stem: A 30-year-old woman at 32 weeks gestation presents with regular contractions and cervical change. Membranes are intact. Which is the most appropriate management?

subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with irregular menses, hirsutism, and acne. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology

subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology

stem: A 28-year-old woman with 6 weeks of amenorrhea presents with right iliac fossa pain and vaginal spotting. Beta-hCG is 2500 IU/L and transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with no adnexal mass. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology

stem: A 32-year-old woman at 30 weeks gestation presents with painless bright-red vaginal bleeding; ultrasound shows the placenta covering the internal os. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Perform immediate digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation
Admit, avoid digital vaginal examination, plan cesarean delivery if bleeding persists
Speculum examination followed by artificial rupture of membranes
subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology

stem: A 28-year-old woman at 26 weeks gestation with no risk factors for diabetes. Which is the most appropriate screening test for gestational diabetes?
opts: Fasting glucose at every antenatal visit
Oral glucose tolerance test at 24–28 weeks
subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology

stem: A 30-year-old man presents with auditory hallucinations, paranoid delusions, and disorganized speech of 3 months' duration, along with declining function at work. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Psychiatry

stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with 2 weeks of repetitive sneezing, clear nasal discharge, and conjunctival folds (Dennie-Morgan lines) during the pollen season. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: ENT

stem: A 28-year-old woman with asthma presents with progressive bilateral nasal obstruction and anosmia. Endoscopy shows pale, grape-like masses in the nasal cavities. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with unilateral purulent nasal discharge, facial pressure, and fever for 10 days that worsened after an initial viral illness. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: ENT

stem: A 30-year-old schoolteacher presents with hoarseness of 4 weeks' duration that worsens by the end of the day and with heavy voice use. Laryngoscopy shows bilateral symmetrical swellings at the junction of the anterior and middle thirds of the vocal cords. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: ENT

stem: A 5-year-old child presents with hearing difficulty and recurrent ear infections. Otoscopy shows a retracted tympanic membrane with a fluid level behind it. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of severe vertigo lasting hours, accompanied by unilateral tinnitus, aural fullness, and fluctuating hearing loss. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with fluctuating ptosis and diplopia that worsen at the end of the day and improve after rest. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Ophthalmology

stem: A 46-year-old man presents with sudden, painless loss of vision in the right eye. Fundoscopy shows a cherry-red spot at the macula. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Ophthalmology

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with gradual, painless loss of peripheral vision in both eyes. Intraocular pressure is elevated and the optic discs show increased cupping. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Ophthalmology

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with blurred vision in the left eye that is worse with eye movement and associated with retro-orbital pain. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Ophthalmology

subject: Forensic Medicine

stem: A 70-year-old man's body is brought to the mortuary several days after death. The forensic examiner notes the sequence of putrefaction of the internal organs. Which organ undergoes putrefaction LAST?
subject: Forensic Medicine

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents within 12 hours of a sexual assault. What is the most appropriate forensic evidence collection?
opts: Full forensic kit including swabs and photographs
subject: Forensic Medicine

stem: A 30-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with intentional self-inflicted knife wounds to the forearm. Besides treating the wounds, what is the forensic priority?
opts: Preserve scene, document injuries, assess for intent
subject: Forensic Medicine

stem: A victim of a fatal assault, conscious and aware that death is near, makes a statement naming his assailant and dies shortly afterward. What is the legal status of this statement?
opts: Dying declaration — admissible in court as substantive evidence
Valid only if recorded by a magistrate
Valid only if witnessed by two persons
subject: Forensic Medicine

stem: A 19-year-old non-obese woman with a strong family history of diabetes (autosomal dominant) presents with mild hyperglycaemia. She is not ketosis-prone and her C-peptide is normal. Which feature best fits maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY)?
opts: Young onset, lean, autosomal dominant inheritance, often sulfonylurea-responsive
subject: Medicine
concept: MODY — young, lean, AD inheritance, sulfonylurea-responsive
discriminator: Young lean diabetic + autosomal dominant family history + C-peptide intact = MODY (not T1/T2)

stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman undergoes a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks. Her results are: fasting 95 mg/dL, 1-hour 175 mg/dL, 2-hour 150 mg/dL. What is the diagnosis and management implication?
opts: Gestational diabetes (OGTT thresholds met) — diet then insulin if needed
subject: Medicine
concept: Gestational diabetes — OGTT thresholds (fasting ≥92, 1h ≥180, 2h ≥153)
discriminator: Pregnancy OGTT meeting ANY threshold (92/180/153) = GDM → diet, insulin if targets unmet

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with apparently new type 2 diabetes and seems to require insulin within 1 year despite initial oral therapy. He is not obese. Glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies are positive. What does this indicate?
subject: Medicine
concept: LADA — adult T2 phenotype but autoimmune (GAD+), progresses to insulin
discriminator: Adult 'T2DM' phenotype + GAD antibodies + early insulin requirement = LADA (slow autoimmune)

stem: A 50-year-old man with 12 years of type 2 diabetes has visual blurring and floaters. Fundoscopy shows neovascularisation of the disc and vitreous haemorrhage. What is the most urgent intervention?
subject: Medicine
concept: Diabetic retinopathy — proliferative stage: neovascularisation → panretinal laser
discriminator: Neovascularisation/vitreous haemorrhage = proliferative diabetic retinopathy → panretinal laser

stem: A 60-year-old diabetic has numbness, tingling, and loss of vibration and ankle reflexes in a stocking-glove distribution, with preserved strength. What is the most likely neuropathy?
subject: Medicine
concept: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy — symmetric stocking sensory loss, reduced reflexes
discriminator: Symmetric stocking sensory loss + absent ankle jerks + preserved power = distal symmetric neuropathy

stem: A 55-year-old diabetic develops sudden severe unilateral periorbital pain with ptosis, a dilated non-reactive pupil, and an inability to move the eye upward or inward. Which feature points to a diabetic mononeuritis rather than a posterior communicating artery aneurysm?
opts: The pupil is always dilated and fixed in diabetic palsy
Pupil-sparing is typical of diabetic CN III palsy (sparse parasympathetic fibres spared)
subject: Medicine
concept: Diabetic CN III palsy — pupil-sparing, painful, ischemic (vs aneurysm which fixes pupil)
discriminator: Painful CN III palsy WITH pupil-sparing = diabetic ischemic mononeuritis; aneurysm fixes the pupil

stem: A 40-year-old diabetic woman has recurrent early satiety, nausea, vomiting of undigested food, and bloating, with glycaemic instability. Gastroscopy is normal. What is the most likely mechanism?
subject: Medicine
concept: Diabetic gastroparesis — autonomic neuropathy, delayed gastric emptying
discriminator: Nausea/vomiting undigested food + normal endoscopy + DM = gastroparesis (vagal neuropathy)

stem: A 55-year-old diabetic with peripheral neuropathy presents with a warm, red, swollen midfoot and a 'rocker-bottom' deformity. X-ray shows fractures and joint dislocation. There is no history of major trauma. What is the diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Charcot neuroarthropathy — painless red swollen foot, rocker-bottom, offloading
discriminator: Neuropathic foot + warm/swollen + rocker-bottom + fractures = Charcot (not infection)

stem: A diabetic man has a painless plantar ulcer with a warm foot and easily palpable pedal pulses. A second patient has a painful, cool foot with absent pulses and rest pain. How do these ulcers differ?
opts: First is arterial, second is neuropathic
First is neuropathic (sensory loss, good perfusion); second is ischaemic (poor perfusion)
subject: Medicine
concept: Diabetic foot ulcer — neuropathic (warm, pulses) vs ischaemic (cool, absent pulses)
discriminator: Painless + warm + palpable pulses = neuropathic ulcer; painful + cool + absent pulses = ischaemic

stem: A 50-year-old man with chronic pancreatitis has steatorrhoea, weight loss, and new-onset diabetes requiring insulin. C-peptide is low and faecal elastase is reduced. What is the diabetes type?
subject: Medicine
concept: Type 3c diabetes — pancreatic disease (chronic pancreatitis/CF) + exocrine insufficiency
discriminator: Diabetes + steatorrhoea + low faecal elastase = type 3c (pancreatogenic), not T1/T2

stem: A 60-year-old woman started on high-dose oral prednisolone for polymyalgia rheumatica develops fasting hyperglycaemia and glucosuria after 2 weeks. She has no prior diabetes. What is the most likely cause?
subject: Medicine
concept: Steroid-induced diabetes — glucocorticoids raise glucose (hepatic output, insulin resistance)
discriminator: New hyperglycaemia after starting glucocorticoids = steroid-induced diabetes

stem: A diabetic man on metformin and a sulfonylurea is scheduled for elective abdominal surgery. What is the most appropriate perioperative glycaemic management?
opts: Hold metformin (lactic acidosis risk with fasting/contrast) and use a variable IV insulin infusion
Continue all oral agents including metformin throughout
Stop insulin if already on it
Give double the sulfonylurea dose pre-op
subject: Medicine
concept: Perioperative diabetes — hold metformin, use IV insulin sliding scale
discriminator: Periop: hold metformin (fasting/contrast/ischaemia → lactic acidosis), use IV insulin

stem: A 48-year-old overweight man has a fasting glucose of 110 mg/dL and a 2-hour post-glucose value of 150 mg/dL on OGTT. HbA1c is 5.9%. What is the correct classification and first step?
opts: Prediabetes (impaired fasting glucose / impaired glucose tolerance) — lifestyle modification
subject: Medicine
concept: Prediabetes — IFG (fasting 100-125) / IGT (2h 140-199); lifestyle first
discriminator: Fasting 110 (IFG) + 2h 150 (IGT) + HbA1c 5.9% = prediabetes → lifestyle, not metformin yet

stem: A 30-year-old type 1 diabetic has frequent asymptomatic nocturnal hypoglycaemic episodes and drives for a living. Which technology most improves her safety?
subject: Medicine
concept: Diabetes technology — CGM for hypoglycaemia unawareness / nocturnal hypo
discriminator: Recurrent asymptomatic (nocturnal) hypoglycaemia → CGM with alerts improves safety

stem: A 52-year-old obese man with type 2 diabetes and BMI 34 is started on a GLP-1 receptor agonist. Which effect is expected and requires counselling?
opts: Weight loss with nausea/vomiting; benefits obesity and CV risk
Weight gain and hypoglycaemia as the main effects
subject: Medicine
concept: GLP-1 receptor agonists — weight loss, GI side effects, CV benefit
discriminator: GLP-1 RA: weight loss + GI (nausea) side effects + CV/renal benefit; low hypo risk

stem: A 64-year-old man on long-term metformin for type 2 diabetes develops numbness and a macrocytic anaemia with low-normal B12. Which association is correct?
opts: Metformin long-term use can cause B12 deficiency
B12 deficiency here is unrelated to metformin
The anaemia is iron-deficiency from metformin
subject: Medicine
concept: Metformin adverse effect — long-term B12 malabsorption/deficiency
discriminator: Chronic metformin → reduced B12 absorption → deficiency (neuropathy, macrocytic anaemia)

stem: A 50-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and no history of cardiovascular disease has an LDL of 110 mg/dL. According to current guidance, what is indicated?
opts: No statin — only treat if LDL >190
Statin therapy for primary CVD prevention (all diabetics ≥40 typically benefit)
Nothing until he has a heart attack
subject: Medicine
concept: Diabetes + CVD risk — statin for primary prevention in most T2DM
discriminator: T2DM is a CVD risk equivalent — statin indicated for primary prevention (not LDL alone)

stem: A 40-year-old type 1 diabetic asks how often her urine should be screened for early kidney disease. She has normal creatinine and no proteinuria on dipstick. What is recommended?
opts: Annual urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (screen for microalbuminuria)
subject: Medicine
concept: Diabetic nephropathy — annual albuminuria screening (ACR) for early detection
discriminator: Annual urine albumin:creatinine ratio screens for microalbuminuria before creatinine rises

stem: An 82-year-old frail woman with type 2 diabetes on a sulfonylurea has had two falls and a hypoglycaemic episode. What is the most appropriate adjustment?
opts: Intensify with insulin to tighten control
De-intensify therapy (stop sulfonylurea, relax targets) to avoid hypoglycaemia
subject: Medicine
concept: Diabetes in the elderly — de-intensify to avoid hypoglycaemia/falls
discriminator: Frail elderly + sulfonylurea hypo/falls = de-intensify (avoid hypo); relaxed targets

stem: A 60-year-old diabetic man develops painful, asymmetric weakness and wasting of the thigh muscles over weeks, with weight loss but preserved sensation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Diabetic amyotrophy — painful asymmetric proximal thigh weakness/wasting
discriminator: Painful asymmetric thigh weakness/wasting in DM = diabetic amyotrophy (radiculoplexus)

stem: A 65-year-old diabetic woman with poor glycaemic control has fever, flank pain, and gas visible within the renal parenchyma on CT. Urine grows E. coli. What is the diagnosis and concern?
opts: Emphysematous pyelonephritis — gas-forming infection, urological emergency
subject: Medicine
concept: Emphysematous pyelonephritis — gas-forming infection in diabetic kidney
discriminator: Diabetic + flank pain + gas in renal parenchyma on CT = emphysematous pyelonephritis (emergency)

stem: A 58-year-old type 2 diabetic has persistent fasting hyperglycaemia on maximal oral therapy. Which insulin regimen is most appropriate to start?
opts: Stop all oral agents and start biphasic twice daily immediately
Once-daily basal (long-acting, e.g. glargine) to target fasting glucose
subject: Medicine
concept: Insulin initiation — start basal (long-acting) for fasting hyperglycaemia
discriminator: Persistently high fasting glucose on orals → add once-daily basal (glargine) first

stem: A diabetic on basal insulin has consistently elevated morning glucose but normal glucose at 3 a.m. (no nocturnal hypoglycaemia). What does this represent?
opts: Dawn phenomenon (early-morning hormonal surge), not Somogyi
subject: Medicine
concept: Dawn phenomenon — morning hyperglycemia WITHOUT nocturnal hypoglycemia
discriminator: Normal 3am glucose + high morning glucose = dawn phenomenon (cortisol/GH surge), not Somogyi

stem: A 55-year-old diabetic has several round, atrophic, hyperpigmented plaques on the shins. They are asymptomatic. Which skin manifestation is this?
subject: Medicine
concept: Diabetic dermopathy — asymptomatic atrophic pigmented shin plaques
discriminator: Atrophic pigmented round plaques on shins in DM = diabetic dermopathy (shin spots)

stem: A 30-year-old woman with pre-existing type 1 diabetes plans pregnancy. What is the most important pre-conceptional intervention to reduce congenital malformation risk?
opts: Achieve tight glycaemic control (HbA1c near normal) before conception
subject: Medicine
concept: Pre-existing diabetes in pregnancy — tighten glycemia pre-conception to cut malformations
discriminator: Pre-existing DM + pregnancy: congenital malformation risk tracks glycaemic control → tighten pre-conception

stem: A 70-year-old woman on a thiazide diuretic for hypertension presents with confusion. Serum sodium is 122 mmol/L. She is clinically volume-depleted. Which mechanism best explains the hyponatremia?
opts: Thiazide-induced volume depletion with impaired free-water excretion
subject: Medicine
concept: Hypovolemic hyponatremia — thiazide causes Na loss and volume depletion
discriminator: Thiazide + volume depletion + low U Na = hypovolemic hyponatremia (not SIADH, which is euvolemic)

stem: A 55-year-old man develops hyponatremia 4 days after a subarachnoid haemorrhage. He is clinically volume-depleted with low urine sodium. Which diagnosis is most likely?
subject: Medicine
concept: Cerebral salt wasting — SAH + hyponatremia + volume depletion
discriminator: SAH + hyponatremia + VOLUME DEPLETION = cerebral salt wasting (vs SIADH which is euvolemic)

stem: A patient's serum sodium measured by flame photometry is 118 mmol/L, but direct ion-selective electrode (after ultracentrifugation) is normal. The patient has severe hypertriglyceridaemia. What explains this?
subject: Medicine
concept: Pseudohyponatremia — lab artifact in hyperlipidemia/hyperproteinemia
discriminator: Marked lipid/protein elevation dilutes Na in the sample → pseudohyponatremia (measured low, true normal)

stem: A 30-year-old man has polyuria and thirst with hypernatremia and dilute urine. After water deprivation, desmopressin is given and urine osmolality rises markedly. What does this indicate?
subject: Medicine
concept: Central vs nephrogenic DI — desmopressin causes concentration in central DI
discriminator: Desmopressin → urine concentration = CENTRAL DI (kidney responds); no response = nephrogenic

stem: A 48-year-old woman with chronic hyponatremia (Na 112 mmol/L) is corrected too rapidly to 132 mmol/L within 12 hours. Two days later she develops dysarthria, dysphagia, and a locked-in-like state. What is the cause?
subject: Medicine
concept: Osmotic demyelination syndrome — over-rapid Na correction
discriminator: Chronic hyponatremia + rapid overcorrection + delayed dysarthria/locked-in = osmotic demyelination

stem: A 2-month-old infant exclusively on formula with inadequate water intake presents with lethargy and a serum sodium of 160 mmol/L. Urine osmolality is low. What is the most likely mechanism?
subject: Medicine
concept: Hypernatremia — free-water deficit from inadequate intake / insensible loss
discriminator: Infant + hypernatremia + inadequate water intake = free-water deficit (not DI, which is ADH-related)

stem: A patient on furosemide with vomiting and metabolic alkalosis has serum potassium of 2.8 mmol/L. Which combination of mechanisms explains the hypokalemia?
opts: Renal K loss (diuretic) + GI loss (vomiting) + shift into cells (alkalosis)
subject: Medicine
concept: Hypokalemia — multifactorial (renal + GI loss + alkalosis shift)
discriminator: Diuretic + vomiting + alkalosis = combined renal/GI K loss plus intracellular shift

stem: A 22-year-old man of Asian descent has recurrent episodes of proximal muscle weakness after heavy carbohydrate meals. Between episodes he is well with normal exam. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Hypokalemic periodic paralysis — episodic weakness after carbs/exercise
discriminator: Episodic flaccid weakness + low K after carbohydrate load/exercise = hypokalemic periodic paralysis

stem: A patient with CKD has a potassium of 7.0 mmol/L. The ECG shows peaked T waves and a prolonged PR interval. Which progression indicates impending catastrophe?
opts: Widening of the QRS complex toward a sine wave
subject: Medicine
concept: Hyperkalemia ECG progression — peaked T → widened QRS → sine wave
discriminator: HyperK ECG: peaked T → prolonged PR → widened QRS → sine wave (pre-arrest)

stem: A 68-year-old man with no renal disease has a reported potassium of 6.9 mmol/L, but he is asymptomatic with a normal ECG. Repeat testing after a drawing technique change shows 4.4 mmol/L. What happened?
subject: Medicine
concept: Pseudohyperkalemia — artifact from hemolysis or prolonged tourniquet/fist clenching
discriminator: Asymptomatic 'hyperkalemia' + normal ECG + normal repeat = pseudohyperkalemia (artifact)

stem: A 60-year-old man with CKD and a potassium of 6.6 mmol/L has peaked T waves but no QRS widening. Which is the MOST appropriate immediate step?
opts: IV calcium gluconate to stabilise the myocardium
subject: Medicine
concept: Hyperkalemia — calcium first for cardiac membrane stabilisation when ECG changes present
discriminator: Any hyperK ECG change (even peaked T) → IV calcium FIRST for cardioprotection, then shift agents

stem: A 64-year-old man with weight loss and bone pain has calcium 12.8 mg/dL, phosphate low, and PTH suppressed (<10 pg/mL). What is the most likely mechanism?
subject: Medicine
concept: Hypercalcemia of malignancy — suppressed PTH (PTHrP), vs primary HPT (high PTH)
discriminator: Hypercalcemia + LOW/normal PTH = malignancy (PTHrP) or vitamin D; HIGH PTH = primary HPT

stem: A 50-year-old alcoholic man has tetany and a corrected calcium of 6.8 mg/dL. Despite IV calcium, the calcium remains low. Magnesium is 1.0 mg/dL. Why is calcium replacement failing?
opts: Hypomagnesemia prevents PTH secretion and action
subject: Medicine
concept: Hypocalcemia — hypomagnesemia causes refractory hypocalcemia
discriminator: Low Mg → impaired PTH secretion/action → calcium replacement fails until Mg corrected

stem: Which of the following is a recognised cause of hypomagnesemia?
opts: Chronic alcohol use with poor intake
subject: Medicine
concept: Hypomagnesemia — causes (alcohol, diuretics, diarrhoea, TPN, aminoglycosides)
discriminator: Hypomagnesemia causes: alcohol, loop/thiazide diuretics, diarrhoea, TPN, aminoglycosides, PPI

stem: A 40-year-old woman in the third trimester develops seizures. Her blood pressure is 160/100 and she has proteinuria. Which magnesium preparation is the treatment of choice for seizure prophylaxis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Magnesium sulfate — eclampsia / pre-eclampsia seizure prophylaxis
discriminator: Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia seizures → IV magnesium sulfate (not calcium)

stem: A patient with CKD stage 4 has an elevated phosphate and low calcitriol. Which complication results from this derangement?
opts: Adynamic bone disease from high calcium
subject: Medicine
concept: CKD-MBD — hyperphosphatemia + low calcitriol → secondary hyperparathyroidism
discriminator: CKD: high PO4 + low calcitriol → low Ca → PTH rises = secondary hyperparathyroidism

stem: A 25-year-old woman has recurrent renal stones, hypokalemia, and a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis despite a normal GFR. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Type 1 distal RTA — normal AG acidosis + hypokalemia + stones/nephrocalcinosis
discriminator: Normal AG metabolic acidosis + hypokalemia + calcium stones = distal (type 1) RTA

stem: A child has proximal muscle weakness, rickets, and glucosuria with a normal plasma glucose. Urine shows phosphaturia, aminoaciduria, and bicarbonate wasting. What syndrome does this represent?
subject: Medicine
concept: Fanconi syndrome — proximal tubular dysfunction (type 2 RTA + glycosuria/phosphaturia/aminoaciduria)
discriminator: Generalized proximal tubule loss (glucose/phosphate/amino acids/bicarbonate) = Fanconi syndrome

stem: A 60-year-old man with long-standing diabetes has a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis and a potassium of 5.8 mmol/L. Which mechanism is most likely?
opts: Hypoaldosteronism / distal H+ and K+ secretion defect (type 4 RTA)
subject: Medicine
concept: Type 4 RTA — hyperkalemic distal RTA from hypoaldosteronism
discriminator: Normal AG acidosis + HYPERkalemia = type 4 RTA (aldosterone deficiency/resistance)

stem: A 70-year-old man with septic shock has a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, elevated lactate (8 mmol/L), and low bicarbonate. Which is the primary mechanism?
opts: Type B lactic acidosis from metformin
Type A lactic acidosis from tissue hypoperfusion
subject: Medicine
concept: Lactic acidosis — type A from hypoperfusion/shock (MUDPILES 'L')
discriminator: Shock + high AG acidosis + high lactate = type A lactic acidosis (hypoperfusion)

stem: A 19-year-old with poorly controlled diabetes vomits repetitively and is found with pH 7.30, HCO3 18, and an elevated anion gap. What best describes the acid-base state?
opts: High anion-gap metabolic acidosis (DKA) with concurrent metabolic alkalosis (vomiting)
subject: Medicine
concept: Mixed acid-base disorder — DKA (high AG acidosis) + vomiting (metabolic alkalosis)
discriminator: High AG + low HCO3 that is LESS low than expected + vomiting = mixed high-AG acidosis + alkalosis

stem: A patient has a normal anion-gap metabolic acidosis. The urine anion gap is positive (urine Na+K − Cl is positive), indicating low urinary ammonium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Normal AG acidosis — positive urine anion gap = RTA (low NH4 excretion); negative = diarrhea
discriminator: Normal AG acidosis: POSITIVE urine anion gap = RTA; NEGATIVE (high NH4) = GI/diarrhea loss

stem: A malnourished chronic alcoholic presents after a binge with abdominal pain, a high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, elevated lactate, and ketonuria, but a normal blood glucose. Which diagnosis fits best?
subject: Medicine
concept: Alcoholic ketoacidosis — high AG acidosis, ketones + lactate, euglycemic
discriminator: Alcoholic + high AG acidosis + ketones + elevated lactate + NORMAL glucose = alcoholic ketoacidosis

stem: A 17-year-old with normal kidney function receives a rapid intravenous infusion of isotonic normal saline. After osmotic equilibrium, which best describes the distribution?
opts: Increased ECF and ICF, decreased sodium
Increased ECF volume, unchanged ICF volume, unchanged plasma sodium
Increased ECF, increased ICF, unchanged sodium
Unchanged ECF, increased ICF, increased sodium
subject: Medicine
concept: Isotonic saline distribution — stays in ECF, no ICF shift, sodium concentration unchanged
discriminator: Isotonic fluid expands ECF only; no osmotic gradient so ICF unchanged; [Na] stays same

stem: A 78-year-old woman on digoxin presents with nausea, bradycardia, and a potassium of 6.4 mmol/L. Which is the most appropriate acute management?
opts: Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Fab); avoid giving calcium
subject: Medicine
concept: Digoxin toxicity — hyperkalemia is a marker; treat with Digoxin-Fab, avoid calcium
discriminator: Digoxin toxicity hyperkalemia = give Digoxin-Fab; AVOID calcium (risk of 'stone heart')

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with a 1-week history of severe anterior neck pain radiating to the ear, fever, and transient palpitations. The thyroid is tender and firm. She recently had a viral upper respiratory infection. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Subacute thyroiditis — painful thyroid after viral illness, transient thyrotoxicosis
discriminator: PAINFUL thyroid + fever + post-viral + transient thyrotoxicosis = de Quervain (subacute) thyroiditis

stem: A 60-year-old man on amiodarone for atrial fibrillation develops thyrotoxicosis with a low uptake on radioactive iodine scan. What is the most likely mechanism?
subject: Medicine
concept: Amiodarone thyroid — type 2 = destructive thyroiditis (low uptake), steroids
discriminator: Amiodarone + thyrotoxicosis + LOW RAI uptake = type 2 (destructive); type 1 (high uptake) = iodine excess

stem: A 35-year-old woman with Graves disease and proptosis develops worsening eye pain, periorbital oedema, and diplopia. She is a smoker. Which factor worsens her orbital disease and what is the mainstay of urgent treatment for severe disease?
opts: Smoking worsens it; high-dose steroids / orbital decompression for severe disease
subject: Medicine
concept: Thyroid eye disease — smoking worsens; steroids/decompression for severe
discriminator: Graves exophthalmos + smoking + severe eye involvement = thyroid eye disease → steroids/decompression

stem: A 50-year-old woman has an elevated TSH (8.5 mIU/L) with a normal free T4 on routine screening. She is asymptomatic. Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Observe and repeat; treat if TSH >10 or symptoms/TPO antibodies develop
subject: Medicine
concept: Subclinical hypothyroidism — observe unless TSH>10 or symptoms/antibodies
discriminator: Elevated TSH + normal T4 + asymptomatic = subclinical hypothyroidism → observe unless TSH>10

stem: A 70-year-old woman with a long-standing multinodular goitre develops palpitations, weight loss, and atrial fibrillation. There is no exophthalmos. What distinguishes this from Graves disease and guides therapy?
opts: Toxic multinodular goitre — nodular goitre, no exophthalmos; treat with radioiodine
subject: Medicine
concept: Toxic multinodular goitre — elderly, nodular goitre, no exophthalmos; radioiodine
discriminator: Elderly + nodular goitre + thyrotoxicosis WITHOUT exophthalmos = toxic MNG (vs Graves)

stem: A 45-year-old woman had a total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid carcinoma and is on thyroxine. Three months later, while on thyroxine, her thyroglobulin is undetectable but anti-thyroglobulin antibodies are negative. What does this indicate?
subject: Medicine
concept: Differentiated thyroid Ca — thyroglobulin as tumour marker (undetectable = no disease)
discriminator: Post-thyroidectomy: undetectable thyroglobulin (+ negative antibodies) = no residual disease

stem: A newborn girl is noted to have ambiguous genitalia and, at 2 weeks, develops vomiting, dehydration, and hypotension. Serum electrolytes show hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: 21-hydroxylase deficiency CAH — salt-wasting + virilization + hypoNa/hyperK
discriminator: Female infant + ambiguous genitalia + salt-wasting crisis (hypoNa/hyperK) = 21-OH deficiency CAH

stem: A 50-year-old man with fatigue and hypotension has hyponatraemia but a normal potassium. He has pale skin with no pigmentation. Which statement is correct?
opts: Findings suggest SECONDARY adrenal insufficiency (no hyperkalaemia/pigmentation)
subject: Medicine
concept: Primary vs secondary adrenal insufficiency — hyperkalaemia + pigmentation only in PRIMARY
discriminator: Adrenal insufficiency WITHOUT hyperkalaemia/pigmentation = secondary (pituitary); primary has both

stem: A woman who had bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing disease 5 years ago now presents with progressive visual field loss and a rapidly enlarging pituitary mass. What is the diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Nelson syndrome — pituitary tumour enlargement after bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing
discriminator: Bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing + enlarging pituitary mass + visual loss = Nelson syndrome

stem: A 55-year-old man has an adrenal mass (3 cm) found incidentally on CT for renal colic. He is hypertensive with hypokalaemia. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Endocrine workup (exclude Cushing, pheochromocytoma, Conn) before any surgery
subject: Medicine
concept: Adrenal incidentaloma — exclude hormonal hyperfunction before considering surgery
discriminator: Incidental adrenal mass → biochemical workup (Cushing/pheo/Conn) before surgery

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with coarse facial features, enlarged hands and feet, and worsening glucose intolerance. Which screening test is most appropriate first?
subject: Medicine
concept: Acromegaly — IGF-1 screening; GH excess from pituitary adenoma
discriminator: Coarse features + enlarging hands/feet + glucose intolerance = acromegaly → check IGF-1 first

stem: A 60-year-old man with a known pituitary macroadenoma suddenly develops a severe headache, bilateral visual loss, and hypotension with hypoglycaemia. What is the urgent diagnosis and action?
opts: Pituitary apoplexy — give glucocorticoids and arrange urgent surgery
subject: Medicine
concept: Pituitary apoplexy — acute haemorrhage/infarction; steroids + urgent decompression
discriminator: Pituitary macroadenoma + sudden HA + visual loss + hypotension/hypoglycaemia = apoplexy (emergency)

stem: A 9-year-old boy has slowed growth, bitemporal hemianopia, and a calcified suprasellar mass on CT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Craniopharyngioma — child, calcified suprasellar mass, bitemporal hemianopia
discriminator: Child + calcified suprasellar mass + bitemporal hemianopia + growth failure = craniopharyngioma

stem: A 30-year-old woman on an antipsychotic for schizophrenia develops galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea. Prolactin is markedly elevated. What should be considered before assuming a prolactinoma?
opts: Prolactinoma confirmed — refer for transsphenoidal surgery
subject: Medicine
concept: Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia — antipsychotics/D2 blockers before prolactinoma
discriminator: Hyperprolactinemia on antipsychotic/metoclopramide = drug-induced; review drug before imaging

stem: A 28-year-old woman in the postpartum period presents with headache, bitemporal hemianopia, and mild diabetes insipidus. MRI shows a homogenously enhancing pituitary mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Lymphocytic hypophysitis — postpartum pituitary mass with DI
discriminator: Postpartum woman + pituitary mass + diabetes insipidus = lymphocytic (autoimmune) hypophysitis

stem: A 7-year-old boy is below the 3rd centile for height with a height velocity below the 25th centile, but normal body proportions. Bone age is delayed. What is the most likely underlying issue if GH deficiency is confirmed?
opts: Growth hormone deficiency causing proportionate short stature with delayed bone age
subject: Medicine
concept: Growth hormone deficiency — proportionate short stature + reduced growth velocity + delayed bone age
discriminator: Child: short stature + low growth velocity + delayed bone age + normal proportions = GH deficiency

stem: A 40-year-old woman has galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea. MRI shows an empty sella with a thin pituitary stalk displaced, but no discrete adenoma. Prolactin is mildly elevated. What explains the hyperprolactinemia?
opts: Stalk effect — interrupted dopamine inhibition from stalk compression
subject: Medicine
concept: Stalk effect — hyperprolactinemia from interrupted dopamine (stalk compression)
discriminator: No adenoma but high prolactin + stalk compression = stalk effect (lost dopamine inhibition)

stem: A 55-year-old man has recurrent episodes of confusion and diaphoresis relieved by eating, occurring fasting or post-exercise. A 72-hour fast reproduces symptoms with a low glucose, elevated insulin, and detectable C-peptide. What is the diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Insulinoma — endogenous hyperinsulinaemic fasting hypoglycaemia (Whipple triad)
discriminator: Fasting hypoglycaemia + HIGH insulin + C-peptide = insulinoma (endogenous); low C-peptide = factitious

stem: A 65-year-old man has bone pain and an elevated alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium and phosphate. X-ray of the pelvis shows cortical thickening and a 'cotton-wool' appearance. What is the diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Paget disease — elevated ALP, normal Ca/PO4, 'cotton-wool' bone on X-ray
discriminator: Bone pain + high ALP + normal Ca/PO4 + cotton-wool bone = Paget disease

stem: A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman has a DEXA T-score of -3.0 at the lumbar spine after a low-trauma wrist fracture. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment to reduce fracture risk?
subject: Medicine
concept: Postmenopausal osteoporosis — bisphosphonate first-line for fracture prevention
discriminator: Postmenopausal osteoporosis (T-score ≤-2.5 + fragility fracture) → bisphosphonate first-line

stem: A 40-year-old man is found to have asymptomatic hypercalcaemia with a normal PTH and a low urine calcium/creatinine ratio. He has a family history of 'high calcium' with no stones or fractures. What is the likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: FHH — benign familial hypercalcemia with LOW urine calcium (not primary HPT)
discriminator: Asymptomatic hypercalcemia + low urine Ca + family history + no complications = FHH (benign)

stem: A 45-year-old man has recurrent renal stones and is found to have primary hyperparathyroidism, a pituitary macroadenoma, and multiple gastric ulcerations. Which syndrome does this represent?
subject: Medicine
concept: MEN1 — parathyroid + pituitary + pancreatic (3 Ps)
discriminator: Parathyroid + pituitary + pancreatic tumours = MEN1 (vs MEN2 = thyroid/pheo/parathyroid)

stem: A 50-year-old woman has a 1.5 cm thyroid nodule. Ultrasound shows microcalcifications, irregular margins, marked hypoechoic echotexture, and a taller-than-wide shape. What is the most appropriate next step?
subject: Medicine
concept: Thyroid nodule — suspicious sonographic features warrant FNA
discriminator: Nodule with microcalcification/irregular margin/hypoechoic/taller-than-wide = suspicious → FNA

stem: A 70-year-old man in the ICU with severe sepsis has a low free T3, a normal TSH, and a normal free T4. He is clinically euthyroid. What explains these thyroid tests?
subject: Medicine
concept: Non-thyroidal illness — low T3, normal TSH/fT4 in acute illness; do not treat
discriminator: Acute severe illness + low T3 + normal TSH/T4 + euthyroid = euthyroid sick syndrome

stem: A 25-year-old East Asian man with untreated hyperthyroidism presents with acute symmetric proximal muscle weakness and a potassium of 2.6 mmol/L during an attack. What is the mechanism and association?
opts: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis — hyperthyroidism triggers hypokalaemic paralysis
Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis without thyroid disease
subject: Medicine
concept: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis — hyperthyroidism → hypokalaemic paralysis (Asian males)
discriminator: Hyperthyroid + acute hypokalaemic weakness (Asian male) = thyrotoxic periodic paralysis

stem: A 6-year-old child has a midline neck swelling that moves upward on protrusion of the tongue and on swallowing. It is non-tender and cystic. What is the diagnosis and management?
opts: Thyroglossal duct cyst — Sistrunk procedure (cyst + tract + hyoid)
subject: Surgery
concept: Thyroglossal duct cyst — midline, moves on tongue protrusion; Sistrunk resection
discriminator: Midline neck cyst moving on tongue protrusion = thyroglossal duct cyst → Sistrunk (tract + hyoid)

stem: A 20-year-old presents with a painless, fluctuant swelling in the anterior triangle of the neck, anterior to the sternocleidomastoid. It has been present since childhood and does not move with tongue protrusion. What is it?
subject: Surgery
concept: Branchial cleft cyst — lateral neck (anterior triangle), no movement on protrusion
discriminator: Lateral neck cyst anterior to SCM, no tongue-protrusion movement = branchial cleft cyst

stem: A singer undergoes thyroid lobectomy and afterwards reports difficulty hitting high notes and a change in vocal pitch, but no breathiness or hoarseness at rest. Which nerve was most likely injured?
opts: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
subject: Surgery
concept: External laryngeal nerve injury — loss of pitch/high notes (not hoarseness); RLN = hoarseness
discriminator: Loss of pitch/high-note control (not hoarseness) = external laryngeal nerve (SLN external) injury

stem: After a total thyroidectomy, a patient develops immediate stridor, respiratory distress, and a fixed midline (paramedian) cord bilaterally. What is the emergency and management?
opts: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury — airway obstruction; urgent tracheostomy/intubation
subject: Surgery
concept: Bilateral RLN injury — airway emergency (bilateral cord fixation) → tracheostomy
discriminator: Bilateral RLN injury → both cords paramedian → airway obstruction → urgent airway (tracheostomy)

stem: A 38-year-old woman has a 2.5 cm papillary thyroid carcinoma with no distant metastases but with a 0.5 cm suspicious central compartment node. What is the recommended initial surgery?
opts: Total thyroidectomy with central compartment lymph node dissection
subject: Surgery
concept: Papillary thyroid Ca — total thyroidectomy + central compartment dissection for ≥1 cm / nodal disease
discriminator: Papillary Ca ≥1 cm or with central nodes → total thyroidectomy + central neck dissection

stem: After total thyroidectomy for a 3 cm follicular variant papillary carcinoma with extrathyroidal extension, which adjuvant therapy is indicated?
subject: Surgery
concept: Differentiated thyroid Ca — adjuvant radioiodine after thyroidectomy
discriminator: Post-thyroidectomy for higher-risk differentiated Ca (size/extension) → RAI ablation

stem: A 60-year-old woman with long-standing Hashimoto thyroiditis develops a rapidly enlarging, painful thyroid mass with compressive symptoms over 2 weeks. Fine-needle aspiration shows atypical lymphoid cells. What is the likely diagnosis and management?
opts: Primary thyroid lymphoma — requires excisional biopsy + chemo/radiotherapy
subject: Surgery
concept: Thyroid lymphoma — rapid enlargement in Hashimoto; excisional biopsy + chemo/RT
discriminator: Rapid painful thyroid enlargement in Hashimoto + lymphoid cells = primary thyroid lymphoma

stem: A patient requires reoperation for recurrent thyroid nodules after a previous partial thyroidectomy. Which complication risk is substantially higher than at first surgery?
opts: Recurrent laryngeal nerve and parathyroid injury (distorted planes)
subject: Surgery
concept: Reoperative thyroid surgery — higher RLN and parathyroid injury risk
discriminator: Reoperative neck surgery → scarred distorted planes → higher RLN/parathyroid injury

stem: A 34-year-old woman with Graves disease and a large multinodular goitre has compressive symptoms and declining response to antithyroid drugs. She is planned for total thyroidectomy. Which pre-operative step is essential to avoid a thyroid storm?
opts: Operate immediately regardless of thyroid state
Achieve euthyroid state with antithyroid drugs + beta-blocker ± Lugol iodine
subject: Surgery
concept: Graves surgery — must be euthyroid pre-op (ATD + beta-blocker ± iodine) to prevent storm
discriminator: Graves thyroidectomy needs euthyroid prep (ATD, beta-blocker, sometimes Lugol) to avoid storm

stem: A patient with primary hyperparathyroidism has a single enlarged parathyroid gland on sestamibi scan and normal other glands on exploration. What is the lesion and procedure?
opts: Solitary parathyroid adenoma — minimally invasive parathyroidectomy
subject: Surgery
concept: Parathyroid adenoma — solitary > MIP; hyperplasia needs 3.5-gland/subtotal
discriminator: Single adenoma on localization = minimally invasive parathyroidectomy; 4-gland disease = different

stem: A patient with long-standing CKD on dialysis develops progressively rising PTH and calcium despite medical therapy and is being evaluated for transplant. What is the underlying process?
opts: Tertiary hyperparathyroidism — autonomous parathyroid hyperplasia from CKD
subject: Surgery
concept: Tertiary hyperparathyroidism — CKD-driven parathyroid hyperplasia becomes autonomous
discriminator: CKD + refractory high PTH/high Ca = tertiary HPT (autonomous hyperplasia); surgery if severe

stem: A patient with primary hyperparathyroidism suddenly develops severe hypercalcaemia (Ca 15 mg/dL) with confusion, abdominal pain, and dehydration. What is the most urgent definitive treatment if medical measures fail?
subject: Surgery
concept: Parathyroid crisis — severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia → urgent parathyroidectomy after stabilisation
discriminator: Symptomatic severe hyperCa from HPT = parathyroid crisis → urgent parathyroidectomy (after resuscitation)

stem: During thyroid lobectomy, the surgeon must ligate the inferior thyroid artery. Why is careful dissection at this site critical for parathyroid preservation?
opts: It supplies the recurrent laryngeal nerve directly
It is the only blood supply to the thyroid
The inferior thyroid artery supplies the inferior parathyroids; ligate laterally to preserve them
subject: Surgery
concept: Inferior thyroid artery — supplies inferior parathyroids; ligate laterally to preserve them
discriminator: Inferior thyroid artery gives branches to inferior parathyroids; ligate distal/lateral to avoid devascularising them

stem: A 58-year-old has a 5 cm adrenal mass found incidentally. Biochemical workup excludes Cushing, pheochromocytoma, and aldosteronism. What is the recommendation?
opts: Surgical resection (size >4 cm raises malignancy concern)
subject: Surgery
concept: Adrenal incidentaloma — resect if >4 cm or functioning; else observe
discriminator: Incidental adrenal mass >4 cm (or any functioning) → resection for malignancy risk

stem: A 45-year-old with a 3 cm aldosterone-producing adrenal adenoma and refractory hypertension is planned for surgery. What is the preferred approach?
subject: Surgery
concept: Adrenalectomy — laparoscopic approach for Conn/pheo/Ca after optimisation
discriminator: Benign adrenal tumours (Conn, pheo, cortisol) → laparoscopic adrenalectomy (minimally invasive)

stem: A patient develops clear rhinorrhoea and a headache 3 days after transsphenoidal pituitary surgery. What is the most likely complication?
opts: CSF leak from an unsealed sella/sphenoid sinus
subject: Surgery
concept: Transsphenoidal pituitary surgery — CSF leak (rhinorrhoea) is a key complication
discriminator: Clear rhinorrhoea after transsphenoidal surgery = CSF leak → bed rest/positioning, may need repair

stem: A patient with clinical Cushing syndrome and a normal pituitary MRI is being evaluated before transsphenoidal surgery. Which test helps confirm the source is pituitary (Cushing disease) rather than ectopic ACTH?
opts: Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (BIPSS) showing central:peripheral ACTH gradient
subject: Surgery
concept: Cushing disease — BIPSS confirms pituitary source before transsphenoidal surgery
discriminator: Pituitary MRI normal in Cushing → BIPSS (central:peripheral ACTH gradient) confirms pituitary source

stem: Before parathyroidectomy for primary hyperparathyroidism, which pre-operative localisation study is most commonly used to identify the abnormal gland?
subject: Surgery
concept: Primary HPT — sestamibi (+US) localises adenoma before parathyroidectomy
discriminator: Pre-parathyroidectomy localisation = sestamibi scan ± neck ultrasound to find the adenoma

stem: A patient with Graves disease is prepared for thyroidectomy. In the days before surgery, Lugol's iodine solution is administered. What is its purpose?
opts: Reduce thyroid vascularity and hormone release (easier, safer surgery)
subject: Surgery
concept: Pre-thyroidectomy iodine (Lugol) — reduces vascularity/hormone release
discriminator: Pre-op Lugol iodine in Graves → reduces gland vascularity and hormone leak at surgery

stem: A patient develops hypocalcaemia with tingling and a positive Chvostek sign on postoperative day 1 after total thyroidectomy, which resolves with calcium. Another has permanent hypocalcaemia requiring lifetime supplements. What explains the difference?
opts: One had Graves, one had cancer
Temporary hypocalcaemia from parathyroid stunning/ischaemia vs permanent from parathyroid excision
subject: Surgery
concept: Post-thyroidectomy hypocalcaemia — transient (ischaemia/stunning) vs permanent (excised)
discriminator: Early transient hypoCa (recovers) = parathyroid ischaemia/stunning; permanent = gland excised/infarcted

stem: What is the single most important preventive measure against thyroid storm in a patient undergoing thyroidectomy for hyperthyroidism?
opts: Operating only when the patient is biochemically euthyroid
Immediate surgery regardless of thyroid state
subject: Surgery
concept: Thyroid storm — prevented by operating only in euthyroid state (storm prophylaxis)
discriminator: Thyroid storm prevention = euthyroid at surgery (ATD + beta-blocker + iodine prep)

stem: During total parathyroidectomy for tertiary hyperparathyroidism, the surgeon implants parathyroid tissue into the forearm muscle. What is the purpose?
opts: Preserve parathyroid function and allow future access if needed
subject: Surgery
concept: Parathyroid autotransplantation — preserves function; forearm site allows re-exploration
discriminator: Autotransplant parathyroid into forearm = preserve function + accessible if graft hyperfunctions

stem: A 65-year-old with a long-standing goitre develops exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea, and cough, with a mediastinal mass on chest X-ray extending below the sternal notch. What is the diagnosis and indication?
subject: Surgery
concept: Substernal goitre — compressive mediastinal extension; surgery indicated
discriminator: Goitre extending retrosternally with compressive symptoms = substernal goitre → surgery

stem: A 70-year-old with a large non-toxic multinodular goitre has progressive dysphagia and tracheal deviation but is euthyroid. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Total or subtotal thyroidectomy for compressive symptoms
subject: Surgery
concept: Non-toxic MNG — surgery for compressive symptoms (dysphagia/tracheal deviation)
discriminator: Non-toxic MNG with compressive symptoms (dysphagia/tracheal deviation) → thyroidectomy

stem: A 50-year-old man has severe hypercalcaemia (Ca 17 mg/dL), a hard, fixed neck mass, and a very high PTH. Imaging shows local invasion. What is the diagnosis and surgery?
opts: Benign parathyroid adenoma — minimally invasive resection
Parathyroid carcinoma — en bloc resection with ipsilateral thyroid lobe
subject: Surgery
concept: Parathyroid carcinoma — hard fixed invasive mass + very high Ca/PTH → en bloc resection
discriminator: Hard fixed invasive parathyroid mass + severe hyperCa/PTH = carcinoma → en bloc resection

stem: A 62-year-old woman reports brief episodes of spinning vertigo for 3 weeks, triggered only when she rolls onto her right side in bed. Each episode lasts under a minute. She has no hearing loss or tinnitus. Dix-Hallpike testing reproduces vertigo with upbeating nystagmus. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Low-salt diet and a thiazide diuretic
MRI of the internal auditory meatus
subject: ENT
concept: BPPV — diagnosis and treatment
discriminator: Vertigo ONLY on position change, <1 min, no cochlear symptoms → posterior canal BPPV → Epley

stem: A 45-year-old male presents with progressive right-sided hearing loss, ringing in the right ear, and a feeling of imbalance for 8 months. Otoscopy is normal. Audiometry shows asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss on the right. Which investigation is the gold standard to confirm the diagnosis?
opts: MRI of the internal auditory meatus with gadolinium
subject: ENT
concept: Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) — investigation of choice
discriminator: Asymmetric SNHL + tinnitus in middle age → rule out CPA tumor → MRI with gadolinium is gold standard

stem: A 28-year-old swimmer presents with intense itching and pain in the right ear for 2 weeks. Otoscopy shows black, cotton-wool-like debris in the ear canal with an intact tympanic membrane. What is the most likely causative organism?
subject: ENT
concept: Otomycosis — organism identification
discriminator: Black cotton-wool debris + itching in a swimmer → Aspergillus niger (most common)

stem: A 68-year-old male with poorly controlled diabetes presents with severe right ear pain for 3 weeks and scanty purulent discharge. Otoscopy shows granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction of the ear canal. He now has right-sided facial weakness. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Topical antibiotic ear drops and review in 1 week
CT scan of the temporal bone and IV antipseudomonal antibiotics
subject: ENT
concept: Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa — diabetic + granulation + CN VII palsy
discriminator: Elderly diabetic + granulation tissue in EAC + facial palsy = skull base invasion → CT + IV antipseudomonal

stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought with hearing difficulty at school. He has had two episodes of acute otitis media in the past year. Otoscopy shows a retracted, dull tympanic membrane with a visible fluid level. Tympanogram is flat (type B). He has failed a 3-month period of watchful waiting. What is the most appropriate management?
subject: ENT
concept: Otitis media with effusion (glue ear) — management after watchful waiting fails
discriminator: Retracted dull TM + fluid level + flat tympanogram + failed observation → grommets

stem: A 50-year-old factory worker presents with difficulty hearing conversations in noisy settings. Audiometry shows a bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with a characteristic notch at 4000 Hz. What is the most likely cause?
subject: ENT
concept: Noise-induced hearing loss — audiometric pattern
discriminator: Bilateral SNHL + 4 kHz notch + occupational noise exposure

stem: A 30-year-old female develops sudden severe vertigo, nausea, and vomiting 1 week after a viral upper respiratory tract infection. She also notices reduced hearing in the left ear. There is no focal neurological deficit. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: ENT
concept: Labyrinthitis vs vestibular neuritis
discriminator: Vertigo + HEARING LOSS after URTI = labyrinthitis; vestibular neuritis spares hearing

stem: A 5-year-old boy with acute otitis media treated 10 days ago returns with fever, earache, and a swelling behind the right ear that pushes the pinna forward and outward. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Continue the same oral antibiotic for another week
CT temporal bone and IV antibiotics with otolaryngology review
Incision and drainage of the external canal
Myringotomy alone in the outpatient clinic
subject: ENT
concept: Acute mastoiditis — complication of AOM
discriminator: Post-auricular swelling pushing pinna forward after AOM = mastoiditis → imaging + IV antibiotics

stem: A 35-year-old male with asthma reports that aspirin triggered a severe reaction 2 years ago. He now has bilateral nasal obstruction and anosmia. Examination shows pale, grape-like, insensate masses in both nasal cavities. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
subject: ENT
concept: Nasal polyps (Samter's triad) — first-line treatment
discriminator: Asthma + aspirin sensitivity + pale insensate grape-like masses = polyps → intranasal steroids first

stem: A 45-year-old male with diabetic ketoacidosis presents with facial pain, nasal obstruction, and a black necrotic eschar on the nasal mucosa. He is febrile and confused. What is the most urgent management step?
opts: Urgent surgical debridement and IV amphotericin B
subject: ENT
concept: Invasive fungal sinusitis (mucormycosis/Aspergillus) — emergency
discriminator: DKA + black necrotic eschar = invasive fungal infection → debridement + amphotericin B

stem: A 20-year-old male presents 2 days after a blow to the nose during a fight. He has bilateral nasal obstruction and a feeling of fullness. Examination shows a bluish, fluctuant swelling on both sides of the nasal septum. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Nasal decongestant spray and review in 1 week
Urgent incision and drainage of the septal hematoma
Closed reduction of the nasal bones
subject: ENT
concept: Nasal septal hematoma — emergency management
discriminator: Post-trauma bilateral bluish fluctuant septal swelling = hematoma → urgent drainage to prevent septal necrosis

stem: A 2-month-old infant has had inspiratory stridor since birth. It is louder when she is supine and during crying, and softer when she is prone. She feeds well and is gaining weight. What is the most likely diagnosis and expected course?

discriminator: Pulsatile mass + bruit + moves LATERALLY not vertically = carotid body tumor

stem: Halfway through a blood transfusion a patient develops fever, chills, loin/back pain, dark urine and hypotension. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
opts: Stop the transfusion immediately, keep the line open, and manage as a transfusion reaction
Continue the transfusion at a slower rate
Stop and discard the unit but disconnect the line
subject: Medicine
concept: Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction - STOP transfusion immediately, keep line, manage reaction
discriminator: Fever/back pain/dark urine during transfusion = haemolytic reaction; stop the blood, keep IV access, manage supportively
