stem: A 55-year-old man with cirrhosis presents with confusion and asterixis. Serum ammonia is elevated. In the liver, ammonia is detoxified by combining with which molecule to form glutamine?
subject: Medicine
concept: Hepatic encephalopathy — ammonia detoxification via glutamine synthetase
discriminator: Ammonia + glutamate → glutamine (glutamine synthetase) is the liver's detoxification pathway

stem: A 60-year-old man with ascites due to cirrhosis presents with fever and abdominal pain. Diagnostic paracentesis shows an ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear (PMN) count of 350 cells/mm³. What is the most appropriate treatment?
subject: Medicine
concept: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis — PMN >250 → cefotaxime + albumin
discriminator: Ascites + fever + PMN >250 cells/mm³ = SBP → cefotaxime + IV albumin (prevents hepatorenal syndrome)

stem: A 58-year-old man with decompensated cirrhosis and ascites develops oliguria and a creatinine rising from 1.0 to 2.6 mg/dL over 2 weeks. Urine sediment is bland and urine sodium is 8 mmol/L. He has received no nephrotoxic drugs and there is no shock or proteinuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Hepatorenal syndrome — functional renal failure in cirrhosis
discriminator: Cirrhosis + progressive creatinine rise + low urine Na (<10) + bland sediment + no shock = hepatorenal syndrome (type 1)

stem: A 52-year-old man with compensated cirrhosis develops new-onset abdominal distension and shifting dullness. He is otherwise stable with normal renal function. What is the first-line treatment?
subject: Medicine
concept: Ascites — first-line medical management
discriminator: New uncomplicated ascites → sodium restriction + spironolactone (aldosterone antagonist) first

stem: A 55-year-old man with chronic liver disease attends for routine review and is found to have a prolonged prothrombin time. Which supplement most directly addresses this coagulation defect?
subject: Medicine
concept: Vitamin K deficiency in chronic liver disease
discriminator: Prolonged PT in chronic liver disease → vitamin K (fat-soluble vitamin needed for factors II, VII, IX, X)

stem: A 45-year-old man with hepatitis B-related cirrhosis is under surveillance. What is the most appropriate screening strategy for hepatocellular carcinoma?
subject: Medicine
concept: Hepatocellular carcinoma — surveillance in cirrhosis
discriminator: Cirrhosis (HBV) → 6-monthly ultrasound + AFP for HCC surveillance

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with ascites, tender hepatomegaly, and right upper quadrant pain of 3 weeks duration. Doppler ultrasound shows thrombosis of the hepatic veins. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Budd-Chiari syndrome — hepatic vein thrombosis
discriminator: Ascites + hepatomegaly + hepatic vein thrombosis = Budd-Chiari syndrome (outflow obstruction)

stem: A 48-year-old man with heavy alcohol use presents with jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, and a Maddrey discriminant function of 40. He has no gastrointestinal bleeding or sepsis. What is the most appropriate treatment?
subject: Medicine
concept: Alcoholic hepatitis — Maddrey DF >32 → corticosteroids
discriminator: Alcoholic hepatitis + Maddrey DF >32 (severe) → prednisolone (reduces mortality)

stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of acute viral hepatitis in children?
subject: Medicine
concept: Hepatitis A — most common acute hepatitis in children
discriminator: Hepatitis A is the most common cause of acute viral hepatitis in children (fecal-oral spread)

stem: A pregnant woman with chronic hepatitis B (HBsAg positive) delivers a baby. After giving hepatitis B immunoglobulin, what additional step most effectively prevents transmission?
opts: First dose of hepatitis B vaccine within 12-24 hours of birth
subject: Medicine
concept: Hepatitis B — vertical transmission prevention
discriminator: HBsAg+ mother → HBIG + first vaccine dose within 12-24 hours of birth

stem: A 35-year-old man is found to have the following serology: HBsAg positive, anti-HBc IgG positive, anti-HBs negative, HBeAg negative, with normal ALT. What does this profile indicate?
subject: Medicine
concept: Hepatitis B serology — chronic infection profile
discriminator: HBsAg+ + anti-HBc IgG+ + anti-HBs− = chronic infection (HBsAg persists >6 months)

stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman in her third trimester presents with acute jaundice, malaise, and markedly elevated aminotransferases. She had recently travelled to a region with poor sanitation. Which hepatitis virus carries the highest mortality in this setting?
subject: Medicine
concept: Hepatitis E — fulminant hepatitis in pregnancy
discriminator: Pregnancy + acute hepatitis (fecal-oral, travel) = hepatitis E → highest mortality in 3rd trimester

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents 24 hours after ingesting a large overdose of paracetamol with jaundice, coagulopathy, and grade 2 hepatic encephalopathy. What is the most appropriate antidote?
subject: Medicine
concept: Fulminant hepatic failure — paracetamol antidote
discriminator: Paracetamol overdose + hepatic failure = N-acetylcysteine (replenishes glutathione)

stem: A 50-year-old man presents with fatigue, joint pain, new-onset diabetes, and slate-grey skin pigmentation. Serum ferritin is markedly elevated with a transferrin saturation of 65%. What is the definitive treatment?
subject: Medicine
concept: Hereditary hemochromatosis — phlebotomy
discriminator: Diabetes + skin pigmentation + raised transferrin saturation (>45%) = hemochromatosis → phlebotomy

stem: A 17-year-old boy presents with a tremor, dysarthria, and deteriorating school performance. Examination shows Kayser-Fleischer rings, and serum ceruloplasmin is low. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
subject: Medicine
concept: Wilson disease — copper chelation with penicillamine
discriminator: Adolescent + tremor + Kayser-Fleischer rings + low ceruloplasmin = Wilson disease → penicillamine

stem: A 35-year-old non-smoker presents with emphysema predominantly in the lung bases and mild transaminitis. Liver biopsy shows PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules in hepatocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease from smoking
subject: Medicine
concept: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency — PAS+ globules, basal emphysema
discriminator: Non-smoker + basal emphysema + PAS-positive diastase-resistant globules = alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

stem: A 22-year-old man is found to have an isolated raised unconjugated bilirubin (40 µmol/L) on routine testing. His haemoglobin, reticulocyte count, and liver enzymes are normal, and there are no symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Gilbert syndrome — benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia
discriminator: Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia + normal Hb/reticulocytes/LFTs = Gilbert syndrome (benign)

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with pruritus and fatigue. Liver biochemistry shows a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase, and anti-mitochondrial antibodies are positive. What is the first-line treatment?
subject: Medicine
concept: Primary biliary cholangitis — AMA positive → UDCA
discriminator: Middle-aged woman + pruritus + raised ALP + AMA+ = PBC → ursodeoxycholic acid

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with jaundice and fatigue. Liver enzymes show a marked hepatocellular pattern (AST 900, ALT 850), IgG is elevated, and anti-smooth muscle antibody is positive. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
subject: Medicine
concept: Autoimmune hepatitis — anti-SMA+ → corticosteroids
discriminator: Young female + hepatocellular injury + elevated IgG + anti-SMA = autoimmune hepatitis → corticosteroids

stem: A 60-year-old man with a history of chronic alcohol-related pancreatitis presents with steatorrhoea and weight loss. Deficiency of which pancreatic enzyme most directly explains the steatorrhoea?
subject: Medicine
concept: Chronic pancreatitis — exocrine insufficiency (lipase → steatorrhoea)
discriminator: Steatorrhoea in chronic pancreatitis = lipase deficiency (fat maldigestion)

stem: A 40-year-old man had acute pancreatitis 6 weeks ago and now presents with a firm epigastric mass and early satiety. CT shows a well-defined cystic lesion in the lesser sac. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Pancreatic pseudocyst — 4-6 weeks after pancreatitis
discriminator: Epigastric mass 4-6 weeks after acute pancreatitis = pancreatic pseudocyst (walled-off fluid)

stem: A 65-year-old man presents with painless jaundice and a palpable non-tender gallbladder. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas
subject: Medicine
concept: Courvoisier's law — painless jaundice + palpable gallbladder
discriminator: Painless jaundice + palpable gallbladder = malignant obstruction (pancreatic head), NOT stones

stem: A 26-year-old man presents with fever, right upper quadrant pain, and a tender liver. Ultrasound shows a single 6 cm abscess in the right lobe. What is the most appropriate management?
subject: Medicine
concept: Amoebic liver abscess — metronidazole + aspiration if large
discriminator: Single large (6 cm) liver abscess in a young man = amoebic → metronidazole + aspiration

stem: A patient's liver function tests show an alkaline phosphatase of 900 U/L with near-normal AST and ALT. Which pattern of liver injury does this represent?
subject: Medicine
concept: Liver biochemistry — cholestatic vs hepatocellular pattern
discriminator: Marked ALP elevation with near-normal aminotransferases = cholestatic (biliary) pattern

stem: A 30-year-old man with a 5-year history of ulcerative colitis presents with fatigue, pruritus, and a persistently raised alkaline phosphatase. MRCP shows multifocal strictures and dilatations of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts ('beaded' appearance). What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Primary sclerosing cholangitis — UC + beaded strictures
discriminator: UC + cholestatic enzymes + multifocal beaded strictures on MRCP = primary sclerosing cholangitis

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with the 'worst headache of her life' of sudden onset 4 hours ago, vomiting and neck stiffness. Non-contrast CT brain is normal. What is the next best step?
opts: Lumbar puncture to look for xanthochromia
Discharge home with simple analgesia after 24 h observation
MRI of the brain as an outpatient
subject: Medicine
concept: Subarachnoid haemorrhage: normal CT does NOT exclude it — proceed to LP
discriminator: Thunderclap headache + normal CT = still rule out SAH with LP

stem: A 28-year-old woman on combined oral contraceptives, 3 weeks postpartum, has progressive bifrontal headache, blurred vision with papilloedema, and a focal seizure. CT shows a haemorrhagic venous infarct. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) recognition
discriminator: Young woman on OCP/postpartum + venous infarct/haemorrhage + papilloedema

stem: A 68-year-old man has sudden right hemiparesis, right hemisensory loss, right homonymous hemianopia and expressive (Broca) aphasia. Which vessel is most likely occluded?
subject: Medicine
concept: Middle cerebral artery occlusion syndrome localisation
discriminator: Aphasia = dominant hemisphere = LEFT MCA; contralateral hemiparesis+hemisensory+hemianopia

stem: A 60-year-old hypertensive diabetic man wakes with isolated right hemiparesis involving face, arm and leg equally. There are NO cortical signs (no aphasia, no neglect, no visual field defect). MRI shows a small deep infarct. This is best described as:
subject: Medicine
concept: Lacunar stroke recognition (pure motor, small vessel)
discriminator: Absence of cortical signs despite dense hemiparesis = subcortical lacunar infarct

stem: A 59-year-old man has acute left-sided weakness of 2 h duration from an ischaemic stroke. His BP is 190/115 mmHg. Before considering IV thrombolysis, what must be done with the blood pressure?
opts: Give thrombolysis immediately regardless of BP
Lower BP to <120/80 mmHg then give thrombolysis
Gently lower BP to ≤185/110 mmHg before thrombolysis
Withhold thrombolysis permanently if BP cannot be lowered
subject: Medicine
concept: BP threshold for IV thrombolysis in ischaemic stroke
discriminator: SBP must be ≤185 mmHg and DBP ≤110 mmHg before alteplase

stem: A 55-year-old hypertensive man has sudden vertigo, vomiting, ataxia and headache. He is drowsy. CT shows a cerebellar haemorrhage (3 cm) with early obstructive hydrocephalus. What is the most appropriate management?
subject: Medicine
concept: Cerebellar haemorrhage — surgical decompression for mass effect
discriminator: Cerebellar bleed + drowsiness/hydrocephalus = surgical emergency

stem: A 40-year-old man is 'awake' with eyes open after a large ventral pontine infarct. He cannot speak or move his limbs, but he can reliably move his eyes vertically to command. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Coma due to bilateral hemispheric damage
subject: Medicine
concept: Locked-in syndrome — preserved vertical eye movement + intact consciousness
discriminator: Intact consciousness + voluntary vertical eye movement only = locked-in

stem: Which combination best satisfies the clinical criteria for brain (brainstem) death?
opts: Deep coma with preserved pupillary light reflex and spontaneous respiration
Deep coma, absent pupillary/corneal/oculocephalic reflexes, absent gag/cough, and a positive apnoea test
Persistent vegetative state with intact brainstem reflexes
Coma with decerebrate posturing to noxious stimuli
subject: Medicine
concept: Brainstem death — clinical criteria (coma + absent brainstem reflexes + apnoea)
discriminator: Absence of ALL brainstem reflexes + apnoea = brainstem death (plus established cause, no sedatives/hypothermia)

stem: A 70-year-old man with cirrhosis continues to seize 10 minutes after receiving a benzodiazepine for status epilepticus. Which second-line agent is preferred here?
subject: Medicine
concept: Second-line agent for status epilepticus — levetiracetam in hepatic impairment
discriminator: Cirrhosis (hepatic impairment) + status = prefer levetiracetam (not hepatically metabolised)

stem: A 34-year-old adult has a FIRST unprovoked generalised tonic-clonic seizure. EEG shows generalised epileptiform activity and MRI is normal. Which factor most strongly supports starting a long-term antiepileptic drug now?
opts: Epileptiform abnormalities on EEG and an abnormal neurologic examination
The single unprovoked seizure with a normal MRI
Absence of any provoking factor and normal imaging
subject: Medicine
concept: First unprovoked seizure — high recurrence risk (epileptiform EEG, abnormal exam) justifies AED
discriminator: Epileptiform EEG + abnormal neuro exam = high recurrence risk -> treat

stem: A 16-year-old girl has brief myoclonic jerks of her arms on waking and occasional generalised tonic-clonic seizures in the morning. Which is the most appropriate first-line antiseizure medication?
subject: Medicine
concept: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy — first-line AED avoiding valproate in a girl
discriminator: JME is photosensitive/myoclonic-on-awakening; avoid valproate in a female of reproductive age

stem: A 7-year-old girl has frequent brief episodes of staring and unresponsiveness with rapid blinking, during which she does not fall, lasting 5–10 seconds, occurring dozens of times a day. EEG shows 3 Hz spike-and-wave. What is the most effective first choice?
subject: Medicine
concept: Typical absence epilepsy — ethosuximide first-line
discriminator: Brief staring + 3 Hz spike-and-wave = absence; ethosuximide is first-line

stem: A 22-year-old collapsed with twitching movements of all limbs for about 20 seconds after standing up quickly, then quickly recovered with full orientation. Which feature most strongly suggests SYNCOPE rather than a seizure?
opts: Rapid full recovery of consciousness within seconds with no post-ictal confusion
Biting the lateral border of the tongue
Confusion and drowsiness for 30 minutes afterwards
subject: Medicine
concept: Syncope vs seizure — post-ictal confusion and recovery distinguish them
discriminator: Rapid alert recovery without post-ictal confusion = syncope (not seizure)

stem: A 32-year-old man has severe, strictly unilateral, tearing and nasal-stuffy headache around the same eye, occurring in clusters every night and making him pace the floor. During an acute attack, the most effective first-line treatment is:
opts: Bed rest in a dark quiet room with simple analgesics
High-flow oxygen therapy and subcutaneous sumatriptan
Oral propranolol at the time of the attack
subject: Medicine
concept: Cluster headache — acute attack treatment (high-flow O2 + SC sumatriptan)
discriminator: Unilateral periorbital pain + autonomic features + restlessness = cluster; high-flow O2 + SC sumatriptan

stem: A 38-year-old woman with migraine takes sumatriptan or ibuprofen on most days (roughly 18 days per month) and now has a daily, dull, diffuse headache that improves transiently with analgesics. What is the most likely diagnosis and key management?
opts: New daily persistent headache — start prophylactic amitriptyline only
Intracranial tumour — urgent MRI is mandatory
Chronic tension headache — increase analgesic frequency briefly
Medication-overuse headache — withdraw the overused analgesic/abortive and re-educate
subject: Medicine
concept: Medication-overuse headache — recognition and withdrawal
discriminator: Daily headache + >10–15 abortive/analgesic days/month = medication overuse; stop the culprit drug

stem: A 68-year-old woman has a new severe temporal headache, jaw claudication while chewing, scalp tenderness, and an ESR of 90 mm/h. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
opts: Wait for the temporal artery biopsy result before any treatment
Start high-dose corticosteroids now, and arrange temporal artery biopsy
Prescribe simple analgesics and review in 2 weeks
Start antibiotics for presumed cellulitis of the temple
subject: Medicine
concept: Giant cell arteritis — urgent steroids before biopsy to prevent blindness
discriminator: New headache in elderly + jaw claudication + high ESR = GCA; treat immediately to save vision

stem: A 29-year-old woman with frequent disabling migraines (5–6 attacks/month) needs preventive therapy. She plans pregnancy in the next year. Which prophylactic is LEAST appropriate?
subject: Medicine
concept: Migraine prophylaxis — sodium valproate is teratogenic, avoid in reproductive-age women
discriminator: Reproductive-age woman planning pregnancy: avoid valproate (teratogenic neural-tube defects)

stem: A 60-year-old woman has brief, electric-shock-like stabbing pains in the right cheek/ jaw triggered by touching her face, chewing and cold air. Neurologic examination, including sensation, is normal. What is the first-line treatment?
subject: Medicine
concept: Trigeminal neuralgia — carbamazepine first-line
discriminator: Lancinating paroxysmal pain + trigger zones + normal sensation = trigeminal neuralgia; carbamazepine

stem: A 34-year-old man awakens with inability to close his LEFT eye and flattening of the left nasolabial fold; BOTH upper and lower face are weak, including forehead wrinkling. No limb weakness. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Start oral corticosteroids within 72 h and protect the eye
subject: Medicine
concept: Bell's palsy — early oral corticosteroids + eye protection
discriminator: Whole-face (upper+lower) peripheral facial palsy = Bell's; treat with steroids within 72 h

stem: Which clinical feature best distinguishes a CENTRAL (upper motor neuron) facial palsy from a PERIPHERAL (lower motor neuron/Bell's) palsy?
opts: Forehead movement is lost in a central palsy
Central palsy always shows loss of taste
Forehead and upper-face movement is spared in a central palsy
subject: Medicine
concept: UMN vs LMN facial palsy — forehead sparing in central lesions
discriminator: Central (cortical) facial palsy spares forehead (bilateral upper-face innervation); peripheral affects all face

stem: A 24-year-old woman has recurrent 'seizures' with asynchronous thrashing, pelvic thrusting, eyes tightly shut, and crying during events, with normal consciousness afterwards. Serum lactate after an episode is normal. Most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES) recognition
discriminator: Asynchronous/ pelvic-thrusting ictus, eyes shut, crying, normal lactate, no post-ictal phase = PNES

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with new headaches and seizures. Imaging shows an extra-axial, contrast-enhancing dural-based mass; histology reveals psammoma bodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Meningioma — extra-axial dural-based tumour with psammoma bodies
discriminator: Extra-axial dural-based mass + psammoma bodies + headache/seizures = meningioma

stem: A 58-year-old hypertensive man has sudden vertigo, hoarseness, dysphagia, and ataxia. Examination shows right-sided Horner syndrome, loss of pain and temperature on the right face AND left body, with intact proprioception. What is the lesion?
subject: Medicine
concept: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome — ipsilateral face + contralateral body pain/temp loss
discriminator: Vertigo+ipsilateral Horner+ataxia+ipsilateral face and contralateral body pain/temp loss = lateral medullary

stem: A 26-year-old woman with epilepsy on levetiracetam becomes pregnant. Which is the most appropriate management of her antiepileptic therapy?
opts: Stop all antiepileptics in the first trimester
Switch to sodium valproate for better seizure control in pregnancy
Continue levetiracetam (the least teratogenic option here) and give folic acid supplementation, monitoring levels
Withhold antiepileptics and only treat if a seizure occurs
subject: Medicine
concept: Epilepsy in pregnancy — continue least-teratogenic AED + folic acid
discriminator: Avoid valproate in pregnancy; continue safest AED (levetiracetam) with folic acid and monitoring

stem: A patient remains in electrographic status epilepticus despite a benzodiazepine AND a second-line agent. What is the appropriate next step?
opts: Induce general anaesthesia (e.g. propofol/midazolam infusion) with continuous EEG monitoring in ICU
Add a third oral antiepileptic and observe on the ward
subject: Medicine
concept: Refractory status epilepticus — anaesthetic agents with continuous EEG in ICU
discriminator: Failure of benzodiazepine + second-line agent = refractory SE; needs anaesthesia + EEG

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with chronic diarrhoea, weight loss, and steatorrhoea. To distinguish small-intestinal mucosal disease from pancreatic insufficiency, which test result would be most informative?
opts: Low serum lipase confirms mucosal disease
Normal D-xylose with raised faecal elastase excludes malabsorption
Low urinary D-xylose indicates mucosal disease
High faecal osmotic gap indicates pancreatic disease
subject: Medicine
concept: Malabsorption workup — D-xylose test distinguishes mucosal vs pancreatic
discriminator: D-xylose is absorbed intact by jejunal mucosa without pancreatic enzymes → low urinary D-xylose = mucosal disease

stem: A patient with chronic watery diarrhoea has a stool osmolality of 290 mOsm/kg with stool sodium 40 mmol/L and potassium 30 mmol/L. What type of diarrhoea is most likely?
subject: Medicine
concept: Faecal osmotic gap — osmotic vs secretory diarrhoea
discriminator: Osmotic gap = 290 − 2(Na+K) = 290 − 2(40+30) = 150 (>50) → osmotic diarrhoea

stem: A 52-year-old man presents with migratory arthralgia, chronic diarrhoea, and weight loss. Small-bowel biopsy shows PAS-positive foamy macrophages in the lamina propria. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
subject: Medicine
concept: Whipple disease — Tropheryma whipplei, PAS+ macrophages → prolonged antibiotics
discriminator: Arthralgia + diarrhoea + PAS+ macrophages = Whipple disease → prolonged antibiotics (ceftriaxone then TMP-SMX)

stem: A 60-year-old man who had a Billroth II gastrectomy years ago presents with diarrhoea, steatorrhoea, and macrocytic anaemia. A glucose breath test shows an early hydrogen peak. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth — blind loop syndrome
discriminator: Post-gastrectomy stasis + steatorrhoea + B12 deficiency + early H2 peak = bacterial overgrowth (blind loop)

stem: A 25-year-old man reports bloating, cramping, and loose stools within 2 hours of drinking milk, which started gradually in his twenties. What is the most appropriate confirmatory test?
subject: Medicine
concept: Lactose intolerance — hydrogen breath test
discriminator: Milk-triggered bloating/diarrhoea in an adult = lactase deficiency → hydrogen breath test

stem: A 50-year-old woman undergoes resection of 100 cm of terminal ileum for Crohn disease. Which two deficiencies is she most at risk of developing?
opts: Vitamin B12 and bile salt malabsorption
subject: Medicine
concept: Ileal resection — B12 and bile salt malabsorption
discriminator: Terminal ileum absorbs B12 and bile salts → resection causes B12 deficiency + bile salt malabsorption

stem: A 45-year-old woman who had a gastrectomy 1 year ago develops palpitations, sweating, and weakness 90 minutes after meals. What is the most likely mechanism?
opts: Reactive hypoglycaemia from excessive insulin secretion
Rapid fluid shift into the bowel lumen
subject: Medicine
concept: Dumping syndrome — late phase (reactive hypoglycaemia)
discriminator: Post-gastrectomy symptoms 1-3 hours after meals = late dumping → reactive hypoglycaemia (excessive insulin)

stem: A 62-year-old woman with pernicious anaemia (positive anti-intrinsic factor antibodies) requires treatment. What is the most appropriate long-term therapy?
opts: Oral vitamin B12 with high-dose tablets
subject: Medicine
concept: Pernicious anemia — lifelong parenteral B12
discriminator: Pernicious anaemia = loss of intrinsic factor → lifelong IM B12 (oral absorption blocked)

stem: A 30-year-old man presents with intensely pruritic vesicles on his elbows, knees, and buttocks. Duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy consistent with coeliac disease. Which medication most effectively controls the skin lesions?
subject: Medicine
concept: Dermatitis herpetiformis — dapsone for skin lesions
discriminator: Pruritic vesicles (elbows/knees/buttocks) + coeliac = dermatitis herpetiformis → dapsone + gluten-free diet

stem: A 35-year-old man develops chronic diarrhoea, steatorrhoea, and megaloblastic anaemia 6 months after returning from an extended stay in South Asia. What is the most appropriate treatment?
subject: Medicine
concept: Tropical sprue — tetracycline + folate
discriminator: Post-travel chronic diarrhoea + steatorrhoea + megaloblastic anaemia = tropical sprue → tetracycline + folate

stem: A 55-year-old man who had a partial gastrectomy for gastric cancer 2 years ago develops fatigue. Blood film shows microcytic, hypochromic anaemia. What is the most likely cause?
subject: Medicine
concept: Post-gastrectomy — iron deficiency anaemia
discriminator: Post-gastrectomy microcytic hypochromic anaemia = iron deficiency (reduced acid + bypassed duodenum)

stem: A 28-year-old woman with chronic diarrhoea and weight loss has a negative anti-tTG IgA test, but coeliac disease is still suspected. Which additional test should be checked?
subject: Medicine
concept: Coeliac disease — IgA deficiency causes false-negative anti-tTG
discriminator: Negative anti-tTG IgA + suspected coeliac → check total IgA (IgA deficiency causes false negatives)

stem: A 6-month-old exclusively breastfed infant develops a rash around the mouth and perineum, diarrhoea, and failure to thrive. Which deficiency is most likely?
subject: Medicine
concept: Zinc deficiency — acrodermatitis enteropathica pattern
discriminator: Periorificial + acral rash + diarrhoea + failure to thrive in infancy = zinc deficiency

stem: In a region of endemic iodine deficiency, a pregnant woman's newborn is at greatest risk of which condition?
subject: Medicine
concept: Iodine deficiency — goitre and cretinism
discriminator: Maternal iodine deficiency → congenital hypothyroidism (cretinism) and goitre

stem: A 40-year-old man with severe anorexia is started on aggressive enteral nutrition after a period of starvation. Within 2 days he develops weakness and cardiac arrhythmia. Which electrolyte disturbance is the most likely cause?
subject: Medicine
concept: Refeeding syndrome — hypophosphataemia
discriminator: Rapid refeeding after starvation → insulin surge → intracellular shift → hypophosphataemia → arrhythmia

stem: An alcoholic man presents confused with ataxia and ophthalmoplegia. Before administering intravenous glucose, which should be given first?
subject: Medicine
concept: Wernicke encephalopathy — thiamine before glucose
discriminator: Give thiamine BEFORE glucose in suspected Wernicke (glucose metabolism consumes thiamine, worsening the encephalopathy)

stem: A 3-year-old child in a low-resource setting presents with night blindness and dry, thickened conjunctiva. Without treatment, what is the most feared progression?
subject: Medicine
concept: Vitamin A deficiency — xerophthalmia progressing to keratomalacia
discriminator: Night blindness + xerophthalmia = vitamin A deficiency → keratomalacia → corneal ulceration/blindness

stem: A 2-year-old child presents with generalised oedema, a distended abdomen, and a flaky-paint dermatitis with depigmented hair. Which form of malnutrition is this?
subject: Medicine
concept: Kwashiorkor — protein deficiency with oedema
discriminator: Oedema + flaky-paint dermatosis + depigmented hair = kwashiorkor (protein deficiency with adequate calories)

stem: A 12-month-old infant presents with severe wasting of muscle and subcutaneous fat, an 'old man' facies, and weight for age below the third centile — but no oedema. What is the diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Marasmus — total calorie deficiency without oedema
discriminator: Severe wasting + no oedema = marasmus (total calorie deficiency)

stem: A 58-year-old strict vegan presents with progressive paraesthesia of the feet, loss of vibration sense, and an unsteady gait, with brisk knee reflexes. Which deficiency is most likely?
subject: Medicine
concept: Vitamin B12 deficiency — subacute combined degeneration of the cord
discriminator: Sensory (vibration/proprioception) loss + upper motor neuron signs = subacute combined degeneration = B12 deficiency

stem: In assessing the nutritional status of an acutely ill hospitalised patient, which protein best reflects recent (short-term) nutritional change?
subject: Medicine
concept: Nutritional assessment — prealbumin vs albumin
discriminator: Prealbumin has a short half-life (~2 days) → reflects recent nutritional change better than albumin

stem: A patient on total parenteral nutrition for 3 weeks develops a fever and rigors. A central line is in situ. What is the most likely complication?
subject: Medicine
concept: Total parenteral nutrition — catheter-related line sepsis

stem: A patient with a functional gastrointestinal tract requires nutritional support. Which feeding route is preferred and why?

concept: Orbital cellulitis vs preseptal - proptosis/EOM restriction/vision loss = orbital, urgent
discriminator: Proptosis + painful EOM restriction + decreased vision = orbital cellulitis -> urgent IV abx + CT

opts: Oral acyclovir (or valacyclovir) urgently plus urgent ophthalmology review

opts: Pinguecula - a yellow nodule at the limbus that does not grow onto the cornea
Pterygium - fibrovascular growth onto the cornea; can threaten vision if it reaches the visual axis

opts: Ectropion - lid turns outward causing epiphora and exposure
Entropion - lid turns inward; lashes traumatise the cornea (risk of ulceration/infection)
subject: Ophthalmology
concept: Entropion vs ectropion - entropion = lid inward, lashes scratch cornea
discriminator: Inward-turning lid with lashes on cornea = entropion; risk of corneal abrasion/ulcer

opts: Acute dacryocystitis (infected nasolacrimal duct) - warm compresses, massage, oral antibiotics; probing if recurrent
subject: Ophthalmology
concept: Dacryocystitis - medial canthal swelling/discharge; infected NLDO
discriminator: Tender medial canthal swelling + purulent reflux from punctum, quiet eye = dacryocystitis (infected NLDO)

stem: A 65-year-old with hypertension and diabetes wakes with sudden, painless vision loss in one eye. Exam shows a relative afferent pupillary defect and an isolated inferior altitudinal visual field defect. Fundoscopy reveals a pale oedematous optic disc with segmental haemorrhages. Diagnosis?
subject: Ophthalmology
concept: NAION - painless altitudinal loss + disc oedema/haemorrhages in hypertensive/diabetic elderly
discriminator: Painless altitudinal VF defect + disc oedema with haemorrhages in vascular patient = NAION

stem: A 15-year-old boy tells his teacher that 'the teacher is trying to kill me' and repeats that classmates are secretly plotting to attack him. He is convinced of this despite evidence to the contrary. He has no prominent depressed or manic mood. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Schizophrenia — persecutory (paranoid) delusions as a positive symptom
discriminator: Fixed persecutory delusion without a mood syndrome = schizophrenia spectrum psychosis

stem: A 22-year-old man presents with delusions and hallucinations that have been continuous for 3 months, with functioning decline. No mood episode is present.Which diagnosis fits best?
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Schizophreniform disorder — 1 to 6 months of psychotic symptoms (prodrome allowed)
discriminator: Continuous psychosis of 1–6 months (with functional decline) = schizophreniform; six months+ = schizophrenia

stem: A 30-year-old man with schizophrenia is started on an antipsychotic. Three months later he has gained 8 kg and his fasting glucose and lipids are elevated. Which agent is MOST responsible for this metabolic syndrome?
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Second-generation antipsychotics (olanzapine) — metabolic syndrome AE
discriminator: Weight gain, hyperglycaemia, dyslipidaemia = metabolic syndrome; typical with SGA olanzapine (vs EPS with FGA)

stem: A patient on an antipsychotic develops rigidity, hyperthermia, fluctuating consciousness and autonomic instability, with a markedly elevated CK. Which condition does this describe, and which drug class change most characteristically precedes it?
opts: Serotonin syndrome after a recent SSRI dose increase
Malignant hyperthermia after an inhaled anaesthetic
Tardive dyskinesia from long-term typical antipsychotics
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome after an antipsychotic dose increase or switch
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — rigidity + hyperthermia + autonomic instability + raised CK
discriminator: Lead-pipe rigidity + hyperthermia + autonomic instability + high CK after antipsychotic = NMS

stem: A 65-year-old woman who has taken a typical antipsychotic for years develops repetitive, involuntary oro-buccal-lingual chewing and grimacing movements. What is the best initial management?
opts: Continue the same dose and reassure
Switch to an atypical antipsychotic (or clozapine) and consider VMAT-2 inhibitor (valbenazine)
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Tardive dyskinesia — reduce/switch antipsychotic; anticholinergics can worsen it
discriminator: Oro-facial stereotypic movements after long-term antipsychotic = tardive dyskinesia; stop/reduce drug, switch to atypical, consider VMAT-2 inhibitor

stem: A 19-year-old man develops painful neck twisting (torticollis), eye deviation (oculogyric crisis) and tongue protrusion within 2 days of starting a high-potency typical antipsychotic. What is the immediate treatment?
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Acute dystonia — anticholinergic (benztropine/diphenhydramine)
discriminator: Acute dystonia within days of high-potency antipsychotic = treat with anticholinergic

stem: A 40-year-old man over 5 days has euphoric mood, grandiosity (plans to quit medicine and start a university), pressured speech and reckless spending, sleeping only 2–3 hours/night yet feeling rested. What is the most specific sleep finding that points to MANIA rather than simple insomnia?
opts: Difficulty falling asleep despite feeling tired
Decreased need for sleep with preserved energy/restored feeling
Early morning awakening with low mood
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Mania — decreased need for sleep (vs insomnia of depression/simple insomnia)
discriminator: Grandiosity + pressured speech + decreased NEED for sleep (not distressed) = mania

stem: A 33-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder presents with a 3-week episode of major depression while on her mood stabiliser. Which is LEAST appropriate?
opts: Add a second mood stabiliser or lamotrigine
Add an atypical antipsychotic such as quetiapine
Use antidepressant monotherapy alone for her depression
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Bipolar depression — avoid antidepressant MONOTHERAPY (mania switch risk)
discriminator: In bipolar depression, antidepressant monotherapy risks triggering mania/hypomania; use mood stabiliser ± atypical antipsychotic

stem: A new mother on day 3 postpartum is tearful, irritable and labile but can care for her baby, with symptoms fluctuating throughout the day and resolving spontaneously. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Postpartum baby blues — transient, day 3–5, self-limiting (<2 weeks)
discriminator: Onset day 3, mild mood lability, retained functioning, self-limiting = baby blues

stem: A mother 2 weeks after delivery is confused, disorganised, has bizarre delusions about her baby being evil, and insomnia. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Reassure and schedule outpatient follow-up in 2 weeks
Start an SSRI and let her rest at home
Refer to a dietician for sleep hygiene
Emergency psychiatric admission with antipsychotic treatment and safety planning for mother and infant
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Postpartum psychosis — psychiatric emergency, urgent admission
discriminator: Delusions + confusion + insomnia postpartum = postpartum psychosis, emergency (infanticide risk)

stem: A 50-year-old man has severe depression with early-morning waking, diurnal mood variation (worse in the morning), anorexia, weight loss and anhedonia with psychomotor retardation. Which feature supports a MELANCHOLIC specifier in depression?
opts: Early-morning awakening with mood worse in the morning and psychomotor changes
Fatigue that improves with restful sleep
Reactive mood that brightens with good news
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Melancholic depression — early-morning wakening, diurnal variation, psychomotor changes
discriminator: Early-morning waking + mood worse AM + appetite/weight loss + psychomotor changes = melancholic

stem: A 30-year-old woman has recurrent, unexpected episodes of intense fear peaking within minutes, with palpitations, sweating, tremor, chest discomfort, choking and a feeling of imminent death. She now avoids crowded places for fear of an episode. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Panic disorder — recurrent unexpected panic attacks peaking in minutes, with avoidance
discriminator: Paroxysmal fear + autonomic surge peaking in minutes + avoidance = panic disorder

stem: A 28-year-old woman with panic disorder asks about treatment. She wants a medication that treats the underlying attack frequency. Which is the most appropriate first-line long-term pharmacotherapy?
opts: Lorazepam as the sole daily treatment
An SSRI (e.g. sertraline or escitalopram), starting low and titrating
A short course of diazepam twice daily indefinitely
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Panic disorder — SSRI first-line
discriminator: Panic disorder is treated long-term with an SSRI (start low, titrate); benzodiazepines are not sole/maintenance treatment

stem: A 78-year-old hospitalised man becomes acutely confused over hours, inattentive, with fluctuating alertness and visual hallucinations; he has an active urinary infection. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Delirium — acute onset, fluctuating, inattention, underlying medical cause
discriminator: Acute/subacute onset + fluctuating + inattention + hallucinations + medical infection = delirium

stem: A postoperative elderly patient is agitated and hallucinating with delirium. Which is the MOST appropriate first-line management approach?
opts: Start a benzodiazepine routinely to sedate immediately
Restrain the patient physically as the primary intervention
Identify and treat the underlying cause, use non-pharmacological measures, and reserve antipsychotics (e.g. low-dose haloperidol) for severe agitation
Give antipsychotics prophylactically to all patients
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Delirium — treat the cause + non-pharmacological first; antipsychotic only for severe agitation
discriminator: Delirium is managed by treating the precipitant + non-pharmacological reorientation; antipsychotics for severe agitation only; avoid benzodiazepines (unless alcohol/benzo withdrawal)

stem: A 72-year-old man has progressive memory loss over 2 years with difficulty naming objects and navigating familiar places; functional decline is emerging. Which pharmacologic treatment is most appropriate for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease?
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Alzheimer disease — cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil) for mild-moderate
discriminator: Gradual amnestic decline + naming/navigation difficulty = AD; mild-moderate treated with cholinesterase inhibitor

stem: A 69-year-old hypertensive, diabetic smoker has stepwise cognitive decline with abrupt worsening, emotional lability, focal neurologic signs and gait difficulty. MRI shows multiple lacunar infarcts and white-matter disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Vascular dementia — stepwise decline + focal signs + vascular risk factors + infarcts on imaging
discriminator: Stepwise decline + focal signs + vascular risk factors + lacunar infarcts = vascular dementia

stem: A 70-year-old man has fluctuating cognition, well-formed visual hallucinations of people and animals, and mild parkinsonism. His family notes marked sensitivity to antipsychotic medications. What is the most likely diagnosis and an important management caveat?
opts: Dementia with Lewy bodies — avoid neuroleptics (severe sensitivity), use cholinesterase inhibitors and handle psychosis carefully
Frontotemporal dementia — start an antipsychotic for behaviour
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Dementia with Lewy bodies — fluctuate + visual hallucinations + parkinsonism; severe neuroleptic sensitivity
discriminator: Fluctuating cognition + visual hallucinations (formed) + parkinsonism + neuroleptic sensitivity = DLB

stem: A 54-year-old man has progressive disinhibition, inappropriate social behaviour, apathy and loss of empathy over 2 years, with relative sparing of memory, plus difficulty producing words. Imaging shows frontal and temporal atrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Frontotemporal dementia — early behavioural disinhibition/apathy + language, younger onset, spared memory
discriminator: Earlier onset + prominent behaviour/personality change + language with spared memory + frontotemporal atrophy = FTD

stem: A chronic heavy drinker stops alcohol abruptly. He has confusion, agitation, tremor, hallucinations and marked autonomic overactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, fever) with a risk of seizures and death. What is this, and what is the treatment?
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Delirium tremens — clouded sensorium + autonomic instability; benzodiazepine treatment
discriminator: Confusion + tremor + hallucinations + marked autonomic overactivity after stopping alcohol = delirium tremens; treat with benzodiazepines

stem: A 42-year-old man with alcohol use disorder wants medication to reduce craving and relapse after detoxification. Which agent reduces drinking by antagonising opioid receptors involved in alcohol's rewarding effect?
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Naltrexone — opioid antagonist reduces alcohol craving/drinking
discriminator: Opioid-receptor antagonist (naltrexone) reduces alcohol reward/craving; disulfiram is aversive; acamprosate is a glutamate modulator

stem: A 35-year-old man with long-standing opioid dependence stops use. He has rhinorrhoea, lacrimation, yawning, piloerection, mydriasis, muscle cramps, diarrhoea and anxiety. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate pharmacotherapy?
opts: Opioid withdrawal — treat with methadone or buprenorphine (and lofexidine adjunctively)
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Opioid withdrawal — sympathomimetic-opposite features; treat with methadone/buprenorphine
discriminator: Rhinorrhoea + mydriasis (opposite of pinpoint) + lacrimation + GI cramps after stopping opioids = withdrawal

stem: A 9-year-old boy has persistent, impairing inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity across school and home, present since age 6. What is the first-line pharmacologic treatment?
subject: Psychiatry
concept: ADHD — stimulant (methylphenidate) first-line
discriminator: Persistent inattention/hyperactivity/impulsivity across settings since childhood = ADHD; stimulants first-line

stem: A 19-year-old woman with severe anorexia nervosa (BMI 14) is started on refeeding. On day 3 she develops weakness, arrhythmia, seizures and confusion. Bloods show low phosphate. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?
opts: Refeeding syndrome — give phosphate/electrolyte replacement and slow, monitored refeeding
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Refeeding syndrome in anorexia nervosa — refeeding-induced hypophosphataemia
discriminator: Severe malnutrition + refeeding + low phosphate + arrhythmia/seizures = refeeding syndrome

stem: A 21-year-old woman of normal weight has recurrent episodes of binge-eating followed by self-induced vomiting several times a week, with dental enamel erosion, parotid swelling and calluses on her knuckles. Which electrolyte disturbance is most characteristic and dangerous?
subject: Psychiatry
concept: Bulimia nervosa — recurrent vomiting causing hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
discriminator: Binge-purge + dental erosion + parotid swelling + knuckle calluses = bulimia; vomiting causes hypokalaemic alkalosis

stem: A 60-year-old woman develops fever, a maculopapular rash, and rising creatinine 10 days after starting a new antibiotic. Urine shows WBC casts and peripheral blood shows eosinophilia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Acute interstitial nephritis — drug exposure + eosinophilia + WBC casts
discriminator: Drug exposure + fever + rash + eosinophilia + WBC casts = AIN (hypersensitivity reaction)

stem: A 45-year-old renal transplant recipient has an asymptomatic rise in serum creatinine 1 year after transplantation, despite stable immunosuppression. What is the most appropriate next step?
subject: Medicine
concept: Renal transplant — rising creatinine requires biopsy before empirical treatment
discriminator: Asymptomatic rising creatinine post-transplant = biopsy first (rejection vs nephrotoxicity vs recurrence)

stem: A 55-year-old man with decompensated cirrhosis and ascites develops progressive oliguria. Urine sodium is 8 mmol/L, urine osmolality is 650 mOsm/kg, and there is no proteinuria or haematuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Hepatorenal syndrome — prerenal AKI in cirrhosis with low urine sodium
discriminator: Cirrhosis + oliguria + low U Na + concentrated urine + bland sediment = hepatorenal syndrome

stem: A 3-year-old child develops bloody diarrhoea followed by oliguria, pallor, and bruising. Blood film shows schistocytes and thrombocytopenia; creatinine is raised. What is the most appropriate management?
subject: Medicine
concept: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome — E. coli O157, supportive care, no antibiotics
discriminator: Child + bloody diarrhoea + MAHA + thrombocytopenia + AKI = HUS (typical, post-enteric)

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with fever, fluctuating confusion, and petechiae. Blood film shows schistocytes; platelets are 20,000/μL. There is no significant renal impairment. What is the most appropriate treatment?
subject: Medicine
concept: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura — ADAMTS13 deficiency, plasma exchange
discriminator: Fever + neurological symptoms + MAHA + thrombocytopenia with MINIMAL renal involvement = TTP → plasma exchange

stem: A 20-year-old man with newly diagnosed Burkitt lymphoma develops oliguria 24 hours after starting chemotherapy. Labs show potassium 6.8 mmol/L, phosphate 7.5 mg/dL, uric acid 14 mg/dL, and calcium 6.0 mg/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Tumour lysis syndrome — post-chemotherapy AKI with hyperK + hyperPO4 + hyperuricemia + hypocalcemia
discriminator: Chemotherapy + oliguria + hyperK + hyperPO4 + hyperuricemia + hypocalcemia = tumour lysis syndrome

stem: According to KDIGO, which urine output criterion defines acute kidney injury?
subject: Medicine
concept: AKI definition — KDIGO urine output criterion
discriminator: KDIGO AKI = Cr rise ≥0.3 mg/dL in 48h OR urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours

stem: A 65-year-old man develops AKI after prolonged hypotension during cardiac surgery. Urine microscopy shows muddy brown granular casts and urine sodium is 60 mmol/L. Which part of the kidney is most likely affected?
subject: Medicine
concept: Acute tubular necrosis — muddy brown casts + high urine sodium
discriminator: Post-hypotension AKI + muddy brown casts + U Na >40 = ATN (tubular injury)

stem: A 58-year-old woman has an eGFR of 35 mL/min/1.73 m² with known diabetic nephropathy. Which CKD stage does this represent?
subject: Medicine
concept: CKD staging — eGFR thresholds

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with bilateral flank pain, hypertension, and haematuria. Imaging shows multiple bilateral renal cysts and his father died of a cerebral aneurysm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: ADPKD — autosomal dominant, bilateral cysts, HTN, berry aneurysms
discriminator: Bilateral cysts + HTN + haematuria + family history of cerebral aneurysm = ADPKD

stem: A 62-year-old hypertensive smoker develops recurrent 'flash' pulmonary oedema. After starting an ACE inhibitor, serum creatinine rises from 1.2 to 2.1 mg/dL within 1 week. What is the most likely cause?
subject: Medicine
concept: Renal artery stenosis — flash pulmonary oedema + ACEi-induced Cr rise >30%
discriminator: Flash pulmonary oedema + >30% Cr rise after ACEi = bilateral renal artery stenosis

stem: A 50-year-old man with advanced CKD (eGFR 12) develops prolonged bleeding after tooth extraction. Platelet count is normal. Which agent most directly corrects the bleeding tendency?
subject: Medicine
concept: Uraemic bleeding — platelet dysfunction corrected by desmopressin
discriminator: CKD + bleeding with NORMAL platelet count = uraemic platelet dysfunction → DDAVP

stem: A 48-year-old woman on peritoneal dialysis presents with abdominal pain and a cloudy effluent bag. What is the most appropriate initial step?
opts: Send effluent for cell count, gram stain, and culture, then start empirical antibiotics
subject: Medicine
concept: Peritoneal dialysis — peritonitis diagnosis and empirical treatment
discriminator: Cloudy effluent + abdominal pain in PD patient = peritonitis → effluent analysis + empirical antibiotics

stem: A patient is being prepared for maintenance haemodialysis. Which vascular access is preferred for long-term dialysis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Haemodialysis access — AV fistula is preferred
discriminator: AV fistula = lowest infection/thrombosis, best long-term patency → preferred access

stem: A 55-year-old man with CKD stage 4 is counselled on dietary modification. Which dietary restriction is most important to slow progression and prevent complications?
subject: Medicine
concept: CKD diet — phosphate and potassium restriction
discriminator: CKD diet: restrict phosphate (CKD-MBD) and potassium (hyperkalaemia); moderate protein

stem: A 60-year-old man with a 20-year history of poorly controlled hypertension has slowly progressive renal impairment with mild proteinuria (<1 g/day). Urine sediment is bland. What is the most likely cause?
subject: Medicine
concept: Hypertensive nephrosclerosis — long-standing HTN, slow decline, mild proteinuria
discriminator: Long-standing HTN + slow CKD + mild proteinuria + bland sediment = hypertensive nephrosclerosis

stem: A 7-year-old boy develops palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs, abdominal pain, and arthralgia 2 weeks after an upper respiratory infection. Urine shows blood and protein. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Henoch-Schönlein purpura — palpable purpura + abdominal pain + arthralgia + renal
discriminator: Palpable purpura (buttocks/legs) + abdominal pain + arthralgia + haematuria = HSP

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with sinusitis, haemoptysis, and rapidly progressive renal failure. Urine shows RBC casts. Which antibody is most likely to be positive?
subject: Medicine
concept: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis — c-ANCA/PR3, ENT + pulmonary-renal
discriminator: Sinusitis + haemoptysis + RPGN + RBC casts = GPA → c-ANCA (PR3)

stem: A 55-year-old woman has rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with haematuria, but NO upper respiratory or sinus involvement. Renal biopsy shows pauci-immune crescentic GN. Which antibody is most likely positive?
subject: Medicine
concept: Microscopic polyangiitis — p-ANCA/MPO, pauci-immune crescentic GN without ENT
discriminator: Pauci-immune crescentic GN WITHOUT ENT involvement = microscopic polyangiitis → p-ANCA (MPO)

stem: A renal biopsy in a patient with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis shows crescentic GN with linear immunofluorescence for IgG along the glomerular basement membrane. Which condition does this represent?
subject: Medicine
concept: RPGN — anti-GBM disease with linear IgG on immunofluorescence
discriminator: Crescentic GN + LINEAR IgG along GBM = anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture)

stem: A 40-year-old man with nephrotic syndrome due to membranous nephropathy develops sudden left flank pain and gross haematuria. What complication should be suspected?
subject: Medicine
concept: Nephrotic syndrome — hypercoagulability → renal vein thrombosis
discriminator: Nephrotic syndrome + sudden flank pain + gross haematuria = renal vein thrombosis

stem: A 30-year-old man with untreated HIV infection develops nephrotic-range proteinuria and progressive renal failure. Biopsy shows collapsing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. What is the most likely cause?
subject: Medicine
concept: HIV-associated nephropathy — collapsing FSGS in HIV
discriminator: HIV + nephrotic-range proteinuria + collapsing FSGS = HIV-associated nephropathy

stem: A 25-year-old woman has persistent microscopic haematuria found on a routine check. She is otherwise well with normal blood pressure, normal renal function, and no proteinuria. Her mother has the same finding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Thin basement membrane disease — benign familial haematuria
discriminator: Isolated persistent haematuria + family history + normal BP/function = thin basement membrane disease

stem: A 60-year-old man with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis develops nephrotic-range proteinuria and renal impairment. Renal biopsy shows apple-green birefringence with Congo red staining. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine
concept: Renal amyloidosis — Congo red apple-green birefringence in chronic inflammation
discriminator: Chronic inflammation + nephrotic syndrome + Congo red apple-green = AA amyloidosis

stem: A 12-year-old girl with recurrent urinary tract infections and hypertension has renal scarring on DMSA scan, most prominent at the upper and lower poles. What is the most likely underlying problem?
subject: Medicine
concept: Reflux nephropathy — VUR causes polar renal scarring
discriminator: Recurrent UTIs + HTN + polar scarring on DMSA = vesicoureteral reflux (reflux nephropathy)

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with his first renal colic. Non-contrast CT shows a radio-opaque stone in the left renal pelvis. Which is the most common composition of such stones?
subject: Surgery
concept: Calcium oxalate — most common renal stone (~80%), radio-opaque
discriminator: Calcium oxalate = ~80% of stones, radio-opaque (only uric acid/cystine are radiolucent)

stem: A 50-year-old man with gout presents with renal colic. Plain abdominal X-ray shows no visible stone, but CT confirms a renal calculus. What is the most likely composition and treatment principle?
opts: Uric acid — radiolucent, treat with urine alkalinization
Calcium oxalate — radio-opaque, treat with thiazide
Struvite — infected urine, treat with antibiotics alone
Cystine — hereditary, treat with hydration only
subject: Surgery
concept: Uric acid stone — radiolucent, gout association, alkalinize urine
discriminator: Gout + radiolucent stone = uric acid → alkalinize urine (and xanthine oxidase inhibitors)

stem: A 19-year-old with a history of childhood renal stones has a stone analysis showing hexagonal crystals. Which inheritance pattern and treatment is correct?
subject: Surgery
concept: Cystine stone — hereditary (cystinuria), hexagon crystals, penicillamine
discriminator: Hexagonal crystals = cystine; autosomal recessive cystinuria → hydration + penicillamine/captopril + alkalinization

stem: A 40-year-old woman with Crohn disease (extensive ileal resection) develops recurrent calcium oxalate stones. What is the underlying mechanism?
subject: Surgery
concept: Enteric hyperoxaluria — fat malabsorption → increased oxalate absorption
discriminator: IBD/bariatric/ileal resection + fat malabsorption → enteric hyperoxaluria → calcium oxalate stones

stem: A 55-year-old woman with recurrent renal stones is found to have hypercalcaemia with low phosphate and elevated PTH. Which stone type is she forming?
subject: Surgery
concept: Primary hyperparathyroidism — hypercalciuria → calcium stones (bones, stones, groans)
discriminator: High Ca + low PO4 + high PTH + stones = primary HPT → calcium-containing stones

stem: A 58-year-old smoker presents with painless gross haematuria, left flank pain, and a palpable abdominal mass. CT shows a 9 cm heterogeneous renal mass extending into the renal vein. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Transitional cell carcinoma of the renal pelvis
subject: Surgery
concept: Renal cell carcinoma — painless haematuria + flank mass + paraneoplastic, smoking
discriminator: Adult + painless haematuria + flank mass + renal vein extension + smoking = RCC

stem: A 3-year-old child is found to have a large, smooth, unilateral abdominal mass that does not cross the midline. There is no haematuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Surgery
concept: Wilms tumour — pediatric abdominal mass <5 years, unilateral, smooth
discriminator: Child <5 + smooth unilateral abdominal mass (no cross midline) = Wilms tumour

stem: A 60-year-old heavy smoker presents with painless gross haematuria. Cystoscopy is normal, but retrograde pyelography shows a filling defect in the renal pelvis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Transitional cell carcinoma of the renal pelvis
subject: Surgery
concept: Upper-tract transitional cell carcinoma — smoking, haematuria, filling defect
discriminator: Smoker + painless haematuria + renal pelvis filling defect (normal cystoscopy) = upper-tract TCC

stem: A 28-year-old man has a painless testicular mass. Tumour markers show an elevated alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and normal human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG). Which histological category does this favour?
subject: Surgery
concept: Testicular germ cell tumour — AFP elevated implies non-seminomatous component
discriminator: Elevated AFP = NON-seminomatous GCT (seminoma has normal AFP; hCG may be raised)

stem: A 1-year-old boy has an undescended right testis that has not spontaneously descended. What is the most important long-term concern and management?
opts: No cancer risk; observe until adulthood
Increased testicular cancer risk + infertility; orchiopexy before puberty
Hormone therapy cures the cancer risk
subject: Surgery
concept: Cryptorchidism — infertility + cancer risk; orchiopexy (not orchiectomy)
discriminator: Undescended testis = infertility + germ-cell cancer risk; fix with orchiopexy (not orchiectomy)

stem: A 26-year-old man presents with infertility and a 'bag of worms' sensation in the left scrotum that diminishes when supine. What is the most likely finding and association?
opts: Left varicocele — dilated pampiniform plexus; associated with left RCC
subject: Surgery
concept: Varicocele — left-sided (venous drainage), infertility, adult right-side suggests RCC
discriminator: Left 'bag of worms' scrotal swelling = varicocele; NEW right-sided varicocele suggests RCC

stem: A couple presents with infertility. The man has a low semen volume and a left varicocele on exam. Which initial step is most appropriate?
opts: Semen analysis; correct varicocele if present before assisted reproduction
subject: Surgery
concept: Male infertility — semen analysis first; varicocele correction improves fertility
discriminator: Infertility workup = semen analysis; varicocele (correctable) is a key reversible cause

stem: A 60-year-old man with poor hygiene has inability to retract the foreskin over the glans, with no acute pain or swelling. A younger man presents acutely with a retracted foreskin trapped behind the glans with pain and oedema. Which pairing is correct?
subject: Surgery
concept: Phimosis vs paraphimosis — cannot retract vs trapped retracted foreskin
discriminator: Phimosis = cannot retract foreskin; paraphimosis = retracted foreskin trapped (acute, needs reduction)

stem: A 55-year-old uncircumcised man presents with a non-healing ulcerative lesion on the glans penis. Which is the strongest associated risk factor?
opts: Poor hygiene / phimosis with HPV infection
subject: Surgery
concept: Penile cancer — HPV + phimosis/poor hygiene; ulcer on glans
discriminator: Glans ulcer in uncircumcised man = penile squamous cell carcinoma (HPV, phimosis risk)

stem: A 50-year-old man reports a progressively curved, painful erection with a palpable firm band on the dorsal penis. What is the diagnosis?
subject: Surgery
concept: Peyronie disease — fibrous plaque causing penile curvature
discriminator: Palpable fibrous plaque + curvature = Peyronie disease (tunica albuginea fibrosis)

stem: A 30-year-old man presents with dysuria, fever, and perineal pain; the prostate is tender and boggy on exam. What is the most appropriate initial antibiotic?
subject: Surgery
concept: Acute bacterial prostatitis — fluoroquinolone, systemic symptoms
discriminator: Acute prostatitis (fever + perineal pain + tender prostate) = fluoroquinolone (cover Gram-negatives)

stem: A 24-year-old pregnant woman at 16 weeks is found to have asymptomatic bacteriuria on screening. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Treat with a pregnancy-safe antibiotic (e.g., nitrofurantoin/cephalexin)
subject: Surgery
concept: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy — treat to prevent pyelonephritis
discriminator: Pregnancy + asymptomatic bacteriuria = TREAT (nitrofurantoin/cephalexin) to prevent pyelonephritis

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with fever, flank pain, and costovertebral angle tenderness. Urinalysis shows leucocytes and nitrites. What is the most likely causative organism?
subject: Surgery
concept: Acute pyelonephritis — E. coli is the most common pathogen
discriminator: Uncomplicated pyelonephritis/UTI = E. coli (~80-90%) from ascending faecal flora

stem: A 70-year-old woman with a urinary catheter develops fever, rigors, and hypotension with a lactate of 3.2 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Intravenous antibiotics + vasopressors for septic shock
subject: Surgery
concept: Urosepsis — source of septic shock; antibiotics + vasopressors
discriminator: Urosepsis with hypotension + lactate >2 = septic shock → antibiotics + vasopressors (fluids + source control)

stem: In which of the following patients is treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria clearly indicated?
opts: An elderly man in a nursing home
A young woman with a single positive screen
subject: Surgery
concept: Asymptomatic bacteriuria — treat in pregnancy and before urologic procedures
discriminator: Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria only in pregnancy and before invasive urologic procedures

stem: A 25-year-old man with a T6 spinal cord injury has recurrent urinary tract infections and incomplete emptying. Which management is most appropriate?
subject: Surgery
concept: Neurogenic bladder — intermittent catheterization to protect upper tracts
discriminator: Spinal cord injury neurogenic bladder = clean intermittent catheterization (protects kidneys)

stem: A 30-year-old man with a cervical spinal cord injury suddenly develops a severe headache, sweating, and a blood pressure of 200/110 mmHg. The trigger is most commonly:
opts: Bladder distension (full catheter bag / blocked catheter)
subject: Surgery
concept: Autonomic dysreflexia — bladder distension is the most common trigger
discriminator: SCI above T6 + sudden hypertension/headache/sweating = autonomic dysreflexia; bladder trigger

stem: An 80-year-old man with long-standing bladder outlet obstruction has constant dribbling incontinence with a palpable bladder. Which type of incontinence is this?
subject: Surgery
concept: Overflow incontinence — chronic retention → dribbling, palpable bladder
discriminator: Incomplete emptying + dribbling + palpable bladder = overflow incontinence

stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of recurrent urethral discharge and prior catheterisation has a weak stream, terminal dribbling, and a palpable bladder. What is the most likely cause?
subject: Surgery
concept: Urethral stricture — obstructive voiding from scarring (catheter/trauma/STD)
discriminator: Weak stream + terminal dribbling + palpable bladder after catheter/STD = urethral stricture

stem: During a hysterectomy, the ureter is most commonly injured at which anatomical relationship?
opts: Where it crosses under the uterine artery ('water under the bridge')
In the posterior abdominal wall lateral to psoas
subject: Surgery
concept: Iatrogenic ureteric injury — at the uterine artery crossing during pelvic surgery
discriminator: Ureter injury in hysterectomy = at the uterine artery crossing (distal third, 'water under the bridge')

stem: A 58-year-old man develops slurred speech and difficulty chewing after a left medullary infarction. On protrusion, the tongue deviates to the left and the left half of the tongue shows wasting and fasciculations. Which nerve is most likely injured?
concept: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) — LMN vs UMN lesion localization

stem: A 38-year-old man presents with acute severe right-sided headache, right ptosis, and diplopia. The right eye is deviated 'down and out', and the right pupil is dilated and non-reactive to light. Which mechanism best explains the pupillary involvement?
opts: Compression of the superficial (peripheral) pupillomotor fibers of the oculomotor nerve by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm
Microvascular ischemia of the central core of the oculomotor nerve sparing the pupillomotor fibers
Compression of the central core of the oculomotor nerve by the superior cerebellar artery
Cavernous sinus thrombosis with involvement of the sympathetic plexus around the internal carotid artery
concept: Oculomotor nerve (CN III) — pupillomotor fiber position; compressive vs ischemic lesions

stem: A 60-year-old hypertensive man wakes with drooping of the left lower face. He can wrinkle his forehead on the left and close the left eye fully. Taste and hearing are normal. Which localization best explains these findings?
opts: Right parotid malignancy involving the facial nerve
concept: Facial nerve (CN VII) — UMN vs LMN facial palsy (forehead sparing)

stem: A newborn has Erb-Duchenne palsy after a difficult delivery, with the arm adducted and internally rotated, the elbow extended, and the wrist flexed. Which group of muscles produces this characteristic posture?
opts: Pectoralis major, teres major, and latissimus dorsi
concept: Brachial plexus upper trunk (Erb-Duchenne) — unopposed muscle action producing the deformity

stem: A 45-year-old woman received an intramuscular injection in the left buttock two weeks ago. She now has a painless limp: when she stands on the left leg alone, the right side of her pelvis drops (positive Trendelenburg sign). Which structure is most likely injured?
concept: Gluteal region — superior gluteal nerve and hip abductor apparatus (Trendelenburg sign)

stem: A 50-year-old man sustains a pelvic fracture in a road traffic accident. He cannot adduct his thigh or cross his legs, and has reduced sensation over the medial side of the thigh. He can extend the knee fully and the patellar reflex is normal. Which nerve is injured?
concept: Obturator nerve (L2-L4) — adductor compartment and medial thigh sensory loss

stem: A 30-year-old man undergoes open shoulder surgery under prolonged traction. He now has weakness of elbow flexion when the forearm is fully supinated, and numbness over the lateral side of the forearm. Flexion with the forearm in mid-pronation (brachioradialis) is strong, and radial sensation is normal. Which nerve is most likely injured?
concept: Musculocutaneous nerve (C5-C6) — biceps/brachialis and lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm

stem: A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and a 30-pack-year smoking history presents with a painless nodule and a cord in his right palm. The ring and little fingers are fixed in flexion at the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints and cannot be extended passively. Which structure is primarily responsible for this contracture?
opts: The collateral ligaments of the metacarpophalangeal joints
concept: Dupuytren contracture — palmar aponeurosis pathology

stem: A 30-year-old diabetic man has a puncture wound over the proximal phalanx of the little finger. Two days later the palm is swollen and tender, and infection has tracked to the ulnar (common flexor) bursa in the wrist. Which anatomical feature best explains this proximal spread of infection?
opts: The sheath of the little finger is continuous with the ulnar bursa, which may communicate with the radial bursa around the flexor pollicis longus (horseshoe abscess)
The sheath of the little finger is continuous with the radial bursa of the thumb
All four digital flexor sheaths merge into a single common bursa in the palm
The little finger sheath terminates blindly in the mid-palm without reaching the wrist
concept: Palmar spaces — flexor tendon sheaths and radial/ulnar bursae (horseshoe abscess)

stem: A 40-year-old man with an odontogenic infection develops dysphagia and fever. CT shows a retropharyngeal collection extending inferiorly BEHIND the alar fascia into the plane between the alar and prevertebral fasciae. Which complication risk is greatest in this patient?
opts: Spread into the posterior mediastinum, potentially to the level of the diaphragm
Direct erosion into the carotid sheath with ipsilateral Horner syndrome
Spread into the anterior mediastinum through the pretracheal space
A self-limited abscess with no inferior extension
concept: Deep neck spaces — the 'danger space' (alar-prevertebral plane) and its mediastinal extension

stem: During repair of an inguinal hernia, the surgeon identifies the walls of the inguinal canal (deep inguinal ring laterally, superficial inguinal ring medially). Which structure forms the FLOOR of the inguinal canal?
concept: Inguinal canal — wall anatomy (floor = inguinal ligament)

stem: A term newborn delivered after shoulder dystocia has decreased spontaneous movement of the right arm. The arm lies comfortably adducted with normal tone, and palpation along the right clavicle makes the infant cry. Which diagnosis is most likely?
opts: Humeral shaft fracture with radial nerve injury
concept: Newborn clavicle fracture — pseudoparalysis vs brachial plexus injury

stem: A 70-year-old woman sustains a displaced INTRACAPSULAR fracture of the femoral neck after a fall. She is at high risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head. Which artery is the dominant blood supply to the adult femoral head and is most vulnerable in this fracture?
opts: The obturator artery via the ligamentum teres
The medial circumflex femoral artery via retinacular branches
The nutrient artery of the femoral shaft
concept: Blood supply of the femoral head — retinacular arteries and intracapsular fracture AVN

stem: A 40-year-old man twists his ankle in an eversion injury. Radiographs show a transverse fracture of the medial malleolus together with a fracture of the fibula at the level of the ankle joint, and the talus is shifted laterally. What is the eponymous name of this injury pattern?
concept: Ankle fractures — Pott's (bimalleolar) fracture-dislocation

stem: A vascular surgeon repairs a traumatic pseudoaneurysm of the superficial femoral artery within the adductor (subsartorial) canal. Which statement about the contents of this canal is correct?
opts: The femoral nerve passes through the canal alongside the artery
The saphenous nerve accompanies the femoral artery through the canal
The deep femoral (profunda femoris) artery is a major content of the canal
The sciatic nerve joins the artery within the proximal canal
concept: Adductor (subsartorial) canal — contents and boundaries

stem: During repair of a paraesophageal hernia, the surgeon must dissect the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm. Which structures accompany the esophagus as it passes through the hiatus at the T10 level?
opts: The anterior and posterior vagal trunks
concept: Diaphragmatic apertures — structures accompanying the esophagus at T10

stem: A 22-year-old man is struck in the epigastrium by a bicycle handlebar. Six hours later he has only mild upper abdominal pain and a soft abdomen. CT shows retroperitoneal air around the duodenum and pancreas with blurring of the right psoas margin. Which anatomical fact best explains the paucity of early peritoneal signs?
opts: The second and third parts of the duodenum are secondarily retroperitoneal, so a rupture leaks into the retroperitoneum
The duodenum is entirely intraperitoneal and covered by the greater omentum
The duodenum lies within the lesser sac, which tamponades any leak
The duodenum is shielded from injury by the transverse mesocolon
concept: Peritoneal relations — retroperitoneal duodenum and the 'silent' retroperitoneal rupture

stem: During laparotomy for blunt hepatic trauma, the surgeon controls brisk hilar bleeding by compressing the free edge of the lesser omentum (Pringle maneuver). Which structures are compressed between the surgeon's fingers?
opts: The hepatic veins and the inferior vena cava
The portal vein and the hepatic artery (with the bile duct)
The celiac trunk and the superior mesenteric artery
The cystic artery and the cystic duct
concept: Porta hepatis — contents of the hepatoduodenal ligament and the Pringle maneuver

stem: During a total abdominal hysterectomy, the surgeon ligates the uterine artery at its crossing with the ureter at the base of the broad ligament. Which anatomical relationship is being exploited, and what is the risk of injury?
opts: The ureter passes UNDER the uterine artery ('water under the bridge') and is at risk of being clamped with it
The ureter passes OVER the uterine artery but is protected by the ovarian ligament
The ureter lies 5 cm lateral to the uterine artery and is never near the operative field
The ureter crosses the uterine artery within the mesovarium, anterior to the ovary
concept: Pelvic ureter — relation to the uterine artery (hysterectomy hazard)

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with a pigmented, bleeding lesion at the anal margin, biopsy confirms malignant melanoma. Where is the lesion located relative to the pectinate line, and to which group of nodes will it most likely metastasize first?
opts: Above the pectinate line — to the inferior mesenteric (para-aortic) nodes
Below the pectinate line — to the superficial inguinal nodes
At the pectinate line — to the internal iliac nodes
Below the pectinate line — to the inferior hypogastric plexus nodes
concept: Anal canal — lymphatic drainage above and below the pectinate line

stem: A 48-year-old woman feels a painless lump in the upper outer quadrant of her right breast. On examination, gentle compression of the lump produces a small skin dimple that was not visible at rest. Which structure is responsible for this dimpling sign?
opts: Dilated subareolar ducts with nipple retraction
The suspensory ligaments of Cooper being shortened or tethered by the tumor
Fixation of the tumor to the pectoralis major fascia
concept: Breast — suspensory (Cooper's) ligaments and the dimpling sign

stem: A 34-year-old woman undergoes total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid carcinoma. During the operation the surgeon first dissects the paratracheal nodes. On which anatomical basis did the surgeon choose this as the first-echelon drainage of the thyroid?
opts: The thyroid drains predominantly to the submandibular nodes
The thyroid drains laterally to the accessory nerve (level V) nodes
The thyroid drains centrally to the paratracheal/central compartment (level VI) nodes, then to the lateral neck
The thyroid drains via the thoracic duct directly to the left axilla
concept: Thyroid — central (level VI) lymph node compartment as first echelon

stem: A 60-year-old man undergoes coronary angiography for inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction, and total occlusion of the right coronary artery (RCA) is found. Angiography also shows that the RCA gives off the posterior descending artery (PDA). What is this pattern of coronary circulation called, and how common is it?
opts: Left dominance — present in about 50% of hearts
Right dominance — present in about 80-85% of hearts
Co-dominance — present in about 25% of hearts
Balanced circulation — present in about 70% of hearts
concept: Coronary arterial dominance — RCA supplying the PDA

stem: A 62-year-old right-handed man suddenly develops weakness of the right face and right arm with a non-fluent (Broca) aphasia, but his right leg is spared. Which cerebral arterial territory is most likely involved?
opts: The superior division of the left middle cerebral artery (MCA)
The left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA)
concept: Cerebral arterial territories — MCA superior division (face/arm + Broca)

stem: A 30-year-old man presents with a 'cape'-like (bilateral shoulder and upper arm) loss of pain and temperature sensation with preserved light-touch, and progressive wasting of the small muscles of both hands. Which spinal cord diagnosis explains these findings?
opts: Syringomyelia of the cervical spinal cord
Brown-Sequard syndrome from a right hemisection
Anterior spinal artery occlusion at the cervical level
concept: Spinal cord tracts — central canal syrinx and dissociated sensory loss

stem: A 28-year-old woman with regular 28-day cycles is investigated for infertility.
