On cycle day 12, ultrasound shows a mature 20 mm dominant follicle and serum estradiol is appropriately elevated, but serial measurements show no mid-cycle LH surge, and follicular rupture never occurs. Which step of the ovarian cycle is failing?
opts: The mid-cycle LH surge, which is required to trigger ovulation
FSH-dependent recruitment and growth of the dominant follicle
Progesterone-mediated secretory transformation of the endometrium
Estrogen negative feedback that limits FSH early in the follicular phase
concept: LH surge — the trigger of ovulation

stem: A 40-year-old woman with 3 days of severe vomiting has pH 7.52, HCO3 35 mEq/L, and serum K+ 2.9 mEq/L. Despite marked metabolic alkalosis, her urine pH is 5.0. Which mechanism best explains this paradoxical aciduria?
opts: Hypokalemia makes distal tubular cells secrete H+ instead of K+, keeping the urine acid despite alkalemia
Low tubular flow during volume depletion prevents bicarbonate excretion
The lungs retain CO2, which the kidneys excrete as carbonic acid
Aldosterone is suppressed, so filtered bicarbonate is completely reabsorbed passively
concept: Metabolic alkalosis — paradoxical aciduria and H+/K+ competition in the distal nephron

stem: A 60-year-old man with heart failure has a low cardiac output. As renal perfusion pressure falls toward 70 mmHg, renin release from the juxtaglomerular cells increases sharply. Which sensor directly initiates this renin release?
opts: Baroreceptors in the afferent arteriole of the kidney
Macula densa cells detecting decreased NaCl delivery
Stretch receptors in the right atrium
concept: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system — the intrarenal baroreceptor mechanism

stem: A 58-year-old man with septic shock and a stiff, hypertrophied left ventricle receives a 500 mL crystalloid bolus. Cardiac output rises only 5%, while central venous pressure jumps from 8 to 16 cm H2O. Which physiological principle best explains this response?
opts: The ventricle is working on the plateau of the Frank-Starling curve, where further preload adds little stroke volume
The bolus raised intrathoracic pressure and mechanically impeded venous return
Sepsis shifted the Starling curve leftward, producing cardiogenic failure
The fluid bolus increased afterload and flattened the curve
concept: Frank-Starling mechanism — the operating point on the curve

stem: A 62-year-old man with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia is given intravenous verapamil. Verapamil blocks calcium channels in cardiac muscle and nodal tissue. Which phase of the cardiac action potential is primarily mediated by calcium influx and therefore targeted by verapamil?
opts: Phase 2 — the plateau, sustained by L-type calcium influx
Phase 4 — the pacemaker sodium funny current
concept: Cardiac action potential — ionic basis of the plateau (phase 2)

stem: During exercise, muscle capillaries receive deoxygenated blood. Deoxygenated hemoglobin carries more CO2 and H+ than oxygenated hemoglobin, which enhances CO2 removal from working muscle. Which physiological principle does this describe?
concept: Haldane effect — CO2 transport by deoxygenated hemoglobin

stem: A 55-year-old man develops sudden dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain 10 days after knee surgery. ABG on room air: PaO2 58 mmHg, PaCO2 33 mmHg. A V/Q scan shows multiple segmental regions that are ventilated but NOT perfused. What is the dominant physiological abnormality?
opts: Diffusion limitation across the alveolar-capillary membrane
concept: Ventilation-perfusion matching — alveolar dead space in pulmonary embolism

stem: A preterm infant develops respiratory distress from surfactant deficiency. Which statement correctly applies the LaPlace relationship to explain why the smallest air sacs are most prone to collapse?
opts: Collapsing pressure is higher in smaller alveoli (P = 2T/r), so they empty into larger ones unless surfactant uniformly lowers surface tension
Larger alveoli develop higher collapsing pressure and collapse first
Surface tension increases as radius increases, protecting small alveoli
Surfactant raises surface tension to keep small alveoli expanded
concept: LaPlace law and surfactant — alveolar stability

stem: A healthy 28-year-old primigravida at 20 weeks gestation has renal function testing. Compared with her non-pregnant baseline, which renal physiological change is expected?
opts: GFR and renal plasma flow rise substantially, partly because afferent arteriolar resistance falls
GFR falls because progesterone constricts the afferent arteriole
GFR is unchanged — the kidney is spared from hormonal changes in pregnancy
GFR rises only during labour and delivery
concept: Pregnancy physiology — GFR and renal plasma flow

stem: The countercurrent multiplier builds the medullary osmotic gradient that makes concentrated urine possible. Which nephron segment performs the active transport that serves as the engine (single effect) of this multiplier?
opts: Active NaCl reabsorption by the thick ascending limb
Water reabsorption from the collecting duct under ADH
Urea recycling across the proximal tubule
Passive sodium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule
concept: Countercurrent multiplier — the single effect of the loop of Henle

stem: Normal urine can be acidified to a pH of about 4.5, far more acidic than plasma. Which cells perform this final acidification of urine in the collecting duct?
opts: Type A intercalated cells, which secrete H+ via an H+-ATPase
Principal cells, which reabsorb sodium through ENaC
Proximal tubule cells, which reclaim filtered bicarbonate via NHE3
Type B intercalated cells, which secrete bicarbonate
concept: Renal acid secretion — type A intercalated cells of the collecting duct

stem: A 55-year-old man with COPD has taken prednisolone 15 mg daily for 6 months. Which statement best explains why his own cortisol production is suppressed during this therapy?
opts: Exogenous glucocorticoid suppresses hypothalamic CRH and pituitary ACTH, so the adrenal cortex atrophies
The adrenal cortex becomes hyperplastic and resistant to ACTH
CRH secretion rises, producing pituitary desensitization
Tissue glucocorticoid receptors are upregulated and consume circulating cortisol
concept: HPA axis — negative feedback suppression by exogenous glucocorticoids

stem: A 45-year-old woman has fatigue, cold intolerance, and a diffuse goiter. Serum TSH is 38 µIU/mL (markedly elevated) with a low free T4. Which statement best explains this pattern?
opts: Loss of T4 negative feedback on the anterior pituitary allows unrestrained TSH secretion
The pituitary is autonomously secreting excess TSH (secondary disease)
TRH is deficient, so TSH accumulates in the blood
concept: Thyroid-pituitary negative feedback (primary hypothyroidism)

stem: A healthy 68-year-old man fasts for 14 hours before elective surgery. Blood glucose at induction is 88 mg/dL. Which mechanism is the primary source of this glucose during an overnight fast?
opts: Hepatic glycogenolysis, with gluconeogenesis rising as glycogen stores deplete
Glycogenolysis in skeletal muscle, which releases glucose into the blood
Direct release of free glucose from adipose tissue lipolysis
Continued glucose absorption from the small intestine
concept: Fuel homeostasis — hepatic glucose output in the fasting state

stem: During the absolute refractory period of a neuron, a second stimulus of any strength fails to produce an action potential. Which molecular event explains this?
opts: Voltage-gated sodium channels are inactivated and cannot reopen until the membrane repolarizes
Sodium channels are closed but available — only the threshold has risen
The sodium-potassium pump is temporarily reversed
Calcium influx dominates the membrane and excludes sodium entry
concept: Action potential — molecular basis of the absolute refractory period

stem: A 30-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis has normal strength at rest, but her grip visibly fatigues with repeated effort. Which electrophysiological mechanism at the neuromuscular junction accounts for this fatigability?
opts: End-plate potential amplitude falls progressively with repetitive stimulation, so transmission eventually fails
Voltage-gated sodium channels in the muscle membrane fail after repeated depolarization
The motor nerve exhausts its acetylcholine vesicle supply within seconds
Calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum becomes deficient with fatigue
concept: Neuromuscular junction — decremental transmission in myasthenia gravis

stem: Which of the following is a parasympathetic effect?
opts: Constriction of the pupil and contraction of the detrusor muscle
Dilatation of the pupil and relaxation of the detrusor
Increase in heart rate and bronchodilatation
Constriction of gastrointestinal sphincters and decreased gut motility
concept: Autonomic nervous system — parasympathetic effector responses

stem: When the patellar tendon is tapped, the quadriceps is stretched and the knee extends. In this reflex, the Ia afferent from the muscle spindle synapses directly (monosynaptically) on which structure to produce the response?
opts: The alpha motor neuron supplying the same (quadriceps) muscle
The gamma motor neuron supplying the same muscle spindle
The alpha motor neuron of the antagonist (hamstring) muscle
concept: Spinal reflexes — monosynaptic stretch reflex circuitry

stem: Shortly after a large meal, blood draining the stomach (gastric venous blood) is transiently more alkaline than arterial blood. Which cellular process explains this 'alkaline tide'?
opts: Each H+ secreted by the parietal cell leaves an equivalent HCO3- behind, which enters the blood
The ingested food buffers carbon dioxide and raises venous pH
Gastrin stimulates the pancreas to secrete bicarbonate into the blood
Gastric blood flow falls after eating, concentrating plasma bicarbonate
concept: Gastric acid secretion — the parietal cell alkaline tide

stem: A 45-year-old man with Crohn disease undergoes resection of the terminal ileum. Two years later he develops macrocytic anemia. Which pair of substances is absorbed specifically in the terminal ileum and deficient after this surgery?
concept: GI absorption — site-specific transport (B12 and bile salts in the ileum)

stem: A 35-year-old man who underwent splenectomy after trauma has a blood film showing Howell-Jolly bodies (small nuclear remnants) inside red cells. Which normal splenic function has been lost?
opts: Pitting — removal of inclusions from otherwise normal red cells
Culling — destruction of senescent red cells at the end of their 120-day life
Erythropoiesis — production of new red cells in the spleen
concept: Spleen and reticuloendothelial system — the pitting function

stem: In the final common pathway of coagulation, a serine protease converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin and also amplifies the cascade by activating factors V, VIII, and XI. Which enzyme is this?
concept: Hemostasis — thrombin in the coagulation cascade

stem: A healthy term newborn is placed in a cool nursery. Unlike an adult, the neonate cannot rely on shivering. Which physiological mechanism is the newborn's primary defense against cold?
opts: Non-shivering thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue
Cutaneous vasodilatation to warm the skin
concept: Thermoregulation — non-shivering thermogenesis in the neonate

stem: A sprinter breathes heavily for several minutes after finishing a 400 m race. Which physiological process primarily explains this sustained post-exercise hyperventilation (oxygen debt)?
opts: Repayment of oxygen debt: resynthesizing ATP-phosphocreatine, clearing lactate, and re-saturating myoglobin
Reflex hyperventilation from a stretched diaphragm after exertion
A sustained rise in pulmonary dead space that keeps CO2 elevated
Reset of the central chemoreceptors to a higher CO2 set-point during the race
concept: Exercise physiology — oxygen debt (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption)

stem: A healthy 30-year-old woman at 32 weeks gestation is compared with her pre-pregnancy baseline. Which statement correctly describes cardiac output in normal pregnancy?
opts: Cardiac output rises by roughly 30-50%, from an early increase in stroke volume plus a modest rise in heart rate
Cardiac output falls about 20% because the uterus compresses the vena cava at all times
Cardiac output is unchanged — the circulation is simply redistributed to the uterus
Cardiac output doubles to about 9 L/min by term
concept: Pregnancy physiology — cardiovascular adaptation (cardiac output)

stem: A 6-month-old boy develops pallor, jaundice, and dark urine 2 days after wearing clothes that had been stored with naphthalene mothballs. Blood film shows bite cells and Heinz bodies, and haemoglobin has fallen from 11 to 7 g/dL. Which biochemical mechanism explains the haemolysis?
opts: Deficient pyruvate kinase prevents ATP generation in late red-cell glycolysis
Deficient NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway leaves reduced glutathione unable to neutralise oxidant stress
Impaired beta-oxidation of fatty acids reduces red-cell membrane stability
Accumulation of galactitol within the red cell causes osmotic lysis
concept: G6PD deficiency — oxidative haemolysis (pentose phosphate pathway)

stem: A 5-month-old infant who was born at home and missed newborn screening has fair skin, eczema, and a musty odour. Plasma phenylalanine is 510 µmol/L. Dietary treatment is planned. Which instruction is correct?
opts: Restrict all protein and give a low-protein vegan diet to protect the brain
Add supplementary leucine and isoleucine to the formula
Provide a low-phenylalanine formula supplemented with tyrosine
Treat with thyroxine and a low-iodine diet
concept: Phenylketonuria — dietary management

stem: A 28-year-old woman has colicky abdominal pain for 3 days, vomiting, and new-onset weakness of the arms. She is tachycardic and hypertensive. Urine left in the light turns dark red-brown. Which explanation best fits these findings?
opts: Porphobilinogen excreted in urine polymerises to porphyrins on standing and in light
Haemoglobin from microscopic haematuria oxidises in air and darkens
Homogentisic acid polymerises to ochronotic pigment in the urine
Myoglobin released from damaged skeletal muscle darkens with oxidation
concept: Acute intermittent porphyria — darkening urine mechanism

stem: A 54-year-old vegetarian has fatigue and a macrocytic anaemia (MCV 112 fL). Serum B12 is 110 pg/mL and red-cell folate is normal. Which additional finding best confirms that B12 deficiency — not folate deficiency — explains the anaemia?
opts: Low serum iron with high total iron-binding capacity
concept: B12 vs folate deficiency — methylmalonic acid as the discriminator

stem: A 47-year-old man with chronic alcohol use has 3 weeks of dyspnoea, ankle oedema, and warm extremities. Oxygen saturation is 98% but venous lactate is 6 mmol/L. Which enzyme defect best explains the lactic acidosis?
opts: Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency blocks the final step of gluconeogenesis
Pyruvate dehydrogenase requires thiamine pyrophosphate; its impairment diverts pyruvate to lactate
Pyruvate carboxylase overactivity shunts pyruvate into oxaloacetate
Lactate dehydrogenase deficiency prevents the conversion of pyruvate to lactate
concept: Thiamine deficiency (wet beriberi) — pyruvate dehydrogenase block

stem: A 19-year-old woman has a photosensitive rash on sun-exposed skin, diarrhoea, and episodes of ataxia after emotional stress. Urine amino acid chromatography shows increased neutral amino acids, including tryptophan. Which deficiency explains the dermatitis?
opts: Niacin deficiency, because conversion of tryptophan to niacin is impaired
Tryptophan deficiency from low dietary intake of meat
Serotonin deficiency from impaired tryptophan hydroxylation
Pyridoxine deficiency from impaired kynureninase activity
concept: Hartnup disease — tryptophan to niacin synthesis

stem: A 34-year-old man starts standard four-drug anti-tuberculosis therapy. Three months later he develops burning pain, tingling, and numbness in both feet with reduced vibration sense. Which vitamin supplement most likely prevents this complication?
concept: Isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy — pyridoxine

stem: A 64-year-old man who lives alone and eats mainly bread, tea, and tinned food presents with bleeding gums, perifollicular haemorrhages on the legs, and poor wound healing. The coagulation screen is normal. Which biochemical step is impaired?
opts: Gamma-carboxylation of glutamic acid residues in clotting factors is blocked
Homocysteine remethylation by methionine synthase is defective
Fatty acid desaturation for membrane synthesis is reduced
Hydroxylation of proline in collagen requires ascorbate; without it, unstable triple helices form
concept: Scurvy — ascorbic acid and collagen hydroxylation

stem: A 58-year-old man with stage 5 chronic kidney disease has bone pain, serum calcium 2.0 mmol/L, and raised parathyroid hormone. Despite adequate 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels, his bone disease persists. Which deficiency best explains this?
opts: 25-hydroxyvitamin D, because of reduced cutaneous synthesis
Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), because renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity is lost
Calcitonin, from reduced parafollicular cell function
Vitamin A, because it antagonises parathyroid hormone action
concept: Chronic kidney disease — calcitriol synthesis (1-alpha-hydroxylase)

stem: Vitamin K acts as a coenzyme in the post-translational modification of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X. Which modification does it drive?
opts: Hydroxylation of proline residues, stabilising the collagen triple helix
N-glycosylation of asparagine residues in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi
Gamma-carboxylation of glutamic acid residues, enabling calcium-dependent membrane binding
Formation of disulfide bonds between cysteine residues
concept: Vitamin K — gamma-carboxylation (Gla residues)

stem: A 19-year-old man with lifelong steatorrhoea has progressive ataxia, loss of proprioception, and areflexia. The blood film shows acanthocytes; plasma cholesterol is low and triglycerides are undetectable. Which deficiency is most important to treat?
concept: Abetalipoproteinemia — vitamin E deficiency

stem: A 6-month-old infant has a protuberant abdomen and recurrent morning irritability that resolves with feeding. Fasting blood glucose is 1.9 mmol/L with lactate 6 mmol/L, uric acid 0.55 mmol/L, and raised triglycerides. Which enzyme is deficient?
concept: Von Gierke disease — glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency

stem: A 19-year-old man has painful muscle cramps and dark urine after sprinting. Ischaemic forearm exercise testing shows a flat rise in venous lactate. Fasting glucose and liver size are normal. Which management advice is most appropriate?
opts: Regular warm-up exercise plus glucose ingestion before exertion to exploit the 'second wind'
Total avoidance of all physical exertion to prevent rhabdomyolysis
A high-fat ketogenic diet with no carbohydrates
Daily oral creatine monohydrate alone, with no dietary change
concept: McArdle disease (myophosphorylase) — management

stem: A 2-day-old boy, previously well, becomes lethargic and vomiting within 24 hours of starting breastfeeds, with rapid breathing. Plasma ammonia is 420 µmol/L and the blood gas shows respiratory alkalosis; liver enzymes are normal. Which intervention has the highest priority?
opts: Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics and observation for 48 hours
Ammonia-scavenging drugs and arginine, stop protein feeds, and prepare for haemodialysis if ammonia does not fall
Intravenous glucose alone and reassessment in 12 hours
Liver biopsy to confirm the enzyme defect before any treatment
concept: Urea cycle defect — neonatal hyperammonaemia management

stem: A 10-day-old infant with jaundice, hepatomegaly, and poor weight gain develops Escherichia coli sepsis. Ophthalmoscopy shows bilateral cataracts. Which biochemical pathway explains the cataracts?
opts: Lactic acid accumulating in the lens from anaerobic glycolysis crystallises it
UDP-glucose epimerase deficiency depletes lenticular glycogen
Aldose reductase converts galactose to galactitol, which accumulates osmotically in the lens
Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the aqueous humour precipitates lens protein
concept: Galactosemia — galactitol and cataract mechanism

stem: A 9-month-old infant develops vomiting, pallor, sweating, and lethargy 30 minutes after his first weaning meals containing fruit and fruit juice. Blood glucose is 2.1 mmol/L and there is fructosuria. Which immediate management is correct?
opts: Continue fruit in small amounts to build tolerance
Give intravenous fructose 10% to correct the hypoglycaemia
Start a lactose-free formula and monitor
Stop fructose, sucrose, and sorbitol, and use glucose-based intravenous fluids
concept: Hereditary fructose intolerance — aldolase B; avoidance therapy

stem: A 6-day-old newborn develops poor feeding, lethargy, and a high-pitched cry. On day 7 he is opisthotonic and the cerumen smells of maple syrup. Sepsis screening is negative. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely?
concept: Maple syrup urine disease — branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency

stem: A 14-year-old boy, tall and thin with long fingers, has had two deep venous thromboses and a pulmonary embolism. Slit-lamp examination shows the lens dislocated downward and inward. Which diagnosis is most likely?
concept: Homocystinuria vs Marfan — direction of lens dislocation

stem: A 52-year-old man reports that his urine turns dark after standing for some hours and progressive low-back stiffness. Examination shows grey-blue pigmentation of the ear cartilage and sclera. Which enzyme is deficient?
concept: Alkaptonuria — homogentisate oxidase deficiency; ochronosis

stem: A 45-year-old woman with cirrhosis has serum sodium 130, chloride 102, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, and albumin 1.8 g/dL. The measured anion gap is 10. What is the most accurate interpretation?
opts: The gap is effectively elevated — correction for hypoalbuminaemia reveals a masked high-anion-gap acidosis
The gap is normal, so no acid-base disturbance exists
The gap is low, indicating a metabolic alkalosis
The gap cannot be interpreted without an arterial blood gas
concept: Anion gap correction for hypoalbuminaemia

stem: A 62-year-old man has an isolated serum alkaline phosphatase of 520 U/L (normal <120). Bilirubin, ALT, GGT, calcium, and phosphate are normal. Which investigation best localises the source of the ALP?
concept: Alkaline phosphatase isoenzymes — bone vs liver; role of GGT

stem: A 60-year-old man presents 90 minutes after the onset of crushing chest pain. The first high-sensitivity cardiac troponin is detectable but below the 99th percentile. Using a contemporary 0/1-hour algorithm, which is the next best step?
opts: Measure CK-MB now and again in 12 hours
Proceed directly to invasive coronary angiography
Repeat high-sensitivity troponin at 1 hour and apply the algorithm's delta (change) value
concept: High-sensitivity troponin — 0/1-hour algorithm

stem: A 32-year-old man has Achilles tendon xanthomas and a paternal uncle who died of myocardial infarction aged 38. Fasting lipids: LDL 6.1 mmol/L, HDL 0.8 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.2 mmol/L. Which mechanism best explains his lipid profile?
opts: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency impairing chylomicron clearance
Familial lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase deficiency with low HDL
Deficient LDL-receptor function reducing hepatic clearance of LDL
Hepatic VLDL overproduction driven by insulin resistance
concept: Familial hypercholesterolaemia — LDL receptor defect

stem: A 58-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has Hb 9.5 g/dL, MCV 78 fL, low serum iron, normal-low transferrin, and ferritin 320 µg/L. Which mediator best explains this pattern of iron studies?
opts: Hepcidin, which degrades ferroportin and traps iron inside macrophages
Erythropoietin deficiency reducing marrow demand for iron
Reduced transferrin synthesis from hepatic inflammation
Antibodies against intrinsic factor blocking ileal B12 absorption
concept: Anaemia of chronic disease — hepcidin-ferroportin axis

stem: A jaundiced patient has dark urine; the dipstick is strongly positive for bilirubin but urobilinogen is absent. Serum bilirubin is predominantly conjugated. Which statement about bilirubin chemistry best explains these findings?
opts: Unconjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and appears in urine whenever the serum level exceeds 2 mg/dL
Urobilinogen is absent because bilirubin is being rapidly conjugated in the liver
Bilirubinuria with absent urobilinogen is the hallmark of haemolytic jaundice
Only conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and filtered by the kidney; absent urobilinogen indicates obstructed biliary flow to the gut
concept: Bilirubin metabolism — conjugated vs unconjugated; urobilinogen cycle

stem: A 65-year-old man develops a prolonged episode of hypotension during coronary artery bypass surgery. A renal biopsy taken 24 hours later shows swollen, pale-staining tubular epithelial cells with intact nuclei and preserved brush borders. What is the most likely underlying mechanism of these cellular changes?
opts: ATP depletion causing failure of the Na+/K+ pump with influx of water
Irreversible membrane damage with loss of membrane integrity
Activation of the receptor-mediated apoptotic cascade
Lysosomal enzyme leakage from rupture of lysosomes
concept: Reversible cell injury — cloudy swelling from ATP depletion

stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic otitis media develops fever, headache, and a right-sided hemiparesis over 1 week. MRI shows a ring-enhancing mass in the left temporal lobe with central necrosis. At surgical drainage, thick pus is aspirated. What type of necrosis does the center of this lesion represent?
concept: Liquefactive necrosis — the abscess cavity

stem: A 30-year-old man presents with a 2-month history of evening fever, night sweats, and a painless left-sided neck swelling. Excision shows matted lymph nodes; on cut section, soft, yellowish-white material with a cheesy consistency oozes from the surface. What type of necrosis is most likely present?
concept: Caseous necrosis — gross morphology of tuberculous lymphadenitis

stem: A 42-year-old woman feels a painless lump in her right breast 3 weeks after a seat-belt injury in a road traffic accident. Mammography shows an ill-defined opacity; biopsy shows lipid-laden macrophages, hemosiderin-laden cells, and fibrous tissue with no atypical epithelial cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Traumatic fat necrosis of the breast — histologic features

stem: A 38-year-old man presents with fever, weight loss, testicular pain, and mononeuritis multiplex. Urinalysis shows hematuria and proteinuria. Renal biopsy shows a small artery whose wall is replaced by smudgy, bright pink, granular material with surrounding neutrophils. What is the most likely vascular change?
concept: Fibrinoid necrosis in systemic vasculitis (polyarteritis nodosa)

stem: A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes presents with a black, swollen, foul-smelling right foot with blistering and cellulitis spreading up to the ankle. The toes are necrotic and the line of demarcation is poorly defined. Which best explains why this is WET gangrene rather than dry gangrene?
opts: Pure arterial ischemia with no collateral circulation
Superadded bacterial infection causing liquefactive decomposition
Venous thrombosis alone without arterial occlusion
Neuropathic changes from diabetic peripheral neuropathy
concept: Wet vs dry gangrene — role of superadded infection

stem: A 24-year-old medical student develops malaise, anorexia, and jaundice. Liver biopsy shows scattered single hepatocytes that are shrunken and deeply eosinophilic, with pyknotic nuclei, and no surrounding inflammatory infiltrate. Which term best describes this hepatocyte change?
concept: Apoptosis — Councilman bodies in viral hepatitis

stem: A 60-year-old man with worsening heart failure develops a right-sided pleural effusion. Thoracentesis yields clear, straw-colored fluid: total protein 1.9 g/dL, LDH 80 U/L, specific gravity 1.009, and very few cells. What is the most likely mechanism of this fluid accumulation?
concept: Transudate vs exudate — mechanism of a transudative effusion

stem: A 12-year-old boy presents with a 2-week history of fever and a tender swelling in the left armpit. He has several healing scratches on his left forearm from a new kitten. Excision biopsy of the node shows granulomas with central stellate microabscesses. Which organism is the most likely cause?
concept: Cat-scratch disease — Bartonella henselae; stellate microabscesses in granulomas

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with 1 week of high fever and right upper quadrant pain. He had an episode of bloody diarrhea 2 months ago. Ultrasound shows a single large abscess in the right lobe of the liver. Aspiration yields thick, reddish-brown ('anchovy sauce') pus. What is the most appropriate initial management?
concept: Amebic liver abscess — medical treatment of choice

stem: A 55-year-old man on long-term oral prednisolone for rheumatoid arthritis undergoes an elective hernia repair. On day 10, the wound edges separate with no evidence of infection. Which phase of normal wound healing has been most directly impaired by his medication?
concept: Glucocorticoids impair wound healing — fibroplasia and collagen synthesis

stem: A 35-year-old man with severe acute pancreatitis develops progressive dyspnea over 48 hours. He is hypoxemic despite high-flow oxygen. Chest X-ray shows bilateral alveolar opacities, and echocardiography is normal. If lung histology were obtained, which finding would most likely be seen?
opts: Thickened alveolar walls with hyaline membranes
concept: ARDS — diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes

stem: A 55-year-old man is brought in 1 hour after vomiting a large amount of blood. He is anxious and pale, with cool extremities and a heart rate of 118/min. Blood pressure is 115/70 mmHg and urine output is low. What do these findings indicate?
concept: Shock stages — non-progressive (compensated) shock

stem: A 24-year-old man sustains a closed fracture of the femoral shaft in a motorcycle accident and undergoes intramedullary nailing. About 48 hours later he becomes acutely dyspneic and confused, and a petechial rash appears over his chest and axillae. Oxygen saturation is 84% on room air. What is the most likely mechanism?
opts: Massive pulmonary thromboembolism from a deep vein thrombosis
Air embolism through the intravenous line
concept: Fat embolism syndrome — post-fracture triad of hypoxia, petechiae, and confusion

stem: A 40-year-old man with a 15-year history of chronic osteomyelitis of the tibia develops proteinuria and pedal edema. Serum creatinine is 1.1 mg/dL. Renal biopsy shows amorphous eosinophilic material in the glomeruli that stains with Congo red and shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light. What is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the underlying cause?
opts: Serum protein electrophoresis and urine Bence-Jones protein
Abdominal fat pad biopsy with Congo red staining
concept: AA (secondary) amyloidosis — confirmatory tissue diagnosis

stem: A 30-year-old Rh(D)-negative woman, who already has one healthy child, delivers her second baby. Within 24 hours the newborn develops progressive jaundice, anemia, and hepatosplenomegaly. A direct Coombs test on the baby's red cells is positive. Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is responsible?
concept: Hemolytic disease of the newborn — Type II hypersensitivity

stem: A 62-year-old hypertensive man on hydralazine develops arthralgia, myalgia, and low-grade fever over 4 months. ANA is positive, but anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies are negative. Urinalysis is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Drug-induced lupus — anti-histone antibodies with renal sparing

stem: A 4-year-old boy has had recurrent pneumonia, suppurative lymphadenitis, and a liver abscess. Cultures grow catalase-positive organisms, including Staphylococcus aureus and Serratia marcescens. On the nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) test, the neutrophils fail to turn blue. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Chronic granulomatous disease — defective respiratory burst; NBT test

stem: A 3-year-old child with Down syndrome presents with pallor, bruising, and hepatosplenomegaly. Complete blood count shows thrombocytopenia and circulating blasts with cytoplasmic blebs. Which type of leukemia is characteristically associated with Down syndrome in early childhood?
concept: Down syndrome — increased risk of acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (GATA1)

stem: A 22-year-old man of Mediterranean origin has had, since childhood, recurrent self-limiting episodes of fever with severe abdominal pain and monoarthritis, each lasting 2–3 days. Examination between attacks is normal. His uncle has a similar history and developed proteinuria in his 40s. Which drug is most appropriate as long-term management?
concept: Familial Mediterranean fever — colchicine prophylaxis prevents attacks and amyloidosis

stem: A 12-year-old girl presents 3 weeks after a sore throat with fever, migratory polyarthritis, and a new systolic murmur. Excision biopsy of a subcutaneous nodule shows a central area of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by large cells with abundant basophilic cytoplasm and characteristic 'owl-eye' nuclei. Which diagnosis do these findings support?
concept: Rheumatic fever — Aschoff bodies and Anitschkow cells

stem: A 28-year-old woman with chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and a perianal fistula undergoes colonoscopy. It shows discontinuous ('skip') lesions with deep transverse ulcers and a cobblestone appearance, mainly in the terminal ileum. Biopsy shows transmural inflammation with non-caseating granulomas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Crohn's disease — transmural inflammation, granulomas, and skip lesions

stem: A 50-year-old man with a 20-year history of heavy alcohol use presents with anorexia and tender hepatomegaly. Liver biopsy shows hepatocyte ballooning, diffuse infiltration by neutrophils, and irregular eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions in hepatocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Alcoholic hepatitis — Mallory hyaline with a neutrophilic infiltrate

stem: Within minutes of a surgical incision, the injured area becomes red and swollen due to arteriolar dilation and increased permeability of venules. Which chemical mediator is primarily responsible for this IMMEDIATE vascular response?
concept: Chemical mediators of acute inflammation — histamine in the immediate phase

stem: An obese 60-year-old man is found to have type 2 diabetes mellitus. Which pancreatic islet change is most characteristic of long-standing type 2 diabetes on histology?
opts: Amyloid deposition in the islets (islet amyloid polypeptide)
Fat replacement of the entire pancreas
concept: Type 2 diabetes — islet amyloid (amylin/IAPP) deposition

stem: A 21-year-old man is brought to the emergency department unconscious after reportedly swallowing ‘a handful’ of tablets. He has pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 6/min, and the ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 148 ms. His friend confirms he takes a benzodiazepine for anxiety. Which statement is correct regarding management?
opts: Give flumazenil and naloxone together immediately
Give flumazenil only after naloxone fails to work
Give naloxone with supportive care and do NOT give flumazenil
Give flumazenil first to confirm the diagnosis before naloxone
concept: Mixed overdose — flumazenil contraindication (possible tricyclic co-ingestion)

stem: A 67-year-old woman on digoxin and furosemide for heart failure presents with nausea, anorexia, and yellow-green visual halos. She has had loose stools for 3 days after a course of antibiotics. The ECG shows sinus rhythm with characteristic ‘scooped’ ST segments. Which electrolyte abnormality most likely precipitated her toxicity?
concept: Digoxin toxicity — hypokalemia as the precipitating factor

stem: A 47-year-old man is brought in 2 hours after ingesting a large quantity of his wife’s amlodipine tablets. He is hypotensive (78/40 mmHg), bradycardic at 42/min, and confused. The ECG shows sinus bradycardia with a normal QRS duration. Which agent is the specific reversal therapy?
concept: Calcium channel blocker overdose — IV calcium as specific therapy

stem: A 63-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin 1 g twice daily presents with 4 days of vomiting, abdominal pain, and lethargy. He stopped eating and drinking 2 days ago. Creatinine is 3.9 mg/dL (baseline 1.0), arterial pH is 7.12, and serum lactate is 9 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Continue metformin and treat the vomiting with an antiemetic
Stop metformin, give IV fluids, and consider hemodialysis
Stop metformin and start an insulin sliding scale alone
Add IV sodium bicarbonate empirically and continue metformin
concept: Metformin-associated lactic acidosis in acute kidney injury

stem: A 52-year-old woman on lithium carbonate for bipolar disorder started naproxen for arthritis 10 days ago. She now has vomiting, a coarse tremor, ataxia, and slurred speech. Which of the following best explains her presentation and the appropriate next step?
opts: Lithium toxicity from NSAID-induced reduced renal clearance — stop lithium and give IV saline
Lithium toxicity from increased lithium absorption — stop lithium and add a thiazide
Naproxen allergy — give an antihistamine and continue lithium
Lithium therapeutic failure — increase the lithium dose
concept: Lithium toxicity — NSAID interaction and management

stem: A 75-year-old woman with osteoarthritis who takes aspirin regularly presents with fever, tinnitus, and deep, rapid breathing. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.48, PaCO2 22 mmHg, and bicarbonate 16 mEq/L; the salicylate level is 55 mg/dL. What is the most important next step in management?
opts: IV sodium bicarbonate with potassium supplementation
concept: Salicylate poisoning — mixed acid-base picture and urinary alkalinization

stem: A farm worker is being treated for organophosphate poisoning with atropine and supportive care. Regarding pralidoxime, which statement is correct?
opts: Pralidoxime reactivates acetylcholinesterase and works best when given within 24–48 hours of exposure, before enzyme ‘aging’
Pralidoxime must be given before atropine to be effective
Pralidoxime reverses muscarinic symptoms better than atropine
Pralidoxime is only useful for carbamate poisoning, not organophosphates
concept: Organophosphate poisoning — pralidoxime (oxime) mechanism and timing

stem: A 22-year-old man undergoing emergency surgery with sevoflurane and succinylcholine develops a rapid rise in temperature to 40.2°C, severe generalized muscle rigidity, and tachycardia. End-tidal CO2 rises markedly despite increased ventilation. Which single intervention is most important?
opts: Ice packs and cold IV fluids alone
concept: Malignant hyperthermia — dantrolene as the specific treatment

stem: A 29-year-old woman with depression is brought in 90 minutes after ingesting amitriptyline. She is confused and hypotensive, and the ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 150 ms. What is the most appropriate immediate therapy?
concept: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose — sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening

stem: A 34-year-old non-pregnant woman presents with dysuria, frequency, and urgency for 2 days. Urine dipstick is positive for nitrites and leukocytes. She has no fever, flank pain, or vomiting. Which antibiotic is the most appropriate first-line choice?
concept: Antibiotic stewardship — first-line drug for uncomplicated cystitis

stem: A 28-year-old woman at 30 weeks of gestation is found to have blood pressure 168/104 mmHg on two occasions. She is otherwise well with no proteinuria. Which antihypertensive is most appropriate, and which class must be avoided?
concept: Antihypertensive therapy in pregnancy — drug safety and teratogens

stem: A 68-year-old man with chronic kidney disease (eGFR 22 mL/min) requires analgesia for renal colic. Which opioid should be avoided because its metabolite accumulates and causes seizures?
concept: Opioid prescribing in renal failure — meperidine and normeperidine neurotoxicity

stem: A 58-year-old man with compensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A) from chronic hepatitis B requires regular analgesia for knee osteoarthritis. He has had a previous variceal bleed. Which analgesic regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Paracetamol at a reduced dose, avoiding NSAIDs
Ibuprofen as needed, avoiding paracetamol entirely
High-dose paracetamol together with an NSAID
concept: Analgesic choice in chronic liver disease

stem: A 61-year-old man with COPD on sustained-release theophylline develops acute bronchitis and is prescribed ciprofloxacin. Three days later he has nausea, palpitations, and a generalized seizure. Which mechanism best explains what happened?
opts: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP450, raising theophylline levels into the toxic range
Ciprofloxacin induces theophylline metabolism, causing a withdrawal effect
Theophylline inhibits ciprofloxacin elimination, causing fluoroquinolone toxicity
An allergic cross-reaction between the two drugs
concept: Drug interaction — fluoroquinolone inhibition of theophylline metabolism (CYP1A2)

stem: A 54-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis on pyridostigmine is admitted with urosepsis and started on IV gentamicin. Twelve hours later she develops marked generalized weakness, ptosis, and shallow breathing. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Give an IV neostigmine bolus only
concept: Aminoglycosides — neuromuscular blockade worsening myasthenia gravis

stem: A 64-year-old man on amiodarone for 14 months for atrial fibrillation presents with a progressive dry cough and exertional dyspnea. He is afebrile. Chest X-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates and oxygen saturation is 91%. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate action?
opts: Amiodarone pulmonary toxicity — stop the drug and arrange further evaluation
Heart failure — increase the diuretic dose
concept: Amiodarone adverse effects — pulmonary toxicity

stem: A 33-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia, stable on clozapine for 6 months, presents with sudden high-grade fever and a severe sore throat. His white cell count is 1,800/mm³ with neutrophils 300/mm³. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Stop clozapine immediately, monitor the FBC, and institute infection precautions
Continue clozapine and treat the sore throat with antibiotics
Reduce the clozapine dose by half and review
Add a second antipsychotic to cover the clozapine gap
concept: Clozapine — agranulocytosis and mandatory monitoring

stem: A 59-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on weekly methotrexate 15 mg is prescribed trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection. Ten days later she presents with mouth ulcers, fever, and pallor. Blood counts show pancytopenia. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Stop both drugs and give leucovorin (folinic acid) rescue
Stop both drugs and give folic acid
Continue both drugs and add growth factors only
concept: Methotrexate toxicity — additive antifolate effect and leucovorin rescue

stem: A 24-year-old woman develops neck twisting, eye rolling, and tongue protrusion 6 hours after receiving intravenous metoclopramide for vomiting. Which drug is the most appropriate treatment?
concept: Metoclopramide — acute dystonia and anticholinergic treatment

stem: A 71-year-old man on warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve presents with an acute severe headache and new left-sided weakness. CT shows an intracranial hemorrhage and the INR is 4.8. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: IV vitamin K plus 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC)
IV vitamin K alone and repeat the INR in 6 hours
Fresh frozen plasma alone, without vitamin K
concept: Warfarin-associated intracranial hemorrhage — urgent reversal

stem: A 45-year-old man with gout presents 4 hours after ingesting a large quantity of colchicine tablets in a suicide attempt. He has already had several episodes of vomiting and diarrhea. Which statement about his prognosis and management is most accurate?
opts: The early GI phase can look reassuring, but a delayed multi-organ failure phase may follow — supportive care and close monitoring are needed
His vomiting and diarrhea indicate the drug has been eliminated — he can be discharged
Colchicine toxicity is self-limiting and requires no specific monitoring
Naloxone is the specific antidote for colchicine
concept: Colchicine toxicity — biphasic course and management

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents 22 hours after a paracetamol overdose with right upper quadrant pain and vomiting. Investigations show ALT 4,800 U/L, INR 2.4, and a paracetamol level of 40 µg/mL. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: IV N-acetylcysteine now and assessment for liver transplantation criteria
Reassure her — the 8-hour NAC window has passed
concept: Paracetamol overdose — late N-acetylcysteine and hepatotoxicity assessment

stem: A 30-year-old man on isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for pulmonary tuberculosis develops burning pain and tingling in both feet after 3 months of treatment. Which supplement prevents and treats this complication?
concept: Isoniazid — peripheral neuropathy and pyridoxine (B6) prophylaxis

stem: A 38-year-old woman remains apneic and unresponsive 40 minutes after a single dose of succinylcholine given for rapid-sequence induction. Peripheral nerve stimulation shows no twitch; temperature, oxygen saturation, capnography, and hemodynamics are all normal. Her brother had a similar episode after surgery. Which investigation confirms the diagnosis?
opts: Plasma cholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase) assay with dibucaine number
concept: Suxamethonium — prolonged apnea from atypical plasma cholinesterase

stem: A 3-day-old neonate with suspected sepsis is treated with chloramphenicol. On day 4 he develops vomiting, poor feeding, abdominal distension, gray discoloration of the skin, and hypothermia. What is the most likely explanation?
opts: Gray baby syndrome — immature hepatic glucuronidation causes chloramphenicol accumulation
Worsening neonatal sepsis — escalate the antibiotics
Hypoglycemia from poor feeding — give IV dextrose
concept: Chloramphenicol — gray baby syndrome in neonates

stem: A 19-year-old non-obese woman with a strong family history of diabetes (autosomal dominant) presents with mild hyperglycaemia. She is not ketosis-prone and her C-peptide is normal. Which feature best fits maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY)?
opts: Young onset, lean, autosomal dominant inheritance, often sulfonylurea-responsive
concept: MODY — young, lean, AD inheritance, sulfonylurea-responsive

stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman undergoes a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks. Her results are: fasting 95 mg/dL, 1-hour 175 mg/dL, 2-hour 150 mg/dL. What is the diagnosis and management implication?
opts: Gestational diabetes (OGTT thresholds met) — diet then insulin if needed
concept: Gestational diabetes — OGTT thresholds (fasting ≥92, 1h ≥180, 2h ≥153)

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with apparently new type 2 diabetes and seems to require insulin within 1 year despite initial oral therapy. He is not obese. Glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies are positive. What does this indicate?
concept: LADA — adult T2 phenotype but autoimmune (GAD+), progresses to insulin

stem: A 50-year-old man with 12 years of type 2 diabetes has visual blurring and floaters. Fundoscopy shows neovascularisation of the disc and vitreous haemorrhage. What is the most urgent intervention?
concept: Diabetic retinopathy — proliferative stage: neovascularisation → panretinal laser

stem: A 60-year-old diabetic has numbness, tingling, and loss of vibration and ankle reflexes in a stocking-glove distribution, with preserved strength. What is the most likely neuropathy?
concept: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy — symmetric stocking sensory loss, reduced reflexes

stem: A 55-year-old diabetic develops sudden severe unilateral periorbital pain with ptosis, a dilated non-reactive pupil, and an inability to move the eye upward or inward. Which feature points to a diabetic mononeuritis rather than a posterior communicating artery aneurysm?
opts: The pupil is always dilated and fixed in diabetic palsy
Pupil-sparing is typical of diabetic CN III palsy (sparse parasympathetic fibres spared)
concept: Diabetic CN III palsy — pupil-sparing, painful, ischemic (vs aneurysm which fixes pupil)

stem: A 40-year-old diabetic woman has recurrent early satiety, nausea, vomiting of undigested food, and bloating, with glycaemic instability. Gastroscopy is normal. What is the most likely mechanism?
concept: Diabetic gastroparesis — autonomic neuropathy, delayed gastric emptying

stem: A 55-year-old diabetic with peripheral neuropathy presents with a warm, red, swollen midfoot and a 'rocker-bottom' deformity. X-ray shows fractures and joint dislocation. There is no history of major trauma. What is the diagnosis?
concept: Charcot neuroarthropathy — painless red swollen foot, rocker-bottom, offloading

stem: A diabetic man has a painless plantar ulcer with a warm foot and easily palpable pedal pulses. A second patient has a painful, cool foot with absent pulses and rest pain. How do these ulcers differ?
opts: First is arterial, second is neuropathic
First is neuropathic (sensory loss, good perfusion); second is ischaemic (poor perfusion)
concept: Diabetic foot ulcer — neuropathic (warm, pulses) vs ischaemic (cool, absent pulses)

stem: A 50-year-old man with chronic pancreatitis has steatorrhoea, weight loss, and new-onset diabetes requiring insulin. C-peptide is low and faecal elastase is reduced. What is the diabetes type?
concept: Type 3c diabetes — pancreatic disease (chronic pancreatitis/CF) + exocrine insufficiency

stem: A 60-year-old woman started on high-dose oral prednisolone for polymyalgia rheumatica develops fasting hyperglycaemia and glucosuria after 2 weeks. She has no prior diabetes. What is the most likely cause?
concept: Steroid-induced diabetes — glucocorticoids raise glucose (hepatic output, insulin resistance)

stem: A diabetic man on metformin and a sulfonylurea is scheduled for elective abdominal surgery. What is the most appropriate perioperative glycaemic management?
opts: Hold metformin (lactic acidosis risk with fasting/contrast) and use a variable IV insulin infusion
Continue all oral agents including metformin throughout
Stop insulin if already on it
Give double the sulfonylurea dose pre-op
concept: Perioperative diabetes — hold metformin, use IV insulin sliding scale

stem: A 48-year-old overweight man has a fasting glucose of 110 mg/dL and a 2-hour post-glucose value of 150 mg/dL on OGTT. HbA1c is 5.9%. What is the correct classification and first step?
opts: Prediabetes (impaired fasting glucose / impaired glucose tolerance) — lifestyle modification
concept: Prediabetes — IFG (fasting 100-125) / IGT (2h 140-199); lifestyle first

stem: A 30-year-old type 1 diabetic has frequent asymptomatic nocturnal hypoglycaemic episodes and drives for a living. Which technology most improves her safety?
concept: Diabetes technology — CGM for hypoglycaemia unawareness / nocturnal hypo

stem: A 52-year-old obese man with type 2 diabetes and BMI 34 is started on a GLP-1 receptor agonist. Which effect is expected and requires counselling?
opts: Weight loss with nausea/vomiting; benefits obesity and CV risk
Weight gain and hypoglycaemia as the main effects
concept: GLP-1 receptor agonists — weight loss, GI side effects, CV benefit

stem: A 64-year-old man on long-term metformin for type 2 diabetes develops numbness and a macrocytic anaemia with low-normal B12. Which association is correct?
opts: Metformin long-term use can cause B12 deficiency
B12 deficiency here is unrelated to metformin
The anaemia is iron-deficiency from metformin
concept: Metformin adverse effect — long-term B12 malabsorption/deficiency

stem: A 50-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and no history of cardiovascular disease has an LDL of 110 mg/dL. According to current guidance, what is indicated?
opts: No statin — only treat if LDL >190
Statin therapy for primary CVD prevention (all diabetics ≥40 typically benefit)
Nothing until he has a heart attack
concept: Diabetes + CVD risk — statin for primary prevention in most T2DM

stem: A 40-year-old type 1 diabetic asks how often her urine should be screened for early kidney disease. She has normal creatinine and no proteinuria on dipstick. What is recommended?
opts: Annual urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (screen for microalbuminuria)
concept: Diabetic nephropathy — annual albuminuria screening (ACR) for early detection

stem: An 82-year-old frail woman with type 2 diabetes on a sulfonylurea has had two falls and a hypoglycaemic episode. What is the most appropriate adjustment?
opts: Intensify with insulin to tighten control
De-intensify therapy (stop sulfonylurea, relax targets) to avoid hypoglycaemia
concept: Diabetes in the elderly — de-intensify to avoid hypoglycaemia/falls

stem: A 60-year-old diabetic man develops painful, asymmetric weakness and wasting of the thigh muscles over weeks, with weight loss but preserved sensation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Diabetic amyotrophy — painful asymmetric proximal thigh weakness/wasting

stem: A 65-year-old diabetic woman with poor glycaemic control has fever, flank pain, and gas visible within the renal parenchyma on CT. Urine grows E. coli. What is the diagnosis and concern?
opts: Emphysematous pyelonephritis — gas-forming infection, urological emergency
concept: Emphysematous pyelonephritis — gas-forming infection in diabetic kidney

stem: A 58-year-old type 2 diabetic has persistent fasting hyperglycaemia on maximal oral therapy. Which insulin regimen is most appropriate to start?
opts: Stop all oral agents and start biphasic twice daily immediately
Once-daily basal (long-acting, e.g. glargine) to target fasting glucose
concept: Insulin initiation — start basal (long-acting) for fasting hyperglycaemia

stem: A diabetic on basal insulin has consistently elevated morning glucose but normal glucose at 3 a.m. (no nocturnal hypoglycaemia). What does this represent?
opts: Dawn phenomenon (early-morning hormonal surge), not Somogyi
concept: Dawn phenomenon — morning hyperglycemia WITHOUT nocturnal hypoglycemia

stem: A 55-year-old diabetic has several round, atrophic, hyperpigmented plaques on the shins. They are asymptomatic. Which skin manifestation is this?
concept: Diabetic dermopathy — asymptomatic atrophic pigmented shin plaques

stem: A 30-year-old woman with pre-existing type 1 diabetes plans pregnancy. What is the most important pre-conceptional intervention to reduce congenital malformation risk?
opts: Achieve tight glycaemic control (HbA1c near normal) before conception
concept: Pre-existing diabetes in pregnancy — tighten glycemia pre-conception to cut malformations

stem: A 70-year-old woman on a thiazide diuretic for hypertension presents with confusion. Serum sodium is 122 mmol/L. She is clinically volume-depleted. Which mechanism best explains the hyponatremia?
opts: Thiazide-induced volume depletion with impaired free-water excretion
concept: Hypovolemic hyponatremia — thiazide causes Na loss and volume depletion

stem: A 55-year-old man develops hyponatremia 4 days after a subarachnoid haemorrhage. He is clinically volume-depleted with low urine sodium. Which diagnosis is most likely?
concept: Cerebral salt wasting — SAH + hyponatremia + volume depletion

stem: A patient's serum sodium measured by flame photometry is 118 mmol/L, but direct ion-selective electrode (after ultracentrifugation) is normal. The patient has severe hypertriglyceridaemia. What explains this?
concept: Pseudohyponatremia — lab artifact in hyperlipidemia/hyperproteinemia

stem: A 30-year-old man has polyuria and thirst with hypernatremia and dilute urine. After water deprivation, desmopressin is given and urine osmolality rises markedly. What does this indicate?
concept: Central vs nephrogenic DI — desmopressin causes concentration in central DI

stem: A 48-year-old woman with chronic hyponatremia (Na 112 mmol/L) is corrected too rapidly to 132 mmol/L within 12 hours. Two days later she develops dysarthria, dysphagia, and a locked-in-like state. What is the cause?
concept: Osmotic demyelination syndrome — over-rapid Na correction

stem: A 2-month-old infant exclusively on formula with inadequate water intake presents with lethargy and a serum sodium of 160 mmol/L. Urine osmolality is low. What is the most likely mechanism?
concept: Hypernatremia — free-water deficit from inadequate intake / insensible loss

stem: A patient on furosemide with vomiting and metabolic alkalosis has serum potassium of 2.8 mmol/L. Which combination of mechanisms explains the hypokalemia?
opts: Renal K loss (diuretic) + GI loss (vomiting) + shift into cells (alkalosis)
concept: Hypokalemia — multifactorial (renal + GI loss + alkalosis shift)

stem: A 22-year-old man of Asian descent has recurrent episodes of proximal muscle weakness after heavy carbohydrate meals. Between episodes he is well with normal exam. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Hypokalemic periodic paralysis — episodic weakness after carbs/exercise

stem: A patient with CKD has a potassium of 7.0 mmol/L. The ECG shows peaked T waves and a prolonged PR interval. Which progression indicates impending catastrophe?
opts: Widening of the QRS complex toward a sine wave
concept: Hyperkalemia ECG progression — peaked T → widened QRS → sine wave

stem: A 68-year-old man with no renal disease has a reported potassium of 6.9 mmol/L, but he is asymptomatic with a normal ECG. Repeat testing after a drawing technique change shows 4.4 mmol/L. What happened?
concept: Pseudohyperkalemia — artifact from hemolysis or prolonged tourniquet/fist clenching

stem: A 60-year-old man with CKD and a potassium of 6.6 mmol/L has peaked T waves but no QRS widening. Which is the MOST appropriate immediate step?
opts: IV calcium gluconate to stabilise the myocardium
concept: Hyperkalemia — calcium first for cardiac membrane stabilisation when ECG changes present

stem: A 64-year-old man with weight loss and bone pain has calcium 12.8 mg/dL, phosphate low, and PTH suppressed (<10 pg/mL). What is the most likely mechanism?
concept: Hypercalcemia of malignancy — suppressed PTH (PTHrP), vs primary HPT (high PTH)

stem: A 50-year-old alcoholic man has tetany and a corrected calcium of 6.8 mg/dL. Despite IV calcium, the calcium remains low. Magnesium is 1.0 mg/dL. Why is calcium replacement failing?
opts: Hypomagnesemia prevents PTH secretion and action
concept: Hypocalcemia — hypomagnesemia causes refractory hypocalcemia

stem: Which of the following is a recognised cause of hypomagnesemia?
opts: Chronic alcohol use with poor intake
concept: Hypomagnesemia — causes (alcohol, diuretics, diarrhoea, TPN, aminoglycosides)

stem: A 40-year-old woman in the third trimester develops seizures. Her blood pressure is 160/100 and she has proteinuria. Which magnesium preparation is the treatment of choice for seizure prophylaxis?
concept: Magnesium sulfate — eclampsia / pre-eclampsia seizure prophylaxis

stem: A patient with CKD stage 4 has an elevated phosphate and low calcitriol. Which complication results from this derangement?
opts: Adynamic bone disease from high calcium
concept: CKD-MBD — hyperphosphatemia + low calcitriol → secondary hyperparathyroidism

stem: A 25-year-old woman has recurrent renal stones, hypokalemia, and a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis despite a normal GFR. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Type 1 distal RTA — normal AG acidosis + hypokalemia + stones/nephrocalcinosis

stem: A child has proximal muscle weakness, rickets, and glucosuria with a normal plasma glucose. Urine shows phosphaturia, aminoaciduria, and bicarbonate wasting. What syndrome does this represent?
concept: Fanconi syndrome — proximal tubular dysfunction (type 2 RTA + glycosuria/phosphaturia/aminoaciduria)

stem: A 60-year-old man with long-standing diabetes has a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis and a potassium of 5.8 mmol/L. Which mechanism is most likely?
opts: Hypoaldosteronism / distal H+ and K+ secretion defect (type 4 RTA)
concept: Type 4 RTA — hyperkalemic distal RTA from hypoaldosteronism

stem: A 70-year-old man with septic shock has a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, elevated lactate (8 mmol/L), and low bicarbonate. Which is the primary mechanism?
opts: Type B lactic acidosis from metformin
Type A lactic acidosis from tissue hypoperfusion
concept: Lactic acidosis — type A from hypoperfusion/shock (MUDPILES 'L')

stem: A 19-year-old with poorly controlled diabetes vomits repetitively and is found with pH 7.30, HCO3 18, and an elevated anion gap. What best describes the acid-base state?
opts: High anion-gap metabolic acidosis (DKA) with concurrent metabolic alkalosis (vomiting)
concept: Mixed acid-base disorder — DKA (high AG acidosis) + vomiting (metabolic alkalosis)

stem: A patient has a normal anion-gap metabolic acidosis. The urine anion gap is positive (urine Na+K − Cl is positive), indicating low urinary ammonium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Normal AG acidosis — positive urine anion gap = RTA (low NH4 excretion); negative = diarrhea

stem: A malnourished chronic alcoholic presents after a binge with abdominal pain, a high anion-gap metabolic acidosis, elevated lactate, and ketonuria, but a normal blood glucose. Which diagnosis fits best?
concept: Alcoholic ketoacidosis — high AG acidosis, ketones + lactate, euglycemic

stem: A 17-year-old with normal kidney function receives a rapid intravenous infusion of isotonic normal saline. After osmotic equilibrium, which best describes the distribution?
opts: Increased ECF and ICF, decreased sodium
Increased ECF volume, unchanged ICF volume, unchanged plasma sodium
Increased ECF, increased ICF, unchanged sodium
Unchanged ECF, increased ICF, increased sodium
concept: Isotonic saline distribution — stays in ECF, no ICF shift, sodium concentration unchanged

stem: A 78-year-old woman on digoxin presents with nausea, bradycardia, and a potassium of 6.4 mmol/L. Which is the most appropriate acute management?
opts: Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Fab); avoid giving calcium
concept: Digoxin toxicity — hyperkalemia is a marker; treat with Digoxin-Fab, avoid calcium

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with a 1-week history of severe anterior neck pain radiating to the ear, fever, and transient palpitations. The thyroid is tender and firm. She recently had a viral upper respiratory infection. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Subacute thyroiditis — painful thyroid after viral illness, transient thyrotoxicosis

stem: A 60-year-old man on amiodarone for atrial fibrillation develops thyrotoxicosis with a low uptake on radioactive iodine scan. What is the most likely mechanism?
concept: Amiodarone thyroid — type 2 = destructive thyroiditis (low uptake), steroids

stem: A 35-year-old woman with Graves disease and proptosis develops worsening eye pain, periorbital oedema, and diplopia. She is a smoker. Which factor worsens her orbital disease and what is the mainstay of urgent treatment for severe disease?
opts: Smoking worsens it; high-dose steroids / orbital decompression for severe disease
concept: Thyroid eye disease — smoking worsens; steroids/decompression for severe

stem: A 50-year-old woman has an elevated TSH (8.5 mIU/L) with a normal free T4 on routine screening. She is asymptomatic. Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Observe and repeat; treat if TSH >10 or symptoms/TPO antibodies develop
concept: Subclinical hypothyroidism — observe unless TSH>10 or symptoms/antibodies

stem: A 70-year-old woman with a long-standing multinodular goitre develops palpitations, weight loss, and atrial fibrillation. There is no exophthalmos. What distinguishes this from Graves disease and guides therapy?
opts: Toxic multinodular goitre — nodular goitre, no exophthalmos; treat with radioiodine
concept: Toxic multinodular goitre — elderly, nodular goitre, no exophthalmos; radioiodine

stem: A 45-year-old woman had a total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid carcinoma and is on thyroxine. Three months later, while on thyroxine, her thyroglobulin is undetectable but anti-thyroglobulin antibodies are negative. What does this indicate?
concept: Differentiated thyroid Ca — thyroglobulin as tumour marker (undetectable = no disease)

stem: A newborn girl is noted to have ambiguous genitalia and, at 2 weeks, develops vomiting, dehydration, and hypotension. Serum electrolytes show hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: 21-hydroxylase deficiency CAH — salt-wasting + virilization + hypoNa/hyperK

stem: A 50-year-old man with fatigue and hypotension has hyponatraemia but a normal potassium. He has pale skin with no pigmentation. Which statement is correct?
opts: Findings suggest SECONDARY adrenal insufficiency (no hyperkalaemia/pigmentation)
concept: Primary vs secondary adrenal insufficiency — hyperkalaemia + pigmentation only in PRIMARY

stem: A woman who had bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing disease 5 years ago now presents with progressive visual field loss and a rapidly enlarging pituitary mass. What is the diagnosis?
concept: Nelson syndrome — pituitary tumour enlargement after bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing

stem: A 55-year-old man has an adrenal mass (3 cm) found incidentally on CT for renal colic. He is hypertensive with hypokalaemia. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Endocrine workup (exclude Cushing, pheochromocytoma, Conn) before any surgery
concept: Adrenal incidentaloma — exclude hormonal hyperfunction before considering surgery

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with coarse facial features, enlarged hands and feet, and worsening glucose intolerance. Which screening test is most appropriate first?
concept: Acromegaly — IGF-1 screening; GH excess from pituitary adenoma

stem: A 60-year-old man with a known pituitary macroadenoma suddenly develops a severe headache, bilateral visual loss, and hypotension with hypoglycaemia. What is the urgent diagnosis and action?
opts: Pituitary apoplexy — give glucocorticoids and arrange urgent surgery
concept: Pituitary apoplexy — acute haemorrhage/infarction; steroids + urgent decompression

stem: A 9-year-old boy has slowed growth, bitemporal hemianopia, and a calcified suprasellar mass on CT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Craniopharyngioma — child, calcified suprasellar mass, bitemporal hemianopia

stem: A 30-year-old woman on an antipsychotic for schizophrenia develops galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea. Prolactin is markedly elevated. What should be considered before assuming a prolactinoma?
opts: Prolactinoma confirmed — refer for transsphenoidal surgery
concept: Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia — antipsychotics/D2 blockers before prolactinoma

stem: A 28-year-old woman in the postpartum period presents with headache, bitemporal hemianopia, and mild diabetes insipidus. MRI shows a homogenously enhancing pituitary mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Lymphocytic hypophysitis — postpartum pituitary mass with DI

stem: A 7-year-old boy is below the 3rd centile for height with a height velocity below the 25th centile, but normal body proportions. Bone age is delayed. What is the most likely underlying issue if GH deficiency is confirmed?
opts: Growth hormone deficiency causing proportionate short stature with delayed bone age
concept: Growth hormone deficiency — proportionate short stature + reduced growth velocity + delayed bone age

stem: A 40-year-old woman has galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea. MRI shows an empty sella with a thin pituitary stalk displaced, but no discrete adenoma. Prolactin is mildly elevated. What explains the hyperprolactinemia?
opts: Stalk effect — interrupted dopamine inhibition from stalk compression
concept: Stalk effect — hyperprolactinemia from interrupted dopamine (stalk compression)

stem: A 55-year-old man has recurrent episodes of confusion and diaphoresis relieved by eating, occurring fasting or post-exercise. A 72-hour fast reproduces symptoms with a low glucose, elevated insulin, and detectable C-peptide. What is the diagnosis?
concept: Insulinoma — endogenous hyperinsulinaemic fasting hypoglycaemia (Whipple triad)

stem: A 65-year-old man has bone pain and an elevated alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium and phosphate. X-ray of the pelvis shows cortical thickening and a 'cotton-wool' appearance. What is the diagnosis?
concept: Paget disease — elevated ALP, normal Ca/PO4, 'cotton-wool' bone on X-ray

stem: A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman has a DEXA T-score of -3.0 at the lumbar spine after a low-trauma wrist fracture. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment to reduce fracture risk?
concept: Postmenopausal osteoporosis — bisphosphonate first-line for fracture prevention

stem: A 40-year-old man is found to have asymptomatic hypercalcaemia with a normal PTH and a low urine calcium/creatinine ratio. He has a family history of 'high calcium' with no stones or fractures. What is the likely diagnosis?
concept: FHH — benign familial hypercalcemia with LOW urine calcium (not primary HPT)

stem: A 45-year-old man has recurrent renal stones and is found to have primary hyperparathyroidism, a pituitary macroadenoma, and multiple gastric ulcerations. Which syndrome does this represent?
concept: MEN1 — parathyroid + pituitary + pancreatic (3 Ps)

stem: A 50-year-old woman has a 1.5 cm thyroid nodule. Ultrasound shows microcalcifications, irregular margins, marked hypoechoic echotexture, and a taller-than-wide shape. What is the most appropriate next step?
concept: Thyroid nodule — suspicious sonographic features warrant FNA

stem: A 70-year-old man in the ICU with severe sepsis has a low free T3, a normal TSH, and a normal free T4. He is clinically euthyroid. What explains these thyroid tests?
concept: Non-thyroidal illness — low T3, normal TSH/fT4 in acute illness; do not treat

stem: A 25-year-old East Asian man with untreated hyperthyroidism presents with acute symmetric proximal muscle weakness and a potassium of 2.6 mmol/L during an attack. What is the mechanism and association?
opts: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis — hyperthyroidism triggers hypokalaemic paralysis
Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis without thyroid disease
concept: Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis — hyperthyroidism → hypokalaemic paralysis (Asian males)

stem: A 45-year-old with fatigue and jaundice has laboratory evidence of haemolysis and a positive direct Coombs (antiglobulin) test. This immune haemolytic anaemia is best classified under which type of hypersensitivity reaction?
concept: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia - Type II hypersensitivity (Coombs positive)

stem: Which of the following findings indicates that haemolysis is the cause of a neonate's hyperbilirubinaemia?
concept: Neonatal hyperbilirubinaemia - haemolysis gives unconjugated (indirect) rise

stem: A patient with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) has microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and neurological features. What is the most common cause of death in TTP?
concept: TTP - most common cause of death is intracranial haemorrhage

stem: A 26-year-old with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia major develops leg oedema and exertional dyspnoea despite regular transfusions. Which is the most likely culpable process?
opts: Dilated cardiomyopathy from transfusional iron overload
concept: Thalassaemia major - iron overload cardiomyopathy from repeated transfusions

stem: A 60-year-old with a urinary tract infection develops fever (40 C), cold peripheries, tachycardia and confusion. WBC is 2100/mm3 and PT/INR is prolonged. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Septic shock with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
concept: Septic shock + DIC - fever, leucopenia, coagulopathy

stem: A 9-month-old breastfed-and-goat's-milk-fed infant has progressive pallor. Hb 6 g/dL, MCV 106 fL, MCHC 39. Which dietary deficiency is most likely?
concept: Folate deficiency - goat's milk (low folate) causes macrocytic anaemia in infants

stem: A 14-year-old girl has Hb 9 g/dL, MCV 70 fL, serum ferritin 8 ng/mL and TIBC 450 ug/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Iron deficiency anaemia - microcytic, low ferritin, high TIBC

stem: A 61-year-old woman has low-grade fever, anaemia, abdominal pain, gum hyperplasia, and circulating blasts with Auer rods; myeloperoxidase (MPO) is positive and WBC is 42,000. Most probable diagnosis?
concept: Acute myeloid leukaemia - Auer rods + MPO positive + gum infiltration

stem: A 45-year-old woman receiving chemo-radiotherapy for breast cancer presents with fatigue. FBC shows Hb 10 g/dL with low serum iron but normal/high ferritin. Which is the most likely cause of her anaemia?
concept: Anaemia of chronic disease - low iron but normal/high ferritin (functional block)

stem: A patient on warfarin (INR 9) presents with a nosebleed. In addition to withholding the warfarin, which is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
concept: Warfarin overdose - vitamin K antidote

stem: A 60-year-old vegetarian has progressive fatigue, glossitis and peripheral paraesthesia with an unsteady gait. FBC shows macrocytosis (MCV 115 fL) and hypersegmented neutrophils. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: B12 deficiency - macrocytic + glossitis + neuropathy (subacute combined degeneration)

stem: A 55-year-old has fatigue, weight loss, massive splenomegaly and a very high WBC with a left shift, basophilia and thrombocytosis. Peripheral blood cytogenetics show the Philadelphia chromosome. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Chronic myeloid leukaemia - Philadelphia chromosome (t9;22 BCR-ABL), massive splenomegaly

stem: A 20-year-old has lifelong mild jaundice, gallstones, splenomegaly and a spherocytosis on the blood film with raised MCHC. Which is the most likely diagnosis and definitive management?
concept: Hereditary spherocytosis - spherocytes, splenomegaly, gallstones; splenectomy if severe

stem: A 12-year-old with sickle cell disease has severe pain in the hands and back, fever 38 C and no localizing chest/abdominal signs. What is the most appropriate initial management of a vaso-occlusive crisis?
opts: Analgesia (paracetamol/NSAIDs/opioids), hydration, oxygen if hypoxic, and detect/prevent complications
concept: Sickle cell vaso-occlusive crisis - analgesia, hydration, oxygen

stem: A young adult has pancytopenia (anaemia, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia) with a hypocellular bone marrow on trephine biopsy and no evidence of infiltration or fibrosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Aplastic anaemia - pancytopenia + hypocellular marrow

stem: A boy develops acute jaundice and dark urine a day after taking an antimalarial and eating fava beans, with a normal blood film except for bite cells and Heinz bodies. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: G6PD deficiency - X-linked, oxidative haemolysis after fava/primaquine, Heinz bodies

stem: A boy has recurrent bleeding into his knees/elbows and easy bruising since early childhood, and his maternal uncle has a similar bleeding disorder. Which factor deficiency is most likely and how is it inherited?
opts: von Willebrand factor deficiency; autosomal recessive
concept: Haemophilia A - factor VIII deficiency, X-linked recessive, joint bleeds

stem: A 30-year-old previously well person develops petechiae and bruising and has an isolated severe thrombocytopenia (platelets 15,000) with an otherwise normal FBC and blood film. No lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis and first-line treatment?
opts: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP); corticosteroids are first line
concept: Immune thrombocytopenia - isolated thrombocytopenia; first-line steroids

stem: A 60-year-old has headache, pruritus after a hot shower, ruddy complexion and an elevated haemoglobin (Hct 60%) with normal oxygen saturation. Which is the most likely diagnosis and genetic marker?
opts: Chronic hypoxia; high EPO with lung disease
concept: Polycythaemia vera - JAK2V617F, aquagenic pruritus, high Hct with normal SpO2

stem: A 70-year-old incidentally has a markedly raised lymphocyte count (WBC 95,000) with a mature lymphocytosis and smudge cells on the film, mild lymphadenopathy, and no anaemia or thrombocytopenia. Most likely diagnosis?
concept: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia - mature lymphocytosis + smudge cells in elderly

stem: A woman with placental abruption develops generalized oozing from venepuncture sites. Laboratories show prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen, thrombocytopenia and a markedly raised D-dimer. Which is the most appropriate description and treatment?
opts: Disseminated intravascular coagulation; treat the underlying cause and support with blood products
concept: DIC - consumption coagulopathy; treat the cause + supportive products

stem: A 65-year-old has bone pain, pathological vertebral fractures, anaemia and renal impairment. Serum shows a monoclonal paraprotein with rouleaux on the film and elevated serum calcium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Multiple myeloma - CRAB (hypercalcaemia, renal, anaemia, bone) + monoclonal paraprotein + rouleaux

stem: A patient with malabsorption and prolonged antibiotic use develops a bleeding tendency. Coagulation tests show a prolonged prothrombin time (PT) with a normal platelet count and aPTT is only mildly prolonged. Which deficiency is most likely?
opts: Vitamin K (affecting factors II, VII, IX, X)
concept: Vitamin K deficiency - prolonged PT (factor VII first) in malabsorption

stem: On a peripheral blood film, which single finding best supports a megaloblastic (B12/folate) anaemia?
concept: Megaloblastic anaemia - hypersegmented neutrophils + macro-ovalocytes

stem: Halfway through a blood transfusion a patient develops fever, chills, loin/back pain, dark urine and hypotension. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
opts: Stop the transfusion immediately, keep the line open, and manage as a transfusion reaction
Continue the transfusion at a slower rate
Stop and discard the unit but disconnect the line
concept: Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction - STOP transfusion immediately, keep line, manage reaction

stem: A 55-year-old man with cirrhosis presents with confusion and asterixis. Serum ammonia is elevated. In the liver, ammonia is detoxified by combining with which molecule to form glutamine?
concept: Hepatic encephalopathy — ammonia detoxification via glutamine synthetase

stem: A 60-year-old man with ascites due to cirrhosis presents with fever and abdominal pain. Diagnostic paracentesis shows an ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear (PMN) count of 350 cells/mm³. What is the most appropriate treatment?
concept: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis — PMN >250 → cefotaxime + albumin

stem: A 58-year-old man with decompensated cirrhosis and ascites develops oliguria and a creatinine rising from 1.0 to 2.6 mg/dL over 2 weeks. Urine sediment is bland and urine sodium is 8 mmol/L. He has received no nephrotoxic drugs and there is no shock or proteinuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Hepatorenal syndrome — functional renal failure in cirrhosis
