stem: A 52-year-old man with compensated cirrhosis develops new-onset abdominal distension and shifting dullness. He is otherwise stable with normal renal function. What is the first-line treatment?
concept: Ascites — first-line medical management

stem: A 55-year-old man with chronic liver disease attends for routine review and is found to have a prolonged prothrombin time. Which supplement most directly addresses this coagulation defect?
concept: Vitamin K deficiency in chronic liver disease

stem: A 45-year-old man with hepatitis B-related cirrhosis is under surveillance. What is the most appropriate screening strategy for hepatocellular carcinoma?
concept: Hepatocellular carcinoma — surveillance in cirrhosis

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with ascites, tender hepatomegaly, and right upper quadrant pain of 3 weeks duration. Doppler ultrasound shows thrombosis of the hepatic veins. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
concept: Budd-Chiari syndrome — hepatic vein thrombosis

stem: A 48-year-old man with heavy alcohol use presents with jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, and a Maddrey discriminant function of 40. He has no gastrointestinal bleeding or sepsis. What is the most appropriate treatment?
concept: Alcoholic hepatitis — Maddrey DF >32 → corticosteroids

stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of acute viral hepatitis in children?
concept: Hepatitis A — most common acute hepatitis in children

stem: A pregnant woman with chronic hepatitis B (HBsAg positive) delivers a baby. After giving hepatitis B immunoglobulin, what additional step most effectively prevents transmission?
opts: First dose of hepatitis B vaccine within 12-24 hours of birth
concept: Hepatitis B — vertical transmission prevention

stem: A 35-year-old man is found to have the following serology: HBsAg positive, anti-HBc IgG positive, anti-HBs negative, HBeAg negative, with normal ALT. What does this profile indicate?
concept: Hepatitis B serology — chronic infection profile

stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman in her third trimester presents with acute jaundice, malaise, and markedly elevated aminotransferases. She had recently travelled to a region with poor sanitation. Which hepatitis virus carries the highest mortality in this setting?
concept: Hepatitis E — fulminant hepatitis in pregnancy

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents 24 hours after ingesting a large overdose of paracetamol with jaundice, coagulopathy, and grade 2 hepatic encephalopathy. What is the most appropriate antidote?
concept: Fulminant hepatic failure — paracetamol antidote

stem: A 50-year-old man presents with fatigue, joint pain, new-onset diabetes, and slate-grey skin pigmentation. Serum ferritin is markedly elevated with a transferrin saturation of 65%. What is the definitive treatment?
concept: Hereditary hemochromatosis — phlebotomy

stem: A 17-year-old boy presents with a tremor, dysarthria, and deteriorating school performance. Examination shows Kayser-Fleischer rings, and serum ceruloplasmin is low. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
concept: Wilson disease — copper chelation with penicillamine

stem: A 35-year-old non-smoker presents with emphysema predominantly in the lung bases and mild transaminitis. Liver biopsy shows PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules in hepatocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease from smoking
concept: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency — PAS+ globules, basal emphysema

stem: A 22-year-old man is found to have an isolated raised unconjugated bilirubin (40 µmol/L) on routine testing. His haemoglobin, reticulocyte count, and liver enzymes are normal, and there are no symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Gilbert syndrome — benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with pruritus and fatigue. Liver biochemistry shows a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase, and anti-mitochondrial antibodies are positive. What is the first-line treatment?
concept: Primary biliary cholangitis — AMA positive → UDCA

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with jaundice and fatigue. Liver enzymes show a marked hepatocellular pattern (AST 900, ALT 850), IgG is elevated, and anti-smooth muscle antibody is positive. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
concept: Autoimmune hepatitis — anti-SMA+ → corticosteroids

stem: A 60-year-old man with a history of chronic alcohol-related pancreatitis presents with steatorrhoea and weight loss. Deficiency of which pancreatic enzyme most directly explains the steatorrhoea?
concept: Chronic pancreatitis — exocrine insufficiency (lipase → steatorrhoea)

stem: A 40-year-old man had acute pancreatitis 6 weeks ago and now presents with a firm epigastric mass and early satiety. CT shows a well-defined cystic lesion in the lesser sac. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Pancreatic pseudocyst — 4-6 weeks after pancreatitis

stem: A 65-year-old man presents with painless jaundice and a palpable non-tender gallbladder. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Carcinoma of the head of the pancreas
concept: Courvoisier's law — painless jaundice + palpable gallbladder

stem: A 26-year-old man presents with fever, right upper quadrant pain, and a tender liver. Ultrasound shows a single 6 cm abscess in the right lobe. What is the most appropriate management?
concept: Amoebic liver abscess — metronidazole + aspiration if large

stem: A patient's liver function tests show an alkaline phosphatase of 900 U/L with near-normal AST and ALT. Which pattern of liver injury does this represent?
concept: Liver biochemistry — cholestatic vs hepatocellular pattern

stem: A 30-year-old man with a 5-year history of ulcerative colitis presents with fatigue, pruritus, and a persistently raised alkaline phosphatase. MRCP shows multifocal strictures and dilatations of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts ('beaded' appearance). What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Primary sclerosing cholangitis — UC + beaded strictures

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with the 'worst headache of her life' of sudden onset 4 hours ago, vomiting and neck stiffness. Non-contrast CT brain is normal. What is the next best step?
opts: Lumbar puncture to look for xanthochromia
Discharge home with simple analgesia after 24 h observation
MRI of the brain as an outpatient
concept: Subarachnoid haemorrhage: normal CT does NOT exclude it — proceed to LP

stem: A 28-year-old woman on combined oral contraceptives, 3 weeks postpartum, has progressive bifrontal headache, blurred vision with papilloedema, and a focal seizure. CT shows a haemorrhagic venous infarct. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) recognition

stem: A 68-year-old man has sudden right hemiparesis, right hemisensory loss, right homonymous hemianopia and expressive (Broca) aphasia. Which vessel is most likely occluded?
concept: Middle cerebral artery occlusion syndrome localisation

stem: A 60-year-old hypertensive diabetic man wakes with isolated right hemiparesis involving face, arm and leg equally. There are NO cortical signs (no aphasia, no neglect, no visual field defect). MRI shows a small deep infarct. This is best described as:
concept: Lacunar stroke recognition (pure motor, small vessel)

stem: A 59-year-old man has acute left-sided weakness of 2 h duration from an ischaemic stroke. His BP is 190/115 mmHg. Before considering IV thrombolysis, what must be done with the blood pressure?
opts: Give thrombolysis immediately regardless of BP
Lower BP to <120/80 mmHg then give thrombolysis
Gently lower BP to ≤185/110 mmHg before thrombolysis
Withhold thrombolysis permanently if BP cannot be lowered
concept: BP threshold for IV thrombolysis in ischaemic stroke

stem: A 55-year-old hypertensive man has sudden vertigo, vomiting, ataxia and headache. He is drowsy. CT shows a cerebellar haemorrhage (3 cm) with early obstructive hydrocephalus. What is the most appropriate management?
concept: Cerebellar haemorrhage — surgical decompression for mass effect

stem: A 40-year-old man is 'awake' with eyes open after a large ventral pontine infarct. He cannot speak or move his limbs, but he can reliably move his eyes vertically to command. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Coma due to bilateral hemispheric damage
concept: Locked-in syndrome — preserved vertical eye movement + intact consciousness

stem: Which combination best satisfies the clinical criteria for brain (brainstem) death?
opts: Deep coma with preserved pupillary light reflex and spontaneous respiration
Deep coma, absent pupillary/corneal/oculocephalic reflexes, absent gag/cough, and a positive apnoea test
Persistent vegetative state with intact brainstem reflexes
Coma with decerebrate posturing to noxious stimuli
concept: Brainstem death — clinical criteria (coma + absent brainstem reflexes + apnoea)

stem: A 70-year-old man with cirrhosis continues to seize 10 minutes after receiving a benzodiazepine for status epilepticus. Which second-line agent is preferred here?
concept: Second-line agent for status epilepticus — levetiracetam in hepatic impairment

stem: A 34-year-old adult has a FIRST unprovoked generalised tonic-clonic seizure. EEG shows generalised epileptiform activity and MRI is normal. Which factor most strongly supports starting a long-term antiepileptic drug now?
opts: Epileptiform abnormalities on EEG and an abnormal neurologic examination
The single unprovoked seizure with a normal MRI
Absence of any provoking factor and normal imaging
concept: First unprovoked seizure — high recurrence risk (epileptiform EEG, abnormal exam) justifies AED

stem: A 16-year-old girl has brief myoclonic jerks of her arms on waking and occasional generalised tonic-clonic seizures in the morning. Which is the most appropriate first-line antiseizure medication?
concept: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy — first-line AED avoiding valproate in a girl

stem: A 7-year-old girl has frequent brief episodes of staring and unresponsiveness with rapid blinking, during which she does not fall, lasting 5–10 seconds, occurring dozens of times a day. EEG shows 3 Hz spike-and-wave. What is the most effective first choice?
concept: Typical absence epilepsy — ethosuximide first-line

stem: A 22-year-old collapsed with twitching movements of all limbs for about 20 seconds after standing up quickly, then quickly recovered with full orientation. Which feature most strongly suggests SYNCOPE rather than a seizure?
opts: Rapid full recovery of consciousness within seconds with no post-ictal confusion
Biting the lateral border of the tongue
Confusion and drowsiness for 30 minutes afterwards
concept: Syncope vs seizure — post-ictal confusion and recovery distinguish them

stem: A 32-year-old man has severe, strictly unilateral, tearing and nasal-stuffy headache around the same eye, occurring in clusters every night and making him pace the floor. During an acute attack, the most effective first-line treatment is:
opts: Bed rest in a dark quiet room with simple analgesics
High-flow oxygen therapy and subcutaneous sumatriptan
Oral propranolol at the time of the attack
concept: Cluster headache — acute attack treatment (high-flow O2 + SC sumatriptan)

stem: A 38-year-old woman with migraine takes sumatriptan or ibuprofen on most days (roughly 18 days per month) and now has a daily, dull, diffuse headache that improves transiently with analgesics. What is the most likely diagnosis and key management?
opts: New daily persistent headache — start prophylactic amitriptyline only
Intracranial tumour — urgent MRI is mandatory
Chronic tension headache — increase analgesic frequency briefly
Medication-overuse headache — withdraw the overused analgesic/abortive and re-educate
concept: Medication-overuse headache — recognition and withdrawal

stem: A 68-year-old woman has a new severe temporal headache, jaw claudication while chewing, scalp tenderness, and an ESR of 90 mm/h. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
opts: Wait for the temporal artery biopsy result before any treatment
Start high-dose corticosteroids now, and arrange temporal artery biopsy
Prescribe simple analgesics and review in 2 weeks
Start antibiotics for presumed cellulitis of the temple
concept: Giant cell arteritis — urgent steroids before biopsy to prevent blindness

stem: A 29-year-old woman with frequent disabling migraines (5–6 attacks/month) needs preventive therapy. She plans pregnancy in the next year. Which prophylactic is LEAST appropriate?
concept: Migraine prophylaxis — sodium valproate is teratogenic, avoid in reproductive-age women

stem: A 60-year-old woman has brief, electric-shock-like stabbing pains in the right cheek/ jaw triggered by touching her face, chewing and cold air. Neurologic examination, including sensation, is normal. What is the first-line treatment?
concept: Trigeminal neuralgia — carbamazepine first-line

stem: A 34-year-old man awakens with inability to close his LEFT eye and flattening of the left nasolabial fold; BOTH upper and lower face are weak, including forehead wrinkling. No limb weakness. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Start oral corticosteroids within 72 h and protect the eye
concept: Bell's palsy — early oral corticosteroids + eye protection

stem: Which clinical feature best distinguishes a CENTRAL (upper motor neuron) facial palsy from a PERIPHERAL (lower motor neuron/Bell's) palsy?
opts: Forehead movement is lost in a central palsy
Central palsy always shows loss of taste
Forehead and upper-face movement is spared in a central palsy
concept: UMN vs LMN facial palsy — forehead sparing in central lesions

stem: A 24-year-old woman has recurrent 'seizures' with asynchronous thrashing, pelvic thrusting, eyes tightly shut, and crying during events, with normal consciousness afterwards. Serum lactate after an episode is normal. Most likely diagnosis?
concept: Psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES) recognition

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with new headaches and seizures. Imaging shows an extra-axial, contrast-enhancing dural-based mass; histology reveals psammoma bodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Meningioma — extra-axial dural-based tumour with psammoma bodies

stem: A 58-year-old hypertensive man has sudden vertigo, hoarseness, dysphagia, and ataxia. Examination shows right-sided Horner syndrome, loss of pain and temperature on the right face AND left body, with intact proprioception. What is the lesion?
concept: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome — ipsilateral face + contralateral body pain/temp loss

stem: A 26-year-old woman with epilepsy on levetiracetam becomes pregnant. Which is the most appropriate management of her antiepileptic therapy?
opts: Stop all antiepileptics in the first trimester
Switch to sodium valproate for better seizure control in pregnancy
Continue levetiracetam (the least teratogenic option here) and give folic acid supplementation, monitoring levels
Withhold antiepileptics and only treat if a seizure occurs
concept: Epilepsy in pregnancy — continue least-teratogenic AED + folic acid

stem: A patient remains in electrographic status epilepticus despite a benzodiazepine AND a second-line agent. What is the appropriate next step?
opts: Induce general anaesthesia (e.g. propofol/midazolam infusion) with continuous EEG monitoring in ICU
Add a third oral antiepileptic and observe on the ward
concept: Refractory status epilepticus — anaesthetic agents with continuous EEG in ICU

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with chronic diarrhoea, weight loss, and steatorrhoea. To distinguish small-intestinal mucosal disease from pancreatic insufficiency, which test result would be most informative?
opts: Low serum lipase confirms mucosal disease
Normal D-xylose with raised faecal elastase excludes malabsorption
Low urinary D-xylose indicates mucosal disease
High faecal osmotic gap indicates pancreatic disease
concept: Malabsorption workup — D-xylose test distinguishes mucosal vs pancreatic

stem: A patient with chronic watery diarrhoea has a stool osmolality of 290 mOsm/kg with stool sodium 40 mmol/L and potassium 30 mmol/L. What type of diarrhoea is most likely?
concept: Faecal osmotic gap — osmotic vs secretory diarrhoea

stem: A 52-year-old man presents with migratory arthralgia, chronic diarrhoea, and weight loss. Small-bowel biopsy shows PAS-positive foamy macrophages in the lamina propria. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
concept: Whipple disease — Tropheryma whipplei, PAS+ macrophages → prolonged antibiotics

stem: A 60-year-old man who had a Billroth II gastrectomy years ago presents with diarrhoea, steatorrhoea, and macrocytic anaemia. A glucose breath test shows an early hydrogen peak. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth — blind loop syndrome

stem: A 25-year-old man reports bloating, cramping, and loose stools within 2 hours of drinking milk, which started gradually in his twenties. What is the most appropriate confirmatory test?
concept: Lactose intolerance — hydrogen breath test

stem: A 50-year-old woman undergoes resection of 100 cm of terminal ileum for Crohn disease. Which two deficiencies is she most at risk of developing?
opts: Vitamin B12 and bile salt malabsorption
concept: Ileal resection — B12 and bile salt malabsorption

stem: A 45-year-old woman who had a gastrectomy 1 year ago develops palpitations, sweating, and weakness 90 minutes after meals. What is the most likely mechanism?
opts: Reactive hypoglycaemia from excessive insulin secretion
Rapid fluid shift into the bowel lumen
concept: Dumping syndrome — late phase (reactive hypoglycaemia)

stem: A 62-year-old woman with pernicious anaemia (positive anti-intrinsic factor antibodies) requires treatment. What is the most appropriate long-term therapy?
opts: Oral vitamin B12 with high-dose tablets
concept: Pernicious anemia — lifelong parenteral B12

stem: A 30-year-old man presents with intensely pruritic vesicles on his elbows, knees, and buttocks. Duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy consistent with coeliac disease. Which medication most effectively controls the skin lesions?
concept: Dermatitis herpetiformis — dapsone for skin lesions

stem: A 35-year-old man develops chronic diarrhoea, steatorrhoea, and megaloblastic anaemia 6 months after returning from an extended stay in South Asia. What is the most appropriate treatment?
concept: Tropical sprue — tetracycline + folate

stem: A 55-year-old man who had a partial gastrectomy for gastric cancer 2 years ago develops fatigue. Blood film shows microcytic, hypochromic anaemia. What is the most likely cause?
concept: Post-gastrectomy — iron deficiency anaemia

stem: A 28-year-old woman with chronic diarrhoea and weight loss has a negative anti-tTG IgA test, but coeliac disease is still suspected. Which additional test should be checked?
concept: Coeliac disease — IgA deficiency causes false-negative anti-tTG

stem: A 6-month-old exclusively breastfed infant develops a rash around the mouth and perineum, diarrhoea, and failure to thrive. Which deficiency is most likely?
concept: Zinc deficiency — acrodermatitis enteropathica pattern

stem: In a region of endemic iodine deficiency, a pregnant woman's newborn is at greatest risk of which condition?
concept: Iodine deficiency — goitre and cretinism

stem: A 40-year-old man with severe anorexia is started on aggressive enteral nutrition after a period of starvation. Within 2 days he develops weakness and cardiac arrhythmia. Which electrolyte disturbance is the most likely cause?
concept: Refeeding syndrome — hypophosphataemia

stem: An alcoholic man presents confused with ataxia and ophthalmoplegia. Before administering intravenous glucose, which should be given first?
concept: Wernicke encephalopathy — thiamine before glucose

stem: A 3-year-old child in a low-resource setting presents with night blindness and dry, thickened conjunctiva. Without treatment, what is the most feared progression?
concept: Vitamin A deficiency — xerophthalmia progressing to keratomalacia

stem: A 2-year-old child presents with generalised oedema, a distended abdomen, and a flaky-paint dermatitis with depigmented hair. Which form of malnutrition is this?
concept: Kwashiorkor — protein deficiency with oedema

stem: A 12-month-old infant presents with severe wasting of muscle and subcutaneous fat, an 'old man' facies, and weight for age below the third centile — but no oedema. What is the diagnosis?
concept: Marasmus — total calorie deficiency without oedema

stem: A 58-year-old strict vegan presents with progressive paraesthesia of the feet, loss of vibration sense, and an unsteady gait, with brisk knee reflexes. Which deficiency is most likely?
concept: Vitamin B12 deficiency — subacute combined degeneration of the cord

stem: In assessing the nutritional status of an acutely ill hospitalised patient, which protein best reflects recent (short-term) nutritional change?
concept: Nutritional assessment — prealbumin vs albumin

stem: A patient on total parenteral nutrition for 3 weeks develops a fever and rigors. A central line is in situ. What is the most likely complication?
concept: Total parenteral nutrition — catheter-related line sepsis

stem: A patient with a functional gastrointestinal tract requires nutritional support. Which feeding route is preferred and why?
opts: Parenteral nutrition, because it is more reliable
Enteral nutrition, because it preserves gut mucosal integrity
Parenteral nutrition, because it avoids aspiration
Enteral nutrition, because it requires no access device
concept: Nutrition support — enteral preferred over parenteral

stem: A 58-year-old man with chronic pancreatitis has steatorrhoea and weight loss despite eating. Which treatment most directly addresses the steatorrhoea?
opts: Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy with meals
concept: Chronic pancreatitis — pancreatic enzyme replacement for steatorrhoea

stem: A 50-year-old woman with coeliac disease remains symptomatic with persistent villous atrophy despite 12 months of strict gluten avoidance. Which complication should now be suspected?
concept: Refractory coeliac disease — enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma

stem: A 60-year-old woman develops fever, a maculopapular rash, and rising creatinine 10 days after starting a new antibiotic. Urine shows WBC casts and peripheral blood shows eosinophilia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Acute interstitial nephritis — drug exposure + eosinophilia + WBC casts

stem: A 45-year-old renal transplant recipient has an asymptomatic rise in serum creatinine 1 year after transplantation, despite stable immunosuppression. What is the most appropriate next step?
concept: Renal transplant — rising creatinine requires biopsy before empirical treatment

stem: A 55-year-old man with decompensated cirrhosis and ascites develops progressive oliguria. Urine sodium is 8 mmol/L, urine osmolality is 650 mOsm/kg, and there is no proteinuria or haematuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Hepatorenal syndrome — prerenal AKI in cirrhosis with low urine sodium

stem: A 3-year-old child develops bloody diarrhoea followed by oliguria, pallor, and bruising. Blood film shows schistocytes and thrombocytopenia; creatinine is raised. What is the most appropriate management?
concept: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome — E. coli O157, supportive care, no antibiotics

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with fever, fluctuating confusion, and petechiae. Blood film shows schistocytes; platelets are 20,000/μL. There is no significant renal impairment. What is the most appropriate treatment?
concept: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura — ADAMTS13 deficiency, plasma exchange

stem: A 20-year-old man with newly diagnosed Burkitt lymphoma develops oliguria 24 hours after starting chemotherapy. Labs show potassium 6.8 mmol/L, phosphate 7.5 mg/dL, uric acid 14 mg/dL, and calcium 6.0 mg/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Tumour lysis syndrome — post-chemotherapy AKI with hyperK + hyperPO4 + hyperuricemia + hypocalcemia

stem: According to KDIGO, which urine output criterion defines acute kidney injury?
concept: AKI definition — KDIGO urine output criterion

stem: A 65-year-old man develops AKI after prolonged hypotension during cardiac surgery. Urine microscopy shows muddy brown granular casts and urine sodium is 60 mmol/L. Which part of the kidney is most likely affected?
concept: Acute tubular necrosis — muddy brown casts + high urine sodium

stem: A 58-year-old woman has an eGFR of 35 mL/min/1.73 m² with known diabetic nephropathy. Which CKD stage does this represent?
concept: CKD staging — eGFR thresholds

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with bilateral flank pain, hypertension, and haematuria. Imaging shows multiple bilateral renal cysts and his father died of a cerebral aneurysm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: ADPKD — autosomal dominant, bilateral cysts, HTN, berry aneurysms

stem: A 62-year-old hypertensive smoker develops recurrent 'flash' pulmonary oedema. After starting an ACE inhibitor, serum creatinine rises from 1.2 to 2.1 mg/dL within 1 week. What is the most likely cause?
concept: Renal artery stenosis — flash pulmonary oedema + ACEi-induced Cr rise >30%

stem: A 50-year-old man with advanced CKD (eGFR 12) develops prolonged bleeding after tooth extraction. Platelet count is normal. Which agent most directly corrects the bleeding tendency?
concept: Uraemic bleeding — platelet dysfunction corrected by desmopressin

stem: A 48-year-old woman on peritoneal dialysis presents with abdominal pain and a cloudy effluent bag. What is the most appropriate initial step?
opts: Send effluent for cell count, gram stain, and culture, then start empirical antibiotics
concept: Peritoneal dialysis — peritonitis diagnosis and empirical treatment

stem: A patient is being prepared for maintenance haemodialysis. Which vascular access is preferred for long-term dialysis?
concept: Haemodialysis access — AV fistula is preferred

stem: A 55-year-old man with CKD stage 4 is counselled on dietary modification. Which dietary restriction is most important to slow progression and prevent complications?
concept: CKD diet — phosphate and potassium restriction

stem: A 60-year-old man with a 20-year history of poorly controlled hypertension has slowly progressive renal impairment with mild proteinuria (<1 g/day). Urine sediment is bland. What is the most likely cause?
concept: Hypertensive nephrosclerosis — long-standing HTN, slow decline, mild proteinuria

stem: A 7-year-old boy develops palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs, abdominal pain, and arthralgia 2 weeks after an upper respiratory infection. Urine shows blood and protein. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Henoch-Schönlein purpura — palpable purpura + abdominal pain + arthralgia + renal

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with sinusitis, haemoptysis, and rapidly progressive renal failure. Urine shows RBC casts. Which antibody is most likely to be positive?
concept: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis — c-ANCA/PR3, ENT + pulmonary-renal

stem: A 55-year-old woman has rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with haematuria, but NO upper respiratory or sinus involvement. Renal biopsy shows pauci-immune crescentic GN. Which antibody is most likely positive?
concept: Microscopic polyangiitis — p-ANCA/MPO, pauci-immune crescentic GN without ENT

stem: A renal biopsy in a patient with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis shows crescentic GN with linear immunofluorescence for IgG along the glomerular basement membrane. Which condition does this represent?
concept: RPGN — anti-GBM disease with linear IgG on immunofluorescence

stem: A 40-year-old man with nephrotic syndrome due to membranous nephropathy develops sudden left flank pain and gross haematuria. What complication should be suspected?
concept: Nephrotic syndrome — hypercoagulability → renal vein thrombosis

stem: A 30-year-old man with untreated HIV infection develops nephrotic-range proteinuria and progressive renal failure. Biopsy shows collapsing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. What is the most likely cause?
concept: HIV-associated nephropathy — collapsing FSGS in HIV

stem: A 25-year-old woman has persistent microscopic haematuria found on a routine check. She is otherwise well with normal blood pressure, normal renal function, and no proteinuria. Her mother has the same finding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Thin basement membrane disease — benign familial haematuria

stem: A 60-year-old man with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis develops nephrotic-range proteinuria and renal impairment. Renal biopsy shows apple-green birefringence with Congo red staining. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Renal amyloidosis — Congo red apple-green birefringence in chronic inflammation

stem: A 12-year-old girl with recurrent urinary tract infections and hypertension has renal scarring on DMSA scan, most prominent at the upper and lower poles. What is the most likely underlying problem?
concept: Reflux nephropathy — VUR causes polar renal scarring

stem: A 42-year-old woman reports progressive difficulty swallowing both liquids and solids for 2 years, with regurgitation of undigested food and a 4 kg weight loss. Barium swallow shows a smooth tapered 'bird-beak' narrowing at the gastro-oesophageal junction. What is the most appropriate definitive management?
concept: Achalasia — definitive management (myotomy vs botox)

stem: A 60-year-old man who smokes and drinks alcohol reports progressive dysphagia — first to solids, now to liquids — with a 6 kg weight loss over 3 months. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Oesophageal carcinoma — solids-then-liquids dysphagia

stem: A 55-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis presents with haematemesis. Upper GI endoscopy reveals tortuous dilated veins in the distal oesophagus. What is the first-line therapeutic intervention?
concept: Oesophageal varices — first-line treatment of acute haemorrhage

stem: A 38-year-old man presents after several episodes of forceful vomiting following a binge, followed by small-volume bright-red haematemesis. He is haemodynamically stable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Mallory-Weiss tear — mucosal tear after retching

stem: A 45-year-old man develops sudden severe lower chest pain and shortness of breath immediately after a bout of violent vomiting. On examination he is febrile with subcutaneous emphysema felt in the neck. What is the most appropriate next step?
concept: Boerhaave syndrome — diagnosis with water-soluble contrast

stem: A 50-year-old man with a long history of NSAID use presents with sudden severe epigastric pain. His abdomen is rigid and board-like, and an erect chest X-ray shows free gas under the diaphragm. What is the most appropriate definitive management?
concept: Perforated peptic ulcer — definitive surgical management

stem: A 40-year-old man reports recurrent epigastric pain that is relieved by eating but wakes him at night. Endoscopy shows a duodenal ulcer. Which pain pattern best characterises his condition?
opts: Right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals
concept: Duodenal ulcer pain — relieved by food, nocturnal

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with melaena and is haemodynamically stable after initial fluid resuscitation. What is the single most appropriate next step?
concept: Upper GI bleed — endoscopy is diagnostic AND therapeutic

stem: A 70-year-old woman presents with right upper quadrant pain, fever with rigors, and jaundice. What is the most appropriate initial management?
opts: IV antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage (ERCP)
concept: Ascending cholangitis — Charcot triad → antibiotics + urgent ERCP

stem: A 68-year-old diabetic man presents with fever, right upper quadrant pain, and vomiting. CT shows gas within the gallbladder wall. What is the most appropriate management?
concept: Emphysematous cholecystitis — gas in GB wall in a diabetic → urgent surgery

stem: A 74-year-old woman presents with colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, and constipation. Abdominal X-ray shows small-bowel obstruction, air in the biliary tree (pneumobilia), and a calcified opacity in the right iliac fossa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Gallstone ileus — Rigler's triad

stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with painless passage of dark red blood per rectum and iron-deficiency anaemia. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
concept: Meckel's diverticulum — rule of 2s, painless PR bleed in a child

stem: A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden severe diffuse abdominal pain that is out of proportion to his near-normal examination. He has a lactate of 5 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Acute mesenteric ischaemia — AF + pain out of proportion

stem: A 9-month-old boy has episodes of sudden crying, drawing up his legs, and passage of red 'currant jelly' stool. A sausage-shaped mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant. What is the most appropriate first-line management?
concept: Intussusception — air enema reduction in a stable infant

stem: A 70-year-old woman presents with vomiting, abdominal distension, and a tender irreducible lump in the right groin below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. The overlying skin is warm and red. What is the most appropriate management?
concept: Strangulated femoral hernia — urgent surgery

stem: A 75-year-old man presents with painless, large-volume bright red bleeding per rectum. He is otherwise well and haemodynamically stable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Diverticulosis — painless bleeding in the elderly

stem: A 60-year-old woman presents with fever, left lower quadrant pain, and leukocytosis. Diverticulitis is suspected. What is the most appropriate imaging to confirm the diagnosis?
concept: Acute diverticulitis — CT diagnosis (barium/colonoscopy contraindicated)

stem: A 68-year-old woman with hypertension presents with sudden crampy left-sided abdominal pain followed by bloody diarrhoea. She has no history of atrial fibrillation. CT shows segmental colonic wall thickening at the splenic flexure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Ischaemic colitis — watershed splenic flexure, non-occlusive

stem: A 78-year-old nursing-home resident presents with gross abdominal distension, constipation, and vomiting. Abdominal X-ray shows a massively dilated loop of colon with a 'coffee bean' appearance. What is the most appropriate initial management?
concept: Sigmoid volvulus — coffee-bean sign → endoscopic detorsion

stem: A 30-year-old woman reports severe tearing pain during defecation with a few drops of bright red blood on the toilet paper. She is otherwise well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Anal fissure — tearing pain + fresh blood on wiping

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with painless bright red bleeding per rectum and a lump that prolapses on defecation but reduces spontaneously. What is the diagnosis?
concept: Haemorrhoids — grading of internal haemorrhoids

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with a tender, fluctuant swelling beside the anus, with fever. What is the most appropriate management?
concept: Perianal abscess — incision and drainage

stem: A 72-year-old woman with aortic stenosis presents with recurrent episodes of intermittent, painless bright red bleeding per rectum and iron-deficiency anaemia. Colonoscopy is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Angiodysplasia — right-colon vascular ectasia (Heyde syndrome)

stem: A 65-year-old woman develops profuse watery diarrhoea 7 days after completing a course of clindamycin. Sigmoidoscopy shows yellow-white adherent plaques. What is the most appropriate treatment?
concept: Pseudomembranous colitis — C. difficile → oral vancomycin

stem: A 28-year-old man with known ulcerative colitis presents with fever, tachycardia, abdominal distension, and dilated colon (>6 cm) on abdominal X-ray. What is the most appropriate initial management?
opts: IV fluids, IV corticosteroids, and surgical review
concept: Toxic megacolon — complication of UC

stem: Chronic acid reflux in Barrett's oesophagus causes the normal squamous epithelium to be replaced by columnar (intestinal-type) epithelium. This transformation is best described as?
concept: Metaplasia - reversible change of one differentiated cell type to another (Barrett's)

stem: The uterine myometrium enlarges during pregnancy, and the prostate enlarges with benign prostatic hyperplasia in older men. Which mechanism best explains the uterine (muscle) growth compared with the prostate?
opts: The uterus grows mainly by hypertrophy (increase in cell size); the prostate grows mainly by hyperplasia (increase in cell number)
The uterus grows by hyperplasia; the prostate by metaplasia
concept: Hypertrophy vs hyperplasia - differentiated cells (muscle) hypertrophy; labile cells (prostate) hyperplase

stem: A malignant tumour shows marked pleomorphism, hyperchromatic nuclei, a high nuclear:cytoplasmic ratio, prominent nucleoli and numerous mitoses. This loss of differentiation is called?
concept: Anaplasia - lack of differentiation, a hallmark of malignancy

stem: On a cervical smear, squamous epithelial cells show nuclear atypia, loss of normal maturation and disordered architecture involving the FULL thickness of the epithelium, but WITHOUT invasion of the basement membrane. This is best described as?
concept: Carcinoma in situ - full-thickness dysplasia without basement-membrane invasion

stem: On histology of an area of recent myocardial infarction, sheets of cells show loss of nuclei, eosinophilic cytoplasm, and an intense neutrophil infiltrate with an inflammatory response. This pattern of cell death is best described as?
concept: Coagulative necrosis - ischaemic cell death in solid organs (MI) with inflammation

stem: A child develops retinoblastoma affecting both eyes at an early age, and a family member has the same condition. A defective gene normally functions as a 'gatekeeper' to restrain cell growth. Which class does this gene belong to, and which gene is it?
concept: Rb tumour suppressor - loss of function allows cancer; hereditary retinoblastoma

stem: A breast cancer shows amplification of a gene encoding a growth-factor receptor tyrosine kinase, targeted by the drug trastuzumab. Which gene is this, and how do oncogenes generally differ from tumour suppressors?
opts: HER2/neu; oncogenes act by gain of function, tumour suppressors by loss of function
Rb; oncogenes act by loss of function
BCR-ABL; oncogenes and suppressors both act by loss of function
p53; oncogenes act by loss of function
concept: HER2/neu oncogene - gain of function (amplification) drives breast cancer

stem: A colorectal carcinoma is reported as T3 N1 M0. What do these designations describe, and what distinguishes it from tumour grading?
opts: TNM describes the anatomic STAGE (tumour size/depth, nodes, metastasis); grading describes the degree of differentiation
Grading and staging are the same thing
concept: Staging (TNM) vs grading - anatomic extent vs differentiation

stem: A patient with cirrhosis develops hepatocellular carcinoma and his alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is markedly elevated. Which statement about tumour markers is correct?
opts: AFP is useful as a screening/monitoring marker for hepatocellular carcinoma, but is not 100% specific
AFP is a specific marker only for colorectal cancer
Tumour markers alone can definitively diagnose cancer
CEA is the marker for hepatocellular carcinoma
concept: Tumour markers - AFP for hepatocellular carcinoma; markers are non-specific, not diagnostic alone

stem: A colorectal carcinoma is found to have multiple liver deposits. Through which route did the tumour most likely reach the liver, and what is the value of a sentinel lymph node biopsy in cancer?
opts: Via the portal vein (portal circulation); sentinel node = first node draining the tumour, for staging
Direct haematogenous spread via the pulmonary artery
Sentinel node = the largest tumour deposit for debulking
concept: Portal vein spread of bowel cancer to the liver; sentinel node concept

stem: A patient with HIV/AIDS has multiple, solitary, darkly pigmented plaques that evolve into nodular, bluish, painful skin lesions. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Kaposi sarcoma - HIV-associated vascular tumour (HHV-8), pigmented plaques/nodules

stem: A 40-year-old woman has spontaneous blood-stained discharge from one nipple. On examination NO lump is palpable and mammography is otherwise unremarkable. Which structure is most likely responsible?
concept: Intraductal papilloma - bloody nipple discharge without a palpable lump

stem: A 35-year-old woman with MEN 2A develops a thyroid lump and chronic diarrhoea; she undergoes total thyroidectomy. Which type of thyroid cancer is most likely, and what explains the diarrhoea?
opts: Medullary carcinoma - arising from parafollicular C cells, needs calcitonin; diarrhoea from calcitonin/peptides
Follicular carcinoma - haematogenous spread to bone
concept: Medullary thyroid carcinoma - MEN 2A, C-cell origin, calcitonin (causes diarrhoea)

stem: A 4-year-old child presents with a large, painless, palpable abdominal mass, hypertension and microscopic haematuria. Imaging shows a renal mass. What is the most common intra-abdominal solid organ tumour of childhood and its characteristic microscopic feature?
concept: Wilms tumour - most common intra-abdominal solid organ tumour of childhood (nephroblastoma)

stem: A 40-year-old woman has a large (6-7 cm), firm, mobile breast lump in the upper outer quadrant that has grown rapidly, but no axillary lymph nodes are palpable. Core biopsy shows a fibroepithelial tumour with prominent stromal overgrowth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Phyllodes tumour - large fibroepithelial tumour with stromal overgrowth (cystosarcoma phyllodes)

stem: A woman presents with a tender, cord-like, linear band beneath the skin of the breast/chest wall. What is the pathophysiology of Mondor's disease?
concept: Mondor's disease - superficial thrombophlebitis of breast/chest wall veins

stem: Which type of colorectal polyp has the HIGHEST malignant potential and is most likely to harbour carcinoma?
concept: Villous adenoma - highest malignant potential of colorectal polyps

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with headaches and new-onset seizures. Imaging shows a well-circumscribed extra-axial tumour arising from and irritating the meninges, and histology reveals psammoma bodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Meningioma - benign extra-axial meningeal tumour with psammoma bodies

stem: A 60-year-old heavy smoker with a central lung mass and hilar lymphadenopathy develops Cushing-like features with a low potassium (hypokalaemic alkalosis) and proximal muscle weakness. Which lung cancer subtype is most associated with this paraneoplastic picture, and what does it produce?
concept: Small cell lung cancer - ectopic ACTH causing Cushing's/hypokalaemic alkalosis

stem: A 50-year-old overweight woman has progressive painless obstructive jaundice, weight loss, and a palpable distended gallbladder (Courvoisier sign). Imaging shows a mass in the head of the pancreas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma - painless obstructive jaundice + Courvoisier sign

stem: A 55-year-old man with cirrhosis and chronic hepatitis B has worsening abdominal pain, weight loss and a sharply elevated alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). Imaging shows a vascular liver mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Hepatocellular carcinoma - cirrhosis/HBV + markedly raised AFP + vascular liver mass

stem: A 55-year-old woman has a hard, irregular, painless breast lump that is fixed to skin, with overlying peau d'orange. Biopsy shows cords of malignant cells invading the stroma, and the tumour is oestrogen-receptor positive. Which single description is most accurate?
opts: Invasive ductal carcinoma - the most common invasive breast cancer; hormone-receptor status guides endocrine therapy
Ductal carcinoma in situ - non-invasive by definition
concept: Invasive ductal carcinoma - most common breast cancer; ER/PR status guides therapy

stem: A 65-year-old has altered bowel habit, rectal bleeding and an 'apple-core' lesion on barium enema. Progression from a benign adenomatous polyp to invasive colorectal carcinoma over years is best described by which concept?
opts: The adenoma-carcinoma sequence (accumulation of mutations, e.g. APC, KRAS, p53)
Direct haematogenous spread from a normal gland
A single inherited germline mutation with no intermediate steps
concept: Adenoma-carcinoma sequence - stepwise genetic progression in colorectal cancer

stem: A 40-year-old has a high-grade cervical lesion and tests positive for high-risk HPV. Which oncogenic mechanism explains HPV-associated cervical carcinogenesis?
opts: HPV E6 and E7 inactivate the p53 and Rb tumour suppressors
HPV encodes a tyrosine kinase receptor like HER2
HPV causes a gain-of-function RAS mutation directly
concept: HPV oncogenesis - E6/E7 inactivate p53 (E6) and Rb (E7)

stem: A 70-year-old man with advanced prostate cancer has new-onset back pain and a raised PSA. A bone scan shows 'hot spots' in the lumbar spine and pelvis. Which statement about prostate cancer bone metastases is correct?
opts: Metastases are typically OSTEOBLASTIC with a raised PSA; back pain may signal spinal cord compression
Metastases are purely osteolytic with a normal PSA
Prostate cancer rarely metastasizes to bone
PSA is a marker for breast, not prostate, cancer
concept: Prostate cancer - osteoblastic bone metastases, raised PSA, cord-compression risk

stem: A 62-year-old man presents with a painful, irreducible right inguinal swelling of 8 hours' duration, with nausea and mild tachycardia. At emergency groin exploration, the hernial sac is found to contain a congested but viable vermiform appendix. What is the correct name for this hernia?
concept: Amyand hernia — appendix within an inguinal hernia sac

stem: A 24-year-old man (70 kg) is brought in 30 minutes after a road traffic accident. He is confused and pale: heart rate 125/min, blood pressure 92/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min, urine output 15 mL/hr. What percentage of circulating blood volume has he lost?
concept: Haemorrhagic shock — ATLS class III (30–40% volume loss)

stem: A 68-year-old man with perforated sigmoid diverticulitis is in the emergency department. After 30 mL/kg of crystalloid, blood pressure remains 82/50 mmHg and the serum lactate is 5.2 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Norepinephrine infusion targeting a MAP of ≥65 mmHg
Immediate CT abdomen with intravenous contrast
concept: Septic shock — first-line vasopressor when fluid-refractory

stem: A 32-year-old woman develops acute urticaria, stridor and hypotension (BP 76/45 mmHg) within minutes of receiving an intravenous penicillin infusion on the ward. What is the single most appropriate immediate treatment?
opts: IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh
IV normal saline 500 mL rapid bolus alone
concept: Anaphylactic shock — adrenaline is the first-line drug

stem: A 28-year-old man falls from a ladder and sustains a C6 spinal cord injury. He is hypotensive (BP 78/50 mmHg) with a heart rate of 52/min, warm peripheries and areflexic limbs. Besides spinal precautions, what is the most appropriate immediate management?
concept: Neurogenic shock — hypotension with bradycardia after spinal cord injury

stem: A 60-year-old man on day 2 after an anterior STEMI is hypotensive (BP 82/55 mmHg) with cool, mottled extremities and oliguria. His jugular venous pressure is elevated and he has bilateral pulmonary crackles. Which finding most strongly indicates cardiogenic rather than hypovolaemic shock?
concept: Cardiogenic shock — elevated JVP and pulmonary oedema point to pump failure

stem: Five minutes after a right subclavian central venous catheter insertion, a 55-year-old man undergoing elective surgery develops sudden hypotension, tachycardia and elevated jugular venous pressure. Breath sounds are absent on the right and the trachea is deviated to the left. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
opts: Chest X-ray to confirm the diagnosis
Immediate needle decompression of the right chest
concept: Tension pneumothorax after central line insertion — obstructive shock

stem: A 30-year-old man with exsanguinating abdominal haemorrhage is receiving a massive transfusion (10 units of packed red cells, fresh frozen plasma and platelets). He develops perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm and a prolonged QT interval on the monitor. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Hyperkalaemia from stored red cell breakdown
concept: Massive transfusion — citrate chelates calcium → hypocalcaemia

stem: A 78-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) has severe generalised abdominal pain for 4 hours that is out of proportion to her minimal abdominal tenderness. Her serum lactate is 6 mmol/L. Which investigation should be performed next?
opts: CT abdomen in the portal venous phase only
CT angiography of the mesenteric vessels
concept: Acute mesenteric ischaemia — CT angiography is the diagnostic test of choice

stem: A 62-year-old woman has colicky periumbilical pain, intermittent bilious vomiting and a palpable sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant for 2 days. CT shows a small-bowel intussusception with a 2.5 cm lead point. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Surgical exploration with resection of the lead point
concept: Adult intussusception — usually has a lead point; treat surgically

stem: A 72-year-old man has massive abdominal distension, crampy pain and absolute constipation for 48 hours. Abdominal X-ray shows a grossly dilated sigmoid loop with a 'coffee bean' sign. There is no peritonism and he is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate first step in management?
concept: Sigmoid volvulus — endoscopic decompression first when there is no ischaemia

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with sudden severe epigastric pain and distension, violent retching without the ability to vomit, and an inability to pass a nasogastric tube. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Acute gastric volvulus — Borchardt triad

stem: A 30-year-old man, 12 hours after damage-control laparotomy for abdominal trauma, has progressive abdominal distension with a tense abdomen, rising peak airway pressures (22 to 38 cm H2O) and urine output falling to 10 mL/hr. Bladder pressure measures 32 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Increase sedation and add a neuromuscular blocker
concept: Abdominal compartment syndrome — bladder pressure >20 mmHg with organ dysfunction → decompression

stem: A 32-year-old woman has low-grade fever, night sweats, weight loss and gradually increasing abdominal distension for 3 months. The abdomen is 'doughy' with shifting dullness but no rigidity. Ascitic fluid is a lymphocytic exudate with an ADA level of 60 U/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Tuberculous peritonitis — chronic lymphocytic exudative ascites with high ADA

stem: On day 4 of severe acute pancreatitis, a 46-year-old man develops periumbilical ecchymosis with a falling haemoglobin (13.1 to 9.8 g/dL). What does this finding indicate?
concept: Cullen sign — periumbilical ecchymosis in haemorrhagic pancreatitis

stem: A 19-year-old woman who has lost 12 kg over 4 months presents with postprandial epigastric bloating and bilious vomiting that is relieved by lying prone or in the knee-chest position. What is the most likely mechanism?
opts: Midgut volvulus around the superior mesenteric artery
Compression of the third part of the duodenum between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery
concept: Superior mesenteric artery (Wilkie) syndrome — duodenal compression after weight loss

stem: A 58-year-old man with acute left lower quadrant pain undergoes emergency laparotomy for generalised peritonitis. The peritoneal cavity is soiled with feculent material from a perforated sigmoid diverticulum. What is the most appropriate surgical procedure?
opts: Hartmann's procedure (resection of the sigmoid with end colostomy)
Simple suture of the perforation with an omental patch
concept: Diverticulitis Hinchey IV (faecal peritonitis) — Hartmann's procedure

stem: A 70-year-old man has sudden severe abdominal and back pain with collapse. He is pale and diaphoretic: blood pressure 80/50 mmHg, heart rate 118/min. A tender, pulsatile epigastric mass is palpable. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Urgent transfer to the operating theatre for laparotomy
Abdominal ultrasound to confirm the mass
Erect chest X-ray to exclude free air
concept: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm — the unstable patient goes straight to the operating theatre

stem: A 44-year-old man with mild acute gallstone pancreatitis is on day 2. His pain has markedly improved, there is no vomiting and bowel sounds have returned. What is the most appropriate nutritional plan?
opts: Keep nil by mouth until the serum amylase normalises
Start oral feeding with a low-fat diet as tolerated
Nasogastric feeding is contraindicated in acute pancreatitis
concept: Acute pancreatitis — early oral/enteral feeding as tolerated (current guideline)

stem: A 50-year-old man with severe acute pancreatitis develops infected pancreatic necrosis confirmed by image-guided aspiration. Which group of organisms is most commonly cultured?
concept: Infected pancreatic necrosis — gut-derived Gram-negative organisms predominate

stem: A 45-year-old woman with known diverticular disease has worsening left lower quadrant pain, fever and generalised tenderness. An erect chest X-ray shows free gas under the right hemidiaphragm. Which investigation is CONTRAINDICATED in this patient?
concept: Suspected colonic perforation — barium enema is contraindicated

stem: Which statement best defines shock in the surgical patient?
opts: Shock is defined by a systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg
Shock is inadequate tissue perfusion; blood pressure may be normal in early (compensated) shock
A normal blood pressure reliably excludes shock
A normalising lactate means resuscitation can be stopped regardless of clinical state
concept: Shock — definition: tissue hypoperfusion, not simply low blood pressure

stem: A 32-year-old man with a stab wound to the abdomen is exsanguinating: blood pressure 65/40 mmHg, heart rate 140/min. He is being wheeled to the operating theatre, but crossmatched blood is not yet available. What should be transfused now?
opts: O-negative packed red cells while crossmatch is pending
Albumin infusion until the blood bank completes the crossmatch
Fresh frozen plasma alone to correct coagulopathy
concept: Haemorrhagic shock — uncrossmatched O-negative blood in exsanguination

stem: A 40-year-old man has acute left lower quadrant pain of 1 day, worse on movement, with no vomiting and no fever. CT shows a 2 cm oval fat-density lesion with a hyperdense rim adjacent to the sigmoid colon at the point of maximal tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Epiploic appendagitis — self-limiting mimic of the acute abdomen

stem: A 62-year-old woman on day 3 after an elective right hemicolectomy has abdominal distension and mild nausea but no significant pain; she passed flatus this morning. Abdominal X-ray shows gas scattered throughout the colon with no dilation and no air-fluid levels. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Supportive care: nasogastric tube if needed, intravenous fluids, analgesia review and ambulation
CT angiography of the mesenteric vessels
concept: Postoperative (paralytic) ileus — recognition and supportive management

stem: A 19-year-old man presents with intermittent fresh rectal bleeding for 6 months. Colonoscopy reveals hundreds of adenomatous polyps carpeting the colon. He has multiple epidermoid cysts on the face and bilateral patches of congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium. His father died of colorectal cancer at age 45. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: FAP — clinical diagnosis (polyposis with extracolonic stigmata)

stem: A 41-year-old woman is diagnosed with adenocarcinoma of the ascending colon. Her mother was treated for endometrial cancer at age 46 and a brother had colon cancer at age 38. Testing of the resected tumour for which abnormality provides the strongest support for Lynch syndrome?
concept: Lynch syndrome — tumour testing (microsatellite instability / mismatch repair)

stem: A 50-year-old asymptomatic man with no family history of colorectal cancer and no personal history of polyps attends for routine health screening. Which one of the following is the most appropriate colorectal cancer screening strategy for this average-risk patient?
opts: CT colonography every 2 years from age 50
concept: Colorectal carcinoma — screening in the average-risk population

stem: A 73-year-old woman presents with progressive fatigue and exertional breathlessness over 3 months. She reports no visible rectal bleeding and no change in bowel habit. Examination shows pallor only. Haemoglobin is 8.4 g/dL with microcytic indices and the faecal immunochemical test is positive. Colonoscopy is most likely to reveal a tumour in which location?
concept: Colorectal carcinoma — right- vs left-sided presentation

stem: A 66-year-old man undergoes an uneventful right hemicolectomy for colon cancer. Histology reports a moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma extending through the muscularis propria into pericolonic tissue (pT3), with 3 of 14 lymph nodes positive (pN1b) and no metastases (M0). What is the most appropriate further management?
concept: Colon cancer — adjuvant treatment of stage III disease

stem: A 64-year-old woman had a curative (R0) resection of a pT3 N0 M0 adenocarcinoma of the sigmoid colon 6 months ago. Which of the following is the most appropriate postoperative surveillance plan?
opts: Serum CEA every 3–6 months for 2–3 years plus colonoscopy at 1 year
Annual serum alpha-fetoprotein with liver ultrasound
concept: Colorectal carcinoma — postoperative surveillance (CEA + colonoscopy)

stem: A 58-year-old woman with left lower quadrant pain, fever of 38.4°C and leukocytosis is diagnosed with acute diverticulitis. CT shows a 4 cm pericolic abscess adjacent to the sigmoid colon, without free intraperitoneal air. She is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate management?
concept: Diverticular disease — Hinchey classification and management of a pericolic abscess

stem: A 55-year-old man is treated successfully for a first episode of uncomplicated acute diverticulitis of the sigmoid colon. His symptoms have fully resolved with antibiotics and dietary modification over the past 3 weeks. What is the most appropriate follow-up?
opts: Colonoscopy in 6–8 weeks to exclude carcinoma
concept: Diverticular disease — exclusion of carcinoma after resolution

stem: A 4-year-old boy passes a small amount of painless bright red blood after defecation, on one occasion. Colonoscopy reveals a single pedunculated polyp in the rectum. Histology shows dilated mucus-filled glands within an inflamed stroma and normal-appearing overlying epithelium. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Polypectomy alone, with no special surveillance if solitary
concept: Juvenile polyp — benign hamartoma and management

stem: A 68-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and chronic constipation presents with a reducible bulge in the right groin that appears on standing and reduces when he lies flat. It does not descend into the scrotum. On examination the cough impulse is felt over the mid-inguinal canal, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. What type of hernia is this?
concept: Inguinal hernia — direct vs indirect anatomy

stem: A 54-year-old woman presents with a small lump in the left groin that is more noticeable after standing. Examination with a finger placed on the pubic tubercle while she coughs shows the lump arising below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, inferior to the inguinal ligament. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Femoral hernia — anatomical localisation

stem: A 79-year-old thin woman with chronic constipation presents with colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and abdominal distension for 48 hours. There is no hernia and no previous abdominal surgery. She reports sharp pain radiating down the medial side of the right thigh when she coughs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Obturator hernia — Howship-Romberg sign in the frail elderly

stem: A 62-year-old woman who had an emergency laparotomy for a perforated peptic ulcer 16 months ago now notices a bulge in her midline scar that has slowly enlarged and becomes uncomfortable on lifting. It is reducible and not tender. She is otherwise fit. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Watchful waiting with an abdominal support belt
Elective mesh repair of the incisional hernia
Weight loss alone before any operative planning
concept: Incisional hernia — indications for elective repair

stem: A 2-month-old boy (born at 34 weeks) is brought in because his mother notices a bulge in the right groin whenever he cries. The bulge reduces easily with gentle pressure. Examination confirms a reducible right indirect inguinal hernia. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Observe and review at school age
Hernia truss until 1 year of age
concept: Paediatric inguinal hernia — timing of repair

stem: A 74-year-old man with a 10-year history of a right inguinal hernia develops colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and abdominal distension. The hernia is now irreducible and tense. The overlying skin is normal, there is no local tenderness, and he is afebrile. What is the most accurate description of this hernia?
concept: Hernia complications — obstructed vs strangulated

stem: A 42-year-old man develops severe acute perianal pain after lifting a heavy object 2 days ago. Examination shows a tender, firm, bluish subcutaneous lump at the anal verge. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Excision of the thrombosed external haemorrhoid
Urgent haemorrhoidectomy of all three columns
concept: Haemorrhoids — thrombosed external haemorrhoid

stem: A 34-year-old man who had a perianal abscess drained 3 months ago now reports intermittent seropurulent discharge from the drainage site. Examination shows an external opening 2 cm from the anal verge, ANTERIOR to the transverse anal line. According to Goodsall's rule, what is the most likely course of the fistula tract?
opts: It runs radially and straight to an internal opening in the same quadrant
It curves posteriorly to open in the posterior midline
It tracks upwards to a supralevator space without an internal opening
It connects to the contralateral anal crypt
concept: Goodsall's rule — fistula tract course

stem: A 35-year-old woman has experienced painful defecation with a few drops of fresh blood for 6 weeks. Examination shows a posterior midline anal fissure with a sentinel skin tag and an oedematous anal papilla. Conservative measures (bulking laxatives and sitz baths) have not helped. What is the most appropriate next treatment?
concept: Chronic anal fissure — medical first-line therapy

stem: A 22-year-old male taxi driver with hirsute buttocks presents with a discharging sinus at the upper end of the natal cleft that has intermittently oozed blood-stained pus for 4 months. There is no acute abscess. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Excision of the sinus tract with open or flap closure
concept: Pilonidal sinus disease — definitive treatment of a chronic sinus

stem: A 79-year-old man presents with massive abdominal distension and absolute constipation. A 'coffee bean' sign on abdominal X-ray confirms sigmoid volvulus, and endoscopic detorsion is successful with prompt resolution of distension. Sigmoidoscopy shows a long, redundant sigmoid colon with viable mucosa. What is the most appropriate further management?
opts: Discharge with laxatives and stool softeners
Elective sigmoid resection during the same admission
Repeat endoscopic detorsion whenever symptoms recur
concept: Sigmoid volvulus — definitive management to prevent recurrence

stem: A 71-year-old woman with chronic constipation presents with sudden colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and absolute constipation. Abdominal X-ray shows a single grossly dilated large bowel loop in the left upper quadrant with two air-fluid levels and dilation of adjacent small bowel. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Caecal volvulus — X-ray pattern

stem: During laparoscopic appendicectomy in a 26-year-old man with clinical acute appendicitis, the appendix is found to be macroscopically normal. No Meckel's diverticulum, inflamed terminal ileum or other pathology is identified. What is the most appropriate action?
opts: Leave the appendix in situ and close
Remove the appendix after completing a careful laparoscopic review
Convert to an open procedure and perform a right hemicolectomy
Abandon surgery and start antibiotics alone
concept: Acute appendicitis — management of a macroscopically normal appendix

stem: A 33-year-old woman undergoes laparoscopic appendicectomy for acute appendicitis. Histology of the specimen shows a 1.2 cm carcinoid tumour confined to the tip of the appendix with clear resection margins. What is the most appropriate further management?
concept: Appendiceal tumours — carcinoid, size-based management

stem: A 74-year-old man develops progressive abdominal distension 4 days after total hip replacement. He passes no stool but small amounts of flatus, and has no vomiting or significant pain. Abdominal X-ray shows dilation of the caecum, ascending and transverse colon with a caecal diameter of 9 cm. CT shows no transition point or obstructing lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome)

stem: A 62-year-old man presents with fresh rectal bleeding and tenesmus for 2 months. Digital rectal examination reveals a firm, ulcerated mass on the anterior rectal wall, and biopsy confirms adenocarcinoma. Which investigation is most useful for local staging to plan treatment?
opts: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
concept: Rectal carcinoma — local staging investigations

stem: A 6-year-old child has a midline neck swelling that moves upward on protrusion of the tongue and on swallowing. It is non-tender and cystic. What is the diagnosis and management?
opts: Thyroglossal duct cyst — Sistrunk procedure (cyst + tract + hyoid)
concept: Thyroglossal duct cyst — midline, moves on tongue protrusion; Sistrunk resection

stem: A 20-year-old presents with a painless, fluctuant swelling in the anterior triangle of the neck, anterior to the sternocleidomastoid. It has been present since childhood and does not move with tongue protrusion. What is it?
concept: Branchial cleft cyst — lateral neck (anterior triangle), no movement on protrusion

stem: A singer undergoes thyroid lobectomy and afterwards reports difficulty hitting high notes and a change in vocal pitch, but no breathiness or hoarseness at rest. Which nerve was most likely injured?
opts: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
concept: External laryngeal nerve injury — loss of pitch/high notes (not hoarseness); RLN = hoarseness

stem: After a total thyroidectomy, a patient develops immediate stridor, respiratory distress, and a fixed midline (paramedian) cord bilaterally. What is the emergency and management?
opts: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury — airway obstruction; urgent tracheostomy/intubation
concept: Bilateral RLN injury — airway emergency (bilateral cord fixation) → tracheostomy

stem: A 38-year-old woman has a 2.5 cm papillary thyroid carcinoma with no distant metastases but with a 0.5 cm suspicious central compartment node. What is the recommended initial surgery?
opts: Total thyroidectomy with central compartment lymph node dissection
concept: Papillary thyroid Ca — total thyroidectomy + central compartment dissection for ≥1 cm / nodal disease

stem: After total thyroidectomy for a 3 cm follicular variant papillary carcinoma with extrathyroidal extension, which adjuvant therapy is indicated?
concept: Differentiated thyroid Ca — adjuvant radioiodine after thyroidectomy

stem: A 60-year-old woman with long-standing Hashimoto thyroiditis develops a rapidly enlarging, painful thyroid mass with compressive symptoms over 2 weeks. Fine-needle aspiration shows atypical lymphoid cells. What is the likely diagnosis and management?
opts: Primary thyroid lymphoma — requires excisional biopsy + chemo/radiotherapy
concept: Thyroid lymphoma — rapid enlargement in Hashimoto; excisional biopsy + chemo/RT

stem: A patient requires reoperation for recurrent thyroid nodules after a previous partial thyroidectomy. Which complication risk is substantially higher than at first surgery?
opts: Recurrent laryngeal nerve and parathyroid injury (distorted planes)
concept: Reoperative thyroid surgery — higher RLN and parathyroid injury risk

stem: A 34-year-old woman with Graves disease and a large multinodular goitre has compressive symptoms and declining response to antithyroid drugs. She is planned for total thyroidectomy. Which pre-operative step is essential to avoid a thyroid storm?
opts: Operate immediately regardless of thyroid state
Achieve euthyroid state with antithyroid drugs + beta-blocker ± Lugol iodine
concept: Graves surgery — must be euthyroid pre-op (ATD + beta-blocker ± iodine) to prevent storm

stem: A patient with primary hyperparathyroidism has a single enlarged parathyroid gland on sestamibi scan and normal other glands on exploration. What is the lesion and procedure?
opts: Solitary parathyroid adenoma — minimally invasive parathyroidectomy
concept: Parathyroid adenoma — solitary > MIP; hyperplasia needs 3.5-gland/subtotal

stem: A patient with long-standing CKD on dialysis develops progressively rising PTH and calcium despite medical therapy and is being evaluated for transplant. What is the underlying process?
opts: Tertiary hyperparathyroidism — autonomous parathyroid hyperplasia from CKD
concept: Tertiary hyperparathyroidism — CKD-driven parathyroid hyperplasia becomes autonomous

stem: A patient with primary hyperparathyroidism suddenly develops severe hypercalcaemia (Ca 15 mg/dL) with confusion, abdominal pain, and dehydration. What is the most urgent definitive treatment if medical measures fail?
concept: Parathyroid crisis — severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia → urgent parathyroidectomy after stabilisation

stem: During thyroid lobectomy, the surgeon must ligate the inferior thyroid artery. Why is careful dissection at this site critical for parathyroid preservation?
opts: It supplies the recurrent laryngeal nerve directly
It is the only blood supply to the thyroid
The inferior thyroid artery supplies the inferior parathyroids; ligate laterally to preserve them
concept: Inferior thyroid artery — supplies inferior parathyroids; ligate laterally to preserve them

stem: A 58-year-old has a 5 cm adrenal mass found incidentally. Biochemical workup excludes Cushing, pheochromocytoma, and aldosteronism. What is the recommendation?
opts: Surgical resection (size >4 cm raises malignancy concern)
concept: Adrenal incidentaloma — resect if >4 cm or functioning; else observe

stem: A 45-year-old with a 3 cm aldosterone-producing adrenal adenoma and refractory hypertension is planned for surgery. What is the preferred approach?
concept: Adrenalectomy — laparoscopic approach for Conn/pheo/Ca after optimisation

stem: A patient develops clear rhinorrhoea and a headache 3 days after transsphenoidal pituitary surgery. What is the most likely complication?
opts: CSF leak from an unsealed sella/sphenoid sinus
concept: Transsphenoidal pituitary surgery — CSF leak (rhinorrhoea) is a key complication

stem: A patient with clinical Cushing syndrome and a normal pituitary MRI is being evaluated before transsphenoidal surgery. Which test helps confirm the source is pituitary (Cushing disease) rather than ectopic ACTH?
opts: Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (BIPSS) showing central:peripheral ACTH gradient
concept: Cushing disease — BIPSS confirms pituitary source before transsphenoidal surgery

stem: Before parathyroidectomy for primary hyperparathyroidism, which pre-operative localisation study is most commonly used to identify the abnormal gland?
concept: Primary HPT — sestamibi (+US) localises adenoma before parathyroidectomy

stem: A patient with Graves disease is prepared for thyroidectomy. In the days before surgery, Lugol's iodine solution is administered. What is its purpose?
opts: Reduce thyroid vascularity and hormone release (easier, safer surgery)
concept: Pre-thyroidectomy iodine (Lugol) — reduces vascularity/hormone release

stem: A patient develops hypocalcaemia with tingling and a positive Chvostek sign on postoperative day 1 after total thyroidectomy, which resolves with calcium. Another has permanent hypocalcaemia requiring lifetime supplements. What explains the difference?
opts: One had Graves, one had cancer
Temporary hypocalcaemia from parathyroid stunning/ischaemia vs permanent from parathyroid excision
concept: Post-thyroidectomy hypocalcaemia — transient (ischaemia/stunning) vs permanent (excised)

stem: What is the single most important preventive measure against thyroid storm in a patient undergoing thyroidectomy for hyperthyroidism?
opts: Operating only when the patient is biochemically euthyroid
Immediate surgery regardless of thyroid state
concept: Thyroid storm — prevented by operating only in euthyroid state (storm prophylaxis)

stem: During total parathyroidectomy for tertiary hyperparathyroidism, the surgeon implants parathyroid tissue into the forearm muscle. What is the purpose?
opts: Preserve parathyroid function and allow future access if needed
concept: Parathyroid autotransplantation — preserves function; forearm site allows re-exploration

stem: A 65-year-old with a long-standing goitre develops exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea, and cough, with a mediastinal mass on chest X-ray extending below the sternal notch. What is the diagnosis and indication?
concept: Substernal goitre — compressive mediastinal extension; surgery indicated

stem: A 70-year-old with a large non-toxic multinodular goitre has progressive dysphagia and tracheal deviation but is euthyroid. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Total or subtotal thyroidectomy for compressive symptoms
concept: Non-toxic MNG — surgery for compressive symptoms (dysphagia/tracheal deviation)

stem: A 50-year-old man has severe hypercalcaemia (Ca 17 mg/dL), a hard, fixed neck mass, and a very high PTH. Imaging shows local invasion. What is the diagnosis and surgery?
opts: Benign parathyroid adenoma — minimally invasive resection
Parathyroid carcinoma — en bloc resection with ipsilateral thyroid lobe
concept: Parathyroid carcinoma — hard fixed invasive mass + very high Ca/PTH → en bloc resection

stem: A 30-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed motor vehicle collision. He is unconscious with snoring respirations and no visible external hemorrhage. During the primary survey, which assessment must be performed first?
opts: Airway assessment with cervical spine protection
Insertion of two large-bore IV cannulas and fluid resuscitation
Full log-roll to examine the spine and back
concept: ATLS primary survey - sequence and first priority

stem: A 24-year-old man is intubated and ventilated after a motorcycle crash. Minutes later his oxygen saturation falls to 82% and his blood pressure drops. He has distended neck veins, absent breath sounds on the left, and tracheal deviation to the right. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
opts: Needle decompression of the left chest
Chest X-ray to check endotracheal tube position
concept: Tension pneumothorax - recognition and immediate decompression

stem: A 45-year-old man is crushed between two vehicles. He has severe chest pain and respiratory distress with SpO2 88% on high-flow oxygen. Inspection shows a segment of the left chest wall moving paradoxically during inspiration, with five ribs fractured in two places. What is the most appropriate initial management?
opts: Emergency open reduction and internal fixation of the flail segment
concept: Flail chest - pathophysiology and initial management

stem: A 29-year-old man sustains a stab wound to the left anterior chest. On examination, air is heard sucking through the wound during inspiration. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Cover the wound with a three-sided occlusive dressing
Apply an airtight dressing sealed on all four sides
Leave the wound exposed to air
Insert a nasogastric tube through the wound
concept: Open (sucking) chest wound - immediate management

stem: A 28-year-old man is stabbed in the right chest. After insertion of a chest drain, 1600 mL of blood drains immediately and his blood pressure remains 85/50 mmHg despite transfusion. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: CT chest to quantify the residual hemothorax
Insertion of a second chest drain
concept: Massive hemothorax - thoracotomy criteria

stem: A 33-year-old man is brought in with a stab wound to the left parasternal area. He is hypotensive with distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds, and FAST shows fluid in the pericardial sac. What is the most appropriate definitive management?
opts: IV fluids and observation in the ICU
concept: Penetrating cardiac trauma - definitive management of tamponade

stem: A 40-year-old man is 5 metres away when an improvised explosive device detonates. He has no external wounds. Examination shows a perforated right tympanic membrane, and over the next hour he develops progressive hypoxia and hemoptysis with diffuse infiltrates on chest X-ray. Which mechanism best explains these injuries?
opts: Quaternary blast injury (burns and toxic fumes)
concept: Blast injury - mechanism classification

stem: A 38-year-old factory worker sustains complete traumatic amputation of the left index finger at the proximal phalanx. The severed part is recovered at the scene. What is the correct method of transporting the amputated part?
opts: Saline-moistened gauze, sealed plastic bag, kept on ice
Direct contact with ice in a sealed container
Immersed in sterile saline on ice
concept: Replantation - preservation of the amputated part

stem: A 26-year-old motorcyclist has an open fracture of the left femur with active pulsatile bleeding from the wound. Direct pressure with dressings has failed to control the hemorrhage and his blood pressure is 85/50 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Apply a pneumatic tourniquet proximal to the wound
Continue direct pressure and elevate the limb
Apply a pneumatic tourniquet distal to the wound
Blindly clamp the bleeding vessel in the wound
concept: Exsanguinating extremity hemorrhage - tourniquet use

stem: A 60 kg woman sustains 30% TBSA burns in a kitchen fire. Using the Parkland formula, how much Ringer lactate should be infused in the first 8 hours after the burn?
concept: Parkland formula - first 8-hour volume

stem: A 6-month-old infant is scalded by hot tea. The burns cover the entire head and both entire upper limbs. Using the age-adjusted (pediatric) assessment of burn surface area, what percentage of TBSA is burned?
concept: Burn surface area - infant modification of the rule of nines
