stem: A 40-year-old woman spills hot cooking oil onto her forearm. The burn is blistered with a mottled red-and-white base, sluggish capillary refill, and reduced but present pain sensation on pinprick. What is the most likely burn depth?
concept: Burn depth - deep partial (deep dermal) burns

stem: A 52-year-old man is rescued from a burning building. He is confused with soot around the mouth, and despite high-flow 100% oxygen he remains confused with a severe lactic acidosis. Carboxyhemoglobin is 8%. What is the most appropriate treatment?
concept: Smoke inhalation - cyanide poisoning

stem: A 24-year-old electrician touches a live high-voltage cable and sustains an electrical injury with a small charred entry wound on the right palm and dark urine. He is hemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate disposition?
opts: Transfer to a regional burn center
Outpatient wound care with review in 1 week
Immediate primary closure of the entry wound
concept: Electrical burns - burn center referral

stem: A 30-year-old man is extricated after being pinned under a collapsed wall for 4 hours. He has a tense, swollen right thigh and dark brown urine. ECG shows peaked T waves and a widened QRS complex. What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?
opts: IV normal saline at maintenance rate
concept: Crush syndrome - hyperkalemia management

stem: A 22-year-old man with a severe head injury and GCS 8 is intubated, ventilated, and sedated for transport. The team will continue neurological monitoring. Which component of the GCS can no longer be reliably assessed?
concept: GCS - effect of intubation on scoring

stem: A 35-year-old man fell 3 metres from a ladder onto concrete, losing consciousness briefly at the scene. He is now alert and oriented with GCS 15, no focal deficit, and no vomiting. Applying the Canadian CT Head Rule, what is the most appropriate next step?
concept: Minor head injury - CT decision rules

stem: A 34-year-old man is struck by a car while crossing the road. He is hypotensive (BP 82/50 mmHg) with a tender, unstable pelvis, and FAST is negative. What is the most appropriate immediate step to control hemorrhage?
opts: Apply a pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters
Apply a pelvic binder at the level of the iliac crests
concept: Pelvic fracture hemorrhage - circumferential pelvic compression

stem: A 55-year-old woman is brought in after a motor vehicle collision with a closed femoral fracture. Heart rate is 130/min, blood pressure 85/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, and urine output is 20 mL/hour; she is confused. What percentage of blood volume has she most likely lost, and what is the appropriate initial therapy?
concept: Classes of hemorrhagic shock - class III

stem: A 28-year-old man is a restrained driver in a low-speed rear-end collision. He is awake, alert, sober, and has no midline cervical tenderness, no neurological deficit, and no distracting injury. What is the most appropriate management of his cervical spine?
concept: Cervical spine - clinical clearance (NEXUS criteria)

stem: A 47-year-old man with severe facial burns and progressive airway edema cannot be intubated after two laryngoscopy attempts, and bag-mask ventilation fails to achieve oxygen saturation above 60%. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: A third laryngoscopy attempt with a different blade
Insertion of a laryngeal mask airway alone
concept: Cannot-intubate-cannot-oxygenate (CICO) - surgical airway

stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought with scalds to both feet and lower legs. The burns have a sharp, symmetrical stocking distribution with no splash marks; the mother says he climbed into a hot bath, and the family presents 2 days after the injury. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Admit the child and initiate a child protection (safeguarding) referral
Reassure the family and discharge with outpatient dressings
Prescribe oral antibiotics and review in 1 week
Apply topical cream and send home
concept: Burns in children - non-accidental injury

stem: A 41-year-old man with exsanguinating hemorrhage from a liver laceration is started on a massive transfusion protocol. Which resuscitation strategy is most appropriate?
opts: Red cells, plasma, and platelets in a 1:1:1 ratio
Red cells alone until cross-match is complete
Crystalloid at 3 times the estimated blood loss
Plasma alone for the first 4 units
concept: Massive transfusion - balanced ratio resuscitation

stem: A 32-year-old man has 35% TBSA deep partial-thickness and full-thickness burns. He is resuscitated, hemodynamically stable, and the wounds are not yet colonized. What is the preferred definitive surgical strategy?
opts: Daily dressings until eschars separate spontaneously
Delayed grafting after 3 weeks of topical therapy
concept: Burn wound - early excision and grafting

stem: A 19-year-old man sustains a severe traumatic brain injury (GCS 7) in a motorcycle crash and is admitted to the intensive care unit. Which statement about seizure prophylaxis is correct?
opts: An antiepileptic is given for the first 7 days only - it reduces early seizures but not late epilepsy
Antiepileptics are continued lifelong to prevent post-traumatic epilepsy
Antiepileptics are contraindicated after traumatic brain injury
Prophylaxis is reserved for penetrating brain injuries
concept: Post-traumatic seizures - prophylaxis window

stem: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden onset of severe pain and numbness of the right leg that began 3 hours ago. On examination, the right foot is pale and cold, with reduced sensation to light touch but preserved motor power. Venous Doppler shows audible flow in the right femoral and popliteal veins, and arterial signals are audible over the right posterior tibial artery. The right calf is not firm. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Observe for 24 hours with serial examination
Heparin alone and reassess in the morning
concept: Rutherford category IIa (viable, marginally threatened) acute limb ischaemia — limb is salvageable and requires urgent revascularization; irreversible ischaemia (grade III) is the only category warranting primary amputation.

stem: A 27-year-old man who has smoked 20 cigarettes daily since age 16 presents with a 6-month history of right foot claudication and a non-healing ulcer on the right great toe. Radial pulses are normal, but distal pedal pulses are absent. Angiography shows segmental occlusion of the distal tibial and pedal arteries with corkscrew collaterals, and normal proximal vessels. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
opts: Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty of the tibial vessels
concept: Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) — a segmental inflammatory-occlusive disease of small- and medium-sized vessels in young male smokers; distal, with normal proximal pulses; the only effective treatment is complete smoking cessation.

stem: A 64-year-old diabetic man reports severe burning pain in the left foot at night, which is relieved by hanging the foot over the edge of the bed. He has a non-healing ulcer on the left heel. On examination the foot is cold and hairless, and it turns deep red when dependant. Femoral and popliteal pulses are palpable but the dorsalis pedis pulse is absent. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Graduated compression stockings with leg elevation at night
Venous duplex ultrasonography to exclude deep vein thrombosis
Duplex arterial assessment and referral for revascularization
Topical antibiotics and a pressure-relieving dressing alone
concept: Critical limb ischaemia — Fontaine stage III (rest pain) with dependent rubor; the pain and rubor are arterial, so management is arterial imaging and revascularization — never venous measures.

stem: A 71-year-old man collapses at home with sudden severe abdominal and back pain. On arrival he is pale and sweaty, with a blood pressure of 78/50 mmHg, pulse 128/min, and a pulsatile abdominal mass. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Urgent CT angiography of the aorta to confirm the diagnosis
Immediate transfer to the operating theatre for laparotomy
Abdominal ultrasound scan in the emergency department
Intravenous fluids and repeat examination in 30 minutes
concept: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm — a clinical diagnosis; in a shocked patient with a pulsatile mass, transfer to the operating theatre precedes any imaging.

stem: A 58-year-old hypertensive man presents with sudden severe tearing interscapular back pain that began 2 hours ago. Blood pressure is 165/95 mmHg in both arms. Chest x-ray shows a widened mediastinum, and CT angiography shows an aortic dissection flap in the descending thoracic aorta without involvement of the ascending aorta and without malperfusion. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Emergency open surgical repair of the descending aorta
Urgent replacement of the ascending aorta and aortic arch
Aggressive blood pressure control with a beta-blocker and analgesia
Immediate endovascular stenting of the entire thoracic aorta
concept: Type B aortic dissection (descending aorta) — uncomplicated type B is managed medically (heart-rate and blood-pressure control), whereas surgery is reserved for complicated type B (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain) or type A.

stem: A 66-year-old man is found on routine screening duplex ultrasonography to have a 75% asymptomatic right internal carotid artery stenosis. He has no history of transient ischaemic attacks or stroke, is an ex-smoker, and has well-controlled hypertension. He remains free of neurological symptoms. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Aggressive medical therapy with regular surveillance
concept: Asymptomatic carotid stenosis — evidence does not support routine intervention; intensive medical therapy (antiplatelet, statin, blood-pressure control, smoking cessation) with surveillance is standard; CEA within 2 weeks is the rule for symptomatic high-grade stenosis.

stem: A 72-year-old man is found to have a pulsatile swelling in the right popliteal fossa on routine examination. Doppler ultrasound shows a popliteal artery aneurysm of 3 cm diameter containing thrombus. A similar but smaller aneurysm is found on the left, and abdominal ultrasound reveals a 4 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm. There is no distal embolisation and the foot is well perfused. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Aspirin and annual ultrasound surveillance of both popliteal aneurysms
Urgent thrombolysis of the right popliteal aneurysm
Elective repair of the right popliteal aneurysm
Aspiration of the swelling under ultrasound guidance
concept: Popliteal artery aneurysm — elective repair is indicated for symptomatic or large (>2 cm) aneurysms, especially with intraluminal thrombus, because of the risk of thrombosis and embolism; bilateral disease and aortic aneurysm association mandate assessment.

stem: A 70-year-old man develops a 3-day history of painful bluish discolouration of the toes of both feet, one day after undergoing coronary angiography. The feet are warm with palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses. There is an area of early gangrene on the tip of the right great toe. His renal function has begun to deteriorate. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Cholesterol atheroembolism (blue toe syndrome) — showering of cholesterol crystals from a disrupted atheromatous plaque (here after angiography) causing small-vessel occlusion with palpable pulses, livedo, and acute kidney injury.

stem: A 52-year-old obese woman presents with a 2-day history of severe painful swelling of the entire right leg. The leg is tense, cyanotic, and covered with fluid-filled blisters; capillary refill is sluggish and the right foot is cool with absent pedal pulses. Doppler confirms extensive iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin alone for 5 days
Insertion of an inferior vena cava filter before anticoagulation
Urgent catheter-directed thrombolysis or surgical thrombectomy
Graduated compression bandaging with leg elevation
concept: Phlegmasia cerulea dolens — massive iliofemoral DVT with venous gangrene; anticoagulation alone is insufficient, and urgent thrombus removal (thrombolysis or thrombectomy) is required to prevent limb loss.

stem: A 61-year-old woman has a 4-month history of an itchy, aching ulcer above the right medial malleolus. The surrounding skin is brown and indurated, and the ankle is mildly swollen at the end of the day. The dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line management?
opts: Endovenous laser ablation of the great saphenous vein
Split-thickness skin grafting of the ulcer
Strict leg elevation with avoidance of compression
concept: Venous leg ulcer — the gaiter-area ulcer with hemosiderin staining and normal pulses is venous; graduated compression is the cornerstone first-line treatment, with surgery reserved for refractory cases.

stem: A 34-year-old intravenous drug user presents with fever, rigors, and a tender, erythematous, cord-like vein on the volar forearm at an old injection site. Blood cultures are drawn. Which organism is most likely to be isolated?
concept: Septic thrombophlebitis in an IV drug user — S. aureus (including MRSA) is the dominant pathogen in injection-site suppurative thrombophlebitis and requires drainage/vein excision plus targeted antibiotics.

stem: A 19-year-old competitive swimmer presents with acute painful swelling of the right arm and dilated superficial veins over the shoulder, which began after an intensive training session 2 days ago. He has no risk factors for malignancy and no central venous catheters. Venography confirms axillary-subclavian vein thrombosis. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Anticoagulation for 3 months and arm elevation
Catheter-directed thrombolysis followed by first-rib decompression
Immediate surgical excision of the thrombosed vein segment
concept: Paget-Schroetter syndrome (effort thrombosis of the axillary-subclavian vein) — in a young, otherwise healthy patient, treatment is aggressive: catheter-directed thrombolysis then surgical decompression of the thoracic outlet (first-rib resection).

stem: A 45-year-old man undergoing general anaesthesia for laparoscopic cholecystectomy has a laryngeal mask airway (LMA) for airway management. Twenty minutes into the procedure he regurgitates, oxygen saturation falls to 82%, and ventilation through the LMA becomes increasingly difficult with audible gurgling. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Increase the fresh gas flow and deepen anaesthesia
Remove the LMA, suction the oropharynx, and intubate the trachea
Continue positive-pressure ventilation through the LMA
Apply cricoid pressure and leave the LMA in situ
concept: Aspiration under a supraglottic airway — an LMA does not protect the trachea; on regurgitation with desaturation, the airway must be converted to a definitive cuffed endotracheal tube after suctioning.

stem: A 24-year-old man involved in a road traffic accident has a clinically diagnosed left tension pneumothorax. A needle decompression is performed at the second intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line, and there is an immediate rush of air with improvement in oxygen saturation and blood pressure. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Remove the needle and observe in the resuscitation bay
Insert a formal tube thoracostomy with underwater seal drainage
Repeat needle decompression every 30 minutes as needed
Urgent chest CT to confirm re-expansion before further action
concept: Tension pneumothorax — needle decompression is only a temporising bridge; a definitive tube thoracostomy must follow once the patient is stabilised.

stem: A 38-year-old man with a severe panfacial fracture is brought to the emergency department unconscious and apnoeic. Two rapid attempts at direct laryngoscopy and intubation have failed, and bag-mask ventilation is impossible due to massive facial swelling. Oxygen saturation is falling. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: A third attempt at direct laryngoscopy with a different blade
Emergency formal tracheostomy with full dissection
Insertion of a nasopharyngeal airway and continued bagging
concept: Cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate (CICO) — the rescue pathway is surgical cricothyroidotomy: it is fast, safe, and the only timely airway in a crashing patient with facial trauma.

stem: A 54-year-old woman who underwent tracheostomy 3 weeks ago for prolonged ventilation develops sudden, brisk, bright-red bleeding from the tracheostomy site and oropharynx. The bleeding is intermittent but profuse, and the patient is becoming hypotensive and tachycardic. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Erosion of the tracheostomy tube into the innominate artery
Simple granulation tissue bleeding at the stoma
concept: Tracheo-innominate artery fistula — a catastrophic late complication of tracheostomy (often 2–4 weeks, at or below the cuff level): sudden copious bright-red bleeding requires immediate overinflation of the cuff and surgical intervention.

stem: A 3-year-old boy suddenly develops coughing and stridor while eating peanuts. On arrival he is in respiratory distress: the right chest is hyper-resonant with diminished breath sounds, and the trachea is shifted to the left. Oxygen saturation is 92% and rising with positioning efforts. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Immediate needle decompression of the right chest
Chest tube thoracostomy on the right
concept: Foreign body aspiration in a child — a ball-valve peanut produces obstructive hyperinflation and mediastinal shift that mimics tension pneumothorax; the treatment is rigid bronchoscopic removal, not chest decompression.

stem: A 50-year-old man develops inspiratory stridor, suprasternal retraction, and oxygen desaturation to 88% immediately after tracheal extubation following a thyroidectomy. He is making vigorous respiratory efforts but no air is entering the lungs. There is no rash, bronchospasm, or facial oedema. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Jaw thrust with 100% oxygen and continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP)
concept: Post-extubation laryngospasm — noisy inspiratory effort with no airflow, no rash/bronchospasm = laryngospasm; first-line is jaw thrust with CPAP and 100% oxygen; pharmacological rescue is second-line.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with 3 days of progressive painful submandibular swelling, trismus, and a swollen, elevated tongue, with drooling and muffled ('hot potato') voice. He is febrile and sitting upright. Flexible nasoendoscopy shows oedematous supraglottic structures. How should his airway be secured?
opts: Rapid-sequence induction with direct laryngoscopy and intubation
Blind nasotracheal intubation in the supine position
Bag-mask ventilation followed by oral intubation once relaxed
concept: Ludwig angina — deep neck space infection with threatened airway; the feared error is losing the airway during induction; awake fibreoptic intubation (or awake tracheostomy) while the patient still breathes spontaneously is the standard approach.

stem: A 54-year-old man receiving cefazolin for wound prophylaxis during surgery develops, within minutes of the infusion, sudden hypotension to 68/40 mmHg, tachycardia, generalised flushing and urticaria, audible wheeze, and increased airway pressures with falling oxygen saturation. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
concept: Perioperative anaphylaxis — the first-line drug is adrenaline (IM or IV bolus depending on severity/circulation), given BEFORE steroids and antihistamines; fluids follow adrenaline.

stem: A 29-year-old man arrives after being stabbed in the left chest. He is pale, tachycardic (130/min), and hypotensive (95/65 mmHg). Breath sounds are absent on the left with dullness to percussion. The trachea is central and his neck veins are flat. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Emergency chest CT to quantify the haemothorax
Large-bore tube thoracostomy on the left
concept: Massive haemothorax after penetrating trauma — clinically evident by absent breath sounds with dullness and shock; in the unstable patient, tube thoracostomy precedes imaging; flat neck veins (not distended) point to hypovolaemia from blood loss rather than tamponade.

stem: A 65-year-old man with severe pneumonia has been mechanically ventilated for 12 days and is expected to require several more weeks of weaning. He is otherwise haemodynamically stable. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention to facilitate weaning?
opts: Continued high-dose sedation with daily sedation breaks
concept: Tracheostomy timing — anticipated prolonged ventilation beyond roughly 10–14 days is an indication for tracheostomy, which eases weaning, suctioning, and communication.

stem: During general anaesthesia with sevoflurane and suxamethonium for an emergency appendicectomy, a 24-year-old man develops generalised muscle rigidity, a rise in end-tidal carbon dioxide to 78 mmHg, and tachycardia. Temperature climbs to 39.5°C. The triggering agents are stopped immediately and the team is called. Which of the following drugs should be administered next?
concept: Malignant hyperthermia — after stopping triggers, the next step is dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV (repeated up to 10 mg/kg); dantrolene is IV only, and verapamil is contraindicated with dantrolene.

stem: A 68-year-old unconscious patient in the emergency department requires airway support after a massive stroke. Which of the following devices provides a definitive airway?
opts: Cuffed endotracheal tube placed through the vocal cords
concept: Definitive airway — a cuffed tube (endotracheal or tracheostomy) placed in the trachea is the only definitive airway; supraglottic and pharyngeal adjuncts are temporising.

stem: A 32-year-old woman in her third trimester of pregnancy is found on ultrasound, performed for abdominal pain, to have a 2.2 cm splenic artery aneurysm. She is otherwise asymptomatic and haemodynamically normal. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Treatment, because of the high risk of rupture in pregnancy
Conservative management with blood pressure control only
concept: Splenic artery aneurysm in pregnancy — pregnancy (especially third trimester) markedly increases rupture risk, with high maternal and fetal mortality; even a small aneurysm in a pregnant woman warrants treatment.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with his first renal colic. Non-contrast CT shows a radio-opaque stone in the left renal pelvis. Which is the most common composition of such stones?
concept: Calcium oxalate — most common renal stone (~80%), radio-opaque

stem: A 50-year-old man with gout presents with renal colic. Plain abdominal X-ray shows no visible stone, but CT confirms a renal calculus. What is the most likely composition and treatment principle?
opts: Uric acid — radiolucent, treat with urine alkalinization
Calcium oxalate — radio-opaque, treat with thiazide
Struvite — infected urine, treat with antibiotics alone
Cystine — hereditary, treat with hydration only
concept: Uric acid stone — radiolucent, gout association, alkalinize urine

stem: A 19-year-old with a history of childhood renal stones has a stone analysis showing hexagonal crystals. Which inheritance pattern and treatment is correct?
concept: Cystine stone — hereditary (cystinuria), hexagon crystals, penicillamine

stem: A 40-year-old woman with Crohn disease (extensive ileal resection) develops recurrent calcium oxalate stones. What is the underlying mechanism?
concept: Enteric hyperoxaluria — fat malabsorption → increased oxalate absorption

stem: A 55-year-old woman with recurrent renal stones is found to have hypercalcaemia with low phosphate and elevated PTH. Which stone type is she forming?
concept: Primary hyperparathyroidism — hypercalciuria → calcium stones (bones, stones, groans)

stem: A 58-year-old smoker presents with painless gross haematuria, left flank pain, and a palpable abdominal mass. CT shows a 9 cm heterogeneous renal mass extending into the renal vein. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Transitional cell carcinoma of the renal pelvis
concept: Renal cell carcinoma — painless haematuria + flank mass + paraneoplastic, smoking

stem: A 3-year-old child is found to have a large, smooth, unilateral abdominal mass that does not cross the midline. There is no haematuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Wilms tumour — pediatric abdominal mass <5 years, unilateral, smooth

stem: A 60-year-old heavy smoker presents with painless gross haematuria. Cystoscopy is normal, but retrograde pyelography shows a filling defect in the renal pelvis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Transitional cell carcinoma of the renal pelvis
concept: Upper-tract transitional cell carcinoma — smoking, haematuria, filling defect

stem: A 28-year-old man has a painless testicular mass. Tumour markers show an elevated alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and normal human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG). Which histological category does this favour?
concept: Testicular germ cell tumour — AFP elevated implies non-seminomatous component

stem: A 1-year-old boy has an undescended right testis that has not spontaneously descended. What is the most important long-term concern and management?
opts: No cancer risk; observe until adulthood
Increased testicular cancer risk + infertility; orchiopexy before puberty
Hormone therapy cures the cancer risk
concept: Cryptorchidism — infertility + cancer risk; orchiopexy (not orchiectomy)

stem: A 26-year-old man presents with infertility and a 'bag of worms' sensation in the left scrotum that diminishes when supine. What is the most likely finding and association?
opts: Left varicocele — dilated pampiniform plexus; associated with left RCC
concept: Varicocele — left-sided (venous drainage), infertility, adult right-side suggests RCC

stem: A couple presents with infertility. The man has a low semen volume and a left varicocele on exam. Which initial step is most appropriate?
opts: Semen analysis; correct varicocele if present before assisted reproduction
concept: Male infertility — semen analysis first; varicocele correction improves fertility

stem: A 60-year-old man with poor hygiene has inability to retract the foreskin over the glans, with no acute pain or swelling. A younger man presents acutely with a retracted foreskin trapped behind the glans with pain and oedema. Which pairing is correct?
concept: Phimosis vs paraphimosis — cannot retract vs trapped retracted foreskin

stem: A 55-year-old uncircumcised man presents with a non-healing ulcerative lesion on the glans penis. Which is the strongest associated risk factor?
opts: Poor hygiene / phimosis with HPV infection
concept: Penile cancer — HPV + phimosis/poor hygiene; ulcer on glans

stem: A 50-year-old man reports a progressively curved, painful erection with a palpable firm band on the dorsal penis. What is the diagnosis?
concept: Peyronie disease — fibrous plaque causing penile curvature

stem: A 30-year-old man presents with dysuria, fever, and perineal pain; the prostate is tender and boggy on exam. What is the most appropriate initial antibiotic?
concept: Acute bacterial prostatitis — fluoroquinolone, systemic symptoms

stem: A 24-year-old pregnant woman at 16 weeks is found to have asymptomatic bacteriuria on screening. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Treat with a pregnancy-safe antibiotic (e.g., nitrofurantoin/cephalexin)
concept: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy — treat to prevent pyelonephritis

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with fever, flank pain, and costovertebral angle tenderness. Urinalysis shows leucocytes and nitrites. What is the most likely causative organism?
concept: Acute pyelonephritis — E. coli is the most common pathogen

stem: A 70-year-old woman with a urinary catheter develops fever, rigors, and hypotension with a lactate of 3.2 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Intravenous antibiotics + vasopressors for septic shock
concept: Urosepsis — source of septic shock; antibiotics + vasopressors

stem: In which of the following patients is treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria clearly indicated?
opts: An elderly man in a nursing home
A young woman with a single positive screen
concept: Asymptomatic bacteriuria — treat in pregnancy and before urologic procedures

stem: A 25-year-old man with a T6 spinal cord injury has recurrent urinary tract infections and incomplete emptying. Which management is most appropriate?
concept: Neurogenic bladder — intermittent catheterization to protect upper tracts

stem: A 30-year-old man with a cervical spinal cord injury suddenly develops a severe headache, sweating, and a blood pressure of 200/110 mmHg. The trigger is most commonly:
opts: Bladder distension (full catheter bag / blocked catheter)
concept: Autonomic dysreflexia — bladder distension is the most common trigger

stem: An 80-year-old man with long-standing bladder outlet obstruction has constant dribbling incontinence with a palpable bladder. Which type of incontinence is this?
concept: Overflow incontinence — chronic retention → dribbling, palpable bladder

stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of recurrent urethral discharge and prior catheterisation has a weak stream, terminal dribbling, and a palpable bladder. What is the most likely cause?
concept: Urethral stricture — obstructive voiding from scarring (catheter/trauma/STD)

stem: During a hysterectomy, the ureter is most commonly injured at which anatomical relationship?
opts: Where it crosses under the uterine artery ('water under the bridge')
In the posterior abdominal wall lateral to psoas
concept: Iatrogenic ureteric injury — at the uterine artery crossing during pelvic surgery

stem: A 26-year-old G1P0 at 20 weeks gestation presents with painless fresh vaginal bleeding. She is Rh-negative and her partner is Rh-positive. Ultrasound confirms a live fetus with no obvious cause for the bleed. Within what time window must anti-D immunoglobulin be administered?
concept: Anti-D prophylaxis — timing after a sensitising event in pregnancy

stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 at 33 weeks presents with sudden severe constant abdominal pain and dark red vaginal bleeding. The uterus is firm and tender. Fetal heart sounds are absent and ultrasound confirms intrauterine fetal demise. Her blood pressure is 115/75 mmHg and the clotting screen is normal. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Vaginal delivery with close monitoring of coagulation status
Expectant management with delivery at 34 weeks
concept: Placental abruption with intrauterine fetal demise — mode of delivery

stem: A 24-year-old primigravida at 35 weeks presents with headache and a blood pressure of 172/112 mmHg confirmed on two readings 15 minutes apart, with 3+ proteinuria. Which medication is most appropriate for immediate blood pressure control?
concept: Severe pre-eclampsia — first-line antihypertensive (labetalol)

stem: A 29-year-old G2P1 at 16 weeks undergoes an ultrasound that reports suboptimal fetal cardiac views. When is the optimally timed detailed fetal anomaly scan performed?
concept: Antenatal screening — timing of the fetal anomaly scan

stem: A 27-year-old woman with a BMI of 32 kg/m² and a first-degree relative with diabetes is at 26 weeks gestation; her fasting glucose was normal at booking. Which test is most appropriate for screening for gestational diabetes?
concept: Gestational diabetes — screening and diagnostic test

stem: A 30-year-old woman at 29 weeks was diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 26 weeks and started on dietary therapy with glucose monitoring. Her fasting glucose is 4.9 mmol/L and her 2-hour postprandial glucose is 6.5 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Continue diet and lifestyle measures with glucose monitoring
concept: Gestational diabetes — stepwise management (diet first)

stem: A 29-year-old primigravida at term in established labour is receiving an oxytocin infusion. The CTG shows uniform decelerations that begin after the peak of each contraction and return slowly to baseline, with reduced baseline variability. Contractions are every 2 minutes. What is the single most appropriate first action?
opts: Stop the oxytocin infusion and reposition the woman left lateral with oxygen
Proceed directly to emergency caesarean section
concept: Intrapartum fetal monitoring — late decelerations (uteroplacental insufficiency)

stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 at 37 weeks with an uncomplicated pregnancy has a CTG that shows a smooth, regular, sine-wave pattern of the fetal heart rate at 130 bpm with no beat-to-beat variability. Which condition is most likely to be associated with this pattern?
concept: Sinusoidal CTG pattern — fetal anaemia

stem: A 27-year-old primigravida in established labour has a partograph whose cervicometric progress line has crossed the action line. Contractions are irregular and weak, and the fetal heart is reassuring. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Continue expectant monitoring for another 4 hours
concept: Progress of labour — partograph action line and augmentation

stem: A 23-year-old G2P1 at 31 weeks presents with preterm prelabour rupture of membranes. She is not in labour, the fetus is well, and there are no signs of chorioamnionitis. Corticosteroids have been given. Which additional management is most appropriate?
concept: PPROM — latency antibiotics (erythromycin)

stem: During a vaginal delivery at 39 weeks of a 4.2 kg baby, the head delivers but the anterior shoulder remains impacted behind the symphysis pubis (turtle sign). McRoberts manoeuvre and suprapubic pressure have failed. Which of the following is contraindicated in this situation?
opts: All-fours position with continued suprapubic pressure
concept: Shoulder dystocia — what NOT to do (fundal pressure)

stem: A 30-year-old G2P1 is in active labour. Immediately after spontaneous rupture of membranes, the umbilical cord is seen at the introitus and the fetal heart rate drops to 60 bpm. The cervix is fully dilated and the vertex is at +2 station with no caput. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Immediate assisted vaginal delivery (vacuum or forceps)
Manual replacement of the cord with oxytocin augmentation
Transfer to theatre with CTG monitoring only
concept: Cord prolapse at full dilatation — expedited vaginal delivery

stem: A 33-year-old G3P2 has a vaginal delivery and develops postpartum haemorrhage from uterine atony. Oxytocin and ergometrine have been given with uterine massage ongoing, but total blood loss reaches 1400 mL. Which adjunct should be given urgently?
opts: Oral tranexamic acid 500 mg twice daily
concept: Postpartum haemorrhage — tranexamic acid (time-critical adjunct)

stem: A 36-year-old G6P5 (grand multipara) in labour at term for 16 hours develops sudden severe constant suprapubic pain. Contractions have stopped and the fetal heart rate is 90 bpm. The abdomen is tender with a distended lower segment, and on vaginal examination the presenting part, previously engaged, is no longer felt. What is the most likely diagnosis and management?
opts: Cord prolapse — elevate the presenting part
Bandl's ring — wait for spontaneous resolution
concept: Uterine rupture in obstructed labour (unscarred uterus) — diagnosis and management

stem: A 24-year-old with severe pre-eclampsia at 34 weeks receives the standard 4 g intravenous magnesium sulfate loading dose. Which maintenance infusion rate is most appropriate?
concept: Magnesium sulfate — maintenance infusion rate

stem: A 38-year-old G1P0 at 12 weeks gestation has a first-trimester combined screening result indicating high risk of trisomy 21, and requests definitive prenatal diagnosis. Which procedure is most appropriate at this gestation?
concept: Prenatal diagnosis — CVS timing (10-13 weeks) vs amniocentesis (15-20 weeks)

stem: A 28-year-old primigravida in labour at term has a vaginal examination that reveals a face presentation with the chin (mentum) directed posteriorly. The cervix is 8 cm dilated and the fetal heart is reassuring. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Allow labour to continue — vaginal delivery is expected
concept: Face presentation — mentum posterior requires caesarean

stem: A 25-year-old G1P0 at term has a prolonged second stage of labour. The fetal head is vertex at +2 station. Which of the following findings would PREVENT instrumental (vacuum or forceps) vaginal delivery?
concept: Instrumental delivery — absolute prerequisites and contraindications

stem: A 34-year-old woman has an uncomplicated monochorionic diamniotic (MCDA) twin pregnancy at 34 weeks. When is planned delivery recommended for uncomplicated monochorionic diamniotic twins?
concept: Multiple pregnancy — delivery timing by chorionicity

stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 at 30 weeks is in established preterm labour with the cervix 5 cm dilated; delivery is expected within hours. Betamethasone has been given. Why is magnesium sulfate being administered at this point?
opts: Uterine relaxation before external cephalic version
concept: Preterm labour — magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection

stem: A 22-year-old primigravida at 10 weeks has been vomiting several times daily for 3 weeks, with 4 kg weight loss and ketonuria. She is dehydrated and being admitted for intravenous fluids. Which of the following should be given BEFORE any intravenous dextrose?
concept: Hyperemesis gravidarum — thiamine before dextrose (Wernicke prophylaxis)

stem: A 31-year-old G2P1 at 33 weeks has a fundal height 4 cm below dates on two consecutive visits, with normal blood pressure. Ultrasound shows an estimated fetal weight below the 3rd centile, oligohydramnios, and absent end-diastolic flow in the umbilical artery Doppler. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Give antenatal corticosteroids and plan delivery
Repeat CTG in 2 weeks and recheck growth
Reassure the mother — constitutionally small baby
concept: Fetal growth restriction — absent end-diastolic flow and delivery planning

stem: A 29-year-old G2P1 at 32 weeks presents with intense itching, worst at night and affecting the palms and soles, for 2 weeks. There is no rash, and liver transaminases are normal. Fasting serum bile acids are 40 µmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy — diagnosis

stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 at 37 weeks had a positive group B streptococcus (GBS) vaginal swab at 36 weeks. She is now in labour with ruptured membranes for 2 hours and is asymptomatic — no fever and no uterine tenderness. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: A 7-day course of oral amoxicillin at home
concept: Group B streptococcus — intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis

stem: A 32-year-old G2P1 who had one previous lower-segment caesarean section is now at 39 weeks with a single vertex fetus, estimated fetal weight 3.3 kg, and no other complications. She asks about her options for this delivery. What is the most appropriate counselling?
opts: Trial of labour can be offered — discuss the approximately 0.5% risk of uterine rupture
Elective repeat caesarean is the only safe option
External cephalic version should be offered first
Vaginal birth is contraindicated after any caesarean section
concept: Previous caesarean — VBAC (trial of labour) counselling

stem: A 31-year-old woman, G2P1, at 20 weeks of gestation with a known 8 cm anterior intramural fibroid presents with acute, sharply localized pain over the mass and a low-grade fever of 37.9°C for 6 hours. The uterus away from the mass is soft, there is no vaginal bleeding, and the fetal heart is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis and management?
opts: Red degeneration of the fibroid — analgesia, hydration and observation
Torsion of a pedunculated fibroid — urgent myomectomy
concept: Uterine fibroids — red (carneous) degeneration in pregnancy

stem: A 42-year-old woman with regular cycles has had progressively heavy, painful periods for 3 years. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a diffusely and uniformly enlarged uterus with no focal mass. MRI shows thickening of the junctional zone to 14 mm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Adenomyosis — imaging diagnosis (junctional zone)

stem: A 26-year-old woman underwent suction evacuation of a complete hydatidiform mole 10 weeks ago. Her β-hCG fell from 180,000 to 400 IU/L, but four consecutive weekly values have been 400–420 IU/L. She has no vaginal bleeding and the uterus is normal on examination. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Proceed to gestational trophoblastic neoplasia staging and chemotherapy
concept: Post-molar gestational trophoblastic neoplasia — diagnosis (hCG plateau)

stem: A 20-year-old university student who is sexually active requests contraception. She often forgets daily pills, wants reliable protection for the next 3 years that she can stop at any time, and prefers to avoid anything inserted vaginally. Her blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg and BMI is 22 kg/m². She has no medical problems. Which contraceptive is most appropriate?
concept: Contraception — long-acting reversible method selection (subdermal implant)

stem: A 33-year-old woman presents with heavy menstrual bleeding and intermenstrual spotting for 5 months. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 1.8 cm echogenic lesion within the uterine cavity whose exact origin cannot be determined. Which investigation best distinguishes a polyp from a submucous fibroid?
concept: Abnormal uterine bleeding (PALM-COEIN) — polyp vs submucous fibroid localisation

stem: A 26-year-old woman with polycystic ovary syndrome (oligomenorrhea, hirsutism and acne; BMI 28 kg/m²) has only 3–4 periods a year. She is sexually active and requests contraception; she does not wish to conceive. Which management best protects her endometrium and addresses her symptoms?
opts: Ten-day courses of progestogen alone each month
concept: PCOS — endometrial protection and symptom control when not seeking pregnancy

stem: A 31-year-old woman with stage II endometriosis diagnosed at laparoscopy has been trying to conceive for 2 years. Her partner's semen analysis is normal and tubal patency is confirmed. A colleague suggested GnRH agonist therapy. Which management is most appropriate to improve her chance of conception?
opts: GnRH agonist suppression for 6 months before attempting conception
concept: Endometriosis — surgery improves fertility; medical suppression does not

stem: A 24-year-old nulliparous woman presents with sudden severe left iliac fossa pain and vomiting over 4 hours. She is afebrile. A tender 7 cm left adnexal mass is palpable. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an enlarged left ovary with absent arterial and venous flow on Doppler. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Urgent laparoscopy with detorsion and ovarian conservation
Intravenous antibiotics for pelvic inflammatory disease
Analgesia and outpatient ultrasound review in 2 weeks
concept: Ovarian torsion — surgical emergency with ovarian conservation

stem: A 34-year-old woman attends routine cervical screening. Primary HPV testing is positive for a high-risk genotype other than 16 or 18, and cytology is negative (NILM). She is asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Repeat HPV and cytology testing in 12 months
concept: Cervical cancer screening — HPV-primary triage of non-16/18 genotypes

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with postcoital bleeding for 3 months. Speculum examination shows a 4 cm friable cervical mass; biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. Examination under anesthesia shows bilateral parametrial involvement without fixation to the pelvic side wall. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Chemoradiotherapy (external beam, brachytherapy and weekly cisplatin)
concept: Cervical cancer — stage IIB is treated with chemoradiotherapy, not surgery

stem: A 57-year-old woman with breast cancer has taken tamoxifen for 3 years. She reports 2 weeks of postmenopausal vaginal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 9 mm. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: CT of the abdomen and pelvis
concept: Endometrial cancer risk — postmenopausal bleeding on tamoxifen requires tissue diagnosis

stem: A 32-year-old woman with a copper intrauterine device was diagnosed with pelvic inflammatory disease and treated with outpatient oral doxycycline and ceftriaxone. After 3 days she remains febrile at 38.6°C with worsening right iliac fossa pain. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 6.5 cm complex right adnexal mass with septations. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Continue the oral antibiotic course at home
Admission for intravenous antibiotics and image-guided or surgical drainage
Add oral fluconazole to the current regimen
Remove the intrauterine device and continue oral therapy at home
concept: Tubo-ovarian abscess — complication of PID requiring admission and drainage

stem: A 26-year-old nulliparous woman at 7 weeks of amenorrhea has mild brown spotting but no pain. Quantitative β-hCG fell from 850 to 610 IU/L over 48 hours. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus and a 2.0 cm left adnexal mass without a fetal pole or free fluid. She is hemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate management?
concept: Ectopic pregnancy — expectant management in spontaneous resolution

stem: A 36-year-old woman presents with 5 months of amenorrhea after years of regular cycles. She reports hot flushes, night sweats and vaginal dryness. FSH is 48 and 51 IU/L on two occasions with a low estradiol; karyotype is normal. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Reassurance with calcium and vitamin D alone
concept: Premature ovarian insufficiency — diagnosis and HRT indication

stem: A 55-year-old woman, para 4, reports a dragging sensation and something coming down for the past year, worse at the end of the day. On examination with Valsalva the cervix comes down to the introitus (stage III prolapse). She has COPD and obesity, is not sexually active, and wishes to avoid surgery. What is the most appropriate management?
concept: Utero-vaginal prolapse — pessary as first-line conservative management

stem: A 48-year-old woman, BMI 34 kg/m², reports leaking urine when she coughs, sneezes or laughs for 6 months. She has no urgency or nocturia, voids normally, and the urine dipstick is negative. Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
concept: Urinary incontinence — stress incontinence and first-line conservative therapy

stem: A 38-year-old woman, G0, with regular 28-day cycles has been trying to conceive for 7 months. Her 41-year-old partner has no children and no known health problems. Neither partner has had a previous pregnancy. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Reassure and reassess at 12 months of trying
Order genetic karyotyping of both partners first
concept: Subfertility — age-adjusted timing of referral (≥35 years)

stem: A 64-year-old woman has had intense vulvar itching and burning for 2 years. Examination shows white, atrophic, parchment-like plaques with fissuring affecting the labia and perianal skin. Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
concept: Lichen sclerosus — diagnosis and first-line ultrapotent steroid

stem: A 44-year-old woman, BMI 36 kg/m², has irregular heavy vaginal bleeding for 7 months. Endometrial biopsy shows complex hyperplasia with cytological atypia. She has completed her family. What is the most appropriate management?
concept: Premalignant disease of the uterus — complex atypical hyperplasia management

stem: A 32-year-old woman has a profuse, frothy, yellow-green, malodorous vaginal discharge with vulvar irritation for 1 week. Speculum examination shows punctate hemorrhagic spots on the cervix (strawberry cervix). A wet mount shows motile flagellated organisms. Which organism is the cause?
concept: Vulvovaginal infections — Trichomonas vaginalis identification

stem: A 58-year-old woman, 6 years postmenopausal, has an incidental finding on ultrasound of a 3.5 cm thin-walled, unilocular, anechoic cyst in the right ovary. There are no septations, solid areas or mural nodules, and CA-125 is normal. She is asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate management?
concept: Benign ovarian cysts — simple cyst in the postmenopausal woman

stem: A 41-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of pelvic pressure. Ultrasound shows an 11 cm solid, well-defined mass whose origin (uterine versus ovarian) cannot be determined. Which investigation best characterizes the origin and tissue type before surgery?
opts: CT of the abdomen and pelvis
concept: Pelvic mass differential — MRI for characterization of indeterminate origin

stem: A 29-year-old woman who had evacuation of a hydatidiform mole 6 months ago has a rising β-hCG, now 150,000 IU/L. Chest X-ray shows multiple bilateral lung nodules; CT shows no liver or brain metastases. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 4 cm myometrial lesion. Her WHO/FIGO prognostic score is 9. Which regimen is most appropriate?
concept: Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia — FIGO stage III, high-risk score → EMA-CO

stem: A 21-year-old competitive long-distance runner (BMI 17.5 kg/m²) has had amenorrhea for 7 months and a recent metatarsal stress fracture. A pregnancy test is negative. FSH is 3.1 IU/L, LH 2.4 IU/L, estradiol 18 pg/mL, and prolactin is normal. Which diagnosis is most likely?
concept: Secondary amenorrhea — functional hypothalamic amenorrhea in energy deficit

stem: A 26-year-old mother is exclusively breastfeeding her 5-month-old infant on demand and has been amenorrheic since delivery. She asks whether she still needs contraception. Which statement about the lactational amenorrhea method (LAM) is correct?
opts: It remains reliable as long as any breastfeeding continues
It is reliable only when the mother is amenorrheic, exclusively breastfeeding, and within 6 months postpartum
It is reliable if the mother breastfeeds at least 6 times daily, regardless of menstrual status
It is the single most effective contraceptive method available
concept: Contraception — lactational amenorrhea method criteria

stem: A term newborn girl is apneic after initial drying and stimulation. Despite 30 seconds of effective positive-pressure ventilation with a visible chest rise, her heart rate remains below 60 bpm. Chest compressions are started. What compression-to-ventilation ratio should be used?
concept: Neonatal resuscitation — chest compression:ventilation ratio

stem: A 9-month-old girl attends a well-baby check. Her mother reports she babbles, reaches for toys, and rolls both ways. Which finding at this age is a red flag for developmental delay?
opts: She does not speak two-word phrases
concept: Developmental milestones — 9-month red flags

stem: A 6-year-old girl is found to have a murmur during school screening. She is asymptomatic and growing well. On examination there is a soft systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border with a fixed, widely split second heart sound. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Congenital heart disease — ostium secundum ASD auscultation

stem: A term newborn girl develops visible jaundice at 18 hours of life. She is feeding well and otherwise vigorous. Her mother is blood group O Rh D-positive and the baby is group B Rh D-positive. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Reassure the parents that this is physiological jaundice
Evaluate for hemolytic disease with blood group, direct Coombs test, hemoglobin, and reticulocyte count
Start phototherapy and discharge without further testing
concept: Neonatal jaundice — jaundice in the first 24 hours is pathological

stem: A 3-week-old boy who is exclusively breastfed has had jaundice since day 10 of life. He is thriving, feeding well, and gaining weight. Total bilirubin is 13.4 mg/dL with a normal direct fraction, and stools are yellow. What is the most appropriate advice?
opts: Stop breastfeeding immediately and refer urgently for a Kasai procedure
Reassure and continue breastfeeding, with follow-up; this is breast milk jaundice
Admit for phototherapy and a sepsis workup
Switch to a lactose-free formula permanently
concept: Neonatal jaundice — breast milk jaundice (late, unconjugated, healthy infant)

stem: A term newborn girl (38 weeks, 3.2 kg) is born after shoulder dystocia with an umbilical cord pH of 6.9 and base deficit of 18 mmol/L. At 4 hours of age she is lethargic, hypotonic, and has subtle seizure activity. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Intravenous phenobarbital alone with supportive care
concept: Birth asphyxia — hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) and therapeutic hypothermia

stem: A term boy born by elective cesarean section without labor develops tachypnea at 2 hours of age: respiratory rate 78/min with mild intercostal retractions and an occasional grunt. Oxygen saturation is 94% on room air. Chest X-ray shows prominent interlobar fissure fluid with streaky perihilar markings. By 36 hours he is much improved. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Respiratory distress in newborn — transient tachypnea of the newborn (TTN)

stem: A term newborn girl has immediate, severe respiratory distress after birth. On examination the abdomen is scaphoid, and bowel sounds are heard over the left hemithorax. Chest X-ray shows bowel loops in the left chest. What is the key immediate management?
opts: Bag-mask ventilation and positioning the infant prone
Orogastric decompression and immediate endotracheal intubation, avoiding bag-mask ventilation
Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) before any other step
concept: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia — delivery-room management

stem: A 35-week newborn girl at 6 hours of age is lethargic with poor feeding, a heart rate of 175/min, and temperature instability. Her mother had chorioamnionitis with membrane rupture 20 hours before delivery. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Observe for 12–24 hours and reassess before any intervention
Blood culture, lumbar puncture, then start empiric intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin without waiting for results
Start antibiotics only once the blood culture is reported positive
Oral amoxicillin with continued breastfeeding and outpatient review
concept: Neonatal sepsis — early-onset sepsis workup and empiric therapy

stem: A term boy born to a diabetic mother (birth weight 4.3 kg) is noted at 2 hours of age to be jittery and sweaty. Bedside glucose is 30 mg/dL. There is no respiratory distress. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Intravenous bolus of 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg, then a continuous dextrose infusion
Oral glucose water and recheck in 2 hours
concept: Neonatal hypoglycaemia — symptomatic infant of diabetic mother

stem: A term girl is born weighing 1.9 kg (below the 3rd percentile for gestational age). Her mother had severe pre-eclampsia with placental insufficiency. Which complication is this infant at highest risk of developing?
opts: Shoulder dystocia with brachial plexus injury
concept: Small for gestational age — metabolic risks

stem: A newborn girl is diagnosed with galactosemia (homozygous deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase) on newborn screening. Which feeding is contraindicated in this infant?
concept: Breastfeeding — contraindications and infant nutrition

stem: A 12-month-old boy has passed loose watery stools 6–8 times in the past 24 hours, without blood. He is alert, drinks eagerly, has no sunken eyes, and his skin pinch returns immediately. Per WHO/IMCI classification he has no dehydration. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Continue feeding, give ORS after each loose stool, and give zinc supplements for 14 days
Supervised ORS 75 mL/kg over 4 hours in a treatment room
Loperamide with plain water and no feeds
concept: Acute diarrhoea — WHO/IMCI Plan A (no dehydration) with zinc

stem: A 15-month-old girl had her first simple febrile seizure two days ago during a febrile illness (39.3°C, generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes, fully alert afterwards, source found to be acute otitis media). Her mother asks how to prevent another seizure. What is the most appropriate advice?
opts: Give paracetamol at the first sign of any fever to prevent seizures
Start daily oral phenobarbital until age 5 years
Control fever for comfort only; antipyretics do not reduce the risk of recurrent febrile seizures
Administer rectal diazepam at the start of every future febrile illness
concept: Febrile seizures — prevention and parental counselling

stem: A 10-month-old boy has had a cough for 3 days. His respiratory rate is 55/min with no chest indrawing and no danger signs; oxygen saturation is 97% and he is feeding well. According to WHO/IMCI classification, what is the most appropriate management?
opts: Admit and start intravenous antibiotics for severe pneumonia
Treat at home with oral amoxicillin and advise return if danger signs develop
Give no antibiotics — this is not pneumonia
Refer urgently for very severe disease
concept: Pneumonia in children — IMCI classification (2–12 months)

stem: A 7-year-old girl has had a dry, persistent cough for 10 days with low-grade fever but minimal chest findings. Chest X-ray shows bilateral patchy interstitial infiltrates, and cold agglutinins are positive. What is the most appropriate treatment?
concept: Atypical pneumonia — Mycoplasma pneumoniae in school-age children

stem: A 3-month-old boy born at 28 weeks gestation with chronic lung disease (still on home oxygen) is about to be discharged in November, before the RSV season begins. Which infant meets criteria for RSV immunoprophylaxis?
opts: All infants born before 37 weeks gestation
A preterm infant of 28 weeks with chronic lung disease requiring ongoing oxygen
Any infant attending daycare during winter
Any infant with a school-age sibling
concept: Bronchiolitis — RSV immunoprophylaxis eligibility

stem: An 8-month-old girl has had fever of 39.5°C for 2 days with no localising source. She is alert and feeding. Urine dipstick shows positive nitrites and leukocyte esterase. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Start oral antibiotics on the basis of the dipstick alone
Obtain a catheter urine sample for culture, then begin empiric antibiotics
Request a renal ultrasound before any treatment
Observe with antipyretics for another 48 hours
concept: Urinary tract infection in children — specimen and culture before treatment

stem: An 18-month-old boy has fever of 40.1°C, lethargy, and neck stiffness. A petechial rash is spreading rapidly over his trunk, blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg, and capillary refill is 4 seconds. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
opts: Lumbar puncture before antibiotics to confirm the diagnosis
Blood culture and immediate intravenous ceftriaxone
Oral amoxicillin and review in the clinic tomorrow
concept: Meningitis — meningococcemia recognition and antibiotic timing

stem: A term newborn boy has not passed meconium in the first 48 hours of life and has progressive abdominal distension with bilious vomiting. Digital rectal examination reveals an empty rectum. Which investigation confirms the diagnosis of Hirschsprung disease?
concept: Hirschsprung disease — diagnostic gold standard

stem: A 30-week preterm girl on day 6 of life develops abdominal distension, bilious gastric aspirates, and blood in the stools. Feeds had been advanced rapidly over the previous 72 hours. Abdominal X-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate management?
opts: Necrotizing enterocolitis — stop feeds, decompress the stomach, and start intravenous antibiotics
Cows' milk protein intolerance — change to an amino-acid formula
concept: Necrotizing enterocolitis — recognition and medical management

stem: A 2-year-old boy has had fever of 39.5°C for 6 days. He has bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, cracked lips, a strawberry tongue, a 1.5 cm right cervical lymph node, and swelling of the hands and feet. He is irritable. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Oral amoxicillin for 10 days for presumed bacterial pharyngitis
Intravenous immunoglobulin (2 g/kg) plus aspirin, started within 10 days of fever onset
Oral prednisolone as the only therapy
Antihistamines and antipyretics, with review in one week
concept: Kawasaki disease — diagnostic criteria and treatment

stem: A 4-year-old girl from a low-resource setting is assessed for undernutrition. Her height-for-age is below −3 standard deviations, while her weight-for-height is within normal limits and there is no oedema. Which term best classifies this pattern of malnutrition?
concept: Growth charts and malnutrition classification — stunting vs wasting

stem: A 2-year-old boy has progressive bowing of the legs and widened wrists since 9 months of age despite routine vitamin D supplementation and adequate sun exposure. Serum calcium is normal, phosphate is very low, alkaline phosphatase is high, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D is normal. His father is short with bowed legs. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: A single high-dose bolus of vitamin D (600,000 IU)
concept: Vitamin D-resistant (hypophosphatemic) rickets — diagnosis and treatment

stem: A 6-week-old girl has prolonged jaundice, constipation since birth, a large tongue, an umbilical hernia, a hoarse cry, and poor feeding. She was born at home and newborn screening was not performed. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Measure serum TSH and free T4
Abdominal ultrasound to evaluate for biliary atresia
Genetic testing for chromosomal anomalies only
Reassure the parents and reassess at 3 months
concept: Congenital hypothyroidism — clinical recognition and confirmation

stem: A 6-week-old baby boy is brought to the EPI centre for his first follow-up immunisation visit. He received BCG and OPV-0 at birth. Which set of vaccines is due at this visit?
opts: First dose of pentavalent (DPT-HepB-Hib), OPV-1, PCV-1 and rotavirus vaccine
A BCG booster and an oral polio booster
First dose of measles vaccine with vitamin A
concept: EPI immunisation schedule — the 6-week visit

stem: A 5-month-old boy is brought during a measles outbreak and his mother insists on early measles vaccination. In the routine EPI schedule the first measles dose is given at 9 months. What is the main reason for this timing?
opts: The vaccine causes severe febrile reactions before 9 months
Infants younger than 9 months do not develop a rash, so the vaccine response cannot be checked
Maternal measles antibodies neutralise the live vaccine before 9 months
Combined measles-rubella vaccine is not available before 9 months
concept: Immunisation — measles vaccine timing (maternal antibody interference)

stem: A 4-month-old girl with a mild upper respiratory infection (runny nose, cough, temperature 37.8°C) is brought for her second DPT dose. The mother asks whether vaccination should be postponed. Which statement is correct?
opts: Postpone vaccination until the cough has fully resolved for at least 2 weeks
Vaccinate today — mild illness with low-grade fever is not a contraindication
Give a half-dose of DPT today to reduce the risk of reactions
Skip this dose permanently now that the schedule has been interrupted
concept: Immunisation — DTP contraindications

stem: A 3-year-old girl on maintenance chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is due for scheduled immunisations. Which vaccine must be withheld while she is significantly immunosuppressed?
concept: Immunisation in immunocompromised children — live vs inactivated vaccines

stem: During an outreach immunisation session a health worker asks which vaccine is damaged by FREEZING and must never be placed in a freezer. Which of the following is correct?
concept: Cold chain — freeze-sensitive vaccines

stem: A 12-year-old boy who had measles at 2 years of age presents with 3 months of declining school performance, personality change and myoclonic jerks. EEG shows periodic slow-wave complexes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Measles complication — subacute sclerosing panencephalitis

stem: A 14-year-old boy develops painful swelling of the right testis 4 days after bilateral parotid swelling and fever. He is otherwise well and afebrile. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Mumps complication — orchitis in the postpubertal male

stem: A newborn girl has bilateral cataracts, a systolic murmur, and a 'blueberry muffin' rash. Her mother recalls a mild maculopapular rash with fever in the first trimester. Which congenital infection is most likely?
concept: Congenital rubella syndrome — TORCH discrimination

stem: A 5-day-old baby girl born at home to an unvaccinated mother presents with refusal to feed, trismus, risus sardonicus and opisthotonic spasms. There is no jaundice. What is the single most effective preventive measure for this disease at the population level?
opts: Routine prophylactic antibiotics for all newborns
concept: Neonatal tetanus — population-level prevention

stem: A 3-year-old boy who was never vaccinated develops acute asymmetric flaccid paralysis of the left leg with preserved sensation and no fever. He had a diarrhoeal illness 10 days earlier. What is the most important public health action?
opts: Order urgent MRI of the spine before anything else
Notify as acute flaccid paralysis and collect two stool specimens 24 hours apart
Start corticosteroids for presumed transverse myelitis
Refer for nerve conduction studies and wait for the results
concept: Poliomyelitis — acute flaccid paralysis surveillance

stem: A 3-year-old boy ingested an estimated 200 mg/kg of paracetamol 3 hours ago and is currently asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Wait for the 4-hour level and treat only if it exceeds the nomogram line
Give activated charcoal and discharge if he remains asymptomatic at 6 hours
Start N-acetylcysteine immediately and obtain a 4-hour paracetamol level
Observe at home and return only if vomiting develops
concept: Acute paracetamol poisoning in children — treatment threshold

stem: A 2-year-old boy was found with an open kerosene container and is now coughing. His parents ask what the main danger is. What is the most dangerous complication of kerosene ingestion?
concept: Kerosene (hydrocarbon) poisoning — target organ and mechanism

stem: A 4-year-old boy with organophosphate poisoning was atropinised and improved. Forty-eight hours later he is alert with dry secretions but develops neck-flexor weakness, proximal limb weakness and shallow breathing. What is the most likely diagnosis and treatment?
opts: Relapse of cholinergic crisis — give more atropine
Intermediate syndrome — supportive ventilation with early pralidoxime
concept: Organophosphate poisoning — intermediate syndrome

stem: A healthy 6-month-old boy is brought for routine vaccination. Which of the following developmental findings is NORMAL for this age?
opts: Uses a neat pincer grasp to pick up a raisin
Rolls from back to front in both directions
concept: Normal development — gross and fine motor milestones at 6 months

stem: A 24-month-old boy has a vocabulary of eight single words and does not combine two words. He passed newborn hearing screening. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Reassure the parents and review again at 3 years of age
Request an urgent MRI of the brain
Refer for audiological assessment and early intervention
concept: Language development — red flags at 2 years

stem: A 4-month-old girl's head circumference has crossed from the 50th to above the 97th percentile in 8 weeks, and her anterior fontanelle is full and tense. Weight and length are at the 50th percentile. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Reassure — head size is genetically determined
Urgent evaluation for raised intracranial pressure (hydrocephalus)
Advise reducing calorie intake to slow head growth
Repeat the measurement at the 6-month visit only
concept: Growth interpretation — head circumference crossing centiles

stem: A 10-month-old girl is below the 3rd centile for weight with normal length and head circumference. During a 5-day admission she gains 300 g when the nursing staff feed her. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Failure to thrive — organic vs non-organic

stem: A 13-year-old boy at the 3rd percentile for height has grown 5 cm in the past year (a normal height velocity), his bone age equals his chronological age, and both parents are short. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
concept: Short stature — familial vs constitutional vs endocrine

stem: A 6½-year-old girl has breast buds (Tanner II), pubic hair and a growth spurt over 4 months. Bone age is 8 years. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Reassurance and review at the annual visit
GnRH analogue therapy after evaluating for an underlying CNS cause
Oestrogen replacement to drive puberty to completion
concept: Precocious puberty — diagnosis and treatment

stem: A 15-year-old boy has no testicular enlargement, scanty pubic hair, height at the 5th percentile and a bone age of 12 years. His father says he 'grew in his late teens'. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty
concept: Delayed puberty — constitutional delay vs pathology

stem: A 15-month-old girl drinks over a litre of unmodified cow's milk daily, has pica and pallor, and Hb 8.2 g/dL with MCV 62 fL, low ferritin and high RDW. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Oral iron alone, with the cow's milk intake unchanged
Oral elemental iron 3-6 mg/kg/day plus counselling to limit cow's milk
concept: Iron deficiency anaemia in a toddler — management

stem: A 4-year-old boy has Hb 10.5 g/dL, MCV 65 fL, an RBC count of 5.6 million/µL and a normal ferritin. The Mentzer index (MCV ÷ RBC) is 11.6. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Microcytic anaemia — thalassaemia trait vs iron deficiency (Mentzer index)

stem: A 3-year-old boy with generalised convulsive status epilepticus is still seizing 10 minutes after two appropriate doses of IV lorazepam. What is the most appropriate second-line agent?
concept: Status epilepticus — second-line anticonvulsant in children

stem: A 7-year-old boy with new-onset diabetic ketoacidosis on IV fluids and insulin develops headache, then bradycardia and a falling Glasgow Coma Scale score. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: A further rapid normal saline bolus to improve perfusion
IV mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg (or 3% saline 2.5-5 mL/kg) and reduce the fluid rate
Obtain a CT head before any intervention
concept: Diabetic ketoacidosis — cerebral oedema recognition and rescue

stem: A 2-year-old girl with 6 hours of fever develops a non-blanching petechial-purpuric rash, cold extremities, tachycardia and lethargy. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Lumbar puncture first to confirm the diagnosis
Blood culture followed immediately by IV ceftriaxone
Oral amoxicillin and review in the morning
IV antihistamines for a presumed allergic rash
concept: Meningococcal septicaemia — recognition and emergency treatment

stem: A 62-year-old woman reports brief episodes of spinning vertigo for 3 weeks, triggered only when she rolls onto her right side in bed. Each episode lasts under a minute. She has no hearing loss or tinnitus. Dix-Hallpike testing reproduces vertigo with upbeating nystagmus. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Low-salt diet and a thiazide diuretic
MRI of the internal auditory meatus
concept: BPPV — diagnosis and treatment

stem: A 45-year-old male presents with progressive right-sided hearing loss, ringing in the right ear, and a feeling of imbalance for 8 months. Otoscopy is normal. Audiometry shows asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss on the right. Which investigation is the gold standard to confirm the diagnosis?
opts: MRI of the internal auditory meatus with gadolinium
concept: Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) — investigation of choice

stem: A 28-year-old swimmer presents with intense itching and pain in the right ear for 2 weeks. Otoscopy shows black, cotton-wool-like debris in the ear canal with an intact tympanic membrane. What is the most likely causative organism?
concept: Otomycosis — organism identification

stem: A 68-year-old male with poorly controlled diabetes presents with severe right ear pain for 3 weeks and scanty purulent discharge. Otoscopy shows granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction of the ear canal. He now has right-sided facial weakness. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Topical antibiotic ear drops and review in 1 week
CT scan of the temporal bone and IV antipseudomonal antibiotics
concept: Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa — diabetic + granulation + CN VII palsy

stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought with hearing difficulty at school. He has had two episodes of acute otitis media in the past year. Otoscopy shows a retracted, dull tympanic membrane with a visible fluid level. Tympanogram is flat (type B). He has failed a 3-month period of watchful waiting. What is the most appropriate management?
concept: Otitis media with effusion (glue ear) — management after watchful waiting fails

stem: A 50-year-old factory worker presents with difficulty hearing conversations in noisy settings. Audiometry shows a bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with a characteristic notch at 4000 Hz. What is the most likely cause?
concept: Noise-induced hearing loss — audiometric pattern

stem: A 30-year-old female develops sudden severe vertigo, nausea, and vomiting 1 week after a viral upper respiratory tract infection. She also notices reduced hearing in the left ear. There is no focal neurological deficit. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Labyrinthitis vs vestibular neuritis

stem: A 5-year-old boy with acute otitis media treated 10 days ago returns with fever, earache, and a swelling behind the right ear that pushes the pinna forward and outward. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Continue the same oral antibiotic for another week
CT temporal bone and IV antibiotics with otolaryngology review
Incision and drainage of the external canal
Myringotomy alone in the outpatient clinic
concept: Acute mastoiditis — complication of AOM

stem: A 35-year-old male with asthma reports that aspirin triggered a severe reaction 2 years ago. He now has bilateral nasal obstruction and anosmia. Examination shows pale, grape-like, insensate masses in both nasal cavities. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
concept: Nasal polyps (Samter's triad) — first-line treatment

stem: A 45-year-old male with diabetic ketoacidosis presents with facial pain, nasal obstruction, and a black necrotic eschar on the nasal mucosa. He is febrile and confused. What is the most urgent management step?
opts: Urgent surgical debridement and IV amphotericin B
concept: Invasive fungal sinusitis (mucormycosis/Aspergillus) — emergency

stem: A 20-year-old male presents 2 days after a blow to the nose during a fight. He has bilateral nasal obstruction and a feeling of fullness. Examination shows a bluish, fluctuant swelling on both sides of the nasal septum. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Nasal decongestant spray and review in 1 week
Urgent incision and drainage of the septal hematoma
Closed reduction of the nasal bones
concept: Nasal septal hematoma — emergency management

stem: A 30-year-old male is involved in a road traffic accident with a head injury. Three days later he notices clear watery fluid dripping from the right nostril when he leans forward. A drop of the fluid on a tissue leaves a double ring (halo sign). Which investigation confirms the fluid is cerebrospinal fluid?
concept: CSF rhinorrhea — confirmatory test

stem: A newborn is noted to have episodes of cyanosis that improve when she cries. A nasogastric tube cannot be passed through the right nostril. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Choanal atresia — newborn presentation

stem: A 30-year-old female has used a topical nasal decongestant spray daily for 4 months to relieve nasal blockage. She now has constant nasal congestion that worsens shortly after each spray. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Continue the spray — it is the only thing that helps
Stop the decongestant and start an intranasal corticosteroid
Switch to a stronger decongestant spray
concept: Rhinitis medicamentosa

stem: A 3-year-old child presents with fever, muffled voice, drooling, and neck stiffness. He refuses to swallow. Examination shows bulging of the posterior pharyngeal wall. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: CT neck and IV antibiotics with surgical drainage
Tongue depressor examination to confirm the bulge
concept: Retropharyngeal abscess — child under 5

stem: A 40-year-old male presents with rapidly progressive swelling under the jaw, severe pain, trismus, and difficulty swallowing. The floor of the mouth is elevated and the tongue is pushed upward. He is sitting forward and drooling. What is the single most important immediate step?
opts: Incision and drainage in the ward
concept: Ludwig angina — airway priority

stem: An 18-year-old university student presents with fever, severe sore throat, and fatigue for 1 week. Examination shows exudative tonsillitis and tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. The spleen is palpable. What is the most important management consideration?
opts: Avoid amoxicillin and give supportive care
concept: Infectious mononucleosis (EBV) — what NOT to do

stem: A 6-year-old unvaccinated child presents with a sore throat, low-grade fever, and a grayish-white membrane covering both tonsils that bleeds on attempted removal. He has marked neck swelling ('bull neck') and a muffled voice. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Diphtheria antitoxin plus penicillin or erythromycin
concept: Diphtheria — treatment

stem: A 55-year-old male smoker presents with a painless swelling in the left side of the throat for 2 months. Examination shows marked enlargement of the left tonsil only, with a firm, non-tender level II lymph node. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: A course of oral antibiotics and review
concept: Tonsillar malignancy — unilateral enlargement in an adult

stem: A 4-year-old child presents with progressive hoarseness of voice. Laryngoscopy shows multiple wart-like papillary lesions on the vocal cords. What is the most likely causative agent?
concept: Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis

stem: A 30-year-old schoolteacher presents with hoarseness that worsens by evening. Laryngoscopy shows bilateral, symmetric, smooth swellings at the junction of the anterior and middle thirds of the vocal cords. What is the most appropriate treatment?
concept: Vocal nodules — management

stem: A 2-month-old infant has had inspiratory stridor since birth. It is louder when she is supine and during crying, and softer when she is prone. She feeds well and is gaining weight. What is the most likely diagnosis and expected course?
opts: Vocal cord paralysis — requires immediate intubation
concept: Laryngomalacia — most common cause of infant stridor

stem: A 1-year-old child presents with a soft, fluctuant swelling in the left posterior triangle of the neck that has been present since birth and is slowly enlarging. The swelling transilluminates brilliantly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Cystic hygroma — neck mass identification
