stem: A 60-year-old male smoker presents with two painless swellings, one in each parotid region, present for 1 year. They are soft and cystic on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Warthin tumor — parotid pathology

stem: A 50-year-old male presents with a slowly enlarging, pulsatile mass at the angle of the jaw, present for 3 years. It moves laterally but not vertically, and a bruit is audible over it. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Carotid body tumor (paraganglioma) — neck mass identification

stem: A 45-year-old has recurrent episodes of vertigo lasting 30-40 minutes, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and a sense of aural fullness in one ear. Between episodes he is well. Dix-Hallpike and neurological examination are normal. Diagnosis?
concept: Meniere's disease - episodic vertigo + fluctuating SNHL + tinnitus + aural fullness

stem: A 3-year-old has a 2-day history of fever and ear pain. Otoscopy shows a bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane with restricted mobility and loss of the light reflex. Most appropriate first-line treatment?
opts: Watchful waiting with no treatment in all cases
concept: Acute otitis media - bulging TM; first-line amoxicillin

stem: A child has right ear pain and tenderness when the ear is pulled, with no fever. Examination shows an inflamed, edematous ear canal with scanty yellow discharge and normal tympanic membrane. Diagnosis and first-line treatment?
opts: Acute otitis externa; topical antibiotic/antiseptic ear drops and keep the ear dry
Furunculosis of the pinna; incision and drainage
concept: Acute otitis externa - tender pinna/canal, normal TM; topical drops + dry ear

stem: A passenger develops ear pain and fullness during aircraft descent. Otoscopy shows a retracted, congested tympanic membrane with a middle-ear effusion. Most likely diagnosis?
concept: Otitic barotrauma - ear pain/fullness on descent, retracted congested TM

stem: A 35-year-old has a long history of chronic, often offensive ear discharge and progressive conductive hearing loss. Otoscopy shows retraction of the pars flaccida with pearly-white keratin debris and a marginal perforation. What is important about this condition?
opts: It is benign and self-limiting; no treatment needed
It is an erosive keratinising lesion that can destroy middle-ear structures; surgical excision is needed
It is managed with topical antibiotics alone
It is a pre-cancerous lesion of the ear canal skin
concept: Cholesteatoma - erosive keratinising lesion; surgical treatment

stem: A 75-year-old reports slowly progressive difficulty hearing in both ears, especially in noisy environments, with normal ears on otoscopy. Pure-tone audiometry shows symmetric high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Most likely diagnosis?
concept: Presbycusis - age-related symmetric high-frequency SNHL

stem: On tuning-fork testing, a patient has Weber lateralizing to the LEFT ear, and Rinne is NEGATIVE on the left (BC > AC) but POSITIVE on the right. Which statement is correct?
concept: Tuning fork - Weber to affected side in conductive loss; Rinne negative

stem: A patient has chronic purulent otorrhoea with an attic (marginal) perforation and a foul smell. Which statement is most important?
opts: This is a safe ear; topical drops are curative
An attic/marginal perforation is an 'unsafe' ear, at risk of cholesteatoma and intracranial complications; needs surgical assessment
It is always malignant otitis externa
It will resolve spontaneously with oral antibiotics
concept: CSOM - safe vs unsafe (marginal/attic perforation)

stem: A 3-year-old has a persistent, unilateral, foul-smelling, blood-stained nasal discharge from the right nostril for 2 weeks. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate next step?
opts: Nasal foreign body; careful anterior rhinoscopy and removal under proper visualization
concept: Nasal foreign body - unilateral foul-smelling/blood-stained discharge in a child

stem: A patient has a 'double worsening' of cold symptoms: nasal congestion and purulent discharge that TRANSIENTLY improved then worsened, with facial pain, no improvement in 10 days. Which feature most strongly supports bacterial (rather than viral) rhinosinusitis?
opts: Symptoms that worsened after initially improving, or persist beyond 10 days with purulence and facial pain ('double worsening')
concept: Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis - 'double worsening' / persistence criteria

stem: A 60-year-old on aspirin has a brisk anterior nosebleed from Little's area that is ongoing. Gentle pressure, decongestant and cautery have controlled the bleeding. However he is at risk of rebleeding. Which measure is most important for initial management?
opts: Immediate posterior nasal packing in all cases
Maintain pressure: sit upright, lean forward, pinch the cartilaginous nose for 10-20 minutes, and treat the bleeding point (silver nitrate/coagulation), plus avoid nasal trauma
Routine hospital admission for every patient
concept: Epistaxis management - anterior packing/pressure + cautery, first aid

stem: A 25-year-old has seasonal sneezing, itchy watery eyes and clear rhinorrhoea. Which is first-line maintenance treatment for allergic rhinitis?
opts: Oral antihistamines alone in all cases
Topical intranasal corticosteroid, with oral/topical antihistamines for symptom relief
concept: Allergic rhinitis - first-line intranasal corticosteroid

stem: A patient sustains nasal trauma and later develops a bilateral nasal obstruction with pain and a bulging, fluctuant septal swelling. This was not drained. Months later she presents with a saddle nose deformity. What best explains the outcome and the initial correct management?
opts: Missed septal hematoma: the septal cartilage lost its blood supply and resorbed; an early hematoma should be drained/I&D and the nose splinted
This is normal healing and needs no treatment
It is caused by an untreated allergy; give antihistamines
It is a septal fracture that always needs immediate open reduction
concept: Septal hematoma - can cause saddle nose via cartilage necrosis; evacuate promptly

stem: A 10-year-old with acute sinusitis develops eyelid swelling, proptosis, pain on eye movement, restricted eye movements and fever. What is the emergency and next step?
opts: Preseptal cellulitis; oral antibiotics at home
Orbital cellulitis; urgent IV antibiotics and imaging (CT) to exclude orbital abscess
Cavernous sinus thrombosis; intensive care and anticoagulation
concept: Orbital cellulitis - complication of sinusitis; urgent IV antibiotics + CT

stem: A 45-year-old of East Asian origin presents with a painless neck mass and unilateral conductive hearing loss from a middle-ear effusion on the same side. He has blood-stained nasal discharge. Which is the most important next investigation?
opts: MRI/endoscopy with biopsy of the nasopharynx
concept: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma - unilateral OME + neck mass in endemic patient; nasopharyngeal biopsy

stem: A 4-year-old has a high fever, severe sore throat, drooling, difficulty swallowing, a muffled voice, and sits in a tripod position. What is the MOST appropriate immediate action?
opts: Examine the throat with a tongue depressor
Secure the airway (senior anaesthetist/ENT; do NOT agitate or examine the throat)
concept: Epiglottitis - airway first; do not examine the throat

stem: A 25-year-old has severe unilateral sore throat, 'hot potato' voice, trismus, and deviation of the soft palate with the uvula pushed to the opposite side. What is the likely diagnosis and most appropriate management?
opts: Acute tonsillitis; oral antibiotics and discharge
Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy); ENT referral for aspiration/incision and drainage plus antibiotics and analgesia
concept: Peritonsillar abscess - trismus + uvula deviation; aspiration/I+D + antibiotics

stem: A 60-year-old heavy smoker with hoarseness for over 3 weeks and progressive voice change is referred. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Reassure that it is a viral laryngitis and review in 6 months
Refer for direct (flexible) laryngoscopy +/- biopsy to exclude laryngeal carcinoma
concept: Laryngeal carcinoma - hoarseness >3 weeks in a smoker warrants specialist evaluation

stem: A patient who has just undergone thyroid surgery develops hoarseness and a breathy voice. Which nerve is most likely affected?
concept: Vocal cord paralysis - recurrent laryngeal nerve injury in thyroid surgery

stem: A 2-year-old has a barking 'seal-like' cough, low-grade fever, hoarseness and inspiratory stridor that worsens at night. There is NO drooling and the child is not toxic. Most likely diagnosis and management?
opts: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis); oral steroid (dexamethasone) and nebulized adrenaline if severe
concept: Croup - barking cough + stridor, not toxic; dexamethasone

stem: A 10-year-old has fever, sore throat and exudative tonsils with painful cervical lymphadenopathy and no cough. Rapid antigen test is positive for Group A streptococcus. Which is the most important reason to treat with antibiotics?
opts: To shorten the illness and prevent acute rheumatic fever and suppurative complications
To prevent viral spread to contacts
It is not needed because it is a virus
concept: GAS tonsillitis - antibiotics to prevent rheumatic fever

stem: A nursing-home resident on an inhaled steroid for COPD develops difficulty eating with a red oropharynx and white, curd-like, removable plaques. Most likely diagnosis?
concept: Oropharyngeal candidiasis - steroid inhaler + white curd-like plaques

stem: A 40-year-old has recurrent painful swelling of the right cheek that worsens at mealtimes. The swelling resolves between meals and a painful mass is felt in Wharton's duct. Which gland and management?
opts: Submandibular gland; sialolithiasis - manage with sialogogues, massage, or ductal removal/ectomy if recurrent
concept: Sialolithiasis - submandibular stone, worse at meals; sialogogues/removal

stem: A 45-year-old develops sudden onset of inability to close the right eye, drooping of the right corner of the mouth and forehead flattening on the right, over 24 hours. There is no other neurological deficit. Most likely diagnosis and treatment?
opts: Bell's palsy; oral corticosteroids (with eye protection)
concept: Bell's palsy - sudden lower motor neuron facial palsy; oral corticosteroids

stem: A 50-year-old awakens with sudden hearing loss in one ear (no vertigo, no ear pain). Audiometry shows moderate unilateral sensorineural hearing loss. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Oral corticosteroids started promptly; urgent audiologic/ENT evaluation
concept: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss - urgent oral corticosteroid

stem: A 12-year-old boy has recurrent seasonal eye itching and redness, worse in summer, with conjunctival hyperaemia, cobblestone papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva, punctate epithelial erosions on fluorescein, and pain on eye movement. Visual acuity is 6/6. Diagnosis?
concept: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis - cobblestone papillae + seasonal, VA preserved

stem: A long-standing diabetic with proliferative retinopathy develops a retinal detachment with visible vitreous haemorrhage and traction bands. Definitive management?
concept: Diabetic tractional retinal detachment - vitrectomy

stem: A 30-year-old presents after an alkali splash to the eye with conjunctival blanching and corneal haze. The single most urgent immediate step is:
opts: Copious immediate irrigation with water or saline
concept: Chemical eye injury - immediate copious irrigation is the priority

stem: A 68-year-old with acute angle-closure glaucoma has markedly elevated intraocular pressure unresponsive to initial topical and oral therapy. Which agent most rapidly lowers IOP by an osmotic mechanism?
concept: Acute angle-closure glaucoma - IV mannitol for rapid osmotic IOP reduction

stem: In acute angle-closure glaucoma, pilocarpine constricts the pupil and opens the angle. What is its mechanism of action?
opts: Beta-2 agonist that increases aqueous outflow
Direct muscarinic agonist contracting ciliary muscle and sphincter, pulling the iris open
Alpha-1 agonist that dilates the pupil
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor reducing aqueous production
concept: Pilocarpine - direct miotic (muscarinic agonist) in AACG

stem: A 19-year-old is struck in the eye with a ball and develops layering of blood in the anterior chamber (hyphema). Mainstay of acute management?
opts: Bed rest with head elevation, eye shield, and avoidance of aspirin/NSAIDs
concept: Traumatic hyphema - bed rest, elevation, shield, avoid anticoagulants

stem: A 70-year-old with hypertension and diabetes has sudden, painless, unilateral visual loss. Fundoscopy shows widespread flame-shaped haemorrhages, dilated tortuous retinal veins, cotton-wool spots and disc oedema ('blood and thunder'). Most likely diagnosis?
concept: Central retinal vein occlusion - 'blood and thunder' fundus

stem: A patient has sudden, painless, monocular visual loss. Which typically presents WITH pain on eye movement and is therefore NOT in the 'painless' differential?
concept: Sudden vision loss - optic neuritis is painful; the others are painless

stem: A diabetic with proliferative retinopathy reports a sudden shower of floaters and a dark veil over one eye with poor vision. The red reflex is absent and the fundus cannot be seen. Most likely diagnosis?
concept: Vitreous haemorrhage - sudden floaters + obscured fundus, absent red reflex

stem: A myopic 55-year-old notices flashes of light, a shower of floaters, and then a shadow/curtain descending over the temporal visual field of one eye. Most appropriate next step?
opts: Urgent ophthalmological assessment for possible retinal detachment
concept: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment - flashes + floaters + curtain

stem: A 22-year-old reports difficulty seeing at night since childhood and progressive narrowing of the visual field. Fundoscopy shows bony spicule pigmentation, attenuated vessels and waxy pallor of the disc. Diagnosis?
concept: Retinitis pigmentosa - night blindness + tunnel vision + bone spicules

stem: A 78-year-old has gradually worsening central blurring and distortion (metamorphopsia) with difficulty reading. Most appropriate initial investigation to monitor disease activity at home?
concept: Age-related macular degeneration - Amsler grid for home monitoring

stem: An 80-year-old with AMD develops rapid central vision loss and distortion. OCT shows subretinal fluid and new vessels under the macula. Which statement is correct?
opts: This is dry AMD and requires antioxidant vitamins only
This is wet (neovascular) AMD and is treated with intravitreal anti-VEGF agents
This is wet AMD and is treated with oral antibiotics
This is dry AMD and requires urgent laser photocoagulation
concept: Wet (neovascular) AMD - anti-VEGF; dry AMD is atrophic/drusen

stem: A 3-month-old has persistent watery discharge and tearing from one eye since birth, with mild medial canthal wetness but no redness or mass. Usual management?
opts: Conservative: massage + observe; most resolve by 1 year, probing if persistent
concept: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction - massage + observe

stem: A 35-year-old has a mild red, mildly tender eye with localized injected vessels that blanch on phenylephrine, and no vision loss. A 60-year-old with rheumatoid arthritis has a severe boring eye pain, a violaceous area of injected sclera that does NOT blanch, and decreased vision. Which distinction is correct?
opts: Both are scleritis; both need systemic immunosuppression
The first is episcleritis (benign, blanches, self-limited); the second is scleritis (severe, violaceous, systemic association)
The first is scleritis; the second is episcleritis
Both are episcleritis and need only lubricants
concept: Episcleritis vs scleritis - phenylephrine blanching distinguishes them

stem: A 28-year-old with untreated anterior uveitis (iritis) returns with a fixed, irregular pupil and glare. What complication has developed, and what helps prevent it?
opts: Posterior synechiae (iris adhered to lens); a cycloplegic (e.g. atropine) helps prevent/adhesiolyse
concept: Anterior uveitis complication - posterior synechiae; cycloplegic prevents

stem: A 6-week-old infant is found to have a dense white pupil (leukocoria) and poor visual fixation in one eye. What is the most important principle in management?
opts: Observe until school age; cataracts in infants are benign
Treat promptly (often surgery within weeks) to prevent deprivation amblyopia
Prescribe corrective glasses and review at 1 year
concept: Congenital cataract - urgent treatment to prevent deprivation amblyopia

stem: After an acute angle-closure attack is controlled medically, what is the definitive preventive treatment?
opts: Laser peripheral iridotomy (creating a hole in the peripheral iris)
concept: Acute angle-closure glaucoma - laser peripheral iridotomy is definitive

stem: An immunocompetent adult has focal necrotizing retinitis with overlying vitritis, described as 'headlight in fog', and a small old scar elsewhere in the fundus. Most likely diagnosis and typical management?
opts: Toxoplasma chorioretinitis; treat with pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine (+folinic acid)
Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy; observe
concept: Toxoplasma chorioretinitis - 'headlight in fog' necrotizing focus + old scar

stem: A child has eyelid swelling and redness. On examination there is proposis, restricted extraocular movements, pain on eye movement and decreased vision. What is the key distinction and management?
opts: This is preseptal cellulitis; oral antibiotics as an outpatient suffice
This is orbital cellulitis; urgent IV antibiotics and CT to assess for abscess
This is allergic oedema; give antihistamines
This is chalazion; warm compresses only
concept: Orbital cellulitis vs preseptal - proptosis/EOM restriction/vision loss = orbital, urgent

stem: A 60-year-old has a vesicular rash on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson sign) with a red painful eye and blurred vision. Most appropriate action?
opts: Oral acyclovir (or valacyclovir) urgently plus urgent ophthalmology review
concept: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus - Hutchinson sign; urgent antiviral + eye review

stem: A 50-year-old farmer with chronic sun exposure has a triangular, fleshy, fibrovascular growth extending from the nasal limbus ONTO the cornea, with mild redness and irritation. Most likely diagnosis and concern?
opts: Pinguecula - a yellow nodule at the limbus that does not grow onto the cornea
Pterygium - fibrovascular growth onto the cornea; can threaten vision if it reaches the visual axis
concept: Pterygium vs pinguecula - pterygium grows onto cornea (UV-related)

stem: An elderly woman has the lower eyelid turning INWARD so the lashes rub against the cornea, causing irritation, redness and a corneal abrasion. Most likely diagnosis and risk?
opts: Ectropion - lid turns outward causing epiphora and exposure
Entropion - lid turns inward; lashes traumatise the cornea (risk of ulceration/infection)
concept: Entropion vs ectropion - entropion = lid inward, lashes scratch cornea

stem: A 4-month-old has a red, tender, swollen lump at the medial canthus with discharge from the punctum on compression; the eye itself is white and quiet. Most likely diagnosis and initial management?
opts: Acute dacryocystitis (infected nasolacrimal duct) - warm compresses, massage, oral antibiotics; probing if recurrent
concept: Dacryocystitis - medial canthal swelling/discharge; infected NLDO

stem: A 65-year-old with hypertension and diabetes wakes with sudden, painless vision loss in one eye. Exam shows a relative afferent pupillary defect and an isolated inferior altitudinal visual field defect. Fundoscopy reveals a pale oedematous optic disc with segmental haemorrhages. Diagnosis?
concept: NAION - painless altitudinal loss + disc oedema/haemorrhages in hypertensive/diabetic elderly

stem: A 15-year-old boy tells his teacher that 'the teacher is trying to kill me' and repeats that classmates are secretly plotting to attack him. He is convinced of this despite evidence to the contrary. He has no prominent depressed or manic mood. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Major depressive disorder with psychotic features
concept: Schizophrenia — persecutory (paranoid) delusions as a positive symptom

stem: A 22-year-old man presents with delusions and hallucinations that have been continuous for 3 months, with functioning decline. No mood episode is present.Which diagnosis fits best?
concept: Schizophreniform disorder — 1 to 6 months of psychotic symptoms (prodrome allowed)

stem: A 30-year-old man with schizophrenia is started on an antipsychotic. Three months later he has gained 8 kg and his fasting glucose and lipids are elevated. Which agent is MOST responsible for this metabolic syndrome?
concept: Second-generation antipsychotics (olanzapine) — metabolic syndrome AE

stem: A patient on an antipsychotic develops rigidity, hyperthermia, fluctuating consciousness and autonomic instability, with a markedly elevated CK. Which condition does this describe, and which drug class change most characteristically precedes it?
opts: Serotonin syndrome after a recent SSRI dose increase
Malignant hyperthermia after an inhaled anaesthetic
Tardive dyskinesia from long-term typical antipsychotics
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome after an antipsychotic dose increase or switch
concept: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome — rigidity + hyperthermia + autonomic instability + raised CK

stem: A 65-year-old woman who has taken a typical antipsychotic for years develops repetitive, involuntary oro-buccal-lingual chewing and grimacing movements. What is the best initial management?
opts: Continue the same dose and reassure
Switch to an atypical antipsychotic (or clozapine) and consider VMAT-2 inhibitor (valbenazine)
concept: Tardive dyskinesia — reduce/switch antipsychotic; anticholinergics can worsen it

stem: A 19-year-old man develops painful neck twisting (torticollis), eye deviation (oculogyric crisis) and tongue protrusion within 2 days of starting a high-potency typical antipsychotic. What is the immediate treatment?
concept: Acute dystonia — anticholinergic (benztropine/diphenhydramine)

stem: A 40-year-old man over 5 days has euphoric mood, grandiosity (plans to quit medicine and start a university), pressured speech and reckless spending, sleeping only 2–3 hours/night yet feeling rested. What is the most specific sleep finding that points to MANIA rather than simple insomnia?
opts: Difficulty falling asleep despite feeling tired
Decreased need for sleep with preserved energy/restored feeling
Early morning awakening with low mood
concept: Mania — decreased need for sleep (vs insomnia of depression/simple insomnia)

stem: A 33-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder presents with a 3-week episode of major depression while on her mood stabiliser. Which is LEAST appropriate?
opts: Add a second mood stabiliser or lamotrigine
Add an atypical antipsychotic such as quetiapine
Use antidepressant monotherapy alone for her depression
concept: Bipolar depression — avoid antidepressant MONOTHERAPY (mania switch risk)

stem: A new mother on day 3 postpartum is tearful, irritable and labile but can care for her baby, with symptoms fluctuating throughout the day and resolving spontaneously. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Postpartum baby blues — transient, day 3–5, self-limiting (<2 weeks)

stem: A mother 2 weeks after delivery is confused, disorganised, has bizarre delusions about her baby being evil, and insomnia. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Reassure and schedule outpatient follow-up in 2 weeks
Start an SSRI and let her rest at home
Refer to a dietician for sleep hygiene
Emergency psychiatric admission with antipsychotic treatment and safety planning for mother and infant
concept: Postpartum psychosis — psychiatric emergency, urgent admission

stem: A 50-year-old man has severe depression with early-morning waking, diurnal mood variation (worse in the morning), anorexia, weight loss and anhedonia with psychomotor retardation. Which feature supports a MELANCHOLIC specifier in depression?
opts: Early-morning awakening with mood worse in the morning and psychomotor changes
Fatigue that improves with restful sleep
Reactive mood that brightens with good news
concept: Melancholic depression — early-morning wakening, diurnal variation, psychomotor changes

stem: A 30-year-old woman has recurrent, unexpected episodes of intense fear peaking within minutes, with palpitations, sweating, tremor, chest discomfort, choking and a feeling of imminent death. She now avoids crowded places for fear of an episode. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Panic disorder — recurrent unexpected panic attacks peaking in minutes, with avoidance

stem: A 28-year-old woman with panic disorder asks about treatment. She wants a medication that treats the underlying attack frequency. Which is the most appropriate first-line long-term pharmacotherapy?
opts: Lorazepam as the sole daily treatment
An SSRI (e.g. sertraline or escitalopram), starting low and titrating
A short course of diazepam twice daily indefinitely
concept: Panic disorder — SSRI first-line

stem: A 78-year-old hospitalised man becomes acutely confused over hours, inattentive, with fluctuating alertness and visual hallucinations; he has an active urinary infection. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Delirium — acute onset, fluctuating, inattention, underlying medical cause

stem: A postoperative elderly patient is agitated and hallucinating with delirium. Which is the MOST appropriate first-line management approach?
opts: Start a benzodiazepine routinely to sedate immediately
Restrain the patient physically as the primary intervention
Identify and treat the underlying cause, use non-pharmacological measures, and reserve antipsychotics (e.g. low-dose haloperidol) for severe agitation
Give antipsychotics prophylactically to all patients
concept: Delirium — treat the cause + non-pharmacological first; antipsychotic only for severe agitation

stem: A 72-year-old man has progressive memory loss over 2 years with difficulty naming objects and navigating familiar places; functional decline is emerging. Which pharmacologic treatment is most appropriate for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease?
concept: Alzheimer disease — cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil) for mild-moderate

stem: A 69-year-old hypertensive, diabetic smoker has stepwise cognitive decline with abrupt worsening, emotional lability, focal neurologic signs and gait difficulty. MRI shows multiple lacunar infarcts and white-matter disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Vascular dementia — stepwise decline + focal signs + vascular risk factors + infarcts on imaging

stem: A 70-year-old man has fluctuating cognition, well-formed visual hallucinations of people and animals, and mild parkinsonism. His family notes marked sensitivity to antipsychotic medications. What is the most likely diagnosis and an important management caveat?
opts: Dementia with Lewy bodies — avoid neuroleptics (severe sensitivity), use cholinesterase inhibitors and handle psychosis carefully
Frontotemporal dementia — start an antipsychotic for behaviour
concept: Dementia with Lewy bodies — fluctuate + visual hallucinations + parkinsonism; severe neuroleptic sensitivity

stem: A 54-year-old man has progressive disinhibition, inappropriate social behaviour, apathy and loss of empathy over 2 years, with relative sparing of memory, plus difficulty producing words. Imaging shows frontal and temporal atrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Frontotemporal dementia — early behavioural disinhibition/apathy + language, younger onset, spared memory

stem: A chronic heavy drinker stops alcohol abruptly. He has confusion, agitation, tremor, hallucinations and marked autonomic overactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, fever) with a risk of seizures and death. What is this, and what is the treatment?
concept: Delirium tremens — clouded sensorium + autonomic instability; benzodiazepine treatment

stem: A 42-year-old man with alcohol use disorder wants medication to reduce craving and relapse after detoxification. Which agent reduces drinking by antagonising opioid receptors involved in alcohol's rewarding effect?
concept: Naltrexone — opioid antagonist reduces alcohol craving/drinking

stem: A 35-year-old man with long-standing opioid dependence stops use. He has rhinorrhoea, lacrimation, yawning, piloerection, mydriasis, muscle cramps, diarrhoea and anxiety. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate pharmacotherapy?
opts: Opioid withdrawal — treat with methadone or buprenorphine (and lofexidine adjunctively)
concept: Opioid withdrawal — sympathomimetic-opposite features; treat with methadone/buprenorphine

stem: A 9-year-old boy has persistent, impairing inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity across school and home, present since age 6. What is the first-line pharmacologic treatment?
concept: ADHD — stimulant (methylphenidate) first-line

stem: A 19-year-old woman with severe anorexia nervosa (BMI 14) is started on refeeding. On day 3 she develops weakness, arrhythmia, seizures and confusion. Bloods show low phosphate. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?
opts: Refeeding syndrome — give phosphate/electrolyte replacement and slow, monitored refeeding
concept: Refeeding syndrome in anorexia nervosa — refeeding-induced hypophosphataemia

stem: A 21-year-old woman of normal weight has recurrent episodes of binge-eating followed by self-induced vomiting several times a week, with dental enamel erosion, parotid swelling and calluses on her knuckles. Which electrolyte disturbance is most characteristic and dangerous?
concept: Bulimia nervosa — recurrent vomiting causing hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis

stem: During a cholera outbreak, the number of new cases reported per week doubles every 3 days. On day 0 there were 25 cases. If this pattern continues, approximately how many cases will there be after 12 days?
concept: Epidemic doubling time calculation

stem: A researcher records the monthly incomes (in thousand rupees) of 9 households in a village: 8, 10, 12, 12, 15, 16, 18, 20, 350. Which measure of central tendency best represents this distribution?
concept: Choice of central tendency measure in skewed data

stem: In a randomized controlled trial, a new antihypertensive drug is compared with placebo. The primary outcome is the mean fall in systolic blood pressure, measured in each of the two groups. Which statistical test is most appropriate to compare the two group means?
concept: Selection of the appropriate test of significance for two independent means

stem: A multicenter trial reports a p-value of 0.03 for its primary outcome. Which statement is the correct interpretation of this p-value?
opts: There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true
There is a 97% probability that the treatment is effective
If the null hypothesis were true, the probability of obtaining results at least this extreme is 3%
The result is clinically significant because it is below 0.05
concept: Correct interpretation of the p-value

stem: A rapid diagnostic test for typhoid was evaluated against blood culture in 2,000 febrile patients. Of 300 patients with culture-confirmed typhoid, 270 tested positive. Of 1,700 patients without typhoid, 1,530 tested negative. What is the negative predictive value (NPV) of this test?
concept: Negative predictive value from a 2×2 table

stem: After monsoon flooding contaminated the shallow wells of a village, 40 children and young adults developed jaundice over 2 weeks. None had blood transfusions, injections, or tattoos. Which is the most likely mode of transmission?
concept: Hepatitis E outbreak - fecal-oral transmission

stem: A nurse sustains a deep needlestick injury while drawing blood from a patient known to be HIV-positive with a high viral load. When should HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) be started?
opts: Start PEP immediately (ideally within hours, and not later than 72 hours) and continue for 28 days
Wait for repeat confirmatory HIV testing of the source patient, then decide
Start PEP only if the nurse tests HIV-positive at 3 months
Give a single antiretroviral drug for 7 days
concept: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis timing and duration

stem: In a randomized controlled trial of a weight-loss drug, 18% of participants in the intervention group never took the study drug. The primary analysis includes all randomized participants in the groups to which they were assigned. What is this analysis called?
concept: Intention-to-treat analysis in RCTs

stem: Using occupational health records from 1990, investigators classify 3,000 chemical plant workers as exposed or unexposed to benzene, then link these records to the national cancer registry up to 2025 to compare cancer incidence. What is the study design?
concept: Retrospective (historical) cohort study identification

stem: In a case-control study, 200 patients with colorectal cancer and 200 matched healthy controls are interviewed about their diet over the past 10 years. Compared with a cohort study, what is the main weakness of this design?
opts: High cost for a small number of outcomes
concept: Recall bias as the principal limitation of case-control studies

stem: A team surveys a town of 5,000 adults on a single day and finds that 85 currently have diabetes mellitus. Which epidemiological measure does the figure of 85/5,000 represent?
concept: Point prevalence vs incidence

stem: In a case-control study of pancreatic cancer and coffee drinking, 80 of 100 cases and 60 of 100 controls reported drinking coffee. Which measure of association is calculated, and what is its value?
concept: Odds ratio calculation in a case-control study

stem: A cohort study of regular exercise reports a relative risk (RR) of 0.6 for myocardial infarction in exercisers compared with sedentary adults. What is the correct interpretation?
opts: Exercise reduces the risk of myocardial infarction by 60%
Exercise reduces the risk of myocardial infarction by 40%
Exercise increases the risk of myocardial infarction by 60%
Risk reduction cannot be interpreted from a relative risk
concept: Interpreting a protective relative risk

stem: A health authority is deciding whether to introduce a population-wide screening programme. Which condition is most suitable for screening?
opts: A common cancer with a long detectable preclinical phase and effective treatment at early stages
A rapidly fatal cancer for which no effective treatment exists
A very rare disease with an inexpensive test
A mild self-limiting infection that resolves without treatment
concept: Suitability criteria for a screening programme

stem: The maternal mortality ratio (MMR) is conventionally expressed as the number of maternal deaths per how many live births?
concept: Maternal mortality ratio denominator

stem: Which statement correctly describes the infant mortality rate (IMR)?
opts: It includes stillbirths in its numerator
It is the number of deaths under 1 year of age per 1,000 live births in a year
It excludes all deaths that occur in the first month of life
It is expressed per 100,000 live births
concept: Infant mortality rate definition

stem: The government passes legislation making salt iodization compulsory across the country to prevent iodine deficiency disorders in the population. This measure is an example of which level of prevention?
concept: Levels of prevention - primordial vs primary

stem: According to Pakistan's Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI), at what age is the first dose of the measles-containing vaccine (MR-1) scheduled?
concept: EPI schedule - timing of first measles dose

stem: A health facility refrigerator malfunctions overnight and the vaccine vials are exposed to -5°C. Which vaccine is MOST likely to have been irreversibly damaged by freezing?
concept: Cold chain - freeze-sensitive vs freeze-tolerant vaccines

stem: A district's population pyramid has a very broad base that narrows steeply through successively higher age groups. Which population structure does this pattern represent?
opts: An ageing population with low fertility
A youthful population with high fertility and high mortality at younger ages
A stationary population with stable birth and death rates
A contracting population with net emigration of adults
concept: Population pyramid interpretation

stem: An asymptomatic 3-year-old child shares a home with his grandfather, who has smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis. The child's chest X-ray is normal. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Give isoniazid preventive therapy for 6-9 months
No action is needed because the child is asymptomatic
concept: Isoniazid preventive therapy for child contacts of smear-positive TB

stem: During a dengue outbreak, health workers find Aedes aegypti larvae breeding in household water storage containers. Which intervention gives the most effective sustained vector control?
opts: Insecticide fogging to kill adult mosquitoes
Source reduction by eliminating or covering breeding containers
Isolation of all febrile patients at home
Antibiotic prophylaxis for all household contacts
concept: Dengue vector control - source reduction

stem: Insecticide-treated bed nets are the cornerstone of malaria vector control in endemic regions because the principal vector:
opts: Bites during the day, mainly outdoors
Breeds only in polluted stagnant water
Transmits the parasite only in urban settings
concept: Malaria vector behavior and rationale for ITNs

stem: A district hospital reports 15 cases of acute watery diarrhea in one week, whereas the area usually records 2-3 cases per week. Following the standard outbreak investigation sequence, what is the FIRST step?
opts: Immediately implement control measures before anything else
Confirm the existence of an outbreak by comparing current and expected incidence
Start an analytic (case-control) study of the suspected food source
Analyze all stool samples in the laboratory before investigating
concept: Outbreak investigation - establishing the existence of an outbreak

stem: In a nutrition survey of children aged 6-59 months, a child has a weight-for-height Z-score of -3.4 and bilateral pitting edema. According to WHO criteria, this child has:
concept: Severe acute malnutrition - WHO anthropometric criteria

stem: A 3-year-old boy drank kerosene stored in a soft-drink bottle and began coughing and gagging immediately. His mother says the child 'choked' on the liquid. The attending doctor explains that kerosene readily enters the airways during swallowing. Which physicochemical property of kerosene is primarily responsible for this aspiration hazard?
opts: Alkaline pH that irritates the pharynx and triggers reflex inhalation
Low viscosity and low surface tension
High lipid solubility with rapid central nervous system penetration
High specific gravity causing it to sink and pool in the stomach
concept: Hydrocarbon (kerosene) poisoning — physicochemical basis of aspiration

stem: A 40-year-old man known to use opium is found drowsy at home. In the emergency department he is comatose with a respiratory rate of 7/min and shallow breathing. Which single finding on examination would most strongly argue AGAINST the opium toxidrome as the explanation for his coma?
concept: Opium (opioid) poisoning — the classic toxidrome and its contradictions

stem: A 45-year-old farmer was treated for acute organophosphate poisoning with atropine and pralidoxime and made a full recovery from the cholinergic crisis. Three weeks later he presents with progressive weakness of both feet, bilateral foot drop, and impaired vibration sense in the legs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Relapse of the acute cholinergic crisis
concept: Organophosphate poisoning — organophosphate-induced delayed neuropathy (OPIDN)

stem: At autopsy, a body shows intense cherry-red (pink) postmortem lividity in dependent areas and the stomach contents smell strongly of bitter almonds. Which poison is the most likely cause of death?
concept: Cyanide poisoning — autopsy findings

stem: A worker collapses minutes after exposure to a chemical with a bitter-almond odour and is brought to the emergency department with suspected cyanide poisoning. Which antidote acts by directly binding cyanide ions to form cyanocobalamin, which is then excreted in the urine?
concept: Cyanide poisoning — antidote mechanism (hydroxocobalamin)

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents with chronic diarrhoea, hyperpigmentation of the skin with raindrop depigmentation, peripheral neuropathy, and white transverse bands across all fingernails (Mees lines). She has been taking an unregulated herbal tonic for months. Which chelating agent is the most appropriate treatment?
concept: Arsenic poisoning — clinical picture and chelation

stem: A 3-year-old boy with pica is brought in with abdominal colic, irritability, and vomiting. He has microcytic anaemia with basophilic stippling on the blood film, and radiographs show dense metaphyseal bands at the wrists. He now develops altered consciousness and seizures. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Parenteral dimercaprol (BAL) plus calcium disodium edetate
concept: Lead poisoning — chelation in encephalopathy

stem: A 2-year-old boy, previously well, develops 3 weeks of irritability, insomnia, profuse sweating, and photophobia. His hands and feet are red, swollen, and painful with peeling of the fingertips, and he is hypotonic. There is no fever. The family recently broke a mercury thermometer at home. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Mercury poisoning — acrodynia (pink disease)

stem: A 25-year-old woman ingests copper sulphate crystals in a suicide attempt and vomits blue-green material repeatedly. She is treated with gastric lavage after demulcents, dimercaprol, and supportive care for haemolysis and metabolic acidosis. Which of the following agents should NOT be added to her management?
opts: Gastric lavage after milk or egg albumin
Intravenous fluids and sodium bicarbonate for acidosis
concept: Copper sulphate poisoning — management and antidote selection

stem: A 40-year-old farmer is bitten on the ankle by a snake while harvesting. Two hours later there is only mild local swelling and mild pain at the bite site, but the 20-minute whole blood clotting test (20WBCT) shows blood that fails to clot. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Excision of the bite wound under local anaesthesia
Tetanus toxoid and antibiotics alone, with daily wound review
Administer polyvalent antivenom without further delay
Observe in hospital without antivenom until local swelling becomes marked
concept: Snake bite — 20WBCT-guided antivenom decision

stem: A 20-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 90 minutes after an alleged sexual assault. She has multiple active bleeding lacerations, a pre-syncopal feeling, and a pulse of 120/min with blood pressure 85/55 mmHg. What is the most appropriate sequence of care?
opts: Complete the full forensic examination first so evidence is not lost
Stabilise and treat the injuries first; carry out the medicolegal examination afterwards with consent
Send her to the police station for a statement before any examination
Perform the medicolegal examination and delay treatment until the investigating officer arrives
concept: Sexual offences — priority of medical care over forensic sampling

stem: A 55-year-old man is brought in unconscious after a road traffic accident with a ruptured spleen and intra-abdominal bleeding. Despite an urgent search his relatives cannot be traced, and surgery cannot wait. What is the correct medicolegal course of action?
opts: Transfer the patient to another hospital that will accept him without consent
Delay surgery until written consent from a relative or guardian is obtained
Proceed with the life-saving surgery, documenting that consent was implied by emergency necessity
Obtain consent from any bystander who accompanied the patient
concept: Consent — the emergency (implied consent) doctrine

stem: A 48-year-old man undergoes an elective cholecystectomy under general anaesthesia and dies on the operating table despite rapid resuscitation. The family had signed a detailed surgical consent form. According to current medicolegal practice, how should this death be handled?
opts: The signed consent form absolves the team of any medicolegal reporting obligation
It is a natural death and needs no reporting to the authorities
It is a medicolegal case and should be reported; autopsy proceeds on the order of the magistrate
It becomes reportable only if the family lodges a formal complaint
concept: Medico-legal cases — perioperative (anaesthetic) death

stem: A 60-year-old woman with 70% burns is conscious and coherent in the casualty ward. She says her son-in-law set her on fire and asks to give her statement before she dies. Who should ideally record her dying declaration?
opts: A police constable from the local station
concept: Dying declaration — recording authority

stem: A man is struck on the head with a glass bottle during a brawl and collapses. At the emergency department he has a scalp wound with irregular, ragged, contused margins, strands of tissue bridging the gap, and bruising of the surrounding scalp. What is the nature of this wound?
opts: An abrasion produced by friction against a rough surface
An incised wound produced by a sharp-edged weapon
A laceration produced by blunt force
A puncture wound produced by a pointed weapon
concept: Mechanical injuries — laceration vs incised wound

stem: A man is found with a bruise on the left arm that is greenish-yellow at the periphery and fading. Based on the colour changes of a healing bruise, approximately how old is this bruise?
opts: More than 3 weeks (brown and fully faded)
concept: Mechanical injuries — ageing of bruises by colour

stem: At autopsy on a body recovered from a house fire, extensive third-degree burns are present. Which single finding most reliably indicates that the burns were sustained BEFORE death (antemortem)?
opts: Pugilistic attitude (fixed flexed posture) of the limbs
Splitting and cracking of the skin over the limbs
Vesication containing fluid rich in leukocytes and fibrin, with a red congested line at the margins
concept: Thermal injuries — antemortem vs postmortem burns

stem: A body is recovered from the sea after several minutes of witnessed immersion. Bystanders pulled the victim out almost immediately, but resuscitation failed. Which biochemical pattern best matches saltwater (seawater) drowning?
opts: Left ventricular failure from acute volume overload
concept: Drowning — fresh vs salt water pathophysiology

stem: At autopsy of a man found dead at home after a domestic dispute, the only significant injury is a fracture of the greater cornu of the hyoid bone with perihyoid haemorrhage. There are no other neck injuries. Which conclusion is best supported by this finding?
opts: Death was due to typical hanging
Death was due to judicial hanging
Death was due to smothering during an assault
Death was due to manual or ligature strangulation
concept: Ligature and manual strangulation — hyoid bone fracture

stem: A body is brought to the mortuary about four hours after death. Rigor mortis is felt in the muscles of the eyelids, jaw, and neck but not yet in the lower limbs. According to Nysten's law, in which muscle group does rigor mortis first appear?
opts: Muscles of the chest and abdomen
concept: Postmortem changes — rigor mortis and Nysten's law

stem: In a medicolegal examination, radiographs are used to estimate the age of an unidentified skeleton. Which epiphysis, being the last to unite in the body, indicates that the person had reached approximately 25 years of age?
opts: The medial end of the clavicle
The lower end of the radius
concept: Age estimation — ossification centres

stem: During the dental examination of a child for medicolegal age estimation, the first permanent molar (the 'six-year molar') has recently erupted while the deciduous incisors are still being shed. Approximately what is the child's age?
concept: Age estimation — dental eruption chronology

stem: A body is found in an open field in summer, and forensic entomology is used to estimate the postmortem interval. The body is colonised by several arthropod species in waves. Which group is typically the FIRST to arrive and lay eggs on a fresh corpse?
concept: Forensic entomology — insect succession in postmortem interval estimation

stem: A family demands the exhumation of a buried body because they suspect poisoning. Under the applicable legal provisions, which authority can order the exhumation of a dead body?
opts: The District Magistrate or a court
The Senior Superintendent of Police on his own authority
A written request from the head of the family
concept: Exhumation — legal authority for the order

stem: A 22-year-old woman is examined 5 hours after an alleged rape. She is haemodynamically stable and consents to the examination. Which investigation most reliably corroborates recent sexual intercourse at this time point?
opts: High vaginal swab for bacterial culture
Microscopic examination of a vaginal swab for motile spermatozoa
concept: Sexual offences — corroborative evidence of recent intercourse

stem: A severely malnourished patient has to undergo surgery. The most important item to replace in order to ensure good wound healing would be:
concept: Vitamin C (ascorbate) is the cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase in collagen cross-linking; deficiency causes defective collagen, poor wound healing, gum bleeding and poor healing of pressure sores.

stem: A 38-year-old male is brought to emergency room after a road traffic accident. He is hypoxic and cyanosed with pulse 120/min, blood pressure 100/70 mmHg and respiratory rate 22/min. The trachea is shifted to the left. There are multiple rib fractures on the right with reduced breath sounds and a hyper-resonant percussion note, and he is deteriorating. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Tension pneumothorax - one-way valve air trapping with mediastinal shift and obstructive shock; clinical diagnosis, decompress immediately

stem: A 1-year-old healthy child is scheduled for elective inguinal hernia repair. The mother asks about pre-operative feeding instructions. The recommended NPO status for this age group is:
opts: 4 hours NPO for both solids and clear fluids
3 hours NPO for solids and clear fluids
2 hours NPO for solids, clear fluids permitted up to 4 hours pre-operatively
4 hours NPO for solids, clear fluids permitted up to 2 hours pre-operatively
concept: Paediatric pre-operative fasting - solids 4-6 h, clear fluids 2 h (traditional 6h/3h for solids)

stem: A 45-year-old female underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy under general anaesthesia two days ago. She now has jaundice with colicky upper abdominal pain and nausea. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms and signs?
opts: Stone in the common bile duct
Injury to the common bile duct
concept: Post-cholecystectomy jaundice within 48 hours - iatrogenic bile duct injury, most often the clip applied to the wrong structure

stem: A 20-year-old girl presents with five days of central abdominal pain that has localised to the right lower quadrant. She is febrile with a tender, firm mass in the right iliac fossa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Appendicular mass - walled-off perforated appendicitis presenting days later as a tender right iliac fossa mass

stem: A 35-year-old primigravida is scheduled for epidural analgesia during labour. During the procedure she has a dural tap and develops a positional headache that has now lasted almost 48 hours. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Normal saline in the epidural catheter
concept: Post-dural puncture headache persisting beyond 24-48 h - epidural blood patch is the treatment

stem: A 27-year-old male is brought to the emergency room after a road traffic accident. He is conscious with pulse 120/min and blood pressure 100/70 mmHg and has a pelvic fracture. Intravenous fluids and oxygen by mask have been started. Which is best for monitoring his progress?
concept: Urine output is the best single bedside monitor of tissue perfusion and response to resuscitation

stem: A 41-year-old man presents 12 hours after a road traffic accident with a compound fracture of the mid-shaft of the right tibia and fibula. He was managed initially at a basic health unit with a POP back slab. According to the Gustilo classification this is a Type IIIA injury. What is the initial most suitable treatment?
concept: Open fracture Type IIIA - urgent debridement with external fixation, then definitive fixation once soft tissue is clean

stem: A young man has an unstable neck from a C3-C4 vertebral fracture with multiple faciomaxillary injuries after falling from a height. His mandible must be fixed under general anaesthesia. What is the best method of intubation?
opts: Awake intubation with a fibreoptic laryngoscope
concept: Unstable cervical spine with facial trauma requiring GA - awake fibreoptic intubation with manual in-line stabilisation

stem: A 52-year-old man has had five operations for fistula-in-ano. What is the key point to evaluate during assessment and surgery in any case of fistula-in-ano?
opts: Internal opening with assessment of all secondary tracts
concept: Fistula-in-ano - the internal opening at the dentate line and all secondary tracts define the anatomy and the operation

stem: A patient with raised intracranial pressure is intubated and ventilated to reduce cerebral oedema using hyperventilation. What is the most appropriate PaCO2 to maintain for the first 12 to 24 hours?
concept: Controlled hyperventilation for raised ICP - PaCO2 30-35 mmHg; avoid aggressive hypocapnia (cerebral ischaemia)

stem: A 32-year-old male is brought to the emergency room after a road traffic accident. He is conscious and talking. During the primary survey you notice rapid breathing, the trachea slightly shifted to the left with engorged neck veins, and multiple rib fractures. Breath sounds are absent on the right with hyper-resonance on percussion. What is your next step in management?
opts: Needle decompression and arrange for chest intubation
Complete the primary survey and inform the surgical team
Send him for urgent chest X-ray for definitive diagnosis
Give oxygen by mask and arrange endotracheal intubation
concept: Tension pneumothorax during primary survey - immediate needle decompression, then chest drain; imaging must not delay

stem: A 37-year-old male had a left chest tube inserted for a traumatic haemothorax 15 days ago. He now has high-grade spiking pyrexia for four days. The chest tube drains frank pus and CT shows a dense, loculated collection confined to the lower two-thirds of the chest. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Placement of a new chest tube
concept: Post-traumatic empyema - the decisive feature is pus (infected phase), treated by drainage; decortication is for the organised chronic phase

stem: A 20-year-old male is brought to the emergency room after a road traffic accident. During the primary survey his pulse is 120/min, blood pressure 90/60 mmHg and respiratory rate 18/min. His left thigh is swollen and deformed, most likely a fractured femur. What should be your next step?
opts: Send the patient for X-ray of the left thigh
Call the orthopaedic team for further management
Immobilise the left lower limb with traction
concept: ATLS primary survey - shocked patient: complete ABCDE first, treating life-threatening problems as found; the femur is a secondary priority

stem: A 25-year-old man presents with trauma to the middle of the arm. There is no external wound. X-ray shows a transverse fracture of the mid-shaft of the humerus with displacement under one centimetre and no angulation. What is the best first treatment option?
concept: Isolated humeral shaft fracture, minimally displaced and unangulated - non-operative management in a sling

stem: A 2-month-old male infant has repeated non-bilious projectile vomiting after feeds since two weeks. On examination visible peristalsis is seen after a feed. You diagnose infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis and schedule him for surgery. What is the next most important step in pre-operative resuscitation?
opts: Intravenous correction of fluid and electrolytes
concept: Pyloric stenosis - pre-operative correction of hypochloremic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis is mandatory before surgery

stem: A 38-year-old male is brought to the emergency room after a road traffic accident. He looks pale with pulse 120/min, blood pressure 90/60 mmHg and respiratory rate 20/min. There are multiple rib fractures on the right with reduced breath sounds and a dull percussion note. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Haemothorax - dull percussion with reduced breath sounds after trauma, versus hyper-resonance in pneumothorax

stem: A 75-year-old lady presents to the emergency room with a painful right hip after a slip in the bathroom. She has advanced dementia with little discomfort. X-ray shows a Garden I fracture - the femoral head is tilted slightly into valgus and impacted on the femoral neck stump with trabeculae in alignment. What is the best treatment?
concept: Garden I impacted femoral neck fracture in a frail, demented, minimally symptomatic 75-year-old - non-operative care

stem: 15 ml of 0.25% plain bupivacaine is administered epidurally for pain relief in labour. Half an hour later she still complains of inadequate analgesia, and the distribution of analgesia is patchy. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Air pockets in the epidural space
concept: Patchy asymmetric epidural block - air pockets in the epidural space (multidose technique) cause non-uniform spread

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with pain, swelling and deformity of the right leg after a fall. X-ray shows more than two fragments of the tibia, minimally displaced, with an intact fibula. What is the most likely type of fracture?
concept: Comminuted fracture - more than two fragments, typically high-energy or direct trauma

stem: A 20-year-old man presents to the emergency room with a fracture of the acromion of the scapula. On X-ray the displacement is minimal. What is the best treatment option?
concept: Minimally displaced acromion fracture - conservative management with sling and early mobilisation

stem: A 36-year-old male is brought to the emergency room after an assault. He is hypoxic with pulse 110/min, blood pressure 100/70 mmHg and respiratory rate 20/min. There are multiple rib fractures on the right with paradoxical movement of a segment of the chest wall. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Flail chest (segmental rib fractures) - paradoxical movement of the chest wall with hypoxaemia

stem: A 20-year-old male presents to the emergency room with green-coloured vomiting, abdominal distension and constipation for two days. He had an appendicectomy one month ago. On examination his abdomen is distended and mildly tender throughout, with a resonant percussion note and sluggish bowel sounds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Post-appendicectomy intestinal obstruction from adhesions - distension, constipation, resonant percussion, sluggish bowel sounds

stem: A 45-year-old alcoholic male presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain radiating to the back for the last 12 hours. On examination the abdomen is soft and distended with tenderness in the epigastric region. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Acute pancreatitis - severe epigastric pain radiating to the back in an alcoholic, with a soft mildly tender abdomen

stem: A 29-year-old female received an epidural for pain relief in labour. She had a wet tap, the procedure was successfully repeated in the space above, and she then developed a post-dural puncture headache. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Stretching of the sixth cranial nerves
concept: Post-dural puncture headache is caused by CSF leak through the dural defect, worsened by gravity when upright

stem: A 28-year-old sportsman fell on his shoulder and developed pain and deformity of the right shoulder. X-rays show a type IV acromioclavicular separation. What is the best treatment option?
concept: Acromioclavicular joint separation Rockwood type IV - surgical stabilisation indicated in an athletic young patient

stem: A 36-year-old woman gives a history of recent blunt trauma to her right breast and presents with a painless lump with skin tethering in the same breast. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Fat necrosis of the breast after blunt trauma - can mimic carcinoma with skin tethering

stem: A 15-year-old school girl presents with a discrete, mobile and painless lump in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Fibroadenoma - discrete, mobile, painless, well-circumscribed breast lump in an adolescent girl

stem: A 22-year-old male suffers from first-degree bleeding haemorrhoids. Which of the following treatments will benefit him most?
opts: Injection sclerotherapy with 5% phenol in almond oil
concept: First-degree haemorrhoids - conservative and office-based treatment; sclerotherapy with 5% phenol is the classic choice

stem: A 40-year-old man with bleeding piles is examined and found to have external haemorrhoids covered by skin. The varicose vein of the pile, i.e. the inferior rectal vein, most likely drains into:
concept: Inferior (superficial) rectal vein drains into the internal pudendal vein; above the pectinate line drainage is to the internal iliac

stem: In a seated adult male, a physician percusses the posterior aspect of the chest along the scapular line in quiet respiration. Lung resonance is most likely to extend down to the level of which rib?
concept: Normal lung resonance in quiet respiration reaches the 6th rib anteriorly and the 10th rib posteriorly (mid-axillary 8th)

stem: A newly married 25-year-old woman has missed her last normal menstrual cycle by four weeks. Her urine pregnancy test is positive. Which hormone is responsible for this pregnancy test?
concept: Urine pregnancy test detects human chorionic gonadotrophin secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast

stem: A young girl is brought to the emergency department with an acute abdomen. Pain began in the umbilicus and radiated towards the right iliac fossa. Tenderness increased on flexing the right thigh and medially rotating it. What is the most likely position of the appendix?
concept: Acute appendicitis - obturator sign localises the inflamed appendix to the pelvis

stem: A young athlete has difficulty turning the sole of the right foot medially but no difficulty turning the sole laterally. Which muscle group is most likely to have been injured?
opts: Extensor hallucis longus / flexor hallucis longus
concept: Inversion (medial rotation) of the sole is performed by tibialis anterior and tibialis posterior; eversion by the peroneal muscles

stem: A patient has difficulty raising the arm above the head after an injury to the right axillary region. On examination the inferior angle of the right scapula is prominent. Which nerve is most likely to have been injured?
concept: Long thoracic nerve (C5,6,7) supplies serratus anterior; injury causes winging of the scapula and loss of abduction above 90 degrees

stem: A 50-year-old woman has a hysterectomy for a uterine fibroid. Within 24 hours she develops colicky right loin pain. Which structure has most likely been ligated?
concept: Pelvic ureter runs close to the uterine artery and cervix; ligation produces colicky loin pain within 24-48 hours of hysterectomy

stem: A boy developed swelling of the ankle joint due to a sprain while playing. Which ligament is most likely to have been involved?
concept: Ankle inversion sprain most commonly tears the anterior talofibular ligament, part of the lateral collateral ligament complex

stem: A 50-year-old woman has fever and excruciating pain on the left side of the face. Vesicles are seen on the left tympanic membrane, on the forehead, on the nose and medial to the left eye. What is the most likely nerve involved?
concept: Herpes zoster in the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve - vesicles in the forehead, nose and medial eye with no involvement of the tympanic membrane territory of VII

stem: Post-natal examination of a newborn revealed a large cystic mass in the lumbar region, filled with CSF and herniating through a vertebral defect. No neurological deficit was found. What is the most likely neural tube defect?
concept: Meningocele - CSF-filled sac through a bony defect with intact neural tissue and no neurological deficit

stem: A young man has a blood pressure of 160/110 mmHg and a blood renin level much higher than normal. What is the most likely stimulus for the increased renin level?
opts: Increased sodium delivery to the distal tubules
concept: Renin is released in response to reduced renal perfusion pressure (decreased afferent arteriolar stretch)

stem: A patient with chronic renal failure has low serum calcium and high serum phosphate. Which change best explains these findings?
opts: Decreased calcium absorption in the gut
Increased calcium loss in the urine
concept: Chronic renal failure - loss of 1-alpha-hydroxylase reduces calcitriol, causing low calcium, low gut absorption and raised phosphate

stem: A patient is exposed in an operating theatre where the air temperature is 21 degrees C and the humidity is 80%. Which route accounts for the greatest heat loss from the body?
concept: Radiation accounts for most heat loss in theatre; vaporisation is second and becomes dominant only in warm, dry, high-airflow conditions

stem: During quiet inspiration, which muscle contraction increases both the anteroposterior and the transverse diameters of the thoracic cavity?
concept: The diaphragm is the principal muscle of quiet inspiration, increasing both AP and transverse thoracic diameters as it descends

stem: A young man had a gastrectomy about three months ago. His haemoglobin is 6 g/dL. What type of anaemia is he most likely to have?
concept: Post-gastrectomy megaloblastic anaemia - loss of intrinsic factor from stomach removal limits vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum

stem: A 35-year-old female reports loss of appetite and weight gain. She wears thick clothes despite a warm day and has a coarse voice and a cold feeling. Which hormone level would most probably be abnormal?
concept: Hypothyroidism - weight gain, cold intolerance, coarse voice and bradycardia from reduced T3/T4

stem: A 66-year-old man reports muscle tremors, muscular rigidity, bradykinesia and gait abnormalities to a neurologist. This problem is due to reduced activity of neurons in which of the following?
concept: Parkinson's disease - loss of dopaminergic neurones in the substantia nigra pars compacta

stem: A man with a head injury has difficulty in uttering words. His speech is limited to only a few words. Where is the damage most likely?
concept: Non-fluent expressive aphasia - damage to Broca's area in the dominant inferior frontal gyrus

stem: An ECG shows an atrial rate of 200-350 per minute, a 3:1 AV block and saw-tooth shaped P waves. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Atrial flutter - saw-tooth flutter waves at 250-350 per minute with a fixed or variable AV conduction ratio

stem: During treadmill exercise, if the heart rate increases to double the normal rate, the duration of the cardiac cycle becomes:
concept: Cardiac cycle duration is the reciprocal of heart rate - 72/min gives 0.83 s, so doubling the rate halves it to about 0.4 s

stem: A 71-year-old man was found to have a reduced left ventricular ejection fraction a few weeks after myocardial infarction. What is the most likely cause of myocardial cell injury in him?
concept: Myocardial infarction causes irreversible injury by ischaemia - coagulative necrosis from ATP depletion and failure of ion pumps

stem: A 30-year-old woman has increased urinary frequency, dysuria, normal urine output, 2+ proteinuria, many white cells in the urine, with normal serum creatinine, normal albumin, normal blood pressure and no peripheral oedema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Acute pyelonephritis - pyuria, bacteriuria and mild proteinuria with preserved renal function and no oedema

stem: An appendicectomy is performed on a 20-year-old girl hospitalised with right lower quadrant pain of 17 hours duration. The surgical specimen is oedematous and erythematous. An infiltrate of which cell type would be characteristic?
concept: Acute appendicitis - acute suppurative inflammation with a neutrophil (polymorphonuclear) infiltrate

stem: A 23-year-old man has been diagnosed with a lipoma on his back, present for five years. Which statement about this condition is most correct?
opts: There would be overlying skin inflammation
concept: Lipoma - a benign tumour of mature adipocytes, soft, mobile, painless, well circumscribed and vascularised

stem: A person sustained a crushing injury of the arm with tissue death due to loss of blood supply. Which type of pathological process is most likely?
concept: Ischaemic infarction of solid tissue - the classic morphology of necrosis from loss of blood supply

stem: A 51-year-old woman has burning micturition, fever with mild chills for two days and increased urinary frequency. What is the most likely causative organism?
concept: Acute uncomplicated cystitis in a woman - ascending infection by E. coli from the gut

stem: A 60-year-old lady has severe lower abdominal pain, high-grade fever and diarrhoea on the fifth post-operative day after vaginal hysterectomy. Her white cell count is 13,000/mm3. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Post-hysterectomy day 5 with fever, pelvic pain and diarrhoea - pelvic sepsis (abscess/infection)

stem: A 23-year-old woman P0+0 at 38 weeks presents with tonic and clonic convulsions. After treatment her urine output is 5 mL/hour and her respiratory rate is 12/min. Which drug was most probably administered?
concept: Magnesium sulphate toxicity - oliguria and respiratory depression (respiratory rate 12) after MgSO4 for eclampsia

stem: A 28-year-old G5P4 at 34 weeks presents with bleeding per vaginum for 12 hours. She is haemodynamically stable. The fundal height corresponds with gestational age and the lie is longitudinal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Painless third-trimester bleeding with a normal fundal height and longitudinal lie = placenta previa

stem: A 30-year-old sixth gravida attends the antenatal clinic at 30 weeks with tiredness, fatigue and breathlessness. She is pale and the fundal height corresponds with gestational age. Her haemoglobin is 8 g/dL. What is the most suitable investigation to determine the type of anaemia?
concept: Iron deficiency anaemia in pregnancy - serum FERRITIN is the investigation, because serum iron is depressed by dilutional anaemia of pregnancy

stem: A 23-year-old woman para 0+3 presents at 35 weeks of gestation with two days of raised blood pressure, headache, visual disturbance and epigastric pain. Blood pressure is 160/120 mmHg, reflexes are brisk and dipstick proteinuria is 4+. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Give intravenous magnesium sulphate and monitor
Give oral antihypertensives and delay delivery until term
Give intravenous magnesium sulphate, control the blood pressure and deliver
concept: Severe pre-eclampsia at 35 weeks - stabilise the mother, control the blood pressure, then deliver because the fetus is near term

stem: A 25-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks is admitted in emergency with convulsions. She has a puffy appearance, pitting oedema of the legs, blood pressure 160/110 mmHg and oliguria. What is the best drug to control the convulsions?
concept: Eclamptic seizure at 36 weeks - magnesium sulphate is both the treatment and the prophylaxis for eclampsia

stem: A 30-year-old woman in her third pregnancy with two previous term intrauterine fetal deaths presents for antenatal care and is unsure of her dates. Ultrasound shows a crown-rump length of 61 mm and a fetal weight of 14 g. What gestational age does this correspond to?
concept: First-trimester dating by crown-rump length; CRL 61 mm is about 12 weeks, and CRL is accurate to within 5-7 days before 14 weeks

stem: A 36-year-old woman P2 presents at the family planning clinic for contraception advice. She is a smoker and had a mastectomy for carcinoma of the breast one year ago. General and pelvic examination reveal no abnormality. What is the best contraception for her?
concept: Contraception in a smoker over 35 after breast carcinoma - the intrauterine device is the best choice

stem: A 4-year-old boy has high-grade fever, cough, conjunctivitis and nasal obstruction with a maculopapular rash that developed four days after these symptoms. Which diagnosis is correct?
concept: Measles - prodrome of fever, cough, coryza and conjunctivitis (the three C's) followed by a maculopapular rash on day 4

stem: A baby girl can roll over, transfers an object from hand to hand, produces a wide variety of recognisable speech sounds and plays with her feet. What is her most likely age?
concept: Developmental milestones - rolling over and object transfer place the infant at six months

stem: Which of the following diseases is included in Pakistan's Expanded Programme on Immunisation?
concept: Pakistan EPI: BCG, oral polio, DPT and measles, with Hib included in the pentavalent formulation

stem: An 8-month-old baby has diarrhoea without blood for one month. He was previously normal and is losing weight, with no other significant history. What step should be taken next to diagnose the condition?
opts: A test for malabsorption should be done
concept: Chronic diarrhoea (over 2 weeks) in an infant with failure to thrive - investigate for malabsorption, not as simple gastroenteritis

stem: A 65-year-old unconscious male is brought to the emergency room after a road traffic accident. He is a known diabetic, has signs of head injury and a swollen, deformed left thigh. His pulse is 130/min, blood pressure 70/40 mmHg and respiratory rate 20/min. What is the most appropriate first step?
opts: Send for CT scan of the brain
Check and correct the blood glucose level
Send for X-rays including the left thigh
concept: Unstable polytrauma - ABCDE with circulation first; treat hypovolaemia before imaging or metabolic causes

stem: A 27-year-old pregnant female is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. She is unconscious with possible head injury. Her pulse is 130/min and blood pressure 90/40 mmHg. What should be the priority in her management?
opts: Order for a CT scan of the brain
Ensure that the baby is fine
Secure the airway and the cervical spine
concept: Trauma in pregnancy - airway with cervical spine protection is the first step of ATLS, whatever the fetal concern

stem: A 50-year-old male presents to the emergency room with pain in the right upper abdomen and fever with rigors for four days. He is jaundiced, with tenderness in the right hypochondrium and lumbar region. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Charcot's triad - fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain indicates acute cholangitis

stem: A 52-year-old male presents with intermittent constipation and occasional bouts of bloody diarrhoea for three months. His appetite is normal but he has lost about 5 kg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Change in bowel habit with weight loss and blood in an older adult - colonic carcinoma until proved otherwise

stem: A 50-year-old male has unilateral claudication of the thigh, calf and sometimes the buttock for a few weeks. On examination the femoral and distal pulses are absent and a bruit is auscultated. What is the site of obstruction?
concept: Absent femoral pulse localises obstruction to the common femoral artery or below

stem: A 65-year-old male comes to the surgical outpatient department with pain in the right inguinoscrotal region for six hours, with vomiting and constipation. On examination there is abdominal distension and a warm, tender swelling in the right groin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Groin swelling plus intestinal obstruction = strangulated inguinal hernia until proved otherwise

stem: A 20-year-old boy presents to the emergency room after a fall on the right side of the neck twelve hours ago. He complains of loss of some function in his right arm. On examination the shoulder abductors and external rotators are affected. Which nerve roots are most likely injured?
concept: Erb's palsy - C5 and C6 injury causes loss of shoulder abduction and external rotation with a waiter's tip deformity

stem: A 27-year-old man with head injury is confused, withdraws and opens his eyes when his arm is pinched. According to the Glasgow Coma Scale, what is his score?
concept: Glasgow Coma Scale - eye, verbal and motor components summed independently; E2 + V4 + M4 = 10

stem: A 78-year-old female is brought to the emergency department after a fall while walking on the pavement. She complains of pain in her left hip and thigh. Her left leg appears shortened and externally rotated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Upper shaft fracture of the femur
concept: Elderly fall with a shortened, externally rotated leg = fractured neck of femur

stem: A 55-year-old male with COPD is admitted to the critical care unit with a severe respiratory infection and his level of consciousness is deteriorating. In this patient the respiratory drive is dependent on:
opts: Impulses from lung receptors to the respiratory centre
Increased blood flow to the brain stem
concept: Chronic CO2 retainers depend on the peripheral hypoxic drive from low PaO2, not the central CO2 response

stem: A 35-year-old male presents four months after suicidal ingestion of caustic soda with dysphagia. Endoscopy revealed multiple strictures starting from 28 cm. What is the best treatment option?
concept: Multiple long-segment strictures after caustic ingestion - surgical oesophageal replacement

stem: A 12-hour-old neonate is undergoing repair of a left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia. Half an hour into the operation he cannot be ventilated, airway pressure rises and he desaturates. Breath sounds are absent over the left hemithorax and the trachea is deviated to the right. What is the most likely cause?
concept: Tension pneumothorax during neonatal ventilation - the lung cannot be ventilated because one hemithorax is under tension

stem: A 45-year-old female is brought to the emergency room after a road traffic accident. She says she was driving fast and hit a tree while wearing a seatbelt. What are the most likely injuries?
opts: Injuries to the thoracic and abdominal walls
concept: Seatbelt injury - lap-belt pattern of mesenteric and bowel injury with minimal external damage

stem: A 55-year-old male presents with painless, progressive jaundice for six weeks, with itching and pale stools. What is the most likely diagnosis?
concept: Painless progressive obstructive jaundice with itching and pale stool in an older adult - periampullary carcinoma

stem: A diagnosed case of acute appendicitis is taken to theatre for appendectomy. The trainee surgeon uses a gridiron incision but cannot find the appendix. What is the most reliable way to locate it?
opts: Follow the taenia coli of the caecum
