stem: A 48-year-old woman with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) develops a saddle nose deformity. What structure has been damaged by the disease?
subject: Medicine-Respiratory
concept: Wegener ENT manifestations — saddle nose from nasal septal destruction
discriminator: Saddle nose deformity in Wegener results from necrotising granulomatous inflammation destroying the nasal septal cartilage, causing collapse of the nasal bridge.

stem: What is the most important clinical feature that distinguishes microscopic polyangiitis from granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener)?
subject: Medicine-Respiratory
concept: Microscopic polyangiitis vs Wegener — ENT involvement is the key discriminator
discriminator: Both are ANCA vasculitides with pulmonary-renal involvement, but only Wegener has prominent ENT involvement (sinusitis, nasal ulcers, saddle nose). Microscopic polyangiitis has NO ENT involvement.

stem: A 25-year-old non-smoker presents with dyspnoea, haemoptysis, and haematuria. CXR shows bilateral ground-glass opacities. Which additional investigation result would most likely confirm the diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Respiratory
concept: Goodpasture diagnosis — anti-GBM antibody confirms
discriminator: Young adult + haemoptysis + haematuria + ground-glass CXR = Goodpasture. Anti-GBM antibody confirms.

stem: A 60-year-old man with ANCA-associated vasculitis (GPA) achieves remission after induction therapy. Which agent is most appropriate for maintenance therapy?
subject: Medicine-Respiratory
concept: ANCA vasculitis maintenance therapy — azathioprine or rituximab
discriminator: After induction of remission in ANCA vasculitis, azathioprine (or rituximab) is used for maintenance. Cyclophosphamide is stopped due to toxicity.

stem: A 40-year-old woman with known microscopic polyangiitis (p-ANCA positive) on treatment develops progressive dyspnoea. CXR shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Pulmonary function tests reveal elevated DLCO. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
subject: Medicine-Respiratory
concept: Alveolar haemorrhage in ANCA vasculitis — elevated DLCO from haemoglobin trapping CO
discriminator: In a patient with known ANCA vasculitis, new dyspnoea + elevated DLCO (paradoxically increased) indicates active alveolar haemorrhage. Haemoglobin in the alveoli binds inhaled CO, increasing DLCO.

stem: A renal biopsy from a patient with RPGN shows linear IgG staining along the GBM on immunofluorescence. Which of the following antibody results would you expect in this patient?
subject: Medicine-Respiratory
concept: Linear IgG on biopsy = anti-GBM disease = Goodpasture
discriminator: Linear IgG staining along GBM is pathognomonic for anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture). The serum anti-GBM antibody will be positive.

stem: Which of the following correctly pairs the pulmonary-renal syndrome with its characteristic antibody?
subject: Medicine-Respiratory
concept: Pulmonary-renal syndrome antibody pairing
discriminator: Microscopic polyangiitis = p-ANCA (anti-MPO). Goodpasture = anti-GBM. Wegener = c-ANCA (anti-PR3).

stem: A 65-year-old man with granulomatosis with polyangiitis develops severe renal failure (creatinine 600 µmol/L) despite induction therapy with steroids and rituximab. What additional therapy should be considered?
opts: Switch to cyclophosphamide at higher dose
subject: Medicine-Respiratory
concept: ANCA vasculitis — plasmapheresis for severe renal involvement (Cr > 500)
discriminator: In ANCA vasculitis (GPA or MPA), plasmapheresis is added when serum creatinine > 500 µmol/L or if dialysis-dependent, to improve renal recovery.

stem: A 19-year-old male college student presents with acute-onset haemoptysis and dark urine. He has no prior medical history. CXR shows bilateral perihilar ground-glass opacities. Blood pressure is 145/95 mmHg. Urinalysis shows haematuria with RBC casts and 2+ protein. Which set of serological findings is most likely?
subject: Medicine-Respiratory
concept: Goodpasture serology — anti-GBM positive with normal complement
discriminator: Young adult + haemoptysis + haematuria + ground-glass CXR + RBC casts = Goodpasture. Anti-GBM is positive, complement (C3) is normal. Low C3 = immune complex GN (PSGN, SLE, MPGN).

stem: A 27-year-old male presents with 3 days of severe diarrhoea and vomiting. He is oliguric, dehydrated, BP 90/60 mmHg, pulse 110/min. Labs: urea 110 mg/dL, creatinine 5.2 mg/dL, Na 132 mmol/L, K+ 5.1 mmol/L. Urine osmolality is 320 mOsm/kg. FeNa is 2.8%. Urine microscopy shows muddy brown granular casts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: ATN vs pre-renal AKI differentiation using FeNa, urine osmolality, and urine sediment
discriminator: FeNa > 2% (2.8%), urine osmolality < 350 (320), and muddy brown granular casts = intrinsic ATN, not pre-renal. Pre-renal would have FeNa < 1% and urine osmolality > 500.

stem: A 65-year-old man with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 22 mL/min) presents with palpitations and weakness. ECG shows peaked T waves in V2–V5 and widened QRS complexes. Serum K+ is 6.9 mmol/L. He is anuric. What is the single best immediate step in management?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Hyperkalemia emergency management — calcium first when ECG changes present
discriminator: Peaked T waves + widened QRS = cardiac membrane instability. IV calcium gluconate stabilises the cardiac membrane FIRST — it does not lower K+. All other options manage K+ but do not stabilise the heart.

stem: A 70-year-old woman with CKD stage 5 presents with severe bone pain and a pathological fracture of the femur. Labs: Ca 8.1 mg/dL (low), PO4 6.2 mg/dL (high), PTH 320 pg/mL (elevated), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 22 ng/mL (low-normal). What is the most likely cause of her bone disease?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Renal osteodystrophy — secondary hyperparathyroidism mechanism in CKD
discriminator: CKD → ↓ 1α-hydroxylase → ↓ calcitriol → ↓ intestinal Ca absorption → ↓ serum Ca → ↑ PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism) → osteitis fibrosa cystica. High PO4 is also typical in CKD-MBD.

stem: A 55-year-old woman with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 28 mL/min) is diagnosed with a UTI and prescribed an antibiotic. She also takes metformin for T2DM, lisinopril, and atorvastatin. Three days later she presents with severe nausea, vomiting, and confusion. Labs: Cr 6.8 mg/dL (baseline 2.4), K+ 6.1, pH 7.12, lactate 8.5 mmol/L. What is the most likely precipitating factor for her acute deterioration?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Metformin contraindication in CKD — lactic acidosis risk when eGFR declines acutely
discriminator: Metformin is contraindicated when eGFR < 30 mL/min. Acute illness (UTI) causing dehydration and further GFR decline can trigger metformin accumulation → lactic acidosis (pH 7.12, lactate 8.5, nausea, confusion).

stem: A 60-year-old man with CKD stage 3b (eGFR 38 mL/min) and T2DM has HbA1c 10.2% despite maximum metformin dose. His current medications include metformin 1000 mg BD, lisinopril 10 mg OD, and atorvastatin 20 mg OD. What is the most appropriate adjustment to his diabetes management?
opts: Reduce metformin dose and add a DPP-4 inhibitor or SGLT2 inhibitor
Continue current regimen — HbA1c target is relaxed in CKD
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Diabetes management in CKD — metformin dose reduction + add-on therapy, avoiding sulfonylureas
discriminator: Metformin dose should be reduced when eGFR 30–45 (max 1000 mg/day total). Sulfonylureas increase hypoglycaemia risk in CKD. SGLT2i/DPP-4i are better add-on choices with renal dose adjustment.

stem: A 68-year-old man with CKD stage 4 presents with severe hyperkalemia (K+ 7.2 mmol/L) and ECG changes (widened QRS, peaked T waves). He is anuric. IV calcium gluconate has been administered. What is the definitive next step for potassium removal?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Dialysis indication in hyperkalemia — anuric patient after membrane stabilisation
discriminator: After calcium stabilises the membrane, an anuric patient with K+ > 6.5 + ECG changes needs definitive K+ removal. Haemodialysis is the fastest and most effective method when the patient is anuric (Kayexalate is too slow and requires gut function).

stem: A 45-year-old male with CKD stage 5 on haemodialysis presents with dyspnoea and orthopnoea. BP 170/95 mmHg. JVP 14 cm H2O. Bilateral crackles up to mid-zones. He has gained 4 kg since last dialysis. Urine output < 100 mL/day. He has not responded to IV furosemide. What is the most appropriate next step?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Dialysis indication — fluid overload (pulmonary oedema) refractory to diuretics
discriminator: AEIOU: O = Overload (pulmonary oedema refractory to diuretics). Anuric patient with fluid overload who has failed diuretics needs urgent dialysis for fluid removal (ultrafiltration).

stem: A 58-year-old woman with T2DM for 12 years is found to have eGFR 52 mL/min, serum Cr 1.4 mg/dL, and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 180 mg/g. BP is 138/86 mmHg. She is on metformin 850 mg BD. Her HbA1c is 7.4%. What is the single best intervention to slow progression of her kidney disease?
opts: Tight glycaemic control alone to HbA1c < 6.5%
Start ACE inhibitor (or ARB) and optimise BP
Add a sulfonylurea for tighter control
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Diabetic nephropathy — ACEi/ARB renoprotection independent of BP control
discriminator: Microalbuminuria (ACR 180 mg/g) in diabetic nephropathy = indication for ACEi/ARB regardless of BP. ACEi/ARB reduces proteinuria and slows CKD progression independently of BP lowering.

stem: A 72-year-old man with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 18 mL/min) has Hb 8.1 g/dL, MCV 88 fL, ferritin 320 ng/mL, TSAT 32%. Serum B12 and folate are normal. Reticulocyte count is low. What is the most likely cause of his anaemia?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: CKD anaemia — erythropoietin deficiency as the primary cause
discriminator: Normocytic anaemia (MCV 88) with low reticulocyte count, adequate iron stores (ferritin > 200, TSAT > 30%), normal B12/folate = erythropoietin deficiency in CKD. EPO production falls as kidney function declines.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents with oliguria after receiving IV contrast for coronary angiography 48 hours ago. His baseline Cr was 1.0 mg/dL; now Cr is 2.8 mg/dL. Urine osmolality is 310 mOsm/kg. FeNa is 0.6%. Urine microscopy shows hyaline casts. What is the most likely type of AKI?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Contrast-induced nephropathy — ATN despite misleading FeNa
discriminator: Contrast is a direct nephrotoxin causing ATN. FeNa can be low (< 1%) early in contrast nephropathy despite intrinsic injury. The key is the timing (48 h post-contrast), oliguria, low urine osmolality, and absence of other causes. Muddy brown casts may appear later.

stem: A 35-year-old man is brought to the ER after ingesting ethylene glycol (antifreeze). Cr is 2.2 mg/dL (baseline 1.0), pH 7.08, HCO3 8, anion gap 28. Serum osmolality is 360 mOsm/kg. What is the most appropriate management?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Dialysis indication — Intoxication (AEIOU): ethylene glycol poisoning
discriminator: Ethylene glycol poisoning with high anion gap metabolic acidosis and AKI = dialysis indicated (Intoxication in AEIOU). Fomepizole (alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor) stops toxic metabolite formation; dialysis removes both parent compound and metabolites.

stem: A 66-year-old woman with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 24 mL/min) has chronic back pain from osteoarthritis. She is currently taking paracetamol with inadequate relief. What is the single best recommendation for her pain management?
opts: Increase paracetamol and consider a low-dose opioid
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: CKD — NSAIDs contraindicated; safe analgesia alternatives in CKD
discriminator: NSAIDs (including COX-2 inhibitors and topical NSAIDs with systemic absorption) are nephrotoxic in CKD — they reduce renal blood flow and worsen GFR. Paracetamol (acetaminophen) is safe, and non-renally cleared opioids (e.g., low-dose oxycodone) can be added cautiously.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with no past medical history presents with oliguria, haematuria, and frothy urine for 3 days. BP is 170/100 mmHg. Labs: Cr 4.8 mg/dL, urea 120 mg/dL, K+ 5.6. Urine microscopy shows dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: RPGN vs ATN vs post-streptococcal GN differentiation
discriminator: Rapid Cr rise + oliguria + haematuria + RBC casts + hypertension + frothy urine (proteinuria) = glomerulonephritis, not tubular injury. The rapid pace (days) and severity (Cr 4.8) point to crescentic (rapidly progressive) GN rather than post-streptococcal GN (which typically has a latent period).

stem: A 32-year-old man recovering from a motor vehicle accident with crush injury to both lower limbs presents with oliguria and dark red-brown urine. Labs: Cr 3.6 mg/dL (baseline 0.9), K+ 6.2, PO4 6.8, uric acid 9.2 mg/dL. Urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood but microscopy shows < 5 RBCs/HPF. Urine myoglobin is positive. What is the most likely cause of his AKI?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Rhabdomyolysis-induced ATN — myoglobinuria causing intrinsic AKI
discriminator: Crush injury + dark urine + dipstick-blood-without-RBCs + positive myoglobin + hyperkalemia + hyperuricaemia + hyperphosphataemia = rhabdomyolysis causing ATN. Myoglobin is directly nephrotoxic and causes tubular obstruction.

stem: A 62-year-old man with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 20 mL/min) has persistent serum K+ of 5.6–5.9 despite dietary counselling. He is on lisinopril 20 mg daily. His urine output is 1.2 L/day. ECG shows no hyperkalemic changes. What is the most appropriate next step in managing his hyperkalemia?
opts: Stop lisinopril, review diet, and consider a potassium binder
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Chronic hyperkalemia in CKD — stepwise management, not emergency intervention when no ECG changes
discriminator: No ECG changes = no membrane emergency → do NOT give calcium. The approach is: address contributors (ACEi/ARB may be culprit), dietary K+ restriction, consider loop/thiazide diuretics if volume status permits, and potassium binders (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate, or Kayexalate if necessary).

stem: A 48-year-old woman with known CKD (eGFR 16 mL/min) is found to have HCO3 16 mmol/L, Ca 8.6 mg/dL, PO4 5.8 mg/dL, PTH 280 pg/mL, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D 20 ng/mL. Which of the following best explains her laboratory abnormalities?
opts: Decreased renal 1α-hydroxylase activity → decreased calcitriol production
Increased PTH → increased bone calcium release → hypercalcaemia
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: CKD-MBD pathophysiology — calcitriol deficiency driving secondary HPT
discriminator: CKD → loss of 1α-hydroxylase → ↓ conversion of 25-OH-D to 1,25-(OH)2-D (calcitriol) → ↓ gut Ca absorption → ↓ serum Ca → ↑ PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism). PTH causes phosphaturia → hypophosphataemia (though PO4 is high here due to reduced GFR).

stem: A 75-year-old man presents with confusion, asterixis, and a pericardial rub on examination. He has no known medical history but appears malnourished. Labs: Cr 8.2 mg/dL, urea 280 mg/dL, K+ 5.8, HCO3 14. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate management?
opts: Uraemic encephalopathy with pericarditis — urgent haemodialysis
Alcoholic ketoacidosis — IV fluids and thiamine
Hyperkalemic cardiac toxicity — IV calcium gluconate
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Dialysis indication — Uraemia (AEIOU) presenting with encephalopathy and pericarditis
discriminator: Uraemic encephalopathy (confusion, asterixis) + uraemic pericarditis (pericardial rub) + severe azotaemia (urea 280, Cr 8.2) = Uraemia in AEIOU. Haemodialysis is urgently indicated.

stem: A 55-year-old woman with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 22 mL/min) presents with K+ 7.0 mmol/L. ECG shows sine wave pattern. She has a history of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Which of the following is the SINGLE BEST initial management?
opts: IV calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% solution over 2 minutes
IV insulin 10 units + 50 mL of 50% dextrose
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Hyperkalemia with life-threatening ECG changes — calcium gluconate is ALWAYS first regardless of other considerations
discriminator: Sine wave pattern = pre-arrest ECG. IV calcium gluconate is the ONLY intervention that immediately stabilises the cardiac membrane. Heart failure does not change this priority — calcium is safe even in HF when given slowly.

stem: A 42-year-old woman with SLE presents with oliguria, oedema, and frothy urine. BP 155/95 mmHg. Labs: Cr 3.2 mg/dL (baseline 0.8), albumin 2.4 g/dL, cholesterol 380 mg/dL. Urine protein: 4.2 g/24h. Urine microscopy shows RBCs and RBC casts. What is the most likely renal pathology?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Lupus nephritis — nephrotic-range proteinuria + active sediment + AKI in SLE
discriminator: SLE + nephrotic syndrome (protein 4.2 g/24h, low albumin, high cholesterol) + active sediment (RBC casts) + AKI = proliferative lupus nephritis (Class III or IV). Requires biopsy and immunosuppression.

stem: A 60-year-old man with CKD stage 5 (eGFR 12 mL/min) who is not yet on dialysis complains of severe pruritus and restless legs at night. Hb is 9.4 g/dL on erythropoietin therapy. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for his symptoms?
opts: Start oral antihistamines and review uraemic toxicity
Increase erythropoietin dose to correct Hb to > 13 g/dL
Start a benzodiazepine for restless legs
Refer for renal transplantation evaluation only
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: CKD — uraemic pruritus and restless legs syndrome management in advanced CKD
discriminator: Pruritus and restless legs are common uraemic symptoms in advanced CKD. Symptomatic management includes antihistamines, emollients, and optimising dialysis adequacy. Do NOT overshoot Hb target with EPO (target 10–11.5 g/dL, > 13 increases thrombotic risk).

stem: A 68-year-old man with known CKD stage 3b (eGFR 38 mL/min), hypertension, and T2DM presents for routine follow-up. Current medications: metformin 1000 mg BD, lisinopril 20 mg OD, atorvastatin 20 mg OD, and amlodipine 5 mg OD. Recent labs: Cr 1.8 mg/dL (stable), K+ 5.2, HbA1c 7.8%. BP 128/76 mmHg. His eGFR has declined from 52 to 38 over 18 months. What is the single best intervention to slow further progression?
opts: Add a sulfonylurea to improve glycaemic control
Add an SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin) if eGFR remains > 25
Add a thiazide diuretic for BP
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: CKD progression — SGLT2 inhibitors for renoprotection in diabetic CKD
discriminator: SGLT2 inhibitors have independent renoprotective effects in diabetic CKD, slowing GFR decline and reducing proteinuria. They are now indicated for CKD with or without diabetes when eGFR > 25. ACEi is already on board. BP is well-controlled.

stem: A 52-year-old man with CKD stage 3a (eGFR 52 mL/min) and hypertension is being started on an ACE inhibitor. Which of the following laboratory changes is expected after initiating ACEi therapy and is considered acceptable?
opts: Serum Cr increase of 15% and K+ increase to 5.8
Serum Cr increase of 25% and K+ increase to 6.5
Serum Cr increase of up to 30% from baseline without further rise
Serum Cr decrease due to improved renal blood flow
No change in Cr or K+ expected
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: ACEi/ARB — benign initial Cr rise of < 30% is acceptable and renoprotective
discriminator: ACEi/ARB causes a benign initial rise in Cr of up to 30% due to haemodynamic effects (reduced efferent arteriolar resistance). This is acceptable and does NOT require discontinuation unless Cr rises > 30% or hyperkalemia is refractory.

stem: A 38-year-old man presents with acute onset of right flank pain radiating to the groin, haematuria, and anuria for 8 hours. He has a history of gout. KUB X-ray shows a radiopaque stone at the right UVJ. Cr is 3.6 mg/dL (baseline 1.0). Ultrasound shows right hydronephrosis and a normal left kidney. What is the most likely type of AKI?
opts: Pre-renal AKI from pain-induced sympathetic activation
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Post-renal AKI — unilateral ureteric obstruction causing anuria (reflex anuria in solitary functioning kidney)
discriminator: Flank pain radiating to groin + radiopaque stone + hydronephrosis + anuria = obstructive (post-renal) AKI. Even unilateral obstruction can cause anuria if the other kidney is non-functional (or reflex anuria).

stem: A 70-year-old woman with CKD stage 5 (eGFR 8 mL/min) who is on haemodialysis is found to have Hb 7.2 g/dL, MCV 78 fL, ferritin 42 ng/mL, TSAT 14%. She is already on recombinant erythropoietin. What is the most likely cause of her persistent anaemia?
opts: EPO resistance due to inadequate dialysis
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: CKD anaemia — iron deficiency (absolute) as cause of EPO hyporesponsiveness
discriminator: Low ferritin (< 100 ng/mL) + low TSAT (< 20%) + microcytic anaemia (MCV 78) = absolute iron deficiency. Despite EPO therapy, the patient cannot mount an adequate erythropoietic response without sufficient iron stores.

stem: A 44-year-old woman with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 28 mL/min) and no history of diabetes has BP 148/92 mmHg despite amlodipine 10 mg daily. Urine ACR is 280 mg/g. She is not on an ACE inhibitor or ARB. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
opts: Add an ACE inhibitor or ARB
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: CKD with proteinuria — ACEi/ARB indicated for BP control and renoprotection regardless of diabetes status
discriminator: Non-diabetic CKD + proteinuria (ACR 280 = A3, severely increased) + uncontrolled BP on single agent = add ACEi/ARB. ACEi/ARB provides renoprotection independent of BP and is indicated in proteinuric CKD with or without diabetes.

stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with tea-coloured urine, periorbital oedema, and hypertension. His mother reports he had a sore throat treated with antibiotics 2 weeks ago. C3 complement level is low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: PSGN diagnosis — timing (2 weeks post-strep) and low C3 are diagnostic
discriminator: Child + cola urine + 2 weeks post-strep infection + low C3 = PSGN, not IgA (which is synpharyngitic with normal C3).

stem: In post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which complement component is characteristically decreased during the acute phase?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Complement profile in PSGN — low C3 via alternative pathway
discriminator: PSGN activates the alternative complement pathway, consuming C3 while C4 (classical pathway) remains normal.

stem: An 22-year-old man presents with frank haematuria that began during an upper respiratory tract infection. He has no oedema, and his blood pressure is 120/75 mmHg. Urinalysis shows red blood cells and 1+ protein. C3 complement is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: IgA nephropathy — synpharyngitic haematuria with normal C3
discriminator: Haematuria DURING a respiratory infection (synpharyngitic) with normal C3 in a young adult is classic for IgA nephropathy.

stem: Which histological finding on immunofluorescence is most characteristic of IgA nephropathy?
opts: Linear IgG deposition along the glomerular basement membrane
Foot process effacement on electron microscopy
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: IgA nephropathy — mesangial IgA deposition
discriminator: Mesangial IgA is the pathognomonic immunofluorescence finding in IgA nephropathy (Berger disease).

stem: A 5-year-old child presents with periorbital and lower extremity oedema, frothy urine, and weight gain over 2 weeks. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein. Serum albumin is 1.6 g/dL. Light microscopy of a renal biopsy shows normal glomeruli. Electron microscopy shows foot process effacement. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Supportive care with fluid restriction only
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: MCD treatment — steroid-responsive nephrotic syndrome in children
discriminator: Child + nephrotic syndrome + normal LM + foot process effacement on EM = minimal change disease → prednisolone is first-line with excellent response.

stem: Which of the following best defines nephrotic-range proteinuria?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Nephrotic syndrome definition — proteinuria threshold
discriminator: Nephrotic-range proteinuria is defined as > 3.5 g/24 h (or urine protein:creatinine ratio > 3.5).

stem: A 9-year-old girl presents with oliguria, cola-coloured urine, and periorbital oedema. Blood pressure is 140/95 mmHg. Urinalysis shows 2+ protein, numerous RBCs, and RBC casts. Which of the following best describes this clinical picture?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Nephritic syndrome — clinical features: haematuria, RBC casts, HTN, oliguria
discriminator: RBC casts + haematuria + hypertension + oliguria = nephritic syndrome, not nephrotic (which has massive proteinuria, low albumin, and frothy urine).

stem: A 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 15 years is found to have microalbuminuria on annual screening. His blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg and HbA1c is 7.2%. Which intervention is most important to slow the progression of diabetic nephropathy?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Diabetic nephropathy — ACEi renoprotection independent of BP
discriminator: ACEi/ARB has an independent renoprotective effect that slows progression of diabetic nephropathy beyond BP and glucose control.

stem: A 48-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes since age 8 presents with nephrotic-range proteinuria. Renal biopsy shows nodular glomerulosclerosis with eosinophilic nodules in the mesangium. What is the most likely histological diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Diabetic nephropathy — Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules
discriminator: Nodular glomerulosclerosis with eosinophilic mesangial nodules (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules) is pathognomonic for diabetic nephropathy.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with lower extremity oedema and frothy urine for 3 weeks. Lab findings: protein 4.2 g/24 h, albumin 2.1 g/dL, cholesterol 320 mg/dL. Renal biopsy shows thickened capillary walls on light microscopy and subepithelial spike-and-dome deposits on electron microscopy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Membranous nephropathy — adult nephrotic syndrome with subepithelial spikes
discriminator: Adult nephrotic syndrome + subepithelial spike-and-dome deposits on EM = membranous nephropathy. Anti-PLA2R antibodies are found in 70-80% of primary cases.

stem: An 8-year-old boy presents with cola-coloured urine and periorbital oedema. His parents report he had impetigo 3 weeks ago. Blood pressure is 130/90 mmHg. C3 level is low. Which of the following is the best next step in management?
opts: Supportive care with fluid and salt restriction
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: PSGN management — supportive care, not immunosuppression
discriminator: PSGN in children is self-limiting; management is supportive (fluid restriction, diuretics for oedema/HTN). Steroids are not indicated.

stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with generalised oedema, frothy urine, and weight gain. Lab: protein 4.8 g/24 h, albumin 1.4 g/dL, cholesterol 350 mg/dL. Light microscopy of a renal biopsy shows normal glomeruli. Electron microscopy shows diffuse foot process effacement with no electron-dense deposits. What distinguishes minimal change disease from focal segmental glomerulosclerosis in this context?
opts: MCD shows segmental sclerosis on LM; FSGS shows normal LM
MCD shows foot process effacement on EM; FSGS shows subepithelial spikes
MCD shows normal LM with foot process effacement; FSGS shows segmental sclerosis on LM
MCD responds poorly to steroids; FSGS responds excellently
MCD presents with haematuria; FSGS presents with nephrotic syndrome
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: MCD vs FSGS — histological distinction on light microscopy
discriminator: MCD: normal LM + foot process effacement on EM. FSGS: segmental sclerotic lesions on LM (some glomeruli, some segments). This is the critical discriminator.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with nephrotic syndrome and hypertension. Renal biopsy shows a tram-track (double contour) appearance of the glomerular basement membrane on light microscopy. C3 is low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: MPGN — tram-track appearance on LM with low C3
discriminator: Tram-track / double contour appearance of the GBM on light microscopy is pathognomonic for MPGN. It is also associated with low C3.

stem: A 46-year-old woman presents with bilateral lower extremity oedema and frothy urine for 2 weeks. Protein excretion is 5.6 g/24 h. Albumin is 2.0 g/dL. Anti-PLA2R antibodies are positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Membranous nephropathy — anti-PLA2R antibodies in primary disease
discriminator: Positive anti-PLA2R antibodies in an adult with nephrotic syndrome is specific for primary membranous nephropathy (70-80% of cases).

stem: A 5-year-old with nephrotic syndrome has generalised pitting oedema. Which mechanism best explains the development of oedema in this patient?
opts: Increased sodium retention as a primary event
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Nephrotic oedema mechanism — decreased oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminaemia
discriminator: In nephrotic syndrome, massive urinary protein loss causes hypoalbuminaemia → decreased plasma colloid osmotic pressure → fluid shifts from intravascular to interstitial space → oedema.

stem: A 30-year-old man is found to have hypertension and proteinuria 1.8 g/day during a routine medical check-up. He has no history of renal disease. Urinalysis shows microscopic haematuria. C3 and C4 are normal. Anti-dsDNA and ANCA are negative. Renal biopsy shows mesangial IgA deposits. What is the most appropriate management to slow progression of renal disease?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: IgA nephropathy — ACEi for proteinuria and renoprotection
discriminator: In IgA nephropathy with proteinuria and hypertension, ACEi/ARB is first-line for renoprotection. Steroids are reserved for persistent proteinuria > 1 g/day despite ACEi.

stem: A 20-year-old man with known IgA nephropathy diagnosed 2 years ago has stable renal function and intermittent macroscopic haematuria during upper respiratory infections. He has no hypertension. Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 0.3. What is the most appropriate management at this point?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: IgA nephropathy — benign course requires only monitoring
discriminator: IgA nephropathy with preserved renal function, no hypertension, and low proteinuria (< 0.5 g/day) has a good prognosis and requires only observation and monitoring — not treatment.

stem: A 16-year-old boy presents with haematuria and progressive renal impairment. He has sensorineural deafness and a family history of renal disease in his maternal uncle. Eye examination reveals anterior lenticonus. Which diagnosis is most likely?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Alport syndrome — hereditary nephritis with deafness and ocular abnormalities
discriminator: Haematuria + sensorineural deafness + anterior lenticonus + family history (X-linked) = Alport syndrome. Importantly, Alport has NO haemoptysis (unlike Goodpasture).

stem: A 34-year-old man presents with peripheral oedema. BP is 110/70 mmHg. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein with no RBCs. Serum albumin is 1.8 g/dL. Cholesterol is 380 mg/dL. Which of the following features would argue AGAINST the diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome in this patient?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Nephrotic vs nephritic — BP is normal in nephrotic, elevated in nephritic
discriminator: Hypertension is a feature of nephritic syndrome, NOT nephrotic syndrome. In nephrotic syndrome, BP is typically normal (unless advanced disease or secondary cause).

stem: A 38-year-old man presents with nephrotic syndrome. Renal biopsy shows segmental sclerotic lesions involving some glomeruli on light microscopy. Immunofluorescence is negative for immune complexes. Electron microscopy shows foot process effacement with areas of detachment from the GBM. Which condition is most likely?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: FSGS histology — segmental sclerosis on LM with podocyte injury
discriminator: Segmental sclerotic lesions on LM (not all glomeruli, not all segments) in a nephrotic adult = FSGS. Unlike MCD which has normal LM.

stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with acute-onset cola-coloured urine, periorbital oedema, and oliguria. His mother reports a sore throat 10 days ago. BP is 135/92 mmHg. C3 is markedly decreased. C4 is normal. Which combination of findings best confirms the diagnosis and indicates the appropriate management approach?
opts: Normal C3 + haematuria DURING infection → IgA nephropathy → ACE inhibitor
Low C3 + haematuria 10 days post-infection → PSGN → supportive care with fluid restriction and diuretics
Low C3 + haematuria DURING infection → PSGN → prednisolone therapy
Normal C3 + haematuria 10 days post-infection → IgA nephropathy → prednisolone
Low C3 + haematuria + RBC casts → MPGN → plasma exchange
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: PSGN vs IgA — integrated timing + C3 + management decision
discriminator: The key discriminator is timing (10 days post-infection = PSGN, not IgA) confirmed by low C3 (alternative pathway activation). PSGN in children is managed supportively, not with immunosuppression.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents with haemoptysis, haematuria, and rapidly progressive renal failure over 2 weeks. BP is 150/92 mmHg. Urinalysis shows RBC casts and 2+ protein. C3 is normal. Chest X-ray shows diffuse alveolar infiltrates. Anti-GBM antibodies are positive. Renal biopsy shows crescentic glomerulonephritis with linear IgG staining on immunofluorescence. What is the single best immediate treatment?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Goodpasture syndrome — rapidly progressive GN with anti-GBM antibodies
discriminator: Haemoptysis + haematuria + rapidly progressive renal failure + anti-GBM antibodies + linear IgG on IF = Goodpasture syndrome. Treatment is plasma exchange + immunosuppression (cyclophosphamide + steroids).

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with malar rash, arthritis, and periorbital oedema. BP is 145/90 mmHg. Urinalysis shows 3+ protein with RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs. Serum creatinine is 2.8 mg/dL. C3 is low and C4 is low. Anti-dsDNA antibodies are positive. What is the most likely renal diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Lupus nephritis — low C3 AND C4 with anti-dsDNA + systemic features
discriminator: Low C3 AND low C4 (both classical pathway) + positive anti-dsDNA + malar rash + arthritis + active urinary sediment = lupus nephritis. Unlike PSGN where only C3 is low, lupus consumes both C3 and C4.

stem: A 50-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B presents with lower extremity oedema, frothy urine, and proteinuria of 5.2 g/24 h. Albumin is 2.0 g/dL. C3 and C4 are normal. Anti-PLA2R antibodies are negative. Renal biopsy shows thickened capillary walls with subepithelial spikes on electron microscopy. Which of the following is the best explanation for the relationship between his hepatitis B and the renal finding?
opts: Hepatitis B virus directly infects podocytes causing foot process effacement
Secondary membranous nephropathy due to HBV immune complex deposition
Hepatitis B causes IgA deposition in the mesangium
Hepatitis B leads to diabetic-type Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules
The hepatitis B is coincidental and unrelated to the renal pathology
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Secondary membranous nephropathy — HBV associaton with negative anti-PLA2R
discriminator: Anti-PLA2R negativity in a patient with membranous nephropathy + HBV suggests secondary membranous nephropathy due to HBV immune complex deposition (HBeAg). Anti-PLA2R is positive in primary but negative in secondary membranous nephropathy.

stem: A 4-year-old girl presents with periorbital and lower extremity oedema, frothy urine, and weight gain of 2 kg over 2 weeks. Urinalysis: 4+ protein. Albumin: 1.6 g/dL. Cholesterol: 380 mg/dL. She is started on prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day. After 6 weeks of daily prednisolone, she still has 3+ proteinuria and persistent oedema. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Perform a renal biopsy before changing therapy
Add ACE inhibitor and discharge with monitoring
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome — biopsy is indicated to diagnose FSGS or other pathology
discriminator: MCD typically responds to 4-8 weeks of prednisolone. Failure to respond after 6 weeks of daily steroids → steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome → biopsy is indicated to look for FSGS, membranous, or another pathology.

stem: A 55-year-old male with known ischemic cardiomyopathy has an LVEF of 30%. He is on bisoprolol 5 mg daily. He has no contraindications. Which additional agents have proven mortality benefit in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: HFrEF mortality benefit — BB + ACEi/ARB + MRA triple therapy
discriminator: The three drug classes with established mortality benefit in HFrEF are beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors (or ARBs), and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (spironolactone/eplerenone).

stem: A 45-year-old male presents with palpitations and lightheadedness. ECG shows an irregularly irregular narrow-complex tachycardia with a ventricular rate of 140/min. Blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg. What is the most appropriate management?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Atrial fibrillation — rate vs rhythm control in haemodynamically stable patient
discriminator: Haemodynamically stable atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular rate: first-line is rate control with beta-blocker or non-dihydropyridine CCB.

stem: A 60-year-old male presents with acute dyspnoea, frothy pink sputum, and respiratory rate of 36/min. BP is 150/95 mmHg, SpO2 is 88% on room air. Chest X-ray shows bilateral alveolar opacities with Kerley B lines. What is the single best next step in management?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Acute pulmonary oedema — combined pharmacologic and ventilatory management
discriminator: Acute pulmonary oedema with hypertension and hypoxia requires simultaneous afterload reduction (GTN), ventilatory support (BiPAP), and volume reduction (furosemide). BiPAP reduces preload and afterload and improves gas exchange without intubation.

stem: A 62-year-old male with diabetes and hypertension presents with chest pain at rest for 45 minutes. ECG shows 1 mm ST depression in V4–V6. High-sensitivity troponin is elevated at 4× ULN. He has no ongoing chest pain and is haemodynamically stable. His TIMI risk score is 4. What is the next step in management?
opts: Conservative medical management with stress test in 48 hours
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: NSTEMI risk stratification — TIMI score and early invasive strategy
discriminator: TIMI score ≥ 4 in NSTEMI indicates high risk and benefit from early invasive strategy (angiography within 24 hours). TIMI components here: age > 65 (1), diabetes (1), known CAD/aspirin use (1), elevated troponin (1) = 4.

stem: A 58-year-old male presents with acute dyspnoea and chest pain 4 days after an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. On auscultation, there is a new loud pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border with a palpable thrill. BP is 85/50 mmHg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Papillary muscle rupture causing acute mitral regurgitation
Acute ischaemic mitral regurgitation from LV dysfunction
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Post-MI mechanical complication — VSD murmur location and timing
discriminator: Pansystolic murmur at LLSB + palpable thrill + inferior MI 4 days ago = ventricular septal rupture. Papillary muscle rupture murmur is at the apex with radiation to the axilla and typically lacks a thrill.

stem: A 40-year-old male presents with a blood pressure of 220/130 mmHg. He has no symptoms, no focal neurological deficits, and fundoscopy shows no papilloedema. Serum creatinine is normal and urinalysis is negative. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: IV labetalol infusion and ICU admission
Oral antihypertensive and outpatient follow-up within 24–48 hours
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Hypertensive urgency vs emergency — definition and management
discriminator: BP > 180/120 without end-organ damage (no neurological symptoms, normal fundoscopy, normal creatinine, negative urinalysis) = hypertensive urgency, not emergency. Management is oral agents with gradual BP reduction over 24–48 hours.

stem: A 68-year-old male presents with exertional syncope, progressive dyspnoea, and chest tightness. On auscultation, there is a late-peaking crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids. Carotid upstroke is delayed. What is the definitive management?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Severe aortic stenosis — indications for valve replacement
discriminator: Exertional syncope + dyspnoea + chest pain in a patient with classic AS murmur and delayed carotid upstroke indicates severe symptomatic AS. Symptomatic severe AS has a dismal prognosis without valve replacement.

stem: A 66-year-old male with type 2 diabetes and stage 3 CKD (eGFR 42 mL/min) presents with 3 hours of crushing chest pain. ECG shows 4 mm ST elevation in V1–V4. BP is 105/70 mmHg. The nearest PCI-capable centre is 150 minutes away. What is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?
opts: Transfer for primary PCI despite the delay
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: STEMI reperfusion — fibrinolysis vs PCI with > 120 min transfer delay and CKD
discriminator: Transfer time (150 min) exceeds 120-minute window for PCI → fibrinolysis indicated. CKD stage 3 is not a contraindication to fibrinolysis. PCI contrast risk in CKD is a consideration but does not override the reperfusion time decision.

stem: A 30-year-old asthmatic uses salbutamol as needed. She reports daytime symptoms 4 times per week and nocturnal symptoms twice per month. FEV1 is 78% predicted. What is the next step according to GINA guidelines?
opts: Add low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) as regular controller
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: GINA asthma step-up — symptoms > 2x/week with FEV1 > 70%
discriminator: Daytime symptoms > 2x/week + FEV1 > 70% = GINA step 2. GINA now recommends low-dose ICS as needed for step 1, but step 2 with symptoms > 2x/week requires regular low-dose ICS controller.

stem: A 28-year-old female presents with acute severe asthma. She has received nebulised salbutamol, ipratropium, and IV hydrocortisone. Despite this, she remains tachypnoeic with respiratory rate 30/min, unable to complete sentences, and SpO2 is 91% on high-flow oxygen. PEFR is 30% of predicted. What is the next step in management?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Acute severe asthma refractory to bronchodilators and steroids — IV MgSO4
discriminator: Acute severe asthma with poor response to initial therapy (nebulised bronchodilators + steroids) requires IV magnesium sulphate as the next step. It is a bronchodilator with proven benefit in acute severe asthma.

stem: A 65-year-old smoker presents with progressive dyspnoea and chronic cough. Spirometry shows FEV1/FVC of 0.55 and FEV1 of 36% predicted. He had 3 exacerbations in the past year and CAT score is 24. What is the GOLD classification?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: COPD GOLD grade (spirometry) and group (symptoms/exacerbations) — combined classification
discriminator: FEV1 30–49% = GOLD 3. CAT ≥ 10 + ≥ 2 exacerbations = Group D. Combined: GOLD 3 Group D.

stem: A 55-year-old male with known COPD presents with acute dyspnoea and confusion. Arterial blood gas on room air shows pH 7.26, PaCO2 78 mmHg, PaO2 50 mmHg. He is drowsy but rousable. What is the most appropriate next step?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: COPD exacerbation with hypercapnic respiratory failure — NIV indication
discriminator: pH < 7.35 + hypercapnia + drowsiness but able to protect airway = hypercapnic respiratory failure in COPD exacerbation requiring NIV (BiPAP). Intubation is reserved for NIV failure or contraindications.

stem: A 22-year-old male presents with sudden-onset pleuritic right chest pain and severe dyspnoea after playing basketball. On examination, he is in respiratory distress with tracheal deviation to the left, absent breath sounds on the right, and a distended neck vein. BP is 80/50 mmHg. What is the immediate intervention?
opts: Needle decompression at the 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line
Tube thoracostomy at the triangle of safety
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Tension pneumothorax — clinical diagnosis and immediate needle decompression
discriminator: Tracheal deviation + absent breath sounds + distended neck veins + hypotension in a patient with acute dyspnoea = tension pneumothorax. Diagnosis is clinical; do NOT wait for imaging. Immediate needle decompression at 2nd ICS midclavicular line.

stem: A 60-year-old male with known cirrhosis presents with right pleural effusion. Diagnostic thoracentesis reveals pleural fluid protein of 3.8 g/dL and serum protein of 5.2 g/dL. Pleural fluid LDH is 320 U/L and serum LDH is 240 U/L (upper limit of normal for LDH is 200 U/L). How many of Light’s criteria are met?
opts: 2 — exudate by both protein and LDH criteria
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Light’s criteria — pleural fluid exudate vs transudate discrimination
discriminator: Light’s criteria: (1) pleural/serum protein > 0.5 (3.8/5.2 = 0.73 → met); (2) pleural/serum LDH > 0.6 (320/240 = 1.33 → met); (3) pleural LDH > 2/3 ULN serum LDH (320 > 133 → met). Three criteria met = exudate.

stem: A 32-year-old male is being treated for pulmonary tuberculosis with standard intensive-phase therapy. Two weeks into treatment, he develops pain and swelling in both ankles. Serum uric acid is elevated. Which anti-tuberculous drug is most likely responsible?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: TB drug side effects — pyrazinamide causing hyperuricaemia and arthralgia
discriminator: Pyrazinamide inhibits renal excretion of uric acid, causing hyperuricaemia that manifests as arthralgia (typically ankles). This is benign and managed with NSAIDs.

stem: A 45-year-old male presents with acute onset fever, rigors, productive cough with rusty-coloured sputum, and pleuritic chest pain. Chest X-ray shows lobar consolidation in the right lower lobe. What is the most likely causative organism?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Community-acquired pneumonia — most common organism and classic presentation
discriminator: Acute onset with rusty sputum, rigors, and lobar consolidation on CXR is classic for Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus). Rusty sputum reflects intra-alveolar haemorrhage and inflammation.

stem: A 50-year-old male with end-stage renal disease on haemodialysis presents with weakness and palpitations. ECG shows peaked T waves and widened QRS complexes. Serum potassium is 7.2 mEq/L. What is the single best immediate step?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Hyperkalemia emergency algorithm — calcium first when ECG changes present
discriminator: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes (peaked T, widened QRS) requires immediate cardiac membrane stabilisation with IV calcium gluconate. Calcium antagonises the cardiac effects of hyperkalemia within minutes.

stem: A 55-year-old male with CKD stage 5 (not on dialysis) presents with fatigue and muscle cramps. K+ is 6.5 mEq/L. ECG shows no peaked T or widened QRS. He is anuric. Which intervention is most appropriate after calcium stabilisation?
opts: IV insulin + dextrose then emergency haemodialysis
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Hyperkalemia in anuric patient — shifting agents then emergency dialysis
discriminator: Calcium is given first if ECG changes present (here it is not mentioned, but protocol is to give calcium if K+ > 6.5 with ECG changes). After cardiac protection, shifting agents (insulin + dextrose) buy time, but definitive therapy in an anuric patient is emergency haemodialysis.

stem: A 10-year-old boy presents with tea-coloured urine and periorbital oedema. His mother reports he had a sore throat 10 days ago. Blood pressure is 130/85 mmHg. C3 complement level is low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Post-streptococcal GN — timing (post-infection), low C3, classic presentation
discriminator: PSGN: occurs 1–3 weeks AFTER a streptococcal infection (here: sore throat 10 days ago). Low C3 is characteristic. IgA nephropathy occurs DURING (synpharyngitic) the infection with normal C3.

stem: A 28-year-old male presents with peripheral and periorbital oedema. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein with no haematuria. Serum albumin is 1.8 g/dL. Renal biopsy shows normal glomeruli on light microscopy but fusion of foot processes on electron microscopy. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Supportive care with salt restriction and diuretics
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Minimal change disease — nephrotic syndrome with steroid-responsive pathology
discriminator: Nephrotic syndrome (heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema) + normal LM + foot process fusion on EM = minimal change disease. It is highly steroid-responsive, especially in younger adults and children.

stem: A 65-year-old with cirrhosis presents with oliguria over 2 days. Urinalysis shows muddy brown granular casts. Urine sodium is 50 mEq/L and FeNa is 3.2%. Serum creatinine rose from 1.0 to 3.5 mg/dL. What is the most likely type of acute kidney injury?
opts: Pre-renal azotaemia due to hepatorenal syndrome
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: AKI differentiation — pre-renal vs ATN using FeNa and urine microscopy
discriminator: FeNa > 2% (here 3.2%) + muddy brown granular casts + high urine Na (> 20 mEq/L) = ATN (intra-renal). Pre-renal would show FeNa < 1%, urine Na < 20, and no casts.

stem: A 35-year-old female with type 1 diabetes for 20 years presents with bilateral lower extremity oedema and frothy urine. BP is 145/90 mmHg. Urinalysis shows 3+ protein. Serum creatinine is 1.8 mg/dL (eGFR 38 mL/min). HbA1c is 8.5%. She is on metformin and insulin. Which intervention has the strongest evidence for slowing progression of diabetic nephropathy?
opts: Tight glycaemic control alone targeting HbA1c < 7%
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Diabetic nephropathy — ACE inhibitor first-line for nephroprotection
discriminator: ACE inhibitors (or ARBs) are the cornerstone of nephroprotection in diabetic nephropathy with proteinuria. They reduce proteinuria and slow CKD progression independent of their antihypertensive effect.

stem: A 68-year-old male with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 28 mL/min) has type 2 diabetes and hypertension. His current medications include metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, and amlodipine 5 mg daily. Which medication adjustment is most appropriate?
opts: Increase metformin dose to improve glycaemic control
Stop lisinopril due to risk of hyperkalemia
Stop amlodipine due to risk of worsening renal function
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: CKD drug precautions — metformin is contraindicated when eGFR < 30
discriminator: Metformin is contraindicated when eGFR falls below 30 mL/min due to risk of lactic acidosis. At eGFR 28, it must be stopped. ACEi and amlodipine are safe and beneficial in CKD.

stem: A 60-year-old male with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 22 mL/min) is found to have haemoglobin of 8.2 g/dL. MCV is 88 fL, ferritin is 250 ng/mL, and transferrin saturation is 35%. He has no evidence of bleeding. What is the most likely cause of his anaemia?
opts: EPO deficiency from chronic kidney disease
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: CKD anaemia — normocytic anaemia from erythropoietin deficiency
discriminator: CKD stage 4 + normocytic anaemia (MCV 88) + adequate iron stores (normal ferritin, TSAT > 30%) + no bleeding = anaemia of CKD due to EPO deficiency. Treatment is recombinant EPO.

stem: A 55-year-old male presents with acute dyspnoea and orthopnoea over 12 hours. He has a history of hypertension and diabetes. BP is 170/100 mmHg, JVP is elevated to 15 cm H2O, and he has bilateral crackles up to the mid-zones. Chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly, prominent upper lobe vessels, and pleural effusions. There is mild pitting pedal oedema. Which feature most strongly suggests this is cardiogenic rather than nephrogenic pulmonary oedema?
subject: Medicine-Renal
concept: Cross-system — cardiogenic vs nephrogenic pulmonary oedema differentiation
discriminator: Cardiomegaly on CXR indicates a cardiac cause (chronic pressure/volume overload leading to enlarged cardiac silhouette). In pure nephrogenic (fluid overload) pulmonary oedema, the heart size is normal — the pulmonary congestion is from excess volume, not pump failure.

stem: A 65-year-old female with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with confusion and a single episode of seizure. Serum sodium is 118 mmol/L. She is euvolemic on examination. Urine sodium is 45 mmol/L and urine osmolality is 520 mOsm/kg. CXR reveals a central hilar mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: SIADH secondary to small cell lung cancer
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: SIADH — euvolemic hyponatremia with high U Na and high U Osm, paraneoplastic from lung cancer
discriminator: Euvolemia + U Na > 20 + U Osm > 300 + lung mass = SIADH; cerebral salt wasting is hypovolemic

stem: A 60-year-old male with type 2 diabetes mellitus missed his last three doses of insulin. He presents with palpitations. ECG shows tall peaked T waves in the precordial leads. Serum potassium is 6.8 mmol/L. What is the IMMEDIATE next step in management?
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes — IV calcium gluconate first for cardiac membrane stabilisation
discriminator: ECG changes (peaked T) mandate immediate cardioprotection before shifting K+; calcium works in seconds

stem: A 45-year-old female with a 3-day history of severe watery diarrhoea undergoes ABG analysis. Results: pH 7.25, PaCO2 24 mmHg, HCO3 10 mmol/L. Serum potassium is 3.2 mmol/L. Anion gap is 10. What is the most likely acid-base disorder?
opts: High anion gap metabolic acidosis from lactic acidosis
Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis from diarrhoea
Mixed metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis with inadequate respiratory compensation
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Diarrhoea causes normal AG (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis from HCO3 loss
discriminator: Normal AG (8-12) + diarrhoea history = HCO3 loss, not acid gain

stem: A 2-month-old infant presents with projectile non-bilious vomiting after feeds. ABG shows: pH 7.56, PaCO2 48 mmHg, HCO3 42 mmol/L. Serum potassium is 2.8 mmol/L, chloride is 88 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Primary respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation
Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from pyloric stenosis
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Pyloric stenosis — hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from loss of gastric HCl
discriminator: High pH + high HCO3 + high pCO2 (compensatory) + low Cl + low K = metabolic alkalosis from vomiting

stem: A 35-year-old male presents with confusion and hyperventilation. ABG: pH 7.20, PaCO2 20 mmHg, HCO3 8 mmol/L. Anion gap is 28. What is the expected PaCO2 based on Winter's formula, and is the respiratory compensation adequate?
opts: Expected PaCO2 12, compensation inadequate (measured PaCO2 too high)
Expected PaCO2 20, compensation adequate (measured matches expected)
Expected PaCO2 24, compensation excessive (measured PaCO2 too low)
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Winter's formula: expected PaCO2 = (1.5 × HCO3) + 8 ± 2 for metabolic acidosis compensation
discriminator: Calculation: (1.5 × 8) + 8 = 20; measured PaCO2 of 20 falls within 20 ± 2 range = adequate compensation

stem: A 55-year-old female 2 days post-thyroidectomy develops perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm. Chvostek sign is positive. Laboratory results: serum calcium 7.8 mg/dL, phosphate 6.0 mg/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Hypoparathyroidism due to surgical removal of parathyroid glands
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Post-thyroidectomy hypocalcemia with low Ca + high PO4 = hypoparathyroidism
discriminator: Post-thyroidectomy + low Ca + high PO4 = hypoparathyroidism (loss of PTH); rickets has low PO4

stem: A 70-year-old male with chronic kidney disease presents with weakness and palpitations. ECG shows peaked T waves and widened QRS complexes. He also has bibasilar crackles and pedal oedema consistent with fluid overload. What is the IMMEDIATE next step?
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes requires IV calcium FIRST regardless of renal status
discriminator: Peaked T + widened QRS = ECG changes → calcium first, even in CKD with fluid overload

stem: A 25-year-old male presents with altered mental status. ABG: pH 7.30, PaCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3 15 mmol/L. Na 140, Cl 105, HCO3 15. What is the anion gap and what type of acidosis does this represent?
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Anion gap calculation: AG = Na - (Cl + HCO3); AG > 12 = high AG metabolic acidosis
discriminator: AG = 140 - (105 + 15) = 20; normal AG 8-12, so 20 is high AG metabolic acidosis

stem: A 50-year-old male with chronic alcoholism presents with vomiting and confusion. ABG: pH 7.48, PaCO2 44 mmHg, HCO3 33 mmol/L. Na 138, Cl 90, HCO3 33. What acid-base disorder is present?
opts: Mixed metabolic alkalosis and respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Metabolic alkalosis with compensatory respiratory acidosis — pH > 7.45, HCO3 > 30, PaCO2 appropriately elevated
discriminator: pH alkalemic + HCO3 high (primary) + PaCO2 elevated (compensatory) = metabolic alkalosis with appropriate compensation

stem: A 30-year-old female on a thiazide diuretic for hypertension presents with muscle cramps. Na 128 mmol/L, K 3.0 mmol/L. She appears euvolemic. Urine Na 40 mmol/L, urine osmolality 450 mOsm/kg. What is the most likely cause of her hyponatremia?
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Thiazide diuretics can cause SIADH-like picture (euvolemic hyponatremia with high U Na, high U Osm)
discriminator: Euvolemic + high U Na + high U Osm = SIADH pattern; thiazides are a classic drug cause

stem: A 40-year-old female on long-term omeprazole presents with perioral tingling and positive Trousseau sign. Serum calcium 7.6 mg/dL, phosphate 3.0 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 450 U/L (elevated). What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Rickets/osteomalacia — low Ca + low PO4 + high ALP = vitamin D deficiency (not hypoparathyroidism)
discriminator: Low Ca + low PO4 + high ALP = vitamin D deficiency; low Ca + high PO4 = hypoparathyroidism

stem: A 22-year-old female with type 1 diabetes presents with nausea, vomiting, and deep rapid breathing. Capillary glucose is 450 mg/dL. ABG: pH 7.15, PaCO2 18 mmHg, HCO3 6 mmol/L. Anion gap is 30. Urine ketones are strongly positive. What is the diagnosis?
opts: High AG metabolic acidosis from lactic acidosis
High AG metabolic acidosis from DKA
Normal AG metabolic acidosis from diarrhoea
Mixed high AG and normal AG metabolic acidosis
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: DKA causes high AG metabolic acidosis from ketoacid accumulation
discriminator: Hyperglycaemia + ketones + high AG + low pH = DKA; lactic acidosis would have elevated lactate

stem: A 55-year-old male presents with confusion. Na 152 mmol/L, K 5.2 mmol/L. He is drowsy and has a fever of 39°C. His urine osmolality is 380 mOsm/kg. Which set of findings would help confirm the diagnosis of diabetes insipidus?
opts: High urine osmolality, low serum osmolality
Low urine osmolality, high serum osmolality, failure to concentrate urine with water deprivation
High urine Na, low urine osmolality
Low serum Na, high urine osmolality
Normal urine osmolality, normal serum osmolality
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Diabetes insipidus — hypernatraemia with inappropriately dilute urine (low U Osm relative to serum) with failure to concentrate on water deprivation
discriminator: Hypernatraemia + U Osm < serum Osm = inability to concentrate urine; water deprivation test confirms

stem: A chronic alcoholic presents with confusion. ABG: pH 7.32, PaCO2 33, HCO3 16. Na 138, Cl 100, HCO3 16. Serum osmolality is 340 mOsm/kg (calculated 290). What is the most likely cause of the high AG metabolic acidosis?
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: MUDPILES — Methanol causes high AG acidosis with elevated osmolal gap
discriminator: High AG + high osmolal gap (measured Osm - calculated Osm > 10) = methanol or ethylene glycol

stem: A 35-year-old male with known CKD stage 5 (not on dialysis) presents with weakness. K 6.5 mmol/L. ECG shows peaked T waves only. What is the most appropriate FIRST step?
opts: Give IV insulin + dextrose followed by calcium gluconate
Give IV normal saline with furosemide
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Hyperkalemia with ANY ECG change requires IV calcium first — peaked T waves count
discriminator: Peaked T waves ARE ECG changes → calcium first, regardless of CKD stage

stem: A 60-year-old female presents with acute dyspnoea. ABG on room air: pH 7.32, PaCO2 55 mmHg, PaO2 60 mmHg, HCO3 26 mmol/L. What is the primary acid-base disorder?
opts: Chronic respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Acute respiratory acidosis — pH < 7.35 + PaCO2 > 45 + HCO3 normal (no renal compensation yet)
discriminator: High PaCO2 + low pH + HCO3 normal (26) = acute, not chronic; chronic would show elevated HCO3

stem: A 70-year-old male with CHF on furosemide presents with confusion. Na 125 mmol/L. He has bilateral pedal oedema and elevated JVP. What is the most likely type of hyponatremia?
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Hypervolemic hyponatremia — oedematous states (CHF) cause dilutional hyponatremia
discriminator: Oedema + elevated JVP = hypervolemic; CHF with furosemide can still be hypervolemic overall

stem: A patient with known high AG metabolic acidosis has the following labs: Na 140, Cl 90, HCO3 15 (baseline HCO3 24). What is the delta-delta gap and what additional disorder is suggested?
opts: ΔAG/ΔHCO3 = 1.0, single high AG metabolic acidosis
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Delta-delta gap: (ΔAG)/(ΔHCO3) > 2 indicates concurrent metabolic alkalosis
discriminator: ΔAG = current AG (20) - normal AG (12) = 8; ΔHCO3 = normal (24) - current (15) = 9; ratio = 8/9 ≈ 0.89... Wait, let me recalculate.

stem: A 45-year-old male with COPD presents with increasing dyspnoea. ABG: pH 7.36, PaCO2 60 mmHg, HCO3 34 mmol/L. What does this ABG indicate?
opts: Chronic respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
Mixed respiratory acidosis and metabolic alkalosis
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Chronic respiratory acidosis — pH near-normal with high PaCO2 and elevated HCO3 (renal compensation)
discriminator: Normal pH + high PaCO2 + high HCO3 = fully compensated chronic respiratory acidosis

stem: A 28-year-old female with anxiety presents with rapid deep breathing. ABG: pH 7.50, PaCO2 25 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L. What is the interpretation?
opts: Chronic respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation
Mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Acute respiratory alkalosis — pH > 7.45 + low PaCO2 + normal HCO3 (no renal compensation yet)
discriminator: Low PaCO2 + high pH + normal HCO3 = acute respiratory alkalosis; anxiety attack is a classic trigger

stem: A 50-year-old female with chronic liver disease presents with confusion. Ammonia level is elevated. ABG: pH 7.48, PaCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3 20 mmol/L. What acid-base disorder does this patient have?
opts: Acute respiratory alkalosis from hepatic encephalopathy-induced hyperventilation
Mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Hepatic encephalopathy causes hyperventilation → acute respiratory alkalosis
discriminator: Low PaCO2 + high pH + mildly low HCO3 (early compensation) in liver disease = respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation

stem: A 32-year-old male presents with an overdose. ABG: pH 7.42, PaCO2 15 mmHg, HCO3 10 mmol/L. Anion gap is 25. What is the most likely ingested substance?
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Salicylate overdose — mixed respiratory alkalosis (direct respiratory stimulation) and high AG metabolic acidosis
discriminator: Normal pH with very low PaCO2 (resp alkalosis) + very low HCO3 (metabolic acidosis) + high AG = salicylate's mixed picture

stem: A 65-year-old female with serum Na 118 mmol/L is started on treatment. After 24 hours, her Na is 130 mmol/L. What is the most significant risk of this rate of correction?
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Maximum safe Na correction is 8-12 mmol/L in 24 hours; > 12 risks osmotic demyelination
discriminator: Na rose from 118 to 130 = 12 mmol/L in 24 hours, which is at the upper limit of safe correction; faster correction causes osmotic demyelination

stem: A 40-year-old female presents with episodic hypertension and weakness. K 2.8 mmol/L. ABG: pH 7.46, HCO3 32 mmol/L, PaCO2 46 mmHg. Urine chloride is 35 mmol/L. What is the most likely cause of her metabolic alkalosis?
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Chloride-unresponsive metabolic alkalosis (U Cl > 20) = hyperaldosteronism; chloride-responsive (U Cl < 20) = vomiting/NG suction
discriminator: U Cl > 20 + hypertension + hypokalaemia + metabolic alkalosis = hyperaldosteronism; U Cl < 20 = GI loss

stem: A 55-year-old male with CKD presents with K 6.2 mmol/L. ECG shows normal sinus rhythm without peaked T waves or QRS widening. What is the appropriate management?
opts: No urgent intervention needed; manage chronic K+ elevation with dietary restriction and Kayexalate
subject: Medicine-Electrolytes
concept: Hyperkalemia WITHOUT ECG changes does not require emergency cardioprotection — manage chronically
discriminator: K 6.2 + normal ECG = no ECG changes → no IV calcium needed; chronic management is appropriate

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with epigastric burning pain that improves after meals but returns 2-3 hours later. He also reports being woken up at night by similar pain. He takes ibuprofen occasionally for knee pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: Duodenal ulcer pain pattern: pain relieved by food, nocturnal recurrence
discriminator: Pain that improves with food but returns 2-3 h later with nocturnal awakening = DU until proven otherwise.

stem: A 55-year-old woman with osteoarthritis presents with epigastric pain that worsens after eating. She has lost 4 kg over 2 months. She takes naproxen daily. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: Gastric ulcer pain pattern: pain worsened by food, weight loss
discriminator: Pain WORSENED by food + weight loss + NSAID use = GU until proven otherwise. GU has malignant potential and requires biopsy.

stem: A 40-year-old woman with dyspepsia and no alarm features tests positive for H. pylori on a urea breath test. What is the recommended first-line eradication regimen?
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: H. pylori first-line triple therapy regimen
discriminator: Triple therapy = PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin for 14 days is standard first-line where clarithromycin resistance is low.

stem: A 38-year-old man with dyspepsia has no alarm features. What is the most appropriate next step in management according to the test-and-treat strategy?
opts: Refer for urgent upper GI endoscopy
Test for H. pylori (stool antigen or urea breath test) and treat if positive
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: H. pylori test-and-treat strategy for uncomplicated dyspepsia
discriminator: No alarm features + dyspepsia = test for H. pylori non-invasively and treat if positive. Endoscopy is reserved for alarm features.

stem: A 60-year-old man with melena and hematemesis presents to the emergency department. His BP is 90/60 mmHg and HR is 110 bpm. What is the most appropriate first step in management?
opts: Urgent upper GI endoscopy within 24 hours
IV fluid resuscitation and cross-match blood
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: Initial management of upper GI bleeding — resuscitation first
discriminator: Hemodynamically unstable GI bleed: resuscitation always precedes diagnostic and therapeutic procedures.

stem: Following resuscitation of a patient with bleeding peptic ulcer, what is the next step in management?
opts: Start oral PPI and discharge if stable
Start high-dose IV PPI infusion and arrange urgent endoscopy within 24 hours
Refer for surgical vagotomy and pyloroplasty
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: Bleeding PUD management after resuscitation — IV PPI + urgent endoscopy
discriminator: High-dose IV PPI (80 mg bolus + 8 mg/h) + endoscopy within 24 h is the standard sequence after resuscitation.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with chronic watery diarrhea, abdominal bloating, and weight loss. She has pallor and a pruritic vesicular rash on her elbows and knees. Which laboratory finding is most likely to be present?
opts: Low serum vitamin B12 with normal folate
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: Celiac disease — anti-tTG IgA serology and dermatitis herpetiformis association
discriminator: Chronic diarrhea + weight loss + malabsorption + pruritic vesicular rash on elbows/knees = celiac disease with dermatitis herpetiformis. Anti-tTG IgA is the first-line serologic test.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with suspected celiac disease has negative anti-tTG IgA serology but high clinical suspicion persists. What is the most appropriate next step?
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: Celiac disease — false-negative anti-tTG due to IgA deficiency
discriminator: If celiac is suspected but anti-tTG IgA is negative, check total IgA — IgA deficiency causes false-negative anti-tTG. In IgA deficiency, check IgG-based tests (anti-DGP IgG or anti-tTG IgG).

stem: A 30-year-old man with chronic diarrhea and weight loss has positive anti-tTG IgA. What is the gold standard test to confirm the diagnosis before starting treatment?
opts: Duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes
Capsule endoscopy of the small bowel
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: Celiac disease — duodenal biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis
discriminator: Positive serology alone is insufficient — duodenal biopsy is required to confirm villous atrophy before committing to lifelong GFD.

stem: A 25-year-old woman is diagnosed with celiac disease. What is the definitive treatment that should be recommended?
opts: Life-long gluten-free diet (avoiding wheat, barley, and rye)
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: Celiac disease — gluten-free diet as definitive treatment
discriminator: GFD is the only definitive treatment for celiac disease. Response to GFD also supports the diagnosis.

stem: A 34-year-old man with chronic diarrhea and malabsorption has been living in rural Bangladesh for the past 2 years. He has negative anti-tTG IgA and negative anti-DGP IgG. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: Tropical sprue vs celiac disease — geographic and serologic differentiation
discriminator: Tropical residence + malabsorption + negative celiac serology = tropical sprue. Treats with tetracycline + folate, not GFD.

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with chronic abdominal pain and altered bowel habits. Her pain is relieved by defecation and associated with bloating. She has no weight loss, no rectal bleeding, and normal physical examination. Basic blood work including CBC, CRP, and TSH is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: IBS — Rome IV criteria: chronic pain + altered bowel habit + no alarm features
discriminator: Pain relieved by defecation + bloating + absence of alarm features (weight loss, bleeding, anemia, age > 50) = IBS by Rome IV criteria.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with chronic abdominal pain and alternating diarrhea and constipation. She has bloating and reports that her symptoms are worse with stress. Weight is stable. Stool is non-bloody. Which finding would be an ALARM feature requiring further investigation?
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: IBS alarm features — nocturnal symptoms suggest organic disease
discriminator: Nocturnal diarrhea is an alarm feature that suggests organic disease (IBD, microscopic colitis) rather than IBS. Functional symptoms do not wake patients from sleep.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with recurrent abdominal pain, non-bloody diarrhea, and bloating is diagnosed with IBS. Initial dietary management includes which of the following?
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: IBS management — low-FODMAP diet
discriminator: Low-FODMAP diet is the evidence-based dietary intervention for IBS, reducing fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, and polyols.

stem: A 29-year-old man with a 40 pack-year smoking history presents with right lower quadrant pain, non-bloody diarrhea, and weight loss. Colonoscopy shows skip lesions with deep ulcerations and strictures in the terminal ileum. Biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: Crohn disease — transmural inflammation, skip lesions, non-caseating granulomas, smoking worsens
discriminator: Skip lesions + terminal ileum + non-caseating granulomas + smoker = Crohn disease. Non-caseating granulomas are pathognomonic.

stem: A 34-year-old non-smoker presents with bloody diarrhea, tenesmus, and lower abdominal cramping. Flexible sigmoidoscopy shows continuous friable mucosa with loss of vascular pattern starting at the rectum. Which of the following histologic findings is most characteristic of this condition?
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: Ulcerative colitis — crypt abscesses on histology
discriminator: Continuous mucosal inflammation from rectum + bloody diarrhea + tenesmus = UC. Crypt abscesses (cryptitis with neutrophil infiltration) are the histologic hallmark.

stem: A 45-year-old man with ulcerative colitis for 12 years comes for routine follow-up. Cholestatic LFTs are noted (elevated ALP and GGT with mildly elevated bilirubin). He has pruritus but no jaundice. What associated condition should be investigated?
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: PSC association with UC — primary sclerosing cholangitis
discriminator: UC patient with cholestatic LFTs + pruritus = PSC until proven otherwise. PSC is strongly associated with UC, not Crohn.

stem: A 28-year-old man with Crohn disease asks about lifestyle modifications. He currently smokes 15 cigarettes per day. Which advice regarding smoking is correct?
opts: Smoking has no effect on Crohn disease activity
Smoking is protective and should be continued
Smoking worsens Crohn disease and should be stopped
Smoking is beneficial for fistulizing Crohn only
Reducing to 5 cigarettes per day is sufficient
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: Smoking effect in Crohn disease (worsens) vs UC (protective)
discriminator: Smoking WORSENS Crohn disease (increases disease activity, need for surgery). The opposite is true for UC (protective). Never confuse these.

stem: A 65-year-old woman on long-term NSAIDs for rheumatoid arthritis is starting treatment. She has a history of gastric ulcer 3 years ago. Which strategy is most appropriate to prevent NSAID-induced peptic ulcer recurrence?
opts: Co-prescribe a PPI with the NSAID
Test and treat H. pylori only
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: NSAID-induced PUD prevention — co-prescribe PPI in high-risk patients
discriminator: Previous PUD + NSAID use + age > 65 = high risk. Co-prescribe PPI for primary/secondary prevention. This patient has multiple risk factors.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents with epigastric pain and watery diarrhea. He has a history of recurrent duodenal ulcers despite H. pylori eradication. Upper GI endoscopy shows multiple post-bulbar duodenal ulcers. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome — recurrent PUD in atypical location + diarrhea
discriminator: Multiple/recurrent ulcers + post-bulbar location + diarrhea + failed H. pylori eradication = Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma causing hypergastrinemia).

stem: A 55-year-old man who underwent successful H. pylori eradication therapy 6 weeks ago returns for follow-up. He is now asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate test to confirm H. pylori eradication?
opts: Repeat serology for H. pylori IgG
Urea breath test or stool antigen test
Rapid urease test on gastric biopsy
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: H. pylori eradication confirmation — non-invasive testing at least 4 weeks after therapy
discriminator: Confirmation of eradication requires non-invasive testing (urea breath test or stool antigen) at least 4 weeks after completing therapy. Serology cannot distinguish active from past infection.

stem: A 32-year-old man with epigastric pain has a positive stool antigen test for H. pylori. He reports a penicillin allergy (urticaria). What is the appropriate first-line eradication regimen?
opts: PPI + bismuth + metronidazole + tetracycline for 10 days
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: H. pylori triple therapy in penicillin allergy — substitute amoxicillin with metronidazole
discriminator: Penicillin allergy requires replacing amoxicillin with metronidazole in triple therapy.

stem: A 62-year-old man with ulcerative colitis diagnosed 9 years ago is in remission on mesalamine. He has never had a colonoscopy. What complication screening should be recommended?
opts: Surveillance colonoscopy for colorectal cancer starting now
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: UC — colorectal cancer surveillance begins 8-10 years after diagnosis
discriminator: UC increases colorectal cancer risk after 8-10 years of disease. Surveillance colonoscopy should begin at this time, regardless of symptoms.

stem: A 48-year-old man presents with hematemesis. Upper GI endoscopy reveals an actively bleeding duodenal ulcer with a visible vessel. What is the most appropriate endoscopic management?
opts: Observation only — visible vessel has low rebleeding risk
Adrenaline injection alone into the ulcer base
Endoscopic therapy with adrenaline injection + mechanical clips or thermal coagulation
Biopsy the ulcer and send for H. pylori testing
Place a nasogastric tube for monitoring
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: Endoscopic management of bleeding PUD — combination therapy for active bleeding or visible vessel
discriminator: Active bleeding or visible vessel on endoscopy requires endoscopic hemostasis. Combination therapy (injection + clips/thermal) is superior to monotherapy.

stem: A 70-year-old woman on warfarin for atrial fibrillation presents with melena and coffee-ground emesis. INR is 4.5. She is hemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate management regarding anticoagulation reversal?
opts: Hold warfarin and monitor INR daily
4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) + IV vitamin K
subject: Medicine-Gastroenterology
concept: Anticoagulation reversal in life-threatening GI bleeding — PCC + vitamin K
discriminator: Life-threatening GI bleeding on warfarin with elevated INR requires rapid reversal with PCC (4-factor) + vitamin K. FFP is slower and less effective.
