stem: A 52-year-old asymptomatic woman undergoes routine blood work. Her HbA1c is 6.8%. Fasting plasma glucose is 7.3 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: DM diagnosis — HbA1c threshold ≥ 6.5%
discriminator: HbA1c ≥ 6.5% alone is diagnostic of diabetes mellitus. FPG ≥ 7.0 confirms.

stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman at 26 weeks gestation undergoes screening. Her 75g OGTT 2-hour plasma glucose is 9.2 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: GDM diagnosis — OGTT in pregnancy at 24–28 weeks
discriminator: OGTT 75g at 24–28 weeks is the gold standard for GDM.

stem: A 50-year-old obese female (BMI 34) presents with polyuria and polydipsia for 2 months. FPG is 8.1 mmol/L, HbA1c 7.2%. What is the single best first-line pharmacotherapy?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: T2DM first-line — metformin in obese patients
discriminator: Obese T2DM → metformin is ALWAYS first-line unless contraindicated.

stem: A 14-year-old male with type 1 diabetes stopped his insulin 2 days ago. He presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, confusion, Kussmaul breathing. Capillary glucose 450 mg/dL. ABG: pH 7.29, HCO3 12. What is the single best initial step?
opts: IV normal saline 1 L over 1 hour
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: DKA management — fluid resuscitation FIRST
discriminator: DKA management sequence: FLUIDS first, then insulin, then K+ monitoring.

stem: A 60-year-old male with type 2 diabetes on insulin missed several doses. He presents with palpitations. ECG shows tall peaked T waves. Serum K+ is 6.4 mmol/L. Most likely cause?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Missed insulin → hyperkalemia mechanism
discriminator: Insulin drives K+ into cells. MISSED insulin = K+ stays extracellular = hyperkalemia. Most repeated exam diabetes pattern.

stem: A 45-year-old T1DM patient reports rising morning glucose despite increasing evening insulin dose. She has night sweats and morning headaches. What phenomenon and correct management?
opts: Dawn phenomenon — increase evening insulin dose
Somogyi phenomenon — decrease evening insulin dose
Waning insulin effect — switch to twice-daily NPH
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Somogyi phenomenon — nocturnal hypoglycaemia with rebound
discriminator: Nocturnal hypoglycaemia + rebound AM hyperglycaemia + worsening with increasing dose = Somogyi. DECREASE dose.

stem: A 55-year-old woman with T2DM has spot ACR 85 mg/g. eGFR 78. BP 128/78. Best intervention to slow nephropathy?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Diabetic nephropathy — ACEi for microalbuminuria
discriminator: Microalbuminuria + diabetes = ACEi/ARB. Independent renoprotection beyond BP and glucose.

stem: A 62-year-old obese T2DM on metformin 2 g daily has eGFR 25 mL/min/1.73m². Most appropriate action?
opts: Add sulfonylurea to reduce metformin requirement
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Metformin contraindication — eGFR < 30
discriminator: Metformin absolutely contraindicated when eGFR < 30 due to lactic acidosis risk.

stem: A 58-year-old T2DM has a plantar ulcer extending to tendon without bone involvement. No gangrene. Wagner grade?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Diabetic foot — Wagner grading system
discriminator: Wagner grade 2 = deep to tendon/capsule without bone. Grade 3 = osteomyelitis.

stem: A 65-year-old T2DM admitted for pneumonia. On metformin and glimepiride. Glucose 420 mg/dL, febrile. Most appropriate regimen adjustment?
opts: Switch to insulin therapy for the duration of illness
Continue metformin and add insulin as needed
Stop all diabetes medications until infection resolves
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Sick-day rules — insulin during illness
discriminator: Illness increases insulin requirements. Oral agents insufficient. Hold metformin if dehydration risk.

stem: A 72-year-old man with T2DM presents confused and dehydrated. Gradual onset over 10 days. Glucose 850 mg/dL. Ketones negative. pH 7.35, HCO3 22. Osmolality 340. Most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: HHS vs DKA differentiation
discriminator: Glucose > 600, no ketones, no acidosis, osmolality > 320, gradual onset in elderly T2DM = HHS.

stem: A 55-year-old T2DM on max metformin has HbA1c 10.2%. eGFR 42. Which add-on therapy should be avoided?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Sulfonylurea caution in CKD
discriminator: Sulfonylureas accumulate in CKD → prolonged severe hypoglycaemia risk.

stem: A 14-year-old with DKA on IV fluids and insulin. Initial K+ 5.0. After 2 hours, K+ drops to 3.8 mmol/L. Most appropriate action?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: DKA K+ monitoring — replace when < 5.3
discriminator: Total body K+ depleted in DKA. Replace K+ when serum < 5.3 mmol/L.

stem: A 60-year-old T2DM with painless plantar ulcer. Foot is warm, dorsalis pedis pulses bounding, claw toes. Most likely type?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Neuropathic foot — warm, pulses present, painless
discriminator: Neuropathic foot: WARM, bounding pulses (AV shunting), painless, claw toes. Cold = ischaemic.

stem: A 58-year-old T2DM on metformin and glibenclamide presents with diaphoresis, confusion, glucose 38 mg/dL. eGFR 32. Most likely contributing factor?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia in CKD
discriminator: Glibenclamide active metabolites accumulate in CKD → prolonged severe hypoglycaemia.

stem: A 22-year-old T1DM on insulin develops vomiting, abdominal pain. Glucose 320. Urine ketones strongly positive. Afebrile. Best next step?
opts: Give extra rapid-acting insulin and encourage fluids
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Sick-day rules — vomiting + ketones = emergency
discriminator: Vomiting + hyperglycaemia + ketones in T1DM = impending DKA. Cannot manage at home.

stem: A 70-year-old with HHS started on IV fluids. After 2 L NS, which electrolyte needs closest monitoring?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: HHS management — K+ monitoring
discriminator: Total body K+ depleted in HHS despite normal initial serum. Fluids and insulin lower K+.

stem: A 65-year-old T1DM on insulin missed a dose. Palpitations, tall peaked T waves on ECG. K+ 6.6. Best immediate intervention?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Hyperkalemia — calcium gluconate for ECG changes
discriminator: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes requires immediate membrane stabilisation with IV calcium gluconate FIRST.

stem: A 48-year-old T1DM with DKA. After 1L NS and insulin, glucose 480→320. K+ 5.4. Most appropriate management?
opts: Add KCl 20 mEq to IV fluids
Continue fluids and insulin, recheck K+ in 1 hour
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: DKA K+ threshold — replace only when < 5.3
discriminator: K+ 5.4 is above the replacement threshold of 5.3. Continue monitoring.

stem: A 55-year-old T2DM with Wagner grade 2 plantar ulcer. Deep to tendon, bone not exposed. Surrounding erythema. Best management?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Wagner grade 2 management
discriminator: Grade 2 (deep to tendon) needs debridement + antibiotics + offloading.

stem: A 56-year-old T2DM on metformin 2 g daily. HbA1c 8.8%. eGFR 38. Appropriate metformin management?
opts: Reduce metformin dose to 1 g daily
Double metformin dose to improve glycaemic control
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Metformin dose adjustment at eGFR 30–45
discriminator: eGFR 30–45: reduce metformin dose (max 1 g/day). Discontinue only if < 30.

stem: A 48-year-old T1DM reports morning hyperglycaemia (210 mg/dL). 3 AM glucose 72. No night sweats. What phenomenon and management?
opts: Dawn phenomenon — adjust timing or increase dose
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Dawn vs Somogyi differentiation
discriminator: Normal 3 AM glucose (72) + AM hyperglycaemia WITHOUT preceding hypoglycaemia = dawn phenomenon.

stem: A 60-year-old T2DM with nephropathy (ACR 120), hypertension (BP 148/92 on amlodipine 10 mg), eGFR 52, no ACEi. Best next step?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: ACEi renoprotection independent of BP control
discriminator: Microalbuminuria + diabetes = ACEi regardless of BP. ADD to existing regimen, don't switch.

stem: A 32-year-old T1DM with DKA. Initial K+ 5.8. After 1h fluids + insulin, K+ drops to 4.9. No ECG changes. Most appropriate management?
opts: Continue fluids and insulin; do not add K+ yet
Start KCl 20 mEq/L in IV fluids immediately
Stop insulin to prevent further K+ decline
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Dynamic K+ threshold in DKA
discriminator: K+ 4.9 is below 5.3 threshold → replacement needed now despite initial K+ being above threshold.

stem: A 65-year-old T2DM with prior inferior STEMI presents with dyspnoea, orthopnoea, JVP elevated, crackles. BP 155/95. Painless plantar ulcer, warm feet, bounding pulses. ACR 145. Which medication benefits BOTH CV and renal disease?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: ACEi — mortality benefit in HF + renoprotection
discriminator: Post-MI HF + diabetic nephropathy + hypertension = ACEi benefits all three.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, palpitations, and fine tremors of her hands. On examination, she has a diffuse, symmetrically enlarged thyroid gland and bilateral proptosis with lid lag. Vital signs show HR 110/min, BP 130/70. What is the single best next step in management?
opts: Start propranolol for symptom control and refer for antithyroid therapy
Start carbimazole alone and monitor thyroid function in 4 weeks
Start Lugol's iodine to block hormone release
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Graves disease: initial management with beta-blocker for catecholamine symptom control before definitive therapy
discriminator: Beta-blocker first for symptom control in newly diagnosed Graves disease — propranolol controls tachycardia, tremor, and anxiety before antithyroid drugs take effect

stem: A 32-year-old woman with Graves disease on carbimazole presents with a sore throat and fever. Her temperature is 38.5°C and she has pharyngeal erythema. What is the most important next step?
opts: Check full blood count for agranulocytosis
Increase carbimazole dose to control hyperthyroidism
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Antithyroid drug side effect: agranulocytosis — sore throat/fever requires immediate FBC check
discriminator: Sore throat + fever on carbimazole/PTU = agranulocytosis until proven otherwise — check FBC before any other intervention

stem: A 26-year-old pregnant woman at 10 weeks gestation presents with heat intolerance, palpitations, and a diffuse goiter. TSH is <0.01 mIU/L, free T4 is 28 pmol/L (normal 9-19). She has no eye signs. What is the most appropriate antithyroid drug for this patient?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: PTU preferred in 1st trimester pregnancy — carbimazole causes aplasia cutis
discriminator: First trimester hyperthyroidism = PTU. Carbimazole/methimazole are teratogenic (aplasia cutis) in the first trimester.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with Graves disease treated with carbimazole for 18 months has persistent goiter and recurrent hyperthyroidism whenever the dose is tapered. She has no plans for pregnancy. What is the most appropriate definitive management?
opts: Continue carbimazole indefinitely at the current dose
External beam radiotherapy to the thyroid
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: RAI is definitive treatment for Graves disease when medical therapy fails or is not tolerated
discriminator: Failed medical therapy in non-pregnant patient without contraindication → RAI is first-line definitive option over surgery

stem: A 35-year-old woman with known Graves disease presents to the emergency department with fever (39.5°C), heart rate 150/min, confusion, and vomiting. She missed her carbimazole dose for 5 days. BP is 100/60. What is the single most important first drug to administer?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Thyroid storm management: propranolol is the first step to control catecholamine-mediated symptoms
discriminator: In thyroid storm, propranolol is given first because it is most immediately life-saving — it controls tachycardia, fever, and agitation by blocking catecholamine effects

stem: A 40-year-old man with Graves disease undergoes total thyroidectomy. On post-operative day 1, he develops tingling in his fingertips and perioral numbness. Physical examination reveals Chvostek sign. ECG shows a prolonged QT interval. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Hypothyroidism due to inadequate levothyroxine replacement
Hypoparathyroidism due to parathyroid gland injury
Hypocalcemia due to hungry bone syndrome
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Post-thyroidectomy hypocalcemia = hypoparathyroidism from parathyroid injury/removal
discriminator: Post-thyroidectomy + Chvostek/Trousseau + prolonged QT = hypoparathyroidism (low Ca, high PO4, low PTH) — not hungry bone syndrome (which occurs after parathyroidectomy, not thyroidectomy)

stem: A 52-year-old woman presents with fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, and weight gain over 6 months. TSH is 58 mIU/L (normal 0.5-4.5) and free T4 is 5 pmol/L (normal 9-19). What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
opts: Levothyroxine 50 mcg PO daily, titrate by TSH every 6-8 weeks
Levothyroxine 200 mcg PO daily as a loading dose
Combination T4/T3 therapy for faster symptom relief
No treatment indicated; repeat TSH in 3 months
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Primary hypothyroidism: start levothyroxine (T4) 1.6 mcg/kg/day — about 50-100 mcg daily depending on weight
discriminator: Levothyroxine (T4) is the standard of care — start low (50 mcg) in older patients and titrate by TSH. T3 therapy is not first-line.

stem: An 80-year-old man with known hypothyroidism on levothyroxine 50 mcg daily presents with confusion, hypotension, hypothermia (35.0°C), and bradycardia. His family reports he has been more withdrawn and eating less for 2 weeks. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Start broad-spectrum antibiotics for presumed sepsis
Administer IV levothyroxine 200-500 mcg and IV hydrocortisone
Increase oral levothyroxine to 100 mcg daily and arrange outpatient follow-up
Administer IV T3 (liothyronine) alone without steroids
Warm the patient passively and observe for 24 hours
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Myxedema coma: IV levothyroxine + hydrocortisone + supportive care
discriminator: Myxedema coma = hypothermia + hypotension + altered mental state in hypothyroid patient. Treat with IV levothyroxine AND hydrocortisone (rule out concurrent adrenal insufficiency).

stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with a 4-month history of progressive central obesity, easy bruising, and thinning of her skin. On examination, she has moon facies, supraclavicular fat pads, purple striae on her abdomen, and proximal muscle weakness. BP is 160/100. Overnight dexamethasone suppression test shows cortisol of 550 nmol/L (normal <50 after suppression). What is the most appropriate next step to localise the source?
opts: CT scan of the adrenal glands
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Cushing syndrome localisation: ACTH level is the single most important test to differentiate ACTH-dependent (pituitary/ectopic) from ACTH-independent (adrenal) causes
discriminator: After confirming Cushing syndrome, the next step is ACTH level. If ACTH is detectable (high/normal) → ACTH-dependent (pituitary vs ectopic). If ACTH is undetectable/low → ACTH-independent (adrenal source).

stem: A 42-year-old woman with Cushing syndrome is found to have an undetectable plasma ACTH level (<1.1 pmol/L). MRI of the adrenals shows a 3 cm left adrenal mass. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: CT-guided biopsy of the adrenal mass
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: ACTH-independent Cushing (undetectable ACTH) from adrenal adenoma → unilateral adrenalectomy
discriminator: Undetectable ACTH + unilateral adrenal mass = adrenal adenoma causing Cushing syndrome → unilateral adrenalectomy is curative. Do not biopsy (risk of hemorrhage, pheochromocytoma must be ruled out).

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with Cushing syndrome. ACTH is 22 pmol/L (normal 1.1-11). High-dose dexamethasone suppression test shows suppression of cortisol to <50% of baseline. MRI pituitary is normal. What is the most likely source?
opts: Ectopic ACTH secretion from a carcinoid tumour
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: High ACTH + suppressible on high-dose dexamethasone = pituitary Cushing disease — even with normal MRI (microadenoma often not visible)
discriminator: High ACTH + suppression on HDDST = pituitary source (Cushing disease). Ectopic ACTH does NOT suppress on HDDST. Normal MRI does not exclude microadenoma — IPSS may be needed.

stem: A 55-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with rapid-onset central obesity, proximal weakness, and severe hypertension. ACTH is 88 pmol/L (normal 1.1-11). High-dose dexamethasone shows no suppression of cortisol. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
opts: Ectopic ACTH secretion from small cell lung cancer
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Ectopic ACTH syndrome: very high ACTH + no HDDST suppression + smoking history + rapid onset
discriminator: Very high ACTH (usually >22 pmol/L) + no HDDST suppression + smoking history + rapid onset = ectopic ACTH until proven otherwise. SCLC is the most common cause.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with Cushing syndrome is found to have a high ACTH level and demonstrates suppression on high-dose dexamethasone testing. MRI shows a 6 mm pituitary adenoma. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
opts: Ketoconazole 600 mg daily with radiation therapy
Gamma knife radiosurgery to the pituitary
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Cushing disease (pituitary ACTH adenoma) — first-line treatment is transsphenoidal surgery
discriminator: Transsphenoidal resection is the gold standard first-line treatment for Cushing disease. Radiosurgery is reserved for residual/recurrent disease or surgical contraindications.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue, darkening of his skin, and dizziness on standing. He has lost 4 kg over 3 months. On examination, BP is 90/60 supine and 75/50 standing. There is hyperpigmentation of the buccal mucosa, palmar creases, and pre-existing scars. Investigations show: Na 128 mmol/L, K 5.9 mmol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Addison disease: hyperpigmentation + hyponatremia + hyperkalemia + hypotension + hypoglycemia
discriminator: Hyperpigmentation + hyponatremia + hyperkalemia + orthostatic hypotension = primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison). Hyperpigmentation differentiates primary from secondary AI (secondary has no hyperpigmentation because ACTH is low).

stem: A 38-year-old man with known Addison disease on hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone presents to the emergency department with severe vomiting, confusion, and hypotension (BP 70/40) after a 3-day history of diarrhoea. He has not been able to take his oral medications. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Increase oral hydrocortisone to 40 mg twice daily and advise rest at home
Administer IV normal saline and IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat
Administer IV dextrose 50% for hypoglycemia first
Check serum cortisol level before giving any medication
Start IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and await cultures
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Adrenal crisis: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg STAT + IV normal saline — do NOT wait for test results
discriminator: Adrenal crisis = hypotension + vomiting + inability to take oral steroids. Treatment is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg + IV NS immediately. Do NOT wait for labs or test results.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with suspected Addison disease undergoes a short Synacthen test. Baseline cortisol is 180 nmol/L. Thirty minutes after 250 mcg IV ACTH, cortisol is 320 nmol/L. What is the interpretation?
opts: Normal adrenal function — no adrenal insufficiency
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Short Synacthen test: cortisol <500 nmol/L at 30 min after ACTH stimulation = adrenal insufficiency. Low baseline + blunted response = primary (inadequate cortisol from adrenal).
discriminator: Short Synacthen = gold standard for Addison. Cortisol <500 at 30 min = adrenal insufficiency. The combination of low baseline + blunted rise is consistent with primary adrenal insufficiency (the adrenal gland itself is the problem).

stem: A 36-year-old man with new-onset hypertension (BP 165/105) is found to have hypokalemia (K 3.0 mmol/L) on routine labs. He is on no medications. He denies headaches, palpitations, or sweating. ABG shows pH 7.48, HCO3 32 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate screening test to establish the diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Conn syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism) screening: aldosterone:renin ratio in a hypertensive patient with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis
discriminator: HTN + hypokalemia + metabolic alkalosis = Conn syndrome. First screen with aldosterone:renin ratio (not just aldosterone, not CT first). High aldosterone + low renin = primary hyperaldosteronism.

stem: A 48-year-old woman with confirmed Conn syndrome has a left adrenal adenoma on CT. Her aldosterone:renin ratio is elevated and saline suppression test confirms autonomous aldosterone production. What is the most appropriate definitive management?
opts: Percutaneous radiofrequency ablation of the adenoma
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Conn syndrome with unilateral adenoma → unilateral adrenalectomy is curative
discriminator: Unilateral Conn adenoma → surgical cure with adrenalectomy. Spironolactone is for bilateral hyperplasia or non-surgical candidates.

stem: A 50-year-old man with hypertension and hypokalemia is diagnosed with Conn syndrome. CT adrenals shows bilateral nodular hyperplasia. He is not a candidate for surgery. What is the most appropriate medical therapy?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Bilateral Conn hyperplasia or non-surgical candidate → spironolactone (mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist)
discriminator: Spironolactone is the specific medical therapy for Conn syndrome — it blocks aldosterone at the mineralocorticoid receptor, correcting both HTN and hypokalemia.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 30-minute episode of severe headache, palpitations, and feeling of impending doom. BP during the episode was 220/130. She is now asymptomatic and BP is 125/80 at rest. She reports 4 similar episodes over the past 3 months, often triggered by exercise. What is the single best diagnostic test?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Pheochromocytoma diagnosis: plasma free metanephrines are the most sensitive test — not VMA
discriminator: Paroxysmal HTN + HA + palpitations + sweating = pheochromocytoma. The best test is plasma free metanephrines (sensitivity 96-100%). VMA is outdated — exam has updated this.

stem: A 40-year-old woman is diagnosed with pheochromocytoma based on elevated plasma metanephrines. CT shows a 4.5 cm right adrenal mass. She is scheduled for laparoscopic adrenalectomy next week. What is the most appropriate pre-operative medication to prevent intra-operative hypertensive crisis?
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Pheochromocytoma pre-op: labetalol (combined alpha + beta blocker) — controls BP and prevents intra-op crisis. NEVER give beta-blocker alone.
discriminator: Labetalol is the first-line pre-op medication for pheochromocytoma because it provides both alpha and beta blockade. Beta-blocker alone causes unopposed alpha agonism → hypertensive crisis.

stem: A 42-year-old woman with a history of a thyroid nodule and episodic hypertension is undergoing adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma. During surgery, manipulation of the adrenal gland causes a sudden rise in BP to 260/130. What is the most appropriate intra-operative management?
opts: Stop surgery and close the incision immediately
Administer IV phentolamine or sodium nitroprusside
Administer IV metoprolol to control heart rate
Administer IV normal saline bolus to expand volume
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Intra-operative hypertensive crisis during pheochromocytoma resection: IV phentolamine (short-acting alpha-blocker) or sodium nitroprusside
discriminator: During pheochromocytoma manipulation, catecholamine release causes severe HTN. Use IV phentolamine (alpha-blocker) or sodium nitroprusside (vasodilator) for acute BP control.

stem: A 52-year-old woman is found to have a 5 cm right adrenal mass on CT during workup for hypertension. She reports episodes of palpitations, diaphoresis, and headaches. Her BP is 150/95. Plasma metanephrines are elevated. She is started on labetalol. What additional pre-operative preparation is essential before adrenalectomy?
opts: Start a high-sodium diet to prevent post-operative hypotension
Start IV fluids for volume expansion 24 hours before surgery
Perform MIBG scan to rule out metastatic disease
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Pre-operative preparation for pheochromocytoma: volume expansion with IV fluids after alpha-blockade to prevent post-resection hypotension
discriminator: After alpha-blockade (labetalol), patients are volume-depleted due to chronic catecholamine-induced vasoconstriction. Volume expansion with IV fluids prevents severe hypotension when the tumour is removed and catecholamines drop.

stem: A patient with Cushing syndrome is found to have an ACTH level of 1.0 pmol/L (low). Which of the following is the most likely cause?
opts: Small cell lung cancer with ectopic ACTH
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Cushing syndrome ACTH logic: low/undetectable ACTH = ACTH-independent (adrenal source: adenoma or carcinoma)
discriminator: Low ACTH in Cushing = adrenal source (autonomous cortisol production suppressing pituitary ACTH). High ACTH = pituitary or ectopic. This is the fundamental ACTH logic tested repeatedly in exam.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with a history of total thyroidectomy for Graves disease 3 days ago develops carpopedal spasm and tingling in her hands and feet. Chvostek sign is positive. Serum calcium is 1.7 mmol/L (normal 2.2-2.6) and phosphate is 2.0 mmol/L (normal 0.8-1.5). What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Oral calcium carbonate 1000 mg three times daily
Intravenous calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% solution
Start activated vitamin D (calcitriol) 0.5 mcg twice daily
Reassure the patient and discharge with oral calcium
subject: Medicine-Endocrinology
concept: Acute hypocalcemia with tetany post-thyroidectomy: IV calcium gluconate is the first step for symptomatic hypocalcemia
discriminator: Symptomatic hypocalcemia (carpopedal spasm, positive Chvostek) with critically low Ca (1.7) requires IV calcium (NOT just oral). IV calcium is the acute management; oral calcium + calcitriol are for ongoing maintenance.

stem: A 70-year-old man with chronic atrial fibrillation presents with acute onset right hemiplegia and aphasia starting 2.5 hours ago. CT brain non-contrast shows no haemorrhage. He is not on anticoagulation. What is the single best next step?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Thrombolysis for acute ischaemic stroke — CT negative + <4.5h window = IV alteplase
discriminator: Acute focal deficit <4.5h with CT ruling out haemorrhage = thrombolysis candidate. Anticoagulation is not for acute management; aspirin is only given if tPA is contraindicated.

stem: A 75-year-old man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation falls at home and presents with headache and confusion. CT brain shows a crescent-shaped hyperdensity over the right cerebral convexity that crosses suture lines. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Subdural vs epidural haematoma — CT morphology
discriminator: Crescent-shaped + crosses sutures = subdural (venous). Lentiform/biconvex + does not cross sutures = epidural (arterial).

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with acute onset aphasia and right arm weakness starting 3 hours ago. CT brain is negative for haemorrhage. His blood pressure is 200/120 mmHg. Which finding is an absolute contraindication to IV alteplase in this patient?
opts: Atrial fibrillation as the embolic source
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Thrombolysis contraindications — elevated blood pressure threshold
discriminator: Sustained BP > 185/110 mmHg is an absolute contraindication to IV alteplase. BP must be lowered below this threshold before thrombolysis.

stem: Which of the following components is included in the ABCD2 score for TIA risk stratification?
opts: Age, Blood pressure, Clinical features, Duration, Diabetes
Age, Atrial fibrillation, Cholesterol, Diabetes, Disability
Age, Blood pressure, CT findings, Duration, Dyslipidaemia
Alcohol use, Body mass index, Claudication, Diabetes, Duration
Atrial fibrillation, Blood pressure, Carotid stenosis, Diabetes, Age
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: ABCD2 score components for TIA risk stratification
discriminator: ABCD2 = Age (≥60 = 1), Blood pressure (≥140/90 = 1), Clinical features (unilateral weakness = 2, speech alone = 1), Duration (≥60 min = 2, 10-59 min = 1), Diabetes (1).

stem: A 65-year-old woman weighing 70 kg is diagnosed with acute ischaemic stroke and deemed eligible for IV alteplase. What is the correct dose and administration regimen?
opts: 0.9 mg/kg IV bolus over 1 minute, max 90 mg
0.9 mg/kg, 10% as bolus, 90% as infusion over 60 minutes, max 90 mg
1.0 mg/kg, 50% bolus, 50% infusion over 30 minutes, max 100 mg
1.5 mg/kg infusion over 90 minutes, max 120 mg
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: IV alteplase dosing for acute ischaemic stroke
discriminator: tPA for stroke: 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg) with 10% bolus + 90% infusion over 60 min. The STEMI dose (1.5 mg/kg) is higher and must not be confused.

stem: A 70-year-old woman on warfarin for mechanical mitral valve presents with acute severe headache, vomiting, and decreased consciousness. CT brain shows a large left basal ganglia haemorrhage. INR is 3.8. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Stop warfarin + oral vitamin K alone
Stop warfarin + IV vitamin K + prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC)
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Anticoagulation reversal in haemorrhagic stroke — active bleeding requires rapid reversal
discriminator: Active ICH on warfarin → urgent reversal with IV vitamin K + PCC/FFP. Vitamin K alone is too slow (takes hours). For major bleeding, PCC is preferred over FFP for more rapid INR correction.

stem: A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a history of left arm weakness and slurred speech that started 30 minutes ago and completely resolved within 45 minutes. MRI brain with DWI shows no restricted diffusion. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Reassure the patient and discharge with outpatient follow-up
Aspirin 300 mg immediately + urgent TIA clinic assessment within 24 hours
CT angiogram of head and neck before any treatment
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: TIA diagnosis and management — symptoms resolved + negative DWI = TIA, not stroke
discriminator: Full neurological recovery within 24h + negative DWI = TIA. Aspirin + urgent TIA clinic < 24h is mandated. Thrombolysis is not indicated as symptoms have resolved.

stem: A 66-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes had a left hemispheric TIA (right arm weakness) one week ago. Carotid duplex ultrasound shows 80% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. What is the most appropriate management for stroke prevention?
opts: Medical management with antiplatelet and statin alone
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Carotid endarterectomy indication — symptomatic > 70% carotid stenosis
discriminator: Symptomatic carotid stenosis > 70% (by NASCET criteria) significantly benefits from CEA. The number needed to treat is low. < 50% → medical management; 50-69% → selected benefit.

stem: A 62-year-old woman describes two episodes of transient vision loss in her left eye, each lasting 5-10 minutes, described as a 'curtain coming down' over her vision. Between episodes, her vision returns to normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Amaurosis fugax — transient monocular vision loss from retinal ischaemia
discriminator: Transient monocular vision loss described as a 'curtain' or 'shade' that resolves completely within minutes = amaurosis fugax. It is the retinal equivalent of a TIA.

stem: A 78-year-old woman becomes unresponsive 3 days after undergoing a left carotid endarterectomy. What is the single most appropriate first step in management?
opts: Start IV alteplase for suspected stroke
Check GCS and perform urgent CT brain
Perform carotid Doppler ultrasound at bedside
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Post-CEA deterioration — first step is GCS assessment and CT brain
discriminator: Any neurological deterioration post-CEA requires immediate CT brain to differentiate haemorrhage from ischaemic stroke. GCS is the first clinical assessment. Do NOT assume the cause without imaging.

stem: A 68-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes developed acute left-sided weakness and slurred speech that completely resolved within 45 minutes of onset. MRI brain with DWI shows no restricted diffusion. He is now asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Aspirin 300 mg immediately and same-day TIA clinic assessment
CT angiogram of carotids before any treatment
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: TIA management — resolved deficit with negative DWI confirms TIA
discriminator: Full symptom resolution + negative DWI = TIA. The 10% stroke risk within 48h mandates immediate aspirin + same-day TIA clinic assessment. Thrombolysis is not for TIA.

stem: A 60-year-old woman reports an episode of transient vision loss in her right eye lasting 8 minutes that resolved spontaneously. She has a history of hypertension and hyperlipidaemia. Cardiovascular and neurological examinations are normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Reassure her that transient symptoms are benign
Start aspirin 300 mg and refer for urgent TIA clinic assessment
Arrange outpatient ophthalmology review in 2 weeks
Start warfarin for presumed retinal vein occlusion
Administer IV alteplase within the 4.5-hour window
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Amaurosis fugax management — treated as TIA, not a benign condition
discriminator: Amaurosis fugax = retinal TIA. It carries the same stroke risk as hemispheric TIA. Aspirin + urgent TIA clinic within 24h is the correct approach. It is NOT benign and NOT for thrombolysis.

stem: A 72-year-old woman on warfarin for atrial fibrillation presents with sudden severe headache, vomiting, and rapidly decreasing consciousness. CT brain shows a hyperdense lesion in the left basal ganglia measuring 4 cm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Acute ischaemic stroke with early oedema
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Haemorrhagic stroke presentation — sudden headache with hyperdense CT lesion
discriminator: Acute onset severe headache + vomiting + decreased consciousness + hyperdense lesion on CT in the basal ganglia (typical hypertensive location) = intracerebral haemorrhage. On warfarin increases the risk.

stem: A 75-year-old man on apixaban for atrial fibrillation presents after a fall. He has a mild headache but no focal neurological deficits. CT brain shows a thin crescent-shaped hyperdensity over the right cerebral convexity crossing suture lines. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Subdural haematoma — CT morphology and clinical context
discriminator: Crescent-shaped extra-axial collection crossing suture lines in an elderly patient on anticoagulation after a fall = acute subdural haematoma. Shape and distribution are characteristic.

stem: A 22-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after a motorcycle accident. He was initially conscious and conversant but has now become progressively drowsy. CT brain shows a lentiform (biconvex) hyperdensity in the left temporal region that does not cross suture lines. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Epidural haematoma — CT morphology and classic lucid interval
discriminator: Lentiform (biconvex) shape + does not cross sutures + temporal location + post-traumatic lucid interval = epidural haematoma from middle meningeal artery tear.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with left hemiplegia and neglect starting 2 hours ago. CT brain is negative. He has a history of gastric ulcer surgery 10 days ago. Blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg. Which finding most affects the decision to administer IV alteplase?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Thrombolysis relative contraindication — recent major surgery
discriminator: Recent major surgery (within 14 days) is a relative contraindication to tPA due to bleeding risk at the surgical site. The decision requires risk-benefit analysis but it is the most significant factor here.

stem: A 62-year-old woman was found with right-sided weakness and global aphasia. The time of symptom onset is unknown; she was last seen well 8 hours ago. CT brain is negative for haemorrhage. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: IV alteplase as per standard protocol
Aspirin 300 mg and stroke unit admission
CT perfusion to determine eligibility for extended-window thrombolysis
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Stroke beyond thrombolysis window — management without tPA
discriminator: Unknown onset > 4.5h (last seen well 8h ago) = outside standard tPA window. Aspirin 300 mg within 24-48h after excluding haemorrhage is the alternative. Extended-window tPA requires advanced imaging and is not the standard in most exam-based protocols.

stem: A 72-year-old man underwent a left carotid endarterectomy 2 days ago. He now has a decreased level of consciousness (GCS 10). What is the most appropriate next step?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Post-CEA neurological deterioration — CT brain is first investigation
discriminator: Any deterioration post-CEA requires urgent CT brain to differentiate haemorrhage from ischaemic stroke. Haemorrhage is a common early complication due to the surgical site and BP fluctuations.

stem: A 55-year-old man with no prior medical history presents with acute confusion and severe headache. His blood pressure is 240/140 mmHg. CT brain is unremarkable. Fundoscopy reveals papilloedema. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Intravenous labetalol for rapid BP reduction
Lumbar puncture to rule out subarachnoid haemorrhage
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Hypertensive encephalopathy — rapid BP control is priority
discriminator: Severe hypertension (240/140) + acute confusion + papilloedema + normal CT = hypertensive encephalopathy. Requires immediate BP reduction with IV antihypertensives, not stroke treatment.

stem: A 75-year-old woman on warfarin for atrial fibrillation presents with minor epistaxis that has stopped. Her INR is 8.1. She is haemodynamically stable with no headache or neurological symptoms. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: IV vitamin K + prothrombin complex concentrate
Continue warfarin and monitor INR in 24 hours
Stop warfarin and start heparin bridging
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Warfarin over-anticoagulation — minor bleeding with elevated INR
discriminator: Elevated INR with minor bleeding (epistaxis, haemodynamically stable): stop warfarin + oral vitamin K. FFP/PCC is reserved for major or life-threatening bleeding. The discriminator is 'minor' vs 'major' bleeding.

stem: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation on warfarin presents with acute right hemiplegia and aphasia starting 3 hours ago. CT brain is negative. His INR is 2.5. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Reverse warfarin with vitamin K and then give tPA
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Thrombolysis contraindication — INR > 1.7 on warfarin
discriminator: INR > 1.7 is an absolute contraindication to IV alteplase regardless of CT findings. The patient is within the 4.5h window but is on warfarin with INR 2.5. tPA cannot be given. Aspirin is the alternative after excluding haemorrhage.

stem: A 64-year-old man had a left hemispheric TIA (right arm weakness resolving in 1 hour) 3 weeks ago. Carotid duplex shows 60% stenosis of the left internal carotid artery. He is on aspirin, statin, and antihypertensives. What is the most appropriate management regarding the carotid stenosis?
opts: Continue optimal medical therapy; CEA may be considered but benefit is marginal
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Carotid endarterectomy decision at 50-69% stenosis — selected benefit
discriminator: The benefit of CEA for symptomatic 50-69% stenosis is modest (NNT higher) compared to > 70% stenosis. Optimal medical therapy is the baseline, and the surgeon's/centre's perioperative risk must be < 3-5% for benefit.

stem: A 66-year-old woman presents with acute right hemiplegia and global aphasia that started 1.5 hours ago. CT brain is negative. However, 20 minutes after arrival, her symptoms begin to improve rapidly — she can now move her right arm against gravity and say a few words. What is the most appropriate management regarding thrombolysis?
opts: Proceed with IV alteplase as originally planned
Withhold tPA as rapid improvement is a relative contraindication
Give half-dose tPA to be cautious
Start aspirin immediately and continue monitoring
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Thrombolysis contraindication — rapidly improving symptoms
discriminator: Rapidly improving neurological symptoms (especially if improvement is significant) is a relative contraindication to tPA. If the deficit is mild or rapidly resolving, the risk of tPA may outweigh the benefit.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with acute right hemiparesis and expressive aphasia starting 2 hours ago. CT brain is negative. His blood glucose is 2.1 mmol/L (38 mg/dL). After IV dextrose, his neurological symptoms completely resolve within 15 minutes. What is the most likely explanation?
opts: The patient had a TIA that coincidentally resolved
The patient was experiencing hypoglycaemia mimicking a stroke (hypoglycaemic hemiplegia)
The patient had a lacunar stroke that resolved spontaneously
The patient had Todd paralysis following a seizure
The patient had a migraine aura with hemiplegia
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Stroke mimic — hypoglycaemia as a contraindication to tPA
discriminator: Focal neurological deficit + hypoglycaemia (glucose < 50 mg/dL or < 3.0 mmol/L) = stroke mimic until proven otherwise. Hypoglycaemia must be corrected before considering tPA. Complete resolution with dextrose confirms the diagnosis.

stem: A 72-year-old woman with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation presents with transient right arm weakness and slurred speech that resolved in 30 minutes. MRI DWI is negative. CT brain is normal. She is haemodynamically stable. When should anticoagulation be initiated for stroke prevention?
opts: Start aspirin now; initiate anticoagulation after ruling out haemorrhagic conversion, usually within 1-2 weeks depending on stroke severity and lesion size
Start warfarin and bridge with heparin
Anticoagulation is not indicated for paroxysmal AF
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: TIA with AF — timing of anticoagulation initiation
discriminator: In TIA (DWI-negative) with AF, aspirin is started immediately for acute protection. Anticoagulation (DOAC or warfarin) is typically initiated after 1-2 weeks for TIA (later for larger strokes) to allow time to rule out haemorrhagic conversion.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents with fever, neck stiffness, and altered consciousness. Lumbar puncture is performed. CSF shows: opening pressure 30 cm H2O, turbid appearance, WBC 1200/mm³ with 90% neutrophils, glucose 25 mg/dL (serum glucose 110 mg/dL), protein 180 mg/dL. Gram stain shows Gram-positive diplococci. What is the single best description of this CSF pattern?
opts: Viral meningitis pattern — lymphocytic predominance, normal glucose
TB meningitis pattern — lymphocytic predominance, low glucose, very high protein
Bacterial meningitis pattern — neutrophil predominance, low glucose, high protein
Fungal meningitis pattern — eosinophil predominance, low glucose
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: CSF pattern recognition — bacterial meningitis
discriminator: Neutrophil predominance + low glucose (CSF:serum < 0.4) + elevated protein + turbid CSF = bacterial meningitis. Gram-positive diplococci suggest Streptococcus pneumoniae.

stem: A 16-year-old female presents with 5 days of fever, headache, photophobia, and vomiting. Neck stiffness is present. Lumbar puncture shows: opening pressure 16 cm H2O, clear fluid, WBC 80/mm³ with 85% lymphocytes, glucose 60 mg/dL (serum glucose 110 mg/dL), protein 55 mg/dL. Gram stain is negative. What is the most likely aetiology?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: CSF pattern for viral (aseptic) meningitis and common aetiologies
discriminator: Lymphocytic predominance + normal glucose + negative Gram stain = viral meningitis. Enteroviruses are the most common cause of aseptic meningitis.

stem: A 30-year-old immunocompromised man presents with subacute fever, headache, and confusion over 3 weeks. CSF shows: WBC 180/mm³ with 80% lymphocytes, glucose 30 mg/dL, protein 320 mg/dL. What CSF pattern is this?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: CSF pattern recognition — TB meningitis
discriminator: Lymphocytic predominance + low glucose + very high protein (> 300) = classic TB meningitis triad. TB has the highest protein elevation among all meningitis types.

stem: An adult patient is diagnosed with suspected community-acquired bacterial meningitis. What is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen before culture results return?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Empiric antibiotics for community-acquired bacterial meningitis in adults
discriminator: Ceftriaxone (covers Neisseria, Streptococcus, Haemophilus) + vancomycin (covers resistant S. pneumoniae) is the standard empiric regimen for adults.

stem: A 10-day-old neonate presents with fever, lethargy, poor feeding, and a bulging fontanelle. CSF analysis is concerning for meningitis. What is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Empiric antibiotics for neonatal meningitis
discriminator: Neonatal meningitis requires coverage for Group B Streptococcus (GBS) and Listeria monocytogenes. Ceftriaxone does NOT cover Listeria; ampicillin + gentamicin covers both GBS and Listeria.

stem: A 45-year-old man is diagnosed with pneumococcal meningitis. Antibiotics are about to be administered. At which point should dexamethasone be given relative to antibiotic administration?
opts: Dexamethasone should be given 24 hours after starting antibiotics
Dexamethasone should be given BEFORE or WITH the first dose of antibiotics
Dexamethasone is not indicated in pneumococcal meningitis
Dexamethasone should be given only if the patient develops septic shock
Dexamethasone should be given after CSF culture confirms the organism
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Dexamethasone timing in bacterial meningitis
discriminator: Dexamethasone must be given before or simultaneously with the first antibiotic dose to reduce neurologic sequelae (especially hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis).

stem: A 40-year-old male experiences a tonic-clonic seizure lasting 8 minutes. Five minutes after it stops, he has another generalised seizure without regaining consciousness. What is the single best next step in management?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Status epilepticus definition and first-line pharmacotherapy
discriminator: Status epilepticus = seizure > 5 min OR recurrent seizures without recovery. First-line treatment is ALWAYS a benzodiazepine (IV lorazepam/diazepam or IM midazolam).

stem: An 18-month-old child presents with a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 8 minutes during a febrile illness. There is no focal onset, no post-ictal focal deficits, and the child had one seizure in 24 hours. Temperature is 39.5°C. The child is now alert and well-appearing with no bulging fontanelle. What is the most appropriate classification of this seizure?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Simple vs complex febrile seizure classification
discriminator: Simple febrile seizure: generalised, < 15 minutes, single in 24 hours, no post-ictal focality, age 6 months–5 years. All criteria met here.

stem: A 2-year-old child with fever has a first-time generalised seizure. After the seizure, the child is drowsy and has a bulging anterior fontanelle. What is the single best next step?
opts: Administer IV phenytoin to prevent recurrence
Perform lumbar puncture to rule out meningitis
Prescribe antipyretics and observe at home
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Febrile seizure with bulging fontanelle — LP is indicated
discriminator: Febrile seizure + bulging fontanelle (sign of increased ICP / meningeal irritation) = LP to rule out meningitis is indicated, NOT CT first.

stem: A 23-year-old university student is diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis. The patient has been started on IV ceftriaxone. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for the patient's close contacts?
opts: Antibiotic prophylaxis with rifampicin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Meningococcal meningitis — contact prophylaxis
discriminator: Close contacts of meningococcal meningitis require chemoprophylaxis with rifampicin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents with acute onset of high fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, and vomiting. He is confused and irritable. LP results: opening pressure 32 cm H2O, turbid fluid, WBC 1500/mm³ (90% neutrophils), glucose 20 mg/dL, protein 210 mg/dL. Gram stain shows Gram-negative diplococci. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: CSF interpretation — Gram-negative diplococci = Neisseria meningitidis
discriminator: Bacterial meningitis pattern + Gram-negative diplococci on Gram stain = Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus), not Streptococcus pneumoniae (Gram-positive diplococci).

stem: A 20-year-old female presents with fever, headache, and behaviour change over 4 days. She has no neck stiffness. MRI brain shows T2 hyperintensity in the right temporal lobe. CSF shows: WBC 60/mm³ (lymphocytes 80%), glucose 65 mg/dL (serum 100 mg/dL), protein 48 mg/dL. What is the most likely causative organism?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: HSV encephalitis — temporal lobe involvement + CSF viral pattern
discriminator: Behavioural change + temporal lobe hyperintensity on MRI + CSF lymphocytic with normal glucose = HSV encephalitis until proven otherwise.

stem: A 35-year-old HIV-positive man (CD4 180) presents with 3 weeks of fever, headache, and progressive confusion. CSF shows: WBC 150/mm³ (lymphocytes 85%), glucose 35 mg/dL, protein 280 mg/dL. Which additional finding would most strongly support TB meningitis over cryptococcal meningitis?
opts: Very high protein > 250 mg/dL with low glucose
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Differentiating TB meningitis from cryptococcal meningitis in HIV
discriminator: Both TB and cryptococcal meningitis are lymphocytic with low glucose, but TB produces significantly higher protein (> 250–500 mg/dL) due to basal exudates. A subacute course with very high protein favours TB.

stem: A 60-year-old man with a history of alcohol use disorder is brought to the ER after a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure that lasted 7 minutes. On arrival, he is post-ictal but breathing spontaneously. IV access is secured. What should be administered first?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Status epilepticus — benzodiazepine is always first-line regardless of aetiology
discriminator: Seizure > 5 minutes = status epilepticus → IV lorazepam first, before thiamine, before phenytoin. Thiamine is given AFTER seizure termination in alcoholics to prevent Wernicke.

stem: A 22-year-old male presents with high fever, hypotension, and a non-blanching purpuric rash over his trunk and extremities. He has neck stiffness and is confused. What is the most likely diagnosis and empiric antibiotic?
opts: Meningococcal meningitis with septicaemia — IV ceftriaxone
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Meningococcal meningitis presentation — purpuric rash and empiric therapy
discriminator: Fever + neck stiffness + hypotension + non-blanching purpuric rash = meningococcal meningitis with meningococcaemia (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome risk). IV ceftriaxone is the empiric antibiotic.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents with headache, fever, and a focal seizure involving the right arm. CT head shows a ring-enhancing lesion in the left frontal lobe. Which is the most common causative organism of cerebral abscess in immunocompetent patients?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Cerebral abscess — most common organism in immunocompetent patients
discriminator: Streptococcus species (especially Streptococcus milleri group) are the most common isolates in cerebral abscess in immunocompetent patients. Toxoplasma is common in HIV, not immunocompetent.

stem: A 35-year-old HIV-positive man with CD4 count 80 cells/mm³ presents with 2 weeks of headache, confusion, and right-sided weakness. MRI brain shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding oedema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Cerebral toxoplasmosis in HIV — multiple ring-enhancing lesions with low CD4
discriminator: HIV + CD4 < 100 + multiple ring-enhancing lesions = cerebral toxoplasmosis until proven otherwise. Single lesion may be lymphoma, but multiple favours toxoplasma.

stem: A 55-year-old man in status epilepticus received IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg 10 minutes ago but the seizure is continuing. What is the next appropriate step?
opts: Proceed directly to anaesthetic agents and ICU
Perform EEG before any further medication
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Status epilepticus — second-line therapy after benzodiazepine failure
discriminator: After first-line benzodiazepine, if seizure continues at 10 minutes, second-line is an antiseizure drug (fosphenytoin/phenytoin or levetiracetam). Anaesthetic agents are third-line at 20–30 minutes.

stem: A 72-year-old man with diabetes and chronic kidney disease presents with suspected bacterial meningitis. Which of the following additions to standard empiric therapy is most appropriate?
opts: Add IV ampicillin for Listeria coverage
Add IV metronidazole for anaerobic coverage
Add IV fluconazole for fungal coverage
No addition — standard ceftriaxone + vancomycin is sufficient
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Empiric antibiotics in elderly/immunocompromised — add ampicillin for Listeria
discriminator: Age > 50 or immunocompromised → add ampicillin to ceftriaxone + vancomycin to cover Listeria monocytogenes, which is not covered by cephalosporins.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with fever and headache is examined. With the patient supine, the examiner flexes the patient's neck. This causes involuntary flexion of both hips and knees. What is this sign called and what does it indicate?
opts: Babinski sign — indicates upper motor neuron lesion
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Meningeal signs — Brudzinski neck sign
discriminator: Neck flexion causing reflexive hip/knee flexion = Brudzinski sign (meningeal irritation). Knee extension with hip flexed causing pain = Kernig sign.

stem: A 5-year-old child presents with fever and a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 12 minutes. The seizure has stopped, the child is drowsy. On examination, there is marked neck stiffness and Kernig sign is positive. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Start anticonvulsant therapy to prevent recurrence
Perform lumbar puncture to rule out meningitis
Prescribe antipyretics and observe for 24 hours
Start IV antibiotics immediately without LP
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Febrile seizure with meningeal signs — LP is the investigation of choice
discriminator: This is NOT a simple febrile seizure (duration > 10 min makes it complex) AND the child now has meningeal signs (neck stiffness, Kernig). LP to rule out meningitis is required. CT is not indicated before LP unless focal deficits or papilloedema.

stem: A 3-year-old child with fever has a generalised seizure that lasts 20 minutes. What feature classifies this as a complex febrile seizure?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Complex febrile seizure criteria — duration > 15 minutes
discriminator: A seizure lasting > 15 minutes is the duration criterion that classifies it as complex. Other complex features: focal onset, multiple in 24 hours, or post-ictal focal deficits.

stem: A 45-year-old immunocompetent man presents with headache, fever, and a right-sided focal seizure. CT head shows a ring-enhancing lesion in the left parietal lobe. Craniotomy and aspiration are performed, and culture grows Streptococcus intermedius. What is the most likely source of this infection?
opts: Contiguous spread from dental infection or sinusitis
Primary pulmonary infection with haematogenous seeding
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Cerebral abscess — pathogenesis and source of Streptococcus milleri group
discriminator: Streptococcus intermedius (S. milleri group) is part of the oral flora. Cerebral abscess from these organisms most commonly arises from contiguous spread: dental infections, sinusitis, or otitis media.

stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with 10 days of fever, headache, and progressive lethargy. CSF shows: WBC 200/mm³ (80% lymphocytes), glucose 30 mg/dL, protein 350 mg/dL. She has no rash. HIV test is negative. CT chest shows apical cavitary lesions. What is the single best next step to confirm the aetiology?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: TB meningitis diagnosis — GeneXpert on CSF when suspected clinically
discriminator: Subacute meningitis + lymphocytic CSF + low glucose + very high protein + apical lung cavitations = TB meningitis. GeneXpert (nucleic acid amplification) on CSF is the best confirmatory test. ZN stain has low sensitivity.

stem: A 65-year-old man with a history of a recent stroke is brought to the ER after a generalised seizure that lasted 6 minutes. On arrival, the seizure has stopped but the patient remains unresponsive. Vital signs are stable. What should be done next?
opts: Start EEG monitoring to rule out non-convulsive status epilepticus
Observe for 30 minutes; if no further seizure, no action needed
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Non-convulsive status epilepticus — EEG indicated when consciousness does not return after seizure
discriminator: After a generalised seizure terminates, failure to regain consciousness raises concern for non-convulsive status epilepticus. EEG is required to diagnose and guide management.

stem: A 55-year-old male presents with resting pill-rolling tremor, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, and masked facies. Which neurotransmitter is deficient in the basal ganglia in this condition?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Parkinson disease — dopamine deficiency in nigrostriatal pathway
discriminator: Substantia nigra pars compacta dopaminergic neurons degenerate → reduced dopamine in striatum. Serotonin, ACh, NE, and GABA are not the primary deficient neurotransmitter in PD.

stem: A 65-year-old female has difficulty initiating movement, frequent falls, a shuffling gait, and cogwheel rigidity. What is the single best first-line pharmacotherapy for her motor symptoms?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Parkinson disease — first-line pharmacotherapy: carbidopa-levodopa
discriminator: Carbidopa-levodopa is the most effective symptomatic therapy for motor symptoms in PD. Dopamine agonists and MAO-B inhibitors are alternatives for mild disease or adjuncts.

stem: A 70-year-old man presents with a 1-year history of right hand tremor that occurs when his hand is resting on the armchair. He also notes slowness of movement and stiffness. On examination, you find cogwheel rigidity and a shuffling gait. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Parkinson disease — classic clinical syndrome recognition
discriminator: Resting tremor + cogwheel rigidity + bradykinesia + postural instability = classic PD triad. Essential tremor is action/postural only, no rigidity or bradykinesia.

stem: A 60-year-old woman has a bilateral hand tremor that worsens when she holds a cup of tea. She has no tremor at rest. Neurologic examination is otherwise normal with no rigidity or bradykinesia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Essential tremor vs Parkinson disease tremor — key discriminator: action vs resting
discriminator: Action/postural tremor (worsens with use) with no rigidity, bradykinesia, or resting component = essential tremor. PD tremor is resting (pill-rolling) and improves with action.

stem: A 68-year-old man with Parkinson disease on carbidopa-levodopa for 5 years now experiences shortening of benefit from each dose, with return of tremor and rigidity 3 hours after each dose. What is the best next step in management?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Parkinson disease — end-of-dose wearing off: add COMT inhibitor
discriminator: End-of-dose wearing off (predictable return of symptoms before next dose) in PD responds to COMT inhibitors (entacapone), which prolong levodopa half-life by inhibiting peripheral metabolism.

stem: A 30-year-old female presents with binocular diplopia that worsens toward the end of the day and intermittent ptosis. Edrophonium test is positive. Which autoantibody is most likely to be found in this patient?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Myasthenia gravis — anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies
discriminator: Anti-AChR antibodies are found in 80-90% of MG patients. The classic presentation (ocular symptoms, fatigable weakness, positive edrophonium test) is diagnostic of MG.

stem: A 35-year-old woman is diagnosed with myasthenia gravis based on fatigable ptosis, diplopia, and a positive edrophonium test. CT chest reveals no thymoma. What is the single best first-line symptomatic treatment?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Myasthenia gravis — first-line symptomatic therapy: pyridostigmine
discriminator: Pyridostigmine (oral anticholinesterase) is the first-line symptomatic therapy for MG. Steroids can worsen weakness initially and are reserved as immunosuppressive adjuncts.

stem: A 28-year-old female presents with drooping of the left eyelid and double vision that is most noticeable at the end of the workday. She has difficulty climbing stairs by evening. Neurologic exam shows ptosis that worsens with sustained upward gaze and proximal limb weakness that fatigues with repetition. Reflexes and sensation are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Myasthenia gravis — clinical recognition: fatigable weakness with ocular onset
discriminator: Fatigable weakness (worse at end of day, worsens with use) + ocular onset (ptosis, diplopia) + normal reflexes + no sensory loss = MG. The key is fatigue with sustained activity.

stem: A 60-year-old man with myasthenia gravis on pyridostigmine reports that after his dose was increased, he developed severe generalized weakness, difficulty swallowing, excessive salivation, and diarrhea. How should his crisis type be confirmed?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: MG crisis vs cholinergic crisis — edrophonium test discrimination
discriminator: Edrophonium (short-acting anticholinesterase) distinguishes the two: improvement = myasthenic crisis (under-treated), worsening = cholinergic crisis (over-treated). Muscarinic side effects (salivation, diarrhea) suggest cholinergic excess.

stem: A 55-year-old woman with known myasthenia gravis on pyridostigmine presents with acute worsening of weakness, dysphagia, and respiratory distress. She took her pyridostigmine this morning but cannot recall if she took extra doses. Edrophonium is administered and her weakness significantly worsens. What is the next best step in management?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Cholinergic crisis — management: stop pyridostigmine, give atropine
discriminator: Edrophonium caused worsening = cholinergic crisis (excess ACh from too much pyridostigmine). Management: stop pyridostigmine, give atropine for muscarinic symptoms, and provide respiratory support.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with ascending weakness and areflexia. Lumbar puncture is performed. Which CSF finding is most characteristic of her condition?
opts: High WBC count with normal protein
High protein with normal WBC count
Low glucose with high WBC count
High protein with high WBC count
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Guillain-Barre syndrome — albuminocytologic dissociation
discriminator: Albuminocytologic dissociation (elevated CSF protein with normal WBC count) is the classic CSF finding in GBS. It distinguishes GBS from infectious causes (which would have pleocytosis).

stem: A 25-year-old female presents with weakness starting in her feet and ascending to her thighs over 5 days. Two weeks ago she had a diarrhoeal illness after eating at a restaurant. On examination, she has symmetric proximal and distal weakness with absent deep tendon reflexes. Sensation is mildly reduced in a glove-and-stocking distribution. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Guillain-Barre syndrome — clinical recognition: ascending paralysis, areflexia, post-infectious
discriminator: Ascending symmetric paralysis + areflexia + post-diarrhoeal (Campylobacter) + mild sensory symptoms = GBS. The ascending pattern and areflexia are the key discriminators.

stem: A 30-year-old male is diagnosed with Guillain-Barre syndrome with rapidly ascending weakness over 3 days. He has no contraindications to therapy. What is the most appropriate treatment?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Guillain-Barre syndrome — disease-modifying therapy: IVIG or plasma exchange
discriminator: IVIG and plasma exchange are equally effective for GBS and are the two proven disease-modifying therapies. Corticosteroids are NOT beneficial and may worsen outcomes.

stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with proximal leg weakness that improves after climbing a few flights of stairs. She also reports dry mouth. Examination reveals decreased reflexes that improve after repeated muscle contraction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome — improves with exercise (post-tetanic potentiation)
discriminator: LEMS is characterized by weakness that IMPROVES with exercise (post-tetanic potentiation), decreased reflexes that potentiate after contraction, and autonomic symptoms (dry mouth). This is the opposite of MG (worsens with use).

stem: A 35-year-old male with Guillain-Barre syndrome has ascending weakness that reached his arms by day 4. His forced vital capacity (FVC) is 18 mL/kg and declining. He has mild dysautonomia with labile blood pressure. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Transfer to ICU for monitoring and possible ventilation
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: GBS — respiratory monitoring and ICU transfer criteria
discriminator: FVC < 20 mL/kg, rapid decline, bulbar weakness, and autonomic instability are indications for ICU admission in GBS. FVC of 18 mL/kg with declining trend and dysautonomia requires ICU-level care.

stem: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is associated with autoantibodies against which target?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome — anti-VGCC antibodies
discriminator: LEMS is caused by anti-VGCC antibodies that target presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels at the NMJ, reducing ACh release. This is distinct from MG (anti-AChR, postsynaptic).

stem: A 40-year-old male presents with acute onset of double vision, difficulty walking, and loss of coordination over 2 days. Examination reveals bilateral ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and absent deep tendon reflexes. Which autoantibody is most likely associated with this condition?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Miller-Fisher syndrome — anti-GQ1b antibodies
discriminator: Ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + areflexia = Miller-Fisher syndrome, a GBS variant. Anti-GQ1b antibodies are present in > 90% of cases and are diagnostic.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis is found to have a thymoma on CT chest. She is well-controlled on pyridostigmine. What additional intervention is indicated?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Myasthenia gravis — thymoma management: thymectomy
discriminator: Thymoma in MG is an indication for thymectomy regardless of symptom severity. Thymectomy improves outcomes and may lead to remission. Thymoma also requires removal for oncologic reasons.

stem: A 72-year-old man on haloperidol for schizophrenia develops rigidity, resting tremor, bradykinesia, and a shuffling gait over several weeks. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Drug-induced parkinsonism — antipsychotic dopamine receptor blockade
discriminator: Antipsychotics (haloperidol) block dopamine D2 receptors and can cause reversible parkinsonism. Key clue: timing correlates with antipsychotic use, and the symptoms are identical to PD.

stem: A 65-year-old woman with no prior neurologic history develops progressive rigidity and slowness over 2 months. She was started on metoclopramide for gastroparesis 3 months ago. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Order DaTscan to confirm Parkinson disease
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Drug-induced parkinsonism — management: stop offending drug
discriminator: Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist that can cause drug-induced parkinsonism. Management is discontinuation of the offending agent. Symptoms typically resolve over weeks to months.

stem: Which of the following statements about corticosteroid use in Guillain-Barre syndrome is correct?
opts: Oral prednisolone is effective as monotherapy
Steroids combined with IVIG provide superior outcomes
Corticosteroids do NOT improve GBS outcomes and may worsen them
Steroids are indicated only for Miller-Fisher variant
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Guillain-Barre syndrome — corticosteroids are not beneficial
discriminator: Multiple trials have shown corticosteroids (oral or IV) do NOT improve GBS outcomes and may delay recovery. This is a well-known exam trap.

stem: A 45-year-old smoker presents with proximal muscle weakness that improves with repeated muscle contraction. He has a 30-pack-year smoking history. Examination shows decreased reflexes with post-tetanic potentiation. What underlying condition must be excluded?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome — SCLC association
discriminator: LEMS is a paraneoplastic syndrome most commonly associated with small cell lung cancer (50-60% of cases). The anti-VGCC antibodies cross-react with calcium channels expressed on SCLC cells.

stem: What is the primary mechanism of action of carbidopa when used in combination with levodopa for Parkinson disease?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Carbidopa — peripheral DOPA decarboxylase inhibitor
discriminator: Carbidopa inhibits peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine by blocking DOPA decarboxylase. This prevents nausea and increases levodopa availability to cross the blood-brain barrier.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with Guillain-Barre syndrome has ascending weakness to the upper thighs. She has no bulbar symptoms. Her FVC is 28 mL/kg and heart rate is 110/min with intermittent hypertension. What is the most appropriate monitoring plan?
opts: Admit to ward with serial FVC and cardiac monitoring
Start IV methylprednisolone to prevent progression
No monitoring needed since FVC is > 20 mL/kg
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: GBS — monitoring: serial FVC and cardiac monitoring for dysautonomia
discriminator: FVC > 20 mL/kg but tachycardia and labile BP (dysautonomia) warrant inpatient monitoring. Autonomic instability can cause arrhythmias and requires cardiac monitoring. FVC should be tracked serially.

stem: A 35-year-old female presents with double vision, difficulty swallowing, and drooping eyelids that started 2 days ago. Over the next 24 hours, weakness progresses to involve her arms and then her legs. Examination shows dilated pupils and absent bowel sounds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Neurology
concept: Botulism — descending paralysis with autonomic features (dilated pupils, ileus)
discriminator: Descending paralysis (cranial nerves → arms → legs) + pupillary dilatation + ileus = botulism. This is the opposite of GBS (ascending). Autonomic features (dilated pupils, ileus) and lack of fatigability distinguish from MG.

stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with bilateral hand pain and stiffness for 8 weeks. The stiffness lasts over 1 hour each morning and improves with activity. On examination, there is tender swelling of the MCP and PIP joints of both hands, with mild wrist swelling. X-rays show periarticular osteopenia without erosions. Which laboratory finding is most specific for confirming the diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: Anti-CCP is the most specific serologic marker for RA, more specific than RF which can be positive in many other conditions
discriminator: Anti-CCP specificity for RA over RF, ANA, and acute-phase reactants

stem: A 40-year-old woman with recently diagnosed rheumatoid arthritis has symmetric synovitis of MCP and PIP joints with elevated RF and anti-CCP. She has no comorbidities. What is the first-line disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) she should be started on?
opts: Methotrexate weekly with folic acid supplementation
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: Methotrexate is the first-line DMARD for RA, given weekly with folic acid to reduce toxicity
discriminator: MTX as first-line before biologics or other DMARDs in treatment-naive RA

stem: A 55-year-old man with a 10-year history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with splenomegaly and recurrent infections. Complete blood count shows neutropenia (ANC 800/mm³). What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: Felty syndrome is the triad of RA, splenomegaly, and neutropenia
discriminator: RA history + splenomegaly + neutropenia = Felty syndrome

stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with gradually worsening knee pain that is worse with walking and climbing stairs and improves with rest. Morning stiffness lasts less than 15 minutes. On examination, there is crepitus on knee movement and bony enlargement of the DIP joints. X-ray of the knee shows joint space narrowing, osteophytes, and subchondral sclerosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: Osteoarthritis is degenerative arthritis with use-related pain, brief morning stiffness, Heberden nodes, and x-ray findings of osteophytes and joint space narrowing
discriminator: Pain worse with activity, brief morning stiffness, DIP bony enlargement (Heberden nodes), and osteophytes on x-ray

stem: A 60-year-old woman has bilateral hand pain. Examination reveals bony swellings at the DIP joints (Heberden nodes) and PIP joints (Bouchard nodes), and squaring of the thumb base. Which of the following differentiates this condition from rheumatoid arthritis?
opts: Presence of morning stiffness lasting 45 minutes
Involvement of the first carpometacarpal joint with absence of MCP synovitis
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: OA involves DIP, PIP, and CMC thumb while sparing MCPs; RA involves MCP and PIP while sparing DIP
discriminator: First CMC (thumb base) involvement and DIP involvement are OA patterns; RA never involves DIP

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with a facial rash that appeared after sun exposure. On examination, there is an erythematous rash over the cheeks and nasal bridge that spares the nasolabial folds. She also reports pain and swelling in both wrists and knees. Which laboratory test is most appropriate as the initial screening test?
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: ANA is the screening test for SLE with >95% sensitivity; anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are confirmatory tests
discriminator: Malar rash sparing nasolabial folds is classic for SLE; ANA is the initial screening test due to high sensitivity

stem: A 32-year-old woman with known SLE presents with periorbital edema and frothy urine. Urinalysis shows proteinuria (3.8 g/24h) and red cell casts. Serum creatinine is 1.8 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for her class III/IV lupus nephritis?
opts: Mycophenolate mofetil or cyclophosphamide with corticosteroids
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: Proliferative lupus nephritis (class III/IV) requires immunosuppression with MMF or cyclophosphamide plus steroids
discriminator: Proteinuria >3 g/24h + red cell casts with known SLE = proliferative lupus nephritis requiring aggressive immunosuppression

stem: A 45-year-old man on hydralazine for hypertension develops arthritis, fever, and a malar rash. Laboratory tests show positive ANA and positive anti-histone antibodies. Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are negative. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: Drug-induced SLE is associated with anti-histone antibodies and resolves upon stopping the offending drug
discriminator: Hydralazine use + anti-histone positivity + negative anti-dsDNA/anti-Smith = drug-induced SLE

stem: A 50-year-old man awakens at night with severe pain in his left big toe. The joint is red, swollen, hot, and exquisitely tender. He reports eating lamb and drinking beer at a dinner party earlier that evening. His temperature is 38.2°C. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: Acute gout is treated with NSAIDs or colchicine; allopurinol is never started during an acute flare
discriminator: Podagra (first MTP) after dietary triggers in a middle-aged man = acute gout; treat with anti-inflammatory, never start urate-lowering during flare

stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with acute onset of a red, swollen, and painful right knee. She has a history of knee discomfort but no prior similar episodes. Joint aspiration yields cloudy fluid. Polarized light microscopy shows positively birefringent rhomboid crystals. X-ray of the knee shows linear calcification in the meniscus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: Pseudogout is caused by CPPD crystals (positively birefringent rhomboids) with chondrocalcinosis on x-ray, typically involving the knee
discriminator: Positively birefringent rhomboid crystals = CPPD (pseudogout); negatively birefringent needle-shaped = MSU (gout); chondrocalcinosis = pseudogout

stem: A 58-year-old woman with hypertension and chronic kidney disease stage 3 presents with acute pain, redness, and swelling of her right first metatarsophalangeal joint. Serum uric acid is 9.2 mg/dL. Joint aspiration reveals negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals. She is not on any urate-lowering therapy. After the acute flare resolves, what is the most appropriate urate-lowering strategy?
opts: Start allopurinol 100 mg daily with colchicine prophylaxis for 3-6 months
Start febuxostat 80 mg daily without prophylaxis
