Prescribe dietary modification alone without medication
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: Allopurinol is started at low dose (100 mg) after flare resolution and titrated up, with colchicine/NSAID prophylaxis for 3-6 months to prevent flares during initiation
discriminator: Start allopurinol at 100 mg after flare resolves, with prophylaxis during the first 3-6 months of therapy

stem: A 72-year-old man presents with acute swelling of the left knee. He has had similar episodes affecting the knee and wrist over the past 3 years. Joint aspiration shows positively birefringent rhomboid crystals. X-ray reveals chondrocalcinosis. The acute inflammation responds poorly to colchicine. Which of the following best characterizes this condition?
opts: Monosodium urate crystal deposition with negatively birefringent needles
Hydroxyapatite crystal deposition with non-birefringent clumps
Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition with positively birefringent rhomboids
Calcium oxalate crystal deposition with bipyramidal crystals
Cholesterol crystal deposition with platelike clefts
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: CPPD crystals are positively birefringent rhomboids; pseudogout involves knees, wrists, shoulders; responds poorly to colchicine
discriminator: Positive birefringence + rhomboid shape + knee involvement + poor colchicine response = CPPD pseudogout

stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with asymmetric oligoarthritis affecting her left knee and right DIP joints. She has nail pitting on examination and a scaly rash on her elbows and scalp. Rheumatoid factor is negative. X-rays show erosive changes at the DIP joints with a pencil-in-cup deformity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: Psoriatic arthritis presents with asymmetric oligoarthritis, DIP involvement, nail pitting, dactylitis, and negative RF
discriminator: DIP involvement + nail pitting + psoriasis skin lesions + RF negative + pencil-in-cup deformity = psoriatic arthritis

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with acute monoarthritis of his right knee. He has had two similar episodes in the past year. He also reports recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and painful red nodules on his shins. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: Behcet disease presents with recurrent oral and genital ulcers, uveitis, arthritis, and erythema nodosum
discriminator: Recurrent oral ulcers + genital ulcers + erythema nodosum + arthritis = Behcet disease (pathergy test positive)

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of severe headache, scalp tenderness, and jaw pain when chewing. Her temperature is 37.8°C. Laboratory studies show ESR 118 mm/h and CRP 65 mg/L. She has no history of headache. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Schedule temporal artery biopsy, then start treatment based on results
Start high-dose prednisolone immediately and perform temporal artery biopsy within 2 weeks
Start methotrexate and monitor symptoms for 4 weeks
Order MRI brain and CT angiography of the head
Administer sumatriptan for migraine and follow up in 2 weeks
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: GCA is a medical emergency requiring immediate high-dose steroids to prevent blindness; biopsy can still be diagnostic up to 2 weeks after starting steroids
discriminator: Age >50 + new headache + jaw claudication + ESR >100 = GCA requiring immediate steroids before biopsy

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with fever, weight loss, and palpable purpura on both lower extremities. He also has mononeuritis multiplex with wrist drop and foot drop. Laboratory studies show positive c-ANCA with anti-PR3 antibodies. Urinalysis shows red cell casts and proteinuria. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: c-ANCA (PR3) is highly specific for GPA (Wegener granulomatosis), which presents with necrotizing vasculitis of respiratory tract and kidney
discriminator: c-ANCA/PR3 positivity = GPA; p-ANCA/MPO = microscopic polyangiitis or EGPA

stem: A 48-year-old man presents with sinusitis, cough with hemoptysis, and progressive dyspnea over 2 months. CT chest shows cavitating pulmonary nodules. Urinalysis shows red cell casts and proteinuria. His c-ANCA titer is strongly positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for induction of remission?
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: ANCA-associated vasculitis with life-threatening organ involvement (renal, pulmonary) requires cyclophosphamide + steroids for induction
discriminator: c-ANCA + cavitating nodules + GN = severe GPA requiring cyclophosphamide + steroids for induction

stem: A 55-year-old woman with long-standing seropositive rheumatoid arthritis presents with progressive dyspnea on exertion and a nonproductive cough. HRCT chest shows usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) pattern with honeycombing. Pulmonary function tests show restrictive pattern with reduced DLCO. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: RA-associated ILD (especially UIP pattern) is a common extra-articular manifestation of RA, occurring in long-standing seropositive disease
discriminator: Long-standing RA + restrictive pattern + honeycombing on HRCT = RA-ILD, not MTX pneumonitis (which is acute/subacute)

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with Raynaud phenomenon, difficulty swallowing, and thickening of the skin on her fingers and face. Laboratory studies show positive ANA. Which autoantibody is most specifically associated with the diffuse cutaneous form of her condition?
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: Anti-Scl-70 is specific for diffuse systemic sclerosis; anti-centromere is associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST)
discriminator: Diffuse skin thickening + Raynaud + dysphagia = diffuse systemic sclerosis → anti-Scl-70; limited/CREST → anti-centromere

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with acute-onset fever, malar rash, and pain in multiple small joints. Laboratory results show positive ANA (titer 1:640), positive anti-dsDNA, low C3 and C4 complement levels, and proteinuria (1.5 g/24h). Which of the following best explains the low complement levels in this patient?
opts: Hepatic dysfunction causing decreased complement production
Complement consumption due to immune complex formation in active SLE
Congenital complement deficiency causing predisposition to SLE
Protein-losing nephropathy causing urinary complement loss
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: Low C3/C4 in active SLE reflects complement consumption by immune complexes deposited in tissues (type III hypersensitivity)
discriminator: Low C3 and C4 with active SLE (positive anti-dsDNA, proteinuria) = complement consumption from immune complex deposition

stem: A 65-year-old man with a 15-year history of seropositive RA develops splenomegaly and recurrent bacterial infections. Labs show WBC 2,800/mm³ with ANC 600/mm³. Bone marrow biopsy shows myeloid hyperplasia. Which complication of RA is most likely responsible?
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: Felty syndrome (RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia) occurs in long-standing seropositive RA; bone marrow shows myeloid hyperplasia (maturation arrest)
discriminator: Long-standing RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia + myeloid hyperplasia on marrow = Felty syndrome

stem: A 40-year-old woman with SLE is being managed on hydroxychloroquine and low-dose prednisolone. She develops new-onset generalized tonic-clonic seizures. MRI brain shows multiple white matter hyperintensities. CSF analysis is normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her seizures?
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: CNS involvement in SLE (neuropsychiatric SLE) can present with seizures, psychosis, and white matter lesions; anti-ribosomal P antibodies are associated
discriminator: Known SLE + new seizures + white matter lesions + normal CSF = CNS lupus until proven otherwise

stem: A 52-year-old woman presents with acute-onset severe pain, redness, and swelling of her left knee. She has had similar episodes affecting the same knee over the past 2 years. She also has hypertension and osteoarthritis. Joint aspiration yields cloudy fluid. Polarized light microscopy shows no crystals. Gram stain is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
opts: Start allopurinol empirically for presumed gout
Administer intravenous vancomycin for presumed septic arthritis
Perform crystal analysis with compensated polarized light microscopy on the same sample
Reassure the patient and prescribe acetaminophen
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: If initial polarized light microscopy shows no crystals, use compensated polarized light to improve sensitivity for crystal detection before starting treatment
discriminator: Negative initial crystal analysis does not rule out crystal arthropathy — compensated polarized light or re-aspiration is needed

stem: A 58-year-old woman presents with dry eyes, dry mouth, and difficulty swallowing solid foods for 6 months. She also reports intermittent joint pain. On examination, there is bilateral parotid gland enlargement. Laboratory tests show positive ANA and positive anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: Primary Sjogren syndrome presents with sicca symptoms (dry eyes/mouth), parotid enlargement, and anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies
discriminator: Sicca symptoms + parotid enlargement + anti-Ro/anti-La = primary Sjogren syndrome

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with tender red nodules on her shins, bilateral ankle arthritis, and hilar lymphadenopathy on chest x-ray. She is otherwise healthy with no significant medical history. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Rheumatology
concept: Lofgren syndrome (erythema nodosum + bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy + arthritis) is a classic presentation of acute sarcoidosis
discriminator: Erythema nodosum + bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy + arthritis = Lofgren syndrome (acute sarcoidosis)

stem: A 35-year-old man from Swat valley presents with 3 days of high fever, rigors, confusion, and oliguria. BP 90/60, HR 110, temperature 40.2°C. Blood film shows ring forms and banana-shaped gametocytes with 12% parasitemia. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: Severe falciparum malaria first-line treatment — IV artesunate
discriminator: Severe falciparum (confusion, organ dysfunction, > 5% parasitemia) requires IV artesunate, not oral therapy or quinine

stem: A 30-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV has a CD4 count of 180 cells/µL and no active infections. At what CD4 threshold should TMP-SMX prophylaxis for PCP be initiated?
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: CD4 threshold for PCP prophylaxis initiation
discriminator: PCP prophylaxis starts at CD4 < 200 — this is the most common and important OI prophylaxis in HIV

stem: A 28-year-old HIV-positive man with CD4 120 presents with subacute dry cough, fever, and hypoxia. CXR shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. LDH is elevated. TMP-SMX is started. When should adjunctive corticosteroids be added?
opts: If PaO2 < 70 mmHg on room air
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: Indication for adjunctive steroids in PCP pneumonia
discriminator: Steroids in PCP are added only when there is moderate-to-severe hypoxia (PaO2 < 70 mmHg or A-a gradient > 35)

stem: A 35-year-old HIV-positive man with CD4 65 presents with 2 weeks of worsening headache, fever, and photophobia. CSF analysis shows elevated opening pressure, low glucose, and India ink stain reveals encapsulated yeast. What is the gold standard diagnostic test for this condition?
opts: CSF India ink preparation or cryptococcal antigen
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: Diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis — India ink and cryptococcal antigen
discriminator: Cryptococcus neoformans is an encapsulated yeast identified by India ink stain or cryptococcal antigen testing in CSF

stem: A 22-year-old woman with dengue fever is on day 5 of illness. Her fever has resolved and she feels better, but her nurse notes that she is now restless with cold extremities, delayed capillary refill, and a rapid thready pulse. At what phase of dengue does shock typically occur?
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: Timing of dengue shock syndrome — defervescence phase
discriminator: Dengue shock syndrome occurs during the defervescence (critical) phase when fever is resolving, not during the febrile phase

stem: A 25-year-old student presents with 5 days of step-ladder fever, dull headache, abdominal discomfort, and relative bradycardia. He recently returned from a trip to Punjab. What is the gold standard diagnostic test in the first week of illness?
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: Typhoid diagnosis — blood culture is gold standard in first week
discriminator: Blood culture has highest sensitivity in week 1; stool culture becomes positive in weeks 2–3

stem: A 32-year-old HIV-positive man with a CD4 count of 55 is diagnosed with cryptococcal meningitis and started on amphotericin B plus flucytosine. When should antiretroviral therapy (ART) be initiated?
opts: After completing the full course of antifungal therapy
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: ART timing in cryptococcal meningitis — delay 4–6 weeks to prevent IRIS
discriminator: Cryptococcal meningitis requires a longer ART delay (4–6 weeks) compared to other OIs (2 weeks) due to high IRIS mortality risk

stem: A 70-year-old man with diabetes presents with suspected sepsis. Which of the following is a component of the qSOFA (quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) score?
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: qSOFA criteria — altered mentation, RR ≥ 22, SBP ≤ 100
discriminator: qSOFA uses only three bedside criteria: altered mentation, RR ≥ 22, SBP ≤ 100 — no labs required

stem: A 24-year-old man with P. vivax malaria is started on chloroquine. After completing chloroquine, what additional treatment is required to prevent relapse, and what test must be done before giving it?
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: Vivax malaria — primaquine for hypnozoite eradication after G6PD screening
discriminator: P. vivax has hypnozoite stage in liver requiring primaquine, but G6PD deficiency causes hemolytic anemia with primaquine

stem: An HIV-positive man with CD4 count of 35 presents with fever, night sweats, weight loss, and chronic diarrhea. Investigations show elevated alkaline phosphatase. Which opportunistic infection is most likely?
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: MAC infection at CD4 < 50 — fever, wasting, diarrhea, elevated ALP
discriminator: MAC presents with disseminated infection: fever, weight loss, diarrhea, and elevated ALP (hepatic involvement) at CD4 < 50

stem: A blood film from a febrile patient returning from an endemic area shows ring forms within red blood cells and crescent-shaped gametocytes. Some parasitized RBCs appear normal in size. What is the most likely species?
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: Falciparum malaria — banana (crescent-shaped) gametocytes on blood film
discriminator: Banana-shaped gametocytes are pathognomonic for P. falciparum; infected RBCs are normal-sized (not enlarged)

stem: A 20-year-old woman with dengue fever has a platelet count of 28,000/µL but no active bleeding, normal vital signs, and stable hematocrit. The on-call intern recommends platelet transfusion. What is the correct management?
opts: Transfuse platelets only if count drops below 20,000
Do not transfuse platelets; monitor clinically and give IV fluids if HCT rises
Give IV methylprednisolone to raise platelet count
Start oral tranexamic acid for prophylaxis
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: Dengue — platelet transfusion is NOT indicated for isolated thrombocytopenia without bleeding
discriminator: Platelet transfusion in dengue is reserved for active bleeding with hemodynamic instability, not for lab values alone

stem: A 30-year-old man from Karachi presents with 10 days of fever, abdominal pain, and constipation. Blood culture grows Salmonella typhi resistant to ciprofloxacin and amoxicillin. What is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic while awaiting sensitivity results?
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: XDR typhoid treatment — ceftriaxone or azithromycin as first-line
discriminator: In Pakistan, XDR typhoid (resistant to fluoroquinolones, amoxicillin, and older cephalosporins) is common; ceftriaxone and azithromycin remain effective

stem: A 35-year-old HIV-positive man with CD4 110 presents with 3 weeks of fever, dry cough, and progressive dyspnea. CXR shows bilateral perihilar interstitial infiltrates. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: PCP in HIV — subacute presentation, interstitial pattern on CXR, CD4 < 200
discriminator: PCP presents subacutely (weeks) with dry cough, hypoxia, bilateral interstitial/perihilar infiltrates at CD4 < 200

stem: A 28-year-old woman from rural Sindh presents with fever, headache, and confusion. She is unconscious with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 9. Her neck is supple. Blood film shows P. falciparum with 8% parasitemia. What complication of falciparum malaria is most likely causing her altered mental status?
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: Cerebral malaria — altered consciousness with P. falciparum, no other obvious cause
discriminator: Cerebral malaria is diagnosed when altered consciousness occurs with P. falciparum infection and no other cause is found; neck is supple (not meningitis)

stem: An HIV-positive patient with CD4 40 presents with 4 weeks of fever, night sweats, and 8 kg weight loss. He has chronic watery diarrhea and abdominal pain. Labs show elevated alkaline phosphatase with mildly elevated transaminases. CXR is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: Disseminated MAC — systemic wasting, diarrhea, elevated ALP at CD4 < 50
discriminator: MAC causes disseminated infection with fever, wasting, diarrhea, and elevated alkaline phosphatase (hepatic involvement) at very low CD4 counts

stem: A 40-year-old HIV-positive woman with CD4 80 presents with 1 week of progressive right-sided weakness and headache. MRI brain shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions at the basal ganglia and gray-white junction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: Cerebral toxoplasmosis — ring-enhancing lesions in basal ganglia at CD4 < 100
discriminator: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions at basal ganglia and gray-white junction in an HIV patient with CD4 < 100 is toxoplasma encephalitis until proven otherwise

stem: An HIV-positive man with CD4 30 complains of floaters and blurred vision in his right eye over the past week. Funduscopy shows retinal hemorrhages with yellow-white exudates. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: CMV retinitis at CD4 < 50 — retinal hemorrhage + exudate (tomato ketchup fundus)
discriminator: CMV retinitis presents with floaters, visual field loss, retinal hemorrhages and exudates (tomato ketchup fundus) at CD4 < 50

stem: A 65-year-old man with urosepsis has a lactate of 4.2 mmol/L, BP 85/50 after 2 L of IV fluids, and is confused. According to the Hour-1 sepsis bundle, which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Order a CT scan of abdomen
Obtain blood cultures and start broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour
Give another 2 L of IV fluids and recheck lactate in 2 hours
Transfer to ICU before initiating treatment
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: Sepsis Hour-1 bundle — blood cultures and broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour
discriminator: The Hour-1 bundle requires simultaneous actions: measure lactate, obtain cultures, start broad-spectrum antibiotics, give IV fluids, and start vasopressors if needed — all within the first hour

stem: A 34-year-old HIV-positive man with CD4 45 starts ART. After 3 weeks, he develops fever, lymphadenopathy, and worsening of his previously controlled cryptococcal meningitis symptoms. CSF shows inflammation but is culture-negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: IRIS — paradoxical worsening of OI symptoms after ART initiation due to immune recovery
discriminator: IRIS occurs weeks after starting ART as immune function recovers, causing inflammatory reaction against residual antigens; CSF is culture-negative excluding active infection

stem: A 26-year-old man presents with 6 days of high-grade fever. On day 4, his fever partially resolved but then recurred. He has severe myalgia, retro-orbital pain, and a petechial rash on his legs. BP 100/70, HR 95, temperature 38.5°C. Platelets 35,000/µL, HCT 48% (baseline 40%). Tourniquet test is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: Dengue — biphasic fever, retro-orbital pain, thrombocytopenia, rising HCT (plasma leak), positive tourniquet test
discriminator: Biphasic fever + retro-orbital pain + thrombocytopenia + rising HCT at defervescence = dengue with plasma leak; the rising HCT indicates hemoconcentration from plasma leakage

stem: A 32-year-old man from Lahore returns from a 2-week trip to rural Balochistan. He has had 4 days of fever (39.5°C), headache, and myalgias. He looks toxic, has mild confusion, and his spleen is palpable. BP 100/65, HR 110. He took paracetamol but no antimalarials. What is the single most appropriate next step?
opts: Start IV ceftriaxone for typhoid and await blood culture results
Obtain STAT thick and thin blood films for malaria
Order dengue NS1 antigen and IgM serology
Start IV fluids and observe for 24 hours
CT scan head to evaluate confusion
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: Fever with travel to endemic area — STAT blood film for malaria is the highest priority
discriminator: Any febrile patient with recent travel to a malaria-endemic area (especially falciparum-endemic rural Balochistan) with confusion must have a STAT malaria film; ceftriaxone without ruling out malaria could be fatal if cerebral malaria is missed

stem: A 38-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV. CD4 count is 35 cells/µL. He has a 2-week history of cough, fever, and dyspnea, a 3-day history of headache and photophobia, and reports floaters in his left eye. CXR shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Funduscopy shows retinal hemorrhages with exudates. Which infection should be treated first?
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: PCP is the most immediately life-threatening OI at this CD4 and requires urgent treatment with TMP-SMX + steroids
discriminator: The patient has features of multiple OIs (PCP: cough + interstitial infiltrates; cryptococcal meningitis: headache + photophobia; CMV: floaters + retinal findings), but PCP with hypoxia is the most acutely life-threatening and must be treated first

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents on day 5 of dengue fever. Her fever resolved 6 hours ago, but she now has cold extremities, delayed capillary refill (4 seconds), pulse 120, BP 80/50, and HCT 52% (baseline 38%). Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Give 1 unit of platelet transfusion immediately
Start IV normal saline at 5 mL/kg/h and transfuse packed RBCs
Give bolus of isotonic crystalloid 15–20 mL/kg over 1 hour, then reassess
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: Dengue shock syndrome management — isotonic crystalloid bolus with careful reassessment
discriminator: Dengue shock at defervescence with rising HCT indicates hypovolemic shock from plasma leak — isotonic crystalloid resuscitation is the mainstay, not platelets, blood, vasopressors first, or steroids

stem: An 8-year-old girl from a peri-urban area of Punjab presents with 7 days of high fever, abdominal pain, and constipation. She has relative bradycardia (temperature 39.5°C, pulse 88) and a tender abdomen. Blood culture grows Salmonella typhi resistant to ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, and amoxicillin. Her weight is 22 kg. What is the best treatment option?
opts: Ciprofloxacin 15 mg/kg twice daily for 10 days
Meropenem 20 mg/kg three times daily for 10 days
subject: Medicine-Infectious
concept: XDR typhoid resistant to ceftriaxone — azithromycin as effective oral option
discriminator: The isolate is ceftriaxone-resistant (XDR typhoid); azithromycin remains effective against XDR strains and provides oral therapy for uncomplicated disease

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with well-demarcated erythematous plaques covered by silvery-white scale on both elbows and knees. The lesions are mildly pruritic. He also reports nail pitting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: Plaque psoriasis — classical morphology and distribution on extensor surfaces with nail pitting
discriminator: Extensor surface distribution + silvery scale + nail pitting is pathognomonic for plaque psoriasis

stem: A 40-year-old woman with chronic plaque psoriasis has her scales gently scraped off during examination. Punctate bleeding points appear at the base. What is this sign called?
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: Auspitz sign — punctate bleeding when psoriatic scale is removed
discriminator: Punctate bleeding after scale removal is specific to psoriasis (Auspitz sign), not other papulosquamous conditions

stem: A 28-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of well-defined erythematous plaques on his elbows and knees. On examination, his fingernails show multiple small pits and onycholysis. What is the significance of the nail findings?
opts: They indicate concurrent fungal infection requiring oral antifungals
They are a common associated feature confirming the diagnosis of psoriasis
They suggest vitamin deficiency and are unrelated to the skin lesions
They are pathognomonic for atopic dermatitis
They indicate the need for immediate systemic immunosuppression
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: Nail pitting is a characteristic feature of psoriasis and supports the diagnosis
discriminator: Nail pitting in the context of extensor plaques confirms psoriasis rather than fungal infection or eczema

stem: A 32-year-old man with known plaque psoriasis develops new psoriatic lesions along a linear scratch mark on his forearm. What is this phenomenon called?
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: Koebner phenomenon — development of psoriatic lesions at sites of trauma
discriminator: Linear distribution of lesions along scratch marks is classic for Koebner phenomenon in psoriasis

stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic plaque psoriasis is started on oral prednisolone 40 mg daily for presumed psoriatic arthritis by his general practitioner. Two weeks after completing the taper, he develops widespread erythema with sterile pustules and fever. What complication has occurred?
opts: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: Systemic steroid withdrawal can precipitate generalized pustular psoriasis (von Zumbusch)
discriminator: History of psoriasis + systemic steroid use + withdrawal + widespread erythema with sterile pustules + fever = generalized pustular psoriasis

stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with intensely pruritic, poorly defined patches on his antecubital and popliteal fossae. His skin is dry and lichenified. He has a history of asthma and allergic rhinitis. Which laboratory finding is most likely to be elevated?
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: Atopic dermatitis is associated with elevated IgE levels
discriminator: Flexural pruritus + personal/family history of atopy (asthma, allergic rhinitis) + elevated IgE = atopic dermatitis

stem: A 2-year-old child presents with severe, persistent atopic dermatitis since infancy. Genetic testing reveals a loss-of-function mutation in a gene encoding an epidermal barrier protein. Which protein is most likely affected?
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: Filaggrin mutation is the most important genetic defect in atopic dermatitis, impairing skin barrier function
discriminator: Loss-of-function mutation in filaggrin (FLG) is the strongest known genetic risk factor for atopic dermatitis

stem: A 22-year-old woman with atopic dermatitis has poorly controlled flexural eczema despite consistent use of emollients. She has severe pruritus affecting sleep. What is the appropriate next step in management?
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: Atopic dermatitis treatment ladder — emollients first, then topical corticosteroids
discriminator: Emollients alone are first-line; topical steroids are added when emollients are insufficient for flares

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with a 4-week history of an expanding annular rash on her trunk. On examination, there is an erythematous ring with a raised scaly border and central clearing. She owns a cat. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: Tinea corporis — annular plaque with raised border and central clearing
discriminator: Annular expanding lesion with raised scaly border, central clearing, and animal contact = tinea corporis (ringworm)

stem: A 28-year-old man has a suspected tinea corporis lesion on his forearm. You perform a scraping from the active border of the lesion and prepare a potassium hydroxide (KOH) mount. What will microscopy most likely show?
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: KOH preparation of dermatophyte infection shows branching septate hyphae
discriminator: KOH dissolves keratin but leaves fungal cell walls intact, revealing branching septate hyphae in dermatophyte infections

stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with patchy scalp alopecia with broken hairs and a scaly, inflamed area. A KOH preparation of hair shafts is positive for fungal elements. The mother asks for a topical antifungal cream. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Topical clotrimazole cream twice daily for 4 weeks
Topical terbinafine cream once daily for 2 weeks
Topical ketoconazole shampoo three times weekly
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: Tinea capitis requires oral antifungal therapy because topicals cannot penetrate the hair follicle
discriminator: Scalp involvement (tinea capitis) always requires oral therapy — topicals cannot penetrate the hair follicle to eradicate dermatophytes

stem: A 35-year-old man with HIV (CD4 count 110 cells/µL) presents with multiple purple, non-blanching nodules on his lower legs and a violaceous lesion on his hard palate. The lesions are painless and non-pruritic. What is the most likely causative agent?
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 (KSHV) and presents with violaceous nodules in HIV patients with low CD4
discriminator: Purple non-blanching nodules + oral involvement + low CD4 = Kaposi sarcoma driven by HHV-8

stem: A 40-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV (CD4 90 cells/µL) is found to have several purple nodules on his legs. Biopsy confirms Kaposi sarcoma. He has no respiratory or GI symptoms. What is the most appropriate first step in management?
opts: Refer for cryotherapy of all visible lesions
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: First-line treatment for HIV-associated Kaposi sarcoma is starting ART to restore immune function
discriminator: HIV-associated KS often regresses with immune restoration from ART alone; chemotherapy is reserved for refractory or visceral disease

stem: A 38-year-old man with HIV (CD4 180) presents with multiple red-purple papules and nodules on his face and arms. Some lesions resemble pyogenic granulomas. He also has pelvic lymphadenopathy. Biopsy shows clumps of bacteria on Warthin-Starry staining. Which treatment is most appropriate?
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: Bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella) mimics Kaposi sarcoma but requires antibiotic therapy, not ART alone
discriminator: Warthin-Starry staining showing clumps of bacteria distinguishes bacillary angiomatosis from KS; antibiotics (erythromycin) are the treatment

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with flaccid, easily ruptured blisters on her trunk and painful oral ulcers. A blister spreads when lateral pressure is applied to perilesional skin. A biopsy shows suprabasal acantholysis. Which autoantibody is most likely present?
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: Pemphigus vulgaris is caused by anti-desmoglein 3 antibodies leading to suprabasal acantholysis
discriminator: Flaccid bullae + oral ulcers + positive Nikolsky + suprabasal acantholysis = pemphigus vulgaris with anti-Dsg3 antibodies

stem: A 72-year-old man presents with tense blisters on his flexural forearms, axillae, and trunk. The blisters are filled with clear fluid and do not rupture easily. Oral mucosa is spared. Lateral pressure on perilesional skin does not extend the blister. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: Bullous pemphigoid presents with tense bullae on flexural areas in elderly patients with a negative Nikolsky sign
discriminator: Tense bullae + elderly + flexural distribution + spared oral mucosa + negative Nikolsky = bullous pemphigoid

stem: A 60-year-old woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes develops a widespread blistering rash. The blisters are tense, located on flexural areas and trunk, and Nikolsky sign is negative. Oral mucosa is clear. A biopsy shows a subepidermal split with eosinophils. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: Bullous pemphigoid — subepidermal split with eosinophils, linear IgG/C3 along basement membrane on DIF
discriminator: Subepidermal split + linear IgG and C3 at BMZ + tense bullae + elderly + negative Nikolsky = bullous pemphigoid

stem: A 28-year-old woman develops widespread target-like macules with central blisters and painful oral, ocular, and genital ulcers 10 days after starting carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia. She has skin detachment involving 15% of her body surface area. What is the most important initial step in management?
opts: Apply silver sulfadiazine to all eroded areas
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: SJS/TEN — immediate withdrawal of the causative drug is the most critical intervention
discriminator: Target lesions + mucosal involvement + skin detachment + recent drug start = SJS/TEN. Stop the causative drug immediately.

stem: A 65-year-old man on allopurinol presents with widespread erythema, target lesions, and skin detachment involving 40% of his BSA. Mucous membranes are severely affected. He is febrile and tachycardic. Which scoring system is used to predict mortality in this condition?
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: SCORTEN is the mortality prediction score for SJS/TEN
discriminator: SCORTEN (SCORing Toxic Epidermal Necrosis) is specifically designed for SJS/TEN mortality prediction using 7 parameters

stem: A 50-year-old man with chronic plaque psoriasis presents with sudden-onset extensive erythema affecting > 90% of his body surface, accompanied by fever, chills, and superficial desquamation. He recently stopped his methotrexate due to nausea. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
opts: Restart methotrexate and escalate the dose
Admit for supportive care and start systemic therapy with acitretin or cyclosporine
Apply potent topical steroids to the entire body
Start intravenous antibiotics for presumed cellulitis
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: Erythrodermic psoriasis requires admission and systemic therapy; systemic steroids must be avoided
discriminator: Sudden-onset widespread erythema (> 90% BSA) in a patient with psoriasis who stopped methotrexate = erythrodermic psoriasis. Needs admission and systemic non-steroid therapy.

stem: A 38-year-old man with known plaque psoriasis develops pain, swelling, and morning stiffness in multiple small joints of his hands and his lower back. Imaging reveals erosive changes and sacroiliitis. Which serological marker is most likely to be negative?
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: Psoriatic arthritis is typically seronegative (negative RF and anti-CCP), distinguishing it from rheumatoid arthritis
discriminator: Psoriatic arthritis is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy — RF and anti-CCP are negative, while HLA-B27 may be positive (especially with axial involvement)

stem: A 55-year-old overweight man presents with an intensely pruritic rash in his groin folds that has been present for 3 weeks. On examination, there is a well-defined erythematous plaque with a raised, scaly border extending from the groin onto the medial thigh, with central clearing. Scrotum is spared. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: Tinea cruris — annular plaque with raised scaly border and central clearing in the groin, sparing scrotum
discriminator: Well-defined annular plaque with raised scaly border, central clearing, and scrotal sparing = tinea cruris

stem: A 30-year-old man with HIV-associated Kaposi sarcoma (CD4 140) develops progressive dyspnea, cough, and hemoptysis. Chest X-ray shows bilateral reticulonodular infiltrates and pleural effusion. Bronchoscopy reveals violaceous endobronchial lesions. What is the next step in management?
opts: Start ART alone and monitor symptoms
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: Visceral Kaposi sarcoma (pulmonary involvement) requires systemic chemotherapy; ART alone is insufficient
discriminator: Pulmonary KS with symptoms requires systemic chemotherapy (liposomal doxorubicin) because ART alone cannot rapidly control visceral disease

stem: A 4-year-old child with severe atopic dermatitis develops grouped vesicles with an erythematous base on eczematous skin, high fever, and lymphadenopathy. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. What is the most likely complication?
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: Eczema herpeticum is disseminated HSV infection in patients with atopic dermatitis, an emergency requiring acyclovir
discriminator: Grouped vesicles on eczematous skin + fever + Tzanck showing multinucleated giant cells = eczema herpeticum (HSV superinfection)

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with a 2-week history of an expanding annular rash on her trunk. She also has well-demarcated plaques on both elbows and reports nail pitting. KOH preparation from the active border of the annular lesion is negative. Which feature would most strongly indicate that the annular lesion is NOT tinea corporis but rather annular psoriasis?
opts: The lesion has a raised border with scale
The center of the lesion is hypopigmented
The patient has nail pitting and other plaques on extensor surfaces
subject: Medicine-Dermatology
concept: Annular psoriasis can mimic tinea corporis; the presence of nail pitting and typical extensor plaques favors psoriasis
discriminator: Nail pitting + extensor plaques + negative KOH = annular psoriasis, not tinea corporis

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep with early morning wakening, and loss of appetite for the past 3 weeks. She feels worthless and has passive thoughts of death. She has no past psychiatric history and no medical comorbidities. What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment?
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: First-line treatment for moderate major depressive disorder is an SSRI
discriminator: Unipolar depression without psychotic features — SSRIs are first-line; ECT is reserved for psychotic or treatment-resistant depression

stem: A 45-year-old man with a 10-year history of schizophrenia maintained on risperidone 4 mg daily presents with acute onset of involuntary upward deviation of the eyes and neck twisting to the left, starting 2 hours after his morning dose. He is conscious and oriented. What is the most appropriate treatment?
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: Acute dystonic reaction from antipsychotics is treated with anticholinergics like benztropine
discriminator: Oculogyric crisis + torticollis in a patient on antipsychotics = acute dystonia. Patient is conscious (not seizing). Responds dramatically to IV/IM anticholinergic.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder on lithium 900 mg daily presents with coarse tremor of the hands, nausea, vomiting, and drowsiness for 2 days. She recently started ibuprofen for knee pain. Serum lithium is 2.6 mEq/L. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Reduce lithium dose to 600 mg daily and repeat level in 1 week
Start propranolol for tremor and continue lithium at same dose
IV normal saline and arrange urgent hemodialysis
Switch lithium to valproate and discharge with outpatient follow-up
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: Severe lithium toxicity (level > 2.5 or with symptoms) requires IV fluids and hemodialysis
discriminator: Coarse tremor + vomiting + drowsiness + lithium level 2.6 + NSAID use = severe lithium toxicity. Level > 2.5 + symptoms = indication for hemodialysis.

stem: A 22-year-old man with schizophrenia is brought to the emergency department with fever (39.5°C), generalized rigidity, altered mental status, and tachycardia. He was started on haloperidol 5 days ago. Lab findings: CK 12,000 U/L, WBC 15,000/mm³. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: NMS presents with rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, and elevated CK after antipsychotic initiation
discriminator: Rigidity + hyperthermia + autonomic instability + elevated CK + recent antipsychotic initiation = NMS. No clonus (rules out serotonin syndrome). Onset is days, not hours.

stem: A 19-year-old man is found unresponsive with shallow breathing at a party. His friends report he may have taken 'something.' On examination: pulse 50/min, BP 90/60, RR 6/min, oxygen saturation 85%, pupils are pinpoint bilaterally. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: Opioid overdose presents with pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, and decreased consciousness — treated with naloxone
discriminator: Pinpoint pupils + respiratory depression + bradycardia + unresponsiveness = opioid toxidrome until proven otherwise. Naloxone is the specific reversal agent.

stem: A 65-year-old woman with a history of major depressive disorder is brought in by her family. Over the past 4 weeks she has refused to eat, believes she is being poisoned by her neighbors, and hears voices telling her she is worthless. She is dehydrated and malnourished. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Increase SSRI dose and add olanzapine
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: ECT is first-line for severe depression with psychotic features
discriminator: Severe depression + psychotic features (paranoid delusions, command auditory hallucinations) + refusal to eat = psychotic depression. ECT is first-line, not last-line.

stem: A 30-year-old man on fluoxetine 40 mg daily for depression was started on tramadol for back pain 2 days ago. He now presents with agitation, hyperthermia (38.8°C), tachycardia (110/min), clonus of the ankles, and hyperreflexia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: Serotonin syndrome is caused by serotonergic drug combinations (SSRI + tramadol) and presents with clonus, hyperreflexia, hyperthermia, and autonomic instability
discriminator: Clonus + hyperreflexia + hyperthermia + onset within days of adding a serotonergic drug = serotonin syndrome. The combination of SSRI + tramadol (which has serotonergic activity) is a classic trigger.

stem: A 55-year-old man is found confused and agitated at home. Empty bottles of amitriptyline (TCA) are found. Heart rate 110/min, BP 85/50, temperature 37.8°C. Pupils are dilated. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with QRS duration 140 ms. What is the most appropriate treatment?
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: TCA overdose with widened QRS is treated with IV sodium bicarbonate
discriminator: TCA overdose + widened QRS (cardiotoxicity) = sodium bicarbonate. Bicarbonate alkalinizes serum and provides sodium to overcome sodium channel blockade.

stem: A 40-year-old man is brought to the ED 3 hours after ingesting 20 g of paracetamol in a suicide attempt. He is awake and oriented, pulse 90/min, BP 120/80. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Wait 4 hours and then check paracetamol level
Perform gastric lavage with normal saline
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: Activated charcoal within 4 hours of paracetamol ingestion reduces absorption
discriminator: Time since ingestion is < 4 hours — activated charcoal is indicated. Level should be checked at 4 hours post-ingestion, but charcoal can be given immediately.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with bipolar disorder comes for routine follow-up. She has been stable on lithium for 2 years. Which of the following is the most important laboratory monitoring to perform at this visit?
opts: Complete blood count and liver function tests
Serum lithium level, renal function tests, and TSH
Serum calcium and vitamin D level
Lipid profile and random blood glucose
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: Lithium requires regular monitoring of serum level, renal function, and thyroid function
discriminator: Lithium monitoring = level (trough, 12 h post-dose) + renal function (Cr, BUN) + thyroid (TSH) every 3–6 months. Lithium causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, renal impairment, and hypothyroidism.

stem: A 28-year-old man is brought to the ED by his friends. He has been acting erratically for the past week — sleeping only 2 hours per night, spending excessive money, talking rapidly, and claiming he is a prophet sent to save the world. He is grandiose, irritable when interrupted, and has pressured speech. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic
Bipolar II disorder, current episode hypomanic
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: Mania is defined by elevated/irritable mood lasting ≥ 1 week with grandiosity, decreased sleep, pressured speech, and functional impairment
discriminator: Duration > 1 week + grandiosity + decreased sleep + risky behavior + functional impairment = mania (not hypomania). No negative symptoms or disorganization pointing to schizophrenia.

stem: A 50-year-old man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and schizophrenia is well controlled on olanzapine. He returns for follow-up. His blood pressure is 130/80, HbA1c 8.2%, and he has gained 12 kg in the past year. What is the most appropriate next step regarding his antipsychotic?
opts: Continue olanzapine; metabolic effects can be managed with lifestyle changes
Switch to haloperidol to reduce metabolic risk
Switch to aripiprazole and monitor metabolic parameters
Add metformin to counteract weight gain without switching
Reduce olanzapine dose by half and monitor HbA1c in 3 months
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: Atypical antipsychotics differ in metabolic side effect profiles; aripiprazole is weight-neutral and has lower metabolic risk
discriminator: Olanzapine causes significant weight gain, hyperglycemia, and dyslipidemia. In a patient with pre-existing diabetes and worsening metabolic control, switching to a metabolically favorable atypical (aripiprazole, ziprasidone, lurasidone) is indicated.

stem: A 60-year-old man who drinks 6 beers daily was admitted for observation after a fall. On day 2 of admission, he becomes agitated, tremulous, and reports seeing insects crawling on the walls. His pulse is 110/min, BP 155/95, and he is diaphoretic. Which of the following medications is most appropriate?
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: Alcohol withdrawal syndrome is treated with benzodiazepines to prevent seizures and delirium tremens
discriminator: Chronic alcohol use + withdrawal symptoms 48–72 hours after cessation + autonomic hyperactivity + visual hallucinations = alcohol withdrawal delirium. Benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide) are first-line.

stem: A 36-year-old woman with depression on sertraline 100 mg daily presents to the ED after a deliberate overdose. She is drowsy but rousable. Family reports she takes no other medications. Her pulse is 88/min, BP 110/70, RR 14/min, oxygen saturation 98%. Pupils are 4 mm and reactive. ECG shows normal sinus rhythm. Which of the following investigations is most important to perform next?
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: A paracetamol level must be checked in every intentional overdose, even if another agent is reported or suspected
discriminator: Any intentional overdose requires paracetamol level screening — paracetamol is in many combination products, patients often do not know what they took, and toxicity is asymptomatic until hepatotoxicity develops.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with major depressive disorder is started on phenelzine (an MAOI). She presents to the ED 2 hours after eating aged cheese and drinking red wine at a party. She has a severe throbbing headache, palpitations, and nausea. Her pulse is 120/min, BP 210/110 mmHg. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Hypertensive crisis due to tyramine interaction
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: MAOIs inhibit tyramine metabolism; tyramine-rich foods cause hypertensive crisis
discriminator: MAOI + tyramine-rich food (aged cheese, red wine, cured meats, pickled foods) = hypertensive crisis. Presentation: severe headache, palpitations, hypertension.

stem: A 38-year-old man with HIV on antiretroviral therapy presents with acute psychosis — paranoid delusions, auditory hallucinations, and disorganized behavior for 2 weeks. He has no prior psychiatric history. He is medically stable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Start olanzapine 10 mg daily as antipsychotic therapy
Refer for urgent CT head and lumbar puncture before starting antipsychotics
Start low-dose haloperidol and titrate upward
Admit for observation without medication for 24 hours
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: New-onset psychosis in an immunocompromised/high-risk patient requires ruling out organic causes (CNS infection, space-occupying lesion) before assuming primary psychiatric illness
discriminator: First-episode psychosis at age 38 + HIV + no psychiatric history = organic cause until proven otherwise. CNS infections (toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis, HIV encephalopathy, CNS lymphoma) must be ruled out.

stem: A 70-year-old woman is brought from a nursing home with confusion, urinary retention, and flushed dry skin for 2 days. Medications include amitriptyline 50 mg for neuropathy, donepezil for Alzheimer disease, and hydrochlorothiazide. Pulse 110/min, BP 100/70, temperature 38.5°C. Pupils are 6 mm and sluggishly reactive. What is the most likely toxidrome?
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: Anticholinergic toxidrome presents with dilated pupils, dry flushed skin, tachycardia, urinary retention, hyperthermia, and delirium
discriminator: Dilated pupils + dry flushed skin + tachycardia + urinary retention + hyperthermia + patient on amitriptyline (anticholinergic TCA) = anticholinergic toxidrome. Classic 'blind as a bat, hot as a hare, dry as a bone, red as a beet, mad as a hatter.'

stem: A 20-year-old farmer is brought to the ED with excessive salivation, lacrimation, sweating, vomiting, diarrhea, and muscle fasciculations. He was spraying pesticides in his fields without protective equipment. Pulse 55/min, BP 90/60, pupils are 1 mm and constricted. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Naloxone 0.4 mg IV and supportive care
Atropine 2 mg IV and pralidoxime 1 g IV
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: Organophosphate poisoning causes cholinergic toxidrome (SLUDGE + miosis) — treated with atropine and pralidoxime
discriminator: SLUDGE (salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI upset, emesis) + miosis + bradycardia + muscle fasciculations + pesticide exposure = organophosphate poisoning. Atropine blocks muscarinic effects; pralidoxime reactivates acetylcholinesterase.

stem: A 32-year-old woman with schizophrenia on clozapine 300 mg daily reports a 3-day history of fever, sore throat, and mouth ulcers. Her temperature is 38.2°C. She looks unwell. Which of the following laboratory investigations is most important to obtain urgently?
opts: Throat swab for rapid streptococcal test
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: Clozapine causes agranulocytosis; fever and sore throat require urgent CBC to rule out neutropenia
discriminator: Clozapine + fever + sore throat + mouth ulcers = agranulocytosis until proven otherwise. CBC with differential is mandatory. Clozapine requires strict hematological monitoring (absolute neutrophil count).

stem: A 24-year-old man with schizophrenia presents with an inability to sit still — he paces constantly, shifts his weight from foot to foot, and reports feeling intensely restless. Symptoms started 2 weeks after increasing his risperidone dose. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Increase risperidone to control psychotic symptoms causing agitation
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: Akathisia (subjective and objective restlessness) from antipsychotics is treated with beta-blockers (propranolol) or benzodiazepines
discriminator: Inability to sit still + pacing + intense subjective restlessness starting after antipsychotic dose increase = akathisia. Unlike acute dystonia (benztropine-responsive), akathisia responds to propranolol or benzodiazepines.

stem: A 44-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is admitted for a manic episode. She has been on lithium but stopped it 3 months ago. She is grandiose, not sleeping, spending money irresponsibly, and becoming aggressive when redirected. Which of the following is the most appropriate acute treatment regimen?
opts: Re-start lithium alone and titrate to therapeutic level
Start valproate or olanzapine for acute mania with possible later lithium maintenance
ECT as first-line for all manic episodes
Start clonazepam 2 mg three times daily as monotherapy
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: Acute mania requires a mood stabilizer (valproate) or atypical antipsychotic (olanzapine) for rapid symptom control; lithium has a slower onset and is better for maintenance
discriminator: Lithium has a slow onset (1–2 weeks for full effect) and requires gradual titration. For acute mania with aggression, valproate or atypical antipsychotics (olanzapine) provide faster symptom control. Lithium is ideal for prophylaxis, not first-line for acute episodes.

stem: A 33-year-old woman with depression is admitted after taking 30 tablets of her mother's amitriptyline (25 mg each) 2 hours ago. She is conscious but drowsy. Pulse 105/min, BP 95/60, RR 14/min. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with QRS of 120 ms. What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?
opts: Wait and observe; QRS < 140 ms is not concerning
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: TCA overdose with QRS ≥ 100 ms indicates sodium channel blockade requiring sodium bicarbonate
discriminator: QRS of 120 ms in TCA overdose = cardiotoxicity. Sodium bicarbonate is indicated when QRS > 100 ms. Charcoal may be given but bicarbonate takes priority for the arrhythmia risk.

stem: A 50-year-old man on a stable dose of lithium for 10 years presents with polyuria and polydipsia (drinking 5–6 L of water per day). Serum sodium is 148 mEq/L, urine osmolality is 200 mOsm/kg (low). He is otherwise well. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
opts: Diabetes mellitus from lithium-induced pancreatic dysfunction
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: Lithium causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus by impairing renal concentrating ability
discriminator: Polyuria + polydipsia + low urine osmolality + high serum sodium + chronic lithium use = nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Lithium accumulates in collecting duct cells and downregulates aquaporin-2 channels.

stem: A 55-year-old man with no prior psychiatric history is brought to the ED by his wife for bizarre behavior over the past month. He has become convinced that the FBI is following him, has installed cameras in his house, and is poisoning his food. He has been sleeping poorly and has lost 5 kg. On exam, he is guarded and suspicious. He denies hallucinations. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Bipolar I disorder, manic episode with psychotic features
Major depressive disorder with psychotic features
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: Delusional disorder is characterized by non-bizarre delusions lasting ≥ 1 month without prominent hallucinations or functional decline
discriminator: Isolated persecutory delusions (non-bizarre: being followed, poisoned, watched) + no hallucinations + no marked functional decline + age 55 + organized personality = delusional disorder. Unlike schizophrenia, there is no negative symptoms or disorganization.

stem: A 30-year-old woman on venlafaxine 225 mg daily for depression presents with confusion, agitation, and jerking movements. On examination: pulse 115/min, BP 145/90, temperature 39.0°C. There is sustained clonus at both ankles, generalized hyperreflexia, and inducible clonus at the wrists. She was recently started on linezolid for a skin infection 3 days ago. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Increase venlafaxine to 300 mg daily for treatment-resistant depression
Stop venlafaxine and linezolid, start cyproheptadine, provide supportive care
Give dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV and stop both medications
Start bromocriptine 5 mg three times daily
Administer naloxone 0.4 mg IV and observe
subject: Medicine-Psychiatry
concept: Serotonin syndrome from SSRI/SNRI + linezolid requires stopping serotonergic agents and administering cyproheptadine
discriminator: Clonus + hyperreflexia + hyperthermia + venlafaxine (SNRI) + linezolid (MAOI activity) = serotonin syndrome. Linezolid has weak MAOI properties and can precipitate serotonin syndrome when combined with SSRIs/SNRIs.

stem: A 35-year-old female presents with fatigue and pallor. She reports heavy menstrual bleeding for the past 8 months. CBC: Hb 8.5 g/dL, MCV 70 fL, MCH 22 pg. Serum iron 25 µg/dL (low), TIBC 480 µg/dL (high), ferritin 6 ng/mL. Peripheral smear shows microcytic hypochromic RBCs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: Iron deficiency anemia — classic iron profile (low Fe, high TIBC, low ferritin) in a patient with menorrhagia
discriminator: Low ferritin (< 15 ng/mL) is the gold standard for absolute iron deficiency; high TIBC confirms IDA over ACD

stem: A 22-year-old asymptomatic female is found to have Hb 11.0 g/dL on routine screening. MCV 68 fL, RBC count 5.8 × 10⁶/µL. Serum ferritin 85 ng/mL, iron 110 µg/dL, TIBC 290 µg/dL. Mentzer index is 11.7. What is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?
opts: Bone marrow biopsy with iron stain
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: Thalassemia trait — Mentzer index < 13 with normal/high ferritin; Hb electrophoresis for confirmation
discriminator: Mentzer index (MCV/RBC) < 13 + normal/high ferritin + normal serum iron suggests thalassemia trait, not IDA

stem: A 55-year-old male with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate presents with fatigue. Hb 9.8 g/dL, MCV 78 fL. Serum iron 30 µg/dL (low), TIBC 200 µg/dL (low), ferritin 350 ng/mL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: Anemia of chronic disease — low serum iron with LOW TIBC and HIGH ferritin in an inflammatory setting
discriminator: High ferritin (acute phase reactant) with low TIBC distinguishes ACD from IDA, where ferritin is low and TIBC is high

stem: A 65-year-old female with rheumatoid arthritis presents with fatigue. Hb 9.0 g/dL, MCV 76 fL. Iron studies: serum iron 25 µg/dL, TIBC 380 µg/dL, ferritin 25 ng/mL. What is the most accurate interpretation?
opts: Concomitant iron deficiency anemia in the setting of anemia of chronic disease
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: Concomitant IDA and ACD — ferritin < 30 in an inflammatory state indicates true iron deficiency despite ferritin being above the usual < 15 cutoff
discriminator: In inflammatory states, ferritin < 30 is diagnostic of concomitant iron deficiency (not < 15 as in non-inflammatory settings)

stem: A 40-year-old female with iron deficiency anemia is started on treatment. Which of the following is the earliest laboratory indicator of response to oral iron therapy?
opts: Rise in serum ferritin at 2 days
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: Timeline of response to oral iron — reticulocyte count rises first (5-7 days), then Hb (2-3 weeks), then MCV normalizes last
discriminator: Reticulocytosis is the earliest measurable response, preceding hemoglobin rise by 1-2 weeks

stem: A 28-year-old female with iron deficiency anemia is prescribed oral iron. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line preparation and dosing regimen?
opts: Ferrous sulfate 200 mg (65 mg elemental iron) orally three times daily on an empty stomach
Ferrous gluconate 100 mg orally once daily with meals
Iron dextran IV infusion 1000 mg over 4 hours
Ferrous sulfate 200 mg orally once daily before bed
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: First-line IDA treatment — oral ferrous sulfate 200 mg TID on empty stomach for optimal absorption
discriminator: Oral ferrous sulfate 200 mg TID on empty stomach is the standard first-line regimen for IDA

stem: A 70-year-old male presents with gradually progressive fatigue, difficulty walking, and tingling in his feet. On examination, he has loss of vibration sense in both legs and an ataxic gait. CBC: Hb 9.2 g/dL, MCV 108 fL. Peripheral smear shows hypersegmented neutrophils. What is the most likely cause of his neurological symptoms?
opts: Vitamin B12 deficiency causing subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: B12 deficiency — macrocytic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (dorsal columns + corticospinal tracts)
discriminator: Macrocytic anemia + hypersegmented neutrophils + SCD (vibration loss + ataxia) = B12 deficiency

stem: A 45-year-old female presents with fatigue and pallor. Labs show Hb 8.0 g/dL, MCV 106 fL. Serum B12 is 120 pg/mL (low). Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies are positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term management?
opts: Intramuscular hydroxocobalamin 1000 mcg every other day for 1 week, then weekly for 1 month, then monthly for life
Intramuscular hydroxocobalamin once and dietary counseling
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: Pernicious anemia — anti-intrinsic factor antibodies confirm autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells; requires lifelong IM B12 replacement
discriminator: Positive anti-intrinsic factor antibodies are diagnostic of pernicious anemia; treatment is lifelong IM B12, not oral

stem: A 60-year-old female presents with fever and easy bruising. CBC shows Hb 8.5 g/dL, WBC 45,000/µL with 65% blasts, platelets 20,000/µL. Bone marrow biopsy shows > 20% myeloblasts. Some blasts contain Auer rods. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) in chronic phase
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: AML — Auer rods are pathognomonic for myeloid lineage; presentation with cytopenias and blasts in an older adult
discriminator: Auer rods in blasts are pathognomonic for AML; they are never seen in ALL

stem: A 55-year-old male is diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia (AML). He has no significant comorbidities and good performance status. Which of the following is the standard induction chemotherapy regimen?
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: AML induction chemotherapy — standard 7+3 regimen: 7 days of cytarabine + 3 days of daunorubicin
discriminator: 7+3 (cytarabine + anthracycline) is the standard induction for AML, distinct from ALL, CML, lymphoma, and APML regimens

stem: A 45-year-old male presents with easy bruising, epistaxis, and fever. CBC: Hb 7.5 g/dL, WBC 50,000/µL with blasts, platelets 15,000/µL. Coagulation profile shows prolonged PT, prolonged aPTT, elevated D-dimer, and low fibrinogen. Peripheral smear shows blasts with multiple Auer rods and bundles. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
opts: All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) plus arsenic trioxide
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: APML (AML M3) presents with DIC; ATRA + arsenic trioxide is first-line, not standard 7+3 chemotherapy
discriminator: Coagulopathy + blasts with multiple Auer rods/bundles = APML (M3). ATRA must be started emergently before cytogenetic confirmation

stem: A 50-year-old male with newly diagnosed APML (AML M3) is started on ATRA and arsenic trioxide. Which of the following complications requires the most urgent monitoring during the first 48-72 hours of treatment?
opts: Differentiation syndrome (capillary leak, pulmonary infiltrates, respiratory distress)
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: Differentiation syndrome (formerly retinoic acid syndrome) is a life-threatening complication of ATRA therapy characterized by fever, respiratory distress, pulmonary infiltrates, and capillary leak
discriminator: Differentiation syndrome is unique to ATRA/arsenic therapy in APML and requires prompt recognition and steroids

stem: A 52-year-old asymptomatic male is found to have WBC 120,000/µL on routine labs. Differential shows neutrophils, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, and 2% blasts. Bone marrow biopsy is hypercellular. Cytogenetics reveals t(9;22) (q34;q11.2). Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line therapy?
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: CML — BCR-ABL+ (Philadelphia chromosome) treated with tyrosine kinase inhibitors (imatinib) as first-line
discriminator: t(9;22) = BCR-ABL = CML. TKIs (imatinib) are first-line, not chemotherapy or transplant

stem: A 72-year-old male presents with painless generalized lymphadenopathy and fatigue. CBC shows WBC 85,000/µL with a predominance of mature-appearing lymphocytes. Peripheral smear shows smudge cells. Flow cytometry shows CD5+, CD23+ B cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: CLL — smudge cells on peripheral smear, CD5+/CD23+ B cells, elderly patient with lymphocytosis
discriminator: Smudge cells + CD5+/CD23+ B-cell phenotype + elderly = CLL

stem: A 25-year-old female presents with painless left-sided neck swelling for 4 weeks. She also reports night sweats and unintentional weight loss. Examination reveals a firm, non-tender left supraclavicular lymph node measuring 3 cm. Excisional biopsy shows Reed-Sternberg cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: Hodgkin lymphoma — Reed-Sternberg cells are pathognomonic; presentation with contiguous nodal spread and B symptoms
discriminator: Reed-Sternberg cells (owl-eye appearance) are pathognomonic for Hodgkin lymphoma

stem: A 30-year-old male with Hodgkin lymphoma undergoes staging. PET-CT shows involvement of cervical, mediastinal, and para-aortic lymph nodes in a contiguous pattern. There is no extranodal involvement. Which of the following chemotherapeutic regimens is most appropriate?
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: Hodgkin lymphoma treatment — ABVD is the standard chemotherapy regimen
discriminator: HL = ABVD; NHL (DLBCL) = R-CHOP; AML = 7+3

stem: A 65-year-old male presents with rapidly enlarging right axillary lymphadenopathy and abdominal pain. PET-CT shows non-contiguous nodal involvement in the axilla, retroperitoneum, and inguinal regions. Excisional lymph node biopsy shows diffuse effacement by large atypical B cells. Immunohistochemistry is CD20+. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate treatment?
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: NHL (DLBCL) — CD20+ large B cells with non-contiguous spread; R-CHOP is standard
discriminator: Non-contiguous spread + CD20+ large B cells = DLBCL, treated with R-CHOP

stem: A 70-year-old male presents with back pain, fatigue, and recurrent infections. CBC shows Hb 9.0 g/dL, creatinine 2.5 mg/dL, and calcium 12.5 mg/dL. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal M-spike of 4.5 g/dL. Skeletal survey shows multiple lytic lesions in the skull and spine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: Multiple myeloma — CRAB criteria (hyperCalcemia, Renal failure, Anemia, Bone lesions) with M-spike and lytic lesions
discriminator: CRAB criteria + M-spike + lytic bone lesions (not blastic) = multiple myeloma

stem: A 62-year-old female with multiple myeloma presents with acute oliguria. Serum creatinine is 4.0 mg/dL (baseline 1.0). Serum calcium is 11.0 mg/dL. Urine protein electrophoresis shows Bence Jones proteinuria (kappa light chains). Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management step?
opts: Aggressive IV hydration and hold nephrotoxic agents
IV bisphosphonate therapy without regard to renal function
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: Myeloma kidney (cast nephropathy) — aggressive IV hydration is first step; avoid nephrotoxic agents and begin anti-myeloma therapy
discriminator: Acute renal failure in myeloma requires immediate hydration and avoidance of NSAIDs/contrast; bisphosphonates need renal dosing

stem: A 68-year-old male with multiple myeloma starting chemotherapy. Which of the following supportive measures is most important to prevent skeletal-related events?
opts: Prophylactic surgical fixation of long bones
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: Myeloma bone disease — bisphosphonates reduce skeletal-related events (pathologic fractures, hypercalcemia, bone pain)
discriminator: Bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid, pamidronate) are the standard of care for myeloma bone disease

stem: A 45-year-old female with newly diagnosed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (NHL) is planned for R-CHOP chemotherapy. She has bulky abdominal disease (12 cm mass) and high LDH. Which of the following prophylactic measures is most important to initiate before starting chemotherapy?
opts: Aggressive IV hydration and allopurinol or rasburicase
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: Tumor lysis syndrome prophylaxis — aggressive IV hydration ± allopurinol/rasburicase before starting chemotherapy in high-risk patients (bulky disease, high LDH)
discriminator: Bulky disease + high LDH = high risk for tumor lysis syndrome; prevention starts before chemotherapy

stem: During the first 48 hours of chemotherapy for a patient with high-grade NHL, which of the following laboratory parameters should be monitored most frequently to detect tumor lysis syndrome?
opts: Hemoglobin and white blood cell count
Potassium, phosphate, calcium, uric acid, and creatinine every 6-8 hours
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: TLS monitoring — K+, Ca++, PO4, uric acid, Cr must be checked every 6-8 hours during the first 48-72 hours of high-risk chemotherapy
discriminator: The hallmark laboratory abnormalities of TLS are hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hyperuricemia, and rising creatinine — all must be monitored frequently

stem: A 55-year-old male is diagnosed with CML in chronic phase. He is started on imatinib. Which of the following is the best method to monitor his response to therapy?
opts: Peripheral smear for blast count monthly
BCR-ABL transcript levels by quantitative PCR
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: CML response monitoring — quantitative PCR for BCR-ABL transcript levels is the standard for molecular monitoring
discriminator: BCR-ABL PCR is the most sensitive method to detect residual disease and molecular response in CML

stem: A 34-year-old female is 6 weeks pregnant and found to have Hb 9.8 g/dL, MCV 74 fL. She is asymptomatic with no significant history. Iron studies: serum ferritin 95 ng/mL, iron 100 µg/dL, TIBC 280 µg/dL. RBC count is 5.2 × 10⁶/µL. Mentzer index is 14.2. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
opts: Start oral ferrous sulfate 200 mg TID
Hemoglobin electrophoresis to evaluate for thalassemia trait
Bone marrow biopsy with iron stain
Start folic acid 5 mg daily and reassure
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: In pregnancy, microcytic anemia with normal ferritin and borderline Mentzer index deserves Hb electrophoresis to rule out thalassemia trait before empirically giving iron
discriminator: Normal ferritin (95) rules out IDA as the cause of microcytosis. Mentzer 14.2 is borderline. Hb electrophoresis clarifies the diagnosis.

stem: A 75-year-old male presents with confusion, polyuria, and constipation. Labs: calcium 13.2 mg/dL, creatinine 2.2 mg/dL, Hb 9.5 g/dL. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal M-spike. Skeletal survey reveals lytic lesions in the skull. Bone marrow biopsy shows 40% plasma cells. Which of the following therapeutic agents should be used with the greatest caution in this patient's current renal state?
subject: Medicine-Hematology
concept: Myeloma with renal impairment — zoledronic acid is nephrotoxic and contraindicated in severe renal impairment; bortezomib is preferred; lenalidomide requires dose adjustment
discriminator: Bisphosphonates (especially zoledronic acid) can worsen renal function and are contraindicated if CrCl < 35; bortezomib is safe in renal failure

stem: A 68-year-old male with hypertension and atrial fibrillation (not on anticoagulation) presents with sudden-onset right-sided weakness and global aphasia. Symptoms began 1 hour ago. CT head non-contrast shows no hyperdensity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Review
concept: Ischemic vs hemorrhagic stroke: CT discriminator
discriminator: CT non-contrast showing no hyperdensity rules out hemorrhage, making ischemic stroke the diagnosis. Cortical signs (global aphasia) indicate large artery (MCA) territory, not lacunar.

stem: A 55-year-old female presents with sudden-onset right-sided weakness and numbness affecting her face, arm, and leg equally. She has no aphasia, no neglect, and no visual field deficit. CT is negative for hemorrhage. What is the most likely stroke subtype?
subject: Medicine-Review
concept: Large artery vs lacunar stroke: cortical signs
discriminator: Pure motor hemiparesis without cortical signs (no aphasia, neglect, or visual deficit) = lacunar stroke, not large artery territory.

stem: A 62-year-old diabetic male had an episode of right arm weakness and slurred speech that lasted 45 minutes and then completely resolved. He is now asymptomatic. CT head is normal. What is the single best test to confirm the diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Review
concept: TIA vs stroke: DWI-MRI discriminator
discriminator: DWI-MRI: restricted diffusion = completed infarct (stroke); no restricted diffusion = TIA.

stem: A 72-year-old male presents with acute-onset right hemiparesis and expressive aphasia. Symptoms started 3 hours ago. CT head shows no hemorrhage. NIHSS is 12. BP is 195/115 mmHg. Glucose is 110 mg/dL. He had hip replacement surgery 3 weeks ago. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Administer IV alteplase immediately — he is within the 4.5-hour window
Lower BP to < 185/110 with IV labetalol, then re-evaluate for thrombolysis
Hold thrombolysis — recent surgery is an absolute contraindication
Give IV alteplase and lower BP simultaneously
subject: Medicine-Review
concept: Thrombolysis in ischemic stroke: BP threshold and contraindications
discriminator: BP must be < 185/110 before thrombolysis. Recent surgery > 14 days ago is not an absolute contraindication.

stem: A 22-year-old college student presents with fever 39.5°C, severe headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia for 24 hours. There is no rash. CSF shows: WBC 1850/μL (85% PMNs), glucose 22 mg/dL, protein 180 mg/dL. Gram stain shows Gram-positive diplococci. What is the most likely causative organism?
subject: Medicine-Review
concept: Bacterial vs viral meningitis: CSF pattern and organism identification
discriminator: CSF with PMN predominance, low glucose, and high protein = bacterial meningitis. Gram-positive diplococci = Streptococcus pneumoniae.

stem: A 30-year-old immunocompetent female presents with fever, confusion, and seizures for 3 days. CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose and mild protein elevation. MRI shows temporal lobe hyperintensity on T2/FLAIR. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Review
concept: Meningitis vs encephalitis: brain parenchymal involvement
discriminator: Encephalitis = brain parenchyma involvement (seizures, confusion, MRI changes). Meningitis = meningeal signs without parenchymal changes. Temporal lobe T2 hyperintensity = HSV encephalitis.

stem: A 23-year-old male with epilepsy is brought to the ED with continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizure activity that has been ongoing for 8 minutes. His girlfriend says he seized briefly 10 minutes ago but did not fully regain consciousness. What is the most appropriate first-line medication?
subject: Medicine-Review
concept: Status epilepticus management: first-line therapy
discriminator: Status epilepticus = seizure > 5 min or recurrent without recovery. First-line: IV benzodiazepine (lorazepam or diazepam).

stem: A 65-year-old male presents with a 1-year history of bilateral hand tremor. The tremor is worse when he is reaching for objects or holding a cup. He has no bradykinesia, rigidity, or postural instability. Family history is positive for tremor. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Review
concept: Parkinson disease vs essential tremor: tremor characteristics
discriminator: Essential tremor = action/postural tremor (worse with use), bilateral, family history, no parkinsonian features. Parkinson = rest tremor, asymmetric, bradykinesia, rigidity.

stem: A 35-year-old female presents with fluctuating double vision and drooping eyelids that worsen as the day progresses. She has difficulty chewing dinner but breakfast is fine. On exam, she has bilateral ptosis worse after upward gaze. Reflexes are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Review
concept: Myasthenia gravis vs GBS: fatigability vs areflexia
discriminator: MG = fluctuating weakness, worse with fatigue/evening, ocular onset common, reflexes intact. GBS = ascending, areflexic, not fatigable.

stem: A 28-year-old male presents with acute ascending numbness and weakness in both legs over 4 days, now involving his arms. He had diarrhoea 2 weeks ago. On exam, he has areflexia in all four limbs and no plantar response. What CSF finding would most strongly support the diagnosis?
opts: High protein with normal cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation)
subject: Medicine-Review
concept: GBS: albuminocytologic dissociation in CSF
discriminator: GBS CSF shows high protein with normal WBC count (albuminocytologic dissociation), typically after the first week.

stem: A 45-year-old male with type 2 diabetes presents with polyuria, polydipsia, and confusion for 5 days. Glucose is 820 mg/dL, serum osmolality 335 mOsm/kg, pH 7.36, HCO3 22, serum ketones negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Medicine-Review
concept: DKA vs HHS: ketosis and acid-base status discriminator
discriminator: HHS: pH > 7.3, HCO3 > 15, no ketones, glucose often > 600, osmolality > 320. DKA: pH < 7.3, HCO3 < 15, ketones positive, AG metabolic acidosis.

stem: A 32-year-old female presents with weight loss, palpitations, heat intolerance, and tremor for 3 months. On exam, she has diffuse goiter, lid lag, and proptosis. TSH is < 0.01, T4 is 22 μg/dL. What test would best distinguish Graves disease from toxic nodular goiter?
subject: Medicine-Review
concept: Graves vs toxic nodular goiter: TSH receptor antibody
discriminator: Graves = positive TSH-R Ab, diffuse goiter, ophthalmopathy, pretibial myxedema. Toxic nodular = no eye signs, nodular goiter, older age, negative TSH-R Ab.
