stem: What is the critical time window for revascularization in acute limb ischemia before irreversible muscle necrosis occurs?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Time window revascularization 6 hours
discriminator: Irreversible ischemia occurs after approximately 6 hours of complete ischemia

stem: A 55-year-old smoker has worsening claudication over 3 days culminating in rest pain. The leg is pale and cool below the knee with reduced but audible Doppler signals. He had a prior diagnosis of PAD with ABI 0.6. Most likely pathology?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Acute-on-chronic thrombosis in PAD
discriminator: Gradual worsening + known PAD + claudication history = acute thrombosis on chronic stenosis

stem: After successful Fogarty embolectomy for acute leg ischemia, the patient develops severe calf pain, tense swelling, and pain on passive dorsiflexion of the foot. What has occurred?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Compartment syndrome after revascularization
discriminator: Revascularization + tense calf + pain on passive stretch = compartment syndrome

stem: Acute limb ischemia with fixed staining (mottling) and rigor in the calf muscles indicates what?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Irreversible ischemia amputation indication
discriminator: Fixed staining + rigor (muscle rigor mortis) = irreversible necrosis = primary amputation

stem: Where do arterial emboli most commonly lodge?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Embolus lodgement sites bifurcation points
discriminator: Emboli lodge at bifurcations — common femoral bifurcation most common in lower limb

stem: A 60-year-old man with AF presents with bilateral leg pain, pallor, and absent femoral pulses. Both legs are cold and paralyzed. What is the most likely site of occlusion?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Saddle embolus aortic bifurcation
discriminator: Bilateral leg ischemia + absent femoral pulses = saddle embolus at aortic bifurcation

stem: Which imaging modality is most appropriate for confirming the diagnosis of acute limb ischemia before intervention?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: CT angiography for acute limb ischemia
discriminator: CT angiography = best modality for acute limb ischemia (fast, defines anatomy, guides intervention)

stem: A patient with acute limb ischemia undergoes successful revascularization. Six hours later the calf is tense and painful with pain on passive stretch. Compartment pressure is 35 mmHg. What is the next step?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Compartment syndrome pressure > 30 mmHg fasciotomy
discriminator: Pressure > 30 mmHg + clinical signs = fasciotomy

stem: Which of the following is a contraindication to intra-arterial thrombolysis for acute limb ischemia?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Thrombolysis contraindications
discriminator: Recent surgery (< 14 days) = contraindication to thrombolysis due to bleeding risk

stem: A 75-year-old bedbound nursing home resident develops acute leg ischemia. The leg shows fixed mottling up to the mid-thigh with rigor. There is a clear demarcation line. What is the management?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Irreversible ischemia palliation vs amputation
discriminator: Irreversible ischemia in bedbound patient with clear demarcation = palliation appropriate

stem: What is the Fogarty catheter made of and how does it work?
opts: Rigid metal tube — cores out the clot
Balloon-tipped catheter — inflated beyond clot, withdrawn to extract embolus
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Fogarty catheter mechanism
discriminator: Fogarty = balloon-tipped catheter passed beyond clot, inflated, withdrawn

stem: A patient with acute leg ischemia has absent motor function and sensation below the knee. Doppler signals are absent. What category of ischemia?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Rutherford classification acute ischemia
discriminator: Absent motor + sensory + Doppler signals = irreversible (Rutherford class III)

stem: What is the immediate medical management to give while preparing for embolectomy in acute embolic limb ischemia?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Heparin in acute limb ischemia
discriminator: Give IV heparin immediately to prevent thrombus propagation

stem: A 45-year-old man with popliteal artery aneurysm presents with acute leg ischemia. Duplex shows thrombosed popliteal aneurysm. Which feature suggests thrombosis rather than embolus?
opts: Palpable pulsatile mass in popliteal fossa
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Popliteal aneurysm thrombosis
discriminator: Popliteal aneurysm + acute ischemia = thrombosis of aneurysm in situ

stem: Following embolectomy, what signs indicate successful revascularization?
opts: Return of pulse, pink color, warmth
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Successful revascularization signs
discriminator: Return of pulse, color, warmth, capillary refill, and pain relief all indicate success

stem: A 50-year-old smoker has a 3-day history of progressive right calf pain now at rest. The foot is pale with absent posterior tibial pulse but Doppler signals audible at ankle. ABI is 0.35. He had ABI 0.55 one month ago. What happened?
opts: Acute thrombosis of previously stenotic superficial femoral artery
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Acute-on-chronic ischemia with ABI change
discriminator: Rapid ABI decline (0.55 → 0.35) in days = acute thrombosis on chronic PAD

stem: After revascularization of an acutely ischemic leg, myoglobinuria and acute kidney injury develop. What is the underlying mechanism?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Reperfusion rhabdomyolysis AKI
discriminator: Post-revascularization + myoglobinuria + AKI = rhabdomyolysis from reperfusion

stem: A patient with acute leg ischemia is found to have a thrombosed popliteal aneurysm with distal embolization. What is the best surgical approach?
opts: Popliteal aneurysm exclusion with bypass + distal embolectomy
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Popliteal aneurysm with distal emboli management
discriminator: Thrombosed popliteal aneurysm + distal emboli = bypass + distal embolectomy

stem: A 40-year-old man with no vascular risk factors has acute right arm ischemia after cardiac catheterization via the brachial artery. What is the most likely cause?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Iatrogenic arterial thrombosis post-catheterization
discriminator: Acute arm ischemia after brachial artery catheterization = iatrogenic thrombosis

stem: A patient develops acute leg ischemia 12 hours after repair of a ruptured AAA. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Embolus from mural thrombus in AAA sac
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Distal embolization after AAA repair
discriminator: Post-AAA repair + acute ischemia = trash foot from atheroembolism (mural thrombus dislodgment)

stem: What is the earliest and most reliable sign of acute compartment syndrome?
opts: Pain out of proportion to injury with pain on passive stretch
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Earliest sign compartment syndrome pain out of proportion
discriminator: Pain out of proportion + pain on passive stretch = earliest and most reliable sign

stem: A 25-year-old man with a tibial shaft fracture in a cast develops severe calf pain, worse with passive toe dorsiflexion. Distal pulses are palpable. What should be done first?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Initial management remove constriction
discriminator: Suspected compartment syndrome → remove constricting bandages/cast first

stem: After splitting the cast, the patient in the previous question still has severe pain with passive stretch. Compartment pressure is 35 mmHg. What is the definitive treatment?
opts: Urgent fasciotomy of all involved compartments
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Fasciotomy indication pressure > 30 mmHg
discriminator: Persistent symptoms + pressure > 30 mmHg after cast removal = fasciotomy

stem: What is the compartment pressure threshold for fasciotomy?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Compartment pressure threshold
discriminator: > 30 mmHg = threshold for fasciotomy

stem: Which statement about distal pulses in compartment syndrome is TRUE?
opts: Pulses are present in early compartment syndrome
Pulse absence is the earliest sign
Pulses should be checked hourly and fasciotomy done when absent
Palpable pulses rule out compartment syndrome
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Pulses in early compartment syndrome
discriminator: Pulses are present in early compartment syndrome — loss is a late sign

stem: Untreated compartment syndrome of the forearm leads to which long-term deformity?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Volkmann contracture after compartment syndrome
discriminator: Untreated forearm compartment syndrome → Volkmann ischemic contracture (flexion deformity)

stem: A patient with a crush injury to the leg presents with dark urine, elevated CK, and acute kidney injury. What is the diagnosis?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Crush syndrome rhabdomyolysis AKI
discriminator: Crush injury + dark urine + high CK + AKI = rhabdomyolysis (crush syndrome)

stem: A 30-year-old man with a forearm fracture develops compartment syndrome. Which compartments of the forearm must be released during fasciotomy?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Forearm compartments fasciotomy
discriminator: Forearm fasciotomy = release both volar and dorsal compartments

stem: How many compartments are there in the leg (calf)?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Leg compartments number
discriminator: Leg has 4 compartments: anterior, lateral, superficial posterior, deep posterior

stem: A patient with circumferential full-thickness burn of the forearm has weak pulses and compartment pressure 42 mmHg. What is the correct surgical procedure?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Escharotomy vs fasciotomy for burns
discriminator: Circumferential burn + elevated pressure = escharotomy (incise eschar, not fascia)

stem: Which of the following is NOT a cause of acute compartment syndrome?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Compartment syndrome causes
discriminator: Chronic venous insufficiency does not cause acute compartment syndrome

stem: A fasciotomy wound is left open after surgery. When is delayed primary closure typically performed?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Fasciotomy wound closure timing
discriminator: Delayed primary closure of fasciotomy at 3-5 days

stem: Which nerve is most commonly affected in anterior compartment syndrome of the leg?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Anterior compartment deep peroneal nerve
discriminator: Anterior leg compartment contains deep peroneal nerve

stem: A patient develops compartment syndrome from a bleeding disorder (hemophilia). What is the specific pathophysiologic mechanism?
opts: Hemorrhage into the compartment causing increased pressure
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Compartment syndrome from bleeding
discriminator: Hemophilia → spontaneous bleeding into compartment → increased pressure

stem: Which of the following is a late sign of compartment syndrome indicating irreversible damage?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Late signs paralysis pulselessness
discriminator: Paralysis and pulselessness = late signs = irreversible damage

stem: What is the critical time window before irreversible muscle necrosis in compartment syndrome?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Time window irreversible necrosis compartment syndrome
discriminator: Irreversible muscle necrosis after 6-8 hours of compartment syndrome

stem: A patient with compartment syndrome has pain out of proportion, tense compartment, and pain on passive stretch. Neurologic exam is normal. What category is this?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Early compartment syndrome classification
discriminator: Pain + tense + pain on stretch but normal neuro = early compartment syndrome = urgent fasciotomy

stem: What is the most reliable diagnostic method for compartment syndrome when clinical signs are equivocal?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Compartment pressure measurement gold standard
discriminator: Compartment pressure measurement = gold standard for equivocal cases

stem: Crush syndrome from a prolonged crush injury releases which substance into the circulation causing systemic complications?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Crush syndrome myoglobin release
discriminator: Myoglobin from damaged muscle → myoglobinuria → AKI

stem: A patient develops compartment syndrome after reperfusion of an acutely ischemic leg. What is the underlying mechanism?
opts: Increased capillary permeability from ischemic endothelial damage → edema
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Reperfusion compartment syndrome mechanism
discriminator: Reperfusion → endothelial injury → capillary leak → edema in fixed compartment

stem: A 20-year-old man has bilateral leg compartment syndrome after a prolonged crush injury from a building collapse. He develops dark urine, oliguria, and serum K+ 6.8 mEq/L. Which electrolyte abnormality is immediately life-threatening?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Crush syndrome hyperkalemia life-threatening
discriminator: Crush syndrome + K+ 6.8 = life-threatening hyperkalemia from muscle breakdown

stem: A patient with compartment syndrome undergoes fasciotomy. The muscle bulges out of the wound and is dusky but contracts when stimulated. What should be done?
opts: Leave muscle in place, close skin loosely
Leave wound open, muscle viable, close later
Apply tight dressing to reduce bulging
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Fasciotomy muscle viability assessment
discriminator: Muscle contracts when stimulated = viable = leave in place, leave wound open

stem: Chronic exertional compartment syndrome differs from acute compartment syndrome in that:
opts: It presents during exercise and resolves with rest
It has pressure > 30 mmHg at rest
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Chronic exertional compartment syndrome
discriminator: Chronic = exercise-induced pain that resolves at rest. No emergency

stem: A 60-year-old man on warfarin for AF develops spontaneous calf pain and tense swelling after minor trauma. INR is 4.5. Compartment pressure is 38 mmHg. What is the management?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Compartment syndrome on anticoagulation
discriminator: Compartment syndrome on warfarin → fasciotomy + correct coagulopathy simultaneously

stem: Which of the following is the best management for preventing AKI in a patient with crush syndrome and rhabdomyolysis?
opts: Aggressive IV crystalloid hydration ± sodium bicarbonate
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Crush syndrome AKI prevention hydration
discriminator: Aggressive hydration (crystalloid) ± alkalinization = mainstay of rhabdomyolysis AKI prevention

stem: A 25-year-old man sustains a midshaft humeral fracture. He cannot extend his wrist or MCP joints and has sensory loss over the dorsal first web space. Which nerve is injured?
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Radial nerve injury — midshaft humerus fracture
discriminator: Wrist drop (cannot extend wrist/MCP) + dorsal 1st web sensory loss = radial nerve

stem: A patient with a surgical neck of humerus fracture cannot abduct the shoulder and has sensory loss over the lateral shoulder (regimental badge area). Which nerve is injured?
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Axillary nerve injury — surgical neck humerus
discriminator: Cannot abduct (deltoid) + regimental badge sensory loss = axillary nerve

stem: A child has a supracondylar humerus fracture and cannot make the OK sign (thumb-index pinch). Which nerve is injured?
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: AIN injury — supracondylar fracture
discriminator: Cannot make OK sign = AIN injury (FPL + FDP index/middle)

stem: A patient with medial epicondyle fracture presents with clawing of the ring and little fingers and sensory loss over the medial 1.5 fingers. Which nerve is injured?
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Ulnar nerve injury — medial epicondyle fracture
discriminator: Claw hand (ring/little) + medial 1.5 finger sensory = ulnar nerve

stem: A patient with fibular neck fracture presents with foot drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot. Which nerve is injured?
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Common peroneal nerve injury — fibular neck fracture
discriminator: Foot drop (cannot dorsiflex) + dorsal foot sensory loss = common peroneal nerve

stem: A 70-year-old woman falls and sustains a displaced intracapsular NOF fracture. She is fit and active. What is the most appropriate surgical management?
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Displaced NOF fracture in fit elderly — hemiarthroplasty
discriminator: Displaced intracapsular NOF = disrupts blood supply → hemiarthroplasty (replace, not fix)

stem: A 75-year-old woman has an undisplaced intracapsular NOF fracture. She has mild dementia but is mobile. What is the most appropriate management?
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Undisplaced NOF fracture management
discriminator: Undisplaced intracapsular NOF → cannulated screws (preserve blood supply)

stem: A 20-year-old man sustains a femoral shaft fracture. On day 2, he develops hypoxia, confusion, and petechiae over the chest and axillae. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Fat embolism syndrome — clinical presentation
discriminator: Long bone fracture + day 2 hypoxia + petechiae + confusion = fat embolism syndrome

stem: What is the pathognomonic triad of fat embolism syndrome?
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Fat embolism triad
discriminator: Hypoxia + petechiae + confusion = classic fat embolism triad

stem: A 10-year-old child has a fracture through the growth plate (physis) that extends into the metaphysis. According to the Salter-Harris classification, which type is this?
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Salter-Harris classification
discriminator: Fracture through physis + metaphysis = Salter-Harris Type II

stem: Which Salter-Harris type has the worst prognosis for growth disturbance?
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Salter-Harris Type V — crush injury worst prognosis
discriminator: Type V (crush of physis) has the worst prognosis for growth arrest

stem: A 6-year-old child falls on an outstretched hand and sustains a fracture. X-ray shows a break on one side of the cortex with the opposite cortex intact (bent). What type of fracture is this?
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Greenstick fracture — pediatric incomplete fracture
discriminator: Incomplete fracture with one cortex broken, opposite bent = greenstick

stem: A 35-year-old man sustains an open tibial fracture in a road traffic accident. Which of the following is the most important immediate management step?
opts: MRI to assess soft tissue injury
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Open fracture management — wound debridement
discriminator: Open fracture → urgent surgical debridement and irrigation is the priority

stem: Which of the following correctly describes a comminuted fracture?
opts: A fracture that extends into a joint
A fracture with more than two bone fragments
A fracture through the growth plate
A spiral fracture caused by twisting
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Comminuted fracture definition
discriminator: Comminuted = bone broken into 3 or more fragments

stem: Which of the following describes the stages of fracture healing in correct order?
opts: Hematoma → granulation → soft callus → hard callus → remodeling
Granulation → hematoma → soft callus → hard callus → remodeling
Hematoma → soft callus → hard callus → granulation → remodeling
Inflammation → soft callus → remodeling → hard callus
Hematoma → remodeling → soft callus → hard callus
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Stages of fracture healing
discriminator: Hematoma → granulation tissue → soft callus (cartilage) → hard callus (bone) → remodeling

stem: A 60-year-old woman falls on an outstretched hand and presents with dinner fork deformity of the wrist. What is the most likely fracture?
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Colles fracture — dinner fork deformity
discriminator: Dinner fork deformity after FOOSH = Colles fracture (distal radius, dorsal displacement)

stem: Which of the following is a late complication of untreated Colles fracture?
opts: Malunion with persistent dinner fork deformity
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Colles fracture complication — malunion
discriminator: Colles fractures commonly malunite if inadequately reduced, leaving dorsal deformity

stem: A fracture that fails to heal within the expected time period (usually 6-9 months) is called:
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Delayed union definition
discriminator: Delayed union = healing taking longer than expected; nonunion = no healing at all

stem: A 15-year-old boy presents with knee pain. X-ray shows a sunburst appearance and Codman triangle at the distal femoral metaphysis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Osteosarcoma — sunburst + Codman triangle
discriminator: Teenage male + distal femur metaphysis + sunburst + Codman triangle = osteosarcoma

stem: A 55-year-old man has osteoarthritis of the hip and is scheduled for elective total hip replacement. What is the most important DVT prophylaxis for this surgery?
opts: No prophylaxis needed for elective surgery
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: DVT prophylaxis in orthopedic surgery
discriminator: Major orthopedic surgery → LMWH prophylaxis (enoxaparin) is first-line

stem: A 45-year-old man has an open fracture of the tibia contaminated with soil. Tetanus immunization status is unknown. What should be administered?
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Tetanus prophylaxis in open fractures
discriminator: Unknown immunization + contaminated wound = both tetanus toxoid + TIG

stem: A 7-year-old boy falls and sustains a supracondylar humerus fracture. The hand is pale with absent radial pulse. What is the most important immediate step?
opts: Emergency open reduction and vascular exploration
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Supracondylar fracture with vascular compromise — emergency OR
discriminator: Supracondylar fracture + pale hand + absent pulse = vascular emergency → immediate exploration

stem: Which of the following is the most common complication of supracondylar humerus fractures?
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Supracondylar fracture complication — Volkmann contracture
discriminator: Volkmann contracture from missed compartment syndrome is the most feared complication of supracondylar fracture

stem: An 80-year-old woman falls and has pain in the left hip. She cannot bear weight. The leg is shortened and externally rotated. X-ray shows no obvious fracture. What is the next best step?
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Occult NOF fracture investigation
discriminator: Elderly + hip pain + inability to bear weight + shortened externally rotated leg but negative X-ray = occult fracture → MRI

stem: A 30-year-old man with a midshaft humerus fracture and radial nerve palsy is managed conservatively. After 4 months, there is no sign of nerve recovery. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Continue conservative management for another 3 months
Surgical exploration of the radial nerve
subject: Surgery-Orthopedics
concept: Radial nerve injury — investigation for recovery
discriminator: No nerve recovery at 4 months → EMG/NCS to assess nerve function

stem: A 28-year-old man is brought to the ER after a high-speed MVC. BP 85/50, HR 130. FAST shows free fluid in Morrison pouch. He transiently improves with 2 L IV fluids then deteriorates. What is the next step?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Unstable trauma FAST+ management
discriminator: Transient responder + FAST+ = unstable → laparotomy, not CT

stem: Which of the following is the most commonly injured solid organ in blunt abdominal trauma?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Most commonly injured solid organ in blunt trauma
discriminator: Spleen = most common solid organ injured in blunt abdominal trauma

stem: A 30-year-old man has blunt trauma to the left lower chest. He has left shoulder tip pain. What is this sign called?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Kehr sign — referred shoulder pain from splenic injury
discriminator: Left shoulder tip pain after splenic trauma = Kehr sign

stem: During FAST scan in a supine trauma patient, where does free intraperitoneal fluid first collect?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Morrison pouch — most dependent space on FAST
discriminator: In supine position, Morrison pouch (hepatorenal recess) is the most dependent peritoneal space

stem: A 32-year-old man with blunt abdominal trauma is hemodynamically stable with a positive FAST. CT shows a Grade II splenic laceration. What is the most appropriate management?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Conservative management of low-grade splenic injury in stable patient
discriminator: Stable patient + Grade II = conservative management

stem: In AAST splenic injury grading, a shattered spleen with hilar injury corresponds to which grade?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: AAST splenic injury grading
discriminator: Shattered spleen with hilar injury = Grade V

stem: A 35-year-old man with blunt trauma is hemodynamically stable. FAST is positive. What is the next imaging investigation?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Stable patient with positive FAST needs CT for grading
discriminator: Stable + FAST+ = CT with IV contrast for injury grading

stem: What is the most common cause of splenic injury?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Most common cause of splenic injury
discriminator: Blunt trauma (RTA, falls) is far more common than penetrating or pathological causes

stem: A 45-year-old man has blunt abdominal trauma. CT shows Grade IV splenic injury with active contrast extravasation. He remains hemodynamically stable. What is the best next step?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Angioembolization for high-grade stable splenic injury with active bleeding
discriminator: Grade IV + active extravasation + stable = angioembolization

stem: A 50-year-old woman undergoes emergency splenectomy after a high-grade splenic injury. When should she receive post-splenectomy vaccinations?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Post-splenectomy vaccination timing
discriminator: Emergency splenectomy → vaccinate 2 weeks after surgery

stem: Against which of the following organisms must post-splenectomy patients be vaccinated?
opts: Strep pneumoniae, H. influenzae type b, Neisseria meningitidis
Bordetella pertussis, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Clostridium tetani
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Encapsulated organisms requiring post-splenectomy vaccination
discriminator: The spleen clears encapsulated bacteria: pneumococcus, H. flu type b, meningococcus

stem: A 60-year-old man had splenectomy 3 months ago. He presents with fever, rigors, rusty sputum, and confusion. CXR shows lobar consolidation. Blood culture shows Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: OPSI from Strep pneumoniae in post-splenectomy patient
discriminator: Post-splenectomy + fever + rigors + Gram+ lancet diplococci = OPSI

stem: Which encapsulated organism is the most common cause of OPSI?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Most common OPSI organism
discriminator: Strep pneumo is the #1 cause of OPSI (Gram+ lancet-shaped diplococcus)

stem: A 70-year-old woman with history of splenectomy presents with fever and hypotension. IV antibiotics are started. Which of the following should be included in the empiric regimen?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Empiric antibiotics for suspected OPSI
discriminator: Suspected OPSI needs broad coverage including ceftriaxone (pneumococcus, Hib, meningococcus) + vancomycin (for resistant pneumococcus)

stem: What is the most important first-line imaging modality in the initial assessment of a trauma patient with suspected intra-abdominal injury?
opts: Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma (FAST)
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: FAST as first-line imaging in trauma
discriminator: FAST is bedside, rapid, non-invasive, and does not require moving the unstable patient

stem: A 22-year-old man is brought in after RTA. He is hypotensive and FAST positive. The team decides to take him to the OR immediately. What is the most likely finding on entering the abdomen?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Spleen is most commonly injured solid organ in blunt trauma
discriminator: Blunt RTA + hemodynamic instability + FAST+ → splenic rupture is most likely

stem: A 38-year-old man is involved in a MVC. He has left lower rib fractures. On examination, there is tenderness over the left upper abdomen. What solid organ is most at risk?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Left lower rib fractures → splenic injury association
discriminator: Left lower rib fractures + LUQ tenderness = splenic injury

stem: A trauma patient arrives with BP 90/60, HR 115 after 2 L IV fluids. FAST is negative. The patient has no external injuries but has a pelvic fracture. What is the most likely source of blood loss?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: FAST negative with pelvic fracture = retroperitoneal bleed
discriminator: Negative FAST + pelvic fracture + instability = retroperitoneal hemorrhage (FAST does not detect retroperitoneal blood)

stem: A patient with splenic injury is being managed conservatively. Which of the following would indicate failure of non-operative management and the need for intervention?
opts: Hb drop of 1 g/dL over 24 hours
Need for 2 units PRBC over 24 hours
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Indicators of failed non-operative management in splenic injury
discriminator: Need for >2 units PRBC or hemodynamic instability = failed conservative management

stem: In which of the following scenarios would splenorrhaphy (splenic repair) be most appropriate?
opts: Hemodynamically unstable patient with Grade IV injury
Stable patient with Grade I superficial laceration found at laparotomy
Any splenic injury in a patient with coagulopathy
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Indications for splenorrhaphy
discriminator: Splenorrhaphy is attempted in stable patients with low-grade injuries where the spleen is salvageable

stem: A 55-year-old man undergoes elective splenectomy for hereditary spherocytosis. When should his pneumococcal vaccine be administered?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Pre-elective splenectomy vaccination timing
discriminator: Elective splenectomy → vaccinate 2 weeks BEFORE surgery for optimal immune response

stem: Post-splenectomy, which laboratory finding is expected as a normal physiological consequence?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Post-splenectomy thrombocytosis
discriminator: Spleen sequesters platelets; after splenectomy, platelet count rises (thrombocytosis)

stem: A 6-year-old child with sickle cell disease is functionally asplenic. Which antibiotic prophylaxis is most important to prevent OPSI?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Antibiotic prophylaxis in asplenic patients (children)
discriminator: Children with asplenia need prophylactic penicillin to prevent pneumococcal OPSI

stem: Which of the following is the correct target for the pneumococcal vaccine series in post-splenectomy adults?
opts: Pneumococcal vaccine is not needed in adults
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Pneumococcal vaccination in asplenic adults
discriminator: Asplenic adults need both PCV13 (conjugate) and PPSV23 (polysaccharide) for optimal coverage

stem: A 40-year-old woman post-splenectomy presents with fever and rigors 18 months after surgery. BP 80/50, HR 130. Blood cultures are pending. Which of the following is the most important immediate intervention?
opts: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (ceftriaxone + vancomycin) and ICU admission
CT abdomen to rule out intra-abdominal abscess
Increase oral fluid intake and paracetamol
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: OPSI is a medical emergency requiring aggressive treatment

stem: A 25-year-old man is brought in after a road traffic accident. He opens eyes only to pain, makes incomprehensible sounds, and withdraws from pain. What is his GCS score?

stem: A patient with head injury has GCS 8. What is the first step in management?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: GCS ≤ 8 requires airway protection
discriminator: GCS ≤ 8 = severe TBI = secure airway first (intubation)

stem: Which of the following describes the classic CT appearance of an extradural (epidural) hematoma?

concept: Extradural hematoma CT appearance

stem: A 25-year-old man had a brief loss of consciousness after a head injury, then fully recovered. Two hours later, he developed severe headache, vomiting, and became unconscious. CT shows a biconvex hyperdense lesion in the temporoparietal region. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Extradural hematoma with lucid interval
discriminator: Lucid interval + biconvex CT = extradural hematoma (middle meningeal artery bleed)

stem: An extradural hematoma typically results from injury to which artery?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Middle meningeal artery source of EDH
discriminator: Middle meningeal artery (branch of maxillary artery) runs in the temporal bone

stem: Which of the following is true regarding subdural hematoma (SDH) compared to extradural hematoma (EDH)?
opts: SDH is arterial; EDH is venous
SDH is crescent-shaped and crosses sutures; EDH is biconvex and limited by sutures
SDH has a classic lucid interval; EDH does not
SDH requires emergency craniotomy; EDH can be managed with burr hole
SDH is limited by sutures; EDH crosses sutures
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: SDH vs EDH CT characteristics
discriminator: SDH = crescent, crosses sutures (bridging veins); EDH = biconvex, limited by sutures (arterial)

stem: A 70-year-old woman on warfarin fell 3 weeks ago. She presents with gradual confusion, headache, and mild left-sided weakness. CT shows a crescent-shaped hypodense collection over the right convexity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Chronic subdural hematoma in elderly
discriminator: Elderly + fall weeks ago + gradual confusion + crescent hypodense = chronic SDH

stem: A patient with an EDH and significant midline shift requires which surgical intervention?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: EDH management — emergency craniotomy
discriminator: EDH with midline shift = time-critical emergency craniotomy

stem: Which of the following describes Cushing reflex?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Cushing reflex — raised ICP late sign
discriminator: Cushing triad: HTN + bradycardia + irregular breathing = late sign of raised ICP

stem: Which of the following is first-line medical therapy for raised intracranial pressure?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: First-line pharmacological ICP management
discriminator: Mannitol (osmotic diuretic) is first-line medical therapy for raised ICP

stem: A patient with severe TBI and raised ICP is being ventilated. What is the target PaCO2 for mild hyperventilation?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Target PaCO2 in hyperventilation for raised ICP
discriminator: Target PaCO2 30-35 mmHg — mild hyperventilation only

stem: A patient with raised ICP should be positioned with the head elevated at what angle and why?
opts: Flat supine — to maintain cerebral perfusion
Head elevated 30°, midline — to promote jugular venous drainage
Head turned to the side — to protect airway
Trendelenburg — to increase cerebral blood flow
Head elevated 90° — to reduce aspiration risk
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Head positioning for raised ICP management
discriminator: Elevated 30° midline optimizes jugular venous outflow and reduces ICP

stem: Which of the following is a late sign of uncal herniation?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Cushing reflex as late herniation sign
discriminator: Cushing reflex indicates brainstem compression and is a late, pre-terminal sign

stem: A patient with head trauma has bilateral periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes) and retroauricular ecchymosis (Battle sign). What is the most likely underlying injury?
opts: Base of skull fracture (anterior cranial fossa)
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Signs of basilar skull fracture
discriminator: Raccoon eyes + Battle sign = base of skull fracture

stem: A patient with head trauma has clear fluid draining from the nose. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Send fluid for beta-2 transferrin to confirm CSF leak
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: CSF rhinorrhea diagnosis — beta-2 transferrin
discriminator: Clear nasal drainage after head injury = CSF leak → confirm with beta-2 transferrin

stem: Which of the following is the most serious complication of a CSF leak following basilar skull fracture?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Meningitis risk from CSF leak
discriminator: CSF leak creates a communication between the subarachnoid space and the external environment → meningitis risk

stem: A skull fracture that is depressed below the level of the inner table of the skull requires elevation if associated with which of the following?
opts: Depressed below the outer table only
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Indications for depressed skull fracture elevation
discriminator: Elevation of depressed skull fracture is indicated if there is an underlying hematoma, dural tear, or significant brain compression

stem: Which of the following is a contraindication to lumbar puncture in a patient with suspected raised ICP?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: LP contraindication in raised ICP
discriminator: Focal signs or papilledema suggests raised ICP → LP risks brain herniation

stem: A 45-year-old man with severe TBI has refractory raised ICP despite mannitol, head elevation, and mild hyperventilation. What is the next surgical option?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Decompressive craniectomy for refractory raised ICP
discriminator: Refractory raised ICP after maximal medical therapy → decompressive craniectomy

stem: An 80-year-old man on antiplatelet therapy has a minor fall. He presents 4 weeks later with progressive confusion, gait disturbance, and urinary incontinence. CT shows bilateral crescent-shaped hypodense collections. What is the diagnosis?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Chronic SDH with classic triad (confusion, gait disturbance, incontinence)
discriminator: Elderly + fall + progressive confusion + gait disturbance + urinary incontinence + crescent hypodense = chronic SDH

stem: Which of the following is the most important reason to document GCS before intubation and sedation in a head injury patient?
opts: It determines the need for ICP monitoring
It provides baseline for prognosis and management decisions
It determines which imaging modality to use
It determines the need for antiseizure prophylaxis
It determines the need for steroids
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Why GCS must be documented before sedation
discriminator: Sedation masks neurological function; GCS before sedation is the true baseline for all subsequent decisions

stem: A 30-year-old man has GCS E4 V5 M6 after a fall. He has no focal deficits but has vomited twice. CT head is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Discharge home with head injury advice
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Mild TBI management with vomiting
discriminator: GCS 15 but vomiting after head injury = admit for observation

stem: A patient with head trauma has a unilateral fixed and dilated pupil (right) and left-sided hemiparesis. Which type of herniation is most likely?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Uncal herniation — CN III palsy + contralateral hemiparesis
discriminator: Ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil (CN III) + contralateral hemiparesis (cerebral peduncle compression) = uncal herniation

stem: Which medication should be avoided in the management of traumatic raised ICP?
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: Corticosteroids not indicated in traumatic brain injury
discriminator: Steroids increase mortality in TBI and are contraindicated

stem: A 22-year-old motorcyclist is found unconscious at the scene. GCS 6 (E1 V2 M3). BP 150/90, HR 55, irregular breathing pattern. CT shows a large biconvex hyperdense lesion in the left temporoparietal region with 12 mm midline shift. What is the most appropriate immediate next step?
opts: Burr hole drainage in the ED
CT angiogram to identify vessel injury
subject: Surgery-Trauma
concept: EDH with Cushing reflex — emergency surgical management
discriminator: GCS 6 + Cushing reflex + biconvex CT with shift = EDH with impending herniation → intubate + emergency craniotomy

stem: A 15-year-old boy wakes with sudden severe left testicular pain and vomiting. The left testis is high-riding and very tender, and the cremasteric reflex is absent. Doppler ultrasound is not immediately available. What is the single best next step?
opts: Give analgesia and review after 4 hours
Send urine culture and start antibiotics
subject: Surgery-Urology
concept: Testicular torsion emergency management
discriminator: Sudden severe pain, vomiting, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex, and no immediate Doppler.

stem: A 72-year-old man with BPH presents with suprapubic pain and inability to pass urine. Bladder scan shows 900 mL. After urethral catheterization, urine output is 420 mL/hour for the next 3 hours. What is the best interpretation and management?
opts: Post-obstructive diuresis; monitor electrolytes and replace part of the urine loss with IV fluids
subject: Surgery-Urology
concept: Post-obstructive diuresis after acute urinary retention
discriminator: High urine output after relief of obstruction.

stem: A 56-year-old diabetic man presents with severe scrotal pain, fever, crepitus, dusky necrotic scrotal skin, and foul-smelling discharge. What is the most urgent intervention?
opts: Emergency surgical debridement with broad-spectrum antibiotics
Hyperbaric oxygen as first-line definitive treatment
subject: Surgery-Urology
concept: Fournier gangrene emergency management
discriminator: Diabetic patient with necrotic scrotal infection and crepitus.

stem: A 30-year-old man has renal colic. KUB shows a radiopaque 4 mm stone at the vesicoureteric junction. He is afebrile, creatinine is normal, and pain is controlled with NSAIDs. What is the best initial management?
opts: Analgesia, hydration advice, and medical expulsive therapy with tamsulosin
subject: Surgery-Urology
concept: Initial management of small uncomplicated distal ureteric stone
discriminator: Small 4 mm distal ureteric stone with no sepsis, renal failure, or uncontrolled pain.

stem: A 42-year-old man with gout has renal colic. KUB X-ray does not show a stone, but ultrasound suggests a calculus in the renal pelvis. Which stone type is most likely?
subject: Surgery-Urology
concept: Radiolucent urinary stone identification
discriminator: Gout plus radiolucent stone.

stem: A 66-year-old man has PSA 22 ng/mL. Biopsy confirms prostate adenocarcinoma, Gleason 4+4=8. Bone scan shows multiple spinal and pelvic metastases. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
subject: Surgery-Urology
concept: Management of metastatic prostate cancer
discriminator: Biopsy-proven high-grade prostate cancer with bone metastases.

stem: A 68-year-old smoker presents with painless total hematuria. Ultrasound shows an irregular bladder mass. What is the most important next diagnostic step?
opts: Reassurance because painless hematuria is benign
subject: Surgery-Urology
concept: Bladder cancer diagnostic workup
discriminator: Older smoker with painless visible hematuria and bladder mass.

stem: A 72-year-old man has hesitancy, weak stream, nocturia, and terminal dribbling. DRE shows a smooth enlarged non-tender prostate. He has no renal failure, hematuria, or recurrent retention. What is the best initial medical treatment?
subject: Surgery-Urology
concept: First-line medical management of uncomplicated BPH
discriminator: Lower urinary tract symptoms with smooth enlarged prostate and no red flags.

stem: A man with renal colic has fever 39.5 C, rigors, hypotension, leukocytosis, and CT showing an obstructing upper ureteric stone with hydronephrosis. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: IV antibiotics plus urgent decompression with ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy
Restrict fluids and wait for culture results
subject: Surgery-Urology
concept: Infected obstructed kidney
discriminator: Obstructing stone plus sepsis.

stem: A 24-year-old man presents with gradually increasing scrotal pain, dysuria, fever, and a tender epididymis. Cremasteric reflex is present and elevation of the scrotum relieves pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Surgery-Urology
concept: Epididymo-orchitis vs torsion
discriminator: Gradual pain, urinary symptoms, fever, preserved cremasteric reflex, and relief with elevation.

stem: A 28-year-old man has a painless scrotal swelling. It transilluminates brilliantly and the testis is difficult to palpate separately. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Surgery-Urology
concept: Hydrocele recognition
discriminator: Painless scrotal swelling that transilluminates.

stem: A 22-year-old man is evaluated for infertility. Examination shows a left-sided scrotal swelling that feels like a 'bag of worms' and becomes more prominent on standing and with Valsalva. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Surgery-Urology
concept: Varicocele recognition
discriminator: Bag-of-worms swelling, left-sided, worse standing/Valsalva, infertility association.

Aspiration/irrigation with intracavernosal phenylephrine; shunt if refractory
Delayed outpatient urology review in 24 hours
subject: Surgery-Urology
concept: Ischemic priapism management
discriminator: Painful prolonged erection with dark deoxygenated blood.

stem: A 35-year-old man after pelvic trauma has blood at the urethral meatus, perineal bruising, and a high-riding prostate on DRE. He cannot pass urine. What is the safest immediate urinary drainage?

subject: Surgery-Urology
concept: Urethral injury and catheterization safety
discriminator: Pelvic trauma plus blood at meatus and high-riding prostate.

subject: Surgery-Urology
concept: Renal trauma evaluation
discriminator: Stable patient with blunt renal trauma and gross hematuria.

concept: Indications for surgical BPH management

Patient with microscopic hematuria only and no hydronephrosis
Patient whose pain resolves completely after NSAID

discriminator: Infection risk plus solitary kidney.

stem: A 69-year-old man presents with severe suprapubic pain, palpable distended bladder, and inability to pass urine for 12 hours. There is no history of pelvic trauma and no blood at the urethral meatus. What is the immediate management?

Pain severity does not correlate with risk

stem: A burn patient has hoarse voice, carbonaceous sputum, and facial burns. SpO2 is 94% on room air. What is the first step?

stem: A patient with circumferential full-thickness burns on the forearm has weak pulses, paraesthesia, and increased pain with passive stretch. What is the next step?

concept: Escharotomy for circumferential full-thickness burns
discriminator: Circumferential burn + neurovascular compromise = escharotomy

stem: What is the key difference between escharotomy and fasciotomy?
opts: Escharotomy is for burns; fasciotomy is for non-burn compartment syndrome
Escharotomy incises fascia; fasciotomy incises eschar
Fasciotomy is superficial; escharotomy is deep
Escharotomy uses a scalpel; fasciotomy uses cautery
subject: Surgery-Burns
concept: Escharotomy vs fasciotomy — indication
discriminator: Escharotomy = burn eschar; fasciotomy = muscle compartment fascia

stem: A burn patient's wound has green-stained dressings with a fruity/grape-like odor. What is the most likely pathogen?

stem: A 50-year-old man has a non-healing ulcer at the margin of a burn scar on his leg from 25 years ago. The ulcer is indurated with raised, friable edges. What is the most likely diagnosis?

subject: Surgery-Burns
concept: Marjolin ulcer — wide local excision
discriminator: Marjolin = SCC → wide local excision with clear margins

stem: A 55-year-old diabetic man presents with perineal pain, swelling, crepitus on palpation, dark purplish discoloration, and foul odor. He is in septic shock. What is the first step?

IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and ICU monitoring
subject: Surgery-Burns
concept: Necrotizing fasciitis — emergency debridement
discriminator: Perineal crepitus + dark skin + diabetic + septic = Fournier → debride immediately

discriminator: Target UOP 0.5-1 mL/kg/hr during burn resuscitation

stem: A 35-year-old man has full-thickness burns of both entire arms. Using the Rule of Nines, what percentage is this?

concept: Rule of Nines — both arms
discriminator: Each arm = 9%; both arms = 18%

stem: Which statement correctly compares Lund-Browder chart to the Rule of Nines?

Lund-Browder adjusts for age-related differences in body proportions
Rule of Nines is preferred for children <1 year
Both are equally accurate for elderly patients
Lund-Browder is only for electrical burns

concept: Lund-Browder chart — adjusts for age proportions
discriminator: Lund-Browder accounts for larger head/head proportion in children

stem: A patient with 30% TBSA burns has received 6 L of Ringer lactate in the first 8 hours but urine output is only 0.2 mL/kg/hr. What is the best next step?

Increase fluid rate to achieve target UOP
CT abdomen to rule out abdominal compartment syndrome

concept: Burn resuscitation — fluid titration based on UOP

stem: A 70-year-old patient with 20% TBSA burns has facial burns, carbonaceous sputum, and has been intubated. What is the next management priority?

subject: Surgery-Burns

stem: A patient in a house fire has stridor, charred facial hair, carbonaceous sputum, and SpO2 93%. What is the single most important immediate step?

subject: Surgery-Burns
concept: Inhalation injury with stridor — emergency intubation
discriminator: Stridor + carbonaceous sputum = impending airway obstruction → intubate NOW

stem: Which topical antimicrobial is commonly used for burn wound care?

concept: Burn wound care — silver sulfadiazine
discriminator: Silver sulfadiazine is the standard topical for burn wounds

stem: A patient with necrotizing fasciitis of the lower limb has gas in the soft tissues on X-ray. Cultures grow a mix of aerobic and anaerobic organisms. Which is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?
subject: Surgery-Burns

discriminator: Necrotizing fasciitis = polymicrobial → piperacillin-tazobactam + clindamycin

stem: A 40-year-old man has full-thickness burns of the entire chest and abdomen (circumferential thoracoabdominal). He develops difficulty ventilating with rising airway pressures. What is the most likely cause?

subject: Surgery-Burns

stem: A 60-year-old woman presents with unilateral left calf swelling and pain. What is the most common symptom of DVT?

stem: What is the best first-line investigation for suspected DVT?

stem: What is the role of D-dimer in DVT diagnosis?

concept: D-dimer role in DVT diagnostic algorithm
discriminator: D-dimer is a rule-out test in low-probability patients (Wells score)

stem: A 65-year-old man with proximal femoral DVT is started on anticoagulation. Which is the correct first-line anticoagulation strategy?

subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: DVT anticoagulation strategy
discriminator: Proximal DVT → LMWH bridge (or DOAC) for anticoagulation

stem: A 70-year-old man presents with sudden onset of severe right leg pain, pallor, and loss of sensation. He has atrial fibrillation and is not anticoagulated. Pulses are absent below the femoral. What is the first medication to administer?

stem: Which of the following is a sign of irreversible limb ischemia indicating that the limb is no longer salvageable?

concept: Irreversible ischemia — motor loss (paralysis)

stem: A 20-year-old man sustains a closed tibial fracture. Four hours later, he has severe pain worse with passive toe movement. The compartment is tense but distal pulses are present. What is the next step?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Compartment syndrome — emergency fasciotomy with clear presentation
discriminator: Pain out of proportion + passive stretch pain + tense compartment = compartment syndrome → fasciotomy (even if pulses present)

stem: What is the most common cause of acute compartment syndrome?

concept: Most common cause of compartment syndrome
discriminator: Tibial fracture is the most common cause of compartment syndrome

stem: What is the most serious complication of missed compartment syndrome?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Complication of missed compartment syndrome
discriminator: Volkmann ischemic contracture is the classic complication of missed compartment syndrome

stem: A 28-year-old man is brought in after RTA. GCS 6 (E1 V2 M3), BP 80/50, FAST shows free fluid in Morrison pouch. What is the next step?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Unstable trauma + FAST+ = OR despite low GCS
discriminator: Hypotension + positive FAST overrides GCS — laparotomy first

stem: A 50-year-old man had splenectomy 3 months ago. He presents with fever, rigors, and rusty sputum. Blood culture grows Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: OPSI from Strep pneumoniae
discriminator: Post-splenectomy + Gram+ lancet diplococci = OPSI (Strep pneumoniae)

stem: A 25-year-old man is hit on the head with a cricket bat. He initially loses consciousness briefly then fully recovers. Two hours later he deteriorates rapidly. CT shows a biconvex hyperdense lesion. What is the management?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: EDH with lucid interval — emergency craniotomy
discriminator: Lucid interval + biconvex CT = EDH → emergency craniotomy

stem: A 70-year-old man on warfarin fell 4 weeks ago and now has progressive confusion. CT shows a crescent-shaped hypodense collection. What is the management?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Chronic SDH management — burr hole drainage
discriminator: Chronic SDH (crescent hypodense) with symptoms → burr hole drainage

stem: A patient has severe head injury with GCS 7. The team intubates and ventilates. For raised ICP, what is the target PaCO2 range?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Target PaCO2 for raised ICP (cross-topic review)
discriminator: 30-35 mmHg — mild hyperventilation avoids cerebral ischemia

stem: Which of the following scenarios differentiates acute compartment syndrome from DVT?
opts: Pain out of proportion to injury with pain on passive stretch
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Differentiating compartment syndrome from DVT
discriminator: Pain out of proportion + pain on passive stretch = compartment syndrome (not DVT)

stem: A 45-year-old man has sudden severe left leg pain and pallor. He has AF. Pulses are absent below the femoral. CTA shows embolic occlusion of the left common femoral artery. What is the definitive management?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Embolic acute limb ischemia — Fogarty embolectomy
discriminator: Embolic occlusion (AF source) → Fogarty balloon catheter embolectomy

stem: Which of the following is the most common source of arterial emboli causing acute limb ischemia?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Most common emboli source
discriminator: Heart (AF, post-MI mural thrombus) is the most common source of emboli

stem: A trauma patient with pelvic fracture is hypotensive with a negative FAST. What is the most likely source of bleeding?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Retroperitoneal hemorrhage from pelvic fracture (FAST negative)
discriminator: Pelvic fracture + hypotension + negative FAST = retroperitoneal hemorrhage

stem: A 65-year-old man has a proximal DVT diagnosed on US. What is the appropriate duration of anticoagulation for a provoked DVT?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Provoked DVT anticoagulation duration
discriminator: Provoked DVT (surgery, trauma, temporary risk factor) → 3 months anticoagulation

stem: Which of the following distinguishes fat embolism syndrome from pulmonary embolism?
opts: Sudden onset of pleuritic chest pain
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Fat embolism vs PE — petechiae as discriminator
discriminator: Petechiae (axillae/chest) are specific to fat embolism syndrome, not PE

stem: A 22-year-old man with tibial fracture has pain out of proportion. The attending physician measures compartment pressure: diastolic BP 80 mmHg, compartment pressure 55 mmHg. What is the ΔP and what action is needed?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: ΔP calculation and decision
discriminator: ΔP = diastolic BP − compartment pressure = 80 − 55 = 25 mmHg (< 30) → fasciotomy

stem: A trauma patient has GCS 9 (E2 V4 M3), BP 110/70, HR 90. FAST is negative. CT head shows a crescent-shaped hyperdensity over the right convexity with 5 mm midline shift. What is the diagnosis?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: Acute SDH — crescent hyperdense
discriminator: Crescent-shaped hyperdensity (acute blood) = acute SDH

stem: Which of the following is the correct first-line DVT prophylaxis in a patient undergoing major orthopedic surgery?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: DVT prophylaxis in orthopedic surgery
discriminator: LMWH + mechanical prophylaxis (TED stockings/IPC) is first-line

stem: A 55-year-old woman has right leg swelling and pain. US shows femoral-pop DVT. She has breast cancer on chemotherapy. What is the most appropriate anticoagulation duration?
subject: Surgery-Vascular
concept: DVT in cancer — extended anticoagulation
discriminator: Cancer-associated thrombosis → anticoagulate as long as cancer is active (or lifelong)

stem: A 30-year-old male presents with acute onset epigastric pain that migrated to the right lower quadrant over 12 hours. He has nausea, low-grade fever, and tenderness at McBurney point. WBC is 14,000/mm³. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Appendicitis — classic pain migration pattern
discriminator: Pain migration from epigastrium to RLQ is the classic sequence of appendicitis (visceral → somatic pain transition).

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with sudden severe epigastric pain. She has a history of NSAID use. On examination, she has board-like rigidity and generalized tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Perforated peptic ulcer — presentation
discriminator: Sudden severe epigastric pain + board-like rigidity + NSAID history = perforated peptic ulcer with peritonitis.

stem: Which of the following is the strongest discriminator between a surgical abdomen requiring laparotomy and a medical cause of abdominal pain?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Surgical vs medical abdomen — discriminators
discriminator: Involuntary guarding and rigidity are signs of peritoneal irritation, indicating a surgical abdomen requiring urgent exploration.

stem: A patient presents with colicky abdominal pain, abdominal distention, vomiting, and obstipation. Abdominal X-ray shows distended small bowel loops with air-fluid levels and no colonic gas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Small bowel obstruction — clinical and radiological features
discriminator: Colicky pain + distention + vomiting + obstipation + small bowel air-fluid levels with absent colonic gas = mechanical small bowel obstruction.

stem: A 70-year-old man presents with abdominal distention, cramping lower abdominal pain, and obstipation. He has a history of constipation and bright red blood per rectum. Abdominal X-ray shows distended colon with a cutoff at the splenic flexure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Large bowel obstruction — clinical and radiological features
discriminator: Distended colon with cutoff at splenic flexure + LBO symptoms suggests obstruction, most often from malignancy.

stem: Which of the following conditions classically presents with pain that is WORSE when supine and RELIEVED when sitting forward?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Pain pattern differentiation — pancreatitis vs pericarditis
discriminator: Pericarditis pain is pleuritic and relieved by sitting forward (leaning forward reduces pericardial-parietal contact). Pancreatitis pain is worse supine. Both radiate to the back, but the positional provocation differs.

stem: A 60-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden severe abdominal pain out of proportion to the physical exam. She has a history of congestive heart failure. Abdominal exam shows minimal tenderness despite severe pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Acute mesenteric ischemia — pain-out-of-proportion
discriminator: Severe abdominal pain with minimal tenderness (pain-out-of-proportion) in a patient with atrial fibrillation = acute mesenteric ischemia from SMA embolus.

stem: A patient with acute pancreatitis has a total Ranson score of 6. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Severe pancreatitis — ICU admission
discriminator: Ranson ≥ 3 = severe pancreatitis. Ranson 6 is severe (30–40% mortality) and requires ICU monitoring.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents 5 days after laparoscopic cholecystectomy with right upper quadrant pain, fever, and jaundice. She has a history of a difficult cholecystectomy with poor visualization of Calot triangle. What is the most likely complication?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Bile duct injury — post-cholecystectomy presentation
discriminator: Pain + fever + jaundice + difficult LC (poor Calot visualization) = bile duct injury until proven otherwise.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with acute onset of generalized abdominal pain, nausea, and distention. He has not passed flatus for 24 hours. He had an appendectomy 10 years ago. Abdominal X-ray shows dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels and no colonic gas. What is the most likely cause of his condition?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Small bowel obstruction — etiology based on history
discriminator: Previous abdominal surgery (appendectomy) + SBO pattern = adhesive obstruction, the most common cause of SBO.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with severe epigastric pain, vomiting, and distention. He is found to have acute pancreatitis. His labs show: age 58, WBC 17,000, glucose 240 mg/dL, LDH 400 U/L, AST 260 U/L. At 48 hours: Hct drops 12%, BUN rises 10 mg/dL, Ca 7.6 mg/dL, PaO₂ 58 mmHg, base deficit 5 mEq/L, fluid sequestration 8 L. Which complication is he at highest risk for?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Severe pancreatitis — prediction of necrotizing pancreatitis
discriminator: Ranson score: all 5 admission + all 6 at-48h = 11/11 (near max). This predicts severe necrotizing pancreatitis with high mortality.

stem: Which of the following is a sign of peritonism that differentiates surgical from non-surgical abdominal pain?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Peritonism — involuntary rigidity as key sign
discriminator: Involuntary rigidity (true guarding) = parietal peritoneal irritation = surgical abdomen.

stem: A patient with known gallstones develops acute RUQ pain, fever, and a positive Murphy sign. US shows gallbladder wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid. LFTs are normal and CBD is 5 mm. After starting antibiotics, which of the following is the most appropriate definitive management?
opts: MRCP to rule out CBD stone
Observation until symptoms resolve, then cholecystectomy in 6 weeks
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Acute cholecystitis — definitive treatment plan
discriminator: Uncomplicated acute cholecystitis (normal LFTs, normal CBD) → early laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the definitive treatment.

stem: A 45-year-old female presents with a 2-day history of colicky periumbilical pain that has now localized to the right lower quadrant. She has a low-grade fever and anorexia. On exam, there is tenderness at McBurney point. Which of the following signs, if present, would be most specific for appendicitis?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Appendicitis — specific physical exam signs
discriminator: Rovsing sign (palpation of the left lower quadrant causes pain in the right lower quadrant) is a specific sign for appendicitis.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents with sudden severe lower abdominal pain, distention, and vomiting. He has a history of chronic constipation. On exam, the abdomen is distended and tympanic. AXR shows a massively dilated sigmoid colon with a 'coffee bean' sign. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Sigmoid volvulus — coffee bean sign
discriminator: Coffee bean sign (bent inner tube) on AXR in a patient with distention = sigmoid volvulus.

stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with acute RUQ pain, fever, and jaundice, but is stable and has no hypotension or confusion. US shows a dilated CBD at 12 mm. LFTs show elevated bilirubin, ALP, and ALT. What is the BEST next step?
opts: MRCP followed by ERCP if positive
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Acute cholangitis with Charcot triad — management
discriminator: Charcot triad (RUQ pain, fever, jaundice) + dilated CBD = acute cholangitis requiring urgent ERCP. MRCP would delay definitive treatment.

stem: A 50-year-old male presents with acute pancreatitis. He has no history of gallstones or alcohol use. Which laboratory finding would suggest hypertriglyceridemia as the etiology?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis — diagnostic level
discriminator: Triglycerides > 1000 mg/dL can cause pancreatitis. Levels > 2000 mg/dL are diagnostic.

stem: An 80-year-old woman with known gallstones presents with acute RUQ pain and fever but no jaundice. BP is 100/60 mmHg and she is mildly confused. US shows gallbladder wall thickening and a dilated CBD. What is the most appropriate next step?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Severe cholangitis with Reynolds pentad — urgent drainage
discriminator: Charcot triad + hypotension + confusion = Reynolds pentad = severe cholangitis requiring urgent biliary drainage via ERCP.

stem: A 28-year-old medical student presents with acute abdominal pain. Which of the following pain patterns is correctly matched with its likely diagnosis?
opts: Epigastric pain radiating to the back, worse supine → acute cholecystitis
RUQ pain radiating to the right shoulder → acute pancreatitis
Colicky RLQ pain that migrates from periumbilical area → acute appendicitis
Severe pain out of proportion to exam → acute diverticulitis
Cramping lower abdominal pain with distention → perforated peptic ulcer
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Pain pattern mapping to surgical diagnoses
discriminator: Pain migration from periumbilical to RLQ is classic for appendicitis. Each option must be correctly matched.

stem: A 65-year-old female presents with acute onset of generalized abdominal pain, vomiting, and distention. She has a history of atrial fibrillation and is not on anticoagulation. On exam, she has minimal tenderness despite severe pain. Bowel sounds are hyperactive initially but have become absent over the last 6 hours. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
opts: Acute mesenteric ischemia with bowel infarction
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Mesenteric ischemia — progression from pain-out-of-proportion to infarction
discriminator: AFib + pain-out-of-proportion → hyperactive then absent bowel sounds + worsening pain = mesenteric ischemia progressing to infarction.

stem: A 50-year-old female is found to have gallbladder polyps on US done for unrelated indications. One polyp is 8 mm and another is 4 mm. What is the most appropriate management?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Gallbladder polyp — surveillance vs surgery
discriminator: Polyps 6–9 mm: surveillance US at 6–12 months. Polyps > 10 mm → cholecystectomy. The largest is 8 mm (< 10 mm), so surveillance is appropriate.

stem: A 40-year-old male with history of heavy alcohol use presents with acute pancreatitis. Which of the following laboratory findings would be most consistent with the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Pancreatic enzymes — simultaneous elevation in pancreatitis
discriminator: Both amylase and lipase are elevated in acute pancreatitis. Lipase is more specific and remains elevated longer.

stem: Which of the following is the correct treatment sequence for a patient with gallstone pancreatitis who has undergone ERCP with sphincterotomy and now has resolving pancreatitis?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Gallstone pancreatitis — definitive management sequence
discriminator: Even after ERCP clears the CBD, the gallbladder must be removed during same admission to prevent recurrent gallstone events.

stem: A 22-year-old male presents with RLQ pain, fever, and anorexia for 24 hours. He has tenderness at McBurney point with guarding. US shows a non-compressible, thickened appendix measuring 8 mm. WBC is 15,000/mm³. Which of the following is the single best next step?
opts: CT scan of abdomen with contrast
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Acute appendicitis — surgical management
discriminator: Classic appendicitis (migratory pain, RLQ tenderness, fever, leukocytosis, thickened appendix on US) → emergency appendectomy. No further imaging needed.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with a 6-hour history of epigastric pain radiating to the back. He is lying curled on his side. He has a history of gallstones. Serum lipase is 1100 U/L. He has a Ranson score of 2. Management is started. Which of the following statements about his prognosis is MOST accurate?
opts: He has severe pancreatitis with 30–40% mortality
He has mild pancreatitis with < 5% mortality and likely to recover
He will definitely develop a pseudocyst within 4 weeks
He requires urgent ERCP within 24 hours
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Integration — Ranson score interpretation and prognosis
discriminator: Ranson 0–2 = mild pancreatitis (0–5% mortality). Despite severe symptoms, the low Ranson score predicts a good outcome.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with generalized abdominal pain, board-like rigidity, and hypotension (BP 80/50). He has a history of NSAID use. What is the most appropriate next step?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Generalized peritonitis with shock — emergency laparotomy before imaging
discriminator: Unstable patient with generalized peritonitis → OR, not CT. Imaging wastes time in a hemodynamically unstable patient.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents with acute abdominal pain and vomiting. Which of the following patterns BEST indicates a surgical cause of abdominal pain?
opts: Vomiting preceded the onset of pain
Pain preceded the onset of vomiting
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Pain before vomiting = surgical abdomen
discriminator: Pain before vomiting suggests peritoneal irritation (surgical). Vomiting before pain suggests gastroenteritis (medical).

stem: A 28-year-old pregnant woman at 24 weeks gestation presents with periumbilical pain that has migrated to the right lower quadrant over 12 hours. She has nausea and tenderness at McBurney point. WBC is 14,000/mm³. What is the most appropriate imaging study?
opts: Ultrasound of the right lower quadrant
No imaging — proceed directly to appendectomy
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Appendicitis in pregnancy — ultrasound first (avoid radiation)
discriminator: Pregnancy mandates ultrasound first to avoid fetal radiation exposure. CT is avoided in pregnancy.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with 5 days of RLQ pain, fever, and a palpable mass. CT shows a perforated appendix with a 5 cm periappendiceal abscess. There is no generalized peritonitis. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: IV antibiotics + percutaneous drainage → interval appendectomy in 6–8 weeks
IV antibiotics alone and discharge when afebrile
Colonoscopy to rule out cecal malignancy
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Perforated appendicitis with abscess — conservative → interval appendectomy
discriminator: Perforated appendix with well-formed abscess and no peritonitis → conservative management (antibiotics ± drainage), then interval appendectomy. Emergency appendectomy risks iatrogenic injury in inflamed tissues.

stem: A 60-year-old man with a history of prior laparotomy presents with colicky abdominal pain, distention, and obstipation. On exam, he has tenderness with involuntary guarding in the right lower quadrant. Abdominal X-ray shows dilated small bowel loops with air-fluid levels. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Nasogastric decompression and observation for 24 hours
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: SBO with peritonism = strangulation → emergency laparotomy
discriminator: SBO + peritoneal signs (guarding) = strangulation until proven otherwise → emergency laparotomy, not observation.

stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with RUQ pain, fever of 39°C, and jaundice. She is hemodynamically stable with no confusion. US shows a dilated CBD at 12 mm. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Urgent ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction
IV antibiotics and observe for 24 hours
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Charcot triad = acute cholangitis → ERCP, not cholecystectomy
discriminator: Charcot triad (RUQ pain, fever, jaundice) = acute cholangitis requiring biliary drainage via ERCP. Cholecystectomy does not address the obstructed bile duct.

stem: A 75-year-old woman presents with RUQ pain, fever, jaundice, hypotension (BP 70/40), and confusion. US shows a dilated CBD. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: CT abdomen with IV contrast for better characterization
IV antibiotics and vasopressors, then ERCP when stable
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy with bile duct exploration
Blood cultures x 2, then start antibiotics and observe
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Reynolds pentad = severe cholangitis with septic shock → emergency ERCP
discriminator: Reynolds pentad (Charcot triad + hypotension + confusion) = septic shock from cholangitis requiring EMERGENCY biliary drainage. Do not wait for stability.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with epigastric pain radiating to the back. Which laboratory finding is MOST sensitive and specific for diagnosing acute pancreatitis?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Pancreatitis — lipase is more sensitive and specific than amylase
discriminator: Lipase is the preferred enzyme for diagnosing acute pancreatitis — more sensitive and specific than amylase.

stem: A 35-year-old man with severe acute pancreatitis develops a fluid collection in the lesser sac 3 weeks after presentation. CT shows a well-defined round fluid collection with a thin wall. The patient is asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Observe — drain at 6 weeks if wall is mature
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Pancreatic pseudocyst — drainage only after 6 weeks (wall maturation)
discriminator: Pseudocyst < 4 weeks = immature wall; drainage risks bleeding/leak. Observe until 6 weeks for wall maturation. Symptomatic or infected pseudocysts require drainage after wall maturity.

stem: A 70-year-old woman presents with a tender, irreducible groin lump below the inguinal ligament. There is no overlying erythema, and she has no signs of peritonism. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Emergency surgical repair during this admission
Ultrasound to confirm the diagnosis before any intervention
Truss support and follow-up in clinic
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Femoral hernia — high strangulation risk, always repair urgently
discriminator: Femoral hernia has the highest risk of strangulation (40%). Even if reducible or non-obstructed, femoral hernias should always be repaired. Their narrow neck predisposes to strangulation.

stem: Which of the following best defines a strangulated hernia?
opts: A hernia that cannot be reduced manually
A hernia that has been present for more than 5 years
An irreducible hernia with signs of vascular compromise and peritonism
A hernia with a wide neck
A hernia causing intermittent colicky pain
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Strangulated hernia definition — irreducible + vascular compromise + peritonism
discriminator: Strangulation = irreducible + peritonism + toxicity (vascular compromise). Irreducible alone = incarcerated, not necessarily strangulated.

stem: A 60-year-old man on warfarin for mechanical mitral valve presents with DVT of the left leg. His INR is 2.5. What is the most appropriate management for his anticoagulation?
opts: Increase warfarin dose to achieve INR 3.0–4.0
Stop warfarin, start therapeutic LMWH, continue until INR is therapeutic again
Add aspirin to current warfarin regimen
Stop warfarin and start direct oral anticoagulant
Continue warfarin at current dose and add compression stockings
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: DVT on warfarin — LMWH bridge for acute management
discriminator: Warfarin alone is insufficient for acute DVT management (takes days to reach therapeutic effect). LMWH bridge provides immediate anticoagulation while warfarin is re-titrated.

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and hypotension (BP 85/55). She has a history of DVT. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Suspected PE with hypotension — IV heparin immediately, then CTPA
discriminator: Suspected PE with hemodynamic instability → DO NOT wait for imaging. Give heparin immediately; CTPA can follow. Unstable PE = treat first, confirm later.

stem: In which of the following scenarios is an IVC filter indicated for DVT management?
opts: First episode of DVT in a young patient
DVT in a patient with active bleeding or contraindication to anticoagulation
Proximal DVT with good response to LMWH
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: IVC filter — indication is contraindication to anticoagulation
discriminator: IVC filter is reserved for patients with VTE who cannot receive anticoagulation (active bleeding, contraindication). It is NOT first-line.

stem: A 70-year-old man with atrial fibrillation presents with sudden onset of right leg pain, pallor, and pulselessness of 4 hours duration. The leg is cold and mottled below the knee. What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacologic step?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Acute limb ischemia — IV heparin to prevent clot propagation
discriminator: Acute limb ischemia → IV heparin immediately to prevent proximal propagation. Aspirin does not provide adequate acute anticoagulation.

stem: In acute limb ischemia, which of the following clinical findings indicates IRREVERSIBLE ischemia requiring amputation rather than revascularization?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Irreversible limb ischemia — paralysis = tissue death, not absent pulses
discriminator: Pulseless ≠ irreversible. Muscle paralysis indicates irreversible ischemia. Pulseless limbs can still be salvaged if revascularized before paralysis develops.

stem: A 30-year-old man sustains a closed tibial fracture in a motorcycle accident. Twelve hours later, he has severe leg pain out of proportion, tense swelling, and pain with passive toe dorsiflexion. Pulses are diminished. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Elevate the leg and apply ice
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Compartment syndrome — acute compartment syndrome = emergency fasciotomy
discriminator: Pain out of proportion + pain with passive stretch + tense swelling = compartment syndrome requiring immediate fasciotomy. Do not wait for pressure measurements in a classic presentation.

stem: A 25-year-old man is brought to the ER after a high-speed RTA. He is hypotensive (BP 75/45) despite 2 L of crystalloid. FAST is positive for free fluid in the RUQ. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: CT abdomen with IV contrast for injury grading
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Unstable trauma + FAST+ = emergency laparotomy, not CT
