discriminator: Unstable patient (transient responder or non-responder) + positive FAST = intra-abdominal hemorrhage requiring emergency laparotomy. CT wastes time.

stem: A 20-year-old man is brought to the ER after a fall from height. He has a GCS of 7 (E1, V2, M4). What is the most appropriate immediate step?
opts: Intubate for airway protection, then CT head
Skull X-ray to screen for fracture
MRI brain for better parenchymal detail
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Severe head injury (GCS ≤ 8) — intubate before CT
discriminator: GCS ≤ 8 = inability to protect airway. Airway (intubation) precedes imaging in ATLS. Do not send to CT before securing the airway.

stem: A 22-year-old man sustains a blow to the head with a baseball bat. He lost consciousness briefly but then woke up and was talking normally. Two hours later, he becomes drowsy, vomits, and develops a right-sided hemiparesis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Lucid interval = extradural hematoma (middle meningeal artery)
discriminator: Lucid interval (brief LOC → awake → deterioration) is classic for EDH from middle meningeal artery tear. The lucid interval is the time between initial concussion and hematoma expansion.

stem: A 65-year-old postmenopausal woman is found to have a 2 cm ER-positive, HER2-negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast with no lymph node involvement. Which of the following is the most appropriate adjuvant endocrine therapy?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Postmenopausal ER+ breast cancer — aromatase inhibitor, not tamoxifen
discriminator: In postmenopausal women, aromatase inhibitors (anastrozole, letrozole) are preferred over tamoxifen because peripheral aromatase conversion is the main estrogen source. Tamoxifen is preferred in premenopausal women.

stem: A 16-year-old boy presents with sudden onset of severe left testicular pain and vomiting for 3 hours. On exam, the left testis is high-riding with an absent cremasteric reflex. Doppler ultrasound is not immediately available. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Observe with scrotal support and ice packs
Arrange urgent Doppler ultrasound at a nearby facility
Immediate surgical exploration of the scrotum
Color Doppler ultrasound before any intervention
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Testicular torsion — clinical diagnosis = immediate exploration, no imaging
discriminator: Clinical torsion (sudden severe pain, absent cremasteric reflex, high-riding testis) + vomiting = surgical emergency. Do NOT wait for imaging. Salvage rate drops after 6 hours. 'Doppler not available' forces the decision to explore clinically.

stem: A 35-year-old man is brought in after a house fire. He has burns to his face, neck, and chest. He is conscious but has a hoarse voice and carbonaceous sputum. SpO2 is 94% on room air. What is the most important immediate step?
opts: Apply Parkland formula for fluid resuscitation
CT scan of the neck and chest
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Inhalation injury — intubate prophylactically before airway edema progresses
discriminator: Hoarse voice + carbonaceous sputum + facial burns = inhalation injury. Airway edema progresses rapidly. Intubate prophylactically before stridor or obstruction develops. Do not wait for desaturation.

stem: A 50-year-old man has a non-healing ulcer at the margin of a burn scar on his leg that he sustained 30 years ago. The ulcer is raised, indurated, and bleeds easily. Biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma. What is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
opts: Wide local excision with clear margins
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Marjolin ulcer — SCC in chronic burn scar → wide local excision
discriminator: Marjolin ulcer = SCC arising from chronic scar/burn. Requires oncologic resection (wide local excision), not simple debridement.

stem: A 30-year-old man with a family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma is found to have a thyroid nodule. What is the most likely histological type if this nodule is malignant?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: MEN2A + thyroid nodule → medullary carcinoma (calcitonin-secreting)
discriminator: Family history of MTC + pheochromocytoma = MEN2A. Thyroid nodule in MEN2A = medullary carcinoma. RET proto-oncogene mutation.

stem: Which nerve is injured in a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Which nerve is injured in a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus?
discriminator: Axillary nerve wraps around the surgical neck of the humerus. Radial = midshaft. Ulnar = medial epicondyle.

stem: Which nerve injury prevents making the OK sign?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Which nerve injury prevents making the OK sign?
discriminator: AIN supplies FPL and FDP (index). Cannot make OK sign = AIN injury. Median nerve proper causes thenar weakness + sensory loss.

stem: A patient presents with a painful swollen calf after prolonged sitting. Wells score is moderate. What is the next step?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: A patient presents with a painful swollen calf after prolonged sitting. Wells score is moderate. What is the next step?
discriminator: Moderate-high Wells = go straight to US. D-dimer is for low-probability patients.

stem: What is the most common cause of small bowel obstruction?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: What is the most common cause of small bowel obstruction?
discriminator: Adhesions are the most common cause of SBO. Malignancy is the most common cause of LBO.

stem: A patient with acute pancreatitis 5 weeks ago has epigastric fullness. US shows a 7 cm fluid collection with thick wall. What is the next step?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: A patient with acute pancreatitis 5 weeks ago has epigastric fullness. US shows a 7 cm fluid collection with thick wall.
discriminator: At 7 cm and 5 weeks (immature wall), this pseudocyst now has a mature wall (>6 weeks = endoscopic drainage).

stem: A woman with a 6 cm breast lump and no axillary nodes — most likely diagnosis?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: A woman with a 6 cm breast lump and no axillary nodes — most likely diagnosis?
discriminator: Large lump + no nodes = phyllodes. Fibroadenomas are <3 cm. Breast cancer usually has nodal involvement.

stem: Which complication of thyroid surgery presents with carpopedal spasm and perioral tingling?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Which complication of thyroid surgery presents with carpopedal spasm and perioral tingling?
discriminator: Tetany + Chvostek + perioral tingling = hypocalcemia from parathyroid injury. RLN = hoarseness. Hematoma = neck swelling + respiratory distress.

stem: In the Surgery Chapter Map — Core Topics bridge review, which concept is best identified by this discriminator: Pain chronology (before/after vomiting), peritonism pattern?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Day 1
discriminator: Pain chronology (before/after vomiting), peritonism pattern

stem: A review question gives this trigger: Appendicitis and Peritonitis. Which linked concept should you revise first?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Day 2
discriminator: Pain migration (periumbilical -> RLQ), CT vs US by age/pregnancy

stem: Which topic best matches the exam discriminator: Colicky vs constant pain = strangulation signal. SBO (adhesions) vs LBO (malignancy)?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Day 3
discriminator: Colicky vs constant pain = strangulation signal. SBO (adhesions) vs LBO (malignancy)

stem: A mixed review stem is built around Perforated Viscus. Which answer is the intended discriminator pair?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Day 4
discriminator: Free air on CXR + peritonism = laparotomy. Graham patch for DU, biopsy for gastric

stem: In the Surgery Chapter Map — Core Topics bridge review, which concept is best identified by this discriminator: Lipase > amylase. Ranson >=3 = severe. Pseudocyst needs 6 weeks to mature?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Day 5
discriminator: Lipase > amylase. Ranson >=3 = severe. Pseudocyst needs 6 weeks to mature

stem: A review question gives this trigger: Gallbladder Disease. Which linked concept should you revise first?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Day 6
discriminator: Murphy = cholecystitis. Charcot = cholangitis -> ERCP. Courvoisier = malignancy

stem: Which topic best matches the exam discriminator: Femoral > inguinal for strangulation. Always repair femoral. Taxia for irreducible without peritonism?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Day 8
discriminator: Femoral > inguinal for strangulation. Always repair femoral. Taxia for irreducible without peritonism

stem: A mixed review stem is built around DVT and Anticoagulation. Which answer is the intended discriminator pair?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Day 9
discriminator: Wells + D-dimer algorithm. Heparin first. DOAC or warfarin for long-term

stem: In the Surgery Chapter Map — Core Topics bridge review, which concept is best identified by this discriminator: 6 Ps. Heparin first. Paralysis = irreversible. CTA then surgical revascularisation?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Day 10
discriminator: 6 Ps. Heparin first. Paralysis = irreversible. CTA then surgical revascularisation

stem: A review question gives this trigger: Compartment Syndrome. Which linked concept should you revise first?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Day 11
discriminator: Pain out of proportion + passive stretch. ΔP < 30. Fasciotomy (not for burn)

stem: Which topic best matches the exam discriminator: Unstable + FAST+ = laparotomy. Stable + FAST+ = CT -> grade -> conservative or splenectomy?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Day 12
discriminator: Unstable + FAST+ = laparotomy. Stable + FAST+ = CT -> grade -> conservative or splenectomy

stem: A mixed review stem is built around Head Injury and ICP. Which answer is the intended discriminator pair?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Day 13
discriminator: Biconvex = EDH = craniotomy. Crescent = SDH = burr hole. GCS <= 8 = intubate

stem: In the Surgery Chapter Map — Core Topics bridge review, which concept is best identified by this discriminator: 5 nerve-fracture pairs. NOF = hemiarthroplasty. Fat embolism = petechiae + hypoxia day 2?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Day 15
discriminator: 5 nerve-fracture pairs. NOF = hemiarthroplasty. Fat embolism = petechiae + hypoxia day 2

stem: A review question gives this trigger: Breast Triple Assessment. Which linked concept should you revise first?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Day 16
discriminator: Triple assessment = exam + imaging + core biopsy. Phyllodes = large + no nodes

stem: Which topic best matches the exam discriminator: Papillary >1 cm = total thyroidectomy. MEN2A = medullary. Tetany = hypoparathyroidism?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Day 17
discriminator: Papillary >1 cm = total thyroidectomy. MEN2A = medullary. Tetany = hypoparathyroidism

stem: A mixed review stem is built around Urology Emergencies. Which answer is the intended discriminator pair?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Day 18
discriminator: Torsion -> explore immediately. Priapism -> phenylephrine. Fournier -> debride

stem: In the Surgery Chapter Map — Core Topics bridge review, which concept is best identified by this discriminator: Inhalation injury -> intubate. Parkland formula. Escharotomy. Marjolin = wide excision?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Day 19
discriminator: Inhalation injury -> intubate. Parkland formula. Escharotomy. Marjolin = wide excision

stem: A review question gives this trigger: Tibial fracture, crush injury. Which linked concept should you revise first?
subject: Surgery-Review
concept: Non-burn (Day 11)
discriminator: Fasciotomy

stem: A 14-month-old infant presents with a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes during a febrile illness (temperature 39.2°C). The child is now alert and interactive. Which age range is classically associated with simple febrile seizures?
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Simple febrile seizure age range
discriminator: The classic age range is 6 months to 5 years; children outside this range with fever and seizure warrant investigation for other causes

stem: What is the maximum seizure duration for a seizure to be classified as a simple febrile seizure?
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Duration threshold for simple vs complex febrile seizure
discriminator: 15 minutes is the cutoff — < 15 min is simple, ≥ 15 min is complex

stem: What is the approximate risk of developing epilepsy in a child who has had a simple febrile seizure?
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Risk of epilepsy after simple febrile seizure
discriminator: 1-2% after simple vs 5-10% after complex — a key prognostic distinction tested on exam

stem: A 2-week-old neonate presents with fever, poor feeding, and lethargy. Lumbar puncture is consistent with bacterial meningitis. Which organism is LEAST likely to be the causative agent?
opts: All are equally likely in this age group
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Neonatal meningitis — age-stratified pathogens
discriminator: Neonates (< 3 months) are infected by GBS, E. coli, and Listeria — NOT by N. meningitidis, which causes meningitis in older children

stem: Which is the most common type of cerebral palsy?
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Cerebral palsy — classification by type
discriminator: Spastic CP accounts for approximately 80% of all cerebral palsy cases

stem: What is the most common malignant brain tumor in children?
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Paediatric CNS tumours — medulloblastoma
discriminator: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumour in children; cerebellar astrocytoma is the most common benign

stem: A 3-year-old child presents to the emergency department with an active generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 6 minutes. There is no intravenous access. What is the most appropriate first-line drug?
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Status epilepticus — first-line management without IV access
discriminator: Without IV access, buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam are first-line; IV options are only relevant once IV access is established

stem: A 2-year-old is diagnosed with bacterial meningitis. What is the recommended dose of dexamethasone to be administered?
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Dexamethasone dose in paediatric bacterial meningitis
discriminator: The exact dose is 0.15 mg/kg IV, given before or with the first antibiotic dose

stem: A term neonate developed severe neonatal jaundice requiring exchange transfusion. At 18 months, the child presents with choreoathetoid movements and fluctuating muscle tone. What serum bilirubin level is typically associated with the development of kernicterus?
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Bilirubin threshold for kernicterus
discriminator: Bilirubin > 20 mg/dL in term neonates is the threshold for kernicterus risk

stem: Which virus is the most common cause of viral meningitis in children?
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Viral meningitis — most common cause
discriminator: Enterovirus accounts for the majority of viral meningitis cases in children; HSV is more associated with encephalitis

stem: A 2-year-old presents with fever (39°C) and a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 4 minutes. This was a single seizure in 24 hours. Post-ictally, the child was drowsy for 10 minutes and then became fully alert and interactive. No neck stiffness or bulging fontanelle. How should this seizure be classified?
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Classification of febrile seizures — simple vs complex
discriminator: Generalized, < 15 min, single in 24 h, normal post-ictal neurology = all criteria for simple febrile seizure

stem: An 18-month-old presents with fever (39.5°C) and a single generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes. The child is now alert and playing. There is no neck stiffness, and examination reveals acute otitis media. Is a lumbar puncture indicated?
opts: Yes — always perform LP after any febrile seizure
Yes — because the child is under 2 years of age
No — not indicated in simple febrile seizure > 12 months with clear fever source
Yes — because a seizure occurred with fever
No — but only after CT brain is normal
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Febrile seizure — LP indication criteria
discriminator: LP is NOT indicated for simple febrile seizure in children > 12 months who are well-appearing with a clear source of fever

stem: A 3-year-old child, born at 30 weeks gestation, presents with delayed walking. Examination reveals scissoring gait, hypertonia in the lower limbs greater than the upper limbs, hyperreflexia, and bilateral Babinski sign. Which type of cerebral palsy is most likely?
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Cerebral palsy — spastic diplegia in preterm infants
discriminator: Preterm birth + lower limb predominant spasticity with scissoring gait = classic spastic diplegic CP from periventricular leukomalacia

stem: A 9-month-old infant presents with fever (39.5°C) and a brief generalized seizure that has resolved. On examination, the infant is irritable, has a bulging anterior fontanelle, and is difficult to console. There is no rash. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Order outpatient EEG for next week
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Meningitis red flags in infants — bulging fontanelle
discriminator: A bulging fontanelle in a febrile infant is a meningitis red flag until proven otherwise; LP is indicated

stem: A 4-year-old presents with fever, neck stiffness, photophobia, and altered consciousness. CSF analysis shows: WBC 1500/μL (90% neutrophils), glucose 20 mg/dL, protein 150 mg/dL. Gram stain shows Gram-positive diplococci. Which empiric antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Empiric antibiotics for bacterial meningitis in children
discriminator: In children 3 mo - 12 y, empiric therapy is cefotaxime/ceftriaxone + vancomycin to cover S. pneumoniae (including resistant strains) and N. meningitidis

stem: A 6-year-old presents with morning headache, projectile vomiting, and an unsteady gait for 3 weeks. Examination reveals bilateral papilledema and left CN VI palsy. CT head shows a midline posterior fossa mass with homogeneous enhancement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Paediatric CNS tumours — medulloblastoma presentation
discriminator: Midline posterior fossa mass + raised ICP + young age + CN VI palsy = medulloblastoma until proven otherwise

stem: A 5-year-old presents with fever, headache, photophobia, and mild neck stiffness. CSF analysis shows: WBC 80/μL (80% lymphocytes), glucose 65 mg/dL (serum glucose 100 mg/dL), protein 40 mg/dL. Gram stain is negative. Which etiology is most likely?
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: CSF interpretation — viral vs bacterial meningitis
discriminator: Lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose and normal-to-mildly elevated protein is classic for viral meningitis

stem: A 2-year-old presents with delayed motor milestones and involuntary writhing movements of all extremities. On examination, muscle tone fluctuates between hypotonia and hypertonia. There is a history of severe neonatal jaundice requiring exchange transfusion. Which type of cerebral palsy is most likely?
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Dyskinetic CP — kernicterus association
discriminator: Involuntary writhing movements + fluctuating tone + history of neonatal jaundice = dyskinetic CP from kernicterus

stem: A 2-year-old has been in generalized tonic-clonic seizure for 25 minutes. IV access has been obtained. What first-line medication should be administered immediately?
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Status epilepticus management — first-line benzodiazepine
discriminator: Benzodiazepines (lorazepam IV or diazepam IV) are first-line for status epilepticus; second-line agents follow if seizure persists

stem: A 3-year-old is diagnosed with bacterial meningitis. At what point should dexamethasone be administered relative to antibiotics?
opts: Only after culture results confirm HIB or pneumococcus
Before or simultaneously with the first dose of antibiotics
After the course of antibiotics is completed
Dexamethasone is contraindicated in paediatric meningitis
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Dexamethasone timing in bacterial meningitis
discriminator: Dexamethasone must be given before or with the first antibiotic dose — NOT after — to effectively reduce hearing loss

stem: A 20-month-old presents with fever (39°C) and a focal seizure involving the right arm lasting 18 minutes. The child had a similar episode 8 hours earlier. Post-ictal examination reveals transient weakness of the left arm. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
opts: Perform LP, consider EEG and neuroimaging
Prescribe rectal diazepam for home use
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Complex febrile seizure — workup indications
discriminator: Multiple complex features (focal onset, duration ≥ 15 min, multiple in 24 h, Todd paresis) warrant LP, EEG, and neuroimaging

stem: A 5-year-old presents with morning headache, projectile vomiting, and truncal ataxia. MRI shows a solid, heterogeneously enhancing midline posterior fossa mass arising from the cerebellar vermis with evidence of leptomeningeal spread. CSF cytology is positive for malignant cells. Which tumour is most likely, and what is the most appropriate management?
opts: Cerebellar astrocytoma — surgical resection alone is usually curative
Medulloblastoma — surgical resection + craniospinal irradiation + chemotherapy
Brainstem glioma — biopsy followed by palliative radiotherapy
Ependymoma — surgical resection alone without adjuvant therapy
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Medulloblastoma vs cerebellar astrocytoma — management
discriminator: Malignant cells in CSF + midline location + leptomeningeal spread = medulloblastoma requiring multimodal therapy

stem: A 4-year-old with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy has severe spasticity limiting mobility and causing discomfort. The parents ask about management options. Which approach is most appropriate?
opts: Orthopedic surgery alone to correct contractures
Physical therapy alone until the child is older
Multidisciplinary approach including PT, OT, speech therapy, and consider baclofen for spasticity
Anticonvulsant monotherapy since the primary issue is neurological
No intervention needed since CP is a progressive condition that will worsen
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Cerebral palsy — multidisciplinary management
discriminator: CP management requires a multidisciplinary team; baclofen (oral or intrathecal) is used for spasticity; CP is non-progressive

stem: A 10-day-old neonate presents with fever, poor feeding, lethargy, and a bulging fontanelle. CSF shows WBC 500/μL (85% neutrophils), glucose 15 mg/dL, protein 200 mg/dL. Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in chains. Which empiric antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Neonatal meningitis — empiric antibiotic selection
discriminator: Neonates (< 3 months) with meningitis receive ampicillin + cefotaxime ± gentamicin to cover GBS, E. coli, and Listeria

stem: A full-term neonate experienced severe perinatal asphyxia requiring resuscitation. At 18 months, the child shows significant motor delay, spasticity in all four limbs (lower > upper), severe intellectual disability, and microcephaly. Which type of cerebral palsy and most likely etiology?
opts: Dyskinetic CP — kernicterus from neonatal jaundice
Spastic diplegic CP — periventricular leukomalacia from prematurity
subject: Paediatrics-Cns
concept: Cerebral palsy — spastic quadriplegia from HIE
discriminator: Full-term + perinatal asphyxia + spastic quadriplegia + microcephaly + intellectual disability = HIE leading to spastic quadriplegic CP

stem: A 15-month-old child presents with a barking cough, inspiratory stridor, and low-grade fever. Symptoms began gradually over 2 days and are worse at night. The child is playful and can lie flat without distress. An AP neck X-ray shows subglottic narrowing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Croup — clinical presentation and X-ray signs
discriminator: Barking cough + gradual onset + age 6 mo–3 y + steeple sign on X-ray = croup. Epiglottitis has drooling, tripod position, and acute high fever.

stem: A 2-year-old with croup has stridor at rest and moderate chest retractions. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
opts: Nebulized budesonide twice daily for 5 days
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Croup treatment — dexamethasone dose
discriminator: Single-dose oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg is the standard first-line treatment for croup. Nebulized adrenaline is added for severe cases but dexamethasone is the cornerstone.

stem: A 4-year-old child presents with acute onset high fever (39.5°C), muffled voice, inspiratory stridor, and drooling. The child refuses to lie down and sits leaning forward with hands on knees. What is the most important immediate step in management?
opts: Examine the throat with a tongue depressor
Secure the airway with controlled intubation
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Epiglottitis — airway management priority
discriminator: Epiglottitis with tripod positioning and drooling indicates imminent airway obstruction. Securing the airway (controlled intubation) is the absolute first priority — before X-rays, before antibiotics, before any other intervention.

stem: A lateral neck X-ray in a 3-year-old with respiratory distress shows swelling of the epiglottis, producing a rounded soft tissue density at the base of the tongue. What is the name of this radiographic sign?
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Epiglottitis — thumbprint sign on lateral neck X-ray
discriminator: Thumbprint sign = swollen epiglottis on lateral neck X-ray in epiglottitis. Steeple sign = subglottic narrowing on AP neck X-ray in croup.

stem: A 6-week-old infant presents with a 3-day history of coryza followed by worsening cough, tachypnea, and difficulty feeding. On auscultation, there are bilateral expiratory wheezes and fine crackles. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent?
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Bronchiolitis — causative agent (RSV)
discriminator: Age < 12 months + coryza → cough → respiratory distress + wheeze and crackles + hyperinflation = bronchiolitis (RSV). Parainfluenza causes croup in older infants/toddlers, not bronchiolitis in young infants.

stem: A 9-month-old infant with bronchiolitis has oxygen saturation of 88% on room air, moderate subcostal retractions, and is feeding poorly. Which intervention is most appropriate?
opts: Oxygen to maintain saturations ≥ 90% and nasogastric hydration
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Bronchiolitis — supportive management
discriminator: Bronchiolitis management is primarily supportive: oxygen for saturations <90%, nasal suctioning, and hydration support. Routine bronchodilators and steroids are not recommended by AAP guidelines.

stem: A 10-month-old infant presents with episodes of paroxysmal coughing followed by a prolonged inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting. The infant is afebrile. Complete blood count shows lymphocytosis. What is the most appropriate antibiotic?
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Pertussis — antibiotic treatment
discriminator: Paroxysmal cough + whoop + post-tussive vomiting + lymphocytosis = pertussis. Azithromycin is the treatment of choice and decreases transmission, though it does not alter the cough course once paroxysmal stage is established.

stem: A 5-year-old unvaccinated child presents with a greyish-white pseudomembrane covering the tonsils and posterior pharynx, with marked cervical lymphadenopathy and neck swelling (bull neck appearance). Which treatment should be administered urgently?
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Diphtheria — antitoxin priority
discriminator: In diphtheria, the antitoxin neutralizes unbound toxin and is the most urgent treatment. Antibiotics kill the bacteria but do not neutralize already-bound toxin. Antitoxin must be given first, without waiting for culture confirmation.

stem: A 2-year-old is brought to the ER after swallowing several of her mother's ferrous sulfate tablets. She is vomiting and appears lethargic. Abdominal X-ray shows radiopaque densities in the stomach. Which chelating agent should be administered?
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Iron poisoning — chelating agent
discriminator: Desferrioxamine is the specific iron chelator. Iron tablets are radiopaque on X-ray — a unique feature. NAC is for paracetamol. Other agents chelate different heavy metals.

stem: A 3-year-old who ingested an unknown number of ferrous sulfate tablets 6 hours ago is brought to the ER. Serum iron level is 480 mcg/dL. The child is awake, alert, and has no metabolic acidosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Observe and recheck serum iron in 2 hours
Perform whole bowel irrigation with PEG-3350
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Iron poisoning — chelation threshold (Fe >500 mcg/dL)
discriminator: Chelation with desferrioxamine is indicated when serum iron exceeds 500 mcg/dL OR if severe symptoms (metabolic acidosis, shock) are present. This child has Fe 480 (below threshold) and is asymptomatic — observation with close monitoring is appropriate.

stem: A 4-year-old child is found unconscious with bradycardia, miosis, excessive salivation, lacrimation, and generalized muscle fasciculations. The mother reports the child was playing in a garden where pesticides are stored. Which two antidotes should be administered?
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Organophosphate poisoning — antidotes
discriminator: SLUDGE + miosis + bradycardia + fasciculations = organophosphate poisoning. Atropine blocks muscarinic effects; pralidoxime reactivates acetylcholinesterase. Both are needed.

stem: A 5-year-old is found drowsy with respiratory rate of 6 breaths/min and pinpoint pupils. Pulse is 70/min. Oxygen saturation is 85%. The child's grandmother takes multiple medications for chronic pain. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Opioid poisoning — naloxone
discriminator: Pinpoint pupils + respiratory depression + sedation = opioid toxidrome. No SLUDGE or fasciculations (rules out OP). Naloxone is the specific reversal agent.

stem: In managing a child with organophosphate poisoning, you administer IV atropine 0.05 mg/kg. After 5 minutes, the child still has excessive secretions and a heart rate of 60/min. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Repeat the same dose of atropine 0.05 mg/kg
Double the atropine dose to 0.1 mg/kg
The dose is too high — reduce to 0.02 mg/kg
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Organophosphate poisoning — atropine dosing escalation
discriminator: In OP poisoning, atropine is given at 0.05 mg/kg IV and the dose is doubled every 5 minutes until atropinization (clear lungs, HR >80, dry secretions). Standard doses are ineffective due to massive acetylcholine excess.

stem: A 2-year-old child is brought to the ER after ingesting an unknown quantity of an organophosphate insecticide 2 hours ago. On examination, the child has excessive salivation, lacrimation, diffuse wheezing, muscle fasciculations, and a heart rate of 55/min. Atropine is administered. Which clinical sign indicates that adequate atropinization has been achieved?
opts: Dry oral secretions and heart rate >80/min
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Organophosphate poisoning — atropinization endpoint
discriminator: Atropinization is defined by: clear lungs (no wheezing/crepitations), heart rate >80/min, and dry oral secretions. Pupil size and fasciculations are not reliable endpoints — atropine blocks muscarinic but not nicotinic effects.

stem: A 3-year-old with a barking cough and inspiratory stridor receives oral dexamethasone but worsens over 4 hours, developing stridor at rest and marked chest retractions. What is the most appropriate next intervention?
opts: Repeat dexamethasone at double the dose
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Croup — nebulized adrenaline for moderate-severe cases
discriminator: When croup does not respond to dexamethasone alone and develops stridor at rest, nebulized adrenaline is indicated for temporary relief of airway edema. Intubation is reserved for cases that fail adrenaline or develop respiratory failure.

stem: A 1-year-old with a 5-day history of cough now has episodes of 10-15 rapid coughs followed by an inspiratory whoop and vomiting. The child is up to date with DTaP vaccinations. Which of the following is true regarding antibiotic therapy?
opts: Antibiotics will shorten the duration of the cough
Azithromycin is given primarily to reduce transmission to others
Antibiotics are not indicated because the child is vaccinated
Amoxicillin is the drug of choice
Doxycycline should be used in children under 2 years
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Pertussis — azithromycin purpose after cough established
discriminator: Once the paroxysmal cough of pertussis develops, azithromycin does NOT change the clinical course. It is given to decrease transmission. The cough can persist for 6-10 weeks regardless of treatment.

stem: A 7-month-old infant presents with acute onset of stridor, drooling, high fever (39.8°C), and cannot lie flat. The parents report the child was well 4 hours ago. A lateral neck X-ray reveals a swollen epiglottis. After the airway is secured, which antibiotic should be started?
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Epiglottitis — antibiotics after airway secured
discriminator: Epiglottitis is bacterial (H. influenzae type b). After the airway is secured, IV ceftriaxone is the recommended antibiotic. The most important step is airway security first — antibiotics come second.

stem: A mother brings her 18-month-old to the ER saying the child swallowed 'several small white tablets' from her handbag 3 hours ago. The child is lethargic, has marked metabolic acidosis, and is vomiting blood-tinged material. Abdominal X-ray shows radiopaque tablets in the stomach. What is the most likely ingested substance?
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Iron poisoning — clinical features and radiopaque tablets
discriminator: Iron tablets are radiopaque on X-ray — a unique feature among common ingestions. Vomiting, hematemesis, metabolic acidosis, and lethargy confirm severe iron poisoning. No other common tablet is visible on plain X-ray.

stem: A 3-year-old with refractory status epilepticus requires endotracheal intubation. Shortly after, the child develops inspiratory stridor, barking cough, and chest retractions. There is no drooling. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Post-extubation croup (acquired croup) — clinical context
discriminator: Post-extubation croup (subglottic edema from endotracheal tube trauma) presents with barking cough and stridor after recent intubation. The absence of drooling, high fever, and acute onset of cough differentiates it from epiglottitis.

stem: A 5-year-old presents with sudden onset of choking while eating peanuts, followed by coughing and stridor. Breath sounds are decreased on the right side. Chest X-ray shows right lung hyperinflation with mediastinal shift to the left. What is the most appropriate next step?
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Foreign body aspiration — bronchoscopy for retrieval
discriminator: Sudden onset choking + asymmetric breath sounds + unilateral hyperinflation = foreign body aspiration, not croup or epiglottitis. Bronchoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

stem: A 2-year-old with suspected organophosphate poisoning is given atropine 0.05 mg/kg IV. After 5 minutes, secretions are slightly decreased but heart rate remains 65/min and lungs have scattered wheezes. Which of the following describes the correct dosing schedule?
opts: Repeat atropine 0.05 mg/kg every 10 minutes as needed
Double the atropine dose and reassess in 5 minutes
Start a continuous atropine infusion at 0.05 mg/kg/h
Give pralidoxime alone and discontinue atropine
Increase atropine to 0.1 mg/kg every 15 minutes
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Organophosphate poisoning — atropine dose escalation regimen
discriminator: The atropine dose doubles every 5 minutes until atropinization is achieved. This is the standard protocol for OP poisoning because standard doses are ineffective against massive cholinergic excess.

stem: A 3-month-old with bronchiolitis and oxygen saturation 87% is started on oxygen and nasogastric hydration. A trial of nebulized salbutamol is given with no clinical improvement. What should be done regarding bronchodilator therapy?
opts: Continue salbutamol every 4 hours as it may take time to work
Discontinue salbutamol as it is ineffective — continue supportive care
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Bronchiolitis — bronchodilator trial: discontinue if no response
discriminator: AAP guidelines: a trial of bronchodilators may be given in bronchiolitis, but if there is no clinical response, they should be discontinued. Routine use is not recommended.

stem: A 2-year-old presents with drowsiness, slow respiration (8/min), and pinpoint pupils. Naloxone is administered and the child becomes more alert with improved respiratory effort. Thirty minutes later, the child becomes drowsy again with respiratory depression. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Give a second dose of naloxone and start a naloxone infusion
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Opioid poisoning — naloxone re-dosing and infusion (half-life shorter than opioids)
discriminator: Naloxone has a shorter half-life (30-90 min) than most opioids, causing symptoms to recur. Repeat boluses or a continuous infusion is needed. Do not confuse this with treatment failure.

stem: A 10-month-old with pertussis develops severe coughing paroxysms with cyanosis and apnea. After the paroxysm, the child vomits and becomes exhausted. Which of the following statements about pertussis cough is correct?
opts: Azithromycin will significantly reduce the cough within 48 hours
The cough typically resolves within 2 weeks of starting antibiotics
The cough may persist for 6-10 weeks regardless of antibiotic therapy
Inhaled corticosteroids will reduce cough severity
The cough is caused by bacterial invasion of the bronchial mucosa
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Pertussis — natural history of cough
discriminator: The pertussis cough is caused by tracheal cytotoxin damage that persists long after bacteria are cleared. It can last 6-10 weeks regardless of antibiotic treatment. Antibiotics only reduce transmission.

stem: A 3-year-old with stridor is being evaluated. The child has a barking cough, low-grade fever, and is comfortable lying flat. Neck X-ray shows subglottic narrowing. The child receives dexamethasone but 6 hours later has stridor at rest. Nebulized adrenaline is given with good effect. When should the child be reassessed for potential discharge?
opts: Immediately after adrenaline, if stridor resolves
After 2 hours, once the adrenaline effect has worn off and stridor does not recur
After 24 hours observation regardless of symptoms
Refer directly for admission — outpatient management is not appropriate
After a repeat dose of dexamethasone with 4 hours observation
subject: Paediatrics-Emergencies
concept: Croup — post-adrenaline monitoring period (2-hour observation)
discriminator: Nebulized adrenaline has a temporary effect (~2 hours). Children who receive adrenaline must be observed for at least 2 hours after administration to ensure stridor does not recur as the effect wears off.

stem: A 3-year-old child presents with acute watery diarrhea for 3 days. On examination, the child is lethargic, has very sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, and skin pinch goes back very slowly. Capillary refill is 4 seconds. No urine output for 8 hours. According to WHO IMCI classification, this child has:
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: WHO IMCI dehydration classification
discriminator: Lethargy + very sunken eyes + very slow skin pinch + prolonged capillary refill + oliguria = severe dehydration (≥10% deficit)

stem: Using the Holliday-Segar method, what is the daily maintenance fluid requirement for a 25 kg child?
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: Holliday-Segar maintenance fluid calculation
discriminator: 100 mL/kg for first 10 kg + 50 mL/kg for next 10 kg + 20 mL/kg for each kg above 20

stem: An 18-month-old child presents with vomiting and loose stools for 2 days. He is thirsty and restless but alert. Mucous membranes are moist, eyes are normal, skin pinch returns quickly, and capillary refill is 2 seconds. He cried tears when examined. According to WHO IMCI classification, what is the dehydration status?
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: WHO IMCI some dehydration classification
discriminator: Thirsty and restless with ALL other parameters normal = some dehydration (3-5% deficit)

stem: A 12 kg child with severe dehydration is in the emergency room. What is the correct first intravenous fluid bolus?
opts: 240 mL of normal saline or Ringer lactate over 15-20 minutes
240 mL of 5% dextrose water over 1 hour
120 mL of Ringer lactate over 30 minutes
360 mL of normal saline over 10 minutes
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: IV bolus for severe dehydration
discriminator: 20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid (NS or RL) is the first bolus for severe dehydration

stem: An 18-month-old boy is brought for evaluation of bowed legs noticed over the past 3 months. On examination, both tibiae and femora are bowed. There is visible widening of the wrists, and palpable beading along the costochondral junctions. The anterior fontanelle is still open. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: Rickets clinical features
discriminator: Bilateral bowing + wrist widening + costochondral beading (rachitic rosary) + delayed fontanelle closure = classic rickets

stem: Which of the following is the characteristic radiographic finding in a child with rickets?
opts: Periosteal reaction along the shaft of long bones
Subperiosteal bone resorption of the phalanges
Metaphyseal cupping, fraying, and widened growth plate
Beaking of the medial proximal tibial metaphysis
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: Rickets radiographic findings
discriminator: Metaphyseal cupping and fraying with widened growth plate is the earliest and most characteristic X-ray finding in rickets

stem: A 14-month-old child from a low-resource setting presents with bilateral pitting pedal edema, apathy, sparse brittle hair with alternating light and dark bands, and flaky paint dermatosis. The abdomen is distended with a palpable liver edge. Subcutaneous fat is preserved in the arms and thighs. Weight-for-age is low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: Kwashiorkor clinical features
discriminator: Edema (hallmark) + preserved subcutaneous fat + skin/hair changes + age > 1 year = kwashiorkor, not marasmus

stem: What is the recommended vitamin K prophylaxis for all newborns at birth?
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: Vitamin K prophylaxis in newborns
discriminator: 1 mg IM is the standard dose for all newborns to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn

stem: A 2-year-old child presents with moderate dehydration per WHO IMCI criteria. He is alert, thirsty, and tries to drink ORS but vomits immediately after each attempt. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
opts: Continue offering ORS by mouth; vomiting is expected
Start intravenous fluids with isotonic crystalloid
Insert a nasogastric tube and give ORS
Keep NPO and reassess in 2 hours
Give antiemetic and resume ORS after 30 minutes
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: ORS vs IV therapy choice
discriminator: ORS works for some/moderate dehydration only if tolerated; persistent vomiting is an indication for IV fluids

stem: According to WHO recommendations, what vitamin A supplementation is indicated for a child presenting with measles in a vitamin A-deficient region?
opts: 200,000 IU given on two consecutive days
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: Vitamin A in measles
discriminator: WHO recommends 200,000 IU vitamin A for two consecutive days for measles to reduce mortality and prevent blindness

stem: A 20-month-old child from a rural area is brought with bilateral pitting pedal edema progressing to involve the legs and hands over 3 weeks. The child is apathetic, with sparse brittle hair that shows alternating bands of light and dark color. The skin has areas of hyperpigmentation and desquamation. Serum albumin is 1.8 g/dL. Urine dipstick is negative for protein. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: Kwashiorkor vs nephrotic syndrome discrimination
discriminator: Negative urine protein + apathy + flag sign hair + flaky skin in a malnourished child = kwashiorkor, not nephrotic syndrome

stem: What is the earliest clinical sign of rickets in an infant?
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: Rickets — earliest clinical sign
discriminator: Craniotabes (ping-pong skull) is the earliest clinical sign of rickets, appearing before bony deformities of the limbs

stem: A 6-month-old infant with hypernatremic dehydration has a serum sodium of 162 mEq/L. Which of the following is the correct approach to fluid correction?
opts: Correct the entire deficit rapidly with 0.45% normal saline over 12 hours
Correct slowly over 48 hours using isotonic fluids to avoid cerebral edema
Administer 3% hypertonic saline bolus to lower serum sodium
Use 5% dextrose water as the primary fluid to dilute serum sodium
Correct deficit with oral water only, no IV fluids
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: Hypernatremic dehydration correction
discriminator: Hypernatremic dehydration requires slow correction over 48 hours to prevent cerebral edema from rapid fluid shifts

stem: A 3-year-old child has sharp angulation below the right knee noticed since he started walking. There is no history of diarrhea or dark skin. X-ray shows beaking of the medial proximal tibial metaphysis. Laboratory results: normal serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and 25-OH vitamin D. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Start vitamin D supplementation 2000 IU daily
Apply bracing and start vitamin D
No intervention needed; bowing will self-correct
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: Blount disease vs rickets
discriminator: Unilateral sharp angulation + medial tibial beaking on X-ray + normal labs = Blount disease, not rickets — requires orthopedic referral

stem: An exclusively breastfed 3-month-old infant is brought for a routine well-child visit in winter. The mother has dark skin and limited sun exposure. Which of the following is recommended to prevent rickets in this infant?
opts: No supplementation needed; breast milk provides adequate vitamin D
Vitamin D 200 IU daily starting at 6 months
Vitamin D 400 IU daily starting at birth
Vitamin D 1000 IU daily starting at 1 year
Sun exposure for 30 minutes daily without supplementation
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: Vitamin D prophylaxis in breastfed infants
discriminator: Exclusively breastfed infants need 400 IU/day vitamin D supplementation because breast milk has low vitamin D content

stem: An 8-month-old infant fed only cow's milk without any supplementation presents with extreme irritability, painful swelling of the lower limbs, and refusal to bear weight. On examination, there are perifollicular hemorrhages, bleeding gums, and the lower limb X-ray shows a subperiosteal hematoma with a 'scorched earth' appearance. What is the most likely deficiency?
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy)
discriminator: Perifollicular hemorrhages + bleeding gums + subperiosteal hematoma + pseudoparalysis in an infant on cow's milk = scurvy (vitamin C deficiency)

stem: Which vitamin deficiency classically presents with the triad of dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia?
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: Niacin deficiency (pellagra)
discriminator: Pellagra (niacin/B3 deficiency) = dermatitis + diarrhea + dementia (the 3 Ds)

stem: A 2-year-old child presents with bowed legs and wrist widening. Investigations show: serum 25-OH vitamin D: 12 ng/mL (low), serum phosphate: low, serum calcium: low-normal, alkaline phosphatase: markedly elevated, PTH: elevated. Which of the following best describes the pathophysiology of these findings?
opts: Vitamin D deficiency leading to reduced intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate with secondary hyperparathyroidism
Renal phosphate wasting with normal vitamin D levels
Vitamin D receptor mutation causing end-organ resistance
Dietary calcium deficiency without vitamin D involvement
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: Rickets pathophysiology and lab interpretation
discriminator: Low 25-OH D + low PO4 + low-normal Ca + high ALP + high PTH = classic vitamin D-deficiency rickets with secondary hyperparathyroidism

stem: A 10 kg child is diagnosed with severe dehydration (10% deficit). An initial IV bolus of 20 mL/kg normal saline is given. After reassessment, the child is hemodynamically stable. What volume of fluid remains to be replaced as the remaining deficit?
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: Dehydration correction — deficit calculation
discriminator: Total deficit = 10% of 10 kg = 1000 mL; subtract the initial bolus (20 mL/kg = 200 mL); remaining deficit = 800 mL

stem: A 14-month-old child presents with pallor, smooth red tongue (glossitis), irritability, and developmental regression. The child is unable to sit without support, though he had achieved this milestone at 10 months. CBC shows macrocytic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils. Which of the following is the most likely deficiency?
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: Vitamin B12 deficiency
discriminator: Macrocytic anemia + hypersegmented neutrophils + developmental regression + glossitis = B12 deficiency; neurological regression distinguishes B12 from folate deficiency

stem: Which vitamin deficiency in infants can present with heart failure (wet beriberi), peripheral neuropathy, and aphonia (hoarse cry)?
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: Thiamine deficiency (beriberi)
discriminator: Beriberi (thiamine/B1 deficiency) has wet (cardiovascular — heart failure) and dry (neuropathy, aphonia) forms

stem: An 8-month-old infant is brought for failure to thrive. On examination, the infant has severe muscle wasting, absent subcutaneous fat, a 'skin and bones' appearance, and an 'old man' facies. There is no edema. Weight-for-height is severely low (< -3 Z-score). The mother reports prolonged breastfeeding without adequate complementary feeding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: Marasmus clinical features
discriminator: Severe wasting + no edema + old man facies + age < 1 year = marasmus (calorie deficiency)

stem: A 15 kg child is admitted with severe dehydration (10% deficit). After the initial 20 mL/kg IV bolus, the child is hemodynamically stable. Using the Holliday-Segar method, calculate the total fluid volume to be given over the next 24 hours (remaining deficit + maintenance).
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: Combined deficit + maintenance fluid calculation
discriminator: Total deficit = 10% of 15 kg = 1500 mL. Bolus given = 300 mL. Remaining deficit = 1200 mL. Maintenance = 10×100 + 5×50 = 1250 mL/day. Total = 1200 + 1250 = 2450 mL.

stem: A 2-year-old child with kwashiorkor is admitted for therapeutic feeding. Which of the following represents the correct sequence of refeeding in severe acute malnutrition?
opts: Start with F100 milk immediately; transition to F75 after 1 week
Start with F75 milk for stabilization; transition to F100 for catch-up growth; then complete recovery feeds
Start with full-cream milk feeds immediately; advance as tolerated
Begin with IV dextrose 10% and advance to oral feeds over 48 hours
Start with F100 mixed with vegetable oil for caloric density; reduce to F75 after weight gain
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: Severe malnutrition — therapeutic feeding protocol
discriminator: F75 (stabilization) → F100 (catch-up growth) → complete recovery feeds is the WHO-recommended sequence

stem: A 6-week-old exclusively breastfed infant presents with sudden-onset intracranial hemorrhage. There is no history of trauma. The mother reports that the baby did not receive any injection at birth. Laboratory findings show prolonged PT and aPTT with normal platelet count. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
subject: Paediatrics-Fluids
concept: Vitamin K deficiency in newborns (late-onset HDN)
discriminator: Late-onset HDN (2-12 weeks) in exclusively breastfed infant with no vitamin K prophylaxis — prolonged PT/aPTT, normal platelets

stem: A newborn is delivered at term and the pediatric team assesses the infant at 1 minute of life. Which of the following is NOT one of the five parameters assessed in the APGAR score?
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: APGAR scoring parameters
discriminator: APGAR assesses Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration — blood pressure is NOT a component

stem: During neonatal resuscitation, a newborn is apneic after initial warming, drying, and stimulation. The heart rate is 90 bpm. What is the NEXT step in the NRP sequence?
opts: Start chest compressions at a 3:1 ratio
Begin positive-pressure ventilation (PPV) with room air
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: NRP sequence — HR thresholds for intervention
discriminator: HR < 100 or apnea → PPV. HR < 60 despite PPV → compressions + epinephrine.

stem: A newborn is noted to have flat facial features, upslanting palpebral fissures, a single palmar crease, and hypotonia. Which of the following is also a characteristic physical finding of this condition?
opts: Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: Down syndrome — characteristic physical features
discriminator: Brushfield spots are white spots on the iris pathognomonic for Down syndrome

stem: Which of the following congenital heart defects is MOST commonly associated with Down syndrome?
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: Down syndrome — most common associated CHD
discriminator: AVSD (endocardial cushion defect) is the classic CHD associated with Down syndrome

stem: Which of the following is the MOST common congenital heart defect overall in the general population?
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: VSD — most common CHD overall
discriminator: VSD is the most common CHD, accounting for ~30% of all congenital heart defects

stem: Which of the following is the MOST common cyanotic congenital heart defect?
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: Tetralogy of Fallot — most common cyanotic CHD
discriminator: TOF is the most common cyanotic CHD in children who survive beyond infancy

stem: During neonatal resuscitation, chest compressions are being performed for a newborn with HR < 60 bpm. What is the recommended dose of intravenous epinephrine?
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: NRP — epinephrine dosage
discriminator: IV epinephrine dose in NRP is 0.01-0.03 mg/kg (0.1-0.3 mL/kg of 1:10,000 solution)

stem: A preterm infant born at 28 weeks gestation is found to have a hemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus on echocardiography. Which of the following medications is most appropriate for medical closure of the PDA?
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: PDA closure — pharmacotherapy in preterm infants
discriminator: Indomethacin or ibuprofen (NSAIDs) close PDA by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis

stem: A newborn presents with severe cyanosis at birth. Echocardiography reveals transposition of the great arteries (TGA). Which medication should be started immediately to maintain ductal patency until surgical repair?
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: Duct-dependent lesions — PGE1 therapy
discriminator: PGE1 maintains ductal patency in duct-dependent cyanotic CHD like TGA, coarctation, HLHS

stem: At what time intervals are APGAR scores routinely assessed in a newborn?
opts: At birth and at 1 hour of life
At 1 minute and 5 minutes of life
At 5 minutes and 10 minutes of life
At 1 minute, 5 minutes, and 30 minutes of life
At 5 minutes only, if the infant appears well
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: APGAR scoring — timing
discriminator: APGAR is routinely assessed at 1 and 5 minutes of life

stem: A 4-month-old infant with known Tetralogy of Fallot is brought to the emergency department during a crying episode with worsening cyanosis. The infant is irritable and tachypneic. What is the MOST appropriate immediate intervention?
opts: Place the infant in the knee-chest position and administer oxygen
Prepare for emergency arterial switch operation
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: Tet spell — acute management
discriminator: Knee-chest position increases SVR, reduces R→L shunt; O2 reduces pulmonary vasoconstriction

stem: A 6-month-old infant with Down syndrome presents with cyanosis during crying. Echocardiography shows a VSD, overriding aorta, right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, and right ventricular hypertrophy. What is the diagnosis?
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: Tetralogy of Fallot — four components and association with Down syndrome
discriminator: The four components of TOF: VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction, RVH. Down syndrome + cyanotic spells = TOF until proven otherwise.

stem: A 7-year-old child is found to have hypertension in the upper extremities on routine examination. Femoral pulses are weak and delayed compared to brachial pulses. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: Coarctation of aorta — clinical presentation
discriminator: Upper limb HTN + diminished/delayed femoral pulses = coarctation until proven otherwise

stem: A 3-year-old asymptomatic child is found to have a harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border on routine examination. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: VSD — murmur characteristics
discriminator: Harsh holosystolic murmur at LLSB is classic for VSD

stem: A newborn presents with severe cyanosis immediately after birth. Chest X-ray shows an egg-on-string appearance. Echocardiography shows the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial medical management?
opts: Start IV prostaglandin E1 and prepare for arterial switch operation
Administer indomethacin and prepare for complete repair at 6 months
Start propranolol and place in knee-chest position
Administer IV epinephrine and start chest compressions
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: TGA — recognition and management
discriminator: TGA: egg-on-string CXR, cyanosis at birth, discordant ventriculoarterial connection. PGE1 maintains ductus until arterial switch.

stem: A newborn with Down syndrome presents with bilious vomiting shortly after birth. Abdominal X-ray shows a 'double-bubble' sign. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: Down syndrome — duodenal atresia association
discriminator: Down syndrome + bilious vomiting + double-bubble sign = duodenal atresia

stem: An 18-month-old child with a known large VSD was lost to follow-up. Now presents with cyanosis and clubbing. Echocardiography shows a right-to-left shunt through the VSD with elevated pulmonary vascular resistance. Which of the following is true regarding management?
opts: Immediate surgical VSD closure is indicated
The condition is irreversible and surgical repair is contraindicated
Start prostaglandin E1 to maintain ductal patency
Balloon angioplasty of the pulmonary artery is indicated
Start indomethacin to close the VSD medically
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: Eisenmenger syndrome — irreversible pulmonary HTN
discriminator: Eisenmenger syndrome = shunt reversal due to irreversible pulmonary HTN; surgical repair is contraindicated

stem: During a delivery room resuscitation, a term newborn is apneic after initial steps. The heart rate is 80 bpm. You begin PPV with room air. After 30 seconds of effective PPV, the heart rate is 55 bpm. What is the next indicated intervention?
opts: Continue PPV and reassess in another 30 seconds
Intubate, start chest compressions at a 3:1 ratio, and give IV epinephrine
Increase oxygen to 100% and continue PPV alone
Place an umbilical venous catheter and start dopamine
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: NRP — escalation when HR < 60 despite PPV
discriminator: HR < 60 despite effective PPV requires intubation, chest compressions, and epinephrine

stem: A 2-week-old preterm infant (born at 29 weeks) has persistent tachypnea, bounding pulses, and a continuous machinery murmur. Echocardiography confirms a large PDA. Renal function is normal and there are no signs of NEC. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
opts: Observe and repeat echo in 6 months — most PDAs close spontaneously
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: PDA in preterm — medical closure indication
discriminator: Symptomatic PDA in preterm with normal renal function → medical closure with indomethacin/ibuprofen

stem: A chest X-ray in a 5-month-old infant with cyanotic spells shows a 'boot-shaped' heart. Which of the following congenital heart defects is most likely present?
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: CXR findings in CHD — boot-shaped heart in TOF
discriminator: Boot-shaped heart = RVH from TOF (RV apex elevated and deviated leftward)

stem: A newborn with Down syndrome has bilious vomiting and a double-bubble sign on abdominal X-ray. After surgical repair, the infant continues to have difficulty passing meconium with abdominal distension. Rectal biopsy shows absence of ganglion cells. Which of the following is the most likely additional diagnosis?
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: Down syndrome — multiple GI associations (duodenal atresia + Hirschsprung)
discriminator: Down syndrome is associated with both duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease. Absent ganglion cells = Hirschsprung.

stem: A 1-day-old full-term newborn is cyanotic. Pre-ductal oxygen saturation (right hand) is 95%, while post-ductal saturation (lower extremity) is 75%. Femoral pulses are weak. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?
opts: Tetralogy of Fallot — place in knee-chest position and give oxygen
Coarctation of aorta or interrupted aortic arch — start PGE1 infusion
Transposition of the great arteries — prepare for arterial switch operation
Total anomalous pulmonary venous return — start PGE1 and schedule repair
Persistent pulmonary hypertension — start inhaled nitric oxide
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: Coarctation — differential cyanosis and management
discriminator: Differential cyanosis (pink upper, blue lower) + weak femoral pulses = coarctation/interrupted arch. PGE1 keeps ductus open.

stem: A 5-year-old child with Down syndrome is being evaluated before starting gymnastics. Which of the following screening investigations is most important to perform due to the increased risk of a specific associated condition?
opts: Hearing assessment for sensorineural hearing loss
Lateral cervical spine X-ray for atlantoaxial instability
Abdominal ultrasound for Wilms tumor screening
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: Down syndrome — atlantoaxial instability screening before sports
discriminator: Down syndrome is associated with atlantoaxial instability; screening X-ray is recommended before high-risk activities like gymnastics

stem: A 3-month-old infant with Down syndrome is being discharged after AVSD repair. During the admission, the mother asks about future malignancy risk. Which of the following malignancies is associated with Down syndrome and should be monitored for?
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: Down syndrome — malignancy risk (ALL)
discriminator: Down syndrome carries increased risk of acute leukemia, particularly ALL

stem: A 6-week-old infant presents with poor feeding, tachypnea, and failure to thrive. On examination, there is a parasternal heave, a harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, and hepatomegaly. Chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly and pulmonary plethora. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and what complication should be prevented with early surgical repair?
subject: Paediatrics-Neonatal
concept: Large VSD — CHF presentation and Eisenmenger prevention
discriminator: Large VSD causes heart failure + failure to thrive + pulmonary plethora. Early repair prevents irreversible Eisenmenger.

stem: A 6-month-old presents with fever of 39.2°C and a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes. The child is now alert and playful. LP shows clear CSF with normal WBC, glucose, and protein.
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: A 6-month-old presents with fever of 39.2°C and a generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 2 minutes. The child is now a
discriminator: Simple febrile seizure: brief (<15 min), generalized, single in 24 h, age 6 mo-5 y, no post-ictal focal signs. LP normal. Reassurance only.

stem: A 3-year-old presents with barking cough, inspiratory stridor, low-grade fever. Neck X-ray shows steeple sign.
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: A 3-year-old presents with barking cough, inspiratory stridor, low-grade fever. Neck X-ray shows steeple sign.
discriminator: Croup: barking cough, steeple sign, gradual onset, low fever. Treatment: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg PO once.

stem: A 2-year-old presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, melena. Abdominal X-ray shows radiopaque material in the stomach.
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: A 2-year-old presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, melena. Abdominal X-ray shows radiopaque material in the stomach.
discriminator: Iron tablets are radiopaque — uniquely visible on abdominal X-ray. Desferrioxamine IV if Fe >500 mcg/dL or severe symptoms.

stem: A 24-week pregnant woman presents with acute severe RLQ pain and vaginal spotting. Tachycardic, hypotensive. US shows empty uterus.
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: A 24-week pregnant woman presents with acute severe RLQ pain and vaginal spotting. Tachycardic, hypotensive. US shows em
discriminator: Ectopic pregnancy: empty uterus + adnexal mass + shock. β-hCG >1500 with empty uterus. Emergency laparoscopy/salpingectomy.

stem: A primigravida at 36 weeks presents with BP 160/110, proteinuria 3+, headache, epigastric pain. Platelets 80,000, AST/ALT elevated.
opts: Severe preeclampsia with HELLP — deliver immediately
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: A primigravida at 36 weeks presents with BP 160/110, proteinuria 3+, headache, epigastric pain. Platelets 80,000, AST/AL
discriminator: HELLP: Hemolysis, Elevated LFTs, Low Platelets. Immediate delivery regardless of gestational age. MgSO4 for seizure prophylaxis.

stem: An Rh-negative mother delivers an Rh-positive baby. Kleihauer test is negative.
opts: No anti-D needed because Kleihauer is negative
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: An Rh-negative mother delivers an Rh-positive baby. Kleihauer test is negative.
discriminator: All Rh-negative mothers with Rh-positive babies need anti-D within 72 h. Negative Kleihauer = no large bleed, so standard dose (300 mcg) is sufficient.

stem: In the Paediatrics — 60-second discriminators bridge review, which concept is best identified by this discriminator: Febrile seizure: brief (<15 min), generalized, age 6mo-5y, no focal signs, alert post-ictal. Meningitis: ill-appearing, photophobia, neck stiffness, focal/prolonged seizure, persistent altered mental state?
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: Febrile seizure vs meningitis
discriminator: Febrile seizure: brief (<15 min), generalized, age 6mo-5y, no focal signs, alert post-ictal. Meningitis: ill-appearing, photophobia, neck stiffness, focal/prolonged seizure, persistent altered mental state

stem: A review question gives this trigger: Fever + meningeal signs. Which linked concept should you revise first?
opts: Isotonic vs hypotonic vs hypertonic dehydration
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: Bacterial vs viral meningitis
discriminator: CSF: PMNs, low glucose, high protein = bacterial; lymphs, normal glucose, normal-mild protein = viral

stem: Which topic best matches the exam discriminator: Spastic (UMNL, most common, 70-80%) -> periventricular leukomalacia. Athetoid/dyskinetic -> basal ganglia (kernicterus). Ataxic -> cerebellar.?
opts: Isotonic vs hypotonic vs hypertonic dehydration
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: Cerebral palsy types
discriminator: Spastic (UMNL, most common, 70-80%) -> periventricular leukomalacia. Athetoid/dyskinetic -> basal ganglia (kernicterus). Ataxic -> cerebellar.

stem: A mixed review stem is built around Child with wasting/edema. Which answer is the intended discriminator pair?
opts: Isotonic vs hypotonic vs hypertonic dehydration
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: Marasmus vs Kwashiorkor
discriminator: Marasmus: severe wasting, no edema, calorie deficiency, skin-and-bones. Kwashiorkor: bilateral pitting edema (hallmark), fatty liver, flag sign hair, flaky paint dermatosis, protein deficiency

stem: In the Paediatrics — 60-second discriminators bridge review, which concept is best identified by this discriminator: Isotonic (Na 130-150): most common, balanced loss. Hypotonic (Na <130): shock out of proportion, seizures. Hypertonic (Na >150): intracellular dehydration, seizures with rapid correction — correct slowly over 48 h?
opts: Isotonic vs hypotonic vs hypertonic dehydration
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: Isotonic vs hypotonic vs hypertonic dehydration
discriminator: Isotonic (Na 130-150): most common, balanced loss. Hypotonic (Na <130): shock out of proportion, seizures. Hypertonic (Na >150): intracellular dehydration, seizures with rapid correction — correct slowly over 48 h

stem: A review question gives this trigger: Bowed legs, rachitic rosary. Which linked concept should you revise first?
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: Rickets signs and labs
discriminator: ↓ Ca/PO4, ↑ ALP, ↑ PTH. X-ray: metaphyseal cupping, fraying, widened growth plate. Vitamin D deficiency. Treatment: cholecalciferol + calcium

stem: Which topic best matches the exam discriminator: HR, RR, tone, reflex irritability, color — each 0-2. Score <3 = severe distress (immediate resuscitation), 4-6 = moderate, 7-10 = normal?
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: APGAR scoring
discriminator: HR, RR, tone, reflex irritability, color — each 0-2. Score <3 = severe distress (immediate resuscitation), 4-6 = moderate, 7-10 = normal

stem: A mixed review stem is built around Newborn with dysmorphic features + murmur. Which answer is the intended discriminator pair?
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: Down syndrome congenital heart disease
discriminator: AVSD (most common, 40-50%), VSD, ASD, TOF. All need echo screening at birth.

stem: In the Paediatrics — 60-second discriminators bridge review, which concept is best identified by this discriminator: Croup: barking cough, steeple sign (subglottic), gradual onset, low fever. Epiglottitis: drooling, tripod positioning, thumbprint sign (epiglottic swelling), acute onset, high fever — DO NOT examine throat?
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: Croup vs Epiglottitis
discriminator: Croup: barking cough, steeple sign (subglottic), gradual onset, low fever. Epiglottitis: drooling, tripod positioning, thumbprint sign (epiglottic swelling), acute onset, high fever — DO NOT examine throat

stem: A review question gives this trigger: Wheezing in infant/toddler. Which linked concept should you revise first?
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: Bronchiolitis vs Asthma
discriminator: Bronchiolitis: first episode, <12 mo, RSV season, coryza -> cough -> wheeze, hyperinflation on X-ray. Asthma: recurrent wheezing, >12 mo, family history/atopy, responds to bronchodilators

stem: Which topic best matches the exam discriminator: Catarrhal stage (most infectious) -> paroxysmal -> convalescent. Lymphocytosis. Azithromycin decreases transmission (not cough course). DTaP prevention?
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: Pertussis clinical triad
discriminator: Catarrhal stage (most infectious) -> paroxysmal -> convalescent. Lymphocytosis. Azithromycin decreases transmission (not cough course). DTaP prevention

stem: A mixed review stem is built around Toddler with vomiting, metabolic acidosis, shock. Which answer is the intended discriminator pair?
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: Iron poisoning
discriminator: Radiopaque tablets on abdominal X-ray (unique). Treatment: desferrioxamine IV if serum Fe >500 mcg/dL or severe symptoms

stem: In the Paediatrics — 60-second discriminators bridge review, which concept is best identified by this discriminator: OP: SLUDGE + fasciculations + bradycardia -> atropine + pralidoxime. Opioid: respiratory depression -> naloxone?
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: OP vs opioid poisoning
discriminator: OP: SLUDGE + fasciculations + bradycardia -> atropine + pralidoxime. Opioid: respiratory depression -> naloxone

stem: A review question gives this trigger: OP poisoning confirmed. Which linked concept should you revise first?
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: Atropine dosing in OP poisoning
discriminator: Start 0.05 mg/kg IV, double dose every 5 min until atropinization (clear lungs, dry secretions, HR >80). Pralidoxime early <24-48 h

stem: Which topic best matches the exam discriminator: Previa: painless, bright red, no pain, high presenting part -> C-section. Abruption: painful, dark blood, board-like uterus, fetal distress -> immediate delivery?
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: Placenta previa vs placental abruption
discriminator: Previa: painless, bright red, no pain, high presenting part -> C-section. Abruption: painful, dark blood, board-like uterus, fetal distress -> immediate delivery

stem: A mixed review stem is built around 1st trimester: pain + bleeding + adnexal tenderness. Which answer is the intended discriminator pair?
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: Ectopic pregnancy
discriminator: TVUS: empty uterus + adnexal mass. β-hCG >1500 with empty uterus = ectopic. Laparoscopy is gold standard. Salpingectomy vs salpingostomy

stem: In the Obstetrics — 60-second discriminators bridge review, which concept is best identified by this discriminator: Tone (uterine atony = most common) -> bimanual massage + oxytocin. Trauma -> repair. Tissue -> manual removal. Thrombin -> replace factors?
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: PPH: causes and initial management
discriminator: Tone (uterine atony = most common) -> bimanual massage + oxytocin. Trauma -> repair. Tissue -> manual removal. Thrombin -> replace factors

stem: A review question gives this trigger: HTN + proteinuria with/without seizures. Which linked concept should you revise first?
opts: Gestational HTN vs preeclampsia vs chronic HTN
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: Preeclampsia vs Eclampsia
discriminator: Preeclampsia: BP >=140/90 + proteinuria after 20 wks. Eclampsia: seizures. MgSO4 is anticonvulsant and prophylactic

stem: Which topic best matches the exam discriminator: Hemolysis (↓ Hb, ↑ LDH, schistocytes), ↑ LFTs, ↓ platelets. Immediate delivery regardless of gestational age?
opts: Gestational HTN vs preeclampsia vs chronic HTN
subject: Paediatrics-Review
concept: HELLP syndrome recognition
discriminator: Hemolysis (↓ Hb, ↑ LDH, schistocytes), ↑ LFTs, ↓ platelets. Immediate delivery regardless of gestational age

stem: A 22-year-old sexually active woman presents with lower abdominal pain and vaginal discharge for 4 days. On bimanual examination, she has cervical motion tenderness and bilateral adnexal tenderness. Temperature is 38.5°C. Which of the following is the minimum criterion sufficient to start empiric treatment for PID?
opts: Cervical motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness on exam
Gram-negative intracellular diplococci on cervical smear
subject: Obgyn-Gynecology
concept: CDC minimum diagnostic criteria for PID
discriminator: PID is a clinical diagnosis — cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, or adnexal tenderness alone is sufficient for empiric treatment per CDC guidelines.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is diagnosed with PID based on cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness. Gram stain of cervical discharge shows gram-negative intracellular diplococci. What is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen?
opts: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose + doxycycline 100 mg PO BD × 14 days + metronidazole 500 mg PO BD × 14 days
Azithromycin 1 g PO single dose + ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BD × 7 days
Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose + azithromycin 1 g PO single dose
Metronidazole 400 mg PO TDS × 7 days + doxycycline 100 mg PO BD × 7 days
Doxycycline 100 mg PO BD × 21 days alone
subject: Obgyn-Gynecology
concept: PID empiric antibiotic regimen — dual/triple therapy
discriminator: PID requires coverage of N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, and anaerobes — ceftriaxone + doxycycline ± metronidazole is the CDC-recommended regimen.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with a copper IUD in situ presents with pelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness, and fever. She is diagnosed with PID. After starting appropriate antibiotics, when should the IUD be removed?
opts: After 48-72 hours if no clinical improvement
After completing the full course of antibiotics
Only if she develops a tubo-ovarian abscess
The IUD should never be removed
subject: Obgyn-Gynecology
concept: IUD management in PID — timing of removal
discriminator: Start antibiotics first. Remove IUD only if no improvement after 48-72 hours — not immediately.

stem: A 26-year-old woman with known Chlamydia trachomatis infection presents with right upper quadrant pain for 3 days. She was treated for PID 2 weeks ago. Laparoscopy reveals violin-string adhesions between the liver capsule and diaphragm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Obgyn-Gynecology
concept: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis)
discriminator: RUQ pain + Chlamydia PID + violin-string adhesions = Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome.

stem: Untreated or inadequately treated PID most commonly leads to which of the following long-term complications?
subject: Obgyn-Gynecology
concept: PID complications — tubal factor infertility
discriminator: Tubal factor infertility is the most common preventable cause of infertility and the most important long-term complication of PID.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with PID is being considered for outpatient management. Which of the following findings would most clearly warrant hospitalization?
subject: Obgyn-Gynecology
concept: PID — indications for hospitalization
discriminator: Failed outpatient therapy, pregnancy, severe illness (T >39°C), and tubo-ovarian abscess are indications for inpatient PID management.

stem: A cervical swab from a patient with PID reveals gram-negative intracellular diplococci. Which is the most likely causative organism?
subject: Obgyn-Gynecology
concept: PID microbiology — gram-negative intracellular diplococci
discriminator: Gram-negative intracellular diplococci on cervical smear are pathognomonic for N. gonorrhoeae.

stem: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication (WHO Category 4) to combined oral contraceptive (COC) use?
opts: Current or past history of venous thromboembolism
Age 30 who smokes 5 cigarettes per day
subject: Obgyn-Gynecology
concept: COC — absolute contraindications (WHO Category 4)
