stem: A 25-year-old motorcyclist sustains a brachial plexus traction injury. He has a flail arm with no movement below the shoulder, complete anesthesia, and a painful Horner syndrome. He also has severe burning pain in the limb. What combination of findings indicates the poorest prognosis for spontaneous recovery?
opts: C5-C6 injury with waiter's tip deformity
C7 nerve root injury with triceps weakness
Upper trunk injury with deltoid weakness
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Preganglionic brachial plexus avulsion — Horner syndrome indicates T1 root avulsion with no recovery
discriminator: Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) = preganglionic T1 avulsion → no spontaneous recovery possible

stem: A 30-year-old man sustains a sharp laceration to his wrist, dividing the median nerve. He presents to the emergency department 6 hours later. The wound is clean. What is the optimal management for the nerve injury?
opts: Observe for 3-6 months for spontaneous recovery
Delayed repair at 3-4 weeks after wound healing
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Nerve repair timing — primary repair within 72 hours for clean sharp lacerations
discriminator: Sharp laceration + clean wound + presentation within hours = primary repair within 72 hours

stem: A 28-year-old man presents with a displaced supracondylar fracture after a fall. On examination, he has a pale, pulseless hand with absent radial pulse, loss of thumb opposition, and paresthesias in the thumb and index finger. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
opts: Perform EMG/NCS to document nerve injury
Urgent orthopedic consultation for reduction and possible vascular exploration
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Combined neurovascular injury in supracondylar fracture — urgent reduction and exploration
discriminator: Pale pulseless hand + nerve deficit (median) + fracture = vascular injury requiring urgent intervention

stem: A 40-year-old man wakes up unable to extend his wrist and fingers after sleeping with his arm draped over a chair. He has no history of trauma. On examination, triceps strength is 5/5. Sensation is mildly reduced over the posterior forearm and dorsal hand. What is the most likely diagnosis and expected course?
opts: Radial nerve laceration — requires immediate surgical repair
Saturday night palsy (radial nerve neurapraxia) — full recovery expected in days to weeks
PIN compression at the supinator — requires surgical decompression
C7 radiculopathy — will not recover without cervical spine surgery
Radial nerve axonotmesis — recovery in 6-12 months
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Saturday night palsy — radial nerve compression neurapraxia, transient, full recovery
discriminator: Nocturnal arm compression + wrist drop + preserved triceps + no trauma + sensory loss posterior forearm/dorsal hand = Saturday night palsy (neurapraxia)

stem: A 50-year-old woman sustains a pelvic fracture in a car accident. She cannot extend her knee and has lost the patellar reflex. Sensation is lost over the anterior thigh and medial leg. Hip adduction is intact. Which nerve is injured?
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Femoral nerve injury — quadriceps weakness, patellar reflex loss, anterior thigh/medial leg sensory loss
discriminator: Pelvic fracture + loss of knee extension + lost patellar reflex + anterior thigh sensory loss + preserved hip adduction = femoral nerve

stem: All of the following are contents of the cubital fossa EXCEPT:
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Cubital fossa contents (medial to lateral: median nerve, brachial artery, biceps tendon)
discriminator: The radial nerve bifurcates at the lateral epicondyle into superficial and deep branches; it does NOT run as part of the midline cubital fossa stack (MB MN: median nerve, brachial artery, biceps tendon).

stem: A 70-year-old woman presents with a painful, irreducible groin swelling below the inguinal ligament, medial to the femoral pulse. On exploration, a hernia sac is found passing through a defect. Through which anatomical space does this hernia pass?
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Femoral hernia passes through femoral canal (medial compartment of femoral sheath, below inguinal ligament)
discriminator: Location below inguinal ligament and medial to femoral vein/pulse = femoral hernia through femoral canal. Inguinal hernias emerge above the inguinal ligament.

stem: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) produced in the choroid plexus of the lateral ventricles flows through which structure to reach the third ventricle?
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Ventricles of brain: CSF flow from lateral ventricles → foramen of Monro → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle → foramina of Luschka/Magendie → subarachnoid space
discriminator: Each lateral ventricle drains into the third ventricle through the interventricular foramen (foramen of Monro). The cerebral aqueduct connects the third and fourth ventricles. The foramina of Luschka and Magendie drain the fourth ventricle.

stem: All of the following cranial nerves run in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus EXCEPT:
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Cavernous sinus contents: lateral wall = CN III, IV, V1, V2; inside sinus = CN VI + ICA
discriminator: CN VI is the only cranial nerve that runs within the cavernous sinus proper (not in the lateral wall), medial to CN V1 and lateral to the ICA.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with numbness and tingling in the thumb, index, and middle fingers, worse at night. On examination, thenar eminence sensation is intact. Which anatomical feature explains the preserved thenar sensation?
opts: Ulnar nerve innervation of the thenar eminence
Radial nerve contribution to thenar skin
Palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises proximal to the flexor retinaculum
Recurrent motor branch of median nerve supplies thenar sensation
The lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve overlaps thenar dermatome
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Carpal tunnel: palmar cutaneous branch of median nerve arises proximal to flexor retinaculum, sparing thenar sensation in CTS
discriminator: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve originates ~5 cm proximal to the wrist crease and passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum. It is NOT compressed in carpal tunnel syndrome, so thenar eminence sensation is spared.

stem: The anterior triangle of the neck is subdivided into four smaller triangles. Which of the following is NOT a subdivision of the anterior triangle?
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Triangles of neck: anterior triangle subdivisions (submental, submandibular, carotid, muscular). Occipital triangle is in the posterior triangle.
discriminator: The anterior triangle (bounded by mandible, midline, SCM) has 4 subdivisions. The occipital triangle belongs to the posterior triangle (bounded by clavicle, SCM, trapezius).

stem: A patient undergoes surgical drainage of an ischiorectal (ischioanal) fossa abscess in the perineum. The surgeon must avoid damaging the neurovascular bundle in the pudendal canal on the lateral wall of the fossa. This fossa is bounded medially by the pelvic diaphragm (levator ani) and laterally by the obturator internus fascia. Which of the following is contained in the pudendal canal (Alcock canal)?
opts: Sciatic nerve and posterior femoral cutaneous nerve
Pudendal nerve, internal pudendal artery, and internal pudendal vein
Inferior rectal nerve and perineal branch of S4
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Pudendal canal (Alcock canal) contents within the ischiorectal fossa lateral wall
discriminator: The pudendal canal is a fascial tunnel on the lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa (obturator internus fascia). It contains the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels. The inferior rectal nerve is a branch that exits medially.

stem: The diaphragm separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominal cavity. Which of the following structures passes through the diaphragm at the level of T10?
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Diaphragm openings: T8 (IVC), T10 (esophagus + vagus nerves), T12 (aorta + thoracic duct + azygos/hemiazygos). The diaphragm is the floor of the thoracic cavity (which contains the mediastinum) and roof of the abdominal cavity.
discriminator: The esophageal hiatus is at T10 (not T8 for IVC, not T12 for aorta). The vagus nerves accompany the esophagus through this hiatus. The mediastinum is directly superior to the diaphragm.

stem: Which of the following cranial fossae contains the pituitary gland (sella turcica), the cavernous sinus, and the foramina rotundum, ovale, and spinosum?
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Cranial fossae: middle cranial fossa houses the sella turcica (pituitary), cavernous sinus, and multiple foramina (rotundum, ovale, spinosum)
discriminator: The sella turcica of the sphenoid bone occupies the center of the middle cranial fossa. The cavernous sinuses lie lateral to it. Foramina rotundum (V2), ovale (V3), and spinosum (middle meningeal artery) open through the greater wing of sphenoid into the middle fossa.

stem: The recurrent laryngeal nerve is most vulnerable to injury during thyroid surgery because of its anatomical relationship to which artery?
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Recurrent laryngeal nerve runs posterior to the inferior thyroid artery in the tracheoesophageal groove
discriminator: The RLN crosses posterior to (or between branches of) the inferior thyroid artery near the lower pole of the thyroid. The inferior thyroid artery is the most important surgical landmark for identifying and preserving the RLN.

stem: A 35-year-old man sustains a mid-shaft humeral fracture in a road traffic accident. On examination, he cannot extend the wrist or metacarpophalangeal joints, and sensation is lost over the dorsum of the first webspace. Which anatomical structure is injured?
opts: Radial nerve at the spiral groove
Axillary nerve at the surgical neck
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Radial nerve injury at spiral groove of humerus → wrist drop, loss of MCP extension, dorsal first webspace sensory loss
discriminator: The radial nerve winds around the humerus in the spiral (radial) groove and is most commonly injured in mid-shaft humeral fractures. Wrist drop (loss of finger and wrist extensors) with sensory loss over the first dorsal webspace is pathognomonic.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with a reducible right groin swelling that appears when standing and disappears when supine. It emerges above the inguinal ligament and descends into the scrotum. On examination, the swelling is lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. This is characteristic of which type of hernia?
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Indirect inguinal hernia: lateral to inferior epigastric vessels, through deep inguinal ring, descends into scrotum
discriminator: Lateral to inferior epigastric vessels = indirect (enters deep ring). Medial = direct (through Hesselbach triangle). Descent into scrotum favors indirect as the sac follows the spermatic cord through the superficial ring.

stem: A 22-year-old man is stabbed in the left axilla. On examination, he cannot abduct the arm beyond 15 degrees and has loss of sensation over the regimental badge area (upper lateral arm). Which nerve is most likely injured?
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Axillary nerve injury: loss of shoulder abduction 15-90°, sensory loss regimental badge area (deltoid region)
discriminator: The axillary nerve (C5-C6) from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus winds around the surgical neck of humerus. It supplies deltoid (abduction 15-90°) and teres minor, plus the superior lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm (regimental badge). Stab wounds to the axilla can injure the posterior cord or the axillary nerve.

stem: A newborn has a brachial plexus injury with the arm adducted and internally rotated, forearm pronated, and wrist flexed (waiter's tip deformity). There is no Horner syndrome. Which part of the brachial plexus is injured?
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Erb-Duchenne palsy: upper trunk (C5-C6) injury → waiter's tip deformity. Klumpke: lower trunk (C8-T1) → claw hand + Horner.
discriminator: Waiter's tip deformity (adducted, internally rotated arm, pronated forearm, flexed wrist) = Erb-Duchenne palsy from C5-C6 upper trunk injury (excessive neck-shoulder separation during delivery). Horner syndrome absent = no T1 involvement (lower trunk intact).

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with a firm, painless mass in the tail of the parotid gland. Examination reveals ipsilateral facial palsy with inability to close the eye and drooping of the mouth corner. Which feature most strongly suggests malignancy?
opts: Size of the mass greater than 2 cm
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Parotid gland malignancy: facial nerve palsy indicates malignant invasion as the facial nerve traverses the parotid gland
discriminator: The facial nerve (CN VII) branches course through the parotid gland. Benign tumors (e.g., pleomorphic adenoma) displace but do not invade the nerve. Facial nerve palsy with a parotid mass is highly suggestive of malignancy until proven otherwise.

stem: A 20-year-old man falls onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH) and develops pain on the dorsolateral aspect of the wrist. Tenderness is elicited in the anatomical snuffbox. Which bone is most likely fractured?
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Anatomical snuffbox: floor formed by scaphoid (and radial styloid, trapezium). Snuffbox tenderness = scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise.
discriminator: The scaphoid forms the floor of the anatomical snuffbox. FOOSH injury + snuffbox tenderness is classic for scaphoid fracture. The scaphoid has a retrograde blood supply (distal to proximal), so proximal pole fractures risk avascular necrosis.

stem: During a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the surgeon identifies a structure posterior to the common bile duct. Aberrant anatomy is suspected. Which of the following is most likely seen?
opts: Cystic artery originating from the left hepatic artery
Accessory cystic duct draining directly into the common hepatic duct
Aberrant right hepatic artery running posterior to the common bile duct
Portal vein running anterior to the common bile duct
Right gastric artery crossing anterior to the cystic duct
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Calot triangle: aberrant right hepatic artery runs posterior to CBD in ~15%. Critical safety in cholecystectomy.
discriminator: The aberrant right hepatic artery is the most important vascular variant in Calot triangle surgery. In ~15% of individuals, the right hepatic artery arises from the superior mesenteric artery and runs posterior to the CBD, making it vulnerable to injury during bile duct dissection.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents with sudden severe headache ('thunderclap'), neck stiffness, and photophobia. CT reveals subarachnoid hemorrhage. Angiography shows a saccular aneurysm. Which is the most common site for a berry aneurysm in the circle of Willis?
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Circle of Willis: most common berry aneurysm site = anterior communicating artery (~30-40%)
discriminator: Berry (saccular) aneurysms most commonly occur at the anterior communicating artery (ACom), followed by the posterior communicating artery and MCA bifurcation. ACom aneurysms often present with SAH and may cause visual field defects (bitemporal) or frontal lobe signs.

stem: A 60-year-old woman presents with fever, proptosis, chemosis, and periorbital edema. She had a furuncle on her upper lip drained 5 days ago. Neurological examination reveals lateral rectus palsy. Which structure is most likely directly involved by the thrombotic process?
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Cavernous sinus thrombosis: facial infection spreads via valveless facial veins → cavernous sinus → proptosis, chemosis, fever, CN VI palsy
discriminator: Infections from the 'danger triangle of the face' (upper lip, nose) spread via the facial vein → superior ophthalmic vein → cavernous sinus. The valveless venous system allows retrograde thrombophlebitis. Cavernous sinus thrombosis causes CN VI palsy (the nerve inside the sinus) plus III, IV, V1, V2 deficits, proptosis, chemosis, and fever.

stem: A surgeon plans an incision through the anterior abdominal wall above the arcuate line. After incising the skin and subcutaneous tissue, the anterior layer of the rectus sheath is divided. Which layer is encountered immediately posterior to the rectus abdominis muscle?
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Rectus sheath above arcuate line: anterior sheath (external oblique + anterior lamina of internal oblique), posterior sheath (posterior lamina of internal oblique + transversus abdominis aponeurosis + transversalis fascia)
discriminator: Above the arcuate line (drawn at the level of the ASIS), the rectus sheath has both anterior and posterior layers. The posterior rectus sheath is formed by the posterior leaf of the internal oblique aponeurosis and the transversus abdominis aponeurosis. Below the arcuate line, the posterior sheath is absent (only transversalis fascia and peritoneum).

stem: Which of the following organs is retroperitoneal?
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Retroperitoneal vs intraperitoneal organs: descending colon (and ascending colon, duodenum, pancreas, kidneys, ureters, aorta, IVC) are retroperitoneal
discriminator: The descending colon is secondarily retroperitoneal (lies behind the peritoneum, covered only on its anterior surface). The stomach, transverse colon, jejunum, and cecum are intraperitoneal (suspended by mesentery).

stem: A 25-year-old man sustains a gunshot wound to the lower neck. He presents with ipsilateral ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis (Horner syndrome) along with a claw hand deformity. Which part of the brachial plexus is injured?
opts: Lower trunk (C8-T1) — Klumpke palsy with sympathetic trunk involvement
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Klumpke palsy: lower trunk (C8-T1) injury → claw hand + Horner syndrome (if T1 sympathetic fibers avulsed)
discriminator: Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) indicates interruption of the cervical sympathetic chain (T1 sympathetic fibers). Combined with claw hand (ulnar/median intrinsic muscle loss = C8-T1 distribution), this is classic for lower trunk/medial cord injury with preganglionic T1 avulsion.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a dull ache in the popliteal region and a palpable pulsatile mass. On exploration, the surgeon notes the deepest structure in the popliteal fossa is dilated. Which structure is most likely involved?
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Popliteal fossa contents (deep to superficial): popliteal artery (deepest), popliteal vein, tibial nerve (most superficial)
discriminator: In the popliteal fossa, the neurovascular bundle is arranged from deep to superficial: artery → vein → nerve (tibial). The popliteal artery is the deepest structure, directly on the popliteal surface of the femur and posterior capsule of the knee joint. Popliteal artery aneurysm is the most common peripheral artery aneurysm.

stem: A patient presents with a stab wound to the posterior abdomen at the T10 dermatome level. Neurological examination reveals ipsilateral loss of proprioception and vibration below the level of the lesion with contralateral loss of pain and temperature beginning 2 dermatomes below the lesion. This pattern is characteristic of injury to which part of the spinal cord?
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Spinal cord tracts: dorsal columns (ipsilateral proprioception/vibration), spinothalamic tract (contralateral pain/temperature), corticospinal tract (ipsilateral motor). Hemisection causes Brown-Séquard.
discriminator: Hemisection of the spinal cord (Brown-Séquard) produces: ipsilateral loss of motor function (corticospinal tract) and proprioception/vibration (dorsal columns), with contralateral loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic tract) beginning 1-2 segments below the lesion.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents with acute onset of severe headache and vomiting. CT shows subarachnoid hemorrhage. Cerebral angiography reveals an aneurysm at the junction of the anterior communicating artery with the anterior cerebral artery. Which anatomical structure is MOST at risk of compression by this aneurysm?
subject: Applied-Anatomy
concept: Anterior communicating artery aneurysm: close to optic chiasm → can cause bitemporal hemianopia from chiasmal compression
discriminator: The anterior communicating artery (ACom) lies superior and anterior to the optic chiasm. Large or ruptured ACom aneurysms can compress the optic chiasm directly, causing bitemporal heteronymous hemianopia (classic chiasmal syndrome). This is the most common compressive complication.

stem: A 55-year-old male with diarrhea has the following labs: Na 140, Cl 110, HCO3 15, albumin 4.0 g/dL. What is the calculated anion gap, and how does it guide the differential diagnosis?
opts: G = 10 — normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
G = 15 — high anion gap metabolic acidosis
G = 20 — high anion gap metabolic acidosis
G = 5 — normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
G = 25 — high anion gap metabolic acidosis
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Anion gap calculation and interpretation
discriminator: AG = Na − (Cl + HCO3) = 140 − (110 + 15) = 15. Normal AG is 8–12, so 15 is elevated, indicating a high-AG metabolic acidosis such as DKA, lactic acidosis, uremia, or toxin ingestion.

stem: A 40-year-old female with diabetic ketoacidosis has an HCO3 of 10 mEq/L. Her PaCO2 is being assessed to determine whether compensation is appropriate. Which formula should be used to calculate the expected PaCO2?
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Winter's formula for compensation in metabolic acidosis
discriminator: Winter's formula is specifically used for metabolic acidosis: Expected PaCO2 = (1.5 × HCO3) + 8 ± 2. The formula (0.7 × HCO3) + 21 ± 1.5 is for metabolic alkalosis compensation.

stem: A 65-year-old female with well-controlled type 2 diabetes on metformin develops metabolic acidosis. Labs: Na 138, Cl 108, HCO3 16 (AG = 14). Which of the following is the most likely cause if the anion gap is normal after albumin correction?
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Causes of normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis
discriminator: AG = 138 − (108 + 16) = 14. After correcting for albumin (assuming normal albumin 4.0, no correction needed), this is near the upper limit of normal but could be slightly elevated. However, the question specifies that after correction it is normal. Diarrhea causes HCO3 loss with Cl retention, producing a normal AG (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis.

stem: A 68-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with worsening dyspnea and productive cough for 3 days. His baseline ABG (3 months ago) showed pH 7.37, PaCO2 58, HCO3 33. Current ABG on room air: pH 7.31, PaCO2 72, HCO3 34. What is the most likely interpretation?
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Acute-on-chronic respiratory acidosis — interpreting ABG against a known baseline
discriminator: The baseline ABG shows chronic respiratory acidosis (pH 7.37 — near-normal due to renal compensation, PaCO2 58, HCO3 33 — elevated from renal HCO3 retention). The current ABG shows a further PaCO2 rise of 14 mmHg with pH dropping to 7.31 and HCO3 essentially unchanged (34). The acute rise caused pH ↓ 0.06, consistent with acute-on-chronic.

stem: A 55-year-old man with chronic kidney disease (stage 4) is seen in follow-up. He feels well. Vital signs normal. ABG: pH 7.36, PaCO2 30, HCO3 15, Na 138, Cl 108. What is the most accurate interpretation?
opts: Normal blood gas — all values within physiological range
Mixed metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Compensated metabolic acidosis — recognizing a primary disorder when pH is normal
discriminator: pH 7.36 is within the normal range but on the acidic side. HCO3 15 is low (metabolic acidosis) — the primary disorder. PaCO2 30 is low (respiratory alkalosis) — compensation. Winter's formula: expected PaCO2 = 1.5(15) + 8 = 30.5 ± 2 = 28.5–32.5. Measured 30 is within range → appropriate compensation. The primary is metabolic acidosis, fully compensated by respiratory alkalosis.

stem: A 65-year-old man with severe COPD (FEV1 30% predicted) presents for routine follow-up. He is comfortable at rest. ABG on room air: pH 7.36, PaCO2 65, HCO3 38, PaO2 60. What is the most likely acid-base status?
opts: hronic respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
Mixed respiratory acidosis and metabolic acidosis
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Chronic respiratory acidosis — recognizing full renal compensation
discriminator: pH 7.36 = near-normal (slightly acidic). PaCO2 65 = high (respiratory acidosis) — primary. HCO3 38 = high (metabolic compensation) from renal HCO3 retention over 3–5 days. Expected chronic compensation: for PaCO2 ↑ 25 above 40, HCO3 should rise by 3 × 2.5 = 7.5 → 24 + 7.5 = 31.5. But actual HCO3 is 38 — even higher, which still falls within chronic compensation range. The near-normal pH confirms full renal compensation.

stem: A 40-year-old male with DKA and ongoing vomiting has the following ABG: pH 7.46, PaCO2 38, HCO3 26, Na 140, Cl 96, albumin 4.0. Which of the following is the best explanation for these unexpected ABG values in a patient with DKA?
opts: oncurrent metabolic alkalosis from vomiting is masking the metabolic acidosis
The patient has combined respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis
The patient has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Mixed metabolic acidosis and metabolic alkalosis — counterbalancing effects on pH and HCO3
discriminator: In DKA, one expects acidemia (↓ pH), low HCO3, and high AG. Here, pH is 7.46 (alkalemia), HCO3 is 26 (normal), and PaCO2 is normal. AG = 140 − (96 + 26) = 18 (elevated). The elevated AG proves a metabolic acidosis is present, but the pH is alkaline — the only way to explain this is a concurrent metabolic alkalosis (from vomiting) raising HCO3 and driving pH alkaline. The two disorders cancel out on pH and HCO3 but leave an elevated AG as the clue.

stem: A 50-year-old male with diabetic ketoacidosis has the following labs: Na 140, Cl 95, HCO3 8, albumin 4.0. His calculated anion gap is 37. Which of the following is the best interpretation of the delta-delta ratio?
opts: elta-delta = 0.5 — suggests concurrent normal AG metabolic acidosis
elta-delta = 1.0 — confirms pure high AG metabolic acidosis
elta-delta cannot be calculated because HCO3 is too low
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Delta-delta ratio calculation and interpretation in high AG metabolic acidosis
discriminator: Delta-delta = (AG − 12) / (24 − HCO3) = (37 − 12) / (24 − 8) = 25 / 16 = 1.56. A delta-delta > 1.0 (typically > 1.2) indicates that the fall in HCO3 is less than expected for the rise in AG, suggesting a concurrent metabolic alkalosis is raising HCO3 (e.g., from vomiting).

stem: The Frank-Starling mechanism describes the direct relationship between:
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Frank-Starling law of the heart
discriminator: Frank-Starling specifically relates ventricular EDV (preload) to SV via sarcomere length-tension relationship. Increasing venous return stretches sarcomeres, increasing cross-bridge formation and force of contraction.

stem: Afferent signals from the carotid sinus baroreceptors travel to the medulla via which cranial nerve?
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Baroreceptor reflex — afferent pathway
discriminator: Carotid sinus baroreceptors → glossopharyngeal (CN IX). Aortic arch baroreceptors → vagus (CN X). This is a classic exam pairing tested repeatedly.

stem: The S3 heart sound occurs during which phase of the cardiac cycle?
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Cardiac cycle — heart sounds
discriminator: S3 = rapid ventricular filling (early diastole, after S2). S4 = atrial contraction (late diastole, before S1). The cadence mnemonic: Ken-tuck-y (S3) vs Ten-nes-see (S4).

stem: Which of the following correctly describes fetal circulation compared to adult circulation?
opts: The ductus arteriosus shunts blood from the right atrium to the left atrium in fetal circulation
Pulmonary vascular resistance is high in the fetus, causing most right ventricular output to bypass the lungs via the ductus arteriosus
Fetal haemoglobin has a lower affinity for oxygen than adult haemoglobin
The foramen ovale shunts blood from the right ventricle to the left ventricle
Placental blood has the lowest oxygen content in fetal circulation
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Fetal vs adult circulation — shunts and haemodynamics
discriminator: In utero, the collapsed fluid-filled lungs have high pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), so ~90% of RV output bypasses the lungs via the ductus arteriosus (→ aorta). The foramen ovale shunts RA → LA. Fetal Hb has HIGHER O₂ affinity (left-shifted curve). The placenta is the organ of gas exchange with the HIGHEST O₂ content.

stem: The normal filtration fraction (GFR ÷ renal plasma flow) is approximately:
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Renal physiology — filtration fraction
discriminator: Normal GFR ~125 mL/min, normal RPF ~625 mL/min. FF = 125/625 = 0.2 = 20%. This is a key numerical value for exam.

stem: The typical resting membrane potential of a neuron is closest to:
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Resting membrane potential — neurophysiology
discriminator: Neuron RMP ≈ -70 mV. Skeletal muscle ≈ -90 mV. Pacemaker cells (SA node) ≈ -60 mV (unstable). The Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation predicts this based on relative permeability to K⁺, Na⁺, and Cl⁻ at rest.

stem: Which transporter is responsible for NaCl reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle?
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Renal countercurrent multiplier — loop of Henle transport
discriminator: Each nephron segment has a unique transporter. TAL = NKCC2 (furosemide target). PCT = NHE3. DCT = NCC (thiazide target). Collecting duct = ENaC (amiloride target). Na⁺-K⁺-ATPase is the basolateral pump present throughout.

stem: Which of the following events occurs FIRST at the chemical synapse during synaptic transmission?
opts: inding of neurotransmitter to postsynaptic receptors
Opening of voltage-gated calcium channels on the presynaptic terminal
xocytosis of synaptic vesicles into the synaptic cleft
iffusion of neurotransmitter across the synaptic cleft
Graded potential generation on the postsynaptic membrane
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Synaptic transmission — sequence of events at the chemical synapse
discriminator: The sequence is: (1) Action potential arrives at presynaptic terminal → depolarisation. (2) Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open → Ca²⁺ influx. (3) Ca²⁺ triggers vesicle exocytosis (SNARE-mediated). (4) Neurotransmitter diffuses across cleft. (5) Binds postsynaptic receptors → ion channels open. (6) Graded potential (EPSP/IPSP). Ca²⁺ influx is the critical first-step trigger.

stem: Renal autoregulation maintains a relatively constant GFR across which range of mean arterial pressure?
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Renal autoregulation — myogenic and tubuloglomerular feedback
discriminator: The autoregulatory range is 80–180 mmHg MAP. Below 80 mmHg, GFR drops linearly (prerenal AKI risk). Above 180 mmHg, GFR rises (hyperfiltration injury).

stem: In skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling, calcium ions required for contraction are primarily released from the:
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Excitation-contraction coupling — calcium source in skeletal muscle
discriminator: The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) is the intracellular calcium store in muscle. T-tubules conduct the action potential inward but do NOT store Ca²⁺. The SR releases Ca²⁺ via ryanodine receptors (RyR1 in skeletal muscle) in response to dihydropyridine receptor (DHPR) activation on T-tubules.

stem: A 60-year-old smoker undergoes spirometry: FEV₁ 1.2 L (42% predicted), FVC 2.8 L (78% predicted), FEV₁/FVC 0.43, TLC 140% predicted. Which pattern is present?
opts: Isolated reduction in DLCO without obstruction or restriction
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Spirometry interpretation — obstructive pattern
discriminator: FEV₁/FVC < 0.70 + TLC ↑ (140%) = obstruction with hyperinflation. The reduced FVC is due to air trapping, NOT restriction (which would show ↓ TLC).

stem: A 65-year-old with known COPD has ABG: pH 7.36, PaCO₂ 58 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 34 mEq/L. What is the acid-base disorder?
opts: hronic respiratory acidosis with appropriate renal compensation
Mixed respiratory acidosis and metabolic alkalosis
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Acid-base physiology — chronic respiratory acidosis compensation
discriminator: In chronic respiratory acidosis, renal compensation raises HCO₃⁻ by ~3–4 mEq/L for every 10 mmHg increase in PaCO₂. Here PaCO₂ ↑ 18 above 40, so expected HCO₃ rise = 24 + (18/10 × 3.5) ≈ 24 + 6.3 ≈ 30; actual HCO₃ = 34 → slightly more compensated, pH 7.36 is near-normal → chronic compensated respiratory acidosis.

stem: In a patient with complete heart block, intermittent prominent a-waves (cannon a-waves) are seen in the JVP. These occur because the:
opts: Right atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: JVP waveform — cannon a-waves
discriminator: Cannon a-waves occur when the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve (AV dissociation). This is classic for complete heart block where the atrium and ventricle beat independently, occasionally causing simultaneous atrial contraction and ventricular systole.

stem: Which of the following electrolyte abnormalities is most associated with prolongation of the QT interval on ECG?
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: ECG — QT interval, electrolyte effects
discriminator: The electrolyte triad that prolongs QT: hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia. Hypercalcaemia shortens QT. Hyperkalaemia causes peaked T waves and widened QRS, not specifically QT prolongation.

stem: A 65-year-old man with long-standing hypertension presents with progressive dyspnoea. Cardiac auscultation reveals a low-pitched extra sound immediately preceding S1 at the apex. This finding most likely represents:
opts: S3 gallop due to volume overload from mitral regurgitation
S4 gallop due to reduced left ventricular compliance from pressure overload
Mid-systolic ejection click from aortic stenosis
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Heart sound identification — S4 gallop
discriminator: Extra sound BEFORE S1 (late diastolic) = S4, caused by atrial contraction against a stiff/hypertrophied LV. Hypertension → pressure overload → LV hypertrophy → reduced compliance → S4. S3 is AFTER S2, not before S1.

stem: A leftward shift of the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve would be caused by:
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: O₂-Hb dissociation curve — factors causing left shift
discriminator: Left shift (↑ O₂ affinity) = ↑ pH (alkalosis), ↓ CO₂, ↓ temperature, ↓ 2,3-DPG. Right shift (↓ O₂ affinity) = ↓ pH (acidosis), ↑ CO₂, ↑ temperature, ↑ 2,3-DPG (anaemia, chronic hypoxia). Hyperventilation → respiratory alkalosis → left shift.

stem: According to West's zones of the lung, which zone has the highest ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) ratio?
opts: ll zones have equal V/Q ratios
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Ventilation-perfusion matching — West's zones
discriminator: Apex (Zone 1): V > Q (high V/Q, alveolar pressure > arterial > venous → dead space effect). Base (Zone 3): Q > V (low V/Q, shunt-like). Zone 2: intermediate. The V/Q ratio increases from base to apex.

stem: A 70-year-old woman weighing 60 kg has a serum creatinine of 1.2 mg/dL. Using the Cockcroft-Gault formula, her estimated creatinine clearance (mL/min) is closest to:
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Renal clearance — Cockcroft-Gault formula for CrCl

stem: At the motor end plate, binding of acetylcholine to nicotinic receptors directly causes:
opts: Opening of voltage-gated sodium channels on the muscle membrane
Release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Influx of sodium ions through the receptor-channel complex, depolarising the end-plate region
ctivation of G-proteins that open potassium channels
irect opening of ryanodine receptors on the sarcoplasmic reticulum
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Motor end plate — nicotinic ACh receptor, end-plate potential
discriminator: The nicotinic ACh receptor at the NMJ is a ligand-gated ion channel (ionotropic). ACh binding opens the channel, allowing Na⁺ influx (and some K⁺ efflux), producing the end-plate potential (EPP). This is NOT voltage-gated — the channel itself is the receptor. The EPP then triggers voltage-gated Na⁺ channels on the adjacent muscle membrane.

stem: The micturition reflex is initiated by which of the following stimuli?
opts: Sympathetic activation causing internal urethral sphincter relaxation
Stretch of the detrusor muscle activating mechanoreceptors in the bladder wall
Voluntary contraction of the external urethral sphincter
Increased urine osmolality detected by osmoreceptors in the bladder
ecreased parasympathetic outflow from the sacral spinal cord
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Micturition reflex — sensory limb and neural control
discriminator: The micturition reflex is a spinal reflex triggered by stretch receptors (mechanoreceptors) in the bladder wall when volume reaches ~150–300 mL. Afferents travel via pelvic nerves (S2–S4) to the pontine micturition centre (Barrington's nucleus). Efferents: parasympathetic (pelvic nerve) → detrusor contraction + internal sphincter relaxation. The external sphincter (pudendal nerve, somatic) is voluntarily controlled.

stem: A 55-year-old smoker with known COPD presents with acute dyspnoea. Spirometry: FEV₁/FVC 0.55, FEV₁ 40% predicted. JVP is raised with a prominent a-wave, there is bilateral pedal oedema and tender hepatomegaly. ABG: pH 7.33, PaCO₂ 62 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 32 mEq/L. Which of the following BEST describes the integrated pathophysiology?
opts: cute asthma exacerbation with respiratory alkalosis and intravascular volume depletion
OPD exacerbation with cor pulmonale and chronic respiratory acidosis with acute-on-chronic decompensation
Restrictive lung disease with right heart failure and compensatory metabolic alkalosis
Left ventricular systolic failure with pulmonary oedema and acute respiratory acidosis
cute pulmonary embolism with obstructive spirometry and acute cor pulmonale
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Integrated multi-system physiology — COPD, cor pulmonale, acid-base
discriminator: This case integrates three systems: (1) Obstructive spirometry (FEV₁/FVC 0.55) = COPD. (2) Raised JVP + pedal oedema + tender hepatomegaly = cor pulmonale (right heart failure from chronic lung disease). (3) pH 7.33 (acidaemic), PaCO₂ 62 (↑), HCO₃⁻ 32 (↑) = chronic respiratory acidosis with acute-on-chronic decompensation (HCO₃⁻ is elevated from renal compensation, but pH is still <7.35 indicating inadequate compensation in the acute setting).

stem: During strenuous exercise, which of the following integrated cardiovascular and respiratory responses is correctly described?
opts: Increased vagal efferent activity decreases heart rate
ecreased 2,3-DPG production shifts the O₂-Hb dissociation curve leftward
Skeletal muscle arterioles dilate while splanchnic and renal arterioles constrict
Renal blood flow increases to maintain glomerular filtration rate during high cardiac output
lveolar ventilation decreases to prevent excessive CO₂ washout and respiratory alkalosis
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Integrated exercise physiology — cardiovascular and respiratory responses
discriminator: Exercise physiology integrates: (1) ↑ sympathetic → selective vasodilation in exercising muscle (local metabolites override sympathetic tone) + vasoconstriction in non-essential beds (splanchnic, renal, skin early). (2) ↑ 2,3-DPG → right shift → more O₂ delivery. (3) ↑ alveolar ventilation matches or exceeds metabolic demands. (4) ↓ vagal tone (not ↑). (5) RBF decreases (not increases).

stem: The sliding filament theory of skeletal muscle contraction involves a specific sequence of molecular events. Arrange the following steps in the correct order: 1. Calcium binds to troponin C 2. ATP is hydrolysed by the myosin head 3. Tropomyosin shifts to expose myosin-binding sites on actin 4. Myosin head binds to actin forming a cross-bridge 5. Power stroke — myosin head pivots, pulling actin filaments toward the M-line
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Muscle contraction — sliding filament and cross-bridge cycling sequence
discriminator: ATP hydrolysis must occur FIRST to energise (cock) the myosin head into the high-energy conformation before it can bind actin. Then Ca²⁺ release → binds troponin → tropomyosin shifts → cross-bridge forms → power stroke. The order is: ATP hydrolysis → Ca binds troponin → tropomyosin shifts → myosin binds → power stroke.

stem: A 45-year-old man with known COPD (baseline PaCO₂ 50 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 30 mEq/L) develops septic shock from pneumonia. ABG: pH 7.15, PaCO₂ 52 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 16 mEq/L, PaO₂ 65 mmHg on 4 L O₂. Na⁺ 138, Cl⁻ 98. What is the most complete acid-base diagnosis?
opts: Mixed disorder: high anion-gap metabolic acidosis plus chronic respiratory acidosis with acute decompensation
Metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
Triple acid-base disorder: metabolic acidosis, metabolic alkalosis, and respiratory acidosis
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: Complex acid-base interpretation — mixed disorders in a patient with baseline chronic respiratory acidosis
discriminator: This patient has a BASELINE chronic respiratory acidosis (known COPD: PaCO₂ 50, HCO₃⁻ 30). Now with sepsis: HCO₃⁻ dropped to 16 (new metabolic acidosis) while PaCO₂ is 52 (slightly above baseline). The anion gap = 138 − (98 + 16) = 24 (elevated, consistent with lactic acidosis from sepsis). The delta-delta (ΔAG/ΔHCO₃) helps confirm pure high-AG metabolic acidosis.

stem: A 35-year-old woman on lithium therapy for bipolar disorder presents with polyuria (6 L/day) and polydipsia over several months. Serum Na⁺ 148 mEq/L, serum osmolality 310 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 180 mOsm/kg. After desmopressin (synthetic ADH) administration, urine osmolality increases to 195 mOsm/kg. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Applied-Physiology
concept: ADH physiology — polyuria differential, water deprivation + desmopressin test
discriminator: Key features: (1) Hypernatraemia (Na 148) + high serum osmolality → water loss (not primary polydipsia). (2) Low urine osmolality (180) despite hyperosmolality → kidney cannot concentrate urine. (3) Minimal response to desmopressin (180 → 195, <50% rise) → nephrogenic DI. (4) Lithium therapy is the most common cause of acquired nephrogenic DI.

stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the five cardinal signs of inflammation described by Celsus?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Cardinal signs of inflammation — rubor, calor, tumor, dolor, functio laesa
discriminator: Pallor is not a cardinal sign; rubor (redness from vasodilation) is the correct vascular sign

stem: Which leukocyte predominates in the first 6–24 hours of an acute inflammatory response?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Neutrophils are the first responders in acute inflammation (6–24 h), followed by mononuclear cells at 24–48 h
discriminator: Time window (6–24 h) exclusively points to neutrophils; mononuclear cells dominate after 24–48 h

stem: The immediate phase of Type I hypersensitivity (15–30 minutes after allergen exposure) is primarily mediated by which of the following?
opts: Prostaglandins from COX-2 activation in macrophages
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Immediate phase of Type I hypersensitivity — IgE cross-linking on mast cells triggers histamine release within minutes
discriminator: Histamine from mast cells mediates the immediate (15–30 min) phase; leukotrienes and cytokines mediate the late (2–8 h) phase

stem: Which mechanism best describes Type II hypersensitivity?
opts: IgE cross-linking on mast cells triggers degranulation
IgG or IgM directed against cell surface or extracellular matrix antigens causes opsonization, complement lysis, or ADCC
Circulating antigen-antibody complexes deposit in tissues and activate complement
T cells mediate tissue injury through macrophage activation or direct cytotoxicity
Antibody binds to a receptor and stimulates it, mimicking the natural ligand
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Type II hypersensitivity — antibody-mediated cytotoxicity against cell surface or extracellular matrix antigens
discriminator: The key is antibody directed against cell SURFACE or ECM antigens (not soluble circulating antigens, which is Type III)

stem: The tuberculin (PPD) skin test elicits a positive reaction after 48–72 hours. Which type of hypersensitivity does this represent?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: PPD skin test is a classic example of Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity mediated by T cells
discriminator: 48–72 hour time course and T cell involvement distinguish Type IV from the other types

stem: In primary intention wound healing, what percentage of normal skin tensile strength is achieved at approximately 7 days?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Wound tensile strength timeline — ~10% at 7 days, ~80% at 3 months (never returns to 100%)
discriminator: 7 days = 10% is a specific number frequently tested in exam; most students overestimate the early strength

stem: A histology section from a myocardial infarct shows preserved architectural outlines of cardiac muscle cells with loss of nuclei and hypereosinophilic cytoplasm. Which type of necrosis is this?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Coagulative necrosis — preserved tissue architecture (ghost outlines) with lost nuclei; most common in ischemic injury to solid organs except brain
discriminator: Preserved architecture (ghost outlines) + ischemic injury = coagulative necrosis; the opposite (lost architecture) = liquefactive

stem: Wound contraction during secondary intention healing is primarily mediated by which cell type?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Myofibroblasts are actin-rich modified fibroblasts responsible for wound contraction in secondary intention healing
discriminator: Myofibroblasts have contractile actin bundles and pull wound edges together; this is unique to secondary intention

stem: Which of the following best distinguishes dystrophic calcification from metastatic calcification?
opts: The size of calcium deposits visible on histology
Whether the calcium is deposited in damaged tissue with normal serum calcium and phosphate levels
The presence or absence of associated inflammation
Whether the calcification is reversible with treatment
The distribution of calcification (single vs multiple organs)
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Key discriminator between dystrophic (damaged tissue, normal Ca/PO4) and metastatic (normal tissue, abnormal Ca/PO4) calcification
discriminator: The condition of the tissue (damaged vs normal) combined with serum calcium/phosphate status is the fundamental distinction

stem: Which of the following features distinguishes apoptosis from necrosis?
opts: Apoptosis involves cell swelling and membrane rupture
Apoptosis elicits a prominent inflammatory response
Apoptosis is a programmed, energy-dependent process that does not trigger inflammation
Apoptosis only occurs in pathologic conditions
Apoptosis affects groups of contiguous cells, while necrosis affects scattered single cells
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Apoptosis — programmed cell death, energy-dependent, no inflammation (vs necrosis — unregulated, pathologic, inflammation-inducing)
discriminator: The absence of inflammation in apoptosis is the key distinguishing feature; cell membrane integrity is maintained, preventing release of DAMPs

stem: A 30-year-old man sustains a laceration on his forearm. Twenty-four hours later, the wound margins are red, warm, and swollen. A swab of the serous exudate is sent for cytology. Which cell type would be most abundant in this sample?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Acute inflammation at 24 h — neutrophils are the predominant cell type in the first 6–24 hours after tissue injury
discriminator: The 24-hour time point and signs of acute inflammation (redness, warmth, swelling) point to neutrophil predominance; macrophages dominate after 48 h

stem: A 35-year-old woman from a high-TB-burden country presents with weight loss, night sweats, and a persistent cough. A cervical lymph node biopsy shows aggregates of epithelioid macrophages surrounded by lymphocytes, with central cheesy necrosis. Multinucleated giant cells with peripherally arranged nuclei are also seen. Ziehl-Neelsen staining reveals acid-fast bacilli. Which type of granuloma is this?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Caseating granuloma with Langhans giant cells and AFB+ is diagnostic of tuberculosis (Type IV hypersensitivity)
discriminator: Central caseation + Langhans giant cells (peripheral nuclei) + AFB+ = TB. Caseation is the key discriminator from sarcoidosis.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus undergoes renal biopsy for proteinuria and declining renal function. Immunofluorescence microscopy shows granular deposition of IgG and C3 along the glomerular capillary walls. Electron microscopy reveals subepithelial electron-dense deposits. Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is responsible for this pattern?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Lupus nephritis is Type III hypersensitivity — immune complex deposition with GRANULAR immunofluorescence pattern
discriminator: GRANULAR (not linear) IgG + C3 deposition = Type III (immune complex-mediated). Linear = Type II (anti-GBM). This IF pattern is the gold standard discriminator.

stem: A 22-year-old male presents with hemoptysis, hematuria, and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Renal biopsy immunofluorescence shows linear deposition of IgG along the glomerular basement membrane. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Goodpasture syndrome — anti-GBM antibody-mediated (Type II hypersensitivity) with LINEAR IgG deposition; lung hemorrhage + RPGN
discriminator: LINEAR IgG along GBM is pathognomonic for Goodpasture (Type II); this is the opposite of granular deposits seen in Type III diseases

stem: A 45-year-old male with a history of heavy alcohol use presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting. Serum amylase is 1200 U/L. During exploratory laparotomy, chalky white, gritty deposits are noted on the omentum and peritoneal surfaces. What type of necrosis is seen in the peritoneal fat?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Fat necrosis in acute pancreatitis — lipase breaks triglycerides into free fatty acids that combine with calcium to form chalky white calcium soaps (saponification)
discriminator: Chalky white, gritty deposits on omental/peritoneal fat + pancreatitis = fat necrosis with saponification

stem: A 60-year-old man with infective endocarditis develops sudden-onset right-sided weakness and aphasia. CT head shows a well-demarcated hypodense area in the left middle cerebral artery territory. If a biopsy of this area were taken, which type of necrosis would be expected on histology?
opts: Liquefactive necrosis with cystic cavity formation
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Brain infarction causes liquefactive necrosis — tissue architecture is completely lost and replaced by a cystic cavity due to glial hydrolases
discriminator: Brain is the only solid organ that undergoes liquefactive (not coagulative) necrosis after ischemic injury because glial cells release abundant hydrolytic enzymes

stem: A 30-year-old asymptomatic female is found to have bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on a routine chest X-ray. Laboratory workup shows elevated serum ACE level. A mediastinal lymph node biopsy reveals non-caseating granulomas with Schaumann bodies and asteroid bodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Sarcoidosis — non-caseating granulomas with Schaumann/asteroid bodies, bilateral hilar LAD, elevated ACE (Type IV hypersensitivity)
discriminator: Non-caseating granulomas + Schaumann/asteroid bodies + hilar LAD + ACE = sarcoidosis. Caseation would point to TB instead.

stem: A 22-year-old woman of African descent develops a raised, firm, pruritic scar at the site of an old ear piercing. The scar extends well beyond the original wound margins and has not regressed over two years. What is the most accurate diagnosis?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Keloid — excessive scar extending beyond original wound borders, does not regress, more common in dark skin; distinguished from hypertrophic scar (stays within borders, may regress)
discriminator: Extension beyond original wound margins is the defining feature of keloid (hypertrophic scar stays within borders)

stem: A 50-year-old diabetic man undergoes incision and drainage of a large thigh abscess. The wound is left open to heal. One week later, the wound bed shows abundant red, granular tissue, and the wound edges appear to be pulling inward. Which of the following correctly describes the healing process occurring here?
opts: Primary intention healing — minimal granulation, edges approximated
Secondary intention healing — prominent granulation with myofibroblast-mediated contraction
Tertiary intention healing — delayed primary closure after debridement
Keloid formation — excessive collagen extending beyond wound margins
Dystrophic calcification — calcium deposition in the wound bed
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Secondary intention healing — open wound with abundant granulation tissue and myofibroblast-mediated wound contraction
discriminator: The combination of an open wound (edges not approximated), abundant red granular tissue, and spontaneous wound contraction points to secondary intention healing

stem: A 60-year-old malnourished patient with a history of partial gastrectomy develops poor wound healing after laparotomy. On examination, his gums are swollen and bleeding, and there are perifollicular hemorrhages on his legs. Which nutritional deficiency most likely explains both his poor wound healing and gingival findings?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) — impaired collagen hydroxylation → poor wound healing, bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages
discriminator: Bleeding gums + perifollicular hemorrhages + poor wound healing = classic triad of scurvy (vitamin C deficiency affecting collagen synthesis)

stem: A 32-year-old woman with SLE develops acute onset of hematuria, proteinuria, and rising creatinine. Renal biopsy immunofluorescence shows GRANULAR deposition of IgG, IgM, IgA, and C3 (full house pattern). Electron microscopy shows numerous subendothelial electron-dense deposits. Separately, her 28-year-old brother presents with hemoptysis, hematuria, and renal biopsy showing LINEAR IgG along the GBM. Based on the immunofluorescence patterns, which hypersensitivity types are responsible for the sister's and brother's conditions, respectively?
opts: Sister: Type II — Brother: Type II
Sister: Type III — Brother: Type II
Sister: Type II — Brother: Type III
Sister: Type III — Brother: Type III
Sister: Type IV — Brother: Type II
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: IF pattern as discriminator: GRANULAR (full house) = Type III (SLE nephritis), LINEAR = Type II (Goodpasture anti-GBM). This question tests the ability to differentiate Type II from Type III using immunofluorescence.
discriminator: Full house granular staining = Type III (immune complex, SLE). Linear IgG = Type II (anti-GBM, Goodpasture). Same family but different diseases with opposite IF patterns.

stem: A 55-year-old male with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 10.2%) and a 40-pack-year smoking history undergoes a below-knee amputation for a non-healing diabetic foot ulcer. The surgical wound is closed primarily. Two weeks post-operatively, the wound has gaped open with purulent discharge. Cultures grow MRSA. Which of the following is the MOST important factor that has impaired his wound healing?
opts: Smoking-induced vasoconstriction and reduced tissue oxygenation
Diabetes mellitus causing microvascular disease and impaired immune function
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Wound infection is the single most important cause of impaired wound healing — it causes dehiscence, prolongs inflammation, and delays closure. In this scenario, infection is the acute precipitating cause of dehiscence.
discriminator: The patient has multiple risk factors (diabetes, smoking), but the acute wound dehiscence with purulent discharge and MRSA confirms that active infection is the most important immediate factor

stem: A 40-year-old male presents with chronic cough, weight loss, and night sweats. Chest X-ray shows a right upper lobe cavity with surrounding infiltrates. Sputum is AFB-positive. Meanwhile, a 35-year-old female is found to have bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with non-caseating granulomas on biopsy. A 28-year-old male with chronic abdominal pain and diarrhea has colonic biopsies showing transmural inflammation with non-caseating granulomas. Which of the following correctly matches each patient with the correct etiology of their granulomatous inflammation?
opts: Patient 1: Sarcoidosis — Patient 2: Tuberculosis — Patient 3: Crohn disease
Patient 1: Tuberculosis — Patient 2: Sarcoidosis — Patient 3: Crohn disease
Patient 1: Tuberculosis — Patient 2: Crohn disease — Patient 3: Sarcoidosis
Patient 1: Fungal infection — Patient 2: Tuberculosis — Patient 3: Crohn disease
Patient 1: Tuberculosis — Patient 2: Tuberculosis — Patient 3: Tuberculosis
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Granuloma differential diagnosis — caseating + AFB+ = TB (lungs), non-caseating + hilar LAD = sarcoidosis, non-caseating + transmural GI = Crohn disease
discriminator: Presence or absence of caseation and the organ system involved (respiratory vs GI) are the key discriminators between TB, sarcoidosis, and Crohn disease

stem: A 45-year-old male with osteoarthritis takes high-dose ibuprofen (a non-selective COX inhibitor) for joint pain. Following a minor respiratory infection, he develops severe abdominal pain, nausea, and hematemesis. Endoscopy reveals multiple gastric and duodenal ulcers. Meanwhile, a 30-year-old asthmatic woman develops acute bronchospasm, urticaria, and hypotension 15 minutes after eating shrimp. Which of the following correctly pairs the PRIMARY mechanism of the adverse effect in each patient?
opts: Ibuprofen: COX-2 inhibition reduces protective prostaglandins — Asthma patient: IgE cross-linking on mast cells releases histamine
Ibuprofen: COX-1 inhibition reduces protective gastric prostaglandins — Asthma patient: IgE cross-linking on mast cells releases histamine
Ibuprofen: Lipoxygenase inhibition reduces leukotrienes — Asthma patient: COX-2 inhibition causes bronchospasm
Ibuprofen: COX-2 inhibition causes platelet dysfunction — Asthma patient: Complement activation causes mast cell degranulation
Ibuprofen: 5-LOX activation increases leukotrienes — Asthma patient: IgG cross-linking on basophils
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: COX-1/COX-2 distinction: COX-1 produces protective prostaglandins in gastric mucosa (inhibition → ulcers). Anaphylaxis is Type I (IgE-mast cell-histamine). Integrates AA pathway with hypersensitivity.
discriminator: Gastric ulcers from NSAIDs = COX-1 inhibition (loss of protective PGE2/PGI2). Anaphylaxis = Type I (IgE/mast cell/histamine). This combines the arachidonic acid pathway with hypersensitivity classification.

stem: A 65-year-old male dies suddenly from a massive myocardial infarction. Autopsy reveals a pale, wedge-shaped area in the posterolateral wall of the left ventricle. Microscopy shows hypereosinophilic cardiomyocytes with pyknotic nuclei and preserved striations, surrounded by a zone of neutrophils. Separately, a 50-year-old female with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis dies from renal failure. Autopsy shows bright pink, amorphous material deposited in the walls of medium-sized arteries, with fibrinoid change and neutrophilic infiltrate. Which two types of necrosis are demonstrated in these two cases, respectively?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Coagulative necrosis (MI — preserved architecture, ghost outlines, wavy fibers) vs Fibrinoid necrosis (immune vasculitis in RA/PAN — bright pink fibrin-like material in vessel walls)
discriminator: Pale wedge + preserved striations + pyknotic nuclei = coagulative necrosis (MI). Bright pink material in vessel walls + rheumatoid arthritis = fibrinoid necrosis (immune complex vasculitis). These are at opposite ends of the necrosis spectrum.

stem: A 55-year-old man with chronic heartburn for 12 years undergoes surveillance endoscopy. Biopsy of the distal esophagus shows columnar epithelium containing goblet cells. Which type of change has occurred?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Barrett esophagus as metaplasia
discriminator: Goblet cells in distal esophagus = specialized intestinal metaplasia = Barrett esophagus

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with fatigue, fever, and gingival bleeding. CBC shows Hb 7.2 g/dL, platelets 22,000/μL, WBC 3,200/μL. Peripheral smear shows blasts with Auer rods. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: AML — Auer rods as pathognomonic feature
discriminator: Auer rods in blasts = pathognomonic for AML (myeloid lineage)

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with massive splenomegaly and night sweats. WBC is 210,000/μL with myeloid left shift. Cytogenetics show t(9;22)(q34;q11). What is the first-line treatment?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: CML — BCR-ABL and imatinib
discriminator: t(9;22) BCR-ABL + massive splenomegaly + extreme WBC = CML → imatinib (TKI)

stem: A 45-year-old woman is found to have a BRCA1 mutation. She has no personal history of cancer. Which cancer is she at highest risk for?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: BRCA1/2 — tumor suppressor genes in breast/ovarian cancer
discriminator: BRCA1 mutation → high risk of breast and ovarian cancer (DNA repair defect)

stem: Which of the following is a paraneoplastic syndrome typically associated with small cell lung carcinoma?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Paraneoplastic syndromes — SCLC (SIADH, Cushing, Lambert-Eaton)
discriminator: SCLC is neuroendocrine → secretes ADH (SIADH) and ACTH (Cushing). Hypercalcemia = SCC.

stem: A 60-year-old man with a history of smoking presents with a lung mass. Biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma. He is found to have serum calcium of 12.8 mg/dL. Which paraneoplastic mechanism most likely explains the hypercalcemia?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: SCC lung → PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia
discriminator: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of lung → PTHrP → hypercalcemia (osteolytic bone metastases less likely with one lesion)

stem: A 35-year-old woman has a rapidly growing cervical lesion. Biopsy shows koilocytotic atypia in the squamous epithelium. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: HPV and cervical carcinogenesis (CIN)
discriminator: Koilocytotic atypia (halo cells) in cervical squamous epithelium = HPV cytopathic effect

stem: Which of the following tumor markers is most appropriate for monitoring treatment response in a patient with colorectal carcinoma?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: CEA — monitoring colorectal cancer recurrence
discriminator: CEA is for monitoring colorectal cancer recurrence, not for screening or diagnosis

stem: A 72-year-old man presents with back pain and fatigue. Serum protein electrophoresis shows an M spike. Skeletal survey reveals multiple lytic lesions in the skull and vertebrae. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely present?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Multiple myeloma — CRAB criteria (hyperCalcemia)
discriminator: M spike + lytic lesions + bone pain = multiple myeloma → hypercalcemia (bone destruction)

stem: A 50-year-old woman has a breast tumor that overexpresses HER2/neu. Which type of genetic alteration is HER2/neu?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: HER2/neu as an oncogene (EGFR family, amplification in breast/gastric cancer)
discriminator: HER2/neu (ERBB2) = receptor tyrosine kinase oncogene, amplified in breast and gastric cancer

stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with acute onset of bone pain, pallor, and petechiae. Bone marrow shows >25% lymphoblasts that are CD19+, CD10+, TdT+, and MPO-negative. Which chromosomal abnormality is most likely associated with a good prognosis in this subtype?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: ALL — B-lineage (CALLA+, TdT+, MPO−) and prognostic cytogenetics
discriminator: CD10 (CALLA)+, CD19+, TdT+, MPO− = B-ALL. Hyperdiploidy = favorable prognosis in pediatric ALL.

stem: A 38-year-old man with CML on imatinib develops worsening fatigue and night sweats. WBC increases despite therapy. Peripheral smear now shows 25% blasts. Bone marrow biopsy confirms blast crisis with myeloid phenotype. What is the next step in management?
opts: Start allogenic stem cell transplant evaluation
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: CML blast crisis — management escalation to transplant
discriminator: Blast crisis (>20% blasts) in CML = TKI-resistant → allogenic SCT (only curative option)

stem: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a benign neoplasm from a malignant neoplasm?
opts: Benign neoplasms never recur after excision
Malignant neoplasms always have a higher growth rate than benign neoplasms
Benign neoplasms are well-differentiated and do not metastasize
Malignant neoplasms are always larger than benign neoplasms
Benign neoplasms have a capsule, malignant neoplasms never have a capsule
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Benign vs malignant neoplasms — differentiation and metastasis
discriminator: Well-differentiated + no metastasis = hallmark of benign neoplasia

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with a painless left neck mass. Excisional biopsy shows effacement of lymph node architecture by atypical lymphoid cells with scattered large binucleate cells with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli (Reed-Sternberg cells). Immunohistochemistry is positive for CD15 and CD30. Which subtype of lymphoma is most likely?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Hodgkin lymphoma — Reed-Sternberg cells, CD15/CD30, nodular sclerosis subtype
discriminator: Reed-Sternberg cells + CD15+/CD30+ = Hodgkin lymphoma. Nodular sclerosis = most common subtype, young women, cervical/mediastinal.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents with painless generalized lymphadenopathy and absolute lymphocytosis (WBC 48,000/μL, 80% lymphocytes on differential). Peripheral smear shows smudge cells. Flow cytometry shows CD5+, CD23+, CD20+ (dim) lymphocytes. Which diagnosis is most likely?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: CLL — smudge cells, CD5+/CD23+, elderly presentation
discriminator: Smudge cells + CD5+/CD23+/CD20(dim) + elderly + lymphocytosis = CLL

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with a CSF leak and nasal obstruction. Biopsy of a midline nasal mass shows sheets of large atypical lymphoid cells with angiocentric growth. In situ hybridization is positive for EBV-encoded RNA (EBER). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: EBV-associated NK/T-cell lymphoma (nasal type)
discriminator: Midline nasal mass + angiocentric growth + EBV (EBER+) = NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type

stem: A 38-year-old man undergoing evaluation for infertility is found to have a right testicular mass. Serum AFP is elevated but β-hCG is normal. Which histological subtype is most likely?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Tumor markers in germ cell tumors — AFP (yolk sac)
discriminator: AFP elevated + β-hCG normal = yolk sac tumor (AFP is produced by yolk sac elements)

stem: A 55-year-old woman is found to have a tumor that invades surrounding tissue and metastasizes to regional lymph nodes first. The primary tumor is in the epithelium of the colon. Which term best describes this category of malignant neoplasm?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Carcinoma vs sarcoma — epithelial vs mesenchymal origin
discriminator: Epithelial origin (colon epithelium) → carcinoma. Lymphatic spread (typical of carcinomas).

stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, and anemia. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a monoclonal spike. Bone marrow biopsy demonstrates 40% plasma cells. Skeletal survey shows multiple lytic lesions. Which CD marker is most likely positive on these neoplastic cells?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Multiple myeloma — plasma cell markers (CD138, CD38, CD56)
discriminator: Plasma cells are CD138+ (syndecan-1), CD38+, CD56+, CD20−, CD34−

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with abdominal pain and an abdominal mass. Biopsy of the mass shows a 'starry-sky' pattern of medium-sized lymphoid cells with numerous tingible-body macrophages. Immunohistochemistry is CD20+, and fluorescence in situ hybridization demonstrates t(8;14). Which gene is most likely overexpressed due to this translocation?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: Burkitt lymphoma — t(8;14) MYC translocation
discriminator: Starry-sky + CD20+ + t(8;14) = Burkitt lymphoma → MYC overexpression

stem: A 35-year-old man with AML presents with DIC before chemotherapy. Peripheral smear shows blasts with multiple Auer rods and hypergranular promyelocytes. Which chromosomal translocation is most likely to be found?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: APML — t(15;17) PML-RARA, Auer rods, DIC risk
discriminator: Hypergranular promyelocytes + Auer rods + DIC in AML = APML → t(15;17)

stem: A 50-year-old woman is diagnosed with breast cancer. Testing reveals amplification of HER2/neu. Which targeted therapy would be most appropriate for this patient?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: HER2-targeted therapy — trastuzumab
discriminator: HER2/neu amplification in breast cancer → trastuzumab (monoclonal antibody against HER2)

stem: A 52-year-old man with a 30-pack-year smoking history presents with cough and weight loss. CT shows a 4 cm central lung mass. Biopsy shows small cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, nuclear molding, and scant cytoplasm. Immunohistochemistry is positive for chromogranin and synaptophysin. Which of the following is true about this tumor?
opts: It is typically treated with surgical resection alone
It is associated with hypercalcemia from PTHrP
It frequently causes paraneoplastic syndromes including SIADH
It has a better prognosis than non-small cell lung cancer
It arises from alveolar type II pneumocytes
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: SCLC — neuroendocrine features, paraneoplastic syndromes, treatment approach
discriminator: Small cells + nuclear molding + chromogranin+ = SCLC (neuroendocrine) → chemo primary, paraneoplastic SIADH/Cushing

stem: A cervical biopsy shows full-thickness dysplasia (severe dysplasia/CIN III) with abnormal mitotic figures extending from the basal layer to the surface. The basement membrane is intact. Which term best describes these histological findings?
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: CIN III/HSIL — full-thickness dysplasia with intact basement membrane (pre-invasive)
discriminator: Full-thickness dysplasia + intact basement membrane = HSIL/CIN III (pre-invasive, not invasive carcinoma)

stem: A 60-year-old woman undergoes colectomy for adenocarcinoma. Post-operatively, her serum CEA level falls to normal. Six months later, she develops rising CEA. CT reveals a 2 cm liver metastasis. Which statement about CEA in this patient is most accurate?
opts: CEA is the most sensitive screening test for colorectal cancer in the general population
Rising CEA after curative resection is highly suggestive of recurrence
CEA level at diagnosis correlates directly with tumor size but has no prognostic value
CEA should be measured annually for colorectal cancer screening
CEA is specific for colorectal adenocarcinoma and is not elevated in other conditions
subject: Applied-Pathology
concept: CEA — monitoring recurrence after colorectal cancer resection
discriminator: Post-resection CEA normalization followed by rising CEA = recurrence until proven otherwise

stem: A 45-year-old man with no drug allergies develops syphilis. Which penicillin formulation is the single best choice for treatment?
opts: Oral amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 14 days
Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM single dose
Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV Q6H for 7 days
Dicloxacillin 500 mg PO Q6H for 10 days
Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg PO BID for 14 days
subject: Clinical-Pharmacology
concept: Penicillin G — natural penicillin indication for syphilis
discriminator: Benzathine penicillin G (long-acting IM formulation) is the specific recommended treatment for early syphilis. Natural penicillins (PCN G) cover Treponema pallidum, not penicillinase-resistant or aminopenicillins.

stem: A 60-year-old woman with a reported IgE-mediated penicillin allergy (anaphylaxis 10 years ago) requires antibiotic prophylaxis for a surgical procedure. Which of the following is safest to administer?
subject: Clinical-Pharmacology
concept: Penicillin allergy cross-reactivity — monobactams are safe
discriminator: Aztreonam (monobactam) shares no significant cross-reactivity with penicillins. Cephalosporins have ~10% cross-reactivity with penicillins in IgE-mediated allergy and should be avoided. Aminopenicillins are contraindicated.

stem: A blood culture from a 55-year-old ICU patient grows Klebsiella pneumoniae resistant to ceftriaxone and cefotaxime. ESBL production is confirmed. What is the single best antibiotic to administer?
subject: Clinical-Pharmacology
concept: ESBL-producing organisms — carbapenem is first-line
discriminator: ESBL-producing Enterobacterales (ceftriaxone-resistant) are treated with carbapenems as first-line therapy. Piperacillin-tazobactam and cefepime may be options only if susceptibility is confirmed and infection is non-severe.

stem: A 72-year-old man on gentamicin for a gram-negative bloodstream infection develops vertigo, nystagmus, and difficulty walking. Audiometry shows high-frequency hearing loss. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Aminoglycoside-induced ototoxicity affecting both cochlear and vestibular divisions
subject: Clinical-Pharmacology
concept: Aminoglycoside ototoxicity — cochlear and vestibular toxicity
discriminator: Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, amikacin, tobramycin) cause both cochlear (hearing loss) and vestibular (vertigo, nystagmus, ataxia) ototoxicity. Risk is increased with prolonged use, high trough levels, and concurrent nephrotoxicity.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with atypical pneumonia is prescribed azithromycin. She has a history of long QT syndrome. Which adverse effect is the greatest concern with this antibiotic?
opts: QT interval prolongation and risk of torsades de pointes
subject: Clinical-Pharmacology
concept: Macrolides — QT prolongation risk (especially in predisposed patients)
discriminator: All macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin) prolong the QT interval by blocking hERG potassium channels. Erythromycin has the highest risk; azithromycin the lowest, but risk remains in patients with pre-existing long QT syndrome.

stem: A 28-year-old man with community-acquired pneumonia is treated with levofloxacin. On day 5 he develops acute-onset right ankle pain, swelling, and difficulty bearing weight. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Gout flare triggered by the infection
subject: Clinical-Pharmacology
concept: Fluoroquinolones — tendon toxicity (Achilles tendinitis/rupture)
discriminator: Fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin, moxifloxacin) are associated with tendinitis and tendon rupture, most commonly affecting the Achilles tendon. Risk factors include age >60, concurrent corticosteroid use, renal impairment, and athletes.

stem: A 50-year-old woman on warfarin for mechanical mitral valve develops a urinary tract infection and is prescribed ciprofloxacin. Three days later, she presents with gum bleeding and easy bruising. INR is 8.5. What is the most likely mechanism?
opts: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2 and CYP3A4, increasing warfarin levels
subject: Clinical-Pharmacology
concept: Fluoroquinolones — CYP inhibition and warfarin interaction
discriminator: Ciprofloxacin is a CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 inhibitor. Warfarin (S-warfarin is metabolised by CYP2C9, R-warfarin by CYP1A2/3A4) levels rise when these enzymes are inhibited, potentiating anticoagulation. This is the key drug interaction.

stem: A 40-year-old woman with a history of recurrent C diff diarrhoea is treated with metronidazole. She drinks a glass of wine at dinner and within minutes develops facial flushing, nausea, vomiting, and palpitations. What is the most likely explanation?
opts: Disulfiram-like reaction due to metronidazole inhibiting aldehyde dehydrogenase
C diff toxin release triggered by alcohol
Alcohol interaction with gut microbiome producing toxic metabolites
subject: Clinical-Pharmacology
concept: Metronidazole — disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol
discriminator: Metronidazole inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, causing accumulation of acetaldehyde when alcohol is consumed → flushing, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, hypotension. This disulfiram-like reaction occurs with metronidazole and some cephalosporins (cefoperazone, cefotetan).

stem: A 65-year-old man with diabetes and peripheral vascular disease is started on vancomycin for MRSA osteomyelitis. During the infusion he develops diffuse flushing, pruritus, and hypotension. There is no urticaria, angioedema, or bronchospasm. What is the best next step?
opts: Stop vancomycin permanently and switch to daptomycin
Slow the infusion rate and consider antihistamine pre-treatment
Change to linezolid and start IV corticosteroids
subject: Clinical-Pharmacology
concept: Vancomycin — red man syndrome vs true IgE allergy
discriminator: Red man syndrome is a non-IgE-mediated histamine release reaction caused by rapid vancomycin infusion. It presents with flushing, pruritus, and hypotension but NOT urticaria, angioedema, or bronchospasm. Management is to slow the infusion rate and pre-treat with antihistamines.

stem: A 32-year-old man with HIV (CD4 80 cells/mm³, not on ART) presents with cryptococcal meningitis. Induction therapy is started with amphotericin B deoxycholate and flucytosine. On day 3, he develops fever (39.5°C), rigors, hypotension, and hypokalemia (K+ 3.0 mEq/L). What is the best explanation?
opts: Flucytosine-induced bone marrow suppression causing febrile neutropenia
Amphotericin B infusion-related reaction with amphotericin-induced potassium wasting
HIV disease progression with disseminated MAC
subject: Clinical-Pharmacology
concept: Amphotericin B — infusion reactions and nephrotoxicity (K+ wasting)
discriminator: Amphotericin B deoxycholate causes infusion-related reactions (fever, rigors, hypotension) and renal tubular toxicity (K+ and Mg2+ wasting). Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and azotemia are expected. Liposomal formulations reduce nephrotoxicity.

stem: A 48-year-old man on rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (RIPE) for pulmonary TB develops orange-coloured urine and tears. The medication list also includes oral contraceptives. Which of the following is the most important management consideration?
opts: Reassure the patient about orange secretions and advise alternative contraception
Stop rifampin immediately and switch to a second-line agent
Reassure and continue all medications; orange secretions indicate therapeutic levels
Check liver function tests and bilirubin
