rule: Epidural haematoma. Mannitol + urgent surgical evacuation.

stem: A 35-year-old man: 6 hours tender, irreducible right inguinal lump. Nausea, no vomiting. Lump above and medial to pubic tubercle, no cough impulse. Management?
rule: Distal oesophageal/GOJ adenocarcinoma = Barrett's oesophagus.

stem: A 70-year-old man: acute urinary retention (bladder to umbilicus). Nocturia and poor stream for 2 years. PSA 3.5. Immediate management?
rule: Acute limb ischaemia. AF is embolic source. IV heparin + embolectomy.

stem: A 15-year-old boy: sudden severe right testicular pain for 4 hours. Right testis high-riding, horizontal. Cremasteric reflex absent. Doppler: absent blood flow. Management?
rule: Irreducible tender inguinal hernia suggests incarceration/strangulation.

stem: A 50-year-old man: painless lump in right breast for 2 months. 2-cm firm, fixed mass in retroareolar area with nipple retraction. Axillary nodes palpable. Next step?
rule: Acute urinary retention then immediate urethral catheterization.

stem: A 45-year-old woman: 3-cm solitary thyroid nodule for 2 months. TSH normal. USG: solid hypoechoic nodule with microcalcifications. Next step?
rule: Testicular torsion. Surgical exploration within 6 hours.

stem: A 60-year-old man: 4 months altered bowel habit, weight loss, intermittent rectal bleeding. DRE: hard, irregular mass 5 cm from anal verge. CEA elevated. Staging investigation?
rule: Male breast cancer. Core needle biopsy is definitive.

stem: A 30-year-old man: deep laceration on volar wrist after glass injury. Loss of sensation over palmar index and middle fingers, weakness of thumb opposition. Nerve injured?
rule: Suspicious thyroid nodule then FNAC.

stem: A 55-year-old man: severe pain and swelling of left calf 7 days after total hip replacement. No fever. Doppler: thrombus in popliteal vein. Immediate treatment?
rule: Rectal cancer. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis is standard staging.

stem: A 40-year-old woman: 2 days severe pain, swelling, erythema of left breast with fever. Breastfeeding 3-month-old. Tender, indurated area in upper outer quadrant. Management?
rule: Median nerve injury at wrist: palmar sensation over lateral 3.5 fingers, thumb opposition weakness.

stem: A 25-year-old man after stab wound to left chest: tachycardic (130), hypotensive (85/60), distended neck veins. Heart sounds muffled. Trachea central. Immediate management?
rule: DVT post-surgery. Therapeutic anticoagulation with LMWH is first-line.

stem: A 60-year-old man: progressive difficulty swallowing solids for 4 months, regurgitation of undigested food. Bird's beak on barium swallow. Definitive diagnostic investigation?
rule: Lactational mastitis. Antibiotics + continued breastfeeding.

stem: A 50-year-old woman: 6 months slowly growing, painless mass in right popliteal fossa. Firm, non-tender, transilluminant. Diagnosis?
rule: Cardiac tamponade (Beck's triad). Needle pericardiocentesis.

stem: A 55-year-old man: 3 months progressive dysphagia and weight loss. Endoscopy: mass in middle third of oesophagus. Biopsy: SCC. Risk factor?
rule: Achalasia. Oesophageal manometry is gold standard.

stem: A 45-year-old man: 2 days severe pain, swelling, erythema of left leg. Skin tense, shiny, well-demarcated edges. Temp 38.8. Small blistering. Diagnosis?
rule: Baker's cyst: transilluminant, firm, non-tender mass in popliteal fossa.

stem: A 30-year-old man: 1 week progressive weakness of both legs and urinary retention. URTI 2 weeks ago. Flaccid paralysis, areflexia, sensory level at T10. MRI: hyperintense thoracic cord lesion. Diagnosis?
rule: Oesophageal SCC = smoking and alcohol.

stem: A 55-year-old woman: 4 months progressive jaundice, pruritus, weight loss. USG: 3-cm mass in head of pancreas with dilated CBD and pancreatic duct. CA19-9 elevated. Curative surgical option?
rule: Erysipelas: well-demarcated, raised, shiny erythema.

stem: A 40-year-old man: 3 days severe perianal pain and swelling. Tender, fluctuant mass at 3 o'clock, 2 cm from anal verge. Temp 38.5. Treatment?
rule: Transverse myelitis: sensory level at T10, MRI shows cord lesion.

stem: A 60-year-old man: 6 months progressive difficulty walking, stiffness in both legs, numbness in hands. Spastic paraparesis, sensory level at T6. MRI: compressive lesion at T5. Management?
rule: Pancreatic head carcinoma. Whipple's procedure is curative.

stem: A 25-year-old man: 2 days severe pain and swelling of right testis. Sexually active with multiple partners. Right testis tender, epididymis thickened. PCR positive for Chlamydia trachomatis. Treatment?
rule: Perianal abscess. I&D under anaesthesia.

stem: A 50-year-old man: 3 months progressive dyspnoea and orthopnoea. Wide pulse pressure, diastolic murmur at left sternal border, Quincke's sign. Echo: severe AR with LV dilation. Definitive treatment?
rule: Spinal cord compression. Surgical decompression is definitive.

stem: A 35-year-old woman: 1 month progressive dyspnoea and chest pain. Rheumatic fever in childhood. Loud S1, opening snap, mid-diastolic rumble at apex. Echo: mitral valve area 1.0 sq cm. Intervention?
rule: Chlamydial epididymitis. Doxycycline or azithromycin.

stem: A 45-year-old man: 2 weeks progressive dysphagia and odynophagia. HIV-positive, CD4 80. Endoscopy: large, deep, linear ulcers in mid-oesophagus. Causative organism?
rule: Severe AR with symptoms and LV dilation then aortic valve replacement.

stem: A 60-year-old man: 3 months progressive dyspnoea and dry cough. Asbestos exposure. CXR: pleural plaques and unilateral pleural effusion. CT: nodular pleural thickening. Diagnosis?
rule: Mitral stenosis. Symptomatic severe MS with suitable valve then balloon valvuloplasty.

stem: A 55-year-old man: 2 months progressive dyspnoea and orthopnoea. Elevated JVP increasing on inspiration (Kussmaul's sign), bilateral pitting oedema, ascites. Echo: thickened pericardium with RV diastolic collapse. Definitive treatment?
rule: CMV oesophagitis: large, deep, linear ulcers in immunocompromised.

stem: A 40-year-old man: 1 week severe epigastric pain radiating to back. Heavy alcohol. Lipase 1,800. CT: pancreatic necrosis 40%. Temp 39, WBC 18,000. Management?
rule: Mesothelioma: asbestos exposure, pleural plaques, nodular pleural thickening.

stem: A 30-year-old woman: 3 months painless lump in left breast. 2-cm, firm, mobile, well-circumscribed mass in upper outer quadrant. USG: solid, homogeneous, smooth margins. Diagnosis?
rule: Constrictive pericarditis. Pericardiectomy is definitive.

stem: A 65-year-old man: 6 months progressive difficulty urinating, nocturia, incomplete bladder emptying. DRE: symmetrically enlarged, firm, smooth prostate. PSA 3.0. First-line pharmacological treatment?
rule: Infected pancreatic necrosis. IV antibiotics + ICU monitoring.

stem: A 45-year-old man: 2 days severe pain and swelling of left leg. Recent hip surgery. Doppler: thrombus in left femoral vein. Immediate treatment?
rule: Fibroadenoma: young woman, firm, mobile, well-circumscribed mass.

stem: A 50-year-old man: 3 months progressive dysphagia and weight loss. Endoscopy: mass in distal oesophagus extending to GOJ. Biopsy: adenocarcinoma. Risk factor?
rule: BPH. Alpha-blockers (tamsulosin) are first-line for symptom relief.

stem: A 35-year-old man: 1 day severe pain and swelling of right great toe. Similar episodes before. Uric acid 9.5. Negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals. First-line treatment?
rule: DVT post-surgery. Therapeutic anticoagulation with LMWH is first-line.

stem: A 65-year-old man: 3 months progressive dysphagia and weight loss. Mass in middle third of oesophagus. Biopsy: SCC. Risk factor?
rule: Distal oesophageal/GOJ adenocarcinoma = Barrett's oesophagus.

stem: A 45-year-old man: 2 days severe pain, swelling, erythema of left leg. Skin tense, shiny, well-demarcated edges. Temp 38.8. Blistering. Diagnosis?
rule: Acute gout. Colchicine, NSAIDs, or steroids.

stem: A 45-year-old man: sudden severe headache, vomiting, and photophobia for 2 hours. Neck stiffness present. CT head shows hyperdensity in the Sylvian fissure. Most likely diagnosis?
rule: Oesophageal SCC = smoking and alcohol.

stem: A 65-year-old man: 6 months progressive dysphagia, initially to solids, now to liquids. 10-kg weight loss. Endoscopy: mass in the middle third of the oesophagus. Biopsy: SCC. Most appropriate treatment for operable disease?
rule: Erysipelas: well-demarcated, raised, shiny erythema.

stem: A 55-year-old woman: 3 months of a slowly growing, painless lump in the left breast. 3-cm, firm, fixed mass with skin dimpling. Axillary lymph nodes palpable. Triple assessment includes all EXCEPT?
rule: SAH: sudden severe headache, neck stiffness, hyperdensity in Sylvian fissure on CT.

stem: A 40-year-old man: 2 days of severe pain, swelling, and erythema of the left leg. The skin is tense and shiny with well-demarcated raised edges. Temperature 39°C. Area of skin blistering and crepitus. Most likely diagnosis?
rule: Oesophageal SCC. Surgical resection is treatment of choice for operable disease.

stem: A 60-year-old man: acute urinary retention (bladder palpable to umbilicus). History of nocturia, poor stream, and terminal dribbling for 3 years. PSA 8.5 ng/mL. DRE: hard, irregular, nodular prostate. Most appropriate next step?
rule: Triple assessment = clinical exam + imaging (mammography/USG) + tissue diagnosis (FNAC/core biopsy). CT is for staging, not part of initial triple assessment.

stem: A 35-year-old man: 1 day of severe pain, swelling, and erythema of the right great toe. History of similar episodes. Uric acid 9.5 mg/dL. Synovial fluid shows needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals. First-line treatment for this acute attack?
rule: Necrotizing fasciitis: crepitus, blistering, severe systemic toxicity. Surgical emergency.

stem: A 55-year-old man: 6 months of progressive difficulty walking, stiffness in both legs, and numbness in the hands. Spastic paraparesis, loss of vibration sense in the legs, and a sensory level at T6. MRI shows an extradural compressive lesion at T5. Most appropriate management?
rule: Suspected prostate cancer (hard, irregular prostate, PSA >4). TRUS-guided biopsy is diagnostic.

stem: A 30-year-old man: 1 week of progressive weakness of both legs and urinary retention. Upper respiratory infection 2 weeks ago. Examination shows flaccid paralysis of both legs with areflexia and a sensory level at T10. MRI spine shows a hyperintense lesion in the thoracic cord. Most likely diagnosis?
rule: Acute gout. Colchicine, NSAIDs, or steroids. Allopurinol NOT during acute attack.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with a 2-month history of progressive dysphagia, initially to solids and now to liquids. He has lost 10 kg. Endoscopy reveals an ulcerated mass in the distal oesophagus extending to the gastro-oesophageal junction. Biopsy shows adenocarcinoma. CT chest and abdomen shows no distant metastases. What is the most appropriate treatment?
rule: Spinal cord compression. Surgical decompression is definitive.

stem: A 60-year-old man with a history of smoking presents with a 3-month history of progressive dyspnoea and a dry cough. Chest X-ray shows a unilateral pleural effusion. CT chest shows pleural plaques and a nodular pleural thickening. Pleural fluid analysis shows protein 4.2 g/dL, LDH 280 U/L, and mesothelial cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
rule: Transverse myelitis: sensory level at T10, MRI shows cord lesion.

stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 at 7 weeks: sudden severe RLQ pain and vaginal spotting. Dizzy on standing. BP 90/60, pulse 120. Urine pregnancy positive. TVUSG: empty uterus, 2-cm right adnexal mass with free fluid. Management?
rule: Resectable distal oesophageal/GOJ adenocarcinoma. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgery is standard.

stem: A 32-year-old at 34 weeks: headache, visual disturbances, epigastric pain for 2 days. BP 165/110, urine protein 3+. Platelets 90,000, AST 180, ALT 200. Diagnosis?
rule: Mesothelioma: asbestos exposure, nodular pleural thickening, exudative effusion.

stem: A 25-year-old at 28 weeks: painless vaginal bleeding for 1 day. No abdominal tenderness. FHR normal. USG: placenta covering internal cervical os. Management?
rule: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy (unstable, free fluid). Emergency laparoscopy + salpingectomy.

stem: A 30-year-old G3P2 at 38 weeks delivers vaginally. Heavy vaginal bleeding (EBL 800 mL). Uterus boggy and soft. Immediate management?
rule: HELLP: haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets.

stem: A 35-year-old woman: secondary infertility for 3 years. History of pulmonary TB. HSG: bilateral tubal blockage with beaded appearance. Cause?
rule: Placenta previa (stable, preterm) then expectant management.

stem: A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman: vaginal bleeding for 2 weeks. BMI 35, diabetes. TVUSG: endometrial thickness 12 mm. Next step?
rule: PPH due to uterine atony. Oxytocin + uterine massage.

stem: A 28-year-old at 30 weeks: severe abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. Uterus tender and hard. FHR absent. Diagnosis?
rule: Genital TB: beaded appearance on HSG is characteristic.

stem: A 30-year-old at 36 weeks: generalized tonic-clonic seizure. History of preeclampsia. BP 170/115, urine protein 4+. First-line anticonvulsant?
rule: Postmenopausal bleeding + endometrial thickness >4 mm then endometrial biopsy.

stem: A 25-year-old woman: oligomenorrhoea, hirsutism, acne for 2 years. BMI 32. USG: bilateral enlarged ovaries with multiple peripheral cysts. First-line for fertility?
rule: Abruptio placentae: painful bleeding, tender hard uterus, fetal death.

stem: A 45-year-old woman: 6 months heavy menstrual bleeding and intermenstrual bleeding. Uterus symmetrically enlarged to 12 weeks. USG: multiple well-defined hypoechoic masses in myometrium. Diagnosis?
rule: Eclampsia. IV magnesium sulphate is first-line.

stem: A 32-year-old at 32 weeks: severe pruritus, especially palms and soles, for 2 weeks. Serum bile acids elevated. No rash. Management?
opts: Oral ursodeoxycholic acid and early delivery planning
rule: PCOS. Clomiphene citrate is first-line for ovulation induction.

stem: A 28-year-old G2P1 at 38 weeks: breech presentation. External cephalic version unsuccessful. Delivery plan?
rule: Uterine fibroids: heavy bleeding, symmetrically enlarged uterus, myometrial masses.

stem: A 35-year-old woman: 3 months postcoital bleeding. Speculum: friable, ulcerated growth on cervix. Next step?
rule: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. Ursodeoxycholic acid + deliver at 36-37 weeks.

stem: A 30-year-old at 20 weeks: blood glucose 210 mg/dL on 75-g OGTT. Fasting glucose 105 mg/dL. Initial management?
rule: Term breech with failed ECV then elective caesarean section.

stem: A 3-day-old term neonate: jaundice. Total bilirubin 18 mg/dL (indirect 17). Mother O Rh-negative, baby A Rh-positive. Direct Coombs positive. Diagnosis?
rule: Cervical cancer. Cervical biopsy is definitive.

stem: A 2-year-old boy: 2 days barking cough, hoarseness, inspiratory stridor. Low-grade fever. Neck X-ray: steeple sign. Treatment?
rule: Gestational diabetes. Initial management is medical nutrition therapy and exercise.

stem: A 4-year-old girl: high fever, drooling, difficulty breathing for 6 hours. Sitting upright with neck extended. Lateral neck X-ray: thumb sign. Immediate management?
rule: ABO incompatibility: mother O, baby A/B, Coombs positive.

stem: A 6-month-old infant: tachypnoea, chest indrawing, cough for 3 days. RR 58/min. No chest indrawing. SpO2 95%. WHO IMCI classification?
rule: Croup. Nebulized epinephrine + dexamethasone.

stem: A 5-year-old boy: generalised oedema, frothy urine, ascites for 1 week. Urine: 4+ proteinuria, no RBCs. Albumin 1.8 g/dL, cholesterol elevated. No haematuria, no HTN. Diagnosis?
rule: Epiglottitis. Secure airway in OT. Do NOT examine throat.

stem: A 3-year-old boy: 5 days high fever, bilateral conjunctival injection, cracked lips, strawberry tongue, cervical lymphadenopathy. Treatment to prevent complications?
rule: IMCI: RR >=50/min in infant = pneumonia (non-severe if no chest indrawing).

stem: A 2-month-old infant: machinery-like murmur at left infraclavicular area. Continuous throughout systole and diastole. Diagnosis?
rule: Nephrotic syndrome in child. Minimal change disease most common in ages 1-10.

stem: A 6-year-old boy: squatting after exertion since early childhood. Central cyanosis and clubbing. CXR: boot-shaped heart. Diagnosis?
rule: Kawasaki disease. IVIG + aspirin to prevent coronary aneurysms.

stem: A 28-week preterm neonate: respiratory distress shortly after birth. Grunting, nasal flaring, chest retractions. CXR: ground-glass appearance with air bronchograms. Immediate management?
rule: PDA: continuous machinery murmur at left infraclavicular area.

stem: A 9-month-old infant: 3 days watery diarrhoea, vomiting, decreased urine output. Lethargic, sunken eyes, skin pinch >3 seconds. Degree of dehydration?
rule: TOF: boot-shaped heart, cyanosis, squatting.

stem: A 3-year-old boy: fever, cough, generalized maculopapular rash for 3 days. Small white spots on buccal mucosa. Treatment?
rule: RDS. Surfactant + CPAP is standard.

stem: A 10-year-old boy: recurrent wheezing and cough for 2 years, triggered by cold air and exercise. No fever. Spirometry: FEV1/FVC 0.65, >12% improvement after bronchodilator. First-line maintenance?
rule: Severe dehydration: lethargy, sunken eyes, skin pinch >2 seconds.

stem: A 1-day-old term neonate: heart rate 70 bpm, no respiratory effort, flaccid and pale. Immediate step in resuscitation?
rule: Measles (Koplik spots). Vitamin A supplementation reduces morbidity/mortality.

stem: A 6-month-old exclusively breastfed infant: irritability, poor feeding, bulging anterior fontanelle. Mother had pulmonary TB, non-compliant. CSF: lymphocytes 200, protein 150, glucose 25. Diagnosis?
rule: Asthma. ICS is first-line maintenance for persistent asthma.

stem: A 55-year-old woman: sudden severe pain in right eye, headache, nausea, blurred vision for 4 hours. Right eye red, fixed mid-dilated pupil. IOP 55 mmHg. Immediate treatment?
rule: Neonatal resuscitation: HR <100 then PPV.

stem: A 65-year-old man: sudden painless loss of vision in right eye lasting 30 min, then partial recovery. History of AF. Fundoscopy: pale retina with cherry-red spot. Diagnosis?
rule: TB meningitis: lymphocytic pleocytosis, high protein, low glucose.

stem: A 50-year-old woman with diabetes for 15 years: blurred vision. Fundoscopy: dot-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton-wool spots. No neovascularization. Stage?
rule: Acute angle-closure glaucoma. Acetazolamide + pilocarpine.

stem: A 25-year-old woman: painful vision loss in right eye, difficulty distinguishing colours. Left leg numbness 6 months ago that resolved. Pupil reacts sluggishly. Swollen optic disc. Diagnosis?
rule: CRAO: sudden painless vision loss, cherry-red spot on pale retina.

stem: A 60-year-old man: gradual painless progressive vision loss in both eyes for 2 years. Reduced visual acuity, brownish opacity in lens. Definitive treatment?
rule: Moderate NPDR: dot-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton-wool spots.

stem: A 45-year-old man: sudden painless vision loss in left eye. Fundoscopy: blood and thunder appearance with dilated, tortuous veins and widespread haemorrhages. Diagnosis?
rule: Optic neuritis: painful vision loss, colour desaturation.

stem: A 4-year-old boy: sudden choking and coughing while eating peanuts. Stridor, decreased air entry on right. CXR: hyperinflation of right lung. Immediate management?
rule: Cataract. Phacoemulsification with IOL is definitive.

stem: A 50-year-old man: profuse bleeding from right nostril for 1 hour. History of hypertension. Bleeding point visible in anterior nasal septum. First-line treatment?
rule: CRVO: blood and thunder fundus, dilated tortuous veins.

stem: A 3-year-old girl: severe ear pain, fever, irritability for 2 days. Tympanic membrane bulging, erythematous, loss of light reflex. Treatment?
rule: Foreign body aspiration. Rigid bronchoscopy for removal.

stem: A 40-year-old woman: progressive hearing loss in right ear for 2 years. Recurrent ear discharge since childhood. Central perforation of tympanic membrane. PTA: 40-dB air-bone gap. Diagnosis?
rule: Epistaxis from Little's area. Chemical cautery is first-line.

stem: A 55-year-old man: unilateral progressive hearing loss, tinnitus, imbalance for 6 months. No ear discharge. Tuning fork tests: lateralization to contralateral ear. Investigation?
rule: Acute otitis media. Oral amoxicillin is first-line.

stem: A 30-year-old woman: recurrent episodes of severe vertigo lasting hours, with tinnitus and aural fullness. PTA: low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Diagnosis?
rule: CSOM tubotympanic: central perforation, conductive hearing loss.

stem: A 60-year-old man: 3 months weight loss and abdominal discomfort. CT: mass in head of pancreas. Biopsy: poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma. Tumour marker most likely elevated?
rule: Suspected acoustic neuroma. MRI with contrast is gold standard.

stem: A tissue sample shows cells with increased mitotic figures, nuclear pleomorphism, and loss of polarity. This best describes:
rule: Ménière's disease: episodic vertigo + tinnitus + aural fullness + SNHL.

stem: A 30-year-old man: fever, pallor, gum bleeding for 1 week. WBC 45,000 with 70% blasts. Blasts MPO positive with Auer rods. Diagnosis?
rule: CA19-9 is the primary tumour marker for pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

stem: A patient with chronic inflammation shows tissue swelling due to proliferation of fibroblasts and new blood vessels. This process is best described as:
rule: Dysplasia: increased mitoses, nuclear pleomorphism, loss of polarity.

stem: A 45-year-old woman: fatigue, pallor. Hb 8, MCV 110, MCH 38. Macro-ovalocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils. B12 80 pg/mL. Underlying cause?
rule: AML: MPO-positive blasts with Auer rods are pathognomonic.

stem: A biopsy of a lymphoid malignancy shows Reed-Sternberg cells. Diagnosis?
rule: Granulation tissue: proliferation of fibroblasts and new blood vessels in chronic inflammation.

stem: A fluid analysis shows protein 1.8 g/dL, specific gravity 1.012, few cells. This fluid is best classified as:
rule: Megaloblastic anaemia. Pernicious anaemia most common cause of B12 deficiency.

stem: A tumour arising from mesenchymal tissue is classified as:
rule: Reed-Sternberg cells are pathognomonic of Hodgkin lymphoma.

stem: A 55-year-old man with progressive dyspnoea and orthopnoea has a wide pulse pressure, diastolic murmur at the left sternal border, and Quincke's sign. Echocardiography shows severe aortic regurgitation with left ventricular dilation. Which pathological process is most likely responsible for the left ventricular dilation?
rule: Transudate: low protein (<2.5 g/dL), low specific gravity (<1.012), few cells.

stem: A 40-year-old woman: 2 months fatigue and pallor. Hb 8, MCV 110, MCH 38. Macro-ovalocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils. B12 80 pg/mL. Which test confirms pernicious anaemia?
rule: Sarcoma = mesenchymal tumour. Carcinoma = epithelial tumour.

stem: A 60-year-old man: 3 months weight loss and abdominal discomfort. CT: mass in head of pancreas. Biopsy shows poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma. Which anatomical structure is most likely to be invaded by this tumour?
rule: Chronic aortic regurgitation causes volume overload (increased preload) leading to left ventricular eccentric hypertrophy and dilation.

stem: A 30-year-old man: fracture of surgical neck of humerus after fall. Weakness of shoulder abduction, loss of sensation over regimental badge area. Nerve injured?
rule: Pernicious anaemia is confirmed by anti-intrinsic factor antibodies (and anti-parietal cell antibodies).

stem: A 45-year-old woman: wrist drop after mid-shaft humeral fracture. Loss of sensation over dorsal first web space. Nerve injured?
rule: Pancreatic head carcinoma commonly invades surrounding structures including the CBD, duodenum, and superior mesenteric vessels.

stem: A 25-year-old man: stabbed in cubital fossa. Inability to flex DIP joints of index and middle fingers, loss of sensation over palmar lateral 3.5 fingers. Nerve injured?
rule: Axillary nerve injury: deltoid weakness, regimental badge area numbness.

stem: A 60-year-old man: claw hand deformity and loss of sensation over medial 1.5 fingers after medial epicondyle fracture. Nerve injured?
rule: Radial nerve injury at spiral groove: wrist drop, dorsal first web space numbness.

stem: A 50-year-old woman: foot drop and loss of sensation over dorsum of foot after fracture of neck of fibula. Nerve injured?
rule: Median nerve injury at cubital fossa: DIP flexion loss, palmar sensation loss.

stem: A 55-year-old man: left-sided stroke affecting internal capsule. Vessel most likely occluded?
rule: Ulnar nerve injury: claw hand, medial 1.5 fingers numbness.

stem: A 30-year-old woman: indirect inguinal hernia. Structure forming the deep (internal) ring?
rule: Common peroneal nerve injury at fibular neck: foot drop, dorsum numbness.

stem: A 60-year-old man: portal hypertension. Most clinically significant site for life-threatening haemorrhage?
rule: Lacunar strokes of internal capsule = lenticulostriate branches of MCA.

stem: A 40-year-old woman: thyroid swelling. Nerve entering larynx posterior to cricothyroid joint?
rule: Deep ring = opening in transversalis fascia.

stem: A 50-year-old man: diaphragmatic hernia through oesophageal hiatus. Vertebral level of oesophageal hiatus?
rule: Oesophageal varices = most life-threatening site.

stem: A 35-year-old woman: mass in femoral triangle. Lateral boundary of femoral triangle?
rule: Recurrent laryngeal nerve enters larynx posterior to cricothyroid joint.

stem: A 50-year-old man with DKA: pH 7.18, HCO3 9 mEq/L, PaCO2 20 mmHg. Primary acid-base disturbance?
rule: Oesophageal hiatus = T10. Aortic hiatus = T12. Caval opening = T8.

stem: A 60-year-old man with CKD: pH 7.30, HCO3 16 mEq/L, PaCO2 32 mmHg. Expected respiratory compensation (Winter's formula)?
rule: Femoral triangle: superior = inguinal ligament, lateral = sartorius, medial = adductor longus.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with anxiety: hyperventilation. ABG: pH 7.52, PaCO2 25 mmHg, HCO3 22 mEq/L. Primary disturbance?
rule: Low pH, low HCO3 = metabolic acidosis. Low PaCO2 = appropriate respiratory compensation.

stem: A 55-year-old man with COPD: pH 7.34, PaCO2 58 mmHg, HCO3 32 mEq/L. Primary disturbance?
opts: Chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
rule: Winter's formula: Expected PaCO2 = 1.5 x HCO3 + 8 ± 2. For HCO3 16: range 30-34.

stem: A 60-year-old man with severe diarrhoea for 3 days: pH 7.28, HCO3 12 mEq/L, PaCO2 28 mmHg. Na 140, Cl 110. Anion gap?
rule: High pH, low PaCO2 = respiratory alkalosis. Normal HCO3 = acute.

stem: A 50-year-old woman with primary hyperparathyroidism: calcium 12.5 mg/dL. Most characteristic ECG finding?
rule: Low pH, high PaCO2 = respiratory acidosis. Elevated HCO3 = chronic with compensation.

stem: A 45-year-old man with Addison's disease: weakness. K+ 6.2 mEq/L, Na 128 mEq/L. Hormonal deficiency explaining these findings?
rule: Anion gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3) = 140 - (110+12) = 18. Diarrhoea = normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.

stem: A 30-year-old woman: secondary amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea. Prolactin elevated. Hypothalamic hormone that normally inhibits prolactin?
rule: Hypercalcaemia shortens QT interval. Hypocalcaemia prolongs QT.

stem: A 55-year-old man with heart failure: reduced cardiac output. According to Frank-Starling mechanism, which intervention increases stroke volume?
rule: Aldosterone deficiency leads to sodium loss + potassium retention.

stem: A 40-year-old man with pulmonary embolism: V/Q mismatch. Best description of physiology?
opts: Ventilation without perfusion then increased dead space
Both ventilation and perfusion reduced equally
rule: Dopamine inhibits prolactin release.

stem: A 55-year-old woman with diabetes, eGFR 25 mL/min/1.73m sq, on metformin. Most appropriate action?
rule: Frank-Starling: increased preload (up to optimal point) increases stroke volume.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with epilepsy planning pregnancy, on valproic acid. Most appropriate advice?
opts: Switch to lamotrigine and supplement folic acid
Double the dose of valproic acid
rule: PE blocks perfusion to ventilated alveoli then increased dead space ventilation.

stem: A 60-year-old man with asthma and hypertension started on beta-blocker. Develops wheezing within hours. Property causing this adverse effect?
rule: Metformin contraindicated if eGFR <30 (risk of lactic acidosis).

stem: A 50-year-old woman with hypertension and bilateral renal artery stenosis started on ACE inhibitor. Develops AKI. Mechanism?
opts: Dilation of efferent arteriole reducing GFR
rule: Valproate is teratogenic. Switch to lamotrigine + folic acid.

stem: A 45-year-old man on warfarin for AF: INR 7.5, minor gum bleeding. Immediate management?
opts: Hold warfarin and administer IV vitamin K
rule: Non-selective beta-blockers block beta-2 receptors then bronchoconstriction.

stem: A 35-year-old woman on OCPs diagnosed with TB, started on rifampicin. Advice regarding contraception?
opts: Rifampicin induces CYP450, reducing OCP efficacy—use additional contraception
rule: In bilateral RAS, ACE inhibitors dilate efferent arteriole then reduced GFR.

stem: A 55-year-old man with AF started on amiodarone. Most concerning adverse effect with long-term use?
rule: INR >7 with bleeding: hold warfarin + IV vitamin K.

stem: A 60-year-old man with heart failure started on spironolactone. Most important electrolyte abnormality to monitor?
rule: Rifampicin induces CYP450 then reduced OCP efficacy.

stem: A 25-year-old man: fatigue and jaundice after starting primaquine. Peripheral film: Heinz bodies and bite cells. Enzyme deficiency?
rule: Amiodarone: pulmonary fibrosis is the most serious long-term adverse effect.

stem: A newborn: vomiting, lethargy, musty odour after feeding. Guthrie test: elevated phenylalanine. Enzyme deficient?
rule: Spironolactone causes hyperkalaemia.

stem: A 30-year-old man: fatigue, pallor. Hb 7, MCV 105, hypersegmented neutrophils, B12 low. Metabolic pathway impaired by B12 deficiency?
rule: G6PD deficiency: oxidative stress then haemolysis with Heinz bodies and bite cells.

stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic alcoholism: confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia. Thiamine administered urgently. Enzyme requiring thiamine as cofactor?
rule: PKU: phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency.

stem: A 60-year-old woman: bone pain, muscle weakness, fractures. Ca low, PO4 low, ALP elevated, 25-OH vitamin D low. Diagnosis?
rule: B12 is cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase.

stem: A 35-year-old woman: photosensitivity, abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric symptoms. Urine: elevated PBG and delta-ALA. Enzyme deficient in acute intermittent porphyria?
rule: Wernicke's encephalopathy. Thiamine is cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase.

stem: A researcher wants to determine incidence of a new infectious disease. Most appropriate study design?
rule: Osteomalacia: vitamin D deficiency then low Ca, low PO4, elevated ALP.

stem: A new screening test for breast cancer evaluated in 1,000 women. Correctly identifies 90/100 true cases. False positive in 50/900 healthy women. Specificity?
rule: Acute intermittent porphyria: PBG deaminase deficiency.

stem: A public health team wants to evaluate efficacy of a new vaccine. Strongest study design?
rule: Cohort study measures incidence by following a disease-free population over time.

stem: According to Pakistan EPI schedule, age for first dose of measles vaccine?
rule: Specificity = TN/(TN+FP) = 850/900 = 94.4%.

stem: A community health survey finds 50/500 people have diabetes. Measure of disease frequency?
rule: RCT provides the strongest evidence for efficacy.

stem: A TB control programme in Pakistan uses DOTS strategy. Most critical component?
rule: Pakistan EPI: measles at 9 months (second dose at 15 months).

stem: A 25-year-old man found dead in closed room with coal fire. Post-mortem: cherry-red discoloration of skin and blood. Cause of death?
rule: Point prevalence = proportion with disease at a given time.

stem: A 30-year-old woman ingested unknown substance. Excessive salivation, lacrimation, miosis, muscle fasciculations, garlic-like odour. Poisoning?
rule: DOTS: Directly Observed Therapy is the cornerstone.

stem: A body recovered from water. Washerwoman appearance of skin and fine foam at mouth and nostrils. Findings indicate?
rule: CO poisoning: cherry-red discoloration (carboxyhaemoglobin).

stem: A forensic pathologist examines a scalp wound. Edges irregular with tissue bridging and surrounding bruising. Wound type?
rule: Organophosphate: cholinergic excess (SLUDGE) + miosis + fasciculations + garlic odour.

stem: A 52-year-old woman on dialysis presents with hypotension, muffled heart sounds and distended neck veins. Echo shows a large circumferential pericardial effusion with right-atrial and right-ventricular diastolic collapse. Immediate treatment?
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Tamponade physiology with RA/RV diastolic collapse = decompress now
rule: Diastolic collapse of RA then RV with clinical hypotension defines tamponade requiring urgent pericardiocentesis; fluid removal via ultrafiltration could make things catastrophically worse by further reducing preload across compressed cardiac chambers.Discriminator: Hypotension + tachycardia + RA/RV diastolic collapse = tamponade; drainage to decompress is the treatmentA) Increase ultrafiltrationUltrafiltration removes intravascular volume and worsens filling pressure across a compressed heart.C) High-dose NSAIDs and colchicineAnti-inflammatory therapy addresses uraemic/w drug-refractory recurrent pericarditis, not acute haemodynamic collapse.D) PericardiectomyPericardiectomy is surgical management of constrictive pericarditis, not acute tamponade.

stem: A 78-year-old woman with syncope has HR 35/min, cananonical carotid pulsations, and wide-complex escape QRS. Atropine gives no sustained improvement. Best next step?
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Symptomatic complete heart block with wide escape → temporise with pacing
rule: Complete heart block with a wideinfra-His escapee responded poorly to atropine — the standard is temporary transvenous pacing with a plan for definitive permanent pacemaker.Discriminator: Wide escape QRS is unstable/I non-reliable; atropine is unreliable in infra-His blockA) Continue atropine infusionIt already failed; repetition amounts to waiting for asystole.C) Adrenaline infusionAdrenaline is a bridge when pacing is unavailable, not a substitute when pacing is accessible.D) Discharge with holterSent-home-on-monitor neglect is what kills these patients within days.

stem: A 55-year-old man with long-standing uncontrolled hypertension develops exertional dyspnoea and orthopnoea. Echo: EF 30%, global hypokinesis, no regional wall-motion abnormality, no CAD on CT angiogram. Most likely cause of his heart failure?
opts: Hypertensive heart disease with dilated (non-ischaemic) cardiomyopathy
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Dilated (non-ischaemic) cardiomyopathy from chronic hypertension
rule: Chronic hypertension drives a hypertensive heart-disease course through diastolic dysfunction, fibrosis and final dilated hypokinetic state (EF 30%) without infarct-pattern regional defects or obstructive coronary disease.Discriminator: Unified global hypokinesis + absence of regional wall-motion defects/ CAD = non-ischaemic dilated cardiomyopathyB) Ischaemic cardiomyopathy requiring revascularisationIschaemic cardiomyopathy would show regional/ territory-dependent wall-motion defects or occlusive disease.C) restrictive cardiomyopathy from amyloidAmyloid gives thick walls with granular speckling, EF preserved until late, often concomitant conduction disease.D) Valve stenosisValvular stenosis produces corresponding valvular obstruction patterns on echo/ auscultation, absent here.

stem: A 62-year-old man with DVT confirmed on ultrasound, Wells score 3 (active cancer, calf swelling, tenderness along deep veins). What is the next step?
opts: Start therapeutic anticoagulation — no further testing needed
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: High-pretest-probability DVT: anticoagulate pending/following imaging without D-dimer
rule: With high pretest probability, D-dimer is not done (it can be false-positive anyway and ''); in addition to the already positive ultrasound, therapeutic anticoagulation begins immediately, typically DOAC or LMWH (in cancer, LMWH preferred at diagnosis).Discriminator: High Wells score (≥2–3): D-dimer unnecessary; anticoagulation started while awaiting/ following sonographyA) D-dimer to rule out DVTD-dimer adds nothing now; the ultrasound is already diagnostic and anticoagulation is urgent.C) Venous duplex after 1 weekWeek-delay doubles embolic risk; anticoagulation cannot wait for convenience.D) ThrombolysisThrombolysis is reserved for limb-threatening phlegmasia or massive PE, not uncomplicated calf/thigh DVT.

stem: A 49-year-old is prepped for dental extraction; history includes a mechanical mitral valve replacement 6 years ago. What prophylaxis is recommended pre-procedure?
opts: Amoxicillin 2 g orally 30–60 min before the procedure
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Endocarditis prophylaxis: prosthetic valve + dental procedure = amoxicillin
rule: Prosthetic valve patients undergoing dental procedures with gum/periapical manipulation receive amoxicillin 2 g (clindamycin if penicillin-allergic/cephalexin/azithro) 30–60 mins pre-procedure; most other cardiac conditions no longer need prophylaxis.Discriminator: High-risk cardiac conditions (prosthetic valve, prior IE, certain CHD) + dental procedures manipulating gingiva = antibiotic prophylaxisA) No prophylaxis — routine dental careProsthetic valves are explicitlytargeted for dental prophylaxis due to life-threatening IE potential.C) Gentamicin IM before the procedureAminoglycosides are not prophylaxis agents for dental work.D) Oral vancomycinOral vancomycin does not generate systemic levels and is not used in prophylaxis.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with 40 minutes of crushing chest pain and diaphoresis. ECG shows a new left bundle branch block with concordant ST-segment elevation in V5-V6. Troponin is pending. What is the immediate management?
opts: Reperfusion therapy as an acute coronary occlusion
Start a calcium channel blocker and observe
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: New LBBB with Sgarbossa-concordant changes is treated as STEMI
rule: Sgarbossa-concordant ST changes in a new LBBB are highly specific for acute coronary occlusion, so the patient is managed as STEMI with immediate reperfusion rather than waiting for troponin.Discriminator: New LBBB + concordant ST changes = occlusive MI until proven otherwise; troponin waits neverA) Wait for troponin before decidingBiomarkers confirm necrosis but reperfusion decisions are made on the ECG; delay costs myocardium.C) Discharge with outpatient echocardiogramAn occlusion pattern with ongoing symptoms needs reperfusion, not outpatient workup.D) Start a calcium channel blocker and observeRate/rhythm control drugs do not address the occluded artery.

stem: A 55-year-old diabetic man 3 days after inferior MI develops a new harsh pansystolic murmur at the left sternal border with worsening hypotension. Echocardiography shows a step-up in oxygen saturation from right atrium to right ventricle. What has occurred?
opts: Papillary muscle infarction with severe MR
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Post-MI VSD — pulmonary step-up confirms left-to-right shunt
rule: A new left-to-right shunt rising oxygen saturation across the ventricular septum confirms ventricular septal rupture, a mechanical complication typically 2–5 days post-MI.Discriminator: O2 step-up RA→RV + harsh LSB murmur post-MI = septal ruptureA) Papillary muscle infarction with severe MRPapillary muscle rupture gives severe MR with a murmur maximal at the apex radiating to axilla and no oxygen step-up.C) RV infarction extensionRV extension causes hypotension with clear lungs, not a new pansystolic murmur or shunt.D) Dressler pericarditisPump failure produces congestion without a new murmur or saturation step-up.

stem: A 68-year-old man on verapamil presents dizzy with HR 38 and BP 95/60; no prior conduction disease documented; potassium 4.1, creatinine 0.9. What is the immediate therapy approach?
opts: Calcium salts + glucagon bridge & temporary pacing input where unresponsive, stopping verapamil
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Calcium-channel-blocker overdose: calcium + glucagon + pacing
rule: CCB toxicity/ idiosyncratic response manifests as profound bradycardia/ vasodilation; management combines IV calcium gluconate (supports excitation-contraction coupling), glucagon (increases cAMP bypass), high-dose insulin-euglycemia therapy in true overdose and temporary transvenous pacing when rhythms gear down; the offending calcium-channel blocker must be stopped.Discriminator: Bradycardia + hypotension from verapamil: give calcium salts, consider glucagon and, if unresponsive, temporary pacing — drug discontinuedB) Adrenaline bolus and dischargeAdrenaline is a short-lived bridge, not a definitive response; potential immediate pacing/calcium is more directed.C) FludrocortisoneFludrocortisone manages neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, not drug-induced heart block.D) Oral potassiumPotassium is normal; measuring potassium replacement doesn't treat an AV-nodal drug effect.

stem: A 55-year-old woman post-hip surgery suddenly becomes hypotensive (BP 82/60) with sharp pleuritic chest pain, HR 128, SpO2 86% on room air; CTPA confirms central saddle pulmonary embolism with RV strain. Immediate treatment?
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Massive (high-risk) PE → reperfusion (lysis) not anticoagulation alone
rule: Hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg for >15 min or requiring support) with confirmed central PE and RV dysfunction categorises high-risk PE where systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg over 2h) is the standard to relieve RV collapse, followed by anticoagulation.Discriminator: Hypotension (SBP <90) + central PE + RV strain = high-risk PE; thrombolysis restores flow fastestA) Therapeutic anticoagulation and monitorAnticoagulation prevents clot extension but does not clear obstructing thrombus in time to rescue a failing right ventricle.C) AspirinAspirin has no role in acute PE treatment.D) Inferior vena cava filter onlyIVC filters are for anticoagulation-contraindicated or recurrent-embolism patients — a substitute, not a reperfusion strategy.

stem: A 50-year-old farmer with excessive salivation, miosis, abdominal cramping and fasciculations after spraying crops; BP 160/90, HR 48. Diagnosis and antidote?
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Organophosphate toxidrome: SLUDGE + fasciculations → atropine + pralidoxime
rule: Combined muscarinic (salivation, miosis, cramps, brady/hypertension variation) and nicotinic (fasciculations) signs after pesticide exposure confirms organophosphate/ carbamate cholinesterase inhibition; high-dose atropine targets muscarinic load and pralidoxime reactivates acetylcholinesterase when given early.Discriminator: Cholinergic muscarinic excess (salivation, miosis, cramps) + nicotinic fasciculations in crop sprayer = organophosphateB) Carbamate with contraindicated atropineAtropine remains indicated (and life-prolonging) even in carbamate cases; withholding it is dangerous.C) Pyrethroid poisoning — decontamination onlyPyrethroids give paresthesia and occasional tremor — not the full cholinergic toxidrome.D) Warfarin rodenticide — vitamin KWarfarin rodenticides bleed, with no cholinergic features.

stem: A 21-year-old athlete collapses and dies during a football match. Autopsy reveals asymmetric septal hypertrophy. Which of his first-degree relatives is at greatest risk of the same condition and should undergo what screening?
opts: All first-degree relatives — clinical exam + echocardiogram ± ECG screening
Female relatives only because of transmission pattern
No screening needed as disease is not inherited
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: HCM: autosomal dominant; cascade screening of first-degree relatives
rule: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the commonest cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes and inherited in ~50–60% as autosomal dominant; first-degree relatives need clinical-exam + 12-lead ECG + echocardiographic screening (adults every 2–5 years, children puberty age-periodically).Discriminator: HCM is AD with incomplete penetrance; SCD in athlete points to family cascade screening pooled echo+ECGB) Only symptomatic relativesHCM often stays silent until the fatal event; 'no symptoms' never rules a family member out.C) Female relatives only because of transmission patternAutosomal-dominant inheritance passes through both sexes equally.D) No screening needed as disease is not inheritedHCM is among the most heritable cardiac muscle-disease patterns known.

stem: A 71-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes has paroxysmal atrial fibrillation on Holter. CHA2DS2-VASc score is 2 (hypertension + diabetes, no stroke, age <75, male). What is indicated?
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2 (male) → anticoagulate, even for paroxysmal AF
rule: With a score of 2 in a male patient, guideline-level risk is high enough that oral anticoagulation (DOAC preferred) is recommended; paroxysmal pattern does not lower the threshold, and aspirin is no longer an acceptable substitute.Discriminator: Paroxysmal AF carries the same stroke risk as persistent; score ≥2 in a man mandates anticoagulationA) Aspirin aloneAspirin's stroke prevention in AF is inadequate and combined major-bleed risk rivals anticoagulation without equivalent efficacy.B) No antithrombotic therapyWith a score of 2, active stroke risk exceeds bleeding risk; withholding therapy is wrong.D) Aspirin plus clopidogrelDual antiplatelet therapy is for acute coronary syndromes/stents, never stroke prevention in AF.

stem: A 58-year-old man on atorvastatin 40 mg develops significant myalgias at week 3; CK 3.5x ULN, no dark urine, renal function normal. What is the appropriate next step?
opts: Stop statin permanently; no rechallenge ever
Pause statin, resume at reduced dose/ alternate statin after symptoms settle, aiming to retain some statin therapy
Continue the same dose and ignore
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Statin myalgia: pause, dechallenge, rechallenging with lower dose/ different statin
rule: Statin-associated muscle symptoms with CK 3–4x ULN warrant temporary discontinuation; after symptoms resolve, rechallenge at lower dose/ hydrophilic alternative (rosuvastatin, pravastatin) or alternate-day rosuvastatin maintains LDL benefit at tolerable exposure.Discriminator: CK >4x ULN with symptoms → stop, dechallenge; CK <10 ULN no rhabdomyolysis; resumption at reduced dose/ alternative statin to retain protectionA) Stop statin permanently; no rechallenge everMost statin-intolerant patients tolerate other statins at lower/ alternate doses; abandonment forfeits major mortality benefit.C) Add niacinNiacin is not a substitute lipid-lowering here.D) Continue the same dose and ignorePersevering on the same dose at CK 3.5x ULN with symptoms can tip into rhabdomyolysis.

stem: A 24-year-old man develops pleuritic chest pain after a viral illness. ECG: diffuse concave ST elevation; echocardiogram normal. What therapy reduces recurrence risk best?
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Acute pericarditis: NSAID + colchicine lowers recurrence
rule: Acute pericarditis is treated with NSAID (aspirin/ibuprofen/indomethacin) plus colchicine for 3 months, which both speeds resolution and substantially cuts recurrence; steroids are reserved for recurrences or connective-tissue/ uraemic/perinatal neoplastic causes.Discriminator: Diffuse concave ST elevation + pleuritic pain = acute pericarditis; colchicine halves recurrenceB) High-dose corticosteroids first-lineCorticosteroids first-line increase recurrence risk in idiopathic/ viral pericarditis.C) Aspirin alone foreverNSAID/aspirin-only courses do not cut recurrence; colchicine does.D) Percutaneous pericardiectomyPericardiectomy is for constrictive disease, not acute self-pericardial inflammation.

stem: A 45-year-old man with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (LDL 8.2 mmol/L) has no known ASCVD. What is the intensity of lipid management?
opts: High-intensity statin ± ezetimibe, target LDL <1.4–1.8 mmol/L if achievable
Diet and exercise alone first, review in 2 years
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: HeFH: high-intensity statin early; combo therapy to reach LDL goals
rule: Familial hypercholesterolaemia carries lifelong extreme LDL burden; management is high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 40–80, rosuvastatin 20–40) from early adulthood with ezetimibe ± PCSK9 inhibitor to reach LDL <1.4 mmol/L (ESC) or <1.8 (varies by region).Discriminator: HeFH (LDL >4.9 mmol/L baseline, tendon xanthomas, family history) = lifelong high-intensity therapy from young ageB) Diet and exercise alone first, review in 2 yearsTwo-year lifestyle-only wait abandons a genetically-determined high-risk patient mid-stream; risk accrues from teenage LDL exposure.C) NiacinNiacin has fallen out of standard use with unfavourable outcome data and tolerability.D) Bile-acid sequestrants monotherapySequestrants alone neither achieve targets nor match statin outcome-evidence and are GI-intolerable long-term.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is admitted with chest pain and transient ST depression in V4-V6. Troponin rises to 3x the 99th percentile. She continues to have pain despite optimal medical therapy. What is the next step?
opts: Discharge after 48 hours of medical therapy
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: High-risk NSTEMI refractory to therapy needs angiography within 24 hours
rule: Refractory chest pain with dynamic ST changes and elevated troponin places her at very high risk, mandating early invasive angiography within 24 hours.Discriminator: Recurrent ischaemia despite therapy = very-high-risk pathway, not discharge-and-watchA) Discharge after 48 hours of medical therapyContinued pain on therapy definesfailure of the conservative pathway; ischaemic risk persists.C) Treadmill exercise test before dischargeStress testing is for low-risk chest pain after ischaemia is stabilized, not during refractory NSTEMI.D) Repeat troponin in 12 hoursSerial troponins classify risk but do not treat ongoing ischaemia.

stem: A 31-year-old woman has fasting triglycerides 14 mmol/L with a clearing-cream serum sample, normal ALT, and an inherited lipid profile from mother with similar pattern; no pancreatitis to date. Highest-priority intervention?
opts: Aggressive lifestyle + fibrate; optimise glycaemic/thyroid/oestrogen factors; avoid secondary-cause triggers (alcohol)
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia: pancreatitis prevention through multifactorial lowering
rule: TG >11.3 mmol/L (set pancreatitis risk) calls for aggressive lifestyle measures (weight, carbohydrate/alcohol cut, omega-3), fibrates ± icosapent ethyl, plus removing secondary factors (glycaemia, thyroid, oestrogens, alcohol) — statins treat ASCVD risk, not TG-centred risk, and can be adjunct later.Discriminator: TG >11.3 mmol/L (1000 mg/dL) — the pancreatitis danger zone — is addressed first with triglyceride-specific therapy, not statinsB) High-dose statin monotherapyStatins modestly reduce triglycerides but at 14 mmol/L pancreatitis prevention requires TG-specific lowering.C) Diet then reassess in 3 yearsA 3-year wait courts pancreatitis; the interval should be weeks-to-months with active therapy.D) Plasma exchange weeklyPlasmapheresis is an acute rescue for TG-crisis/ pancreatitis, not routine maintenance.

stem: A 60-year-old man with HFrEF (EF 28%) on sacubitril-valsartan, evidence-based beta blocker and spironolactone remains in symptomatic congestion with persistent EF 26%. Which drug should be added to reduce death and hospitalisation regardless of EF?
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: SGLT2 inhibitors reduce CV death/hospitalisation across the EF range
rule: SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin/empagliflozin) reduce cardiovascular death and heart failure hospitalisation in HFrEF and HFpEF and are added once a patient remains symptomatic on triple therapy.Discriminator: On maximal GDMT + persistent symptoms → SGLT2 inhibitor, the only class benefiting HFrEF and HFpEF equallyB) VerapamilNon-dihydropyridine CCBs are negative inotropes contraindicated in HFrEF.C) FlecainideFlecainide is contraindicated in structural heart disease.D) AmlodipineAmlodipine may be used for angina/HTN in HF but does not reduce death or hospitalisation.

stem: A 75-year-old man with exertional syncope has an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, slow-rising pulse, and echocardiographic aortic valve area 0.9 cm² with mean gradient 45 mmHg. Management?
opts: Nitrates for symptom control and review
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Symptomatic severe AS → valve replacement
rule: Symptomatic severe AS (any of angina/syncope/dyspnoea, AVA <1.0 cm² with an appropriate gradient) is a class I indication for valve replacement — nitrates risk precipitate collapse, and no drug therapy relieves the mechanical obstruction.Discriminator: Exertional syncope + small valve area + high gradient = symptomatic severe AS; area >0.6 and gradient >40 qualifyA) Nitrates for symptom control and reviewNitrates can precipitate syncope in AS preload-dependent physiology; symptom relief means fixing the valve.C) Balloon mitral valvotomyBalloon mitral valvotomy addresses rheumatic mitral stenosis, a different valve and different path.D) Statin therapy onlyStatin therapy does not slow symptomatic progression in calcific AS to a clinically meaningful degree.

stem: A 70-year-old woman with a long-standing multinodular goitre develops palpitations, weight loss, and atrial fibrillation. There is no exophthalmos. What distinguishes this from Graves disease and guides therapy?
opts: Toxic multinodular goitre — nodular goitre, no exophthalmos; treat with radioiodine
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Toxic multinodular goitre — elderly, nodular goitre, no exophthalmos; radioiodine
rule: Toxic multinodular goitre causes thyrotoxicosis in older patients with a longstanding nodular goitre and lacks the exophthalmos and diffuseness of Graves disease (intel #60: exophthalmos = Graves). Therapy is radioiodine (or surgery); antithyroid drugs are not first-line. Recognising the absence of eye signs avoids misdiagnosing Graves.Discriminator: Elderly + nodular goitre + thyrotoxicosis WITHOUT exophthalmos = toxic MNG (vs Graves)A) Graves — start antithyroid drugs firstGraves has exophthalmos and a diffuse goitre; TMG is nodular without eye signs.B) Thyroiditis — observe onlyThis is thyrotoxic, not thyroiditis; observation is insufficient.C) Thyroid cancer — urgent surgeryThere is no suggestion of malignancy; urgent cancer surgery is wrong.

stem: A 30-year-old woman on an antipsychotic for schizophrenia develops galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea. Prolactin is markedly elevated. What should be considered before assuming a prolactinoma?
opts: Prolactinoma confirmed — refer for transsphenoidal surgery
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia — antipsychotics/D2 blockers before prolactinoma
rule: Many drugs elevate prolactin by blocking dopamine D2 receptors — antipsychotics (risperidone, typicals), metoclopramide, domperidone, verapamil, opioids. A careful drug history is essential before attributing hyperprolactinemia to a prolactinoma. Discontinuation (where safe) normalises prolactin. True prolactinoma is treated with dopamine agonists.Discriminator: Hyperprolactinemia on antipsychotic/metoclopramide = drug-induced; review drug before imagingB) Prolactinoma confirmed — refer for transsphenoidal surgerySurgery is for prolactinoma, not drug-induced hyperprolactinemia; the drug should be reviewed first.C) Primary hypothyroidismHypothyroidism can raise prolactin mildly but not typically with galactorrhoea on an antipsychotic.D) Pregnancy is the only causePregnancy is one cause but not the only one; drugs are a key consideration here.

stem: A woman with placental abruption develops generalized oozing from venepuncture sites. Laboratories show prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen, thrombocytopenia and a markedly raised D-dimer. Which is the most appropriate description and treatment?
opts: Disseminated intravascular coagulation; treat the underlying cause and support with blood products
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: DIC - consumption coagulopathy; treat the cause + supportive products
rule: Disseminated intravascular coagulation is a consumption coagulopathy driven by massive tissue factor release (obstetric abruption, sepsis, malignancy), causing bleeding with prolonged PT/aPTT, thrombocytopenia, low fibrinogen and high D-dimer. The cornerstone is treating the underlying cause with supportive blood product replacement (platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate).Discriminator: Placental abruption + bleeding + low fibrinogen/platelets + high D-dimer = DIC; treat cause + supportiveB) Haemophilia; give factor VIIIhaemophilia is a single-factor (VIII/IX) deficiency, not a consumption coagulopathy with low fibrinogenC) Immune thrombocytopenia; corticosteroidsITP gives isolated thrombocytopenia without prolonged PT or low fibrinogenD) Vitamin K deficiency; vitamin Kvitamin K deficiency gives prolonged PT but not thrombocytopenia or low fibrinogen

stem: A 60-year-old with a urinary tract infection develops fever (40 C), cold peripheries, tachycardia and confusion. WBC is 2100/mm3 and PT/INR is prolonged. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Septic shock with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Septic shock + DIC - fever, leucopenia, coagulopathy
rule: In sepsis, release of procoagulants and consumption of clotting factors produces DIC, reflected by thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen and high D-dimer. Leucopenia and a coagulopathy on top of shock point to septic shock with DIC rather than simple infection or embolic/cardiogenic causes. A recalled exam pattern (Q76).Discriminator: Source of sepsis + hypotension/confusion + low WBC + prolonged PT = septic shock with DICA) Uncomplicated UTIuncomplicated UTI does not cause shock, leucopenia and coagulopathyC) Cardiogenic shockcardiogenic shock has a raised JVP/pulmonary oedema and does not explain the coagulopathyD) Massive pulmonary embolismmassive PE causes acute right-heart strain, not leucopenia with prolonged PT

stem: A patient with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) has microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and neurological features. What is the most common cause of death in TTP?
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: TTP - most common cause of death is intracranial haemorrhage
rule: In thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura the classical pentad includes fever, microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, renal and neurological involvement. Severe thrombocytopenia predisposes to intracranial haemorrhage, the most common lethal event. Treatment is plasma exchange. A recalled exam pattern (Q25).Discriminator: TTP: intracranial haemorrhage is the most common cause of death (thrombocytopenia + microangiopathy)B) Myocardial infarctioncardiac ischaemia is not the leading cause of death in TTPC) Pulmonary embolismpulmonary embolism is not the typical fatal eventD) Hepatic failurehepatic failure is not the main cause of death in TTP

stem: A 30-year-old previously well person develops petechiae and bruising and has an isolated severe thrombocytopenia (platelets 15,000) with an otherwise normal FBC and blood film. No lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis and first-line treatment?
opts: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP); corticosteroids are first line
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Immune thrombocytopenia - isolated thrombocytopenia; first-line steroids
rule: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an autoimmune process (antiplatelet antibodies) causing isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal blood film, no splenomegaly, and mucocutaneous bleeding. First-line treatment is corticosteroids (plus, if severe, IVIg). It is a diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out leukaemia/TTP/vitamin K deficiency.Discriminator: Isolated severe thrombocytopenia, normal film, no splenomegaly = ITP; first-line corticosteroidsB) TTP; plasma exchangeTTP has microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with schistocytes and fever/neuro/renal signsC) Acute leukaemia; chemotherapyleukaemia shows blasts/pancytopenia and organ infiltrationD) Vitamin K deficiency; vitamin Kvitamin K deficiency causes coagulopathy (prolonged PT), not isolated low platelets

stem: A 14-year-old girl has Hb 9 g/dL, MCV 70 fL, serum ferritin 8 ng/mL and TIBC 450 ug/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Iron deficiency anaemia - microcytic, low ferritin, high TIBC
rule: Iron deficiency anaemia is microcytic/hypochromic with low ferritin, low serum iron, and high total iron-binding capacity (TIBC). Ferritin is the most specific marker; here it is clearly low (8). This is a recalled exam pattern (Q103). Thalassaemia minor also gives microcytosis but with normal/high ferritin and mild anaemia.Discriminator: Microcytic (MCV 70) + low ferritin + high TIBC = iron deficiency (ferritin is diagnostic if low)B) Thalassaemia minorthalassaemia minor has microcytosis but normal/high ferritin and often only mild anaemiaC) Sickle cell anaemiasickle cell anaemia is normocytic with sickling on crisis, not this iron profileD) Vitamin B12 deficiencyB12 deficiency is macrocytic (high MCV), not microcytic

stem: On a peripheral blood film, which single finding best supports a megaloblastic (B12/folate) anaemia?
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Megaloblastic anaemia - hypersegmented neutrophils + macro-ovalocytes
rule: Megaloblastic anaemia (B12 or folate deficiency) shows macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils (neutrophils with >5 nuclear lobes) on the film, along with an elevated MCV. Microcytes/target cells suggest iron deficiency or thalassaemia; spherocytes suggest spherocytosis; sickling suggests sickle cell disease.Discriminator: Hypersegmented neutrophils + macrocytosis = megaloblastic (B12/folate) anaemiaB) Microcytes and target cellsmicrocytes and target cells suggest iron deficiency or thalassaemia, not megaloblastic changeC) Spherocytesspherocytes suggest spherocytosis/AIHAD) Sickle-shaped cellssickle cells suggest sickle cell disease

stem: A 70-year-old incidentally has a markedly raised lymphocyte count (WBC 95,000) with a mature lymphocytosis and smudge cells on the film, mild lymphadenopathy, and no anaemia or thrombocytopenia. Most likely diagnosis?
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia - mature lymphocytosis + smudge cells in elderly
rule: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is common in older adults, with a persistent mature lymphocytosis (often >5,000 and seen at very high counts), smudge cells on the film, and lymphadenopathy. It may be asymptomatic and is staged with the Rai system; treatment is reserved for symptoms/cytopenias. Smudge cells are a characteristic artefactual finding.Discriminator: Elderly + high mature lymphocyte count + smudge cells = CLLB) Acute lymphoblastic leukaemiaALL is a childhood blast-cell acute leukaemia, not an elderly mature lymphocytosisC) Hairy cell leukaemiahairy cell leukaemia often has pancytopenia and hairy cytoplasmic projectionsD) Follicular lymphomafollicular lymphoma is primarily nodal lymphoma, not a marked peripheral lymphocytosis with smudge cells

stem: A boy develops acute jaundice and dark urine a day after taking an antimalarial and eating fava beans, with a normal blood film except for bite cells and Heinz bodies. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: G6PD deficiency - X-linked, oxidative haemolysis after fava/primaquine, Heinz bodies
rule: G6PD deficiency is an X-linked trait causing acute oxidative haemolysis when exposed to fava beans and oxidant drugs (primaquine, sulfonamides, dapsone). It presents with jaundice, dark urine, and Heinz bodies/bite cells on the film. It is more common in males and is diagnosed by enzyme assay (best measured when not in crisis).Discriminator: Triggers (fava beans, oxidant drugs) + acute haemolysis + Heinz bodies = G6PD deficiency (X-linked)B) Hereditary spherocytosisspherocytosis causes persistent spherocytes and gallstones, not trigger-related Heinz bodiesC) Autoimmune haemolytic anaemiaAIHA is Coombs positive without the drug/fava trigger patternD) Thalassaemia majorthalassaemia major is a transfusion-dependent chronic microcytic anaemia

stem: A patient with malabsorption and prolonged antibiotic use develops a bleeding tendency. Coagulation tests show a prolonged prothrombin time (PT) with a normal platelet count and aPTT is only mildly prolonged. Which deficiency is most likely?
opts: Vitamin K (affecting factors II, VII, IX, X)
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Vitamin K deficiency - prolonged PT (factor VII first) in malabsorption
rule: Vitamin K is required for synthesis of factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S). Malabsorption, liver disease or broad-spectrum antibiotics (reducing gut flora) cause vitamin K deficiency, giving a prolonged PT - factor VII has the shortest half-life, so PT rises first. Treatment is vitamin K.Discriminator: Malabsorption/antibiotics + prolonged PT + normal platelets = vitamin K deficiency (factors II, VII, IX, X)B) Factor VIIIfactor VIII deficiency (haemophilia

stem: A 60-year-old has headache, pruritus after a hot shower, ruddy complexion and an elevated haemoglobin (Hct 60%) with normal oxygen saturation. Which is the most likely diagnosis and genetic marker?
opts: Chronic hypoxia; high EPO with lung disease
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Polycythaemia vera - JAK2V617F, aquagenic pruritus, high Hct with normal SpO2
rule: Polycythaemia vera is a myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by the JAK2 V617F mutation, presenting with an elevated haematocrit, aquagenic pruritus (itch after shower), thrombotic risk and splenomegaly, with normal arterial oxygen saturation (excluding secondary causes). Management includes venesection, aspirin and cytoreduction.Discriminator: Erythrocytosis + aquagenic pruritus + normal SpO2 = polycythaemia vera (JAK2 mutation)A) Secondary polycythaemia; low EPOsecondary polycythaemia follows chronic hypoxia (low SpO2) with high EPOC) Chronic hypoxia; high EPO with lung diseaselung-disease hypoxia causes secondary polycythaemia with low SpO2, not PVD) Iron deficiency; low MCViron deficiency is microcytic and does not raise the haematocrit with pruritus

stem: A 45-year-old woman receiving chemo-radiotherapy for breast cancer presents with fatigue. FBC shows Hb 10 g/dL with low serum iron but normal/high ferritin. Which is the most likely cause of her anaemia?
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Anaemia of chronic disease - low iron but normal/high ferritin (functional block)
rule: Anaemia of chronic disease (inflammation/malignancy) features low serum iron with NORMAL or HIGH ferritin (an acute-phase reactant) because hepcidin sequesters iron in stores. This contrasts with iron deficiency, where ferritin is low. A recalled exam pattern (Q182).Discriminator: Chronic illness + low serum iron + normal/high ferritin = anaemia of chronic disease (hepcidin blocks iron release)A) Iron deficiency anaemiairon deficiency has LOW ferritin, unlike the normal/high ferritin hereC) Vitamin B12 deficiencyB12 deficiency is macrocytic with neurological signs, not this profileD) Haemolytic anaemiahaemolytic anaemia shows reticulocytosis and raised LDH/bilirubin

stem: A 12-year-old with sickle cell disease has severe pain in the hands and back, fever 38 C and no localizing chest/abdominal signs. What is the most appropriate initial management of a vaso-occlusive crisis?
opts: Analgesia (paracetamol/NSAIDs/opioids), hydration, oxygen if hypoxic, and detect/prevent complications
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Sickle cell vaso-occlusive crisis - analgesia, hydration, oxygen
rule: Vaso-occlusive (painful) crises are managed with prompt analgesia, adequate hydration and oxygen if hypoxic, plus identifying triggers (infection, dehydration). Blood transfusion is reserved for complications such as acute chest syndrome or stroke, not every crisis. Hydroxyurea reduces crisis frequency. This is exam-relevant management.Discriminator: Painful crisis in sickle cell = analgesia, hydration, oxygen; transfusion only for specific complications (e.g. stroke, chest syndrome)B) Blood transfusion for all crisestransfusion is not needed for every crisis, only for complicationsC) Prophylactic antibiotics onlyantibiotics alone do not relieve the pain of a vaso-occlusive crisisD) Immediate splenectomysplenectomy is not the treatment for an acute painful crisis

stem: A patient on warfarin (INR 9) presents with a nosebleed. In addition to withholding the warfarin, which is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Warfarin overdose - vitamin K antidote
rule: Warfarin acts as a vitamin K antagonist, inhibiting clotting factors II, VII, IX and X. Its antidote is vitamin K (with prothrombin complex concentrate if life-threatening bleeding). Protamine sulphate reverses heparin; desmopressin is used in von Willebrand disease/platelet dysfunction. A recalled exam pattern (Q5).Discriminator: Warfarin (vitamin K antagonist) reversal = vitamin K; protamine reverses heparinB) Protamine sulphateprotamine sulphate reverses heparin (unfractionated), not warfarinC) Desmopressindesmopressin (DDAVP) is used in VWD/platelet function disorders, not to reverse warfarinD) Platelet transfusionplatelet transfusion does not correct vitamin K-dependent factor deficiency

stem: A 60-year-old vegetarian has progressive fatigue, glossitis and peripheral paraesthesia with an unsteady gait. FBC shows macrocytosis (MCV 115 fL) and hypersegmented neutrophils. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: B12 deficiency - macrocytic + glossitis + neuropathy (subacute combined degeneration)
rule: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes a megaloblastic macrocytic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils, glossitis, and neurological features (peripheral neuropathy, subacute combined degeneration of the cord from impaired myelin). Vegans and pernicious anaemia are common causes. Unlike folate deficiency, B12 deficiency has neurological involvement.Discriminator: Macrocytosis + glossitis + peripheral neuropathy/gait = B12 deficiency (also causes neurological signs)A) Iron deficiency anaemiairon deficiency is microcytic without neuropathy or hypersegmentationC) Thalassaemia minorthalassaemia minor is microcytic and mildD) Anaemia of chronic diseaseACD is normocytic with low iron but high/normal ferritin and no neuropathy

stem: A young adult has pancytopenia (anaemia, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia) with a hypocellular bone marrow on trephine biopsy and no evidence of infiltration or fibrosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Aplastic anaemia - pancytopenia + hypocellular marrow
rule: Aplastic anaemia is a stem-cell disorder causing bicytopenia/pancytopenia with a hypocellular (empty) marrow that lacks blast infiltration or fibrosis. Causes include drugs, toxins, viral (parvovirus/EBV), and idiopathic. Management is supportive care, immunosuppression (anti-thymocyte globulin) or stem-cell transplant.Discriminator: Pancytopenia with a HYPOCELLULAR marrow (no blasts/fibrosis) = aplastic anaemiaB) Acute myeloid leukaemiaAML shows blasts and a hypercellular marrow, not an empty hypocellular marrowC) Multiple myelomamyeloma shows plasma cells and an M-protein, not pancytopenia with an empty marrowD) Iron deficiency anaemiairon deficiency is not pancytopenic and has an iron-deficient (not hypocellular) picture

stem: A 61-year-old woman has low-grade fever, anaemia, abdominal pain, gum hyperplasia, and circulating blasts with Auer rods; myeloperoxidase (MPO) is positive and WBC is 42,000. Most probable diagnosis?
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Acute myeloid leukaemia - Auer rods + MPO positive + gum infiltration
rule: Acute myeloid leukaemia presents with circulating blasts containing Auer rods, positive myeloperoxidase (MPO), and organ infiltration (gum hyperplasia points to the monocytic subtype M4/M5). This distinguishes it from ALL (MPO negative, PAS positive, children) and CML (BCR-ABL, chronic phase). A recalled exam pattern (Q135).Discriminator: Blasts + Auer rods + MPO positive = AML; gum hyperplasia is classic for monocytic AMLA) Chronic lymphocytic leukaemiaCLL is a mature lymphocytic leukaemia of older adults without blasts/Auer rodsB) Acute lymphoblastic leukaemiaALL is MPO negative, PAS positive, common in childrenC) Chronic myeloid leukaemiaCML has a chronic phase with basophilia and the BCR-ABL fusion, not gum-infiltrating blasts with Auer rods

stem: A boy has recurrent bleeding into his knees/elbows and easy bruising since early childhood, and his maternal uncle has a similar bleeding disorder. Which factor deficiency is most likely and how is it inherited?
opts: von Willebrand factor deficiency; autosomal recessive
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Haemophilia A - factor VIII deficiency, X-linked recessive, joint bleeds
rule: Haemophilia A is an X-linked recessive deficiency of factor VIII causing recurrent haemarthroses and deep soft-tissue bleeding, classically in males with maternal transmission. Treatment is factor VIII replacement (and tranexamic acid). Factor IX deficiency is haemophilia B; the maternal-uncle pattern points to X-linked inheritance.Discriminator: Recurrent haemarthroses + maternal lineage = haemophilia A (factor VIII, X-linked recessive)B) Factor IX deficiency; autosomal dominantfactor IX deficiency is haemophilia B; it is still X-linked, not autosomal dominantC) von Willebrand factor deficiency; autosomal recessiveVWD is autosomal, affects mucocutaneous bleeding (not deep joints), and is not X-linkedD) Vitamin K-dependent factors; autosomal recessivevitamin K-dependent factor deficiency differs and is not X-linked recessive joint bleeding

stem: A 55-year-old has fatigue, weight loss, massive splenomegaly and a very high WBC with a left shift, basophilia and thrombocytosis. Peripheral blood cytogenetics show the Philadelphia chromosome. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Chronic myeloid leukaemia - Philadelphia chromosome (t9;22 BCR-ABL), massive splenomegaly
rule: Chronic myeloid leukaemia is a myeloproliferative neoplasm with reciprocal translocation t(9;22) producing the Philadelphia chromosome (BCR-ABL fusion). It presents with a very high leucocyte count with left shift and basophilia, splenomegaly, and often thrombocytosis. First-line targeted therapy is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (imatinib). A plan anchor (CML BCR-ABL).Discriminator: High WBC + left shift + basophilia + splenomegaly + Philadelphia chromosome = CML (BCR-ABL)A) Acute myeloid leukaemiaAML has circulating blasts with Auer rods and marrow failure, not a chronic left shift with splenomegalyC) Chronic lymphocytic leukaemiaCLL shows a mature lymphocytosis with smudge cells in older adults, not basophilia/Ph chromosomeD) Myelofibrosismyelofibrosis has teardrop cells and a dry tap with an enlarged spleen but is Ph negative

stem: A 26-year-old with transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia major develops leg oedema and exertional dyspnoea despite regular transfusions. Which is the most likely culpable process?
opts: Dilated cardiomyopathy from transfusional iron overload
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Thalassaemia major - iron overload cardiomyopathy from repeated transfusions
rule: Repeated transfusions in thalassaemia major cause transfusional iron overload (haemosiderosis). Myocardial iron deposition produces a dilated cardiomyopathy with heart failure (oedema, exertional dyspnoea). This is a recalled exam pattern (Q67). Chelation therapy (deferasirox/desferrioxamine) is used to prevent it.Discriminator: Transfused thalassaemia major + oedema/dyspnoea = iron-overload dilated cardiomyopathy (ferritin/LIC)A) Chronic renal failurechronic renal failure is not the typical cause of the heart failure hereC) Liver cirrhosis alonecirrhosis does not cause exertional dyspnoea and oedema primarily as a cardiac complicationD) Pulmonary embolismpulmonary embolism is not the expected process with transfusion history

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with painless bright red bleeding per rectum and a lump that prolapses on defecation but reduces spontaneously. What is the diagnosis?
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Haemorrhoids — grading of internal haemorrhoids
rule: Internal haemorrhoids are above the dentate line (painless). Grading: first degree bleed but don't prolapse; second degree prolapse on defecation but reduce spontaneously; third degree require manual reduction; fourth degree are irreducible. External haemorrhoids are below the dentate line and painful when thrombosed.Discriminator: Painless bleeding + prolapse that reduces spontaneously = second-degree internal haemorrhoidsA) External haemorrhoidsExternal haemorrhoids are below the dentate line and painful, especially when thrombosed.C) Third-degree internal haemorrhoidsThird-degree internal haemorrhoids require manual reduction — this one reduces spontaneously.D) Anal fissureAnal fissure causes tearing pain during defecation, not painless bleeding.

stem: A 55-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis presents with haematemesis. Upper GI endoscopy reveals tortuous dilated veins in the distal oesophagus. What is the first-line therapeutic intervention?
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Oesophageal varices — first-line treatment of acute haemorrhage
rule: Endoscopic band ligation is first-line for acute oesophageal variceal haemorrhage — it is superior to sclerotherapy (fewer perforation and stricture complications). Octreotide is an adjunct that lowers portal pressure; TIPS is a rescue after failed endoscopic therapy.Discriminator: Cirrhosis + haematemesis + distal oesophageal varices → endoscopic band ligation is first-lineA) SclerotherapySclerotherapy is now second-line — banding has better outcomes and fewer complications.C) Octreotide infusion aloneOctreotide reduces portal pressure as a pharmacologic adjunct but is not the primary intervention.D) Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS)TIPS is reserved for refractory or recurrent bleeding after endoscopic therapy fails.

stem: A 30-year-old woman reports severe tearing pain during defecation with a few drops of bright red blood on the toilet paper. She is otherwise well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Internal-Medicine-I
concept: Anal fissure — tearing pain + fresh blood on wiping
rule: Anal fissure causes a sharp, tearing pain during defecation with fresh blood on the paper. Haemorrhoids bleed painlessly; a fistula causes discharge; carcinoma causes occult bleeding.
