CT/PET/MRI brain are not the standard localising studies for primary HPT.Discriminator: Pre-parathyroidectomy localisation = sestamibi scan ± neck ultrasound to find the adenomaB) CT chestCT chest is not used to localise parathyroid adenomas in primary HPT.C) PET scanPET is not the standard localising modality for parathyroid disease.D) MRI brainMRI brain is irrelevant to parathyroid localisation.
Immediate transfer to the operating theatre for laparotomy

Thyroglossal duct cyst — Sistrunk procedure (cyst + tract + hyoid)Concept: Thyroglossal duct cyst — midline, moves on tongue protrusion; Sistrunk resection | Cognitive: Analysis/synthesisWhy C: A thyroglossal duct cyst is a remnant of the thyroglossal tract, presenting as a midline (or paramedian) neck mass that classically rises on tongue protrusion and swallowing. Definitive treatment is the Sistrunk procedure — excision of the cyst, the tract, and the midportion of the hyoid bone — to prevent recurrence. A branchial cleft cyst is lateral and does NOT move on protrusion.Discriminator: Midline neck cyst moving on tongue protrusion = thyroglossal duct cyst → Sistrunk (tract + hyoid)A) Branchial cleft cyst — simple excisionBranchial cleft cysts are lateral and do not move on tongue protrusion.B) Thyroid nodule — hemithyroidectomyA thyroid nodule is in the thyroid gland, not a midline suprahyoid cyst.D) Lymphadenopathy — antibioticsLymphadenopathy is discrete, firm nodes, not a cystic midline mass.

External branch of the superior laryngeal nerveConcept: External laryngeal nerve injury — loss of pitch/high notes (not hoarseness); RLN = hoarseness | Cognitive: InterpretationWhy D: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve innervates the cricothyroid muscle (adjusts vocal pitch/tension). Injury causes difficulty with high-pitch phonation and a 'tired voice' in singers, WITHOUT the hoarseness/breathiness of recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) injury, which affects all intrinsic laryngeal muscles. Recognising the distinction matters for vocal professionals and surgical technique (the nerve runs close to the superior thyroid artery).Discriminator: Loss of pitch/high-note control (not hoarseness) = external laryngeal nerve (SLN external) injuryA) Recurrent laryngeal nerveRLN injury causes hoarseness/breathiness and a paramedian cord, not just pitch loss.B) Vagus nerveVagus injury would cause more widespread deficits including RLN palsy.C) Hypoglossal nerveHypoglossal injury causes tongue deviation, not vocal pitch change.
subject: Applied-Anatomy-&-Surgery
concept: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm — a clinical diagnosis; in a shocked patient with a pulsatile mass, transfer to the operating theatre precedes any imaging.
rule: The triad of sudden abdominal/back pain, shock, and a pulsatile abdominal mass makes ruptured AAA a clinical diagnosis. In an unstable patient every minute of imaging — CT or ultrasound — consumes survival time. Immediate transfer to theatre for emergency open or endovascular repair is the correct action; imaging adds nothing that changes the decision and delays definitive haemorrhage control.Discriminator: Shock + sudden abdominal/back pain + pulsatile mass = ruptured AAA until proven otherwise; no scan is needed to act in the unstable patient — the operating theatre is the next step.A) Urgent CT angiography of the aorta to confirm the diagnosisCT angiography in a shocked ruptured AAA patient costs the definitive intervention its only resource — time; in this scenario the diagnosis is already made clinically, so CT is a dangerous detour.C) Abdominal ultrasound scan in the emergency departmentBedside ultrasound can confirm an aneurysm but will not change management in the unstable patient, and time spent scanning delays haemorrhage control.D) Intravenous fluids and repeat examination in 30 minutesObservation and fluid resuscitation alone delay the only life-saving step — surgical haemorrhage control; this patient is in decompensating rupture, not a volume-responsive state.

stem: A 70-year-old with a large non-toxic multinodular goitre has progressive dysphagia and tracheal deviation but is euthyroid. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Total or subtotal thyroidectomy for compressive symptoms

Temporary hypocalcaemia from parathyroid stunning/ischaemia vs permanent from parathyroid excisionConcept: Post-thyroidectomy hypocalcaemia — transient (ischaemia/stunning) vs permanent (excised) | Cognitive: InterpretationWhy C: Post-thyroidectomy hypocalcaemia may be transient (within 24-48h) due to parathyroid ischaemia, bruising, or 'stunning' — recovering with temporary calcium — or permanent if the glands were inadvertently excised or infarcted (lifelong replacement needed). The timing and durability distinguish them; both present with Chvostek/Trousseau and low calcium. Vigilance for the immediate, potentially severe, drop is essential.Discriminator: Early transient hypoCa (recovers) = parathyroid ischaemia/stunning; permanent = gland excised/infarctedA) Different surgeonsSurgeon identity does not explain the transient-vs-permanent biology.B) One had Graves, one had cancerPathology (Graves vs cancer) does not determine transient vs permanent hypocalcaemia.D) Vitamin D deficiency onlyVitamin D deficiency may contribute but does not explain the post-op temporal pattern.

CSF leak from an unsealed sella/sphenoid sinusConcept: Transsphenoidal pituitary surgery — CSF leak (rhinorrhoea) is a key complication | Cognitive: Analysis/synthesisWhy D: Transsphenoidal pituitary surgery traverses the sphenoid sinus and sella, risking a CSF leak (clear, watery rhinorrhoea, often postural/worse on bending), which can lead to meningitis if untreated. Management is head-up rest, sometimes a lumbar drain, and surgical repair of the defect if persistent. It is a hallmark complication distinct from routine post-op oedema.Discriminator: Clear rhinorrhoea after transsphenoidal surgery = CSF leak → bed rest/positioning, may need repairA) Normal post-operative oedemaClear rhinorrhoea is not normal oedema; it indicates a leak.B) Meningitis without leakMeningitis can be a CONSEQUENCE of an unrecognised leak, not the primary event here.C) Recurrent tumour bleedingTumour bleeding would cause worsening mass effect/haemorrhage, not clear rhinorrhoea.
subject: Applied-Anatomy-&-Surgery
concept: Non-toxic MNG — surgery for compressive symptoms (dysphagia/tracheal deviation)
rule: A non-toxic (euthyroid) multinodular goitre that causes compressive symptoms (dysphagia, tracheal deviation/compression, cosmetic concerns) is an indication for subtotal or total thyroidectomy. Radioiodine is more suited to toxic (hyperthyroid) MNG or when surgery is contraindicated. Long-term levothyroxine 'suppression' is ineffective for established multinodular goitres and risks iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis/arrhythmia. Observation is inappropriate with compressive symptoms.Discriminator: Non-toxic MNG with compressive symptoms (dysphagia/tracheal deviation) → thyroidectomyB) Radioiodine ablationRadioiodine is preferred for TOXIC MNG; compressive non-toxic goitre needs surgery.C) Observation onlyObservation is wrong with compressive symptoms.D) Levothyroxine suppression long-termLong-term suppressive thyroxine is ineffective and risky in MNG.

stem: A 7-year-old girl has had a dry, persistent cough for 10 days with low-grade fever but minimal chest findings. Chest X-ray shows bilateral patchy interstitial infiltrates, and cold agglutinins are positive. What is the most appropriate treatment?
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Atypical pneumonia — Mycoplasma pneumoniae in school-age children
rule: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the classic cause of atypical (walking) pneumonia in school-age children, presenting with a prolonged dry cough and interstitial infiltrates; it lacks a cell wall, so treatment is a macrolide such as azithromycin.Discriminator: School-age child + protracted dry cough + patchy interstitial infiltrates + cold agglutinins = Mycoplasma → macrolide (azithromycin) because Mycoplasma lacks a cell wallA) Oral amoxicillinAmoxicillin is a β-lactam that acts on the cell wall; Mycoplasma has no cell wall, so it is ineffective.C) Intravenous ceftriaxoneCeftriaxone also targets cell-wall synthesis and does not cover Mycoplasma pneumoniae.D) Oral oseltamivirOseltamivir is an antiviral for influenza; this clinical picture is bacterial atypical pneumonia, not flu.

stem: A 4-year-old girl from a low-resource setting is assessed for undernutrition. Her height-for-age is below −3 standard deviations, while her weight-for-height is within normal limits and there is no oedema. Which term best classifies this pattern of malnutrition?
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Growth charts and malnutrition classification — stunting vs wasting
rule: Stunting is chronic malnutrition reflected in a low height-for-age, while wasting is acute malnutrition reflected in a low weight-for-height; this child's pattern — short but not wasted — defines stunting.Discriminator: Low height-for-age with normal weight-for-height = stunting (chronic); low weight-for-height = wasting (acute); low weight-for-age = underweightB) Wasting (acute malnutrition)Wasting (low weight-for-height) reflects acute malnutrition and is not present here, as weight-for-height is normal.C) UnderweightUnderweight (low weight-for-age) blends both indices; this child's normal weight-for-height means weight-for-age would not be the best classification.D) Normal nutritional statusHeight-for-age below −3 SD is clearly abnormal; this is not normal nutritional status.

stem: An 18-month-old boy has fever of 40.1°C, lethargy, and neck stiffness. A petechial rash is spreading rapidly over his trunk, blood pressure is 82/50 mm Hg, and capillary refill is 4 seconds. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
opts: Lumbar puncture before antibiotics to confirm the diagnosis
Blood culture and immediate intravenous ceftriaxone
Oral amoxicillin and review in the clinic tomorrow
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Meningitis — meningococcemia recognition and antibiotic timing
rule: A febrile child with a rapidly spreading purpuric rash, meningism, and shock has meningococcemia; blood cultures should be drawn and IV ceftriaxone given immediately — lumbar puncture must not delay antibiotics when the child is unstable.Discriminator: Fever + petechial/purpuric rash + meningism + shock = meningococcemia → blood culture and IV ceftriaxone IMMEDIATELY; never delay antibiotics for LP in an unstable childA) Lumbar puncture before antibiotics to confirm the diagnosisPerforming LP before antibiotics in an unstable child risks herniation and delays life-saving therapy; treat first, LP once stabilised.C) CT head before starting antibioticsCT before antibiotics causes unacceptable delay; imaging is only considered for focal signs or raised ICP after stabilisation.D) Oral amoxicillin and review in the clinic tomorrowMeningococcemia with shock is a paediatric emergency requiring IV antibiotics and resuscitation, not outpatient care.

stem: A 24-month-old boy has a vocabulary of eight single words and does not combine two words. He passed newborn hearing screening. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Reassure the parents and review again at 3 years of age
Request an urgent MRI of the brain
Refer for audiological assessment and early intervention
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Language development — red flags at 2 years
rule: A 24-month-old should use roughly 50 words and begin combining two words; fewer than 25-50 words or absence of phrases is a language-delay red flag warranting audiological and developmental referral — early intervention, not watchful waiting, is the standard.Discriminator: By 2 years expect ~50 words and 2-word phrases; fewer than 25-50 words or no phrases = refer for audiology + early intervention, even with a normal newborn screenA) Reassure the parents and review again at 3 years of ageWatchful waiting to 3 years forfeits the early-intervention window.B) Request an urgent MRI of the brainImaging has no role in primary language delay without neurological signs.D) Start levothyroxine empiricallyHypothyroidism has other features (growth failure, constipation, coarse features); it is not treated empirically.

stem: A healthy 6-month-old boy is brought for routine vaccination. Which of the following developmental findings is NORMAL for this age?
opts: Uses a neat pincer grasp to pick up a raisin
Rolls from back to front in both directions
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Normal development — gross and fine motor milestones at 6 months
rule: Rolling in both directions is achieved by about 6 months; independent sitting (~8 months), a neat pincer grasp (~9-10 months) and specific 'mama/dada' (~12 months) are all later milestones, so only rolling is age-appropriate.Discriminator: 6 months: rolls both ways, sits with support, babbles; sitting unsupported ~8 mo, pincer grasp ~9-10 mo, specific words ~12 moA) Uses a neat pincer grasp to pick up a raisinA neat pincer grasp is a 9-10 month skill; a 6-month-old uses a whole-hand (palmar) grasp.C) Sits steadily without supportSitting steadily without support is an ~8-month milestone.D) Says 'mama' and 'dada' specificallySpecific use of 'mama'/'dada' comes around 12 months; at 6 months there is babbling.

stem: A 6-month-old has clusters of brief symmetric flexor spasms that started last week, with developmental regression and an EEG showing hypsarrhythmia. Which is the best initial drug class for this epilepsy syndrome?
opts: Vigabatrin or corticosteroid (ACTH) as first-line treatment
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Infantile spasms (West syndrome) treatment
rule: Infantile spasms respond to vigabatrin or adrenocorticotropic hormone/steroids (with hormonal therapy often favoured); carbamazepine and phenytoin are ineffective and can worsen the pattern; early treatment improves developmental outcome.Discriminator: Cluster flexor spasms + regression + hypsarrhythmia = infantile spasms; vigabatrin (esp. tuberous sclerosis) or ACTH/steroids is first-line, not traditional AEDsB) CarbamazepineCarbamazepine is ineffective in infantile spasms.C) PhenytoinPhenytoin similarly has no role in this epileptic encephalopathy.D) Valproate aloneValproate monotherapy is not the standard first-line for infantile spasms and carries caution in young infants.

stem: A 6-hour-old neonate born at term after prolonged rupture of membranes (24 hours) and maternal fever develops grunting, poor perfusion and oxygen requirement. Which empirical antibiotic pair is the standard first-line for early-onset neonatal sepsis?
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Empiric early-onset neonatal sepsis therapy
rule: Early neonatal sepsis (first 72 h, typically group B Streptococcus and enteric gram-negatives) is empirically treated with ampicillin plus an aminoglycoside (gentamicin); this combination covers GBS, Listeria, and E. coli with synergistic activity.Discriminator: Early-onset sepsis (GBS + E. coli) → ampicillin + gentamicin for synergy/coverage; cephalosporins alone risk resistance and do not cover Listeria ideallyB) Ceftriaxone aloneCeftriaxone monotherapy risks resistance, poor Listeria/enterococcal activity and calcium-precipitation concerns in neonates.C) Metronidazole aloneMetronidazole treats anaerobes, not the dominant early-onset pathogens.D) AzithromycinAzithromycin has no place in empiric early-onset sepsis.

stem: A newborn screening blood spot from a baby born at term shows a high TSH and low T4 at day 3 of life. The infant is asymptomatic and feeding well. What is the correct action?
opts: Start levothyroxine immediately and confirm with venous sample; recall urgently
Treat only if the baby develops symptoms
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Congenital hypothyroidism screening response
rule: Screening-identified congenital hypothyroidism mandates immediate confirmatory venous TSH/free-T4 and levothyroxine initiation (10-15 µg/kg/day); delayed treatment beyond the first weeks causes irreversible intellectual impairment, so asymptomatic presentation does not permit watchful waiting.Discriminator: High TSH + low T4 newborn screen = congenital hypothyroidism until proven otherwise; levothyroxine start is time-critical to protect neurodevelopment, never wait for symptomsB) Repeat the screen at 6 weeksDelaying diagnosis and treatment for weeks risks permanent neurodevelopmental damage.C) Treat only if the baby develops symptomsSymptoms are often subtle/absent in the newborn period; the biochemistry, not symptomatic status, drives therapy.D) Start iodine drops onlyIodine drops are not the therapy for thyroid dysgenesis — the commonest cause.

stem: A 10-year-old monitored at school has hypertension found by the school nurse; his arm blood pressure is 140/90, leg blood pressure 105/70, and femoral pulses feel weak and delayed. What is the most likely diagnosis and confirmatory test?
opts: Coarctation of aorta — confirm with echocardiography/CT angiography
Essential hypertension — confirm with ambulatory monitoring
Renal artery stenosis — confirm with renin sampling
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Coarctation recognition in the older child
rule: Four-limb BP discrepancy with weak delayed femoral pulses is the classic coarctation signature in older children (who escape newborn detection); echocardiography shows the narrowed segment and gradient, with CT/MRI angiography for anatomy.Discriminator: Upper-limb hypertension with lower-limb hypotension and delayed femoral pulses in a child = coarctation; imaging confirmsB) Essential hypertension — confirm with ambulatory monitoringEssential hypertension in children is a diagnosis of exclusion and does not produce a leg-arm gradient.C) Renal artery stenosis — confirm with renin samplingRenal artery stenosis does not explain the leg-weak-pulse asymmetry.D) Phaeochromocytoma — confirm with metanephrinesPhaeochromocytoma causes paroxysmal spells of hypertension, not a limb-pressure gradient.

stem: A 3-year-old with a close adult contact recently diagnosed with sputum-positive pulmonary tuberculosis has a positive interferon-gamma release assay; chest X-ray shows right hilar lymphadenopathy with no parenchymal lesion; he is asymptomatic. What is the correct management?
opts: Treat as latent TB infection — isoniazid (or rifampicin-based regimen) after excluding active disease
No treatment since he is asymptomatic
Start four-drug anti-TB therapy for active pulmonary disease
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Childhood TB: latent infection treatment
rule: An asymptomatic child with a positive IGRA and chest X-ray showing hilar lymphadenopathy without parenchymal disease fits latent TB infection (or primary complex); treatment with INH (6-9 months) or a short rifampicin course prevents progression to active disease, especially in the under-5s.Discriminator: Positive IGRA + contact + chest X-ray with only nodal changes, asymptomatic = LTBI (or primary complex) — treat to prevent progression, often INH 6-9 months or 3-4 months rifampicinB) No treatment since he is asymptomaticChildren under 5 with TB exposure and positive IGRA progress to disseminated/miliary TB and must be treated even if asymptomatic.C) Start four-drug anti-TB therapy for active pulmonary diseaseFour-drug therapy is for active tuberculosis, which this X-ray/clinical picture does not establish (no parenchymal lesion, no symptoms).D) BCG vaccine nowBCG is preventive vaccination for uninfected infants, not treatment of established infection.

stem: A 14-year-old boy took a large paracetamol overdose 4 hours ago. He has mild nausea but no pain; the 4-hour paracetamol level is in the probable-toxicity range on the treatment nomogram. What is the correct treatment?
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Paracetamol toxicity — NAC timing
rule: Paracetamol level plotted on the treatment nomogram above the line indicates risk of hepatotoxicity; IV N-acetylcysteine should begin immediately (within 8 h ideally) — waiting for transaminase rise forfeits the protective window.Discriminator: Level above the nomogram line at 4 h (or 150 µg/mL at 4 h) → NAC immediately; never wait for LFT derangement — earliest NAC is most hepatoprotectiveB) Wait for liver enzymes tomorrowLiver enzymes rise only after hepatocyte injury is underway; NAC is time-critical.C) Activated charcoal aloneCharcoal is only helpful within 1 h and alone is inadequate.D) Intravenous fluids onlyIV fluids do not prevent paracetamol hepatotoxicity.

stem: A 5-month-old with a large perimembranous ventricular septal defect has poor weight gain, tachypnoea and recurrent chest infections; echo shows a big left-to-right shunt. What is the correct approach?
opts: Surgical closure (or device closure where suitable) for symptomatic large defect despite medical therapy
subject: Paediatrics
concept: VSD management in infancy
rule: Large symptomatic VSDs causing failure to thrive and recurrent chest infections despite optimal medical therapy (diuretics, nutrition, +/- ACE-inhibitor/antireflux) warrant closure in infancy; small defects are observed for spontaneous closure.Discriminator: Large VSD + failure to thrive + recurrent infections = surgery now (medical failure); small defects may close spontaneouslyB) Wait until school age unconditionallyWaiting until school age with failure to thrive and infections is harmful when closure is feasible in infancy.C) Give antibiotics onlyAntibiotics do not address the haemodynamic burden.D) Restrict fluids permanentlyFluid restriction does not treat the shunt and risks poor growth further.

stem: A 2-year-old with a mild croup-like cough for 2 days is brought distressed with stridor at rest, marked chest retractions, and SpO2 91% on room air after failed nebulised epinephrine and dexamethasone. What is the escalating step?
opts: Repeat nebulised epinephrine, add heliox, consider intubation in ICU when obstruction is severe
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Severe croup escalation
rule: Severe croup failing first-line epinephrine and dexamethasone warrants repeated nebulised epinephrine, observed care in ICU, heliox improves laminar airflow, and elective intubation (smaller tube) when exhaustion/hypoxia threatens; it is viral (usually para-influenza).Discriminator: Stridor at rest + desaturation after epinephrine/steroid = severe croup: repeat epinephrine, heliox, ICU, possible intubation; antibiotics do not treat viral croupB) Oral antibioticsAntibiotics are ineffective in viral laryngotracheobronchitis.C) Chest physiotherapyPhysiotherapy does not relieve subglottic oedema.D) Discharge with reassurance and paracetamolDesaturation with rest stridor is never a home-care disposition.

stem: A 10-month-old, exclusively breastfed, presents with irritability, poor growth, frontal bossing, widening wrists and bowed legs; calcium 2.0 mmol/L, phosphate low, alkaline phosphatase markedly raised. X-ray shows cupping and fraying of metaphyses. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
opts: Vitamin D deficiency rickets — vitamin D with calcium supplementation
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Nutritional rickets diagnosis and treatment
rule: Nutritional (vitamin D deficiency) rickets in an exclusively breastfed infant with limited sunlight presents with skeletal deformities, hypocalcaemia/hypophosphataemia, high ALP and cupped-frayed metaphyses; treatment is vitamin D (stoss or daily) with adequate calcium, plus sunlight and dietary education.Discriminator: Bowed legs + frontal bossing + wrist widening + rachitic rosary + low calcium/phosphate + high ALP + metaphyseal cupping = vitamin D-deficient ricketsB) Hypophosphatasia — enzyme replacementHypophosphatasia has LOW alkaline phosphatase — opposite of this picture.C) Osteogenesis imperfecta — bisphosphonatesOsteogenesis imperfecta causes recurrent fractures with blue sclerae, not metaphyseal cupping with high ALP.D) Scurvy — vitamin CScurvy causes bleeding gums/perifollicular haemorrhage and pseudoparalysis, without the wrist-cupping/ALP pattern.

stem: A 14-month-old previously thriving boy has dropped from the 50th to the 10th centile for weight over 4 months despite good appetite. Examination shows no organomegaly, and there are no chronic symptoms. What is the single most important next evaluation step?
opts: Detailed dietary history, social history and plotted growth review before labelling
Reassure that centile drift is normal at this age
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Growth faltering evaluation
rule: Weight crossing two centile lines (e.g., 50th → 10th) defines growth faltering; evaluation begins with a detailed history of feeding, dietary intake, developmental and social factors (neglect, feeding behaviour, maternal health) and plotted serial growth, before investigations.Discriminator: Crossing ≥2 major centile lines in weight = growth faltering; first step in the paediatric approach is shared history (feeding, family, social), not immediate admission or testsB) Start appetite stimulantsAppetite stimulants treat nothing and are not paediatric practice here.C) Admit for total parenteral nutritionAdmission and TPN are for severe failure with acute decompensation, not first-line for a well-appearing child.D) Reassure that centile drift is normal at this ageCrossing two major centile lines is not explained by normal variation at this age.

stem: A 4-year-old with dengue shock syndrome has poor perfusion, weak pulses, and a narrow pulse pressure after 40 mL/kg of crystalloids. What is the correct escalation?
opts: Give a bolus of colloid or additional crystalloid, reassess haematocrit and clinical status repeatedly; do not transfuse based on haemoconcentration alone
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Dengue shock management — refractory shock
rule: Dengue shock is hypovolaemic from plasma leakage; after the first 40 mL/kg, persistent shock warrants further fluid (crystalloid or colloid), guided by serial haematocrit and clinical response — blood products are reserved for bleeding/falling Hb, not for haemoconcentration, and diuretics worsen the hypovolaemic state.Discriminator: Compensated shock in dengue → crystalloid 10-20 mL/kg; refractory → second crystalloid/colloid bolus with repeated Hct-guided reassessment; transfusion only if bleeding/haemoglobin fallsB) Immediate blood transfusionTransfusion in haemoconcentrated shock risks worsening viscosity; only for overt bleeding or falling Hb.C) Inotrope infusion onlyInotropes are adjunct in refractory hypotensive shock after volume, not a substitute for volume.D) Furosemide to offloadDiuretics are contraindicated in the leak phase of dengue shock.

stem: A 2-year-old girl has 2 days of watery diarrhoea. She is lethargic, with sunken eyes, dry mucosa, slow skin pinch, and a palpable radial pulse. She has not passed urine for 8 hours. How much deficit does she have and what is the first step?
opts: 10% dehydration — IV bolus 20 mL/kg crystalloid then reassess
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Dehydration classification and shock management
rule: Two or more of lethargy, sunken eyes, dry mucosa, slow skin pinch, and no urine define severe dehydration (≥10%), which in the presence of a weak radial pulse/shock warrants IV fluid bolus (20 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid) with reassessment — ORS is unsafe in shock.Discriminator: Lethargy + sunken eyes + dry mucosa + slow skin pinch + no urine 8h = severe (≥10%) dehydration; the child with signs of shock gets an IV bolus, not ORSB) 5% dehydration — start ORS at homeSome dehydration (5%) has fewer signs and a normal urine output; this child is in shock territory.C) 15% dehydration — urgent blood transfusionBlood transfusion is not first-line for hypovolaemic dehydration unless there is severe anaemia/haemorrhage.D) 2% dehydration — reassure motherThe lethargy, sunken eyes, slow pinch and oliguria objectively grade far beyond 2%.

stem: A 15-year-old girl with severe calorie restriction and excessive exercise has body mass index 15, heart rate 42, and cold peripheries. Her mother worries about 'just being diet-conscious'. Which finding is the strongest argument that this is a medical emergency requiring admission?
opts: Marked bradycardia with risk of arrhythmia
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Anorexia nervosa — medical instability criteria
rule: In anorexia nervosa, bradycardia below 45-50 bpm, orthostatic instability, electrolyte disturbance, hypoglycaemia or very low BMI indicate medical instability and risk of arrhythmia/refeeding syndrome; admission with monitored refeeding is required.Discriminator: Severe malnutrition + bradycardia (<45) = medical instability (refeeding/arrhythmia risk) → admission; the diagnosis is eating disorder, not dietingB) Desire to lose weightWeight concern is a diagnostic feature, not a severity criterion.C) School performance declineSchool decline reflects psychosocial impact but is not the acute admission driver.D) Preference for saladsFood choice alone does not define medical instability.

stem: A 12-hour-old term infant has recurrent focal clonic seizures. Bedside glucose is 1.8 mmol/L which corrects with a dextrose bolus infusion, yet he seizes again. Examination is otherwise unremarkable; calcium and magnesium are pending. What is the next most appropriate step after confirming normoglycaemia?
opts: Evaluate seizure aetiology systematically — check calcium/magnesium, add an anticonvulsant (phenobarbital) for ongoing seizures, and consider HIE/infection/metabolic causes
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Neonatal seizure workup and treatment
rule: Neonatal seizures are a symptom, not a diagnosis: after treating hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia and hypomagnesaemia, sepsis/meningitis (LP), hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy and metabolic/inborn errors must be considered; phenobarbital is the first-line anticonvulsant for ongoing seizures.Discriminator: Neonatal seizure not resolved by glucose correction = pursue electrolyte/metabolic/structural/infective causes; phenobarbital is first-line anticonvulsantB) Discharge homeRecurrent seizures with ongoing cause are never a discharge situation.C) Stop all feeds and waitStopping feeds without identifying the cause risks metabolic decompensation and hypoglycaemia recurrence.D) Give only oral diazepamOral diazepam is not first-line for neonatal seizures.

stem: A 3-year-old boy has 6 days of fever, bilateral non-exudative conjunctivitis, cracked lips, strawberry tongue, and a generalised polymorphous rash; no cervical lymphadenopathy. CRP and ESR are high; echocardiography shows normal coronaries today. What is the correct next step?
opts: Treat as incomplete Kawasaki disease — IVIG and aspirin within 10 days of fever
Observe only until the rash resolves
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Incomplete Kawasaki disease recognition
rule: Incomplete Kawasaki is suspected with fever ≥5 days plus fewer than 4 classic criteria when inflammatory markers are elevated; IVIG + aspirin within 10 days reduces coronary aneurysm risk and normal coronaries on day 6 do not exclude the diagnosis.Discriminator: Fever ≥5 days + 3-4 clinical features + inflammatory markers = incomplete Kawasaki; echocardiography does not rule it out early — treat to prevent coronary aneurysmsB) Observe only until the rash resolvesObservation forfeits the 10-day therapeutic window; coronary damage is the preventable outcome.C) Start corticosteroids aloneCorticosteroids are reserved for IVIG-resistant disease, not first-line.D) Discharge as viral illnessA fever unresponsive to antibiotics with mucocutaneous features and high inflammatory markers is not a benign viral illness to discharge.

stem: A 16-month-old boy has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 3 minutes with fever 39°C, on the first day of an upper respiratory infection. He is fully recovered in the emergency room, with a normal neurological examination. Which statement is correct?
opts: Simple febrile seizure — reassure, no routine neuroimaging or EEG, child likely to outgrow
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Simple febrile seizure evaluation
rule: A generalised febrile seizure under 15 minutes in a child fully recovered with normal neuro exam is simple; evaluation targets the source of fever, and routine neuroimaging, EEG and lumbar puncture (without meningeal signs) are not indicated; most children outgrow them by school age.Discriminator: Generalised seizure <15 min, single in 24 h, age 6-60 months, full recovery = simple febrile seizure; no routine LP/EEG/imaging; excellent prognosisB) Complex febrile seizure — urgent MRIComplex features (focal, >15 min, repeated in 24 h) would prompt further evaluation, but this is simple.C) Epilepsy — start long-term anticonvulsant nowA febrile seizure is not epilepsy; no long-term anticonvulsants.D) Meningitis — lumbar puncture mandatoryLumbar puncture is reserved for meningeal signs, suspected sepsis, or infants with equivocal examination.

stem: A 17-year-old girl took an overdose of iron tablets 6 hours ago. She has vomiting, abdominal pain, severe metabolic acidosis and hyperglycaemia; abdominal X-ray shows radio-opaque tablets in the gut. What is the specific treatment?
opts: Whole-bowel irrigation with plain water only
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Iron poisoning — deferoxamine
rule: Iron poisoning with systemic toxicity (acidosis, hyperglycaemia, shock) requires IV deferoxamine chelation; N-acetylcysteine is the paracetamol antidote; whole-bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol can remove tablets but never replaces chelation in established toxicity.Discriminator: Severe metabolic acidosis + shock + radio-opaque tablets + vomiting = significant iron toxicity; chelation with deferoxamine is the antidoteB) N-acetylcysteineNAC treats paracetamol overdose, not iron.C) Sodium bicarbonate aloneBicarbonate corrects acidosis but does not remove iron.D) Whole-bowel irrigation with plain water onlyWBI alone is decontamination, insufficient when chelation is indicated.

stem: A 4-year-old boy has bloody diarrhoea for 4 days, then becomes pale and oliguric; Hb 7.1, platelets 35,000, creatinine 2.4, fragmented red cells on smear. Which management is potentially harmful here?
opts: Supportive care with careful fluid balance and transfusion if symptomatic
Antibiotics and anti-motility drugs for the presumed ongoing enteritis
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome — antibiotics worsen outcome
rule: Typical HUS follows Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli (STEC); antibiotics and antimotility agents are associated with worse renal and neurological outcomes; management is supportive (fluids, electrolytes, transfusion, dialysis as needed).Discriminator: Bloody diarrhoea → anaemia + thrombocytopenia + AKI = HUS; antibiotics and antimotility agents increase toxin release and worsen diseaseA) Supportive care with careful fluid balance and transfusion if symptomaticSupportive care is the correct mainstay of HUS management.C) Monitor electrolytes dailyElectrolyte monitoring is mandatory in AKI with renal failure.D) Dialysis for anuriaDialysis is indicated for anuria/fluid overload/electrolyte crisis.

stem: A 2-year-old drank kerosene from a bottle thirty minutes ago. He is coughing but conscious and protecting his airway, with mild tachypnoea. What is the correct immediate management?
opts: Do not induce vomiting; observe/respiratory support with chest X-ray as indicated
Induce vomiting with syrup of ipecac immediately
Gastric lavage with a large-bore tube
subject: Paediatrics
concept: Hydrocarbon ingestion — aspiration prevention
rule: Hydrocarbon ingestion (kerosene) injures by aspiration; vomiting, gastric lavage and activated charcoal all increase aspiration risk and worsen chemical pneumonitis — management is supportive, avoiding emesis, with oxygen and chest X-ray when respiratory signs exist.Discriminator: Kerosene/hydrocarbons = aspiration pneumonitis risk; never induce vomiting, no lavage/charcoal; support respirationB) Induce vomiting with syrup of ipecac immediatelyInduced vomiting aspirates the hydrocarbon directly into the lungs — the classic harmful intervention.C) Gastric lavage with a large-bore tubeGastric lavage is contraindicated due to aspiration risk.D) Activated charcoalActivated charcoal does not adsorb hydrocarbons and risks aspiration.

stem: A 62-year-old man has an isolated serum alkaline phosphatase of 520 U/L (normal <120). Bilirubin, ALT, GGT, calcium, and phosphate are normal. Which investigation best localises the source of the ALP?
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Alkaline phosphatase isoenzymes — bone vs liver; role of GGT
rule: Alkaline phosphatase is produced by bone, liver, and placenta; GGT (or 5'-nucleotidase) confirms a hepatobiliary origin. A normal GGT with raised ALP points to bone, and a bone-specific ALP isoenzyme assay confirms the source — here most consistent with Paget disease of bone.Discriminator: Isolated raised ALP with NORMAL GGT = bone source (Paget disease); GGT rises only when ALP originates from the hepatobiliary systemA) Liver biopsyLiver biopsy is invasive and unnecessary when other liver tests — particularly GGT — are normal; a normal GGT argues against a hepatobiliary source.C) ERCPERCP evaluates biliary obstruction; normal GGT and bilirubin make a biliary cause very unlikely.D) 24-hour urinary calciumUrinary calcium assesses calcium handling, not the tissue origin of alkaline phosphatase.

stem: A 14-year-old boy, tall and thin with long fingers, has had two deep venous thromboses and a pulmonary embolism. Slit-lamp examination shows the lens dislocated downward and inward. Which diagnosis is most likely?
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Homocystinuria vs Marfan — direction of lens dislocation
rule: Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency causes homocystinuria: a Marfanoid habitus with ectopia lentis directed down-and-in, plus a strong thrombotic tendency from hyperhomocysteinaemia — distinguishing it from Marfan syndrome.Discriminator: Downward/inward lens dislocation + thromboembolism = homocystinuria; Marfan dislocates UPWARD and causes arterial (aortic) disease, not venous thrombosisA) Marfan syndromeMarfan syndrome dislocates the lens upward and causes aortic dissection, not recurrent venous thromboembolism; the downward dislocation and thromboses point away from Marfan.B) Ehlers-Danlos syndromeEhlers-Danlos gives skin hyperextensibility and joint laxity with bleeding, not lens dislocation and pulmonary embolism.D) Wilson diseaseWilson disease causes Kayser-Fleischer rings, tremor, and liver disease — not lens dislocation or venous thrombosis.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has Hb 9.5 g/dL, MCV 78 fL, low serum iron, normal-low transferrin, and ferritin 320 µg/L. Which mediator best explains this pattern of iron studies?
opts: Hepcidin, which degrades ferroportin and traps iron inside macrophages
Erythropoietin deficiency reducing marrow demand for iron
Reduced transferrin synthesis from hepatic inflammation
Antibodies against intrinsic factor blocking ileal B12 absorption
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Anaemia of chronic disease — hepcidin-ferroportin axis
rule: Interleukin-6 from chronic inflammation stimulates hepcidin, which binds and degrades ferroportin — the only cellular iron exporter; iron is therefore trapped in macrophages and enterocytes, giving low serum iron with high ferritin and a normal-low TIBC: anaemia of chronic disease.Discriminator: Inflammation → IL-6 → hepcidin → ferroportin internalised → iron trapped in stores → low serum iron + HIGH ferritin + normal-low TIBC = ACDB) Erythropoietin deficiency reducing marrow demand for ironEPO deficiency explains the anaemia of chronic kidney disease, but it does not produce the high-ferritin, low-transferrin pattern of ACD.C) Reduced transferrin synthesis from hepatic inflammationTransferrin is often normal-low in ACD, but the master regulator of the whole pattern — iron trapping in stores — is hepcidin blocking ferroportin.D) Antibodies against intrinsic factor blocking ileal B12 absorptionIntrinsic-factor antibodies cause pernicious anaemia — macrocytic with low B12 — not a microcytic anaemia with high ferritin.

stem: A 52-year-old man reports that his urine turns dark after standing for some hours and progressive low-back stiffness. Examination shows grey-blue pigmentation of the ear cartilage and sclera. Which enzyme is deficient?
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Alkaptonuria — homogentisate oxidase deficiency; ochronosis
rule: Alkaptonuria results from homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency; homogentisic acid accumulates, is excreted in urine (darkening on standing/alkalisation), and polymerises in cartilage and sclera to cause ochronosis and early spondylosis.Discriminator: Urine darkening on standing + ochronotic ear/sclera pigmentation + back stiffness = alkaptonuria; homogentisic acid accumulates because its oxidase is missingA) TyrosinaseTyrosinase deficiency is oculocutaneous albinism — absent pigment, not ochronosis or darkening urine.B) Phenylalanine hydroxylasePAH deficiency is phenylketonuria — musty odour and intellectual disability, not ochronosis.C) Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylaseIts deficiency is porphyria cutanea tarda — blistering photosensitive skin lesions, not darkened urine with ochronotic pigmentation.

stem: A 5-month-old infant who was born at home and missed newborn screening has fair skin, eczema, and a musty odour. Plasma phenylalanine is 510 µmol/L. Dietary treatment is planned. Which instruction is correct?
opts: Restrict all protein and give a low-protein vegan diet to protect the brain
Add supplementary leucine and isoleucine to the formula
Provide a low-phenylalanine formula supplemented with tyrosine
Treat with thyroxine and a low-iodine diet
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Phenylketonuria — dietary management
rule: In classic PKU, phenylalanine hydroxylase is deficient, so phenylalanine accumulates and tyrosine becomes conditionally essential; treatment is a phenylalanine-restricted diet with tyrosine supplementation.Discriminator: Musty odour + eczema + fair skin + phenylalanine 510 = PKU; because PAH cannot make tyrosine from phenylalanine, tyrosine becomes an essential amino acidA) Restrict all protein and give a low-protein vegan diet to protect the brainBlanket protein restriction starves the infant of all essential amino acids; only phenylalanine must be curtailed while every other amino acid is provided.B) Add supplementary leucine and isoleucine to the formulaLeucine and isoleucine are the branched-chain amino acids restricted in maple syrup urine disease, not in PKU.D) Treat with thyroxine and a low-iodine dietThyroxine treats congenital hypothyroidism, which also causes developmental delay but not a musty odour or eczema.

stem: A newborn screened at 48 hours has a low T4 but a normal to high TSH. The mother is euthyroid. Which is the most appropriate interpretation and first-line test refinement?
opts: Compensated primary hypothyroidism - confirm with repeat TSH and free T4 before starting thyroxine
Secondary to maternal Graves disease - propranolol
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Congenital hypothyroidism screening interpretation
rule: Screening shows low T4 with raised TSH, the classic pattern of primary congenital hypothyroidism. Confirmatory testing (repeat TSH/free T4) is done urgently, and thyroxine started without delay once confirmed, ideally before 2 weeks of age to protect neurodevelopment.Discriminator: Low T4 with elevated TSH = primary hypothyroidism until proven otherwise; confirm before treatment (but do not delay if confirmed)B) Transient physiologic dip - no actionA physiologic TSH surge resolves by 24-48 hours; a low T4 with high TSH at 48 h is not physiologic.C) Central hypothyroidism - pituitary MRICentral hypothyroidism gives low T4 with low or normal TSH.D) Secondary to maternal Graves disease - propranololMaternal Graves disease causes transient hyperthyroidism, not this pattern.

stem: A 6-year-old has recurrent unexplained hypoglycaemia after fasting. After a supervised fast, laboratory tests show low glucose, low insulin, low C-peptide and elevated beta-hydroxybutyrate with normal lactate. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Ketotic hypoglycaemia of childhood - fasting biochemistry pattern
rule: Ketotic hypoglycaemia of childhood is the commonest cause of fasting hypoglycaemia in young children. Appropriate ketogenesis (high beta-hydroxybutyrate), suppressed insulin/C-peptide and normal lactate distinguish it from fatty-acid oxidation defects (which are hypoketotic) and from insulin excess.Discriminator: Fasting hypoglycaemia with ketosis, low insulin/C-peptide, normal lactate = ketotic hypoglycaemia; MCAD is hypoketoticA) InsulinomaInsulinoma shows inappropriately HIGH insulin and C-peptide with suppressed ketones.C) Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiencyMCAD deficiency is hypoketotic with abnormal acylcarnitine profile.D) Glycogen storage disease type IGSD I gives lactic acidosis and hepatomegaly with hypoglycaemia.

stem: A 55-year-old man on long-term phenytoin has tingling, a positive Chvostek sign, and low ionized calcium with a low-normal PTH. Vitamin D store is normal. Which is the most likely explanation?
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Hypomagnesaemia causing hypocalcaemia - PTH resistance
rule: Phenytoin and other anticonvulsants can cause hypomagnesaemia. Hypomagnesaemia impairs PTH secretion and end-organ response, producing hypocalcaemia that fails to correct until magnesium is replaced. Vitamin D is normal, excluding simple deficiency.Discriminator: Hypocalcaemia with inadequate PTH response + long-term phenytoin = hypomagnesaemia (phenytoin depletes magnesium)A) Phenytoin-induced functional hypoparathyroidismPhenytoin acts through magnesium depletion, not direct parathyroid suppression.B) Vitamin D deficiencyVitamin D store is stated normal.D) Chronic kidney diseaseCKD would show hyperphosphataemia and raised PTH in early disease.

stem: A 30-year-old woman has a calcium of 10.8 mg/dL with normal albumin. PTH is suppressed and 25(OH)D is normal. 24-hour urinary calcium is high. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Hypercalcaemia differential - PTH-independent with high urine calcium
rule: Suppressed PTH with hypercalcaemia indicates PTH-independent cause. A high 24-hour urinary calcium (especially with low-normal calcium intake) suggests malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia (PTHrP or osteolysis). Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia is excluded by low urinary calcium and normal PTH.Discriminator: Hypercalcaemia + suppressed PTH + HIGH urine calcium = PTH-independent (malignancy is the archetype); FHH has LOW urine calciumA) Primary hyperparathyroidismPrimary hyperparathyroidism shows raised or inappropriately normal PTH, not suppressed.B) Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemiaFHH shows low urinary calcium with mild hypercalcaemia and normal PTH.D) SarcoidosisSarcoidosis gives elevated calcitriol with suppressed PTH but typically LOW urinary calcium is not the key clue.

stem: A 40-year-old butcher develops papulovesicular lesions on his hands and forearms that progress to black eschars; he hasn't any direct cattle contact but handles imported hides and wool. Organism and its virulence mechanism?
opts: Bacillus anthracis — edema toxin/ lethal factor ( protective antigen + EF/ LF)
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Cutaneous anthrax characteristics
rule: Cutaneous anthrax: painless pruritic papule progress vesicle then black eschar with surrounding oedema within 1-5 days after exposure to spores from hides/wool; toxin includes protective-antigen + edema-factor/ lethal-factor components causing tissue oedema; treat ciprofloxacin/ doxycycline.Discriminator: Occupational hide/wool exposure + painless papule vesicle progress to black eschar = cutaneous anthraxB) Clostridium tetani — tetanospasminTetanus produces the neurotoxin tetanospasmin, not a cutaneous eschar syndrome.C) Yersinia pestis — coagulase-like activityY pestis causes bubonic/ pneumonic plague with lymphadenitis; coccobacillus may show 'safety-pin' appearance; no black eschar on hide exposure typically.D) Brucella — intracellular survivalBrucellosis pathogenesis relies on intracellular survival, unrelated mechanism to toxin-driven eschar.

stem: A 6-week-old boy is brought with fever 39°C, bulging fontanelle and poor feeding. CSF: protein 180 mg/dL, glucose 20 mg/dL (blood 90), 1200 neutrophil-dominant cells. Gram stain: gram-negative coccobacilli. Most likely organism?
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Age-organism matching in bacterial meningitis
rule: Haemophilus influenzae type b, a gram-negative coccobacillus, causes meningitis predominantly between ages 2 months and 3 years; the early-infancy age with gram-negative coccobacilli matches Hib best (GBS = gram-positive cocci, neonatal; Listeria = gram-positive rods; meningococcus = gram-negative diplococci).Discriminator: Gram-negative coccobacillus in early-infancy meningitis = Hib; Group B strep is gram-positive cocci in the neonatal windowA) Neisseria meningitidisMeningococcus is a gram-negative DIPLOCOCCUS (pairs), peak in adolescents/young adults.C) Streptococcus agalactiaeGroup B strep is gram-positive spherical cocci, classically first-week-of-life sepsis/meningitis.D) Listeria monocytogenesListeria is a gram-positive rod affecting neonates, pregnant women, elderly, immunosuppressed.

stem: A 7-year-old with fever and sore throat now has a blanching sandpaper rash with pastia lines and strawberry tongue; rapid antigen test for group A streptococcus positive; and she is allergic to penicillin. Medication choice?
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Scarlet fever + penicillin-allergy alternatives
rule: Scarlet fever from Streptococcus pyogenes erythrogenic toxin is treated 10 days amoxicillin/penicillin; in macrolide-allergic (true penicillin allergy) children azithromycin is acceptable (with macrolide-resistance awareness), whereas amoxicillin is not; cephalosporin only when allergy isn't Type-I-severe.Discriminator: Sandpaper rash/strawberry tongue/Pastia lines = scarlet fever; penicillin-allergic children treated with azithromycin or cephalosporin if only mild allergyB) AmoxicillinAmoxicillin is beta-lactam contraindicated with true penicillin allergy.C) CefiximeCephalosporin viable only when allergy is not IgE-type/anaphylaxis; safer first-line in true documented penicillin allergy is macrolide.D) DoxycyclineDoxycycline avoid in <8 years (dental discoloration) unless no alternative.

stem: A 29-year-old intravenous drug user presents with fever for 7 days; echo shows vegetation of the tricuspid valve; blood cultures repeated twice positive. What is the most likely organism and first-line therapeutic base?
opts: Staphylococcus aureus — empiric IV antistaphylococcal beta-lactam (anti-MSSA/MRSA local epidemiology guidance)
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: IE organism profile in IV drug users + empirical treatment
rule: Right-sided (tricuspid) infective endocarditis in IV drug users is overwhelmingly Staphylococcus aureus (>60%); empiric treatment generally anti-staphylococcal penicillin-sensitive strategies/ vancomycin (for MRSA-suspect or penicillin-allergic), refined once susceptibilities emerge.Discriminator: IE + tricuspid/right-sided vegetation and IV drug-use context: S. aureus first; empirical antistaphylococcal therapy while cultures finaliseB) Viridans group Streptococcus onlyViridans group strep classically arises from post-dental/ oral manipulations on native left-sided valves, not the IVDU setting.C) Candida — amphotericin surgical route prerequisiteCandida endocarditis usually follows central catheter or immunocomprised clusters; not the default IVDU organism.D) Pseudomonas for all endocarditisPseudomonas IE is uncommon; typically device/ burns/ water exposure; not default for IVDU here.

stem: A 60-year-old diabetic farmer was bit on hand by a healthy-appearing dog 30 minutes ago; he has no chronic immunosuppression and previous rabies pre-exposure vaccination documented two years ago. Management?
opts: Wound washing + 2 booster doses of rabies vaccine (day 0 and day 3), no immunoglobulin
Full rabies vaccine series + immunoglobulin standard
No intervention because dog was healthy
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Rabies post-exposure in pre-vaccinated person
rule: In immunised individuals (documented pre-exposure or a prior complete series), post-exposure management is two booster doses of vaccine (days 0 and 3) with no passive immunoglobulin, since antibodies are already primed and RIG would specifically blunt the active response.Discriminator: Previously vaccinated person = 2-day booster series (day 0/3), no RIG neededB) Full rabies vaccine series + immunoglobulin standardThe complete 5-dose vaccine + RIG package is for unimmunised individuals — same status does not apply here.C) Rabies immunoglobulin onlyImmunoglobulin-only regimen neither induces active lasting immunity nor is indicated for fully immunised persons.D) No intervention because dog was healthyRabies exposure from an unvaccinated/ unknown-status animal is never dismissed on how healthy the animal appears.

stem: A 45-year-old in dairy-farming household presents with high spiking fevers, arthralgia and sweating episodes with normal chest exam; blood cultures at 5 days grow gram-negative coccobacilli; brucella standard agglutination titre 1:320. Best treatment regimen?
opts: Doxycycline + rifampicin (or doxycycline + gentamicin) for 6 weeks
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Brucellosis dual/triple antibiotic regimen
rule: Brucellosis requires combination therapy to prevent relapse: doxycycline 6 weeks plus rifampicin (or plus gentamicin/streptomycin first 1-2 weeks then doxycycline ± rifampicin for 6 weeks); monotherapy carries unacceptable relapse rates, and beta-lactams don't reach intracellular brucellae effectively.Discriminator: Brucella blood-culture positive/ high titre: doxycycline + rifampicin (or doxycycline + aminoglycoside first 2-3 weeks) — never monotherapyB) Ciprofloxacin monotherapyCiprofloxacin monotherapy does not prevent relapse; it may be combined, but is not a standalone regimen.C) Penicillin GPenicillins are not effective against Brucella intracellular forms.D) Cephalexin courseCephalexin likewise neither covers intracellular brucellae nor prevents relapse.

stem: A 5-year-old presented with dysentery and is treated with ciprofloxacin; 2 days later he develops sudden severe abdominal distension with bloody stool and shock. Which complication is he facing?
opts: Intussusception precipitated by Shigella-associated lymphoid swelling
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Shigella-associated intussusception/ bloating
rule: Dysentery age (5 or under) with acute intermittent colicky pain, sausage-shaped mass, and red-current-jelly stool — intussusception, is triggered/enhanced by Peyer's patch enlargement (Shigella, adenovirus, and rotavirus associations); immediate reduction is needed (enema/air/pneumatic or surgical).Discriminator: Dysentery age 3-5 with sudden colicky distension and current-jelly stool — Shigella causes intestinal lymphoid Peyer's patch hyperplasia leading to intussusceptionB) Exercise-induced asthmaAsthma involves the airway, irrelevant to sudden colicky abdominal pathology.C) Pseudomembranous colitisPseudomembranous colitis follows antibiotic exposure in adults/elderly or prolonged courses — a 2-day post-ciprofloxacin event in a child with acute colick presentation doesn't fit.D) Spontaneous bacterial peritonitisSBP complicates ascites/cirrhosis; the clinical pattern here is intestinal telescoping, not peritoneal fluid infection.

stem: An 8-year-old boy with measles-like prodrome and koplik spots received vitamin A; he now has severe barking cough and stridor, oxygen saturating 92%. What complication has potentially developed and what is the key management step?
opts: Post-measles croup/laryngotracheitis — nebulised epinephrine/steroid and airway care
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Measles complication: post-measles croup/ airway compromise
rule: Measles weakens respiratory epithelium and precipitates viral/bacterial superinfections; croup develops with exacerbating stridor + oxygen desaturation, which mandates in-hospital airway support: dexamethasone/ nebulised epinephrine, oxygen, escalation to intubation if obstruction progresses.Discriminator: Barking cough + stridor + desaturation in a measles child identifies severe croup/laryngotracheobronchitis — airway is the primary threatB) Simple upper-respiratory involvement — outpatientStridor with SpO2 92% is airway emergency, not outpatient territory.C) Koplik spots resolution therapyKoplik spots are diagnostic eruption signs, not a therapeutic target.D) Measles inclusion-body encephalitis management onlyNeurological involvement is a possible late complication — the acute airway compromise is the current life-threat.

stem: A 26-year-old woman 3rd-trimester pregnancy is found to have HBsAg positive, HBeAg positive, HBV DNA high. What newborn prophylaxis prevents transmission most effectively?
opts: Hepatitis B immunoglobulin + hepatitis B vaccine within 12 hours of birth
Vaccine-only delayed to 6 weeks with HBIG at delivery to mother
caesarean section to prevent all vertical transmission
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: HBV mother-to-child prevention: HBIG + vaccine birth dose
rule: Neonatal prophylaxis pairing HBIG with the birth-dose vaccine within 12 hours cuts vertical transmission >90%, making breastfeeding safe; caesarean provides no additional protection beyond the vaccine+HBIG package.Discriminator: HBsAg+ (esp. HBeAg+/DNA high) newborn → HBIG plus vaccine within 12 hours; breastfeeding permitted with this packageB) Vaccine-only delayed to 6 weeks with HBIG at delivery to motherVaccine alone may leave an early gap for high-viraemia mothers — HBIG bridge is the combination standard.C) caesarean section to prevent all vertical transmissionCaesarean isn't indicated for HBsAg-positive mothers who receive the neonatal prophylaxis package.D) Breastfeeding-avoidance as sole measureBreastfeeding is encouraged under vaccine+HBIG prophylaxis; withholding it deprives the infant unnecessarily.

stem: A 33-year-old labourer with chronic HBV infection has: HBsAg positive, HBeAg negative, anti-HBe positive, ALT mildly raised 80, HBV DNA 12,000 IU/mL, and biopsy shows active hepatitis with bridging fibrosis. Management?
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Chronic HBV HBeAg-negative hepatitis needs antiviral therapy
rule: HBeAg-negative chronic infection with HBV DNA high, ALT elevated and biopsy fibrosis crosses into the treatment-needed territory ('immune-active hepatitis'), standard first-line daily tenofovir or entecavir given high-resistance barrier and long therapy horizon.Discriminator: HBeAg-negative chronic HBV with ALT elevated + HBV DNA high + biopsy fibrosis = treatA) Reassure and review annuallyBiopsy fibrosis + DNA load + ALT rise means not inactive-carrier state; managing as such risks cirrhosis.C) Interferon-alphaInterferon is largely replaced by oral antivirals given tolerability, cost and contraindication profile.D) Liver transplantation nowTransplant indication is decompensated cirrhosis/HCC, not compensated active hepatitis responding to oral therapy.

stem: A 48-year-old man with a contaminated deep puncture wound and no documented immunisation history arrives with trismus, opisthotonus-triggered episodes, risus sardonicus. What is the appropriate initial package?
opts: Human tetanus immunoglobulin + metronidazole + wound debridement + supportive-ventilatory care; NOT immunisation-only
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Tetanus management: passive immunoglobulin + toxin removal + supportive care
rule: Tetanus management is three-pronged: human tetanus immunoglobulin neutralises circulating (not yet bound) toxin; metronidazole kills the anaerobic organism; debridement removes the source, while spasm control/muscle relaxants/ventilation protect airway; definitive active immunisation begins concurrently in unimmunised patients.Discriminator: Trismus + risus + opisthotonus after dirty wound with no immunisation = tetanus; TIG neutralises unbound toxin, metronidazole killsClostridium, ventilatory supportB) Antigen-antibody culture and waitWaiting on cultures wastes the therapeutic window; identification is clinically clear.C) Passive-only immunisationPassive immunisation alone without antiseptic source-control and supportive care leaves the intoxication under-treated.D) Broad-spectrum antibiotics onlyAntibiotics alone do not neutralise circulating/ already bound toxin.

stem: A 55-year-old gardener with chronic lung disease has a plmmonary cavitary lesion hairball-like fungus ball in an upper lobe with air crescent on CT; Aspergillus skin test/serum IgE unremarkable but Aspergillus serum IgG raised. Diagnosis and management?
opts: Aspergilloma (chronic cavitary colonisation) — antifungal/ surgical if symptomatic/haemoptysis
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Aspergilloma in pre-existing cavity (saprophytic colonisation)
rule: Aspergillomafungus ball colonises pre-existing cavities (classically old TB), taking a mobile ball with air-crescent sign; management scheduled surveillance/asymptomatic, or antifungal/ embolisation/ surgery when hemoptysis significant.Discriminator: Air-crescent ball-in-cavity + no invasiveness marker + IgG-positive but IgE-normal = aspergilloma; not invasive nor allergic formsA) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis — steroidsABPA targets asthmatics with high IgE/ eosinophilia and central bronchiectasis — different axis of aspergillosis.C) Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis — voriconazole empiricInvasive pulmonary aspergillosis is the immunosuppressed halo/ cavitary progressive disease, vorionazole IV approach.D) TuberculomaTuberculoma is solid granuloma, no mobile fronded ball or air-crescent.

stem: A 12-year-old girl with fever 4 days, retro-orbital headache, myalgias and petechiae; platelets 40,000, haematocrit rising, reflexes brisk; she has mild abdominal tenderness and persistent vomiting. What is the critical classification and warning that she is entering the danger window?
opts: Dengue with warning signs (severe dengue threshold) — plasma leakage phase at defervescence; admit and monitor fluid
Simple dengue fever — supportive outpatient only with review after 1 week
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Dengue warning signs + critical phase
rule: Persistent vomiting, abdominal tenderness with lethargy, falling platelets and rising haematocrit mark warned dengue entering the plasma-leak phase around fever defervescence — the critical moment best handled with close monitoring and careful crystalloid resuscitation.Discriminator: Persistent vomiting + abdominal tenderness + rising haematocrit with falling platelets = warning signs; danger sits at defervescence (plasma leak)B) Simple dengue fever — supportive outpatient only with review after 1 weekThese features cross from simple dengue into warning-sign dengue — outpatient weekly follow-up is unsafe/fast enough.C) Chikungunya feverChikungunya causes severe polyarthralgia without classic plasma-leakage dynamics or petechial phase-dynamics platelet-drop profile.D) Scrub typhusScrub typhus typically includes eschar, regional lymph nodes, severe headache, and responds to doxycycline/azithro.

stem: A 30-year-old Pakistani man returning from rural Sindh has 10 days of high fever, relative bradycardia, rose-coloured spots on abdomen, and tender hepatosplenomegaly; WBC low. Blood culture grows a gram-negative rod producing H2S on SS agar. Diagnosis?
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Enteric fever classic presentation + SS agar colony
rule: Sustained high fever with relative bradycardia, rose-spot rash, hepatosplenomegaly and leucopenia is classic enteric (typhoid) fever, endemic across Pakistan; confirmation by blood culture (up to 80% positive first week) on selective media.Discriminator: Relative bradycardia + rose spots + stepwise fever + gram-negative rod growing on MacConkey = S typhiB) BrucellosisBrucella gives undulant fever with articular/ sex-organ involvement from raw milk, no rose spots; coccobacilli but different clinical constellation.C) DengueDengue has retro-orbital pain, thrombocytopenia, rash but not relative bradycardia stepwise typhoid pattern.D) Malaria vivaxVivax malaria is diagnosed by blood film; no rose spots or primary GI symptoms.

stem: A 22-year-old student has 4 days of fever, temperature 39.5, cervical lymphadenopathy, pharyngitis with grey exudates, and generalised maculopapular rash spreading after amoxicillin was started by a chemist; drink-sharing contact with a known infectious monospot-negative mononr. Most likely diagnosis?
opts: Streptococcus pyogenes pharyngitis with drug rash
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: EBV infectious mononucleosis + amoxicillin rash association
rule: Infectious mononucleosis (EBV) triad — fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy (+ splenomegaly/ atypical lymphocytes) — retains its classic feature of a morbilliform rash specifically after amoxicillin/ampicillin exposure; contact history supports EBV; heterophile (monospot) can be negative early.Discriminator: Pharyngitis + cervical lymphadenopathy + splenomegaly/ hepatosplenomegaly + amoxicillin-triggered morbiliform rash = EBV mononucleosisB) CMV mononucleosis-like syndromeCMV mono syndrome is heterophile-negative but pharyngitis/ cervical nodes are much milder, not the focal exudate-heavy pharyngitis pattern given.C) Streptococcus pyogenes pharyngitis with drug rashStreptococcal pharyngitis (GAS) produces purulent tonsillar exudate with tender anterior nodes; the classical amox-triggered generalised rash pattern + mono clusters is not it.D) ToxoplasmosisToxoplasmosis gives fever + lymphadenopathy usually posterior cervical/ generalised, not focal exudative pharyngitis.

stem: A 50-year-old immunosuppressed transplant recipient presents with progressive cognitive decline, hemiparesis and non-contrast CT showing hypodense white matter lesions without mass effect or contrast enhancement. Most likely pathogen?
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: PML in immunosuppressed population
rule: PML, by JC polyomavirus reactivation in immunocompromised immunosuppressed hosts, presents subacutely with focal deficits, cognitive decline, non-contrast-positive white matter lesions (oligodendrocyte destruction); no mass effect/ ring enhancement — treating the primary/ lowering immunosuppression.Discriminator: Immunosuppressed + focal neuro logic decline + white-matter lesions without mass/contrast = progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy by JC virusB) Cryptococcus neoformansCryptococcus gives meningitis/ cryptococcomas with capsule, not PML white-matter pattern.C) Toxoplasma gondiiToxoplasma produces multiple ring-enhancing lesions frequently with mass effect — opposite imaging signature.D) Streptococcus pneumoniaePneumococcus causes bacterial meningitis, different CSF/clinical pathway.

stem: A 6-month-old boy has 3 days fever, crusting oral lesions, and painful red eyes with keratitis; mother noticed large cavitating vesicles at corners of the mouth and around the genitals after a family wedding where a relative with 'lip fever' kissed the child. Most likely organism?
opts: Herpes simplex type 1 (gingivostomatitis/ eczema herpetic…, oropharyngitis)
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Primary HSV-1 gingivostomatitis + ocular/kissing link
rule: Primary HSV-1 infection presents as fever, painful gingivostomatitis with vesicles/ ulcers of oral mucosa often triggered by nonimmune oral contact with a shedding adult; ocular involvement (keratoconjunctivitis) is a serious complication needing ophthalmic aciclovir referral.Discriminator: Gingivostomatitis in young child + kissing contact from adult cold-sore carrier + eye involvement = primary HSV-1B) Varicella zosterVaricella causes generalised pruritic teardrop vesicles of different stages, not clustered peri-oral/ genital+ ocular involvement pattern.C) Coxsackie A16Coxsackie A16 = hand, foot and mouth syndrome with limb lesions/ oral ulcers; no kissing-contact adult source pattern.D) Candida albicansCandidal oral thrush is white plaques (pseudomembranous) without vesicles or ocular keratitis pattern.

stem: A 42-year-old butcher has tender left inguinal adenopathy and positive(fname track) node fever, seborisation; occupational raw-meat/ animal-fluid exposure; blood culture growing gram-negative coccal-rod pleomorphic organisms requiring CO2 for growth. Diagnosis?
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Brucellosis occupational + culture profile
rule: Brucella is a gram-negative coccobacillus growing slowly (needs CO2-rich atmosphere) associated with occupational livestock/raw-product exposure; presenting undulant fevers, articular pains, hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy; diagnosed by blood/bone-marrow culture or serology, treated with doxycycline + rifampicin/gentamicin.Discriminator: Occupational raw-animal exposure + undulant/ positional fever + CO2-requiring gram-negative coccobacillus = BrucellaB) TularemiaTularemia is a small gram-negative coccobacillus from rabbits/ticks with ulceroglandular presentation — its growth needs cysteine, classically not CO2-pattern.C) PasteurellosisPasteurella multocida from bites causing cellulitis/abscess, common cat/dog-oriented exposure.D) Cat-scratch diseaseCat-scratch disease: Bartonella henselae, regional node near a cat scratch, self-resolution usually.

stem: A 20-year-old soldier presents with fever, and severe polyarthritis (knees/ ankles) after a diarrheal episode a week earlier; HLA-B27 positive; unilateral conjunctivitis noted. Best-matching diagnosis and organism trio class?
opts: Reactive arthritis after GIT/ GU infection — Chlamydia/ Shigella/ Salmonella/ Yersinia/ Campylobacter
Septic arthritis — blood/ joint aspiration mandatory
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Reactive arthritis classic triad + HLA-B27 organisms
rule: Reactive arthritis follows GI/ genitourinary infections, classically by Chlamydia, Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia, Campylobacter, with the triad arthritis + urethritis/ cervicitis + conjunctivitis presenting in HLA-B27 carriers; management is NSAIDs/ sulfasalazineTNFi if severe — antibiotics don't alter the established arthritis.Discriminator: Post-infectious asymmetric oligoarthritis + conjunctivitis/ urethritis pattern + HLA-B27 = reactive arthritis; identity through post-dysentery organismsB) Septic arthritis — blood/ joint aspiration mandatorySeptic arthritis would require monoarticular focus with positive joint aspiration; post-infectious arthritis is culture-negative.C) Rheumatoid arthritis early-onsetRA looks for symmetrical small-joint involvement with RF/anti-CCP, morning stiffness — not the post-dysenteric pattern.D) Reiter-like overlap from disseminated NeisseriaDisseminated gonococcal infection causes pustular skin lesions/ tenosynovitis; arthritis-dermatitis triad, different pattern.

stem: A village stray dog bit a farmer's leg through trousers 60 hours ago; wound is on lower leg, moderate and bleeding stopped; WHO category III exposure (saliva contact through torn skin). What should be done now?
opts: Nothing — wound has healed surface-wise, animal healthy
Wash wound extensively with soap + water, start rabies vaccine course (with immunoglobulin if possible) immediately, suture avoided
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (Category III): wound care + vaccine + RIG
rule: Category III exposures (transdermal bites/scratches or saliva on broken skin) require immediate thorough soap-and-water irrigation, rabies vaccine series, and rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into/ around the wound within 7 days if the animal cannot be observed; delayed RIG beyond day 7 is unnecessary once antibody responses generate.Discriminator: Transdermal bite from unvaccinated stray = Category III → immediate wound irrigation + vaccine ± rabies immunoglobulin infiltrationA) Nothing — wound has healed surface-wise, animal healthyRabies has essentially 100% mortality once symptoms start; 'the dog looked healthy' is a fatal reassurance.C) Only tetanus boosterTetanus boost is adjunct — never the rabies response.D) antibiotics aloneAntibiotics manage secondary wound infection risk, not rabies itself.

stem: An organism isolated from a CSF sample of a neutropenic patient with pneumonia grows a gram-negative rod requiring charcoal yeast extract with iron and L-cysteine. It does not gram-stain well but stains with silver/ direct fluorescent antibody. Diagnosis basis and therapy choice?
opts: Legionella pneumonia — macrolide or fluoroquinolone; NOT beta-lactam
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Legionella culture requirements + treatment
rule: Legionella pneumophila is an intracellular gram-negative bacillus that requires charcoal-yeast extract agar with iron and L-cysteine, stains poorly with Gram and is treated with macrolides (azithromycin) or fluoroquinolones — beta-lactams are ineffective due to intracellular habitat.Discriminator: Charcoal-yeast-extract + iron + cysteine, poor gram stain, intracellular lung infection = Legionella; treated with macrolide/ FQB) Mycobacterium tuberculosis — anti-TB therapyMycobacteria grow on Löwenstein-Jensen with slow colonies; acid-fast, not this profile.C) Pseudomonas — ceftazidimePseudomonas grows readily on standard media, gram-negative but no special medium or fade-out gram stain issue.D) Coxiella burnetii — doxycyclineCoxiella (Q fever) does not require CYE agar; serological/ PCR diagnostic; doxycycline therapy.

stem: A 28-year-old woman had hepatitis A-like illness; serology now shows anti-HAV IgG positive, IgM negative, ALT normal. Interpretation?
opts: Past immunisation/ cured infection — immunity present
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Hepatitis A IgG vs IgM meaning
rule: Hepatitis A never becomes chronic; anti-HAV IgG without IgM and normal ALT indicates resolved past infection or vaccination with durable immunity.Discriminator: IgM = current/recent; IgG without IgM with normal ALT = resolved/past or vaccinatedA) Current acute hepatitis A infectionIgM negative rules out acute infection.C) Chronic carrier stateHAV does not form chronic carrier states.D) Pre-vaccination window with fulminant riskWith normal ALT and IgG-only positivity there is no fulminant pre-window; she is simply immune.

stem: A 40-year-old woman on Repeat-level anti-TB therapy for 2 months develops yellow sclerae, fatigue and peripheral neuropathy; ALT 260, AST 240; bilirubin 4 mg/dL. Which two drugs are the likeliest culprits and what is management of the neuropathy?
opts: Isoniazid + rifampicin hepatotoxicity; B6 repletion for INH neuropathy
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Anti-TB drug hepatotoxicity (INH/Rifampicin/PZA) and INH neuropathy
rule: INH, rifampicin and pyrazinamide are the hepatotoxic trio, with INH additionally causing a B6-deficiency peripheral neuropathy prevented/treated by pyridoxine supplementation.Discriminator: Transaminitis/jaundice with INH-related peripheral neuropathy points to INH (± rifampicin/PZA) — B6 deficiency mechanismB) Ethambutol optic toxicity; stop itEthambutol causes ocular/optic-neuritis (colour vision/visual acuity) — not transaminitis or neuropathy.C) Pyrazinamide joint pains; urate-lowering therapyPyrazinamide causes hyperuricaemia/arthritis but the triad agent pair is INH+Rifampicin here.D) Streptomycin ototoxicity; stop the injectionStreptomycin causes ototoxicity/neephrotoxicity, not hepatic injury.

stem: A 3-year-old is brought with high fever, drooling, tripod posture, inspiratory stridor and a thumb-print epiglottitis on lateral X-ray; immunisations are incomplete. Immediate action?
opts: Secure airway (anaesthetist/ ENT standby), avoid throat examination, then IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone)
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Epiglottitis airway-first principle
rule: Epiglottitis (classically H. influenzae type b in under-immunised children) threatens acute airway obstruction: securing the airway (in theatre, under anaesthesia) precedes everything; direct throat examination risks precipitating arrest; ceftriaxone then treats the organism.Discriminator: Drooling + tripod + thumbprint sign + unimmunised child = epiglottitis — one of the few absolute airway-first presentationsB) Swab the throat immediatelyThroat examination may precipitate airway arrest in a child with epiglottitis.C) Oral amoxicillin outpatientOutpatient oral therapy is insufficient for a potentially obstructing airway; admission with airway control is the standard.D) Steam inhalation and observeSteam inhalation is croup supportive, not epiglottitis-suitable management.

stem: A 6-year-old boy from a malaria-endemic area has 3 days of fever with rigors, pallor, and dark reddish-brown urine; peripheral smear shows ring forms and banana-shaped gametocytes; parasitemia 4%; Hb 6.8. Which is correct?
opts: Oral chloroquine full course on outpatient basis
IV artesunate + full-course oral artemisinin-based combination therapy; screen/pre-empt severe disease markers
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Severe/complicated falciparum malaria management
rule: Banana-shaped gametocytes and multiple-ring forms identify falciparum; anaemia 6 g plus haemoglobinuria (blackwater) shift this into severe malaria, treated with IV artesunate (or quinine if unavailable), then a full ACT course; chloroquine resistance and outpatient-only handling are unacceptable.Discriminator: Falciparum (banana gametocytes) + anaemia + haemoglobinuria = severe malaria risk → parenteral artesunate if any severity criteria, ACTA) Oral chloroquine full course on outpatient basisChloroquine resistance plus severe criteria make oral-only outpatient chloroquine unsafe and inadequate.C) Primaquine monotherapyPrimaquine clears hypnozoites (vivax/ovale) and gametocytes but never treats acute falciparum blood-stage disease alone.D) Quinine IM aloneIM quinine is a fallback when IV artesunate unavailable — inferior and painful, not the standard answer.

stem: An organism grows on chocolate agar (supplemented) requiring both factor X and V; meningitis picture in an unvaccinated toddler. Identification?
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: H. influenzae growth requirements
rule: Haemophilus species require X and/or V factors: H. influenzae needs both, classically cultured on chocolate (heat-lysated) agar; the clinical setting (unvaccinated child's meningitis) corroborates Hib.Discriminator: Needs both X (haematin) + V (NAD) factors grown on chocolate agar = H influenzaeA) Neisseria meningitidisN. meningitidis is fastidious but grows well on blood/chocolate, Thayer-Martin; factor X/V is not its requirement.C) Moraxella catarrhalisMoraxella catarrhalis grows readily on blood agar, causing otitis/sinusitis not classic meningitis in children.D) LegionellaLegionella requires charcoal yeast agar with iron and L-cysteine.

stem: A 27-year-old clinical laboratory worker absentmindedly handled cultures without gloves; three days later she has fever, chills and headache after a needle-prick handling Brucella culture at the lab. Best immediate response?
opts: Post-exposure prophylaxis with doxycycline + rifampicin for the window of suspicion
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
