concept: Brucella laboratory-acquired infection prophylaxis
rule: Brucella is a top-tier laboratory hazard (aerosol/ percutaneous infection risk): accidental exposure prophylaxis is doxycycline 100 mg Bd + rifampicin 600-900 mg daily for 3-6 weeks over the incubation window (7-21 days) with clinical monitoring; no licensed human vaccine exists.Discriminator: Laboratory needle-prick/ aerosol exposure to live Brucella cultures = PEP regimen (doxycycline + rifampicin) due to high infectivity/ incubationB) Observation onlyWaiting without prophylaxis after a known high-risk exposure wastes the best opportunity to abort infection.C) Pre-exposure vaccination nowNo approved human brucella vaccine — pre-exposure immunisation is a veterinary practice only.D) Amebicidal therapyAmebicidal therapy is irrelevant to Brucella exposure.

stem: A 24-year-old student has fever, severe headache and neck stiffness. CSF: clear, 200 lymphocytes, protein 55, glucose parallel to blood. Rapid improvement seen after first dose of what medication challenge would confirm clinical suspicion of tuberculous meningitis in ambiguous cases?
opts: Anti-TB therapy over weeks with slow improvement is the practical differentiator, not an overnight response
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: TB meningitis CSF pattern + response kinetics vs viral meningitis
rule: This CSF — lymphocytes, elevated protein, mildly low glucose — sits with tuberculous meningitis (viral meningitis keeps protein near-normal and glucose iso- with blood); response scale is weeks not days, whereas HSV responds far faster; neuroimaging basal enhancement and duration >5 days of symptoms also predict TB.Discriminator: Lymphocytic CSF with HIGH protein and LOW-normal glucose = TB; lymphocytes with normal glucose/protein = viralA) Steroid trial only axisSteroids alone bring no organism-confirmed benefit diagnosis-wise; they're adjunct in confirmed TBM.C) Single-dose artesunateArtesunate targets malaria — unrelated to this CSF pattern and clinical course.D) Acyclovir trialAcyclovir empiric therapy is reserved for HSV clues (seizures/temporal changes/HSV PCR availability).

stem: A 19-year-old man has a painful genital ulcer with a unilateral inguinal bubo; Gram stain/ culture from aspiration shows small gram-negative rods, VNTR strain typing available. Likely pathogen?
subject: Biochemistry-&-Microbiology
concept: Chancroid clinical/culture profile
rule: Chancroid: painful, undermining, non-indurated genital ulcer with tender suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo), caused by Haemophilus ducreyi gram-negative rod, treated azithromycin 1 g single dose or ceftriaxone IM.Discriminator: Painful genital ulcer + unilateral suppurative inguinal node = chancroid (H. ducreyi); differs from LGV (painless primary + bubo) and syphilis (painless chancre)B) Treponema pallidumSyphilitic chancre characteristically painless with rubbery painless lymph nodes.C) Herpes simplexHerpes presents with multiple vesicles/ulcers, inguinal nodes may be tender but ulcer stages differ; bubo-suppurative pattern is chancroid.D) Lymphogranuloma venereumLGV: transient painless primary lesion, followed by painful suppurative inguinal bubo ( chronic sequelae (rectal strictures/ elephantiasis).

stem: A 60-year-old male smoker presents with two painless swellings, one in each parotid region, present for 1 year. They are soft and cystic on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Warthin tumor — parotid pathology
rule: Bilateral, soft, cystic parotid swellings in an elderly male smoker are characteristic of Warthin tumor (papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum).Discriminator: Bilateral parotid swellings + male smoker + cystic = Warthin tumorA) Pleomorphic adenomaPleomorphic adenoma is usually unilateral, firm, and the most common overall.C) MumpsMumps is acute, febrile, and inflammatory.D) Parotid abscessAn abscess is painful and acute.

stem: A 60-year-old has a vesicular rash on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson sign) with a red painful eye and blurred vision. Most appropriate action?
opts: Oral acyclovir (or valacyclovir) urgently plus urgent ophthalmology review
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus - Hutchinson sign; urgent antiviral + eye review
rule: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus involves the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. A vesicle on the nasal tip (Hutchinson sign) indicates nasociliary involvement and high risk of ocular disease (keratitis, uveitis, raised IOP). It requires urgent systemic antiviral (acyclovir/valacyclovir) and ophthalmology review; topical steroids are only for specific ocular inflammation under supervision.Discriminator: Vesicular rash on nose tip (nasociliary involvement) + eye signs = HZO; urgent antiviral + ophth reviewA) Topical antibiotics and reassuranceantibiotics do not treat VZV; this needs antiviral therapyC) Oral antihistaminesantihistamines do not treat viral infection or prevent ocular complicationsD) Topical steroids alonetopical steroids alone risk worsening; systemic antiviral is required

stem: In acute angle-closure glaucoma, pilocarpine constricts the pupil and opens the angle. What is its mechanism of action?
opts: Beta-2 agonist that increases aqueous outflow
Direct muscarinic agonist contracting ciliary muscle and sphincter, pulling the iris open
Alpha-1 agonist that dilates the pupil
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor reducing aqueous production
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Pilocarpine - direct miotic (muscarinic agonist) in AACG
rule: Pilocarpine is a direct muscarinic (cholinergic) agonist. In AACG it causes miosis and ciliary muscle contraction, pulling the peripheral iris away from the trabecular meshwork, opening the angle. Contraindicated in anterior uveitis.Discriminator: Pilocarpine is a direct-acting miotic: contracts ciliary muscle (opens angle) and sphincter (miosis), breaking the pupillary blockA) Beta-2 agonist that increases aqueous outflowbeta-2 agonists are not used in glaucoma; timolol is a beta-blocker reducing aqueous productionC) Alpha-1 agonist that dilates the pupilalpha-1 agonists (phenylephrine) DILATE the pupil and would worsen AACGD) Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor reducing aqueous productionacetazolamide is the carbonic anhydrase inhibitor; pilocarpine is the miotic

stem: A 30-year-old presents after an alkali splash to the eye with conjunctival blanching and corneal haze. The single most urgent immediate step is:
opts: Copious immediate irrigation with water or saline
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Chemical eye injury - immediate copious irrigation is the priority
rule: Chemical (especially alkaline) eye burns cause rapid penetration and necrosis; the definitive immediate treatment is copious irrigation with water or saline for 20-30 minutes, started at the scene. pH measurement and other drops come after irrigation is underway.Discriminator: Any chemical eye injury: irrigate copiously FIRST, before anything else (even before pH)B) Instil topical antibiotic drops firstantibiotic drops are secondary; irrigation must come first to limit tissue necrosisC) Give a cycloplegic drop firsta cycloplegic is comfort care and not the urgent sight-saving stepD) Measure the pH, then decidemeasuring pH must not delay irrigation - start water/saline immediately

stem: After an acute angle-closure attack is controlled medically, what is the definitive preventive treatment?
opts: Laser peripheral iridotomy (creating a hole in the peripheral iris)
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Acute angle-closure glaucoma - laser peripheral iridotomy is definitive
rule: Laser peripheral iridotomy creates a hole in the peripheral iris, allowing aqueous to bypass the pupillary block and reach the trabecular meshwork, definitively preventing recurrence of angle closure. It is performed once the acute attack is medically controlled, and prophylactically in the fellow eye.Discriminator: Definitive AACG treatment = laser peripheral iridotomy (after pressure control) to bypass the pupillary blockA) Lifelong topical antibioticsantibiotics do not prevent angle closureC) Cataract extraction only, no lasercataract surgery may help but iridotomy is the definitive angle-closure procedureD) Oral diuretics indefinitelychronic diuretics are not the definitive preventive treatment

stem: A 70-year-old with hypertension and diabetes has sudden, painless, unilateral visual loss. Fundoscopy shows widespread flame-shaped haemorrhages, dilated tortuous retinal veins, cotton-wool spots and disc oedema ('blood and thunder'). Most likely diagnosis?
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Central retinal vein occlusion - 'blood and thunder' fundus
rule: CRVO presents with acute painless loss and a characteristic fundus of engorged tortuous veins, flame haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and disc oedema ('blood and thunder'). Associated with hypertension, diabetes, glaucoma and hypercoagulable states. Macular oedema managed with anti-VEGF/steroids.Discriminator: Sudden painless loss + dilated tortuous veins + flame haemorrhages + disc oedema = CRVOA) Central retinal artery occlusionCRAO shows a pale retina with a cherry-red macula, not widespread haemorrhagesC) Vitreous haemorrhagevitreous haemorrhage obscures the fundus (no clear vessels) rather than showing venous congestionD) Retinal detachmentretinal detachment shows a demarcation line/tear, not a haemorrhagic venous pattern

stem: A 4-month-old has a red, tender, swollen lump at the medial canthus with discharge from the punctum on compression; the eye itself is white and quiet. Most likely diagnosis and initial management?
opts: Acute dacryocystitis (infected nasolacrimal duct) - warm compresses, massage, oral antibiotics; probing if recurrent
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Dacryocystitis - medial canthal swelling/discharge; infected NLDO
rule: Dacryocystitis is infection of the lacrimal sac, usually from obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct. It presents with a tender, red swelling at the medial canthus with reflux of pus from the punctum on compression; the conjunctiva is typically quiet (unlike cellulitis). Management is warm compresses, massage and oral antibiotics, with probing/dilation if recurrent. It differs from preseptal/orbital cellulitis, which involve the lid/orbit more broadly.Discriminator: Tender medial canthal swelling + purulent reflux from punctum, quiet eye = dacryocystitis (infected NLDO)A) Preseptal cellulitis; urgent IV antibioticspreseptal cellulitis is diffuse lid erythema/swelling without a focal sac and punctal refluxC) Orbital cellulitis; urgent CTorbital cellulitis has proposis/EOM restriction, not a focal medial canthal sacD) Conjunctivitis; topical antibioticsconjunctivitis has a diffusely red eye, not a focal canthal swelling

stem: A child has eyelid swelling and redness. On examination there is proposis, restricted extraocular movements, pain on eye movement and decreased vision. What is the key distinction and management?
opts: This is preseptal cellulitis; oral antibiotics as an outpatient suffice
This is orbital cellulitis; urgent IV antibiotics and CT to assess for abscess
This is allergic oedema; give antihistamines
This is chalazion; warm compresses only
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Orbital cellulitis vs preseptal - proptosis/EOM restriction/vision loss = orbital, urgent
rule: Preseptal cellulitis is confined to the eyelid (no proposis, no EOM restriction, normal vision) and is treated with oral antibiotics. Orbital cellulitis extends behind the septum causing proposis, restricted/painful eye movement, decreased vision and systemic toxicity; it is an emergency requiring urgent IV antibiotics and imaging (CT) to exclude an abscess, with ENT/orbital source often from sinusitis.Discriminator: Proptosis + painful EOM restriction + decreased vision = orbital cellulitis -> urgent IV abx + CTA) This is preseptal cellulitis; oral antibiotics as an outpatient sufficeoral outpatient care is for preseptal; this child has orbital signs needing admissionC) This is allergic oedema; give antihistaminesallergic oedema is bilateral, itchy, and lacks infection signs/EOM restrictionD) This is chalazion; warm compresses onlya chalazion is a painless lid lump, not acute swelling with proposis

stem: A 28-year-old with untreated anterior uveitis (iritis) returns with a fixed, irregular pupil and glare. What complication has developed, and what helps prevent it?
opts: Posterior synechiae (iris adhered to lens); a cycloplegic (e.g. atropine) helps prevent/adhesiolyse
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Anterior uveitis complication - posterior synechiae; cycloplegic prevents
rule: Posterior synechiae form when iris inflamation causes adhesion of the iris to the lens, producing a fixed, irregular pupil and risk of angle-closure glaucoma. Cycloplegic/mydriatic drops (e.g. atropine, cyclopentolate) keep the pupil mobile and prevent synechiae; they are a cornerstone of anterior uveitis management alongside steroids.Discriminator: Recurrent/untreated iritis -> posterior synechiae (pupil fixed/irregular); cycloplegics prevent by dilating and resting the irisA) Cataract; prevent with early surgerycataract is not the acute complication described; the fixed irregular pupil is synechiaeC) Retinal detachment; prevent with laserretinal detachment is not the mechanism hereD) Glaucoma; prevent with mioticsmiotics would worsen synechiae risk; cycloplegics (dilators) are used

stem: An elderly woman has the lower eyelid turning INWARD so the lashes rub against the cornea, causing irritation, redness and a corneal abrasion. Most likely diagnosis and risk?
opts: Ectropion - lid turns outward causing epiphora and exposure
Entropion - lid turns inward; lashes traumatise the cornea (risk of ulceration/infection)
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Entropion vs ectropion - entropion = lid inward, lashes scratch cornea
rule: Entropion is inversion of the eyelid margin so the lashes contact the cornea, causing irritation, epithelial defects and risk of infection/ulceration, especially in the elderly (involutional). Ectropion is eversion (outward) causing epiphora and exposure. Management of entropion may require lid surgery to protect the cornea.Discriminator: Inward-turning lid with lashes on cornea = entropion; risk of corneal abrasion/ulcerA) Ectropion - lid turns outward causing epiphora and exposureectropion is outward eversion with tearing/exposure, not inward lashes on corneaC) Blepharospasmblepharospasm is involuntary lid squeezing, not a structural inversionD) Ptosisptosis is lid drooping, not inversion

stem: An immunocompetent adult has focal necrotizing retinitis with overlying vitritis, described as 'headlight in fog', and a small old scar elsewhere in the fundus. Most likely diagnosis and typical management?
opts: Toxoplasma chorioretinitis; treat with pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine (+folinic acid)
Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy; observe
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Toxoplasma chorioretinitis - 'headlight in fog' necrotizing focus + old scar
rule: Toxoplasma chorioretinitis classically presents with a focal area of retinal necrosis with overlying vitritis ('headlight in fog') adjacent to a pigmented old scar. Immunocompetent patients are treated with pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine (with folinic acid to reduce bone-marrow toxicity); sight- or life-threatening disease may need steroids.Discriminator: Focal necrotizing retinitis + overlying vitritis + old scar = toxoplasma; treat with pyrimethamine/sulfadiazineA) CMV retinitis; treat with ganciclovirCMV retinitis occurs in immunocompromised hosts, is perivascular ('tomato ketchup'), and lacks an old toxoplasma scarC) Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy; observeAPMPPE is multifocal placoid and not necrotizing with a single old scarD) Syphilitic retinitis; treat with penicillinsyphilitic retinitis has a different picture and is not 'headlight in fog' with a solitary old scar

stem: A diabetic with proliferative retinopathy reports a sudden shower of floaters and a dark veil over one eye with poor vision. The red reflex is absent and the fundus cannot be seen. Most likely diagnosis?
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Vitreous haemorrhage - sudden floaters + obscured fundus, absent red reflex
rule: Vitreous haemorrhage (from PDR, trauma, retinal tear) presents with sudden floaters and a dark veil; the red reflex is lost and the fundus is not visible. It mandates urgent assessment to exclude an associated retinal tear/detachment.Discriminator: Sudden floaters + veiled vision + absent red reflex/fundus view = vitreous haemorrhageA) Central retinal artery occlusionCRAO shows a pale retina with cherry-red spot, not an obscured vitreousC) Anterior uveitisanterior uveitis has a visible inflamed anterior segment, not an absent red reflex from bloodD) Acute angle-closure glaucomaAACG has a mid-dilated fixed pupil and high pressure, not floaters with lost red reflex

stem: A 3-month-old has persistent watery discharge and tearing from one eye since birth, with mild medial canthal wetness but no redness or mass. Usual management?
opts: Conservative: massage + observe; most resolve by 1 year, probing if persistent
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction - massage + observe
rule: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction is common and usually resolves spontaneously by 12 months with lacrimal massage. Probing/dilation is reserved for persistent cases; acute dacryocystitis (red swollen medial canthus) needs antibiotics.Discriminator: Neonatal watery eye without mass/redness = congenital NLDO; conservative first (massage), resolves <1yA) Immediate surgical dacryocystorhinostomyimmediate DCR is far too aggressive for a self-limiting neonatal obstructionC) Topical antibiotics indefinitelychronic antibiotics are not indicated without infectionD) Oral antihistaminesantihistamines do not treat a mechanical duct obstruction

stem: A myopic 55-year-old notices flashes of light, a shower of floaters, and then a shadow/curtain descending over the temporal visual field of one eye. Most appropriate next step?
opts: Urgent ophthalmological assessment for possible retinal detachment
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment - flashes + floaters + curtain
rule: Rhegmatogenous RD classically begins with flashes (vitreoretinal traction) and floaters (vitreous detachment/tear), followed by a shadow or curtain from the detaching retina. Risk factors include myopia, aphakia/pseudophakia, trauma and lattice degeneration. It is an urgent sight-saving referral.Discriminator: Flashes + floaters + curtain in a myope = rhegmatogenous RD until proven otherwise; urgentA) Reassure and review in 2 weeksdelaying risks irreversible macula-off detachment and permanent lossC) Start topical antibioticsantibiotics are irrelevant; there is no infectionD) Prescribe reading glassesglasses do not address an acute retinal detachment

stem: A 22-year-old reports difficulty seeing at night since childhood and progressive narrowing of the visual field. Fundoscopy shows bony spicule pigmentation, attenuated vessels and waxy pallor of the disc. Diagnosis?
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Retinitis pigmentosa - night blindness + tunnel vision + bone spicules
rule: Retinitis pigmentosa is an inherited rod-cone dystrophy causing early night blindness and progressive peripheral field loss (tunnel vision), with classic fundus bone-spicule pigmentation, vessel attenuation and waxy disc pallor. A standard recalled pattern.Discriminator: Night blindness + tunnel (ring) vision + bone-spicule pigment + attenuated vessels = RPA) Age-related macular degenerationAMD causes central (not peripheral/night) loss and drusen, not bone spiculesC) Central serous retinopathycentral serous causes a central serous detachment, not night blindness or spiculesD) Diabetic retinopathydiabetic retinopathy has microaneurysms/haemorrhages, not bone-spicule pigment

stem: A 42-year-old man with alcohol use disorder wants medication to reduce craving and relapse after detoxification. Which agent reduces drinking by antagonising opioid receptors involved in alcohol's rewarding effect?
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Naltrexone — opioid antagonist reduces alcohol craving/drinking
rule: Naltrexone (an opioid receptor antagonist) reduces the rewarding effects of alcohol and craving, decreasing relapse. Disulfiram causes an aversive acetaldehyde reaction if alcohol is drunk; acamprosate modulates glutamate and also reduces relapse.Discriminator: Opioid-receptor antagonist (naltrexone) reduces alcohol reward/craving; disulfiram is aversive; acamprosate is a glutamate modulatorA) Disulfiramdisulfiram is aversive (blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase causing a reaction with alcohol), not an opioid antagonistB) Acamprosateacamprosate modulates glutamate/NMDA signalling to reduce relapse, not opioid receptorsD) Haloperidolhaloperidol is an antipsychotic with no role in alcohol-craving reduction

stem: A 65-year-old woman who has taken a typical antipsychotic for years develops repetitive, involuntary oro-buccal-lingual chewing and grimacing movements. What is the best initial management?
opts: Continue the same dose and reassure
Switch to an atypical antipsychotic (or clozapine) and consider VMAT-2 inhibitor (valbenazine)
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Tardive dyskinesia — reduce/switch antipsychotic; anticholinergics can worsen it
rule: Tardive dyskinesia (TD) is an extrapyramidal syndrome of oro-bucco-lingual stereotypic movements after long-term dopamine blockade. Initial management is a trial of reducing/stopping the causative antipsychotic or switching to a lower-risk atypical (clozapine), and a VMAT-2 inhibitor (valbenazine/deutetrabenazine) is FDA-approved for TD.Discriminator: Oro-facial stereotypic movements after long-term antipsychotic = tardive dyskinesia; stop/reduce drug, switch to atypical, consider VMAT-2 inhibitorA) Increase the antipsychotic doseincreasing the offending antipsychotic worsens TD — it must be reduced or switchedB) Add an anticholinergic (e.g. benztropine)anticholinergics (benztropine) can WORSEN tardive dyskinesia, unlike acute dystonia/drug-induced parkinsonismC) Continue the same dose and reassurereassuring while continuing the same dose risks irreversible movement disorder; action is required

stem: A 30-year-old man with schizophrenia is started on an antipsychotic. Three months later he has gained 8 kg and his fasting glucose and lipids are elevated. Which agent is MOST responsible for this metabolic syndrome?
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Second-generation antipsychotics (olanzapine) — metabolic syndrome AE
rule: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotics such as olanzapine and clozapine cause significant weight gain and metabolic syndrome (hyperglycaemia, dyslipidaemia), whereas first-generation agents (haloperidol, fluphenazine) more often cause extrapyramidal symptoms.Discriminator: Weight gain, hyperglycaemia, dyslipidaemia = metabolic syndrome; typical with SGA olanzapine (vs EPS with FGA)A) Haloperidolhaloperidol (FGA) mainly causes extrapyramidal symptoms/akathisia, not marked metabolic syndromeB) Loxapine (fluphenazine)fluphenazine (FGA) causes EPS; it is not the main cause of metabolic syndromeD) Chlorpromazine at low dosechlorpromazine is low-metabolic relative to olanzapine — olanzapine is the archetype for metabolic weight gain

stem: A 70-year-old man has fluctuating cognition, well-formed visual hallucinations of people and animals, and mild parkinsonism. His family notes marked sensitivity to antipsychotic medications. What is the most likely diagnosis and an important management caveat?
opts: Dementia with Lewy bodies — avoid neuroleptics (severe sensitivity), use cholinesterase inhibitors and handle psychosis carefully
Frontotemporal dementia — start an antipsychotic for behaviour
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Dementia with Lewy bodies — fluctuate + visual hallucinations + parkinsonism; severe neuroleptic sensitivity
rule: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is marked by fluctuating cognition, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, and parkinsonism. Patients have severe, sometimes fatal sensitivity to antipsychotics, so these are avoided; cholinesterase inhibitors are used and psychosis handled conservatively.Discriminator: Fluctuating cognition + visual hallucinations (formed) + parkinsonism + neuroleptic sensitivity = DLBA) Alzheimer disease — start donepezil onlyAD lacks the prominent parkinsonism, visual hallucinations and severe neuroleptic sensitivity that define DLBC) Vascular dementia — antiplatelet therapyvascular dementia has stepwise vascular/focal signs, not this triad of fluctuation, visual hallucinations and parkinsonismD) Frontotemporal dementia — start an antipsychotic for behaviourgiving an antipsychotic for DLB psychosis is dangerous (severe neuroleptic sensitivity); it must be avoided

stem: A 40-year-old man over 5 days has euphoric mood, grandiosity (plans to quit medicine and start a university), pressured speech and reckless spending, sleeping only 2–3 hours/night yet feeling rested. What is the most specific sleep finding that points to MANIA rather than simple insomnia?
opts: Difficulty falling asleep despite feeling tired
Decreased need for sleep with preserved energy/restored feeling
Early morning awakening with low mood
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Mania — decreased need for sleep (vs insomnia of depression/simple insomnia)
rule: In mania, sleep is decreased in NEED — the patient sleeps few hours yet feels rested and energetic. This contrasts with the insomnia of depression (tired but unable to sleep, early-morning awakening) where energy is low. Reduced need for sleep is a core and specific manic feature.Discriminator: Grandiosity + pressured speech + decreased NEED for sleep (not distressed) = maniaA) Difficulty falling asleep despite feeling tireddifficulty falling asleep while tired is characteristic of depression/anxiety insomnia, not manic decreased-need sleepC) Early morning awakening with low moodearly-morning awakening with low mood is a hallmark of depression, not maniaD) Hypersomnia and daytime nappinghypersomnia is typical of atypical depression, not mania

stem: A 19-year-old woman with severe anorexia nervosa (BMI 14) is started on refeeding. On day 3 she develops weakness, arrhythmia, seizures and confusion. Bloods show low phosphate. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management?
opts: Refeeding syndrome — give phosphate/electrolyte replacement and slow, monitored refeeding
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Refeeding syndrome in anorexia nervosa — refeeding-induced hypophosphataemia
rule: Refeeding syndrome occurs when rapid nutrition is given to a severely malnourished patient, causing insulin-driven shifts and severe hypophosphataemia (also hypoK/hypoMg) with arrhythmias, seizures, weakness and confusion. Management is cautious, monitored refeeding with phosphate/electrolyte replacement.Discriminator: Severe malnutrition + refeeding + low phosphate + arrhythmia/seizures = refeeding syndromeA) Hypoglycaemia — give IV dextrose onlythe key derangement is hypophosphataemia from refeeding, not isolated hypoglycaemia; both replacement and slow refeeding are requiredC) Serotonin syndrome — stop the antidepressantserotonin syndrome follows serotonergic drugs with clonus/hyperreflexia, not this electrolyte-driven pictureD) Alcohol withdrawal — give a benzodiazepineno alcohol use here; the problem is refeeding hypophosphataemia, not alcohol withdrawal

stem: A chronic heavy drinker stops alcohol abruptly. He has confusion, agitation, tremor, hallucinations and marked autonomic overactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, sweating, fever) with a risk of seizures and death. What is this, and what is the treatment?
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Delirium tremens — clouded sensorium + autonomic instability; benzodiazepine treatment
rule: Delirium tremens (DTs) is the severe end of alcohol withdrawal: clouded consciousness, tremor, hallucinations and marked autonomic instability, with risk of seizures and death. It is a medical emergency treated with benzodiazepines (e.g. diazepam/lorazepam) plus thiamine and supportive care.Discriminator: Confusion + tremor + hallucinations + marked autonomic overactivity after stopping alcohol = delirium tremens; treat with benzodiazepinesA) Alcoholic hallucinosis — treat with antipsychoticsalcoholic hallucinosis has a clear sensorium without the autonomic storm of DTs; the treatment for DTs is benzodiazepines, not primary antipsychoticsB) Wernicke encephalopathy — give thiamine onlythiamine treats/prevents Wernicke encephalopathy but does not control autonomic DTs; benzodiazepines are neededD) Alcoholic dementia — long-term carethis is an acute withdrawal emergency, not chronic alcoholic dementia requiring only long-term care

stem: A 72-year-old man has progressive memory loss over 2 years with difficulty naming objects and navigating familiar places; functional decline is emerging. Which pharmacologic treatment is most appropriate for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease?
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Alzheimer disease — cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil) for mild-moderate
rule: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) are first-line for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer disease, modestly stabilising cognition/function. Memantine (NMDA antagonist) is typically added/used in moderate-severe disease.Discriminator: Gradual amnestic decline + naming/navigation difficulty = AD; mild-moderate treated with cholinesterase inhibitorA) Memantine monotherapymemantine is for moderate-to-severe AD, not first-line for mild-moderate (cholinesterase inhibitor is used first)B) Haloperidolhaloperidol is an antipsychotic and only for significant agitation/psychosis, not a cognitive treatmentC) Amitriptylineamitriptyline is an anticholinergic antidepressant that can worsen cognition in AD

stem: A 9-year-old boy has persistent, impairing inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity across school and home, present since age 6. What is the first-line pharmacologic treatment?
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: ADHD — stimulant (methylphenidate) first-line
rule: ADHD (persistent impairing inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity across ≥2 settings, onset before 12 years) is first-line treated with stimulants such as methylphenidate, which improve core symptoms. Multi-modal care (behavioural/psychoeducation) complements medication.Discriminator: Persistent inattention/hyperactivity/impulsivity across settings since childhood = ADHD; stimulants first-lineB) Benzodiazepinesbenzodiazepines do not treat ADHD core symptoms and can impair attentionC) Antipsychotics routinelyantipsychotics are not first-line for core ADHD (only for severe aggression/comorbidity)D) Guarana/caffeine supplementscaffeine/supplements are not evidence-based first-line treatment for ADHD

stem: A 54-year-old man has progressive disinhibition, inappropriate social behaviour, apathy and loss of empathy over 2 years, with relative sparing of memory, plus difficulty producing words. Imaging shows frontal and temporal atrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Frontotemporal dementia — early behavioural disinhibition/apathy + language, younger onset, spared memory
rule: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) presents at a younger age (50s-60s) with early, marked behavioural disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy (behavioural variant) or language impairment (progressive aphasias), with relative preservation of memory early and frontotemporal atrophy on imaging.Discriminator: Earlier onset + prominent behaviour/personality change + language with spared memory + frontotemporal atrophy = FTDB) Alzheimer diseaseAD is typically amnestic early and older-onset, without prominent early disinhibition/apathy with spared memoryC) Dementia with Lewy bodiesDLB features visual hallucinations, fluctuation and parkinsonism rather than early personality changeD) Vascular dementiavascular dementia has stepwise decline with focal signs and vascular risk factors, not the behavioural syndrome of FTD

stem: A new mother on day 3 postpartum is tearful, irritable and labile but can care for her baby, with symptoms fluctuating throughout the day and resolving spontaneously. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Postpartum baby blues — transient, day 3–5, self-limiting (<2 weeks)
rule: Baby blues affect up to 50–80% of women, begin around day 3–5 postpartum, are mild (tearfulness, lability) with preserved functioning, and resolve within 2 weeks without treatment. Persistent symptoms >2 weeks with functional impairment herald postpartum depression.Discriminator: Onset day 3, mild mood lability, retained functioning, self-limiting = baby bluesB) Major postpartum depressionPPD requires symptoms persisting >2 weeks with functional impairment — day-3 self-limiting lability is not PPDC) Postpartum psychosispostpartum psychosis features confusion, delusions and is a psychiatric emergency — not present hereD) Generalised anxiety disorderGAD is persistent excessive worry, not day-3 transient tearfulness

stem: A 78-year-old hospitalised man becomes acutely confused over hours, inattentive, with fluctuating alertness and visual hallucinations; he has an active urinary infection. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Delirium — acute onset, fluctuating, inattention, underlying medical cause
rule: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and cognition with a clear underlying medical cause (here a urinary infection). It is common in hospitalised elderly and is an emergency that resolves when the cause is treated.Discriminator: Acute/subacute onset + fluctuating + inattention + hallucinations + medical infection = deliriumB) Dementiadementia is chronic, progressive and not typically triggered acutely by infection; it lacks the acute fluctuating inattention of deliriumC) Major depression (pseudodementia)depression (pseudodementia) has prominent low mood and 'don't know' answers, not acute fluctuating consciousness with hallucinationsD) Schizophreniaschizophrenia begins with psychosis, not acute confusion with inattention from a medical infection

stem: A mother 2 weeks after delivery is confused, disorganised, has bizarre delusions about her baby being evil, and insomnia. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Reassure and schedule outpatient follow-up in 2 weeks
Start an SSRI and let her rest at home
Refer to a dietician for sleep hygiene
Emergency psychiatric admission with antipsychotic treatment and safety planning for mother and infant
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Postpartum psychosis — psychiatric emergency, urgent admission
rule: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency: rapid-onset delusions/hallucinations, confusion and insomnia in the weeks after delivery with high risk of harm to the infant and mother. It requires urgent psychiatric admission, antipsychotic/mood treatment and safety planning.Discriminator: Delusions + confusion + insomnia postpartum = postpartum psychosis, emergency (infanticide risk)A) Reassure and schedule outpatient follow-up in 2 weeksthis is an emergency with risk to the infant — outpatient reassurance is dangerousB) Start an SSRI and let her rest at homean SSRI is not emergency treatment and home management is unsafe hereC) Refer to a dietician for sleep hygienesleep hygiene is wholly inadequate for psychotic symptoms

stem: A 50-year-old man has severe depression with early-morning waking, diurnal mood variation (worse in the morning), anorexia, weight loss and anhedonia with psychomotor retardation. Which feature supports a MELANCHOLIC specifier in depression?
opts: Early-morning awakening with mood worse in the morning and psychomotor changes
Fatigue that improves with restful sleep
Reactive mood that brightens with good news— END OF PAPER —
subject: ENT,-Ophthalmology-&-Psychiatry
concept: Melancholic depression — early-morning wakening, diurnal variation, psychomotor changes
rule: Melancholic features include early-morning awakening, diurnal variation (worse in the morning), anorexia/weight loss, anhedonia, and psychomotor retardation or agitation, often with a better response to ECT/physical treatments.Discriminator: Early-morning waking + mood worse AM + appetite/weight loss + psychomotor changes = melancholicA) Hypersomnia and increased appetitehypersomnia with increased appetite are ATYPICAL (reverse) features, the opposite of melancholicC) Fatigue that improves with restful sleepmelancholic depression does not sleep restfully — early-morning wakening is the markerD) Reactive mood that brightens with good newsemptiness/loss of reactivity (mood does not brighten) characterises melancholia, not reactive brightening

stem: An 18-year-old woman is about to start isotretinoin for severe nodulocystic acne. Which measure is mandatory before and during treatment?
opts: Two forms of contraception and monthly pregnancy testing
subject: Dermatology,-Community-Medicine-&-Forensic
concept: Isotretinoin — teratogenicity requires dual contraception plus pregnancy tests
rule: Isotretinoin is profoundly teratogenic; females need two forms of contraception plus monthly pregnancy tests, along with monthly LFTs and lipid monitoring.Discriminator: Isotretinoin + woman of reproductive age — the exam answer is always dual contraception.A) Monthly eye examinationOphthalmology review is not the mandatory monthly monitor; teratogenicity is the core concern.B) Weekly full blood countLFTs and lipids are the blood monitors — monitored monthly, not weekly FBC.D) Annual electrocardiogramECG is not part of isotretinoin monitoring.

stem: After applying permethrin 5% cream overnight for scabies, the application is repeated after one week. What is the reason for this second application?
opts: To kill mites hatching from eggs present at the first application
It is unnecessary — a single application always suffices
subject: Dermatology,-Community-Medicine-&-Forensic
concept: Scabies — repeat application after 1 week to hit newly hatched mites
rule: Permethrin is repeated after one week because eggs survive the first application; the second dose kills mites hatching in the interim and prevents reinfestation.Discriminator: The rationale for the scheduled repeat is the egg-hatch cycle — the stem asks exactly that.B) It is unnecessary — a single application always sufficesGuidelines mandate the repeat; single application leaves hatching eggs untreated.C) To treat bacterial superinfectionSuperinfection is treated separately with antibiotics, not extra scabicide.D) To prevent post-scabetic itchPost-scabetic itch persists 2-4 weeks and is hypersensitivity, not a reason to retreat.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has sharply demarcated depigmented macules over the hands and around the mouth, with a white forelock. Which autoimmune condition is most commonly associated with this disorder?
subject: Dermatology,-Community-Medicine-&-Forensic
concept: Vitiligo — most common autoimmune association is thyroid disease
rule: Vitiligo is an autoimmune destruction of melanocytes; thyroid disease (hypo/hyperthyroidism) is the most commonly associated autoimmune condition, so screening is advised.Discriminator: "Sharply demarcated depigmented macules + white forelock" is vitiligo; the question asks its classic association.A) Addison diseaseAddison disease is associated but far less common than thyroid disease in vitiligo.B) Pernicious anaemiaPernicious anaemia is associated with vitiligo but is not the most frequent.D) Type 1 diabetes mellitusType 1 diabetes co-occurs, but thyroid disease tops the list.

stem: A dermatologist plans isotretinoin for a young man with severe nodulocystic acne. What cumulative dose is the usual treatment target?
subject: Dermatology,-Community-Medicine-&-Forensic
concept: Power number — isotretinoin cumulative dose 120-150 mg/kg
rule: The standard cumulative isotretinoin target is 120-150 mg/kg (at 0.5-1 mg/kg/day), which lowers relapse rates in severe acne.Discriminator: The stem asks the cumulative target — 120-150 mg/kg is the fixed power number.A) 50-75 mg/kg50-75 mg/kg is far below the relapse-reducing cumulative target.B) 80-100 mg/kg80-100 mg/kg is insufficient as a course target.C) 200-250 mg/kg200-250 mg/kg exceeds the standard course and adds toxicity without benefit.

stem: A farmer in a rural area has a painless chronic ulcer with a raised violaceous border on his forearm, following an insect bite months earlier. Which vector transmits the causative organism?
subject: Dermatology,-Community-Medicine-&-Forensic
concept: Cutaneous leishmaniasis — Phlebotomus sandfly vector
rule: A painless chronic ulcer with a violaceous border after a bite is cutaneous leishmaniasis, transmitted by the Phlebotomus sandfly (Leishmania tropica/L. major).Discriminator: Painless chronic ulcer + violaceous border + bite history is the leishmaniasis vignette; the vector question follows.A) Anopheles mosquitoAnopheles mosquitoes transmit malaria.B) Culex mosquitoCulex mosquitoes transmit filariasis and West Nile virus.C) Tsetse flyTsetse flies transmit African trypanosomiasis.

stem: A 50-year-old man with dark skin has a rapidly enlarging pigmented lesion on the sole of his foot with irregular borders. Which melanoma subtype is most likely?
subject: Dermatology,-Community-Medicine-&-Forensic
concept: Acral lentiginous melanoma — palms, soles, nail beds; common in dark skin
rule: Acral lentiginous melanoma arises on palms, soles and subungual sites and is the most common melanoma subtype in Asian and Black populations.Discriminator: "Sole of the foot in a dark-skinned patient" is the acral lentiginous location clue.A) Superficial spreading melanomaSuperficial spreading melanoma is the commonest subtype in fair-skinned populations on intermittently sun-exposed skin.B) Nodular melanomaNodular melanoma is a rapidly growing nodule but is not site-selective for the sole.D) Lentigo maligna melanomaLentigo maligna melanoma occurs on chronically sun-damaged facial skin of the elderly.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has multiple tender erythematous nodules over the anterior shins with low-grade fever. In Pakistan, which underlying causes should be actively sought?
subject: Dermatology,-Community-Medicine-&-Forensic
concept: Erythema nodosum — TB, sarcoidosis, streptococcal causes
rule: Erythema nodosum (tender anterior shin nodules = septal panniculitis) is a reactive pattern; in our setting TB, sarcoidosis and streptococcal infection head the workup list.Discriminator: Tender shin nodules = erythema nodosum; the question localises the cause list to Pakistan, where TB leads.A) Systemic lupus erythematosusSLE is not a primary cause of erythema nodosum.B) Rheumatoid arthritisRheumatoid arthritis is not an erythema nodosum cause.C) Drug allergyDrugs are a recognised cause but fungal "drug allergy" is not the lead answer in this setting.

stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic plaque psoriasis has skin biopsy showing a thickened stratum corneum with retained nuclei in the keratinocytes. Which histopathology term describes the retained-nuclei finding?
subject: Dermatology,-Community-Medicine-&-Forensic
concept: Histopathology terminology — parakeratosis
rule: Parakeratosis is retained nuclei in the stratum corneum, classically seen in psoriasis. Hyperkeratosis (thickened corneum) coexists in psoriasis but is not the retained-nuclei finding.Discriminator: The stem asks specifically for the retained-nuclei feature, not the simple thickening.A) HyperkeratosisHyperkeratosis is thickening of the stratum corneum — but no retained nuclei.C) AcanthosisAcanthosis is thickening of the stratum spinosum (e.g. acanthosis nigricans).D) SpongiosisSpongiosis is intercellular oedema of the epidermis — the hallmark of eczema.

stem: A patient with acanthosis nigricans has biopsy showing thickened stratum spinosum. Which histopathology term describes this thickening?
subject: Dermatology,-Community-Medicine-&-Forensic
concept: Histopathology terminology — acanthosis
rule: Acanthosis is thickening of the stratum spinosum — and it names the disease acanthosis nigricans.Discriminator: "Thickened stratum spinosum" is the literal definition of acanthosis.A) ParakeratosisParakeratosis is retained nuclei in the stratum corneum (psoriasis).B) HyperkeratosisHyperkeratosis thickens the stratum corneum, not the spinosum.C) AcantholysisAcantholysis is loss of cell-cell adhesion (pemphigus).

stem: A 2-year-old with atopic dermatitis develops fever and widespread painful vesicles with punched-out erosions over the eczematous skin within 24 hours. What is the most appropriate next step?
subject: Dermatology,-Community-Medicine-&-Forensic
concept: Eczema herpeticum — disseminated HSV on eczema is an emergency
rule: Eczema herpeticum is disseminated HSV superinfection of eczematous skin and is a medical emergency requiring IV acyclovir.Discriminator: "Punctuated vesicles + punched-out erosions + fever" in an atopic child is the eczema herpeticum pattern.A) Topical mupirocin to erosionsMupirocin treats bacterial impetiginization, not disseminated HSV.B) Oral antihistamines and observeObservation with antihistamines would delay emergency antiviral therapy.C) Increase topical steroid potencyMore topical steroid is contraindicated — infection is the issue.

stem: A 70-year-old man has a basal cell carcinoma being treated surgically. For which location is Mohs micrographic surgery most likely to be added?
subject: Dermatology,-Community-Medicine-&-Forensic
concept: Mohs surgery — cosmetically sensitive facial locations
rule: Mohs micrographic surgery is preferred for BCC in cosmetically sensitive areas such as the face, where tissue-sparing margin control matters; excisional surgery elsewhere cures >95%.Discriminator: The stem asks where Mohs is added — the face is the specified cosmetically sensitive zone.B) BackBack lesions are low-risk sites where simple excision with clear margins suffices.C) Lower legsLower legs are non-cosmetic sites; simple excision is standard.D) AbdomenAbdomen is not a Mohs-priority site.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents with a painful shingles rash on the trunk. Antiviral therapy is most effective if started within which window?
subject: Dermatology,-Community-Medicine-&-Forensic
concept: Power number — zoster antivirals within 72 hours
rule: Antivirals (acyclovir/valacyclovir) for herpes zoster must be started within 72 hours of rash onset to reduce acute pain and the risk of postherpetic neuralgia.Discriminator: The stem asks the therapy window — 72 hours from rash onset is the fixed number.A) Within 1 week of crustingCrusting means the replicative phase has passed; starting then is too late for maximal benefit.C) Only after postherpetic neuralgia developsWaiting for PHN is wrong — antivirals are preventive, given early.D) Only in immunocompromised patientsAntivirals benefit immunocompetent patients within the window as well.

stem: A 30-year-old man with coeliac disease develops intensely pruritic grouped vesicles on the elbows and knees. DIF shows granular IgA at the dermal papillae tips. Before starting dapsone, which blood test is essential?
subject: Dermatology,-Community-Medicine-&-Forensic
concept: Dermatitis herpetiformis — dapsone and G6PD screening
rule: DH (pruritic grouped vesicles on extensors, granular IgA at dermal papillae, coeliac link) responds dramatically to dapsone, but dapsone causes haemolysis — check G6PD first.Discriminator: The stem plants the DH diagnosis and the dapsone start; G6PD is the pre-dapsone safety check.B) Serum creatinineRenal monitoring matters for other drugs; dapsone has haemolysis as its key risk in G6PD deficiency.C) Thyroid function testsThyroid tests are not a dapsone prerequisite.D) Chest X-rayChest X-ray screens sarcoidosis/TB, not dapsone toxicity.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has itchy purple, flat-topped, polygonal papules on the flexor wrists with fine white lace-like lines on the surface. Before starting treatment, which serology is important?
subject: Dermatology,-Community-Medicine-&-Forensic
concept: Lichen planus association with hepatitis C
rule: Lichen planus (pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar papules with Wickham striae) is associated with hepatitis C; LFTs and HCV serology are checked.Discriminator: "Purple polygonal planar papules + Wickham striae on flexor wrists" is lichen planus, and the stem asks for its key association.B) Hepatitis B surface antigenHBV is not the recognised lichen planus association — HCV is.C) HIV antibody testHIV does not drive lichen planus workup; molluscum/leishmaniasis vigilance does.D) EBV serologyEBV is not linked with lichen planus.

stem: In bullous pemphigoid, the autoantibodies are directed against which structure of the basement membrane zone?
subject: Dermatology,-Community-Medicine-&-Forensic
concept: Bullous pemphigoid — anti-BP180/BP230 hemidesmosomal antibodies
rule: Bullous pemphigoid targets hemidesmosomal proteins BP180 (BPAG2) and BP230 (BPAG1) at the basement membrane zone, giving linear IgG on DIF.Discriminator: The stem names the disease; the question is the molecular target — hemidesmosomes.A) Desmoglein 3Desmoglein 3 is the pemphigus vulgaris target, giving suprabasal acantholysis.B) Type VII collagenType VII collagen is attacked in epidermolysis bullosa acquisita, not BP.C) Tissue transglutaminaseTissue transglutaminase relates to coeliac disease, a dermatitis herpetiformis association.

stem: In a randomized controlled trial, a new antihypertensive drug is compared with placebo. The primary outcome is the mean fall in systolic blood pressure, measured in each of the two groups. Which statistical test is most appropriate to compare the two group means?
opts: Start PEP immediately (ideally within hours, and not later than 72 hours) and continue for 28 daysConcept: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis timing and duration | Cognitive: Analysis/synthesis (occupational exposure management)Why A: Occupational HIV PEP should begin as soon as possible (ideally within 2 hours) and no later than 72 hours after exposure, with a 28-day course of antiretrovirals. Waiting for the source's confirmatory test or for the worker to seroconvert forfeits the window of effectiveness.Discriminator: Deep parenteral exposure to a high-viral-load source → start PEP immediately, within 72 h, 28 daysB) Wait for repeat confirmatory HIV testing of the source patient, then decideWaiting for the source's repeat serology delays PEP beyond the effective window.C) Start PEP only if the nurse tests HIV-positive at 3 monthsStarting PEP only after the worker seroconverts is pointless - PEP prevents, it does not treat established infection.D) Give a single antiretroviral drug for 7 daysA single drug for 7 days is inadequate; standard PEP is a combination regimen for 28 days.

9 monthsConcept: EPI schedule - timing of first measles dose | Cognitive: Recall (EPI schedule)Why B: In Pakistan's EPI schedule, the first measles-containing vaccine dose (MR-1) is given at 9 months, with a second dose (MR-2) at 15 months. The 9-month timing balances maternal antibody decline with early measles risk.Discriminator: EPI Pakistan: MR-1 at 9 months, MR-2 at 15 monthsA) 6 months6 months is too early - maternal antibodies still interfere and immunogenicity is reduced.C) 12 months12 months is the schedule in several high-income countries (MMR at 12-15 months), not the EPI.D) 15 months15 months is the timing of the EPI second dose (MR-2), not the first.
subject: Dermatology,-Community-Medicine-&-Forensic
concept: Selection of the appropriate test of significance for two independent means
rule: The outcome is a continuous variable compared between two independent groups (drug vs placebo), so the independent (unpaired) t-test is appropriate.Discriminator: Continuous outcome (mean BP fall) + two independent groups → unpaired t-testA) Chi-square testChi-square compares proportions or categories, not continuous means.B) Paired t-testPaired t-test is for before-after or matched measurements in the same subjects.D) Pearson correlation coefficientCorrelation examines the relationship between two continuous variables, not a difference between groups.

stem: A team surveys a town of 5,000 adults on a single day and finds that 85 currently have diabetes mellitus. Which epidemiological measure does the figure of 85/5,000 represent?
opts: Primordial preventionConcept: Levels of prevention - primordial vs primary | Cognitive: Interpretation (prevention level classification)Why A: Primordial prevention targets the population as a whole through policy and social measures (such as salt iodization legislation) to prevent risk factors for disease from emerging in the first place. Primary prevention reduces individual exposure to established risk factors.Discriminator: Population-level, policy-driven action to prevent the emergence of risk factors before disease exists = primordial preventionB) Primary preventionPrimary prevention acts on individuals to reduce established risk factors (e.g. immunization, smoking cessation).C) Secondary preventionSecondary prevention is early detection and treatment of existing disease (screening).D) Tertiary preventionTertiary prevention limits disability and rehabilitates patients with established disease.

100,000 live birthsConcept: Maternal mortality ratio denominator | Cognitive: Recall (indicator definition)Why C: The maternal mortality ratio is defined as maternal deaths per 100,000 live births. The denominator is live births, not women of reproductive age.Discriminator: MMR = maternal deaths per 100,000 live birthsA) 1,000 live births1,000 live births is the denominator of the infant mortality rate, not the MMR.B) 10,000 live births10,000 is not used for either indicator; the MMR uses 100,000.D) 100,000 women of reproductive ageWomen of reproductive age form the denominator of the maternal mortality RATE, not the ratio.
subject: Dermatology,-Community-Medicine-&-Forensic
concept: Point prevalence vs incidence
rule: The survey counts all existing cases of diabetes in the population on one day, giving point prevalence (85/5,000). Incidence measures NEW cases arising over a period of time, not existing cases at a single time point.Discriminator: Existing cases counted on a single day ÷ population at that time = point prevalenceA) Incidence rateIncidence rate measures new cases developing over a defined period, not existing cases on one day.C) Attack rateAttack rate applies to the proportion of an exposed group developing illness during an outbreak.D) Cumulative incidenceCumulative incidence requires following a population over time for new events - not a one-day snapshot.

stem: A researcher records the monthly incomes (in thousand rupees) of 9 households in a village: 8, 10, 12, 12, 15, 16, 18, 20, 350. Which measure of central tendency best represents this distribution?
opts: The medial end of the clavicleConcept: Age estimation — ossification centres | Cognitive: Recall (final epiphyseal union)Why A: The medial (sternal) end of the clavicle is the last epiphysis in the body to unite, at about 23-25 years, so its fusion indicates the individual has passed approximately 25 years; all other major epiphyses close earlier.Discriminator: Medial end of the clavicle unites last (about 25 years); the other centres close far earlier in the ossification timetableB) The lower end of the radiusThe lower end of the radius unites at about 18-19 years, well before the clavicle.C) The iliac crestThe iliac crest epiphysis unites around 16-17 years — an important juvenile-adult landmark but not the last.D) The head of the humerusThe head of the humerus unites at about 20 years, earlier than the medial clavicle.

HydroxocobalaminConcept: Cyanide poisoning — antidote mechanism (hydroxocobalamin) | Cognitive: Recall (antidote-action pairing)Why D: Hydroxocobalamin (vitamin B12a) chelates cyanide directly to form harmless cyanocobalamin, which is renally excreted — a key mechanism question for cyanide antidotes.Discriminator: Hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide as cyanocobalamin; cyanocobalamin is the product, not the antidoteA) CyanocobalaminCyanocobalamin (vitamin B12) is the harmless compound FORMED when hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide — it is the product, not the antidote.B) Sodium thiosulfateSodium thiosulfate acts as a sulfur donor converting cyanide to thiocyanate — it does not directly bind cyanide ions.C) Sodium nitriteSodium nitrite works by inducing methemoglobinemia, which then binds cyanide — a different mechanism from direct chelation.
subject: Dermatology,-Community-Medicine-&-Forensic
concept: Choice of central tendency measure in skewed data
rule: The outlier of 350 pulls the mean to 51.2, which misrepresents the typical household. The median (15) is resistant to outliers and is the appropriate central-tendency measure for positively skewed data.Discriminator: One extreme outlier (350) skews the mean upward; the median (15) stays robustA) Mean (51.2)The mean (51.2) is inflated by the single 350 outlier and does not represent the typical household.C) Mode (12)The mode (12) is the most frequent value but ignores the spread of the rest of the distribution.D) Range (342)The range is a measure of dispersion, not central tendency.

stem: A body is found in an open field in summer, and forensic entomology is used to estimate the postmortem interval. The body is colonised by several arthropod species in waves. Which group is typically the FIRST to arrive and lay eggs on a fresh corpse?
opts: Stabilise and treat the injuries first; carry out the medicolegal examination afterwards with consentConcept: Sexual offences — priority of medical care over forensic sampling | Cognitive: Analysis/synthesis (priority sequencing in the examined victim)Why B: In any medicolegal case the doctor's first duty is to the patient: life-threatening injuries are treated first, and the forensic examination is performed afterwards, with consent, once the patient is stable.Discriminator: Haemodynamic instability + bleeding → resuscitation and injury care precede the forensic examinationA) Complete the full forensic examination first so evidence is not lostDelaying stabilisation to perform the forensic examination first can be fatal and is never correct.C) Send her to the police station for a statement before any examinationThe patient needs medical care before any police statement; the doctor must not substitute the police for the clinical response.D) Perform the medicolegal examination and delay treatment until the investigating officer arrivesDelaying treatment until the investigating officer arrives subordinates medical care to the legal process — the wrong priority.

Administer polyvalent antivenom without further delayConcept: Snake bite — 20WBCT-guided antivenom decision | Cognitive: Interpretation (bedside test → treatment trigger)Why C: An incoagulable 20-minute whole blood clotting test is an indication of systemic (hemotoxic) envenomation and mandates antivenom even when local swelling is still mild — waiting for florid local signs delays life-saving therapy.Discriminator: A non-clotting 20WBCT indicates systemic coagulopathy even with trivial local signs → antivenom nowA) Excision of the bite wound under local anaesthesiaWound excision has no role in snake bite management and may worsen tissue injury and infection risk.B) Tetanus toxoid and antibiotics alone, with daily wound reviewAntibiotics and tetanus are adjuncts, not definitive therapy, once systemic coagulopathy has been demonstrated.D) Observe in hospital without antivenom until local swelling becomes markedObserving without antivenom while the blood is incoagulable risks fatal bleeding — the abnormal clotting test is the trigger, not the degree of local swelling.

Death was due to manual or ligature strangulationConcept: Ligature and manual strangulation — hyoid bone fracture | Cognitive: Interpretation (skeletal findings in asphyxial deaths)Why D: The hyoid bone is the classic site of fracture in manual and ligature strangulation because pressure is applied low in the neck; surrounding haemorrhage proves the fracture was vital. In typical hanging the force is applied high above the thyroid cartilage and produces a high oblique ligature mark, with laryngeal or cervical spine injury rather than an isolated clean hyoid fracture.Discriminator: An isolated hyoid fracture at the greater cornu with surrounding haemorrhage is the classic skeletal signature of manual or ligature strangulationA) Death was due to typical hangingTypical hanging applies force high in the neck (above the thyroid cartilage) and characteristically produces a high oblique mark; an isolated hyoid fracture is not its signature injury.B) Death was due to judicial hangingJudicial hanging produces fracture-dislocation of the second cervical vertebra (the 'hangman's fracture') with cord injury — not an isolated hyoid fracture.C) Death was due to smothering during an assaultSmothering involves occlusion of the nose and mouth and leaves no neck injury at all, so a fractured hyoid with haemorrhage excludes it.
subject: Dermatology,-Community-Medicine-&-Forensic
concept: Forensic entomology — insect succession in postmortem interval estimation
rule: Blowflies (Calliphoridae) are the primary colonisers of a fresh corpse, often arriving within minutes to a few hours of death, and their developmental stages are the main tool for estimating the postmortem interval; beetles and mites appear in later waves of decomposition.Discriminator: Blowflies detect and colonise a corpse within minutes to hours; beetles arrive in later decomposition stagesB) Dermestid beetlesDermestid beetles arrive in the dry/skeletal stages of decomposition, many weeks after death — they are late colonisers.C) Carrion beetles (Silphidae)Carrion beetles appear after the blowfly maggot masses, feeding later in the decomposition sequence.D) Ants and mitesAnts and mites can be incidental or late arrivals and are not the primary first-wave colonisers used for PMI dating.

stem: A 2-year-old boy, previously well, develops 3 weeks of irritability, insomnia, profuse sweating, and photophobia. His hands and feet are red, swollen, and painful with peeling of the fingertips, and he is hypotonic. There is no fever. The family recently broke a mercury thermometer at home. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: CyanideConcept: Cyanide poisoning — autopsy findings | Cognitive: Interpretation (postmortem pattern recognition)Why B: Bright cherry-red lividity and congestion with a bitter-almond odour from the stomach contents are the classic autopsy findings of cyanide poisoning; carbon monoxide also colours the lividity pink but does not produce the almond odour.Discriminator: Cherry-red lividity alone is shared with CO poisoning; the bitter-almond gastric odour points to cyanideA) Carbon monoxideCarbon monoxide also produces cherry-red lividity and pink tissues, but there is no bitter-almond odour of the gastric contents.C) MethanolMethanol produces cyanosed or congested organs with putamen necrosis and ocular findings — not cherry-red lividity or an almond odour.D) StrychnineStrychnine causes convulsive death with intense rigor and asphyxial changes — not cherry-red lividity or an almond smell.

Proceed with the life-saving surgery, documenting that consent was implied by emergency necessityConcept: Consent — the emergency (implied consent) doctrine | Cognitive: Analysis/synthesis (legal principle applied to a life-threatening scenario)Why C: In an emergency threatening life, consent is implied by necessity: the doctor may perform the intervention required to save life or prevent serious harm, documenting the situation and informing the administration afterwards.Discriminator: Life-threatening emergency + no relative traceable → consent is implied by necessity; proceed and documentA) Transfer the patient to another hospital that will accept him without consentTransferring a patient who cannot consent and who needs immediate surgery is unsafe and does not resolve the legal question.B) Delay surgery until written consent from a relative or guardian is obtainedDelaying surgery to hunt for relatives would endanger the patient's life — the emergency exception to consent applies.D) Obtain consent from any bystander who accompanied the patientA bystander has no legal standing to give consent; consent here is implied by the clinical necessity itself.

Vesication containing fluid rich in leukocytes and fibrin, with a red congested line at the marginsConcept: Thermal injuries — antemortem vs postmortem burns | Cognitive: Interpretation (vital reaction vs heat artifacts)Why D: Antemortem burns show a vital reaction: blisters with protein-rich fluid containing leukocytes and fibrin and a congested red margin. Pugilistic attitude, skin splitting, and heat stiffening are heat effects that occur in both antemortem and postmortem burning.Discriminator: Only a vital reaction (inflammatory exudate in blisters + marginal hyperemia) proves the burn was antemortem; posture, splitting, and stiffening occur in postmortem burning tooA) Pugilistic attitude (fixed flexed posture) of the limbsThe pugilistic attitude results from heat coagulation of muscles and occurs whether the body was burned before or after death.B) Splitting and cracking of the skin over the limbsSplitting of the skin from heat is a postmortem artifact of burning and carries no vital significance.C) Heat stiffening of the musclesHeat stiffening of muscles is again a purely physical heat effect, identical in bodies burned after death.
subject: Dermatology,-Community-Medicine-&-Forensic
concept: Mercury poisoning — acrodynia (pink disease)
rule: Acrodynia (pink disease) is chronic inorganic mercury poisoning in young children: irritability, photophobia, sweating, hypotonia, and red, painful, desquamating extremities; the absence of fever and the mercury exposure separate it from Kawasaki disease.Discriminator: Red swollen peeling extremities + sweating + photophobia + NO fever + mercury exposure = acrodyniaB) Kawasaki diseaseKawasaki disease requires fever for at least 5 days plus conjunctivitis, rash, and cervical lymphadenopathy — no fever and the presence of sweating and photophobia point away from it.C) Erythema multiformeErythema multiforme presents with target lesions and mucosal involvement, not the sweating, photophobia, hypotonia, and peeling digits of acrodynia.D) Infantile eczema with secondary infectionInfantile eczema is pruritic and chronic but does not cause photophobia, sweating, hypotonia, or the redness and peeling confined to the extremities.

stem: A patient on furosemide with vomiting and metabolic alkalosis has serum potassium of 2.8 mmol/L. Which combination of mechanisms explains the hypokalemia?
opts: Renal K loss (diuretic) + GI loss (vomiting) + shift into cells (alkalosis)
subject: Grand-All-Subject
concept: Hypokalemia — multifactorial (renal + GI loss + alkalosis shift)
rule: Hypokalemia here arises from three mechanisms: loop diuretic causes renal potassium wasting, vomiting causes gastric loss, and metabolic alkalosis drives extracellular K into cells. Recognizing the multifactorial cause guides both replacement and correction of the underlying driver (stop diuretic, treat vomiting/alkalosis).Discriminator: Diuretic + vomiting + alkalosis = combined renal/GI K loss plus intracellular shiftA) Only dietary deficiencyDietary deficiency alone rarely causes severe hypokalemia this rapidly.B) Only transcellular shift from insulinInsulin shift is one factor; the dominant losses here are renal and GI.C) Magnesium excessMagnesium excess does not cause hypokalemia; magnesium DEFICIENCY is associated.

stem: A 35-year-old non-smoker presents with emphysema predominantly in the lung bases and mild transaminitis. Liver biopsy shows PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules in hepatocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease from smoking
subject: Grand-All-Subject
concept: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency — PAS+ globules, basal emphysema
rule: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes early-onset panacinar (basal) emphysema and liver disease from accumulated misfolded AAT in hepatocytes (PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules). The combination of basal emphysema in a non-smoker plus these globules is diagnostic.Discriminator: Non-smoker + basal emphysema + PAS-positive diastase-resistant globules = alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiencyA) Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease from smokingSmoking-related emphysema is apical and occurs in smokers, without the hepatic globules.B) Cystic fibrosisCystic fibrosis causes bronchiectasis and pancreatic insufficiency, not basal emphysema with hepatic globules.C) Non-alcoholic fatty liver diseaseNAFLD shows steatosis (fat), not PAS-positive diastase-resistant globules.

stem: A 48-year-old overweight man has a fasting glucose of 110 mg/dL and a 2-hour post-glucose value of 150 mg/dL on OGTT. HbA1c is 5.9%. What is the correct classification and first step?
opts: Prediabetes (impaired fasting glucose / impaired glucose tolerance) — lifestyle modification
subject: Grand-All-Subject
concept: Prediabetes — IFG (fasting 100-125) / IGT (2h 140-199); lifestyle first
rule: Prediabetes is defined by intermediate values: impaired fasting glucose (fasting 100-125 mg/dL), impaired glucose tolerance (2-h OGTT 140-199 mg/dL), or HbA1c 5.7-6.4%. It is not yet diabetes, so first-line management is intensive lifestyle modification (diet, exercise, weight loss) to prevent progression; metformin is reserved for high-risk individuals. Annual screening is advised.Discriminator: Fasting 110 (IFG) + 2h 150 (IGT) + HbA1c 5.9% = prediabetes → lifestyle, not metformin yetA) Diabetes mellitus — start metforminThese values are below diabetes thresholds; metformin is not first-line for prediabetes generally.B) Normal — no action neededPrediabetes warrants lifestyle intervention to prevent progression.C) Gestational diabetesGDM is pregnancy-specific; this is an OGTT in a non-pregnant adult.

stem: A 58-year-old type 2 diabetic has persistent fasting hyperglycaemia on maximal oral therapy. Which insulin regimen is most appropriate to start?
opts: Stop all oral agents and start biphasic twice daily immediately
Once-daily basal (long-acting, e.g. glargine) to target fasting glucose
subject: Grand-All-Subject
concept: Insulin initiation — start basal (long-acting) for fasting hyperglycaemia
rule: When oral therapy no longer controls glycaemia, especially with predominant fasting hyperglycaemia, the standard initiation step is adding a once-daily basal (long-acting, e.g., glargine/detemir) insulin while continuing oral agents. This is simpler and lower-hypo-risk than jumping to multiple daily injections. Rapid-acting/prandial or biphasic regimens are added later if post-prandial control remains poor. IV insulin is for inpatient acute management.Discriminator: Persistently high fasting glucose on orals → add once-daily basal (glargine) firstA) Three-times-daily prandial rapid-acting onlyPrandial-only without basal leaves fasting glucose uncontrolled.B) Stop all oral agents and start biphasic twice daily immediatelyImmediate biphasic MDI is more complex than needed as a first step.C) IV insulin infusion as outpatientIV insulin is inpatient/acute, not an outpatient initiation.

stem: A 12-year-old girl with recurrent urinary tract infections and hypertension has renal scarring on DMSA scan, most prominent at the upper and lower poles. What is the most likely underlying problem?
subject: Grand-All-Subject
concept: Reflux nephropathy — VUR causes polar renal scarring
rule: Vesicoureteral reflux causes reflux nephropathy: infected urine refluxes into the kidney, producing focal scarring at the poles (intrarenal reflux), recurrent UTIs, hypertension, and progressive CKD. Diagnosis is by micturating cystourethrography; management includes antibiotic prophylaxis and surgical correction for high-grade reflux.Discriminator: Recurrent UTIs + HTN + polar scarring on DMSA = vesicoureteral reflux (reflux nephropathy)A) Posterior urethral valvesPosterior urethral valves cause obstruction in male infants, not polar scarring.B) Renal artery stenosisRenal artery stenosis causes hypertension without recurrent UTIs.C) Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney diseaseADPKD causes cysts, not polar scarring.

stem: A 9-year-old boy has slowed growth, bitemporal hemianopia, and a calcified suprasellar mass on CT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
subject: Grand-All-Subject
concept: Craniopharyngioma — child, calcified suprasellar mass, bitemporal hemianopia
rule: Craniopharyngioma is a benign but locally aggressive tumour arising from Rathke pouch, typically in children/young adults, presenting with a calcified suprasellar mass causing bitemporal hemianopia (chiasmal compression) and hypothalamic/pituitary hormone deficiencies (growth failure). Treatment is surgical resection, often with radiotherapy; diabetes insipidus commonly follows.Discriminator: Child + calcified suprasellar mass + bitemporal hemianopia + growth failure = craniopharyngiomaA) Pituitary adenomaPituitary adenomas are rarely calcified and usually present in adults, not with this mass in a child.B) MeningiomaMeningiomas are extra-axial and uncommon in children, and less often calcified suprasellar.C) Glioma of the optic nerveOptic nerve glioma causes unilateral vision loss, not bitemporal hemianopia with a calcified mass.

stem: A 78-year-old woman on digoxin presents with nausea, bradycardia, and a potassium of 6.4 mmol/L. Which is the most appropriate acute management?
opts: Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Fab); avoid giving calcium
subject: Grand-All-Subject
concept: Digoxin toxicity — hyperkalemia is a marker; treat with Digoxin-Fab, avoid calcium
rule: In acute digoxin toxicity, hyperkalemia reflects blocked Na/K-ATPase and correlates with severity; potassium-lowering (especially insulin) and Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Fab) are indicated. Calcium is traditionally AVOIDED in digoxin toxicity because it can precipitate severe dysrhythmia ('stone heart'). This contrasts with non-digoxin hyperkalemia, where calcium is first-line for ECG changes.Discriminator: Digoxin toxicity hyperkalemia = give Digoxin-Fab; AVOID calcium (risk of 'stone heart')A) IV calcium gluconate immediatelyCalcium is avoided in digoxin toxicity due to arrhythmia risk.B) Insulin and dextrose aloneInsulin/dextrose may be used but Fab is definitive; calcium is the key avoided agent.C) Potassium supplementationPotassium would worsen toxicity; it is already elevated.

stem: A 40-year-old diabetic woman has recurrent early satiety, nausea, vomiting of undigested food, and bloating, with glycaemic instability. Gastroscopy is normal. What is the most likely mechanism?
subject: Grand-All-Subject
concept: Diabetic gastroparesis — autonomic neuropathy, delayed gastric emptying
rule: Diabetic autonomic neuropathy can involve the vagus, causing gastroparesis — delayed gastric emptying with early satiety, nausea, vomiting of old food, and erratic glucose absorption. Endoscopy is typically normal (rule out obstruction/ulcer). Management is glycaemic control, small frequent meals, prokinetics (metoclopramide/erythromycin), and antiemetics.Discriminator: Nausea/vomiting undigested food + normal endoscopy + DM = gastroparesis (vagal neuropathy)A) Peptic ulcer diseasePUD would show a lesion on endoscopy, which was normal here.C) Mechanical gastric outlet obstructionMechanical obstruction would show a luminal block on scope/imaging.D) Pancreatic exocrine insufficiencyPancreatic insufficiency causes steatorrhea, not vomiting of undigested food.

stem: A 48-year-old woman on peritoneal dialysis presents with abdominal pain and a cloudy effluent bag. What is the most appropriate initial step?
opts: Send effluent for cell count, gram stain, and culture, then start empirical antibiotics
subject: Grand-All-Subject
concept: Peritoneal dialysis — peritonitis diagnosis and empirical treatment
rule: Peritonitis is the major complication of peritoneal dialysis, presenting with abdominal pain and cloudy effluent (WBC >100/μL). Management is effluent cell count, Gram stain, and culture followed by empirical intraperitoneal antibiotics (covering Gram-positives). Catheter removal is reserved for refractory or fungal peritonitis.Discriminator: Cloudy effluent + abdominal pain in PD patient = peritonitis → effluent analysis + empirical antibioticsA) Remove the peritoneal catheter immediatelyCatheter removal is reserved for refractory, fungal, or tunnel infections.B) Switch to haemodialysis permanentlyPermanent switch to haemodialysis is not first-line.D) Observe for 48 hoursObservation delays treatment of a potentially serious infection.

stem: A 66-year-old man undergoes an uneventful right hemicolectomy for colon cancer. Histology reports a moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma extending through the muscularis propria into pericolonic tissue (pT3), with 3 of 14 lymph nodes positive (pN1b) and no metastases (M0). What is the most appropriate further management?
subject: Grand-All-Subject
concept: Colon cancer — adjuvant treatment of stage III disease
rule: Positive regional lymph nodes make this stage III colon cancer, for which adjuvant chemotherapy meaningfully improves survival; radiotherapy is not used for colon primaries.Discriminator: Node-positive (stage III) colon cancer → adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., oxaliplatin-based); radiation is for rectal cancerA) Observation alone with surveillanceA: Observation is appropriate for low-risk stage I/II disease, not node-positive (stage III) colon cancer.C) Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by surgeryC: Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy is used for locally advanced RECTAL cancer, not for colon primaries.D) Palliative chemotherapyD: Palliative chemotherapy is for metastatic disease; this patient is M0.

stem: During total parathyroidectomy for tertiary hyperparathyroidism, the surgeon implants parathyroid tissue into the forearm muscle. What is the purpose?
opts: Preserve parathyroid function and allow future access if needed
subject: Grand-All-Subject
concept: Parathyroid autotransplantation — preserves function; forearm site allows re-exploration
rule: In total/subtotal parathyroidectomy (e.g., tertiary HPT, MEN), viable parathyroid tissue is autotransplanted, often into the forearm sternocleidomastoid or brachioradialis, to preserve calcium homeostasis and — being superficial — allow easy re-exploration if graft-dependent hyperparathyroidism recurs. It does not address thyroid disease or nerve/chyle issues.Discriminator: Autotransplant parathyroid into forearm = preserve function + accessible if graft hyperfunctionsA) Treat thyroid diseaseIt preserves parathyroid, not thyroid, function.B) Mark the recurrent laryngeal nerveIt does not mark or protect the RLN.D) Prevent chyle leakChyle leak is unrelated to parathyroid autotransplantation.
